entries.content:
为什么要逐卷读

每日读经计划带我们在一年里走遍全本圣经，但步子很快，一天常常四五章。逐卷研读是另一种读法：一次只读一卷书，一天一章，在一章里停下来，看几处值得细看的地方——一个希腊词、一处旧约的回声、各译本之间的差异、作者的一个写作手法。目的不是多知道一些资料，而是像约翰所盼望的那样，在他的书里遇见耶稣、信他，并且因他的名得生命。

作者与写作背景

这卷书没有在开头署名。书中的见证人自称「耶稣所爱的那门徒」（约13:23；约21:20），书末说：「为这些事作见证，并且记载这些事的，就是这门徒。」（约21:24）早期教会几乎一致认为他就是西庇太的儿子使徒约翰。二世纪的爱任纽曾在少年时听过坡旅甲讲道，而坡旅甲是约翰的门徒；爱任纽记载约翰晚年住在以弗所，并在那里写了这卷福音书。多数学者把成书时间定在主后85至95年之间。现代学界对作者身份有不同的看法，但书中处处可见亲历者的细节：石缸的数目（约2:6）、一百五十三条鱼（约21:11）、「那时约有午正」（约4:6）。

钥匙经文：20:31

1. 作者亲口说明写作目的。 四福音中只有约翰这样做：「但记这些事要叫你们信耶稣是基督，是神的儿子，并且叫你们信了他，就可以因他的名得生命。」全书所记的神迹、对话、讲论，都是为这个目的挑选出来的（约20:30说耶稣另外行了许多神迹，「没有记在这书上」）。所以读每一章都可以问：这一段要我相信耶稣是谁？

2. 一个字母的差别：「开始相信」还是「继续相信」？ 「叫你们信」的希腊文动词，古抄本有两种写法：pisteusēte（不定过去时，有「开始相信」的意味）和 pisteuēte（现在时，「持续地相信」）。前者像是一卷向未信的人传福音的书；后者像是写给已信的人，劝他们坚守下去。学者至今没有定论。卡森则从句子结构指出，这句话应当读成「叫你们信基督、神的儿子，就是耶稣」，是在回答「弥赛亚是谁？」这个问题，因此他认为本书首先是一卷向犹太人和归信犹太教的外邦人传福音的书。无论原文是哪一种，这卷书都向两种读者说话：慕道的人在这卷书里遇见基督，信了多年的人在这卷书里被托住，继续信下去。

3. 「信」是动词，不是名词。 约翰福音用「信」这个动词大约98次，比其他三卷福音书加起来还多，却一次也没有用名词「信心」（pistis）。对约翰来说，信不是一样拥有的东西，而是一个不断发生的动作：来就他、接待他、吃他、住在他里面。他常写「信入」（pisteuō eis，「信」加上表示方向的介词），信是朝着一个人走过去。

全书的结构
  • 序言（约1:1-18）：道成肉身。全书的主题在这里先奏一遍。
  • 神迹之书（约1:19–12:50）：耶稣在世人面前行神迹、讲论，引起信与不信两种反应。
  • 荣耀之书（约13:1–20:31）：耶稣的「时候」到了。洗脚、楼上讲论、大祭司的祷告、受难、复活。
  • 尾声（21章）：提比哩亚海边，彼得被恢复。
七个神迹与七个「我是」

约翰从不把耶稣的神迹叫作「异能」，而叫作「神迹」（sēmeia，记号、指标）。记号的意义不在本身，而在它所指向的。他选了七个：变水为酒（2章）、医治大臣的儿子（4章）、医治毕士大池边的瘫子（5章）、五饼二鱼（6章）、在海面上行走（6章）、医治生来瞎眼的（9章）、叫拉撒路复活（11章）。

与七个神迹并行的，是耶稣七句带着喻象的「我是……」：生命的粮（约6:35）、世界的光（约8:12）、羊的门（约10:7）、好牧人（约10:11）、复活和生命（约11:25）、道路、真理、生命（约14:6）、真葡萄树（约15:1）。此外还有几处单独的「我是」（egō eimi），最震撼的是约8:58：「还没有亚伯拉罕就有了我。」这句话叫人想起出3:14神在荆棘火中向摩西启示自己的名（希腊文七十士译本作 egō eimi），听的人听懂了，所以拿石头要打他。

读这卷书的三把钥匙

1. 留意误解。 约翰最常用的写法，是让人物把耶稣的话听成字面意思：尼哥德慕以为「重生」是再进母腹（3章），撒玛利亚妇人以为「活水」是井水（4章），众人以为「这殿」是圣殿（2章）。每当你读到一个误解，就停下来问：耶稣真正说的是哪一层？

2. 留意关键词。 信、生命、光、真理、见证、世界、荣耀、时候、常在（menō，也译「住」「存留」）。这些词在书中反复出现，意思一层层加深。

3. 留意节期。 逾越节（2、6、11-19章）、住棚节（7-8章）、修殿节（10章）。耶稣常在节期中说话，显明自己就是那节期所预表的实体：住棚节点灯，他说「我是世界的光」；住棚节浇水，他说「人若渴了，可以到我这里来喝」。

与另外三卷福音书的不同

约翰福音约有九成的内容是另外三卷没有的：没有登山宝训，没有赶鬼，几乎没有比喻，却有长篇的对话与讲论。二世纪末的亚历山大的革利免称它为「属灵的福音」。这不是说其他福音不属灵，而是说约翰默想同一位耶稣多年之后，写出了更深一层的见证。他不是在纠正其他福音，而是与它们并列，带我们更深地认识同一位主。

默想

默想： 约翰说他写这卷书是要叫人「信」，而且这个「信」可能是「开始相信」，也可能是「继续相信」。我今天读这卷书，是带着哪一种需要？是想第一次看清耶稣是谁，还是在疲乏中需要被托住、继续信下去？
entries.content_en:
Why Read Book by Book

The daily plan takes us through the whole Bible in a year, but at a brisk pace, often four or five chapters a day. Book study is another way to read: one book at a time, one chapter a day, stopping inside each chapter to look closely at a few places that reward it. That might be a Greek word, an Old Testament echo, a difference between translations, or one of the author's literary habits. The aim is not to collect information but, as John hoped, to meet Jesus in his book, believe in him, and have life in his name.

Author and Setting

The book carries no name at the top. Its witness calls himself "the disciple whom Jesus loved" (John 13:23; John 21:20), and the closing lines say, "This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things" (John 21:24). The early church agreed almost unanimously that this was John the son of Zebedee. In the second century Irenaeus, who as a boy had heard Polycarp preach (Polycarp was a disciple of John), recorded that John lived at Ephesus in his old age and wrote his Gospel there. Most scholars date it between AD 85 and 95. Modern scholarship holds a range of views on authorship, but the book is full of eyewitness detail: the number of stone jars (John 2:6), the 153 fish (John 21:11), "it was about the sixth hour" (John 4:6).

The Key Verse: 20:31

1. The author states his purpose outright. John is the only Gospel writer who does this: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name." Every sign, conversation and discourse was selected for this purpose (John 20:30 says Jesus did many other signs "not written in this book"). So in every chapter we can ask: what does this passage want me to believe about who Jesus is?

2. One letter of difference: "come to believe" or "go on believing"? The ancient manuscripts have two forms of the verb "believe" here: pisteusēte (aorist, suggesting "come to believe") and pisteuēte (present, "keep on believing"). The first makes John an evangelistic book for those who don't yet believe; the second makes it a book for believers, to help them hold on. Scholars haven't settled it. Carson, arguing from the sentence's grammar, reads it as "that you may believe that the Christ, the Son of God, is Jesus," answering the question "Who is the Messiah?", and so sees John first as an evangelistic book for Jews and Gentile converts to Judaism. Whichever the original was, the book speaks to both kinds of reader: seekers meet Christ in this book, and long-time believers are held up by it and keep believing.

3. "Believe" is a verb, not a noun. John uses the verb "believe" about 98 times, more than the other three Gospels combined, yet never once uses the noun "faith" (pistis). For John, believing isn't something you possess but something you keep doing: coming to him, receiving him, eating him, abiding in him. He often writes "believe into" (pisteuō eis, the verb plus a preposition of direction). Believing means moving toward a person.

The Shape of the Book
  • Prologue (John 1:1-18): The Word became flesh. The book's themes are sounded here first, like an overture.
  • The Book of Signs (John 1:19–12:50): Jesus performs signs and teaches in public, drawing out both belief and unbelief.
  • The Book of Glory (John 13:1–20:31): Jesus' "hour" has come. The foot-washing, the Upper Room discourse, the high-priestly prayer, the passion and the resurrection.
  • Epilogue (ch. 21): By the Sea of Tiberias, Peter is restored.
Seven Signs and Seven "I Am" Sayings

John never calls Jesus' miracles "mighty works" (dynameis). He calls them "signs" (sēmeia), markers whose meaning lies not in themselves but in what they point to. He selects seven: water into wine (ch. 2), healing the official's son (ch. 4), healing the paralyzed man at Bethesda (ch. 5), feeding the five thousand (ch. 6), walking on the sea (ch. 6), healing the man born blind (ch. 9), and raising Lazarus (ch. 11).

Alongside the signs run seven "I am" sayings with images: the bread of life (John 6:35), the light of the world (John 8:12), the door of the sheep (John 10:7), the good shepherd (John 10:11), the resurrection and the life (John 11:25), the way, the truth and the life (John 14:6), the true vine (John 15:1). There are also several bare "I am" statements (egō eimi), most startlingly John 8:58: "before Abraham was, I am." This echoes God's self-revelation at the burning bush in Exodus 3:14 (where the Greek Septuagint has egō eimi). His hearers understood him perfectly, which is why they picked up stones.

Three Keys for Reading John

1. Watch for misunderstandings. John's favorite technique is to let a character take Jesus' words at the literal level. Nicodemus thinks being "born again" means re-entering the womb (ch. 3). The Samaritan woman thinks "living water" means well water (ch. 4). The crowd thinks "this temple" means the building (ch. 2). Whenever you meet a misunderstanding, stop and ask what level Jesus was really speaking on.

2. Watch the key words. Believe, life, light, truth, witness, world, glory, hour, abide (menō, also "remain," "dwell"). These words recur throughout the book, gaining depth each time.

3. Watch the feasts. Passover (chs. 2, 6, 11–19), Tabernacles (chs. 7–8), Dedication (ch. 10). Jesus often speaks at a feast, revealing himself as the reality the feast pointed to. At Tabernacles, when great lamps were lit, he says "I am the light of the world." At Tabernacles, when water was poured out, he says "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink."

How John Differs from the Other Gospels

About ninety percent of John's material appears in none of the other three: no Sermon on the Mount, no exorcisms, almost no parables, but long conversations and discourses. Around AD 200 Clement of Alexandria called it "the spiritual Gospel." He didn't mean the others weren't spiritual. He meant that John, after meditating on the same Jesus for many years, wrote a witness that goes a layer deeper. John isn't correcting the other Gospels. He stands beside them and helps us see further into the same Lord.

Meditation

Reflect: John says he wrote this book so that we might "believe," and that believing may mean "coming to believe" or "going on believing." Which of these needs do I bring to this book today? Do I want to see clearly, for the first time, who Jesus is? Or am I weary and need to be held up so that I can keep believing?

entries.title_en: In the Beginning Was the Word, and the Word Became Flesh

verse_parts.text: 太初有道，道与神同在，道就是神。
道成了肉身，住在我们中间，充充满满地有恩典有真理。我们也见过他的荣光，正是父独生子的荣光。

entries.verse_text: 太初有道，道与神同在，道就是神。道成了肉身，住在我们中间，充充满满地有恩典有真理。我们也见过他的荣光，正是父独生子的荣光。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第一章分三段。序言（1-18节）像一首诗，从永恒说到创造，从创造说到道成肉身。施洗约翰的见证（19-34节）把镜头拉到约旦河外的伯大尼，宗教领袖派人来问「你是谁」，约翰却一直把话题引向另一位。最初的门徒（35-51节）中，一个人带另一个人来见耶稣：安得烈带彼得，腓力带拿但业。全章的问题是「他是谁？」，答案从「道」「神」「光」一路到「神的羔羊」「弥赛亚」「以色列的王」「人子」，一章之内就给了耶稣十几个称号。

深读 1:1「太初有道，道与神同在，道就是神」

1. 「太初」是有意的回声。 「太初」希腊文是 en archē，正是七十士译本创1:1「起初神创造天地」的开头两个字。约翰要读者一开卷就想起创世记，但他又往前推了一步：创世记从神造天地说起，约翰从天地被造以先说起。

2. 「有」与「成了」的对比。 这一节三次用「有/是」（ēn），这是未完成时，意思是「一直都在」。到第3节说万物「是藉着他造的」，换成了另一个动词 egeneto（成了、出现）。万物是「成了」的，道却是「本有」的。到了第14节，约翰又用这个「成了」：「道成了肉身」。那位本来就在的，进入了有开始的世界。整篇序言就靠这两个动词撑起来。

3. 「与神同在」：面向着神。 「同在」的希腊文是 pros ton theon。pros 加上宾格，常有「朝向」的意思，所以许多解经家把它理解为「面对面」，好像道在永恒中就面向着父，与父相交。有学者提醒不要把一个介词读得太重，在当时的希腊文里它也可以只是「与……一起」。但约翰在18节又说子「在父怀里」，可见他确实想让我们看到一种亲密的关系，不只是位置上的并列。

4. 「道就是神」：一个冠词的分量。 希腊文是 theos ēn ho logos，字面是「神是那道」。「道」有冠词，「神」没有冠词，而且放在句首加强语气。这个文法很精确。如果「神」也加冠词，意思就成了「道等于神的全部」，好像道就是父本身；可是约翰刚说过道「与神同在」，可见二者有分别。但没有冠词也不是说「道是一位神」（某些译本这样翻），因为放在动词前、作表语的名词，通常表示性质或身份，不是泛指。有一本英文译本把它译成「神是什么，道也是什么」，很贴近原意：道与父有分别，却完全拥有神的本性。

5. 为什么叫「道」？ 希腊文 logos 有「话语」「理性」的意思。约翰用这个词，根源首先在旧约：神说话就有了世界（「神说，要有光」；「诸天藉耶和华的命而造」，诗33:6），箴言8章又把神的智慧描写成在创世以先就与神同在、参与创造的那一位。对希腊读者，logos 也是哲学家用来说明宇宙秩序背后那个理性原则的词，所以两边的读者都听得懂这个字。但约翰的意思要从旧约来理解，而他宣告的是：这道是一个位格，而且他来了。中文译者借用了「道」字，中国读者自然会联想到老子。但老子的「道」是非位格、不可名状的原则，约翰的「道」却是那位创造万物、与父相交、成了肉身的神。约翰不是在回答老子；这两个「道」只是同一个字，不是同一个意思。

要点：第一节用最少的字，同时说了道的永恒（太初有道）、道与父的分别与相交（与神同在）、道的神性（道就是神）。后面整卷书，都是在展开这三句。
深读 1:5「光照在黑暗里，黑暗却不接受光」

1. 一个动词，两种译法。 「接受」的希腊文是 katelaben，这个字可以是「抓住、领会」，也可以是「抓住、制服」。所以译本分成两派：和合本译「黑暗却不接受光」，英文钦定本译「黑暗却不明白它」，这是「领会」的意思；一些较新的中文译本译作「黑暗不能胜过光」，英文ESV、NIV译「黑暗没有胜过它」，这是「制服」的意思。

2. 约翰自己用法的线索。 同一个动词在约12:35又出现：「免得黑暗临到你们」，那里显然是「追上、压倒」的意思。这是支持「胜过」的有力证据。但约翰很喜欢一字双关（第三章会看到更明显的例子），也许他有意两层都要：黑暗既不明白光，也压不住光。

3. 时态的对比。 「照」是现在时（phainei），光一直在照；「不接受/不胜过」是不定过去时，把整件事概括起来看。在序言里，这首先是在总结光从创造以来在黑暗世界中的历史。但读完整卷书再回来看这一节，我们难免会想到那次决定性的较量：十字架是黑暗最用力的一次，「那时候是夜间了」（约13:30），可是第三天光依然照着。

要点：无论选哪一种译法，这一节都是在宣告结局：光一直在照，黑暗没有得胜。
深读 1:14「道成了肉身，住在我们中间」

1. 「肉身」是很刺耳的字。 约翰没有说道「成了人」或「取了身体」，而是说成了 sarx，就是肉体，人的软弱、会累、会饿、会死的那一面。同一卷书里，耶稣会走累了坐在井旁（约4:6），会在拉撒路墓前哭（约11:35），会在十字架上说「我渴了」（约19:28）。第1节那位「就是神」的道，在第14节成了会渴的肉身。

2. 「住」原文是「支帐棚」。 「住」是 eskēnōsen，来自 skēnē（帐棚）。七十士译本称会幕就用这个字。读过出埃及记的人立刻会想起：会幕立好以后，「云彩遮盖会幕，耶和华的荣光就充满了帐幕」（出40:34）。所以约翰紧接着说：「我们也见过他的荣光。」神的同在从前住在旷野的帐幕里，现在住在一个人的身体里。

3. 「恩典真理」是出埃及记34章的回声。 在出埃及记33章，摩西求神：「求你显出你的荣耀给我看。」神说：「你不能看见我的面，因为人见我的面不能存活。」于是神从摩西面前经过，宣告自己是「有丰盛的慈爱和诚实」（出34:6），希伯来文 ḥesed we'emet。许多解经家认为，约翰的「充充满满地有恩典有真理」就是这句话的回声（七十士译本译 ḥesed 用的是另一个字，所以这是意思上的呼应，不是逐字的翻译）。他在17-18节接着说：「律法本是藉着摩西传的；恩典和真理都是由耶稣基督来的。从来没有人看见神，只有在父怀里的独生子将他表明出来。」原文在这两句之间没有「但是」：律法本身就是神的恩赐，约翰不是把律法与恩典对立，而是说律法所指向的，在基督里完全显明了。摩西在山上求而不得看见的，门徒在一张人的脸上看见了。

4. 「独生子」与18节的异文。 「独生」（monogenēs）的重点可能不在「生」，而在「独一、无可比拟」，来11:17称以撒为亚伯拉罕的 monogenēs，而亚伯拉罕还有以实玛利。（也有学者认为传统的「独生」译法仍然成立。无论如何，信经所认信的子「在万世之先为父所生」，并不只建立在这一个字上。）18节还有一个有名的异文：较早的抄本作「独一的神」（monogenēs theos），后来的抄本作「独生子」。和合本跟随后者，英文ESV作「那独一的神」，NIV（2011年版）作「那位独一的子，他本身就是神」。不论哪一种，意思都是：只有那位自己就是神的，才能把神表明出来。

要点：神不只是从远处向人说话，他亲自来住在我们中间。会幕、荣光、恩典真理，旧约里神同在的每一个记号，约翰都放在这一个人身上。
深读 1:29「看哪，神的羔羊，除去世人罪孽的」

1. 哪一只羔羊？ 约翰没有解释，因为他的读者心里已经有好几只：逾越节的羊羔（出12章），它的血使灭命的越过；赛53:7的羔羊，「他像羊羔被牵到宰杀之地」，默然不语、担当众人的罪孽；还有创22:8亚伯拉罕的那句话：「神必自己预备作燔祭的羊羔。」有些犹太启示文学（年代有争议）里还有一只得胜的羊羔，带领神的子民争战（启示录也这样描写基督）。施洗约翰说这话时，心里想的也许主要是那位要来施行审判、得胜的弥赛亚；写福音书的约翰回头看，看见了更完整的意义。还要注意：逾越节的羊羔严格来说不是赎罪祭，「除去罪孽」这一层，主要来自以赛亚书53章那位替众人担罪的仆人。这一个称号，把这几条线都收进来了。

2. 约翰福音的结尾把耶稣的死与逾越节连在一起。 约翰特别记下，耶稣被定罪是在「预备逾越节的日子，约有午正」（约19:14）。有解经家认为这正是宰杀逾越节羊羔的那一天；也有人（如卡森）认为「预备日」指逾越节期间的星期五，这样就与另外三卷福音书的记载一致。无论哪一种，约翰都要我们把耶稣的死与逾越节连在一起：他死后兵丁没有打断他的腿，约翰引经说「他的骨头一根也不可折断」（约19:36），这是出12:46对逾越节羊羔的规定（参诗34:20）。第一章的这句呼喊，到十九章才完全展开。

3. 「罪孽」是单数。 希腊文是 tēn hamartian tou kosmou，「世界的罪」，单数。约翰不是在列一张罪的清单，而是把世人在神面前全部的罪债与罪责总括起来。羔羊是祭牲，他除去罪的方法，是在十字架上替我们死、担当我们的罪，而且一次就完成了（约19:30「成了」）。「除去」（airōn）是现在分词，说明他就是那位除去罪的；这不是说这工作还没有完成，而是说这位羔羊的身份与他所成就的救恩分不开。

深读 1:51「你们将要看见天开了，神的使者上去下来在人子身上」

1. 雅各的梯子。 这是创28:12的直接回声：雅各梦见一个梯子立在地上，梯子的头顶着天，「神的使者在梯子上，上去下来」。连顺序都一样，先「上去」再「下来」。雅各醒来说：「这不是别的，乃是神的殿，也是天的门。」（创28:17）耶稣说，那座连接天地的梯子，就是「人子」自己。

2. 拿但业与雅各。 这个回声不是偶然的。几节之前，耶稣称拿但业是「真是以色列人，他心里是没有诡诈的」（约1:47）。「以色列」是雅各后来的名字，而雅各原本是那个「用诡计」骗取祝福的人（创27:35；七十士译本这里用的正是「诡诈」dolos 一字）。耶稣好像在说：你是一个没有雅各诡诈的以色列人，你要看见比雅各所看见的更大的事。

3. 为第二章作铺垫。 雅各把那地方叫「伯特利」，意思是「神的殿」。下一章耶稣就要说：「你们拆毁这殿，我三日内要再建立起来。」（约2:19）神与人相会的地方，不再是一个地点，而是一个人。

默想

默想： 第一章给了耶稣十几个称号：道、神、光、羔羊、弥赛亚、神的儿子、以色列的王、人子。哪一个称号是我今天最需要的？是那位「除去世人罪孽」的羔羊，还是那位住在我们中间的道？拿但业还没有来，耶稣就已经看见他在无花果树底下（约1:48）。那位先看见我、先找到我的主，今天要我对谁说：「你来看！」
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 1 has three parts. The Prologue (vv. 1–18) reads like a poem, moving from eternity to creation and from creation to the incarnation. John the Baptist's testimony (vv. 19–34) pulls the camera to Bethany beyond the Jordan, where religious leaders send people to ask "Who are you?" and John keeps turning the subject to someone else. The first disciples (vv. 35–51) come one by one, each bringing another: Andrew brings Peter, and Philip brings Nathanael. The chapter's question is "Who is he?", and the answers run from "the Word," "God" and "the light" to "the Lamb of God," "Messiah," "King of Israel" and "Son of Man." Within one chapter Jesus is given more than a dozen titles.

Going Deeper: 1:1 "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God"

1. "In the beginning" is a deliberate echo. The Greek en archē is exactly how the Septuagint opens Genesis 1:1, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." John wants his readers to think of Genesis from the very first words, but then he goes one step further back. Genesis starts with God making the world; John starts before the world was made.

2. "Was" versus "came to be." This verse uses "was" (ēn) three times. It's the imperfect tense, meaning "was already there, continuously." When verse 3 says all things were made through him, John switches to a different verb, egeneto ("came to be," "came into existence"). All things came to be; the Word simply was. Then in verse 14 John uses that "came to be" verb again: "the Word became flesh." The one who always was entered a world of beginnings. The whole Prologue is held up by these two verbs.

3. "With God": facing toward God. "With" here is pros ton theon. Pros with the accusative often carries the sense of "toward," so many interpreters hear it as "face to face": the Word in eternity facing the Father in communion. Some scholars warn against overloading a preposition, since in the Greek of the day it could simply mean "with." But in verse 18 John adds that the Son is "at the Father's side" (literally, "in the bosom of the Father"), so he clearly wants us to see an intimate relationship, not just two beings side by side.

4. "The Word was God": the weight of one article. The Greek is theos ēn ho logos, literally "God was the Word." "Word" has the article; "God" doesn't, and it comes first for emphasis. The grammar is precise. If "God" also had the article, it would mean "the Word is the whole of God," as if the Word were the Father himself, yet John has just said the Word was with God, so the two are distinct. But the lack of an article doesn't mean "the Word was a god" (as one translation renders it), because a predicate noun placed before the verb typically describes nature or identity rather than one of a class. The New English Bible captures it well: "what God was, the Word was." The Word is distinct from the Father, yet fully shares the nature of God.

5. Why "the Word"? The Greek logos means both "word" and "reason." John's roots are first in the Old Testament: God speaks the world into being ("And God said, Let there be light"; "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made," Ps 33:6), and Proverbs 8 pictures God's Wisdom as present with him before creation and at work in it. For Greek readers logos was also the philosophers' term for the rational principle behind the order of the universe, so the word registered with both audiences. But John's meaning comes from the Old Testament, and what he announces is that the Word is a person, and he has come. Chinese Bibles translate it 道 (dao), and a Chinese reader naturally thinks of Laozi. But Laozi's Dao is an impersonal principle that cannot be named, while John's Word is the God who made all things, lives in communion with the Father, and became flesh. John wasn't answering Laozi. The two share a word, not a meaning.

The point: In the fewest possible words, verse 1 states the Word's eternity ("in the beginning was the Word"), his distinction from and communion with the Father ("with God"), and his deity ("was God"). The rest of the book unfolds these three phrases.
Going Deeper: 1:5 "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it"

1. One verb, two translations. The verb is katelaben, which can mean "grasp" in the sense of understanding or "grasp" in the sense of seizing and overpowering. So translations split into two camps. The KJV has "the darkness comprehended it not," and the Chinese Union Version's "did not accept it" (接受) sits on the same side. The ESV and NIV have "the darkness has not overcome it," as do several newer Chinese translations.

2. A clue from John's own usage. The same verb appears again in John 12:35, "lest darkness overtake you," where it clearly means "catch up with and overwhelm." That's strong evidence for "overcome." But John loves double meanings (chapter 3 has a clearer example), and he may intend both: the darkness neither understood the light nor could put it out.

3. A contrast of tenses. "Shines" is present tense (phainei): the light keeps on shining. "Has not overcome" is aorist, which views the action as a whole. In the Prologue it first sums up the light's history in a dark world since creation. But read the whole book and come back, and you can hardly help thinking of the decisive contest. The cross was darkness's greatest effort ("and it was night," John 13:30), yet on the third day the light was still shining.

The point: Whichever translation you choose, the verse announces the outcome in advance. The light keeps shining, and the darkness has not won.
Going Deeper: 1:14 "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us"

1. "Flesh" is a jarring word. John doesn't say the Word "became a man" or "took a body." He says he became sarx, flesh: human weakness, the part of us that tires, hungers and dies. In this same book Jesus is worn out from walking and sits down by a well (John 4:6), weeps at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35), and says "I thirst" on the cross (John 19:28). The Word who "was God" in verse 1 became, in verse 14, flesh that could thirst.

2. "Dwelt" literally means "pitched his tent." The verb is eskēnōsen, from skēnē (tent), the word the Septuagint uses for the tabernacle. Anyone who knew Exodus would recall that when the tabernacle was finished, "the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle" (Ex 40:34). So John goes straight on: "and we have seen his glory." God's presence once dwelt in a tent in the wilderness; now it dwells in a human body.

3. "Grace and truth" echoes Exodus 34. In Exodus 33 Moses asks, "Please show me your glory." God answers, "You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." So God passes before Moses and proclaims himself "abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (Ex 34:6), in Hebrew ḥesed we'emet. Many interpreters hear John's "full of grace and truth" as an echo of that phrase (the Septuagint renders ḥesed with a different word, so it's an echo of meaning rather than a word-for-word match). In verses 17–18 he goes on: "the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known." There's no "but" between the two halves in Greek. The law was itself God's gift; John isn't setting law against grace but saying that what the law pointed to has been fully revealed in Christ. What Moses asked for on the mountain and couldn't see, the disciples saw in a human face.

4. "Only Son" and the variant in verse 18. The stress of monogenēs may fall less on "begotten" and more on "unique, one of a kind." Hebrews 11:17 calls Isaac Abraham's monogenēs, though Abraham also had Ishmael. (Some scholars still defend "only begotten." Either way, the creeds' confession that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father doesn't rest on this one word.) Verse 18 also has a famous textual variant. The earlier manuscripts read "the only God" (monogenēs theos), while later ones read "the only Son." The Chinese Union Version follows the latter; the ESV has "the only God," and the NIV (2011) "the one and only Son, who is himself God." Either way the meaning is that only one who is himself God can make God known.

The point: God didn't just speak to us from a distance. He moved in. The tabernacle, the glory, the steadfast love and faithfulness, every Old Testament sign of God's presence, John places on this one person.
Going Deeper: 1:29 "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!"

1. Which lamb? John doesn't explain, because his readers already had several lambs in mind. There was the Passover lamb (Ex 12), whose blood made the destroyer pass over. There was the lamb of Isaiah 53:7, "like a lamb that is led to the slaughter," silent, bearing the iniquity of many. And there was Abraham's word in Genesis 22:8, "God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering." Some Jewish apocalyptic texts (their dating is debated) also picture a conquering lamb leading God's people in battle (Revelation portrays Christ this way too). When John the Baptist spoke, he may mainly have had in mind a Messiah who would come in judgment and victory; John the evangelist, looking back, saw the fuller meaning. Note too that the Passover lamb wasn't strictly a sin offering. The idea of "taking away sin" comes mainly from Isaiah 53's servant, who bears the sin of many. This one title gathers all these threads.

2. The end of the Gospel ties Jesus' death to Passover. John notes that Jesus was condemned on "the day of Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour" (John 19:14). Some interpreters see this as the day the Passover lambs were slaughtered; others (Carson, for example) take "Preparation" to mean the Friday of Passover week, in line with the other three Gospels. Either way, John wants us to connect Jesus' death with Passover. After his death the soldiers didn't break his legs, and John quotes, "Not one of his bones will be broken" (John 19:36), which was the rule for the Passover lamb in Exodus 12:46 (cf. Ps 34:20). The cry of chapter 1 is only fully unfolded in chapter 19.

3. "Sin" is singular. The Greek is tēn hamartian tou kosmou, "the sin of the world," in the singular. John isn't listing sins; he sums up the whole world's guilt before God. A lamb is a sacrifice, and Jesus takes away sin by dying in our place on the cross, bearing it himself, once for all ("It is finished," John 19:30). "Takes away" (airōn) is a present participle, describing him as the one who takes away sin. That doesn't make the work unfinished; it tells us that who the Lamb is cannot be separated from what he has done.

Going Deeper: 1:51 "You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man"

1. Jacob's ladder. This directly echoes Genesis 28:12, where Jacob dreams of a ladder set on the earth with its top reaching heaven, "and behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it." Even the order matches: first ascending, then descending. Jacob wakes and says, "This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven" (Gen 28:17). Jesus says the ladder joining heaven and earth is the Son of Man himself.

2. Nathanael and Jacob. The echo isn't accidental. A few verses earlier Jesus calls Nathanael "an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit" (John 1:47). "Israel" was Jacob's later name, and Jacob was the man who came "deceitfully" to steal the blessing (Gen 27:35, where the Septuagint uses the same word for deceit, dolos). It's as if Jesus is saying: you are an Israelite without Jacob's deceit, and you will see greater things than Jacob saw.

3. Setting up chapter 2. Jacob named the place Bethel, "house of God." In the next chapter Jesus will say, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19). The meeting place of God and humanity is no longer a location but a person.

Meditation

Reflect: Chapter 1 gives Jesus more than a dozen titles: Word, God, Light, Lamb, Messiah, Son of God, King of Israel, Son of Man. Which one do I most need today? The Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, or the Word who dwelt among us? Jesus saw Nathanael under the fig tree before Nathanael ever came (John 1:48). The Lord who saw me and found me first: who might he want me to say "Come and see" to today?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第二章由两个场景组成，一个在加利利的婚筵上，一个在耶路撒冷的圣殿里。变水为酒（1-11节）是七个神迹的第一个，场面安静，只有用人和门徒知道发生了什么。洁净圣殿（12-22节）则是公开的冲突。结尾的三节（23-25节）像一个小注脚，告诉我们耶稣怎样看待那些因神迹而「信」的人。这两个场景放在一起，说的是同一件事：旧的秩序（洁净礼仪的石缸、献祭的圣殿）要让位给更新、更丰盛的那一位，就是耶稣自己。

还有一个小细节：「第三日」（约2:1）。第一章用「次日」把日子一天天往下数（约1:29、35、43），有学者算出来，迦拿的婚筵落在全书的第七天。这和创世记第一章遥相呼应：约翰福音以「太初」开始，在第一个「七天」的结尾，新创造的荣耀第一次显出来。这个算法不是每个解经家都接受，但它提醒我们，约翰很在意时间。

深读 2:4「母亲，我与你有什么相干？我的时候还没有到」

1. 和合本的「母亲」原文是「妇人」。 希腊文是 gynai，和合本译成「母亲」，并加小字注明原文作「妇人」。中文里称母亲为「妇人」显得冷淡，但在希腊文里这是一个有礼貌的称呼，耶稣也这样称呼撒玛利亚妇人（约4:21）和抹大拉的马利亚（约20:15）。不过，儿子这样称呼自己的母亲确实不寻常，这暗示一种距离：在这件事上，她不再只是以母亲的身份对他说话。

2. 「我与你有什么相干」是一句闪族习语。 字面是「这对我和对你是什么？」（ti emoi kai soi）。旧约里这句话表示双方在这件事上立场不同，有时带着责备甚至敌意（如士11:12，王上17:18）。耶稣在这里的语气不一定严厉，但意思是划出界线：他行事的时间表，不由母亲决定，也不由婚筵的需要决定，而由父决定。

3. 「我的时候」是贯穿全书的一条线。 这是约翰福音第一次提到耶稣的「时候」。接下来这个词会一再出现：「没有人下手，因为他的时候还没有到」（约7:30；约8:20）；然后在受难前夕突然转变：「人子得荣耀的时候到了」（约12:23），「耶稣知道自己离世归父的时候到了」（约13:1），「父啊，时候到了」（约17:1）。所以耶稣在迦拿说「我的时候还没有到」，心里想的不只是这场婚筵，而是十字架。

4. 耶稣只在两个场景里直接称呼他的母亲，两次都称她「妇人」。 在约翰福音里，耶稣直接对母亲说话，只在开头的迦拿和结尾的十字架下（约19:25-27），而且两次都用 gynai 称呼她（和合本两处都译为「母亲」）。在迦拿，「时候还没有到」；在十字架下，时候到了。这两个场景像书挡一样，把耶稣的公开事奉夹在中间。

要点：耶稣的「时候」由父来定，最终指向十字架。马利亚不知道他会怎样做，却把缺乏带到他面前，并对用人说：「他告诉你们什么，你们就做什么。」（约2:5）我们也可以这样交托，因为这位主把最好的酒留在后头，而为此付上代价的是他自己。
深读 2:6-10 六口石缸

1. 数量惊人。 「每口可以盛两三桶水」，这里的「桶」（metrētēs）约等于三十九公升。六口缸加起来大约四百五十到七百公升，相当于六百到九百多瓶葡萄酒。一个乡村婚筵用不了那么多。这是故意的：弥赛亚时代的一个标志就是酒的丰盛。摩9:13说那日「大山要滴下甜酒」，赛25:6说万军之耶和华要在这山上为万民摆设「陈酒的筵席」。

2. 石缸是做什么用的？ 约翰特别注明它们是「照犹太人洁净的规矩」摆在那里的。这些规矩不是摩西律法本身，而是后来犹太人（特别是法利赛人）的传统（参可7:3-4）：石器被认为不会沾染不洁，所以用来盛洁净礼仪的水，比如饭前洗手。耶稣用的，正是当时犹太人洁净礼仪的器皿。

3. 「直到缸口」。 用人把缸倒满了水，「直到缸口」（约2:7）。约翰记下这个细节，强调缸是满满的。旧的器皿装满了，水却变成了新酒。约翰没有说洁净的礼仪是错的，而是说洁净礼仪所指向的那一位现在来了，并且远远超过它。

4. 管筵席的不知道，用人知道。 管筵席的尝了，就说：「你倒把好酒留到如今！」（约2:10）这句话的讽刺很深：他夸的是新郎，其实应该夸的是另一位，就是那位真正的新郎（约3:29施洗约翰就这样称呼耶稣）。而知道真相的，是打水的用人。神迹的意义，常常向那些顺服地做了事的人显明。

深读 2:11「这是耶稣所行的头一件神迹……显出他的荣耀来」

1. 「头一件」原文是「起头」。 希腊文是 archēn tōn sēmeiōn，直译为「神迹的起头」。archē 正是约1:1「太初」的那个字。它的意思首先就是「第一个」，但也可以带着「开端、典范」的意味：这个神迹为后面的神迹定了调，它们都要「显出他的荣耀」。

2. 「神迹」是记号，不是表演。 约翰从不用对观福音常用的 dynameis（异能）来称耶稣的神迹，而是用 sēmeia（记号）。一个路标的价值不在路标本身，而在它指向的地方。变水为酒的意义，不是耶稣能解决婚筵缺酒的尴尬，而是它「显出他的荣耀来」。这呼应约1:14：「我们也见过他的荣光。」序言里宣告的事，在迦拿第一次被看见了。

3. 神迹引出的反应。 「他的门徒就信他了。」门徒在第一章已经跟从他，这里却说他们「信」了，可见信是会加深的。约翰整卷书所记的，就是信心这样一层层加深。

深读 2:19「你们拆毁这殿，我三日内要再建立起来」

1. 两个都译作「殿」的字。 约翰在这段里用了两个不同的希腊字，和合本都译成「殿」。14-15节耶稣赶出牛羊的「殿」是 hieron，指整个圣殿区，包括外院；19-21节「你们拆毁这殿」的「殿」是 naos，指圣所本身，就是神同在的地方。这两个字的分别并不严格（20节犹太人说「这殿是四十六年才造成的」，用的也是 naos，指的是整个工程），但 naos 更常指圣所，很适合用来指向他的身体。约翰随即解释：「耶稣这话是以他的身体为殿。」（约2:21）呼应约1:14，神的同在已经「支帐棚」在他的身体里了。还要注意「你们拆毁」是一个带讽刺的命令式：耶稣不是在威胁要拆毁圣殿，而是预言他们将要拆毁他的身体，就是把他钉在十字架上，而他要在三日内把这殿再建立起来。

2. 又一个误解。 「这殿是四十六年才造成的，你三日内就再建立起来吗？」（约2:20）这是约翰福音第一个典型的误解：听的人只听到字面意思。希律从主前20年左右开始重建圣殿，四十六年后，大约是主后27-28年，与耶稣开始传道的时间吻合，这也是约翰的年代记载可靠的一个旁证。

3. 门徒也是后来才明白。 约翰很诚实地记下：「所以到他从死里复活以后，门徒就想起他说过这话，便信了圣经和耶稣所说的。」（约2:22）有些话要等到复活之后才能懂。约翰在书中好几次这样说（约12:16；约14:26）。这对今天的读者也是一种安慰：今天读不懂的，不一定是白读。

4. 「我为你的殿心里焦急，如同火烧」。 门徒想起诗69:9（约2:17）。七十士译本的诗篇用过去时（「已经吞噬了我」），约翰引用时却用将来时：「必吞噬我」。诗篇69篇是一首义人受苦的诗，约翰改成将来时，似乎是在暗示：耶稣为父殿的热心，最终要把他自己吞噬，这就是十字架。

5. 为什么约翰把洁净圣殿放在开头？ 马太、马可、路加都把这件事放在受难周，约翰却放在事奉的开头。有学者认为耶稣洁净过两次圣殿；也有学者认为约翰是按主题而不是按时间来安排，把它放在前面作为整卷书的纲领。不论哪一种，约翰的用意都很清楚：从一开始，耶稣与圣殿的冲突，焦点就在于：神同在的地方究竟在哪里，是这座殿，还是这个人？

深读 2:24「耶稣却不将自己交托他们」

这里有一个中文看不出来的文字游戏。23节说许多人「信了他的名」，24节说耶稣「不将自己交托他们」。「信」和「交托」在希腊文里是同一个字 pisteuō。直译就是：「许多人信了他……耶稣却不把自己『信』给他们。」

他们的「信」是被神迹吸引的，耶稣知道这种信还没有扎根，「因他知道人心里所存的」（约2:25）。约翰在这里第一次提醒我们：信有不同的深度。有一种信只停留在神迹上，另一种信却是信入他这个人。下一章的尼哥德慕，就是一个「因为看见神迹」来找耶稣的人（约3:2）。

默想

默想： 管筵席的说：「你倒把好酒留到如今！」耶稣把最好的留在后头，而那代价是他的「时候」，就是十字架。我生命里有哪一处「酒用尽了」，是我可以像马利亚那样带到他面前的？耶稣「知道人心里所存的」，我对他的信，是停留在他能为我做什么，还是已经开始把自己交托给他？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 2 has two scenes, one at a wedding feast in Galilee and one in the temple at Jerusalem. Water into wine (vv. 1–11) is the first of the seven signs, and it's quiet: only the servants and the disciples know what happened. The cleansing of the temple (vv. 12–22) is open confrontation. The last three verses (vv. 23–25) are a short footnote showing how Jesus regards people who "believe" because of signs. Together the two scenes say one thing: the old order, the stone jars of purification and the temple of sacrifice, is giving way to someone newer and richer: Jesus himself.

There's also a small detail: "on the third day" (John 2:1). Chapter 1 counts the days forward with "the next day" (John 1:29, 35, 43), and some scholars calculate that the wedding at Cana falls on the book's seventh day. That would echo Genesis 1: John's Gospel opens with "in the beginning," and at the end of its first "seven days" the glory of a new creation appears for the first time. Not every interpreter accepts this count, but it reminds us that John pays close attention to time.

Going Deeper: 2:4 "Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come"

1. "Woman" is respectful in Greek. The word is gynai. To modern ears it sounds cold for a son to call his mother "woman" (the Chinese Union Version softens it to "mother," with a note that the original says "woman"). But in Greek it was a polite form of address; Jesus uses it for the Samaritan woman (John 4:21) and Mary Magdalene (John 20:15). Still, it's unusual for a son to address his own mother this way, and it suggests some distance: in this matter she is no longer speaking to him simply as his mother.

2. "What does this have to do with me?" is a Semitic idiom. Literally it's "What is this to me and to you?" (ti emoi kai soi). In the Old Testament the phrase signals that two parties stand differently in a matter, sometimes with reproach or even hostility (e.g., Judg 11:12; 1 Kgs 17:18). Here Jesus' tone isn't necessarily harsh, but it draws a line: his timetable isn't set by his mother or by the wedding's needs, but by the Father.

3. "My hour" is a thread through the whole book. This is the first mention of Jesus' "hour" in John. The word keeps returning: "no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come" (John 7:30; John 8:20). Then, on the eve of the passion, it suddenly shifts: "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" (John 12:23); "Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father" (John 13:1); "Father, the hour has come" (John 17:1). So when Jesus says at Cana that his hour hasn't come, he's thinking not just of this wedding but of the cross.

4. Jesus addresses his mother in only two scenes, and both times he calls her "woman." In John, Jesus speaks directly to his mother only at Cana at the start and at the cross at the end (John 19:25–27), and both times he addresses her as gynai. At Cana, the hour has not yet come; at the cross, it has. The two scenes act like bookends around Jesus' public ministry.

The point: Jesus' "hour" is set by the Father, and it points to the cross. Mary didn't know what he would do, but she brought the need to him and told the servants, "Do whatever he tells you" (John 2:5). We can entrust things to him the same way, because this Lord keeps the best wine for last and pays the cost himself.
Going Deeper: 2:6–10 The Six Stone Jars

1. The quantity is staggering. "Each holding twenty or thirty gallons." Six jars hold roughly 120 to 180 gallons (450 to 700 liters), something like 600 to 900-plus bottles of wine. A village wedding could never drink that much. That's the point: one mark of the messianic age was an abundance of wine. Amos 9:13 says that in that day "the mountains shall drip sweet wine," and Isaiah 25:6 says the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples "a feast of well-aged wine."

2. What were the stone jars for? John notes that they stood there "for the Jewish rites of purification." These rites came not from the law of Moses itself but from later Jewish, especially Pharisaic, tradition (cf. Mark 7:3–4). Stone vessels were considered unable to contract impurity, so they held water for purification rituals such as washing hands before meals. Jesus used the very vessels of Jewish purification practice.

3. "Up to the brim." The servants filled the jars "up to the brim" (John 2:7), and John records the detail to stress that the jars were full. The old vessels were filled full, and the water became new wine. John isn't saying the purification rites were wrong. He's saying that the one purification pointed to has now arrived, and he far surpasses them.

4. The master of the feast doesn't know; the servants do. The master tastes it and says, "You have kept the good wine until now" (John 2:10). The irony runs deep. He praises the bridegroom, but the one he should be praising is another, the true Bridegroom (which is what John the Baptist calls Jesus in John 3:29). And the ones who know the truth are the servants who drew the water. The meaning of a sign is often revealed to those who simply did what they were told.

Going Deeper: 2:11 "This, the first of his signs... manifested his glory"

1. "The first" is literally "the beginning." The Greek is archēn tōn sēmeiōn, "the beginning of the signs." Archē is the same word as "in the beginning" in John 1:1. Its first meaning is simply "first," but it can also carry the sense of "beginning" or "pattern": this sign sets the tone for the signs that follow, all of which reveal his glory.

2. A sign is a pointer, not a performance. John never calls Jesus' miracles dynameis (mighty works), as the other Gospels do, but sēmeia (signs). A signpost's value isn't in the post but in where it points. The meaning of water into wine isn't that Jesus could rescue a wedding from embarrassment, but that it "manifested his glory." This echoes John 1:14: "we have seen his glory." What the Prologue announced is seen for the first time at Cana.

3. The response the sign draws out. "And his disciples believed in him." The disciples had already followed him in chapter 1; now they "believe," which shows that faith can deepen. John's whole book traces this deepening, layer by layer.

Going Deeper: 2:19 "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up"

1. Two words, both translated "temple." John uses two different Greek words in this passage, though many translations render both as "temple." The temple Jesus clears of cattle and sheep in verses 14–15 is the hieron, the whole temple complex, outer courts included. The temple of "destroy this temple" in verses 19–21 is the naos, the sanctuary itself, the place of God's presence. The distinction isn't rigid (in verse 20, "forty-six years to build this temple," naos refers to Herod's whole project), but naos is more often used of the sanctuary, and it suits the reference to his body. John then explains: "he was speaking about the temple of his body" (John 2:21). This echoes John 1:14: God's presence has already "pitched its tent" in his body. Note too that "Destroy" is an ironic imperative. Jesus isn't threatening to tear down the temple; he's foretelling that they will destroy the temple of his body by crucifying him, and he will raise it in three days.

2. Another misunderstanding. "It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?" (John 2:20). This is John's first classic misunderstanding: the hearers catch only the literal meaning. Herod began rebuilding the temple around 20 BC, so forty-six years later is about AD 27–28, which fits the start of Jesus' ministry and is one small confirmation of John's chronology.

3. The disciples also understood only later. John honestly records, "When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken" (John 2:22). Some words can only be understood after the resurrection; John says this several times (John 12:16; John 14:26). That's a comfort for readers today too: what we can't understand now isn't wasted reading.

4. "Zeal for your house will consume me." The disciples remember Psalm 69:9 (John 2:17). The Septuagint has the verb in the past tense ("has consumed me"), but John quotes it in the future: "will consume me." Psalm 69 is a psalm of the suffering righteous one, and by shifting to the future John seems to hint that Jesus' zeal for his Father's house will finally consume him. That is the cross.

5. Why does John put the temple cleansing at the start? Matthew, Mark and Luke all place it in passion week; John places it at the beginning of the ministry. Some scholars think Jesus cleansed the temple twice. Others think John arranged his material by theme rather than chronology, putting this first as a key to the whole book. Either way John's intent is clear: from the beginning, the conflict between Jesus and the temple is about where God's presence dwells.

Going Deeper: 2:24 "But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them"

There's wordplay here that most translations can't show. Verse 23 says many "believed in his name"; verse 24 says Jesus "did not entrust himself to them." "Believe" and "entrust" are the same Greek verb, pisteuō. Literally: "Many believed in him... but Jesus did not believe himself to them."

Their belief was drawn by the signs, and Jesus knew it hadn't taken root yet, "for he himself knew what was in man" (John 2:25). Here John first warns us that belief comes in different depths. One kind stops at the signs; another kind believes into the person himself. In the next chapter, Nicodemus is a man who comes to Jesus precisely because of the signs he's seen (John 3:2).

Meditation

Reflect: "You have kept the good wine until now." Jesus saves the best for last, and the cost is his "hour," the cross. Where in my life has "the wine run out," something I can bring to him as Mary did? Jesus "knew what was in man." Does my faith in him stop at what he can do for me, or have I begun to entrust myself to him?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第三章分三段。尼哥德慕夜访（1-15节）：一位法利赛人、犹太人的官，夜里来见耶稣，对话从「重生」开始，到「人子被举起来」结束。神爱世人（16-21节）：讲论转向更广的宣告，光来到世间，人要么来就光，要么躲在黑暗里。施洗约翰最后的见证（22-36节）：约翰的门徒为跟从耶稣的人越来越多而不安，约翰却说：「他必兴旺，我必衰微。」

尼哥德慕是约翰福音里一条安静的线索。他「夜里」来（约3:2），后来在公会里替耶稣说了半句公道话（约7:50-51），最后在耶稣死后，带着约一百斤的没药和沉香来安葬他（约19:39）。这样的分量是给君王用的。约翰特别注明他就是「先前夜里去见耶稣的」，好像在说：那个夜里来的人，似乎一步一步走向了光。他是否完全公开地信了，解经家有不同看法。约翰福音里的「夜」常有象征意味：犹大出去的时候，「那时候是夜间了」（约13:30）。

深读 3:3「人若不重生，就不能见神的国」

1. 一个字，两个意思。 「重生」的「重」，希腊文是 anōthen。这个字可以是「再一次」，也可以是「从上头」。和合本译作「重生」，并在小字里注明「或作从上头生」。英文译本也分成两派：传统的「born again」与较新译本的「born from above」。

2. 尼哥德慕听成了「再一次」。 他问：「人已经老了，如何能重生呢？岂能再进母腹生出来吗？」（约3:4）他把 anōthen 理解为时间上的「第二次」。但约翰自己在同一章用这个字的时候，意思明显是「从上头」：「从天上来的是在万有之上」（约3:31，「从天上来的」就是 ho anōthen erchomenos）。耶稣在十九章对彼拉多说：「若不是从上头赐给你的，你就毫无权柄办我。」（约19:11）用的也是这个字。所以耶稣强调的是来源：这个新生命不是人能自己再来一次的，它是从神那里来的。

3. 两层意思其实都对。 从上头来的生命，对人来说确实是第二次的出生。这是约翰典型的双关，误解的人只抓住了一半。

4. 「神的国」在约翰福音里很少见。 对观福音常说「神的国」，约翰福音却只在这里（约3:3、5）用这个词。约翰平常用的对应说法是「永生」。所以本章从「见神的国」开始，到「得永生」（约3:15-16）结束，两个说法讲的是同一样东西：神掌权的那种生命，现在就可以进入。

要点：重生不是宗教上的自我改进（不是修身养性），不是「再来一次」，而是一个从上头来、由神主动赐下的新开始。
深读 3:5-8「从水和圣灵生的」

1. 「水和圣灵」是什么意思？ 解经家有几种看法：有人认为「水」指肉身的出生（羊水），有人认为指洗礼。但在希腊文里，「水和圣灵」共用一个介词（ex hydatos kai pneumatos），看起来是一次出生的两个方面，而不是两次出生。

2. 以西结书的背景。 许多福音派解经家（如卡森）认为，最好的背景是结36:25-27：「我必用清水洒在你们身上，你们就洁净了……我也要赐给你们一个新心，将新灵放在你们里面。」水象征洁净，灵象征新生命，这正是先知应许的新约。所以耶稣接着说：「你是以色列人的先生，还不明白这事吗？」（约3:10）原文这里有冠词：「那位以色列的先生」（「先生」就是老师）。一位精通圣经的老师，应该从以西结书就认得出这个应许。

3. 风与灵是同一个字。 「风随着意思吹」（约3:8）的「风」，和「圣灵」的「灵」，在希腊文里都是 pneuma，希伯来文的 ruach 也是如此。以西结书37章的枯骨异象里，先知向「气息」（ruach）说预言，枯骨就活了。耶稣用这个双关告诉尼哥德慕：你看不见风，却看得见它的果效；圣灵的工作也是这样，人不能控制，却能经历。

深读 3:14-15「摩西在旷野怎样举蛇，人子也必照样被举起来」

1. 民数记21章的故事。 以色列人在旷野发怨言，神使火蛇进入百姓中间。摩西为百姓祷告，神吩咐他造一条蛇挂在杆子上，摩西就用铜造了一条，「凡被蛇咬的，一望这铜蛇就活了」（民21:9）。治疗的方法不是做什么，而是「望」。耶稣说，信他也是这样：「叫一切信他的都得永生。」

2. 「举起来」是双关。 希腊文 hypsoō 有「举高」也有「高举、尊荣」的意思。约翰福音三次说人子要被「举起来」（约3:14；约8:28；约12:32-34），在约12:33约翰直接解释：「耶稣这话原是指着自己将要怎样死说的。」钉十字架被举起来，同时就是被高举、得荣耀。赛52:13（七十士译本）说到受苦的仆人「必被举起，大得荣耀」（按七十士译本直译；和合本作「必被高举上升，且成为至高」），用的正是「举起」和「荣耀」这两个字。在约翰福音里，十字架不只是耶稣的羞辱，也是他的荣耀。

3. 「必」字。 「人子也必照样被举起来」，希腊文的 dei 表示神计划中的必然。本章有三个这样的「必」：「你们必须重生」（约3:7），「人子也必照样被举起来」（约3:14），「他必兴旺，我必衰微」（约3:30）。新生、十字架、谦卑，都在神的计划之中。

深读 3:16「神爱世人，甚至将他的独生子赐给他们」

1. 神「怎样」爱：重在方式。 英文常译作「God so loved」，读者容易以为「so」是在说爱的程度有多大。希腊文的 houtōs 更常表示「这样地、以这种方式」。和合本没有把 houtōs 单独译出，「甚至」对应的是后面的 hōste。所以这节经文首先说的是神怎样爱：神是以赐下儿子的方式来爱世人。紧跟着的 hōste 加上直述语气的「赐」，强调这不是假设，而是真实发生的结果。当然，以这种方式去爱，本身就显出了爱的深度。这「赐」紧接着约3:14的「被举起来」：神赐下儿子，是让他上十字架，替我们承受我们该受的审判，使信他的人「不致灭亡」（约3:16），不再在神的震怒之下（约3:36）。

2. 「世人」是谁？ 原文是「世界」（kosmos）。这个字在约翰福音出现了将近八十次，常指与神为敌的人类世界：「世界却不认识他」（约1:10）；「世人……不爱光，倒爱黑暗」（约3:19）。所以神爱「世界」，令人惊讶的不是世界有多大，而是世界有多坏。神爱的是背叛他的人。

3. 「信」和「永生」。 「叫一切信他的」，原文是「信入他」（pisteuōn eis auton），信是朝向一个人。「永生」（zōē aiōnios）字面是「属于那个世代的生命」，就是神国来临时的生命。约翰说这生命现在就可以拥有：「信子的人有永生」（约3:36），是现在时。

4. 这话是谁说的？ 希腊文没有引号。耶稣对尼哥德慕的话是到15节为止，还是一直到21节？各译本标点不同：和合本在16节另起引号，英文ESV在15节结束引语，NIV加注说「有解经者认为引语到15节结束」，16-21节可能是约翰的默想。不论是哪一种，这段话都是福音书作者在圣灵默示下给我们的话，权威并没有不同。

要点：神爱世界，不是因为世界可爱；世界不可爱，他仍然爱。这爱的证据，就是他赐下了独生子。
深读 3:30「他必兴旺，我必衰微」

1. 门徒的不安。 约翰的门徒来报告：「你所见证的那位，现在施洗，众人都往他那里去了。」（约3:26）这听起来像是在抱怨竞争。

2. 新郎的朋友。 施洗约翰用婚礼作比喻：「娶新妇的就是新郎；新郎的朋友站着，听见新郎的声音就甚喜乐。」（约3:29）在犹太婚俗中，新郎的朋友负责安排婚事、把新娘带到新郎面前。他的工作完成的时候，正是他退到一旁的时候。旧约常以神为以色列的丈夫（何2:16-20；赛62:5），施洗约翰称耶稣为「新郎」，是一个很高的称呼。

3. 喜乐满足了。 「故此，我这喜乐满足了。」施洗约翰的喜乐不在于自己被看见，而在于新郎被看见。「满足」（peplērōtai）这个动词（plēroō），耶稣后来在楼上讲论中也用来说门徒的喜乐（约15:11；约17:13）。

默想

默想： 被蛇咬的人不是靠努力得医治，而是「一望这铜蛇就活了」（民21:9）。神以赐下儿子的方式，爱这个与他为敌的世界。今天我是在努力让自己变好，还是抬头仰望那被举起来的一位？施洗约翰退后，不是失落，而是「听见新郎的声音就甚喜乐」。在服事、家庭或工作中，我在哪里还在争着被看见？如果我的喜乐在于基督被看见，那里会有什么不同？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 3 has three parts. Nicodemus comes by night (vv. 1–15): a Pharisee and ruler of the Jews comes to Jesus at night, and the conversation runs from being "born again" to the Son of Man being "lifted up." God so loved the world (vv. 16–21): the discourse widens into a broad announcement. The light has come into the world, and people either come to it or hide in the dark. John the Baptist's final witness (vv. 22–36): John's disciples are troubled that more and more people are following Jesus, but John says, "He must increase, but I must decrease."

Nicodemus is a quiet thread through John's Gospel. He comes "by night" (John 3:2). Later he speaks half a sentence in Jesus' defense before the council (John 7:50–51). Finally, after Jesus' death, he brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury him (John 19:39), a quantity fit for a king. John notes that he was the one "who earlier had come to Jesus by night," as if to say that the man who came in the dark seems to have moved step by step toward the light. Whether he came to full, open faith is debated. Night in John often carries symbolic weight: when Judas goes out, "it was night" (John 13:30).

Going Deeper: 3:3 "Unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God"

1. One word, two meanings. "Again" translates the Greek anōthen, which can mean "again" or "from above." The Chinese Union Version renders it "born again" with a note, "or, born from above." English translations split the same way: the traditional "born again" and the newer "born from above."

2. Nicodemus hears "again." He asks, "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" (John 3:4). He takes anōthen as a second time. But when John himself uses the word later in this chapter, it clearly means "from above": "He who comes from above is above all" (John 3:31, "who comes from above" being ho anōthen erchomenos). In chapter 19 Jesus tells Pilate, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above" (John 19:11), with the same word. So Jesus is stressing the source. This new life isn't something a person can do over by himself; it comes from God.

3. Both meanings are true. Life from above really is, for us, a second birth. It's a typical Johannine double meaning, and the man who misunderstands has grasped only half of it.

4. "Kingdom of God" is rare in John. The other Gospels speak of the kingdom of God often; John uses the phrase only here (John 3:3, 5). His usual equivalent is "eternal life." So this chapter begins with "seeing the kingdom of God" and ends with "having eternal life" (John 3:15–16). Both describe the same thing: the life of God's reign, which can be entered now.

The point: New birth isn't religious self-improvement or a second attempt. It's a new beginning that comes from above and that God himself gives.
Going Deeper: 3:5–8 "Born of water and the Spirit"

1. What do "water and Spirit" mean? Interpreters hold several views. Some think "water" refers to physical birth (the amniotic fluid), others to baptism. But in Greek "water and Spirit" share a single preposition (ex hydatos kai pneumatos), which suggests two aspects of one birth rather than two births.

2. The background in Ezekiel. Many evangelical interpreters (Carson among them) think the best background is Ezekiel 36:25–27: "I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean... And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you." Water stands for cleansing and spirit for new life; this is the new covenant the prophet promised. That's why Jesus goes on, "Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?" (John 3:10). The Greek has the article: "the teacher of Israel." A master of the Scriptures should have recognized this promise from Ezekiel.

3. Wind and Spirit are the same word. "The wind blows where it wishes" (John 3:8): "wind" and "Spirit" are both pneuma in Greek, as both are ruach in Hebrew. In Ezekiel 37's valley of dry bones, the prophet prophesies to the "breath" (ruach), and the bones live. Jesus uses the double meaning to tell Nicodemus: you can't see the wind, but you can see what it does. The Spirit's work is like that. No one controls it, but it can be experienced.

Going Deeper: 3:14–15 "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up"

1. The story in Numbers 21. Israel grumbled in the wilderness, and God sent fiery serpents among the people. Moses prayed, and God told him to make a serpent and set it on a pole, so Moses made one of bronze: "if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live" (Num 21:9). The cure wasn't something to do but somewhere to look. Jesus says believing in him is like that: "that whoever believes in him may have eternal life."

2. "Lifted up" is a double meaning. The Greek hypsoō means both "raise up" and "exalt." Three times John says the Son of Man must be "lifted up" (John 3:14; John 8:28; John 12:32–34), and in John 12:33 John explains outright: "He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die." Being raised on the cross is also being exalted in glory. Isaiah 52:13 in the Septuagint says the suffering servant "shall be lifted up and glorified," using exactly these two words. In John the cross isn't only Jesus' humiliation; it is also his glory.

3. The word "must." "So must the Son of Man be lifted up." The Greek dei signals necessity within God's plan. This chapter has three such "musts": "You must be born again" (John 3:7), "so must the Son of Man be lifted up" (John 3:14), and "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30). New birth, the cross and humility all lie within God's plan.

Going Deeper: 3:16 "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son"

1. "So" stresses the manner. Readers often take "God so loved" to describe how much God loved. The Greek houtōs more often means "in this way." So the verse first tells us how God loved: by giving his Son. The following hōste with the indicative "gave" stresses that this is not hypothetical but an actual result. Of course, loving in this way also shows the depth of the love. This "gave" follows directly on John 3:14's "lifted up": God gave his Son to the cross, to bear the judgment we deserved, so that believers "should not perish" (John 3:16) and are no longer under God's wrath (John 3:36).

2. Who is "the world"? The word is kosmos, which appears nearly eighty times in John and often means humanity in rebellion against God: "the world did not know him" (John 1:10); "people loved the darkness rather than the light" (John 3:19). So the surprise in God loving "the world" isn't how big the world is but how bad it is. God loves people who have turned against him.

3. "Believe" and "eternal life." "Whoever believes in him" is literally "believes into him" (pisteuōn eis auton): believing is moving toward a person. "Eternal life" (zōē aiōnios) is literally "the life of the age," the life of the coming kingdom. John says it can be possessed now: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life" (John 3:36), in the present tense.

4. Who is speaking here? Greek has no quotation marks. Do Jesus' words to Nicodemus end at verse 15 or run through verse 21? Translations punctuate differently: the ESV closes the quotation at verse 15, the Chinese Union Version opens a new quotation at verse 16, and the NIV notes that "some interpreters end the quotation with verse 15," making verses 16–21 the evangelist's reflection. Either way, these are words the Gospel writer gives us under the Spirit's inspiration, with the same authority.

The point: God's love isn't drawn out by the world's loveliness; it comes in spite of the world's unloveliness. The proof of that love is that he gave his only Son.
Going Deeper: 3:30 "He must increase, but I must decrease"

1. The disciples' unease. John's disciples report, "He who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him" (John 3:26). It sounds like a complaint about competition.

2. The friend of the bridegroom. John the Baptist answers with a wedding picture: "The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice" (John 3:29). In Jewish custom the bridegroom's friend arranged the wedding and brought the bride to the groom. The moment his work was done was the moment he stepped aside. The Old Testament often pictures God as Israel's husband (Hos 2:16–20; Isa 62:5), so calling Jesus "the bridegroom" is a high title.

3. Joy made complete. "Therefore this joy of mine is now complete." The Baptist's joy lies not in being seen himself but in the bridegroom being seen. The verb behind "complete" (peplērōtai, from plēroō) is the one Jesus later uses of his disciples' joy in the Upper Room (John 15:11; John 17:13).

Meditation

Reflect: The bitten Israelites weren't healed by effort; they looked at the bronze serpent and lived (Num 21:9). God loved a hostile world by giving his Son. Today, am I trying to improve myself, or looking up at the one who was lifted up? John the Baptist stepped back not in loss but rejoicing "greatly at the bridegroom's voice." In my service, family or work, where am I still competing to be seen? What would change there if my joy lay in Christ being seen?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第四章分两大段。撒玛利亚妇人（1-42节）是约翰福音里最长的一段一对一对话：从「给我水喝」开始，经过活水、五个丈夫、在哪座山上敬拜，到耶稣说出「我就是」，最后整座城的人出来见他。医治大臣的儿子（43-54节）是第二个神迹，回到加利利的迦拿。

这一章和第三章刚好成对：尼哥德慕是犹太人、男人、宗教领袖，在夜里来；撒玛利亚妇人是外族、女人，也许还处在社会边缘，在正午遇见耶稣。尼哥德慕从「我们知道」开始，最后却不明白；妇人从一句话也不懂开始，最后却跑回城里作见证。耶稣向两个完全不同的人，说了同一个福音。

深读 4:4-9「必须经过撒玛利亚」

1. 「必须」是地理还是神意？ 从犹太到加利利，经过撒玛利亚是最直接的路。犹太史家约瑟夫记载，加利利人上耶路撒冷过节时常常走这条路。所以「必须」可以只是说路线。但约翰用的是 edei，正是第三章「必」的那个字（约3:7、14、30）。在约翰福音里，这个字常带着神计划的意味。也许两层都有：这条路是最近的，而在这条路上，有一个人是父要耶稣去找的（约4:23「父要这样的人拜他」）。

2. 井旁相遇是旧约的一个熟悉场景。 亚伯拉罕的仆人在井旁遇见利百加（创24章），雅各在井旁遇见拉结（创29章），摩西在井旁遇见西坡拉（出2章），每一次都以婚姻结束。有学者指出，约翰刚在上一章称耶稣为「新郎」（约3:29），这一章就让他坐在「雅各井」旁，遇见一个女人。但这次的相遇完全出人意料：她已经有过五个丈夫。如果约翰真有意借用这个场景，那么新郎要迎娶的新妇就是他的子民，如今连撒玛利亚人也在其中。

3. 正午与疲乏。 「耶稣因走路困乏，就坐在井旁。那时约有午正。」（约4:6）这是约1:14「道成了肉身」最具体的画面之一：那创造万物的道，走累了，口渴了。妇人在正午最热的时候来打水，许多解经家认为这暗示她刻意避开其他打水的妇女。

4. 「没有来往」原文可能更具体。 「原来犹太人和撒玛利亚人没有来往」（约4:9），这个动词（synchrōntai）可能有「共用器皿」的意思。若是如此，妇人的惊讶就更具体了：一个犹太人，竟然愿意用撒玛利亚人的水罐喝水。按照当时一些犹太人的看法，这会使他在礼仪上不洁。耶稣跨过的不只是种族的界线，还有洁净礼仪的界线。

深读 4:10-15「他也必早给了你活水」

1. 「活水」又是一个双关。 「活水」（hydōr zōn）在日常用语里指流动的水，泉水、溪水，相对于积在池里的死水。妇人自然听成了这个意思：「井又深，你从哪里得活水呢？」（约4:11）这又是约翰福音典型的误解：她只听到字面的意思，耶稣说的却是属灵的事。

2. 旧约里的活水。 耶2:13，神说：「我的百姓做了两件恶事，就是离弃我这活水的泉源，为自己凿出池子，是破裂不能存水的池子。」神自己就是活水的泉源。耶稣说他能赐活水，等于宣告他做的是只有神能做的事。

3. 活水是什么？ 约翰在约7:37-39给了答案：耶稣在住棚节说「人若渴了，可以到我这里来喝」，约翰解释：「耶稣这话是指着信他之人要受圣灵说的。」所以活水就是圣灵自己，以及他所带来的新生命，它不是一次性的，而是「在他里头成为泉源，直涌到永生」（约4:14）。

4. 「难道你比他还大吗？」 妇人问耶稣是否比雅各还大（约4:12）。约翰的读者知道答案：是的。这是约翰喜欢用的反讽：书中人物随口问的问题，答案正是福音。

深读 4:16-26 五个丈夫与「这和你说话的就是他」

1. 揭露罪，却不羞辱人。 耶稣说「你去叫你丈夫」，妇人说「我没有丈夫」，耶稣说：「你说没有丈夫是不错的。你已经有五个丈夫，你现在有的并不是你的丈夫。」（约4:17-18）经文没有说明她的五段婚姻是怎么结束的，可能是丧偶，也可能是被休，当时只有男人能休妻。耶稣的话揭露了真相，却没有羞辱她。但她现在与一个不是她丈夫的人在一起，这是罪，耶稣没有回避这一点；他揭露罪，是为了把活水赐给她。她的反应是：「我看出你是先知。」

2. 一个有争议的象征读法。 有解经家把「五个丈夫」读成象征，指王下17:24-34中被带到撒玛利亚的五族人和他们的神。但经文本身没有暗示要这样读，多数解经家仍把它理解为她真实的生命经历。

3. 话题转到敬拜，不是逃避。 妇人问：该在基利心山还是耶路撒冷敬拜？（约4:20）这常被说成转移话题。但对一个被人看不起的撒玛利亚女人来说，「我可以在哪里、怎样亲近神」也许正是她心底的问题。

4. 「我就是」。 妇人说：「我知道弥赛亚要来。」耶稣回答：「这和你说话的就是他！」（约4:26）希腊文是 egō eimi, ho lalōn soi，直译「我是，那正在对你说话的」。这是约翰福音第一次出现耶稣口中的 egō eimi。在这里它首先的意思是「我就是那弥赛亚」，但熟悉约翰福音的读者，会在后来（约6:20；约8:58；约18:5-6）听到这两个字越来越深的回声。在整卷书里，耶稣第一次明说自己是弥赛亚，听见的竟是一个撒玛利亚妇人。

深读 4:23-24「用心灵和诚实拜他」

1. 「时候将到，如今就是了」。 敬拜的地点之争（基利心山或耶路撒冷）要被超越，不是因为地点不重要，而是因为神的同在现在住在耶稣身上（约2:19-21）。

2. 「救恩是从犹太人出来的」。 耶稣并没有说两边都对。「你们所拜的，你们不知道；我们所拜的，我们知道，因为救恩是从犹太人出来的。」（约4:22）神的救恩是透过以色列的历史、律法和先知临到的，弥赛亚是犹太人。但这救恩不停留在犹太人中间，它现在临到了撒玛利亚。

3. 「心灵和诚实」是什么？ 和合本译「用心灵和诚实」，中文读者容易理解为「真心诚意」，与外在仪式相对。这不算错，但希腊文的意思更深。原文「心灵和诚实」共用一个介词（en pneumati kai alētheia），是一个整体概念，正像约3:5的「水和圣灵」。解经家对「灵」是直接指圣灵，还是指圣灵所开启的那种敬拜，看法不一；但从约3:5-8和约7:39看，这种敬拜离不开圣灵的工作。「诚实」（alētheia）就是约翰福音常说的「真理」，而耶稣说「我就是道路、真理、生命」（约14:6）。所以真正的敬拜，是在圣灵里、透过那位是真理的耶稣而献上的敬拜。真心是需要的，但真心本身还不够；敬拜需要按着神所启示的真理，借着他所赐的灵。

4. 「神是个灵」。 这不是说神是一股无形的气或力量，而是说神是有位格的灵，不受物质、地点限制，所以不能只在某一座山上被敬拜。

要点：耶稣没有让妇人在两座山之间选一座，而是把她带到自己面前。真正的敬拜，以圣灵和真理为中心，而真理就是基督。
深读 4:46-54「那人信耶稣所说的话就回去了」

1. 「你们」是复数。 耶稣说：「若不看见神迹奇事，你们总是不信。」（约4:48）「你们」是复数，不只是对这位大臣说，也是对加利利众人说，他们欢迎耶稣是因为看过他在耶路撒冷所行的事（约4:45）。这呼应约2:23-25：因神迹而生的信，还不够深。

2. 信在神迹之前。 大臣没有争辩，只是再求一次。耶稣说「回去吧，你的儿子活了」，经文说：「那人信耶稣所说的话就回去了。」（约4:50）他在看见以先就信了，信的是耶稣的话。

3. 信心的两步。 第二天他知道儿子好转的时辰正是耶稣说话的时辰，于是「他自己和全家就都信了」（约4:53）。同一个人，信了两次：先是信耶稣的话足以依靠，后来是全然地信（约4:53的「信」没有宾语，是一种完整的信）。约翰福音里的信，就是这样一步步加深的。

4. 「救世主」。 撒玛利亚人说：「知道这真是救世主。」（约4:42）这个称号在新约中只出现在这里和约一4:14。在罗马世界，这类称号常被用来尊称皇帝。撒玛利亚人认出的救主，不是凯撒，而是一个坐在井旁口渴的犹太人。

默想

默想： 耶稣口渴地坐在井旁，等的是一个也许被人避开的妇人；他揭开她的过去，是为了把活水给她。我是否相信，他看见我的全部，仍然要把活水给我？被这样寻找的人，也能去寻找别人：我身边有没有一个我一直避开的人？我是否也像那妇人一样，用别的池子（成就、关系、娱乐）止渴，却越喝越渴？大臣「信耶稣所说的话就回去了」，今天有没有一句主的话，是我需要在看见以先就去相信的？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 4 has two main parts. The Samaritan woman (vv. 1–42) is the longest one-on-one conversation in John: it starts with "Give me a drink," moves through living water, five husbands and which mountain to worship on, reaches Jesus' "I am he," and ends with a whole town coming out to see him. The healing of the official's son (vv. 43–54) is the second sign, back at Cana in Galilee.

This chapter pairs with chapter 3. Nicodemus is a Jew, a man and a religious leader who comes at night; the Samaritan woman is a foreigner, a woman, perhaps on the edge of society, who meets Jesus at noon. Nicodemus begins with "we know" and ends up not understanding; the woman begins understanding nothing and ends up running back to town to bear witness. Jesus gives the same gospel to two completely different people.

Going Deeper: 4:4–9 "He had to pass through Samaria"

1. Geography or divine purpose? Going through Samaria was the most direct route from Judea to Galilee. The Jewish historian Josephus records that Galileans often took this road to the festivals in Jerusalem. So "had to" may simply describe the route. But John uses edei, the same word as the "must" of chapter 3 (John 3:7, 14, 30), and in John the word often carries the sense of God's plan. Perhaps both are true: it was the shortest road, and on that road was a person the Father wanted Jesus to find (John 4:23, "the Father is seeking such people to worship him").

2. Meeting at a well is a familiar Old Testament scene. Abraham's servant meets Rebekah at a well (Gen 24), Jacob meets Rachel at a well (Gen 29), Moses meets Zipporah at a well (Ex 2), and each time it ends in marriage. Some scholars note that John has just called Jesus "the bridegroom" (John 3:29) and now sits him by "Jacob's well," where he meets a woman. But this meeting is completely unexpected: she has already had five husbands. If the motif echoes here, the bride the bridegroom gathers is his people, now including Samaritans.

3. Noon and weariness. "Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour" (John 4:6). This is one of the most concrete pictures of John 1:14, "the Word became flesh": the Word who made all things is tired and thirsty. The woman comes to draw water at the hottest hour, which many interpreters take as a hint that she was avoiding the other women.

4. "No dealings" may be more specific. "For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans" (John 4:9): the verb (synchrōntai) may mean "do not share vessels." If so, the woman's surprise is concrete: a Jew is willing to drink from a Samaritan's water jar. By the view of some Jews at the time, that would make him ritually unclean. Jesus crosses not only an ethnic line but a line of ritual purity.

Going Deeper: 4:10–15 "He would have given you living water"

1. "Living water" is another double meaning. In everyday speech "living water" (hydōr zōn) meant flowing water, from a spring or stream, as opposed to stagnant water in a cistern. The woman naturally hears it that way: "the well is deep. Where do you get that living water?" (John 4:11). This is another typical Johannine misunderstanding: the literal hearing set against the spiritual meaning Jesus intends.

2. Living water in the Old Testament. In Jeremiah 2:13 God says, "my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water." God himself is the fountain of living water. When Jesus says he can give living water, he is claiming to do what only God does.

3. What is the living water? John gives the answer in John 7:37–39. At the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus says, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink," and John explains: "this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive." So the living water is the Spirit himself and the life he brings. It isn't a one-time drink; it "will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life" (John 4:14).

4. "Are you greater than our father Jacob?" The woman asks whether Jesus is greater than Jacob (John 4:12). John's readers know the answer: yes. It's the kind of irony John loves, where a character's question has the gospel as its answer.

Going Deeper: 4:16–26 Five Husbands and "I who speak to you am he"

1. Exposing sin without shaming. Jesus says, "Go, call your husband." She says, "I have no husband." Jesus replies, "You are right in saying, 'I have no husband'; for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband" (John 4:17–18). The text doesn't say how her five marriages ended. She may have been widowed or divorced, and at the time only men could divorce. Jesus' words expose the truth without humiliating her. Yet she is now living with a man who is not her husband, which is sin, and Jesus doesn't skip over it. He exposes sin in order to give living water. Her response: "Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet."

2. A disputed symbolic reading. Some interpreters read the "five husbands" as a symbol of the five peoples settled in Samaria, with their gods, in 2 Kings 17:24–34. But the text gives no hint that it should be read this way, and most interpreters still take it as her real life story.

3. The turn to worship isn't evasion. She asks whether to worship on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem (John 4:20). This is often called changing the subject. But for a despised Samaritan woman, "where and how can I come near to God?" may be the real question of her heart.

4. "I am he." The woman says, "I know that Messiah is coming." Jesus answers, "I who speak to you am he" (John 4:26). The Greek is egō eimi, ho lalōn soi, literally "I am, the one speaking to you." This is the first egō eimi on Jesus' lips in John. Here it first means "I am the Messiah," but readers who know the Gospel will hear deeper echoes of these words later (John 6:20; John 8:58; John 18:5–6). In the whole book, the first person Jesus plainly tells that he is the Messiah is a Samaritan woman.

Going Deeper: 4:23–24 "Worship in spirit and truth"

1. "The hour is coming, and is now here." The dispute over where to worship (Gerizim or Jerusalem) is being surpassed. Not because place doesn't matter, but because God's presence now dwells in Jesus (John 2:19–21).

2. "Salvation is from the Jews." Jesus doesn't say both sides are right: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews" (John 4:22). God's salvation came through Israel's history, law and prophets, and the Messiah is a Jew. But that salvation doesn't stay among the Jews; it has now reached Samaria.

3. What are "spirit and truth"? The Chinese Union Version renders it "with heart-spirit and sincerity," which readers easily take as "with genuine sincerity," as opposed to outward ritual. That isn't wrong, but the Greek goes deeper. One preposition governs both words (en pneumati kai alētheia), making them a single idea, as with "water and Spirit" in John 3:5. Interpreters differ on whether "spirit" means the Holy Spirit directly or the kind of worship the Spirit opens up, but in light of John 3:5–8 and John 7:39 such worship cannot be separated from the Spirit's work. "Truth" (alētheia) is John's word for the truth revealed in Jesus, who says, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). So true worship is offered in the Spirit and through Jesus, who is the truth. Sincerity is needed, but sincerity alone isn't enough; worship must follow the truth God has revealed, by the Spirit he gives.

4. "God is spirit." This doesn't mean God is an impersonal force. It means God is personal spirit, not bound by matter or place, so he can't be worshiped only on one mountain.

The point: Jesus doesn't make the woman choose between two mountains; he brings her to himself. True worship centers on the Spirit and the truth, and the truth is Christ.
Going Deeper: 4:46–54 "The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him"

1. "You" is plural. Jesus says, "Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe" (John 4:48). "You" is plural. He's speaking not only to the official but to the Galileans, who welcomed Jesus because they had seen what he did in Jerusalem (John 4:45). This echoes John 2:23–25: faith born of signs is not yet deep enough.

2. Faith before the sign. The official doesn't argue; he simply asks again. Jesus says, "Go; your son will live," and the text says, "The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way" (John 4:50). He believed before he saw, and what he believed was Jesus' word.

3. Two steps of faith. The next day he learns that his son recovered at the very hour Jesus spoke, "And he himself believed, and all his household" (John 4:53). The same man believes twice: first that Jesus' word could be trusted, then believing outright (John 4:53 has "believed" with no object, a settled, complete faith). This is how faith deepens in John.

4. "The Savior of the world." The Samaritans say, "we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world" (John 4:42). The title appears in the New Testament only here and in 1 John 4:14. In the Roman world, titles like this were often used to honor the emperor. The Savior the Samaritans recognized wasn't Caesar but a thirsty Jew sitting by a well.

Meditation

Reflect: Thirsty and tired by a well, Jesus waited for a woman others perhaps avoided, and he uncovered her past in order to give her living water. Do I believe he sees all of me and still offers it? Those who have been sought like this can seek others: is there someone near me I keep avoiding? Am I, like the woman, drinking from other cisterns (achievement, relationships, entertainment) and getting thirstier the more I drink? The official "believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way." Is there a word of the Lord I need to believe today, before I see?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第五章是一个转折点。医治瘫子（1-15节）是第三个神迹，地点在耶路撒冷的毕士大池，时间是安息日。安息日的冲突（16-18节）：犹太人逼迫耶稣，不只因为他在安息日医病，更因为他「称神为他的父，将自己和神当作平等」。耶稣的讲论（19-47节）分两部分：先说子与父的关系（19-30节），再像在法庭上一样，传召为他作见证的证人（31-47节）。

从这一章开始，约翰福音里「犹太人」想要杀耶稣（约5:18）成为一条持续的线索。约翰福音里的「犹太人」常常是指反对耶稣的宗教领袖，而不是整个民族。耶稣自己、他的门徒、约翰本人，都是犹太人。

深读 5:2-9 毕士大池与三十八年

1. 考古相符的细节。 「旁边有五个廊子」（约5:2），过去有学者认为「五个廊子」只是象征（如摩西五经）。十九世纪以来，考古学家在耶路撒冷圣安妮教堂旁发现了一个中间有隔墙的双池，四边加上中间，正好可容五个廊子，与约翰的描述相符。这是约翰福音目击细节可靠的又一个例子。

2. 第4节在哪里？ 有些圣经版本在3-4节有一段话：天使按时下池搅动池水，先下去的病就痊愈。最早、最好的希腊文抄本没有这段话，现代译本多半把它放在脚注里，本读经应用采用的和合本和ESV都略去了第4节。3节下半「等候水动」也不见于同一批早期抄本。这段话很可能是后来的抄写者为了解释第7节「水动的时候」而加上的说明。病人自己的话反映了当时人们的信念，但约翰并没有说这个信念是真的。

3. 「你要痊愈吗？」 这个问题看起来多余，却直指人心。病人没有回答「要」，而是解释为什么好不了：「没有人把我放在池子里。」（约5:7）他把希望放在池水上，耶稣却完全绕过池水：「起来，拿你的褥子走吧！」医治他的不是池子，而是耶稣的话。

4. 三十八年。 有解经家联想到申2:14，以色列人从加低斯巴尼亚到过撒烈溪，在旷野漂流了三十八年。这个联想有趣，但约翰没有点明，最稳妥的读法是：这个数字说明他的病有多久、多绝望。

5. 「不要再犯罪」。 耶稣后来在殿里对他说：「你已经痊愈了，不要再犯罪，恐怕你遭遇的更加利害。」（约5:14）这不表示所有疾病都是某个罪的直接后果，耶稣在约9:3明确否认了这种推论。但耶稣提醒他：还有比疾病更可怕的，就是罪带来的永远后果（「更加利害」很可能是指这一点）。

深读 5:17-18「我父做事直到如今，我也做事」

1. 神在安息日做不做事？ 创2:2说神在第七日「安息了」。但当时犹太教师也承认，神在安息日并没有停止一切：他仍然托住世界，仍然使人出生、使人死亡，仍然施行审判。与耶稣同时代而年长的犹太哲学家斐洛就说神从不停止工作；后来的拉比文献更记载了这样的讨论：神在安息日仍然做两件事，就是赐生命和审判。

2. 耶稣宣告了同样的特权。 耶稣说：「我父做事直到如今，我也做事。」意思是：父在安息日不停止的工作，我也不停止。听的人立刻明白：「将自己和神当作平等。」（约5:18）

3. 紧接着的正是那两件事。 耶稣接下来说的，正好就是犹太教师说神在安息日仍做的两件事：「父怎样叫死人起来，使他们活着，子也照样随自己的意思使人活着」（约5:21，赐生命）；「父不审判什么人，乃将审判的事全交与子」（约5:22，审判）。耶稣不是偶然打破规矩，他是在宣告自己做的正是神的工作。

深读 5:19-30 子与父：平等，又出于父

1. 「子凭着自己不能做什么」。 这句话（约5:19）乍听像是在说子比父低。但下一句马上说：「父所做的事，子也照样做。」子不能做父没有做的事，但父所做的一切，子都做。这不是能力不足，而是完全的合一：子从不离开父单独行事。

2. 尊荣的平等。 「叫人都尊敬子如同尊敬父一样。不尊敬子的，就是不尊敬差子来的父。」（约5:23）在严格的一神信仰中，没有人能要求被尊敬「如同」神一样，除非他自己就是神。

3. 「在自己有生命」。 「父怎样在自己有生命，就赐给他儿子也照样在自己有生命。」（约5:26）「在自己有生命」，就是生命不靠任何别的来源，这是只有神才有的属性。子「也照样」在自己有生命。许多教父（如奥古斯丁）从这节经文看出子从父永远受生的关系；加尔文等人则认为它是指道成肉身的中保从父领受赐生命的权柄。两种读法都肯定子在自己有生命、与父同等。

4. 现在与将来。 请比较两节：「时候将到，现在就是了，死人要听见神儿子的声音，听见的人就要活了」（约5:25）；「时候要到，凡在坟墓里的，都要听见他的声音，就出来」（约5:28）。第一节有「现在就是了」，第二节没有。前者说的是现在：属灵上死了的人，听见子的声音就出死入生（约5:24）。后者说的是将来：身体的复活和最后的审判。约翰福音同时有这两层：永生现在就开始，复活在末日完成。

要点：耶稣在这里不是说他像神，而是说他做神所做的事、受神所受的尊荣、拥有神所拥有的生命；同时他在差遣中完全顺从父，而这顺从出于与父同一的旨意，不表示他在本质上低于父。
深读 5:31-47 证人一个一个上台

1. 法庭的场景。 申19:15规定，凡事要凭两三个人的口作见证才能定案。耶稣说：「我若为自己作见证，我的见证就不真。」（约5:31）意思是：按你们的标准，单凭我自己的话不够，那么我来传召证人。

2. 四个（或五个）证人。 接下来耶稣一个一个列出：施洗约翰（约5:33）；父交给他的工作，就是他所行的神迹（约5:36）；父自己（约5:37）；圣经（约5:39）；摩西（约5:46，也可以看作圣经见证的代表）。「见证」是约翰福音的关键词之一，整卷书就像一场审判，读者是陪审员。

3. 「你们查考圣经」是命令还是陈述？ 希腊文 ereunate 的形式，可以是命令语气（「你们要查考」），也可以是直述语气（「你们正在查考」）。英文钦定本（KJV）译作命令「你们要查考圣经」；和合本的「你们查考圣经，因你们以为内中有永生」，与ESV、NIV一样，读作直述较自然。从上下文看，直述也较合理：耶稣不是叫他们去读圣经，他们已经读得很勤了，问题是他们读了，却没有看见圣经所指向的那一位。「给我作见证的就是这经。然而，你们不肯到我这里来得生命。」（约5:39-40）

4. 摩西指着谁写？ 「他书上有指着我写的话。」（约5:46）最直接的经文是申18:15：「耶和华你的神要从你们弟兄中间给你兴起一位先知像我。」但耶稣的意思可能更广：整部摩西五经，从女人的后裔（创3:15）到逾越节的羔羊，都在指向他。

5. 信的障碍。 「你们互相受荣耀，却不求从独一之神来的荣耀，怎能信我呢？」（约5:44）耶稣指出，不信不只是头脑的问题，也是心的问题：太在乎人的称赞，就很难接受一位被人弃绝的弥赛亚。这对看重面子的我们，是很直接的提醒。

默想

默想： 那人躺了三十八年，没有人帮他，他甚至不知道医治他的是谁（约5:13），耶稣却先来到他面前。「那听我话、又信差我来者的，就有永生……是已经出死入生了。」（约5:24）我是把这句话当作已经成就的事实来领受，还是仍在等自己够好？我读圣经，会不会也像那些人一样，查考了很多，却没有「到他这里来得生命」？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 5 is a turning point. The healing of the paralyzed man (vv. 1–15) is the third sign, at the Pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem, on a Sabbath. The Sabbath conflict (vv. 16–18): the Jews persecute Jesus not only for healing on the Sabbath but because he was "calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God." Jesus' discourse (vv. 19–47) has two parts: first the relationship of the Son to the Father (vv. 19–30), then, as in a courtroom, a call to the witnesses who testify about him (vv. 31–47).

From this chapter on, "the Jews" seeking to kill Jesus (John 5:18) becomes a continuing thread. In John, "the Jews" often means the religious leaders who opposed Jesus, not the whole people. Jesus himself, his disciples and John were all Jews.

Going Deeper: 5:2–9 The Pool of Bethesda and Thirty-Eight Years

1. A detail that fits the archaeology. "Which has five roofed colonnades" (John 5:2): some critics once read the five porticoes as merely symbolic (the five books of Moses). Since the nineteenth century, excavations beside the Church of St. Anne in Jerusalem have revealed a double pool with a central dividing wall; four sides plus the middle would give exactly five colonnades, which fits John's description. It's another example of the reliability of John's eyewitness detail.

2. Where is verse 4? Some Bibles have a passage at verses 3–4 saying an angel stirred the water from time to time, and the first one in was healed. The earliest and best Greek manuscripts don't have it, so most modern translations put it in a footnote; both the ESV and the Chinese Union Version used in this app omit verse 4. The end of verse 3 ("waiting for the moving of the water") is missing from the same early manuscripts. It was most likely added by a later copyist to explain the sick man's reference to the water being "stirred up" in verse 7. The man's words reflect what people believed, but John doesn't say the belief was true.

3. "Do you want to be healed?" The question seems unnecessary, but it goes to the heart. The man doesn't answer "yes"; he explains why he can't get well: "I have no one to put me into the pool" (John 5:7). His hope is in the water. Jesus bypasses the water entirely: "Get up, take up your bed, and walk." It wasn't the pool that healed him but Jesus' word.

4. Thirty-eight years. Some interpreters recall Deuteronomy 2:14, where Israel wandered thirty-eight years from Kadesh-barnea to the brook Zered. The connection is intriguing, but John doesn't make it. The safest reading is that the number shows how long and how hopeless his illness was.

5. "Sin no more." Later Jesus finds him in the temple and says, "See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you" (John 5:14). This doesn't mean every illness is the direct result of a particular sin; Jesus explicitly rejects that inference in John 9:3. But he warns him that worse than any bodily illness are, most likely, the eternal consequences of sin.

Going Deeper: 5:17–18 "My Father is working until now, and I am working"

1. Does God work on the Sabbath? Genesis 2:2 says God "rested" on the seventh day. But Jewish teachers of the time also recognized that God didn't stop everything on the Sabbath: he still upheld the world, still caused births and deaths, still judged. Philo, a Jewish philosopher and an older contemporary of Jesus, already said that God never ceases working; later rabbinic writings record the discussion that on the Sabbath God still does two things, giving life and judging.

2. Jesus claims the same prerogative. "My Father is working until now, and I am working." In other words, the work the Father doesn't stop on the Sabbath, I don't stop either. His hearers understood at once: "making himself equal with God" (John 5:18).

3. What follows is exactly those two works. What Jesus says next is precisely the two things Jewish teachers said God still does on the Sabbath: "as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will" (John 5:21, giving life); "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son" (John 5:22, judging). Jesus isn't breaking a rule by accident. He is announcing that what he does is God's own work.

Going Deeper: 5:19–30 The Son and the Father: Equal, and from the Father

1. "The Son can do nothing of his own accord." At first this verse (John 5:19) sounds as if the Son is lower than the Father. But the next sentence says, "For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise." The Son can't do what the Father isn't doing, but everything the Father does, the Son does. This isn't a lack of power but complete unity: the Son never acts independently of the Father.

2. Equal honor. "That all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him" (John 5:23). Under strict monotheism, no one can demand to be honored "just as" God is honored, unless he himself is God.

3. "Life in himself." "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself" (John 5:26). To have life in oneself is to depend on nothing outside oneself for life, which belongs to God alone. The Son "also" has life in himself. Many church fathers (Augustine, for example) saw here the Son's eternal generation from the Father; Calvin and others took it of the incarnate Mediator receiving from the Father the authority to give life. Both readings affirm that the Son has life in himself, equal with the Father.

4. Present and future. Compare two verses: "an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live" (John 5:25); "an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out" (John 5:28). The first has "and is now here"; the second doesn't. The first speaks of the present: the spiritually dead hear the Son's voice and pass from death to life (John 5:24). The second speaks of the future: bodily resurrection and final judgment. John holds both: eternal life begins now, and resurrection is completed on the last day.

The point: Jesus isn't saying he is like God. He says he does what God does, receives the honor God receives and has the life God has, while in his mission he fully obeys the Father, an obedience that flows from one shared will, not from any lesser divinity.
Going Deeper: 5:31–47 The Witnesses Take the Stand

1. A courtroom scene. Deuteronomy 19:15 requires two or three witnesses to establish a matter. Jesus says, "If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not deemed true" (John 5:31). In other words: by your standard my own word isn't enough, so I will call witnesses.

2. Four (or five) witnesses. Jesus lists them one by one: John the Baptist (John 5:33); the works the Father gave him, his signs (John 5:36); the Father himself (John 5:37); the Scriptures (John 5:39); and Moses (John 5:46, who can also be counted as the chief example of Scripture's witness). "Witness" is one of John's key words. The whole book is like a trial, with the reader as juror.

3. Is "search the Scriptures" a command or a statement? The Greek form ereunate can be imperative ("search!") or indicative ("you search"). The KJV took it as a command ("Search the scriptures"); the ESV and NIV, and most naturally the Chinese Union Version, read it as a statement: "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life." The context favors the statement. Jesus isn't telling them to read the Bible; they already read it diligently. The problem is that they read without seeing the one the Scriptures point to: "it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life" (John 5:39–40).

4. Of whom did Moses write? "He wrote of me" (John 5:46). The most direct text is Deuteronomy 18:15: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you." But Jesus may mean more broadly that all of Moses' writings, from the offspring of the woman (Gen 3:15) to the Passover lamb, point to him.

5. What blocks belief. "How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?" (John 5:44). Jesus shows that unbelief isn't only a problem of the head but of the heart. If you care too much about people's praise, it's hard to accept a rejected Messiah.

Meditation

Reflect: For thirty-eight years no one helped him, and he didn't even know who healed him (John 5:13), yet Jesus came to him first. "Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life... he has passed from death to life" (John 5:24). Do I receive that as something already done, or am I still waiting until I'm good enough? When I read the Bible, am I like those who searched diligently but would not "come to him that they may have life"?
