entries.title: 凡事都当造就人：聚会中的方言与先知讲道
entries.title_en: Let All Things Be Done for Building Up: Tongues and Prophecy in the Gathering

verse_parts.text: 弟兄们，这却怎么样呢？你们聚会的时候，各人或有诗歌，或有教训，或有启示，或有方言，或有翻出来的话，凡事都当造就人。

entries.verse_text: 弟兄们，这却怎么样呢？你们聚会的时候，各人或有诗歌，或有教训，或有启示，或有方言，或有翻出来的话，凡事都当造就人。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十四章把第十二、十三章的原则，应用在哥林多教会的聚会上。这一章分三段。作先知讲道比说方言更能造就教会（1-19节）：「说方言的，是造就自己；作先知讲道的，乃是造就教会。」保罗宁可「用悟性说五句教导人的话，强如说万句方言」。为不信的人着想（20-25节）：若外人进来，听见众人说方言，会以为「你们癫狂了」；若听见先知讲道，就可能「将脸伏地，敬拜神」。聚会的次序（26-40节）：「凡事都当造就人」，说方言要轮流，并要有人翻出来；作先知讲道也要轮流，其余的人要慎思明辨，因为「神不是叫人混乱，乃是叫人安静」。中间有一段关于「妇女在会中要闭口不言」的话（33-36节），是新约中较难解的经文之一。

这一章的中心是26节：「凡事都当造就人。」聚会的目的，不是让人显出自己的恩赐，而是让众人被建立。这正是第十三章所说的爱。

深读 14:1-19 造就教会

1. 追求爱，切慕恩赐。 「你们要追求爱，也要切慕属灵的恩赐，其中更要羡慕的，是作先知讲道。」（林前14:1）保罗先说「追求爱」，正是接续第十三章。他没有贬低恩赐，却把恩赐放在爱的底下：恩赐是用来表达爱、服事人的。

2. 先知讲道是什么？ 「但作先知讲道的，是对人说，要造就、安慰、劝勉人。」（林前14:3）「作先知讲道」原文是说预言（和合本在林前11:4-5只作「讲道」），不等于今天讲台上的讲道。它是什么，有不同的理解：

  • 许多终止论者（如加芬）认为，这是神直接的启示，带着神自己的权威，属于使徒时代的根基（弗2:20）。
  • 许多延续论者（如古德恩）认为，这是人受圣灵感动所说、能帮助会众的话，但权威低于圣经，所以「其余的就当慎思明辨」（林前14:29）。
  • 也有人（如加尔文）认为，在今天，这恩赐主要表现在解释和应用圣经上。

不论哪一种理解，保罗的重点都是：作先知讲道是用人听得懂的话，叫人得造就、安慰、劝勉。

3. 说方言是什么？ 「那说方言的，原不是对人说，乃是对神说，因为没有人听出来。然而，他在心灵里却是讲说各样的奥秘。」（林前14:2）方言是什么，也有不同的看法：有人认为是说话的人没有学过的外国语言，像五旬节那天一样（徒2:6-8）；也有人认为是一种不属于人间语言的祷告和赞美（参林前13:1「天使的话语」）。保罗承认说方言有价值：「说方言的，是造就自己」（林前14:4），他自己「说方言比你们众人还多」（林前14:18）。但在聚会中，没有翻出来的方言不能造就别人。

4. 用灵，也用悟性。 「我要用灵祷告，也要用悟性祷告；我要用灵歌唱，也要用悟性歌唱。不然，你用灵祝谢，那在座不通方言的人，既然不明白你的话，怎能在你感谢的时候说『阿们』呢？」（林前14:15-16）敬拜不只是情感的经验，也需要头脑明白。别人要能跟着说「阿们」，才算是一同敬拜。

5. 五句与万句。 「但在教会中，宁可用悟性说五句教导人的话，强如说万句方言。」（林前14:19）这句话对今天的教会仍然适用：讲台上无论用了多少术语、说得多么高深，都不如几句让人听得懂、能带回家的话。

要点：聚会中的恩赐，要用人听得懂的方式，造就、安慰、劝勉别人。五句造就人的话，强如一万句只造就自己的话。
深读 14:20-25 为不信的人着想

1. 在心志上作大人。 「弟兄们，在心志上不要作小孩子。然而，在恶事上要作婴孩，在心志上总要作大人。」（林前14:20）哥林多人看重方言，却只看重它的新奇和热闹，像小孩子一样。保罗要他们在思想上成熟。

2. 方言是给不信的人的记号。 「律法上记着：主说：我要用外邦人的舌头和外邦人的嘴唇向这百姓说话；虽然如此，他们还是不听从我。这样看来，说方言不是为信的人作证据，乃是为不信的人。」（林前14:21-22）保罗引用赛28:11-12：以色列人不肯听先知的话，神就让他们听见听不懂的亚述话，作为审判的记号。这段经文很难解。常见的理解是：在聚会中，不信的人听见没有翻出来的方言，不会因此悔改，反倒说「你们癫狂了」（林前14:23）；这方言就成了一个记号，显明他们的不信。

3. 「神真是在你们中间了」。 「若都作先知讲道，偶然有不信的，或是不通方言的人进来，就被众人劝醒，被众人审明，他心里的隐情显露出来，就必将脸伏地，敬拜神，说：『神真是在你们中间了。』」（林前14:24-25）这是聚会最好的结果：一个外人进来，不是被奇怪的现象吓走，而是听见神的话，被神光照，认罪悔改，敬拜神。

要点：聚会最美的时刻，不是我们显得多属灵，而是慕道友和新朋友也能说：「神真是在你们中间了。」为此，我们要用他听得懂的话，把神的话讲给他听。
深读 14:26-40 聚会的次序

1. 凡事都当造就人。 「弟兄们，这却怎么样呢？你们聚会的时候，各人或有诗歌，或有教训，或有启示，或有方言，或有翻出来的话，凡事都当造就人。」（林前14:26）从这里可以看见，早期教会的聚会有许多人参与。

2. 次序。 说方言的「只好两个人，至多三个人，且要轮流着说，也要一个人翻出来。若没有人翻，就当在会中闭口」；作先知讲道的「只好两个人或是三个人，其余的就当慎思明辨」（林前14:27-29）。「先知的灵原是顺服先知的；因为神不是叫人混乱，乃是叫人安静。」（林前14:32-33）和合本译作「安静」的这个词，原文是平安。圣灵的工作不会叫人失控，属灵的人可以安静、等候、轮流。

3. 「妇女在会中要闭口不言」。 「妇女在会中要闭口不言，像在圣徒的众教会一样，因为不准她们说话。她们总要顺服，正如律法所说的。她们若要学什么，可以在家里问自己的丈夫，因为妇女在会中说话原是可耻的。」（林前14:34-35）大多数解经家认为，这段话不能理解为妇女在聚会中完全不可以开口，因为保罗在林前11:5已经提到妇女在聚会中祷告、说预言（和合本作「讲道」）；所以这里的「闭口」是指某种特定的说话。主要有以下几种理解：

  • 不参与评断先知讲道：许多互补派学者（如卡森、古德恩）认为，这段话紧接在29节「其余的就当慎思明辨」之后，指的是妇女不在会众面前公开评断先知的话，因为这涉及教导的权柄（参提前2:12）。
  • 不在聚会中插嘴发问：许多学者，特别是平等派学者（如克雷格·基纳〔Craig Keener〕）认为，当时的妇女大多没有受过教育，可能在聚会中大声发问、打断讲话，所以保罗说「可以在家里问自己的丈夫」；这是为了聚会的秩序，不是一条永远禁止妇女说话的命令。
  • 后来加进去的经文：也有一些学者（如戈登·费依，多属平等派）认为，这两节可能是后来抄写的人加进去的，因为少数西方抄本把这两节放在第40节之后；他们也认为，这两节与林前11:5和上下文不协调。但现存的抄本都有这两节，今天通行的希腊文本和大多数福音派解经家都认为这是保罗原来的话。

「正如律法所说的」也不容易理解，因为旧约没有一节经文直接这样说。保罗在林前14:21把以赛亚书也称为「律法」，可见「律法」可以泛指旧约。有人认为是指创世记第二章的创造次序（参林前11:8-9；提前2:13），也有人认为是指创3:16，或泛指旧约的原则。华人教会在这件事上的做法也不一样：有的教会有女传道人讲道、教导，有的教会讲台只由弟兄负责，姊妹仍然祷告、作见证，也教导妇女和孩子。无论采取哪一种做法，都要记得：神的灵「浇灌凡有血气的」，「你们的儿女要说预言」（珥2:28；徒2:17-18）。彼得在五旬节宣告，这应许已经应验；腓利的四个女儿也是说预言的（徒21:9）。主耶稣让马利亚坐在他脚前听道（路10:39），又让妇女作复活的第一批见证人（约20:17-18）；保罗在这里也假定姊妹要学道。姊妹的恩赐是神给教会的礼物，不可轻看；持不同做法的教会，也不必因此彼此论断。

不论怎样理解这里的「顺服」和「闭口」，这段经文都不是要姊妹忍受丈夫的暴力，也不是要她在教会里对虐待保持沉默。受害的姊妹可以离开危险，也应当报警（罗13:4）；教会必须聆听、保护她，不可为了「家丑不可外扬」而遮掩，也不可让施害的人保留职分，或再接近受害人和孩子。

4. 主的命令。 「若有人以为自己是先知，或是属灵的，就该知道，我所写给你们的是主的命令。」（林前14:37）保罗所写的，不只是他个人的意见，而是主的命令。

5. 不要禁止，也要规矩。 「所以我弟兄们，你们要切慕作先知讲道，也不要禁止说方言。凡事都要规规矩矩地按着次序行。」（林前14:39-40）这一句平衡了两边：不要因为怕混乱就禁止圣灵的恩赐；也不要因为追求恩赐，就让聚会失去次序。放在今天的华人教会，这几节对两边都有话说。灵恩的教会要问：众人同时大声说方言、没有人翻出来，外人进来能说「阿们」吗？有人说「主告诉我」，有没有人按圣经「慎思明辨」？若有人藉「神的启示」要人嫁给谁、奉献多少，或不可离开教会，那就是辖制，不是先知讲道。非灵恩的教会也要问：我们是不是因为怕，就一概「禁止」，或者看不起有不同经历的弟兄姊妹？讲台上满是术语、外人听不懂的，也是另一种没有翻出来的方言。两边要记得，量度的尺是同一把：这能不能造就人，能不能叫人更认识基督？

要点：神不是叫人混乱的神，乃是赐平安的神。聚会中的一切，都要规规矩矩、按着次序，好叫众人在基督这根基上被建立（参林前3:11）。
默想

默想： 「作先知讲道的，是对人说，要造就、安慰、劝勉人。」请回想一句曾经扶持过我的话：也许是在我最灰心的时候，一位长辈拍拍我的肩膀说：「神没有忘记你」；也许是小组里一位弟兄姊妹为我祷告时说的一句经文；也许只是一条短信。那几句话不长，却在我心里留了很多年。也许我想不起有谁这样扶持过我；也许我在教会里听到的，更多是批评和论断。可是有一句话，主已经亲口对我说了：神在这末世藉着他的儿子向我们说话（来1:2），他对我说的，不是定罪，而是「你的罪赦了」（可2:5）。我也想起自己说过的一些话，不是造就人，而是伤人：在家里对孩子说过的重话，在教会里传过的闲话。这是罪；但这些罪也在他的赦免里面，所以我可以不再为自己辩护，先向主认罪，也去向那人认错。我常常以为，造就人是牧师和讲员的事。可是保罗说「各人或有诗歌，或有教训」，每个人都可以说几句造就人的话；即使我没有说预言的恩赐，我说话的目标也和先知讲道一样：造就人（弗4:29；帖前5:11）。今天，我能不能求主把一个人放在我心里，把我从主那里听见的恩典，用几句简单的话说给他听？我能说造就人的话，不是因为我口才好，而是因为我先被主的话造就了。他对我说的那句「你的罪赦了」，就是我一切话语的源头。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 14 applies the principles of chapters 12 and 13 to the Corinthian church's gatherings. It has three parts. Prophecy builds the church more than tongues (vv. 1–19): "The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church." Paul "would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue." Thinking of unbelievers (vv. 20–25): if outsiders come in and hear everyone speaking in tongues, they will say "you are out of your minds"; if they hear prophecy, they may fall "on his face" and "worship God." Order in the gathering (vv. 26–40): "Let all things be done for building up"; tongues and prophecy should take turns, with interpretation or weighing, because "God is not a God of confusion but of peace." In the middle is a passage on women keeping "silent in the churches" (vv. 33–36), among the harder texts in the New Testament.

The center of the chapter is verse 26: "Let all things be done for building up." The purpose of the gathering is not for people to display their gifts, but for everyone to be built up. This is the love of chapter 13.

Going Deeper: 14:1–19 Building Up the Church

1. Pursue love, desire the gifts. "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:1). Paul begins with "pursue love," continuing chapter 13. He doesn't belittle the gifts, but he puts them under love: gifts are tools of love.

2. What is prophecy? "On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation" (1 Corinthians 14:3). What New Testament prophecy is has been understood in different ways:

  • Many cessationists (e.g. Richard Gaffin) hold that it was direct revelation from God, carrying God's own authority, belonging to the foundation laid in the apostolic age (Eph 2:20).
  • Many continuationists (e.g. Wayne Grudem) hold that it is Spirit-prompted speech that helps the congregation, with less authority than Scripture, which is why "the others weigh what is said" (1 Corinthians 14:29).
  • Others (e.g. Calvin) hold that today this gift is expressed mainly in explaining and applying Scripture.

On any view, Paul's point is that prophecy uses words people can understand, for their upbuilding, encouragement and consolation.

3. What are tongues? "For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit" (1 Corinthians 14:2). Views differ on what tongues are. Some take them to be foreign languages the speaker had never learned, as at Pentecost (Acts 2:6–8); others take them to be prayer and praise not in any human language (cf. 1 Corinthians 13:1, "the tongues of men and of angels"). Paul grants that tongues have value: "The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself" (1 Corinthians 14:4), and he himself speaks "in tongues more than all of you" (1 Corinthians 14:18). But in the gathering, uninterpreted tongues cannot build others up.

4. With the spirit and with the mind. "I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also. Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say 'Amen' to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying?" (1 Corinthians 14:15–16). Worship is not only an emotional experience; it also needs the mind to understand. Others must be able to say "Amen" for it to be shared worship.

5. Five words and ten thousand. "Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue" (1 Corinthians 14:19). This still applies to the church today: however learned a sermon sounds, however much specialized vocabulary it uses, a few words people can understand and take home are worth more.

The point: Gifts in the gathering are to be used in ways others can understand, for their upbuilding, encouragement and consolation. Five words that build others up are better than ten thousand that build up only oneself.
Going Deeper: 14:20–25 Thinking of Unbelievers

1. Mature in thinking. "Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature" (1 Corinthians 14:20). The Corinthians prized tongues, but like children they prized the novelty and the excitement. Paul wants them to mature in their thinking.

2. Tongues as a sign for unbelievers. "In the Law it is written, 'By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.' Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers" (1 Corinthians 14:21–22). Paul cites Isaiah 28:11–12: when Israel would not listen to the prophets, God made them hear unintelligible Assyrian speech, a sign of judgment. The passage is difficult; a common reading is that in the gathering, unintelligible tongues bring unbelievers not to repentance but to a sign of their unbelief, leaving them to say "you are out of your minds" (1 Corinthians 14:23).

3. "God is really among you." "But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all, the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you" (1 Corinthians 14:24–25). This is the best outcome of a gathering: an outsider comes in and, rather than being driven away by strange phenomena, hears God's word, is searched by God, confesses and repents, and worships God.

The point: A gathering is at its best not when we look spiritual, but when an outsider says, "God is really among you." So we speak God's word in words he can understand.
Going Deeper: 14:26–40 Order in the Gathering

1. All things for building up. "What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up" (1 Corinthians 14:26). Here we see that the early church's gatherings involved many participants.

2. Order. For tongues, "let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church"; for prophecy, "let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said" (1 Corinthians 14:27–29). "The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Corinthians 14:32–33). The Spirit's work does not make people lose control; spiritual people can be quiet, wait and take turns.

3. "The women should keep silent in the churches." "The women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church" (1 Corinthians 14:34–35). Most interpreters conclude that this cannot mean women may never speak at all in the gathering, since in 1 Corinthians 11:5 Paul has already mentioned women praying and prophesying there; so the "silence" here concerns a particular kind of speech. The main readings are these:

  • Not taking part in weighing prophecies: many complementarian scholars (e.g. D. A. Carson, Wayne Grudem) note that this follows directly on verse 29, "let the others weigh what is said," and take it to mean that women should not publicly judge the prophets' words before the congregation, since that involves the authority to teach (cf. 1 Tim 2:12).
  • Not interrupting with questions: many scholars, especially egalitarians (e.g. Craig Keener), hold that most women then had little education and may have been calling out questions and interrupting, so Paul says "let them ask their husbands at home"; this is for the order of the gathering, not a permanent command forbidding women to speak.
  • A later addition: some scholars, mostly egalitarian (e.g. Gordon Fee), think these two verses may have been added later by a copyist, because in a few Western manuscripts they appear after verse 40; they also argue the verses fit poorly with 1 Corinthians 11:5 and the flow from verse 33 to verse 36. But no extant manuscript lacks them, and the standard Greek text (NA28) and most evangelical commentators retain them as Paul's own words.

"As the Law also says" is not easy either, since no Old Testament verse says this directly. In 1 Corinthians 14:21 Paul calls Isaiah "the Law," so the word can refer to the Old Testament generally. Some take it as the creation order of Genesis 2 (cf. 1 Corinthians 11:8–9; 1 Tim 2:13), others as Genesis 3:16, others as a general Old Testament principle. Chinese churches differ in practice: some have women pastors who preach and teach, others reserve the pulpit for men while sisters still pray, testify, and teach women and children. Whatever the practice, we must remember that God pours out his Spirit "on all flesh," and "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy" (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17–18). Peter declared this promise fulfilled at Pentecost, and Philip's four daughters prophesied (Acts 21:9). Jesus let Mary sit at his feet as a learner (Luke 10:39) and made women the first witnesses of his resurrection (John 20:17–18); Paul here also assumes that sisters will learn. Sisters' gifts are God's gift to the church and must not be despised; and churches with different practices need not judge one another over this.

However "submission" and "silence" here are understood, this passage never requires a wife to endure her husband's violence, or a sister to keep quiet about abuse in the church. A woman who is being harmed may leave danger, and should report it to the police (Rom 13:4). The church must listen to her and protect her; it may not hide abuse to save face, and it may not leave the abuser in office or give him access again to victims or children.

4. A command of the Lord. "If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 14:37). What Paul writes is not merely his personal opinion but the Lord's command.

5. Do not forbid, and keep order. "So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:39–40). This sentence balances both sides: don't forbid the Spirit's gifts out of fear of disorder, and don't let the gathering lose its order in pursuit of gifts. In Chinese churches today these verses speak to both sides. Charismatic churches should ask: when everyone prays aloud in tongues at once with no interpretation, can an outsider say "Amen"? When someone says "the Lord told me," does anyone weigh it by Scripture? If someone uses a "revelation" to tell a person whom to marry, how much to give or that they may not leave the church, that is control, not prophecy. Non-charismatic churches should ask: have we simply "forbidden" out of fear, or looked down on brothers and sisters whose experience differs? A pulpit full of jargon outsiders cannot follow is another kind of uninterpreted tongue. Both sides use the same measure: does this build people up, and does it help them know Christ?

The point: God is not a God of confusion but of peace. Everything in the gathering should be done decently and in order, so that all are built up on Christ the foundation (cf. 1 Corinthians 3:11).
Meditation

Reflect: "The one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation." Recall a few words that once held me up: perhaps when I was most discouraged, an older believer patted my shoulder and said, "God has not forgotten you"; perhaps a verse a brother or sister prayed over me in small group; perhaps just a short text message. Those words were few, but they stayed with me for years. Perhaps I can't remember anyone speaking to me like that; perhaps what I have mostly heard at church is criticism. Yet there is one word the Lord has spoken to me himself: in these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:2), and what he says to me is not condemnation but "your sins are forgiven" (Mark 2:5). I also remember words I have spoken that did not build up but wounded: harsh words to my children at home, gossip passed on at church. This is sin; but these sins too are covered by his forgiveness, so I can stop defending myself, confess them to the Lord, and go and own them to the person I hurt. I often think building others up is the work of pastors and speakers. But Paul says "each one has a hymn, a lesson," and everyone can speak a few words that build others up; even if I do not prophesy, the aim of my speech is the same as prophecy's: building up (Eph 4:29; 1 Thess 5:11). Today, can I ask the Lord to lay one person on my heart, and pass on to them, in a few simple words, the grace I have heard from him? I can speak words that build up not because I am eloquent, but because his word has built me up first. His "your sins are forgiven" is the source of every word I speak.

entries.title: 基督已经从死里复活：死啊，你得胜的权势在哪里？
entries.title_en: Christ Has Been Raised: O Death, Where Is Your Victory?

verse_parts.text: 但基督已经从死里复活，成为睡了之人初熟的果子。

entries.verse_text: 但基督已经从死里复活，成为睡了之人初熟的果子。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十五章是全书的高峰，讲死人复活。哥林多教会中「有人说没有死人复活的事」（林前15:12），保罗用全章来回答。这一章分五段。福音的核心（1-11节）：基督照圣经所说为我们的罪死了，埋葬了，第三天复活了，并且显给许多人看。若基督没有复活（12-19节）：我们所传的、所信的都是枉然，我们仍在罪里。基督已经复活（20-28节）：他是「睡了之人初熟的果子」，他必作王，直到「尽末了所毁灭的仇敌就是死」。为什么天天冒死（29-34节）：若没有复活，信徒的受苦就没有意义。复活的身体与最后的得胜（35-58节）：所种的是必朽坏的，复活的是不朽坏的；「死啊！你得胜的权势在哪里？」

这一章的转折点在20节：「但基督已经从死里复活。」前面的「若」字，都在这一句面前倒塌了。复活不是福音的附录，而是福音的中心：没有复活，就没有基督教的信仰。

深读 15:1-11 福音的核心

1. 「第一」要紧的事。 「我当日所领受又传给你们的：第一，就是基督照圣经所说，为我们的罪死了，而且埋葬了；又照圣经所说，第三天复活了。」（林前15:3-4）「第一」是指最重要的事。这几句话有固定的格式，「领受」和「传给」又是传递传统的用语（参林前11:23），所以许多学者认为，这是早期教会的一段信条，可能在耶稣受死后几年之内就已经形成，保罗信主后不久就领受了。保罗信主大约三年后，曾在耶路撒冷见过矶法和雅各（加1:18-19），很可能就是那时领受的。福音的核心是历史事件：基督死了，埋葬了，复活了，而且这一切都是「照圣经所说」，应验了旧约（参赛53:5-12；诗16:10；何6:2）。「为我们的罪」说明了基督受死的意义：他是替我们承担罪的刑罚。

2. 许多见证人。 「并且显给矶法看，然后显给十二使徒看；后来一时显给五百多弟兄看，其中一大半到如今还在，却也有已经睡了的。以后显给雅各看，再显给众使徒看，末了也显给我看。」（林前15:5-8）「其中一大半到如今还在」，等于是说：你们可以去问他们。雅各是主的弟弟，耶稣在世的时候，连他的弟兄也不信他（约7:5），后来却成了耶路撒冷教会的领袖（徒15:13）。这份名单没有提到妇女，许多学者认为，这可能是因为当时的法庭不太看重妇女的见证，而这是一段公开传讲的信条；但四福音都记载，最先来到空坟墓的是妇女，马太福音和约翰福音也记载，复活的主最先向她们显现（太28:9-10；约20:14-18）。

3. 「是蒙神的恩才成的」。 「我原是使徒中最小的，不配称为使徒，因为我从前逼迫神的教会。然而，我今日成了何等人，是蒙神的恩才成的。」（林前15:9-10）保罗称自己「如同未到产期而生的人一般」（林前15:8）。这个词的意思有不同理解，许多人认为是因为他不是在耶稣在世的时候跟随他，而是在逼迫教会的时候被主拦住。他比众使徒格外劳苦，「这原不是我，乃是神的恩与我同在」。

要点：福音的核心是历史事实：基督为我们的罪死了，埋葬了，第三天复活了，并且有许多见证人；连逼迫教会的人，也因这恩典成了「何等人」。
深读 15:12-19 若基督没有复活

1. 「没有死人复活的事」。 「既传基督是从死里复活了，怎么在你们中间有人说没有死人复活的事呢？」（林前15:12）这些哥林多人可能受了希腊哲学（特别是柏拉图一派）的影响，认为身体是灵魂的监牢，死后灵魂得释放就好了，身体复活是不可思议的事（参徒17:32）。也有学者认为，他们以为自己已经进入了完全属灵的境界，不再需要身体的复活（参林前4:8；提后2:18）。

2. 一连串的「若」。 保罗从反面推论：「若基督没有复活，我们所传的便是枉然，你们所信的也是枉然」（林前15:14）；「基督若没有复活，你们的信便是徒然，你们仍在罪里。就是在基督里睡了的人也灭亡了。」（林前15:17-18）基督教的信仰不是一套道德教训，也不是一种心理安慰；它建立在一件历史事件上。若基督没有复活，十字架就只是一场悲剧，我们的罪也没有被除去。

3. 比众人更可怜。 「我们若靠基督只在今生有指望，就算比众人更可怜。」（林前15:19）这句话很诚实：信徒为主受苦、舍弃、牺牲，若死后什么都没有，那确实是白白受苦。基督教的盼望，从来不只是今生过得更好。

要点：基督教的信仰建立在复活这件历史事件上。若基督没有复活，我们仍在罪里；但他确实复活了，一切都改变了。
深读 15:20-28 初熟的果子

1. 「但基督已经从死里复活」。 「但基督已经从死里复活，成为睡了之人初熟的果子。」（林前15:20）「初熟的果子」是收割时先献给神的第一捆庄稼（利23:10-11），它保证后面还有整个收成。基督的复活不只是一件孤立的神迹，而是一个保证：所有属他的人，将来也必复活。

2. 亚当与基督。 「死既是因一人而来，死人复活也是因一人而来。在亚当里众人都死了；照样，在基督里众人也都要复活。」（林前15:21-22；参罗5:12-21）这不是说所有人都要得救，因为23节接着说：「以后，在他来的时候，是那些属基督的。」在亚当里的众人，因为与亚当联合而死；在基督里的众人，因为与基督联合而活。圣经在别处也说，所有的人都要复活，有的复活得生，有的复活定罪（约5:28-29）；这里的「在基督里……都要复活」，是指复活得生命。

3. 尽末了的仇敌。 「因为基督必要作王，等神把一切仇敌都放在他的脚下。尽末了所毁灭的仇敌就是死。」（林前15:25-26；参诗110:1；诗8:6）今天我们仍然面对死亡，死仍是仇敌，不是朋友；但它已经是一个注定要被毁灭的仇敌。

4. 「子也要自己服」。 「万物既服了他，那时子也要自己服那叫万物服他的，叫神在万物之上，为万物之主。」（林前15:28）这节经文不是说子在本质上次于父，或说子的国会结束（「他的国也没有穷尽」，路1:33）。许多解经家（如奥古斯丁、加尔文）认为，这是指：子道成肉身，作了中保，完成救赎的工作以后，就把国交与父，叫三一神得着一切的荣耀（参第十一章关于「神是基督的头」的说明）；在新天新地里，宝座仍是「神和羔羊的宝座」（启22:3）。子与父同质、同等、同荣。

要点：基督的复活是初熟的果子，保证属他的人都要复活。死仍是仇敌，但已经是注定被毁灭的仇敌。
深读 15:29-34 为什么天天冒死

1. 为死人受洗。 「不然，那些为死人受洗的，将来怎样呢？若死人总不复活，因何为他们受洗呢？」（林前15:29）这是新约中最难解的经文之一，历来有几十种解释。主要的有：

  • 有人（如戈登·费依）认为，哥林多有些人为已经去世的人代受洗礼；保罗只是提到这个做法，说明连他们也相信复活，并没有赞同。
  • 也有人（如锡塞尔顿）认为，这是指有些人因为已经去世的信徒（例如亲人临终前的见证）而信主受洗，盼望将来与他们重聚。
  • 一些较早的解经家认为，「死人」指受洗的人自己必死的身体：受洗就是承认自己将来要死，也盼望复活。

耶稣基督后期圣徒教会（俗称摩门教）根据这节经文，为去世的人举行代洗，并认为逝者可以接受或拒绝这代行的仪式。可是圣经没有一处吩咐这样做，而且圣经清楚地教导：「人人都有一死，死后且有审判」（来9:27），每一个人都要在今生亲自信靠基督。华人家庭常有为逝者超度、做七、烧纸钱的习俗，好像活人还能为死人做些什么。福音却告诉我们，人在神面前的结局，不靠后人的仪式；基督在十字架上已经「成了」（约19:30）。这也让在丧事中被要求做这些事的信徒，可以存着平安婉拒。

2. 天天冒死。 「我们又因何时刻冒险呢？……我是天天冒死。我若当日像寻常人，在以弗所同野兽战斗，那于我有什么益处呢？若死人不复活，我们就吃吃喝喝吧！因为明天要死了。」（林前15:30-32；引赛22:13）「同野兽战斗」可能是比喻，指在以弗所遇见凶猛的敌人（参林前16:9；徒19章）；也有人认为是实际的经历。保罗的意思是：若没有复活，他为福音所受的苦就毫无意义，不如及时行乐。

3. 滥交是败坏善行。 「你们不要自欺；滥交是败坏善行。」（林前15:33）这句话出自希腊喜剧诗人米南德，当时已成了俗语。今天「滥交」多指性关系混乱，但和合本这里是指与坏人来往，在上下文中就是与那些否认复活的人来往。错误的教导会带来错误的生活。

要点：复活的盼望使信徒的受苦有意义。若没有复活，人就只剩下「吃吃喝喝」；但因为有复活，为主受苦不是徒然的。
深读 15:35-49 复活的身体

1. 种子的比喻。 「或有人问：『死人怎样复活，带着什么身体来呢？』无知的人哪，你所种的，若不死就不能生。并且你所种的不是那将来的形体，不过是子粒……但神随自己的意思给他一个形体。」（林前15:35-38）种子和长出来的植物，是同一个生命，却是很不一样的形体。复活的身体也是这样：与现在的身体有连续（是同一个人），也有改变（是全新的样式）。

2. 四个对比。 「所种的是必朽坏的，复活的是不朽坏的；所种的是羞辱的，复活的是荣耀的；所种的是软弱的，复活的是强壮的；所种的是血气的身体，复活的是灵性的身体。」（林前15:42-44）「灵性的身体」不是说没有形体、只有灵魂，而是指完全被圣灵掌管、充满圣灵生命的身体（参罗8:11）。复活的主可以被摸、可以吃东西（路24:39-43），我们将来的身体也要像他「荣耀的身体」（腓3:21）。

3. 不只是灵魂得释放，也不是轮回。 信徒死后，灵魂会立刻与主同在（腓1:23；林后5:8），但这还不是最终的盼望；最终的盼望是身体复活。圣经的盼望不是希腊思想所说的灵魂脱离身体就好，也不是佛教和民间信仰所说的轮回转世。轮回是一次又一次地回到这个充满苦难的世界；而且，轮回讲的是业报，人下一世的光景要看自己积了多少功德；复活却不是靠功德换来的，是神白白「使我们……得胜」（林前15:57）。复活是神亲自使我们这同一个人，带着改变了的身体，进入永远不再有死亡的新天新地。

4. 两个亚当。 「首先的人亚当成了有灵的活人」；「末后的亚当成了叫人活的灵」……「我们既有属土的形状，将来也必有属天的形状。」（林前15:45-49）我们从亚当那里得了必死的身体；从基督那里，我们要得着复活的身体。

要点：复活的身体与现在的身体是同一个人，却完全改变：不朽坏、荣耀、强壮，被圣灵充满，像基督荣耀的身体。
深读 15:50-58 死被得胜吞灭

1. 都要改变。 「我如今把一件奥秘的事告诉你们：我们不是都要睡觉，乃是都要改变，就在一霎时，眨眼之间，号筒末次吹响的时候。」（林前15:51-52；参帖前4:16）主再来的时候，已经死了的信徒要复活，还活着的信徒要改变。第50节说「血肉之体不能承受神的国」，这是指现在必朽坏、必死的身体（同节下半：「必朽坏的不能承受不朽坏的」），不是说复活的身体没有形体。

2. 死啊，你的毒钩在哪里？ 「那时经上所记『死被得胜吞灭』的话就应验了。死啊！你得胜的权势在哪里？死啊！你的毒钩在哪里？死的毒钩就是罪，罪的权势就是律法。」（林前15:54-56；引赛25:8；何13:14）死之所以可怕，是因为罪；罪之所以有权势，是因为律法显明、甚至激动人的罪（罗7:8-11），又定人的罪（加3:10）。可是基督已经担当了我们的罪，满足了律法的要求，「为我们受了咒诅」（加3:13），所以死的毒钩已经被拔除了。

3. 感谢神。 「感谢神，使我们藉着我们的主耶稣基督得胜。」（林前15:57）得胜不是我们自己争取来的，是神「使我们……得胜」。

4. 不是徒然的。 「所以，我亲爱的弟兄们，你们务要坚固，不可摇动，常常竭力多做主工；因为知道，你们的劳苦在主里面不是徒然的。」（林前15:58）复活的盼望不是叫人逃避现实，而是叫人在今天更坚定地事奉。因为有复活，今天为主所做的每一件小事，都不会白费。

5. 面对亲人的离世。 华人的丧礼表达了对逝者深切的孝心和不舍，也常常带着对死亡的恐惧、许多忌讳和祭拜的仪式。信徒不参与上香、跪拜、烧纸钱，却可以用守灵陪伴、追思礼拜（或称安息礼拜）、献花、诗歌和见证来尽孝、安慰家人（参第八章和第十章；若从前在压力下随从过，主的恩典比我们的软弱更大）。信徒可以哀哭，耶稣在拉撒路的坟前也「哭了」（约11:35）；但我们的忧伤，不「像那些没有指望的人一样」（帖前4:13）。至于那些没有信主就离世的亲人，圣经清楚地说，人得救只有靠着基督（徒4:12）；但我们不知道每一个人临终时在神面前的光景，定人结局的也不是我们。我们可以把他们交托给那位「审判全地的主」：他必行公义，也是我们在耶稣基督身上所认识、满有怜悯的神（创18:25；诗145:9）。若我为自己当初没有开口、或开口太晚而自责，这份懊悔也可以交在主面前。我们今天能做的，是趁着还有今日，带着这份盼望，温柔地陪伴还活着的家人，把复活的盼望告诉他们。若你自己还没有信靠这位复活的主，今天就可以向他认罪，把自己交托给他。

要点：基督已经胜过死亡，死的毒钩已经被拔除。所以我们可以带着盼望哀哭，也可以坚固不摇动地事奉主。
默想

默想： 「若基督没有复活……就是在基督里睡了的人也灭亡了。」如果保罗只写到第19节，我的盼望也就停在那里。想起一位我所爱、已经在主里睡了的人：也许是祖母，也许是父亲，也许是一位朋友。我记得那天的灵堂，记得盖棺时的哭声，记得回家后那个空出来的位子。我的哀伤，是不是还停在第19节：他走了，我只剩下回忆，我们「比众人更可怜」？也许我的眼泪里，不只有思念，还有懊悔：有些话一直没有说出口，有些探望一拖再拖，有些争执到最后也没有和好。保罗说：「死的毒钩就是罪」（林前15:56）；可是这根毒钩，基督已经替我承受了，我的懊悔也可以带到他的十字架前，他的血也为这些罪流了。保罗接着写下了一个「但」字：「但基督已经从死里复活，成为睡了之人初熟的果子。」（林前15:20）这个「但」字，不是建立在我的感觉上，而是建立在那个空了的坟墓上，建立在矶法、雅各、五百多位弟兄亲眼看见的那一位身上。他复活了，所以那位在主里睡了的人，也必复活；我们还要在主面前重聚，带着不朽坏、荣耀的身体；更要紧的是，我们要一同亲眼看见那位为我们死、又为我们复活的主。若我想起的那一位，我不知道他是否信了主，我也把他交在那位公义又怜悯的主手里。我今天也许仍然会哭，这不是没有信心；耶稣也哭过。但我可以在眼泪中，和保罗一同说：「感谢神，使我们藉着我们的主耶稣基督得胜。」
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 15 is the summit of the letter: the resurrection of the dead. Some in the Corinthian church were saying "that there is no resurrection of the dead" (1 Corinthians 15:12), and Paul gives the whole chapter to answering them. It has five parts. The heart of the gospel (vv. 1–11): Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many. If Christ has not been raised (vv. 12–19): our preaching and your faith are in vain, and you are still in your sins. Christ has been raised (vv. 20–28): he is "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep," and he must reign until "the last enemy to be destroyed is death." Why face danger every hour? (vv. 29–34): without resurrection, believers' suffering has no meaning. The resurrection body and the final victory (vv. 35–58): what is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable; "O death, where is your victory?"

The turning point of the chapter is verse 20: "But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead." All the "ifs" before it collapse before this sentence. The resurrection is not an appendix to the gospel but its center: without the resurrection there is no Christian faith.

Going Deeper: 15:1–11 The Heart of the Gospel

1. Of first importance. "For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). These lines have a fixed form, and "received" and "delivered" are the language of handing on tradition (cf. 1 Corinthians 11:23), so many scholars think this is an early church creed that Paul received soon after his conversion, perhaps formed within a few years of Jesus' death; about three years after his conversion Paul met Cephas and James in Jerusalem (Gal 1:18–19), a likely occasion for receiving it. The heart of the gospel is historical events: Christ died, was buried and was raised, all "in accordance with the Scriptures," fulfilling the Old Testament (cf. Isa 53:5–12; Ps 16:10; Hos 6:2). "For our sins" gives the meaning of his death: he bore the penalty of our sins in our place.

2. Many witnesses. "And that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me" (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). "Most of whom are still alive" amounts to saying: you can go and ask them. James was the Lord's brother; during Jesus' ministry "not even his brothers believed in him" (John 7:5), yet James became a leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13). This list does not mention the women, perhaps, as many suggest, because women's testimony carried little legal weight then and this was a creed for public proclamation. But all four Gospels record that women were first at the empty tomb, and Matthew and John record that the risen Lord appeared first to them (Matt 28:9–10; John 20:14–18).

3. "By the grace of God I am what I am." "For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am" (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). Paul calls himself "one untimely born" (1 Corinthians 15:8). The word's sense is debated; many take it to mean that he did not follow Jesus during his earthly ministry but was stopped by the Lord while persecuting the church. He worked harder than any of them, "though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me."

The point: The heart of the gospel is historical fact: Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and was seen by many witnesses; by this grace even a persecutor of the church became what he is.
Going Deeper: 15:12–19 If Christ Has Not Been Raised

1. "No resurrection of the dead." "Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?" (1 Corinthians 15:12). These Corinthians may have been influenced by Greek philosophy (especially the Platonic strand), which saw the body as the prison of the soul: at death the soul is released, and a bodily resurrection is unthinkable (cf. Acts 17:32). Others think they believed they had already arrived at full spiritual life and needed no bodily resurrection (cf. 1 Corinthians 4:8; 2 Tim 2:18).

2. A chain of "ifs." Paul argues from the opposite side: "if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14); "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins. Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished" (1 Corinthians 15:17–18). The Christian faith is not a set of moral teachings or a psychological comfort; it rests on a historical event. If Christ has not been raised, the cross is only a tragedy and our sins have not been taken away.

3. Most to be pitied. "If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are of all people most to be pitied" (1 Corinthians 15:19). This is honest: if believers suffer, give up and sacrifice for the Lord, and there is nothing after death, they have truly suffered for nothing. Christian hope has never been merely "a better life now."

The point: The Christian faith rests on the historical event of the resurrection. If Christ has not been raised, we are still in our sins; but he has been raised, and everything has changed.
Going Deeper: 15:20–28 The Firstfruits

1. "But in fact Christ has been raised." "But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). The "firstfruits" were the first sheaf of the harvest offered to God (Lev 23:10–11), the guarantee that the whole harvest would follow. Christ's resurrection is not an isolated miracle but a guarantee: all who belong to him will also be raised.

2. Adam and Christ. "For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:21–22; cf. Rom 5:12–21). This does not mean everyone will be saved, for verse 23 goes on: "then at his coming those who belong to Christ." All who are in Adam die because they are united to Adam; all who are in Christ live because they are united to Christ. Elsewhere Scripture says that all will be raised, some to life and some to judgment (John 5:28–29); "made alive" in Christ here means resurrection to life.

3. The last enemy. "For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:25–26; cf. Ps 110:1; Ps 8:6). We still face death today, and death is still an enemy, not a friend; but it is an enemy already doomed to destruction.

4. "The Son himself will also be subjected." "When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:28). This verse does not mean that the Son is lesser in nature than the Father, or that the Son's kingdom will end ("of his kingdom there will be no end," Luke 1:33). Many interpreters (so Augustine and Calvin) take it to refer to the Son, as the incarnate Mediator, handing over the kingdom to the Father once the work of redemption is complete, so that the triune God receives all the glory (cf. the note in chapter 11 on "the head of Christ is God"); in the new creation the throne is still "the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Rev 22:3). The Son is of one being with the Father, equal in power and glory.

The point: Christ's resurrection is the firstfruits, guaranteeing that all who belong to him will be raised. Death is still an enemy, but an enemy already doomed.
Going Deeper: 15:29–34 Why Face Danger Every Hour?

1. Baptized on behalf of the dead. "Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf?" (1 Corinthians 15:29). This is among the hardest verses in the New Testament, with dozens of proposed explanations. The main ones are:

  • Some (e.g. Gordon Fee) think some in Corinth were being baptized in place of people who had died, and that Paul mentions the practice only to show that even they believed in resurrection, without approving it.
  • Some (e.g. Anthony Thiselton) think people came to faith and were baptized because of believers who had died (for example, a relative's testimony on their deathbed), hoping to be reunited with them.
  • Some older interpreters hold that "the dead" refers to the baptized person's own mortal body: baptism acknowledges that one will die and hopes for resurrection.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints draws on this verse to perform baptisms on behalf of the dead, holding that the deceased may accept or reject the proxy ordinance. But Scripture nowhere commands this, and it teaches plainly that "it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment" (Heb 9:27); each person must personally trust in Christ in this life. Chinese families often hold rites to help the dead (超度, the seventh-day rites, burning paper money), as if the living could still do something for them. The gospel says that a person's standing before God does not depend on rites performed by descendants; Christ's work on the cross is "finished" (John 19:30). This lets believers who are pressed to join these rites decline in peace.

2. Dying every day. "Why am I in danger every hour?... I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'" (1 Corinthians 15:30–32, quoting Isa 22:13). "Fought with beasts" may be a figure for fierce opponents in Ephesus (cf. 1 Corinthians 16:9; Acts 19); others take it as a literal experience. Paul's point is that without resurrection his suffering for the gospel would be meaningless, and he might as well live for pleasure.

3. Bad company. "Do not be deceived: 'Bad company ruins good morals'" (1 Corinthians 15:33). These words come from the Greek comic poet Menander and had become a proverb. In context this means keeping company with those who deny the resurrection. Wrong teaching leads to wrong living.

The point: The hope of resurrection gives believers' suffering its meaning. Without resurrection, all that is left is "eat and drink"; but because there is resurrection, suffering for the Lord is not in vain.
Going Deeper: 15:35–49 The Resurrection Body

1. The seed. "But someone will ask, 'How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?' You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel... But God gives it a body as he has chosen" (1 Corinthians 15:35–38). The seed and the plant are the same life in very different forms. So it is with the resurrection body: there is continuity (it is the same person) and transformation (an entirely new kind of body).

2. Four contrasts. "What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). A "spiritual body" does not mean a bodiless soul, but a body wholly governed by the Holy Spirit and filled with his life (cf. Rom 8:11). The risen Lord could be touched and could eat (Luke 24:39–43), and our future bodies will be like "his glorious body" (Phil 3:21).

3. Not merely the soul set free, not reincarnation. Believers who die are at once with the Lord (Phil 1:23; 2 Cor 5:8), but that is not yet the final hope; the final hope is the resurrection of the body. The hope of Scripture is not the Greek idea of the soul escaping the body, nor the cycle of rebirth in Buddhism and the transmigration of souls in folk religion. Reincarnation means returning again and again to this world of suffering; and reincarnation runs on karma, the next life depending on the merit one has stored up, whereas resurrection is not earned by merit; it is God who "gives us the victory" (1 Corinthians 15:57), bringing the same person, with a transformed body, into a new heavens and new earth where death will be no more.

4. Two Adams. "'The first man Adam became a living being'; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit... Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven" (1 Corinthians 15:45–49). From Adam we received mortal bodies; from Christ we will receive resurrection bodies.

The point: The resurrection body is the same person, yet wholly transformed: imperishable, glorious, powerful, filled with the Spirit, like Christ's glorious body.
Going Deeper: 15:50–58 Death Swallowed Up in Victory

1. All changed. "Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet" (1 Corinthians 15:51–52; cf. 1 Thess 4:16). When the Lord returns, believers who have died will be raised, and believers still living will be changed. "Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God" (1 Corinthians 15:50) refers to our present perishable, mortal state ("nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable"), not to bodily existence as such.

2. O death, where is your sting? "Then shall come to pass the saying that is written: 'Death is swallowed up in victory.' 'O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?' The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law" (1 Corinthians 15:54–56, quoting Isa 25:8; Hos 13:14). Death is terrible because of sin; sin has power because the law exposes and even provokes sin (Rom 7:8–11) and condemns us (Gal 3:10). But Christ has borne our sin and satisfied the law's demands, "becoming a curse for us" (Gal 3:13), so death's sting has been drawn.

3. Thanks be to God. "But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 15:57). The victory is not something we win; God "gives us the victory."

4. Not in vain. "Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58). The hope of resurrection doesn't make us escape reality; it makes us serve more steadfastly now. Because of the resurrection, every small thing done for the Lord today counts.

5. When a loved one dies. Chinese funerals express deep filial love and grief, and often carry fear of death, many taboos and rites of offering. Believers do not offer incense, bow in the rite or burn paper money, but can honor the departed and comfort the family by keeping vigil with them, a memorial service, flowers, hymns and testimony (cf. chapters 8 and 10; and if we once went along under pressure, the Lord's grace is greater than our weakness). Believers may weep; Jesus too "wept" at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35); but we do not grieve "as others do who have no hope" (1 Thess 4:13). As for relatives who died without coming to faith, Scripture is clear that salvation is in Christ alone (Acts 4:12); but we do not know how things stood between each person and God at the end, and judging them is not ours to do. We can entrust them to "the Judge of all the earth," who will do what is just, and who is the merciful God we have come to know in Jesus Christ (Gen 18:25; Ps 145:9). If I blame myself for never speaking, or speaking too late, I can bring that regret to the Lord too. What we can do today, while it is still today, is gently walk alongside the family who remain and tell them of this resurrection hope. If you have not yet trusted the risen Lord yourself, you can confess your sins to him and entrust yourself to him today.

The point: Christ has conquered death, and its sting has been drawn. So we can weep with hope, and serve the Lord steadfast and immovable.
Meditation

Reflect: "If Christ has not been raised... then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished." If Paul had stopped at verse 19, my hope would stop there too. I think of someone I loved who has fallen asleep in the Lord: perhaps a grandmother, a father, a friend. I remember the funeral hall, the weeping when the coffin was closed, the empty place at home afterward. Is my grief still stuck at verse 19: they are gone, I have only memories, and we are "of all people most to be pitied"? Perhaps my tears hold not only longing but regret: words I never said, visits I kept putting off, a quarrel never mended. Paul says, "The sting of death is sin" (1 Corinthians 15:56); but Christ has taken that sting for me, and I can bring my regrets to his cross too; his blood was shed for these sins as well. Then Paul writes one word, "But": "But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). That "but" does not rest on my feelings; it rests on an empty tomb, on the one whom Cephas, James and more than five hundred brothers saw with their own eyes. He is risen, so the one who fell asleep in him will rise too, and we will meet again before the Lord, with imperishable and glorious bodies; and, best of all, together we will see with our own eyes the Lord who died and rose for us. If the one I am thinking of is someone I do not know came to faith, I entrust them too into the hands of the Lord who is just and merciful. Today I may still weep, and that is not a lack of faith; Jesus wept too. But through my tears I can say with Paul: "Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ."

verse_parts.text: 凡你们所做的都要凭爱心而做。

entries.verse_text: 凡你们所做的都要凭爱心而做。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十六章是全书的结尾，看起来只是一些实际的安排和问安，却处处显出福音带来的新关系。这一章分四段。为圣徒捐钱（1-4节）：每逢七日的第一日，各人照自己的进项抽出来留着，由众人举荐的人送到耶路撒冷。保罗和同工的行程（5-12节）：保罗要住在以弗所，因为「有宽大又有功效的门」为他开了；提摩太要来，亚波罗暂时不来。最后的劝勉（13-18节）：「你们务要警醒，在真道上站立得稳，要作大丈夫，要刚强。凡你们所做的都要凭爱心而做。」又要敬重司提反一家这样服事圣徒的人。问安与祝福（19-24节）：「若有人不爱主，这人可诅可咒。主必要来！」最后以恩典和爱作结。

这一章的中心是第14节。一封充满责备的信，最后落在「爱」字上：保罗不是要赢得辩论，而是要哥林多人在基督里彼此相爱，等候主再来。这封信以恩典开头（林前1:3-4），也以恩典结束（林前16:23）。

深读 16:1-4 为圣徒捐钱

1. 为耶路撒冷的穷人。 「论到为圣徒捐钱，我从前怎样吩咐加拉太的众教会，你们也当怎样行。」（林前16:1）这笔捐项是为「耶路撒冷圣徒中的穷人」（罗15:26；参林后8-9章）。外邦教会为犹太信徒捐钱，不只是救济，更是表明犹太人和外邦人在基督里是一家。

2. 有计划、按比例。 「每逢七日的第一日，各人要照自己的进项抽出来留着，免得我来的时候现凑。」（林前16:2）这里有几个原则：

  • 定期：「每逢七日的第一日」。「留着」可能是指在自己家里存起来；但保罗特别指定这一天，也可能表示早期教会已经在这一天（主复活的日子）聚会（参徒20:7）。
  • 人人有分：「各人」都要参与，不只是有钱的人。
  • 按比例：「照自己的进项」，收入多的多给，收入少的少给（参林后8:12）。
  • 有计划：平时就预备，不是临时被情绪推动。

3. 透明与问责。 「及至我来到了，你们写信举荐谁，我就打发他们，把你们的捐资送到耶路撒冷去。」（林前16:3）保罗不独自经手这笔钱，而是让教会举荐的人一同送去，「免得有人……挑我们的不是。我们留心行光明的事，不但在主面前，就在人面前也是这样」（林后8:20-21）。今天的教会处理奉献，也要公开、有多人负责、经得起查账，不要碍于情面，让一个人独自管钱、没有人敢查账。这不是不信任同工，而是保护同工，也保护教会的见证；若发现问题，也不可为了面子而遮掩。

4. 这不是成功神学。 保罗从来没有说，奉献是一种投资，给得越多，神就会让你越富有。奉献的动力是恩典：「他本来富足，却为你们成了贫穷，叫你们因他的贫穷，可以成为富足」（林后8:9）；奉献的态度是甘心，「捐得乐意的人是神所喜爱的」（林后9:7）。马其顿的教会「在极穷之间」仍然乐捐（林后8:2）；神看重的不是数目，而是被恩典感动的心。所以，教会不可用公布名单或比较数目给人压力，收入少的弟兄姊妹也不必因奉献得少而羞愧。

要点：奉献是对基督恩典的回应：定期、按比例、有计划，也要公开透明，在主面前、在人面前都光明正大。
深读 16:5-12 保罗和同工

1. 「主若许我」。 「我如今不愿意路过见你们；主若许我，我就指望和你们同住几时。」（林前16:7）保罗有计划，却把计划交在主手里（参雅4:15）。后来他的行程果然有所改变（参林后1:15-17）。

2. 宽大的门，也有许多反对的人。 「但我要仍旧住在以弗所，直等到五旬节；因为有宽大又有功效的门为我开了，并且反对的人也多。」（林前16:8-9）开了的门和反对的人同时存在（参徒19章）。保罗没有因为反对的人多，就认为门没有开。

3. 提摩太。 「若是提摩太来到，你们要留心，叫他在你们那里无所惧怕；因为他劳力做主的工，像我一样。所以，无论谁都不可藐视他。」（林前16:10-11）提摩太年轻，也可能比较胆怯（参提前4:12；提后1:7）。保罗请一个骄傲的教会，好好接待一位年轻的同工。华人教会常常论资排辈，年轻传道人也容易被轻看。

4. 亚波罗。 「至于兄弟亚波罗，我再三地劝他同弟兄们到你们那里去；但这时他决不愿意去，几时有了机会他必去。」（林前16:12）哥林多教会中有人说「我是属亚波罗的」（林前1:12），可是保罗称他为「兄弟」，还再三劝他去。保罗和亚波罗之间没有竞争（参林前3:5-9）；亚波罗也有自己的判断，保罗尊重他（原文没有说是谁的意愿，所以也有人理解为神的旨意）。

要点：福音的同工不是彼此竞争的对手，而是一同在主手中、按主的时间服事的弟兄。
深读 16:13-18 凡事凭爱心

1. 四个命令。 「你们务要警醒，在真道上站立得稳，要作大丈夫，要刚强。」（林前16:13）「要作大丈夫」原文的意思是要勇敢、要有担当。这句话不是只对弟兄说的，姊妹也同样要在真道上刚强。

2. 凭爱心而做。 「凡你们所做的都要凭爱心而做。」（林前16:14）前一节的四个命令，可能让人变得刚硬；这一节却说，一切都要凭爱心。有刚强没有爱，就变成好斗；有爱心没有真道，就变成软弱。第十三章所说的爱，在这里成了全书最后的命令。

3. 司提反一家。 「你们晓得司提反一家，是亚该亚初结的果子，并且他们专以服事圣徒为念。我劝你们顺服这样的人，并一切同工同劳的人。」（林前16:15-16）司提反一家是保罗亲自施洗的（林前1:16）。他们得到尊重，不是因为口才或地位，而是因为「专以服事圣徒为念」。「顺服」这样的人，是指尊重、跟随那些忠心服事的人，不是盲目服从，更不是给任何人辖制别人的权柄。若有带领的人滥用属灵权柄、欺压或伤害人，信徒不必顺服。受害的人不必留在危险之中，也不必勉强与不安全的人和好；任何人都可以、也应当向警方举报犯罪（罗13:4）。即使施害的人认罪悔改、得蒙饶恕，也不表示他可以恢复职分，或再接近受害人和孩子。教会不可为了「家丑不可外扬」而遮掩，反要保护受害人、公正地处理（参第五章、第六章和第十一章的说明）。

4. 叫我心里快活。 「他们叫我和你们心里都快活。这样的人，你们务要敬重。」（林前16:18）教会中那些默默服事、使别人「心里都快活」的人，我们应当看见他们、感谢他们。

要点：在真道上站立得稳，与凭爱心而做，是同一个呼召，因为我们所跟随的基督，是「充充满满地有恩典有真理」的那一位（约1:14）。教会要敬重那些默默服事圣徒的人。
深读 16:19-24 主必要来！

1. 家里的教会。 「亚居拉和百基拉并在他们家里的教会，因主多多地问你们安。」（林前16:19）亚居拉和百基拉曾在哥林多与保罗一同制造帐棚（徒18:2-3），现在在以弗所，他们的家就是教会聚会的地方。今天许多华人教会，也是从一个家庭查经开始的。

2. 圣洁的亲嘴问安。 「你们要亲嘴问安，彼此务要圣洁。」（林前16:20）这是当时家人和亲友之间问安的方式；今天在华人教会，可能是握手、拥抱或一句真诚的问候。重点是：信徒彼此是一家人。

3. 亲笔问安。 「我－保罗亲笔问安。」（林前16:21）保罗常请人代笔，最后亲手写几句，表明这封信是他写的（参罗16:22；加6:11；帖后3:17）。

4. 「主必要来！」 「若有人不爱主，这人可诅可咒。主必要来！」（林前16:22）「可诅可咒」原文是 anathema，是很重的话：拒绝爱主的人，是在神的审判之下。这是严肃的警告，不是许可信徒去咒诅人，而且紧接着就是「主必要来」和恩典（林前16:23）。这里说的是拒绝主的人，不是爱主却还软弱、挣扎的信徒；我们爱他，是因为他先爱我们（约一4:19）。这句话也在问每一个读者：我爱主吗？趁主还没有再来，不爱主的人今天仍可以回转，投靠这位赐恩典的主。

「主必要来」原文是一句亚兰话。可以分成 maran atha，意思是我们的主已经来了，或必要来，和合本就是这样理解；也可以分成 marana tha，意思是我们的主啊，请来，许多现代译本这样理解。两种读法都可能。《十二使徒遗训》第十章记载，早期一些教会在圣餐中用这句祷告；启22:20也说「主耶稣啊，我愿你来！」。保罗在说希腊话的教会里保留这句亚兰话，说明最早说亚兰话的犹太信徒已经称耶稣为「主」。若这是一句祷告，他们也已经在向他祷告。

5. 恩典与爱。 「愿主耶稣基督的恩常与你们众人同在！我在基督耶稣里的爱与你们众人同在。阿们！」（林前16:23-24）这封信责备了分门结党、淫乱、诉讼、骄傲、守主的晚餐时各顾各，最后的一句话却是：我的爱与你们「众人」同在。保罗爱这个让他头痛的教会，因为基督先爱了他们。

要点：全书以恩典和爱作结，也以盼望作结：「主必要来！」我们今天在爱中等候他。
默想

默想： 「主必要来！」读完哥林多前书，我好像看见了一个和我的教会很像的教会：有分门结党，有骄傲，有淫乱的事，有为钱打官司，有在聚会中各顾各的，也有对复活的怀疑。保罗没有放弃他们，最后的一句话是：「我在基督耶稣里的爱与你们众人同在。」我也可以回想这十六章：哪一章最像在说我？是第一章那句「我是属保罗的」，第八章那种自以为有知识的骄傲，第十一章那位独自吃饭、我却从没留意的弟兄，还是第十三章那段我几乎读不下去的爱？这些都不是要把我推开，而是要把我带回十字架前，带到那位「为我们的罪死了，而且埋葬了」、「第三天复活了」的主面前（林前15:3-4）。保罗在信的开头，就称这群问题重重的人为「蒙召作圣徒的」（林前1:2），并且应许：「他也必坚固你们到底，叫你们在我们主耶稣基督的日子无可责备。神是信实的」（林前1:8-9）。所以，「主必要来」对我不是威吓，而是盼望：那位要来的，正是为我死的那一位。今天读完这卷书，我不急着给自己定什么新计划，只想用早期教会的祷告来结束：

主耶稣啊，谢谢你，在我最像哥林多人的时候，你仍然爱我，为我舍了自己。我愿你来。在你再来以前，求你使我在真道上站立得稳，叫我凡事都凭爱心而行。愿你的恩常与我们众人同在。阿们。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 16 closes the letter. It looks like nothing more than practical arrangements and greetings, yet everywhere it shows the new relationships the gospel creates. It has four parts. The collection for the saints (vv. 1–4): on the first day of every week, each puts something aside as he may prosper, to be carried to Jerusalem by people the church approves. Plans for Paul and his co-workers (vv. 5–12): Paul will stay in Ephesus, because "a wide door for effective work has opened"; Timothy will come, and Apollos will not come yet. Final exhortations (vv. 13–18): "Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love." And honor people like the household of Stephanas who serve the saints. Greetings and blessing (vv. 19–24): "If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!" The letter ends with grace and love.

The center of the chapter is verse 14. A letter full of rebuke ends on the word "love": Paul is not trying to win an argument, but to see the Corinthians love one another in Christ as they wait for the Lord's return. The letter that opened with grace (1 Corinthians 1:3–4) closes with grace (1 Corinthians 16:23).

Going Deeper: 16:1–4 The Collection for the Saints

1. For the poor in Jerusalem. "Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do" (1 Corinthians 16:1). This collection was "for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem" (Rom 15:26; cf. 2 Cor 8–9). Gentile churches giving for Jewish believers was not only relief; it showed that Jews and Gentiles are one family in Christ.

2. Planned and proportionate. "On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come" (1 Corinthians 16:2). Several principles appear here:

  • Regular: "on the first day of every week." The money was probably set aside at home ("store it up"), but the singling out of this day also suggests the early church was already gathering on it, the day of the Lord's resurrection (cf. Acts 20:7).
  • Everyone takes part: "each of you," not only the wealthy.
  • Proportionate: "as he may prosper"; those who earn more give more, those who earn less give less (cf. 2 Cor 8:12).
  • Planned: prepared beforehand, not moved by emotion on the spot.

3. Transparency and accountability. "And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem" (1 Corinthians 16:3). Paul does not handle the money alone; people the church accredits carry it together, "so that no one should blame us about this generous gift... for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord's sight but also in the sight of man" (2 Cor 8:20–21). Churches today should handle giving openly too, with several people responsible and books that can bear an audit, not leaving, out of deference, one person handling money no one dares to audit. This is not distrust of those who serve but protection for them and for the church's witness; and if problems are found, they must not be hidden to save face.

4. Not prosperity teaching. Paul never says giving is an investment, so that the more you give, the richer God will make you. The motive for giving is grace: "though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor 8:9); and the attitude is gladness, for "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Cor 9:7). The Macedonian churches gave joyfully "in their extreme poverty" (2 Cor 8:2); God looks not at the amount but at a heart moved by grace. So churches should not pressure people by publishing names or comparing amounts, and those with little need not be ashamed of a small gift.

The point: Giving is a response to Christ's grace: regular, proportionate and planned, and handled openly, so that it is honorable before the Lord and before people.
Going Deeper: 16:5–12 Paul and His Co-workers

1. "If the Lord permits." "For I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits" (1 Corinthians 16:7). Paul makes plans but holds them in the Lord's hand (cf. Jas 4:15). His plans did in fact change later (cf. 2 Cor 1:15–17).

2. A wide door, and many adversaries. "But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries" (1 Corinthians 16:8–9). The open door and the many adversaries exist side by side (cf. Acts 19). Paul did not conclude from the opposition that the door was closed.

3. Timothy. "When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am" (1 Corinthians 16:10), and no one is to despise him (1 Corinthians 16:11). Timothy was young and perhaps timid (cf. 1 Tim 4:12; 2 Tim 1:7). Paul asks a proud church to receive a young co-worker well. Chinese churches often rank people by seniority, and young pastors are easily looked down on.

4. Apollos. "Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity" (1 Corinthians 16:12). Some in Corinth said "I follow Apollos" (1 Corinthians 1:12), yet Paul calls him "brother" and urged him to go. There was no rivalry between Paul and Apollos (cf. 1 Corinthians 3:5–9), and Apollos had his own judgment, which Paul respected (some take "will" here as God's will).

The point: Gospel co-workers are not rivals but brothers, serving together in the Lord's hands and on the Lord's timetable.
Going Deeper: 16:13–18 All in Love

1. Four commands. "Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong" (1 Corinthians 16:13). "Act like men" means be courageous and take responsibility; it is not addressed only to brothers, for sisters too are to be strong in the faith.

2. Done in love. "Let all that you do be done in love" (1 Corinthians 16:14). The four commands before it could make people hard; this verse says that everything is to be done in love. Strength without love becomes combativeness; love without the truth becomes weakness. The love of chapter 13 becomes the letter's final command.

3. The household of Stephanas. "You know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints, be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer" (1 Corinthians 16:15–16). Paul himself baptized the household of Stephanas (1 Corinthians 1:16). They are honored not for eloquence or status, but because they "devoted themselves to the service of the saints." To "be subject to" such people means respecting and following those who serve faithfully; it is not blind obedience, still less authority for anyone to dominate others. Where a leader abuses spiritual authority or harms people, believers owe no such submission. Victims need not remain in danger or reconcile with someone unsafe, and anyone may, and should, report crimes to the police (Rom 13:4). Even if the offender repents and is forgiven, that does not restore his office or give him access to victims or children. The church must not cover it up to save face; it must protect victims and deal with the matter justly (cf. the notes in chapters 5, 6 and 11).

4. They refreshed my spirit. "For they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such men" (1 Corinthians 16:18). Those in the church who serve quietly and refresh others' spirits should be noticed and thanked.

The point: Standing firm in the faith and doing everything in love are one calling, because the Christ we follow is "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). The church should honor those who quietly serve the saints.
Going Deeper: 16:19–24 Our Lord, Come!

1. The church in their house. "Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 16:19). Aquila and Priscilla had made tents with Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:2–3); now in Ephesus their home is where the church meets. Many Chinese churches today also began as a Bible study in someone's home.

2. A holy kiss. "Greet one another with a holy kiss" (1 Corinthians 16:20). This was how family and close friends greeted one another then; in Chinese churches today it may be a handshake, a hug or a heartfelt word. The point is that believers are family.

3. In his own hand. "I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand" (1 Corinthians 16:21). Paul often dictated his letters and added a few lines in his own hand at the end to show the letter was his (cf. Rom 16:22; Gal 6:11; 2 Thess 3:17).

4. "Our Lord, come!" "If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!" (1 Corinthians 16:22). "Accursed" translates anathema, a very strong word: whoever refuses to love the Lord stands under God's judgment. This is a solemn warning, not permission for believers to curse people, and it leads straight into "Our Lord, come!" and grace (1 Corinthians 16:23). It speaks of those who reject the Lord, not of believers whose love is real but weak and struggling; we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). It also asks every reader: do I love the Lord? Before he comes, anyone who does not love him may still turn to him today and receive his grace.

The Aramaic can be divided maran atha, "our Lord has come / is coming" (the CUV's reading), or marana tha, "Our Lord, come!" (the ESV and many modern versions). Both are possible. The Didache (chapter 10) shows some early churches using it as a prayer at the Lord's Supper, and Rev 22:20 prays "Come, Lord Jesus!" Either way, that Paul keeps the Aramaic in a Greek-speaking church shows the earliest Aramaic-speaking Jewish believers already called Jesus "our Lord"; on the prayer reading, they were praying to him.

5. Grace and love. "The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen" (1 Corinthians 16:23–24). This letter has rebuked divisions, sexual immorality, lawsuits, pride and selfishness at the Lord's Supper; yet its last sentence is: my love be with you "all." Paul loves this church that has given him so much grief, because Christ loved them first.

The point: The letter ends with grace and love, and with hope: "Our Lord, come!" Today we wait for him in love.
Meditation

Reflect: "Our Lord, come!" Having read 1 Corinthians, I seem to see a church much like my own: divisions, pride, sexual immorality, lawsuits over money, people looking after themselves at the gathering, even doubts about the resurrection. Paul did not give up on them; his last sentence is, "My love be with you all in Christ Jesus." I can look back over these sixteen chapters too: which one sounds most like me? The "I follow Paul" of chapter 1, the pride of "knowledge" in chapter 8, the brother in chapter 11 who eats alone and whom I never noticed, or the love in chapter 13 that I could hardly bring myself to read? None of these is meant to push me away; they are meant to bring me back to the cross, to the Lord who "died for our sins... was buried... was raised on the third day" (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). At the start of the letter Paul called these troubled people "saints" (1 Corinthians 1:2), and promised that God "will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful" (1 Corinthians 1:8–9). So "Our Lord, come!" is not a threat to me but a hope: the one who is coming is the one who died for me. Today, having finished this book, I am in no hurry to make myself a new plan; I want only to end with the early church's prayer:

Lord Jesus, thank you that when I was most like the Corinthians, you still loved me and gave yourself for me. Come, Lord Jesus. Until you come again, make me stand firm in the faith, and let all that I do be done in love. May your grace be with us all. Amen.

entries.content:
这卷书在讲什么

哥林多后书是保罗书信中最个人、最坦白的一封。在这封信里，保罗不只是教导，也把自己的心掏出来给哥林多人看：他在亚细亚「甚至连活命的指望都绝了」（林后1:8）；他「多多地流泪」写信（林后2:4）；他在特罗亚因为找不到提多，「心里不安」（林后2:13）；他到了马其顿，「外有争战，内有惧怕」（林后7:5）；他身上还有「一根刺」，三次求主叫它离开，主却没有挪去（林后12:7-8）。

为什么一位使徒要这样讲自己的软弱？因为哥林多教会里来了一些人，他们看不起保罗：说他「气貌不扬，言语粗俗」（林后10:10），说他反复不定（林后1:17），说他没有像样的荐信（林后3:1）。这些人自称是使徒，夸口自己的出身、口才和属灵经历。保罗的回答出人意料：他不去证明自己比他们更强，反而夸自己的软弱，因为主对他说：「我的恩典够你用的，因为我的能力是在人的软弱上显得完全。」（林后12:9）

所以，这卷书的中心不是保罗，而是钉十字架又复活的基督：「他因软弱被钉在十字架上，却因神的大能仍然活着。」（林后13:4）基督为我们的罪受苦，然后进入荣耀；我们与他联合，跟从他、服事他，也走同样先受苦、后得荣耀的路。

作者与写作背景

1. 作者。 「奉神旨意作基督耶稣使徒的保罗和兄弟提摩太」（林后1:1）。保罗是这封信的作者，这一点几乎没有人怀疑。

2. 保罗和哥林多教会的往来。 根据两封哥林多书信和使徒行传，许多学者把事情的经过大致整理如下：

  • 保罗建立哥林多教会，在那里住了一年半（徒18:1-18）。
  • 他写了一封信，现在已经失传（林前5:9）。
  • 他从以弗所写了哥林多前书（林前16:8）。
  • 他又去了一趟哥林多，那是一次痛苦的探访（林后2:1；参林后12:14；林后13:1-2「第三次」）。很可能就在那次，有人当众顶撞、伤害了他（林后2:5；林后7:12）。
  • 回到以弗所后，他「多多地流泪」写了一封严厉的信（林后2:3-4；林后7:8），并且差提多送去。
  • 他离开以弗所，到特罗亚等提多，没有等到，就往马其顿去（林后2:12-13；参徒20:1）。
  • 在马其顿，提多终于来了，带来好消息：多数哥林多人已经悔改，重新接纳保罗（林后7:6-16）。
  • 保罗于是写了哥林多后书，大约在主后55-56年。

那封流泪写的信是哪一封，学者有不同的看法。较早的解经家多认为就是哥林多前书；今天多数学者认为是另一封已经失传的信；也有人认为它保存在哥林多后书10–13章里。

3. 「最大的使徒」。 保罗在信中两次讽刺地称对手为「那些最大的使徒」（林后11:5；林后12:11），又直接说他们是「假使徒」（林后11:13）。他们是犹太人出身、自称是基督仆人的教师（林后11:22-23），却「另传一个耶稣」（林后11:4）。他们带着荐信而来（林后3:1），以口才和异象自夸（林后10:10；林后11:6；林后12:1），并且向教会要钱，甚至欺压人（林后11:20）。有学者（如恩斯特·凯斯曼、查尔斯·巴瑞特）认为「最大的使徒」是指耶路撒冷的使徒，与林后11:13的「假使徒」不同；但多数学者（如维克多·弗尼什、默里·哈里斯）认为，这两个称呼指的是同一群人：林后11:5紧接在林后11:4讲「另传一个耶稣」的人之后，林后11:13-15也还在同一段论证里。

4. 这卷书是一封信，还是几封信合成的？ 1–9章的语气大致是和好与安慰，10–13章却忽然变得严厉。有些学者（如巴瑞特、弗尼什）认为10–13章是保罗后来另写的一封信；也有学者（如较早的阿道夫·豪斯拉特、詹姆斯·肯尼迪）认为10–13章就是那封流泪写的信。还有更复杂的分割理论，例如把林后2:14–7:4或8、9两章看作另外的书信。另一些学者（如保罗·巴尼特、大卫·加兰、哈里斯）认为全书是一封信：保罗可能分几次写成，中间又听到新的消息；或者1–9章主要是对已经悔改的多数人说的，10–13章是对仍被假使徒影响的人说的。现存的所有古抄本，都把哥林多后书当作一封完整的信。无论采取哪一种看法，这卷书都是神所默示的话，信息是一致的。

钥匙经文：4:7

1. 「这宝贝」。 上一节说：「那吩咐光从黑暗里照出来的神，已经照在我们心里，叫我们得知神荣耀的光显在耶稣基督的面上。」（林后4:6）宝贝就是福音，就是神显在基督面上的荣耀。

2. 「放在瓦器里」。 瓦器是当时最便宜、最容易破的器皿，常用来装油、装水，甚至用来收藏贵重的东西（参耶32:14，地契就是放在瓦器里保存的）。保罗说，神把最宝贵的福音，放在最普通、最脆弱的人身上。

3. 「要显明这莫大的能力是出于神，不是出于我们」。 神这样做是有意的。如果器皿本身华丽坚固，人就会去欣赏器皿；正因为器皿只是粗陋易碎的瓦器，人才看得出能力不是出于器皿，而是出于神。

全书结构

哥林多后书可以大致分成五个部分：

  • 患难中的安慰与行程的改变（林后1:1–2:13）：「愿颂赞归与……赐各样安慰的神」；保罗解释他为什么没有按原来的计划去哥林多。
  • 新约职事的荣耀与软弱（林后2:14–7:4）：这是全书最长、神学最丰富的一段，讲新约的荣耀（3章）、瓦器里的宝贝（4章）、复活的盼望（林后5:1-10）、劝人与神和好的职分（林后5:11-21），以及保罗向哥林多人敞开的心（林后6:1–7:4）。
  • 提多带来的好消息（林后7:5-16）：哥林多人「依着神的意思忧愁」，生出了悔改。
  • 为耶路撒冷圣徒的捐献（8–9章）：「他本来富足，却为你们成了贫穷」（林后8:9）。
  • 对假使徒的回应（10–13章）：保罗「像愚妄人」自夸（林后11:17），夸的却是他的软弱；第三次去哥林多之前的最后警告；以三一神的祝福结束（林后13:14）。
怎样读这卷书

1. 留意「软弱」和「能力」。 这一对词贯穿全书。神的能力不是绕过软弱，而是在软弱中显明出来（林后4:7；林后12:9-10；林后13:4）。

2. 留意「安慰」和「患难」。 在林后1:3-7这五节经文里，「安慰」这个词（包括名词和动词）在原文中出现了十次。保罗不是在顺境中学会安慰别人，而是在患难中先被神安慰。

3. 留意保罗怎样衡量一个人的服事。 假使徒看重荐信、口才、外表和成就；保罗看重的是心中有没有基督、生命有没有被改变、是不是像基督一样为人舍己。今天许多教会用人数、名气、规模和网络影响力来衡量服事，保罗的话是很有分量的提醒。这也问到我们自己：我暗暗用什么来衡量自己和别人？

默想

默想： 「我们有这宝贝放在瓦器里，要显明这莫大的能力是出于神，不是出于我们。」（林后4:7）我们很容易只把自己好的一面给人看：在教会里总是说「感谢主，一切都好」，在朋友圈里只放笑脸、成绩和旅行的照片，在家人面前不敢承认自己失败了。这背后常常是怕丢面子，也是想靠自己的形象站立得住。保罗却把自己的眼泪、惧怕和那根拿不掉的刺，都写在信里给人看。他不是在诉苦，而是要人看见：撑着他的，不是他自己。我们的主耶稣也没有保全自己的体面，他「因软弱被钉在十字架上」，为我这个常常要面子的人赤身受了羞辱；他「却因神的大能仍然活着」（林后13:4）。因为他已经替我担当了我的罪和我的羞辱，我就不必再靠一个完美的形象活着。在开始读哥林多后书的时候，我能不能把一件一直不敢让人知道的软弱带到神面前，不是求他先替我把它藏好、补好，而是求他就在这裂缝里显出他的能力，叫人看见的是他，不是我？我这瓦器有裂缝，主的恩典却够我用。
entries.content_en:
What This Book Is About

2 Corinthians is the most personal and candid of Paul's letters. Here Paul does more than teach. He opens his heart to the Corinthians: in Asia "we despaired of life itself" (2 Corinthians 1:8); he wrote to them "with many tears" (2 Corinthians 2:4); in Troas "my spirit was not at rest" because he could not find Titus (2 Corinthians 2:13); in Macedonia there was "fighting without and fear within" (2 Corinthians 7:5); and he carried "a thorn... in the flesh," which he asked the Lord three times to remove, and the Lord did not take it away (2 Corinthians 12:7–8).

Why would an apostle speak this way about his weakness? Because some people had come into the Corinthian church who looked down on Paul. They said his "bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account" (2 Corinthians 10:10), that he wavered (2 Corinthians 1:17), that he had no proper letters of recommendation (2 Corinthians 3:1). They called themselves apostles and boasted of their background, eloquence and spiritual experiences. Paul's answer is surprising. He does not try to prove he is stronger than they are. He boasts of his weaknesses, because the Lord said to him, "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9).

So the center of this book is not Paul but Christ crucified and risen: "he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God" (2 Corinthians 13:4). Christ suffered for our sins and then entered glory; united to him, those who follow and serve him walk the same road, suffering first and glory after.

Author and Setting

1. Author. "Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother" (2 Corinthians 1:1). Paul's authorship is almost universally accepted.

2. Paul's dealings with the Corinthian church. From the two Corinthian letters and Acts, many scholars piece the story together roughly like this:

  • Paul founded the church and stayed a year and a half (Acts 18:1–18).
  • He wrote a letter that has not survived (1 Cor 5:9).
  • He wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (1 Cor 16:8).
  • He made a visit to Corinth that was painful (2 Corinthians 2:1; cf. 2 Corinthians 12:14; 2 Corinthians 13:1–2, "the third time"). Probably on that visit someone publicly opposed and wounded him (2 Corinthians 2:5; 2 Corinthians 7:12).
  • Back in Ephesus, he wrote a severe letter "with many tears" (2 Corinthians 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 7:8) and sent Titus with it.
  • He left Ephesus and waited for Titus at Troas. When Titus did not come, he went on to Macedonia (2 Corinthians 2:12–13; cf. Acts 20:1).
  • In Macedonia Titus finally arrived with good news: most of the Corinthians had repented and welcomed Paul again (2 Corinthians 7:6–16).
  • Paul then wrote 2 Corinthians, around AD 55–56.

Scholars differ on which letter was the "tearful letter." Older interpreters mostly took it to be 1 Corinthians. Most scholars today think it was another letter that has been lost. Some think it is preserved in 2 Corinthians 10–13.

3. The "super-apostles." Twice Paul ironically calls his opponents "these super-apostles" (2 Corinthians 11:5; 2 Corinthians 12:11), and he calls them plainly "false apostles" (2 Corinthians 11:13). They were Jewish teachers (2 Corinthians 11:22) who claimed to be servants of Christ (2 Corinthians 11:23) but preached "another Jesus" (2 Corinthians 11:4). They came with letters of recommendation (2 Corinthians 3:1), boasted of eloquence and visions (2 Corinthians 10:10; 2 Corinthians 11:6; 2 Corinthians 12:1), and took money from the church, even mistreating it (2 Corinthians 11:20). Some scholars (such as Ernst Käsemann and C. K. Barrett) think the "super-apostles" were the Jerusalem apostles, distinct from the "false apostles" of 2 Corinthians 11:13. Most (such as Victor Furnish and Murray Harris) think the two names refer to the same group, since 2 Corinthians 11:5 follows directly on those who preach "another Jesus" in 2 Corinthians 11:4, and 2 Corinthians 11:13–15 continues the same argument.

4. One letter, or several combined? Chapters 1–9 are mostly about reconciliation and comfort. Chapters 10–13 suddenly turn severe. Some scholars (such as C. K. Barrett and Victor Furnish) think chapters 10–13 are a later letter Paul wrote separately. Others (earlier, Adolf Hausrath and J. H. Kennedy) think chapters 10–13 are the "tearful letter" itself. There are more complex partition theories too, for example treating 2 Corinthians 2:14–7:4, or chapters 8 and 9, as separate letters. Still others (such as Paul Barnett, David Garland and Murray Harris) think the book is one letter. Paul may have written it in stages and received fresh news along the way, or he may address chapters 1–9 mainly to the repentant majority and chapters 10–13 to those still swayed by the false apostles. Every surviving ancient manuscript presents 2 Corinthians as a single letter. Whichever view one takes, the book is God's inspired word, and its message is one.

Key Verse: 4:7

1. "This treasure." The previous verse says, "For God, who said, 'Let light shine out of darkness,' has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6). The treasure is the gospel, the glory of God shown in the face of Christ.

2. "In jars of clay." Clay jars were the cheapest and most breakable vessels of the day, used for oil and water and even for keeping valuables (cf. Jer 32:14, where deeds of purchase are stored in an earthenware vessel). Paul says God puts his most precious gospel in the most ordinary, fragile people.

3. "To show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us." God does this on purpose. If the vessel were splendid and strong, people would admire the vessel. Because it is a battered clay jar, people can see that the power comes from God, not from the jar.

Structure

2 Corinthians falls broadly into five parts:

  • Comfort in affliction and a change of plans (2 Corinthians 1:1–2:13): "Blessed be... God of all comfort"; Paul explains why he did not come to Corinth as first planned.
  • The glory and weakness of new covenant ministry (2 Corinthians 2:14–7:4): the longest and richest section of the letter, on the glory of the new covenant (ch. 3), treasure in jars of clay (ch. 4), the hope of resurrection (2 Corinthians 5:1–10), the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:11–21), and Paul's heart opened to the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 6:1–7:4).
  • Good news from Titus (2 Corinthians 7:5–16): the Corinthians "felt a godly grief" that led to repentance.
  • The collection for the saints in Jerusalem (chs. 8–9): "though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor" (2 Corinthians 8:9).
  • Answering the false apostles (chs. 10–13): Paul boasts "as a fool" (2 Corinthians 11:17), but of his weaknesses; final warnings before his third visit; and the closing blessing of the triune God (2 Corinthians 13:14).
How to Read This Book

1. Watch for "weakness" and "power." This pair runs through the whole letter. God's power does not bypass weakness. It is shown in weakness (2 Corinthians 4:7; 2 Corinthians 12:9–10; 2 Corinthians 13:4).

2. Watch for "comfort" and "affliction." In the five verses of 2 Corinthians 1:3–7, the Greek word for "comfort" (noun and verb) appears ten times. Paul did not learn to comfort others in easy times. He was first comforted by God in affliction.

3. Watch how Paul measures ministry. The false apostles prized letters of recommendation, eloquence, appearance and achievement. Paul asks whether Christ is in the heart, whether lives have been changed, and whether the servant gives himself for others as Christ did. For churches today that measure ministry by numbers, fame, size and online reach, this is a weighty reminder. It also asks us: what do I quietly use to measure myself and others?

Meditation

Reflect: "But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us" (2 Corinthians 4:7). It is easy to show people only our good side: at church we always say, "Thank God, everything is fine"; online we post only smiles, achievements and holiday photos; with family we dare not admit we have failed. Behind this is often the fear of losing face, and the hope of standing on our own image. Paul, though, wrote his tears, his fears and the thorn that would not go away into a letter for others to read. He was not complaining. He wanted people to see that what held him up was not himself. Our Lord Jesus did not protect his own dignity either. He "was crucified in weakness," stripped and shamed for me, who so often cares about face; and he "lives by the power of God" (2 Corinthians 13:4). Because he has already borne my sin and my shame in my place, I no longer have to live by a flawless image. As I begin 2 Corinthians, can I bring to God one weakness I have never dared let anyone know, not asking him first to hide it or patch it, but to show his power through that very crack, so that people see him and not me? This jar of clay is cracked, but the Lord's grace is sufficient for me.
