entries.verse_text: 若有人在基督里，他就是新造的人，旧事已过，都变成新的了。神使那无罪的，替我们成为罪，好叫我们在他里面成为神的义。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第五章有三段。帐棚与房屋（1-10节）：「我们这地上的帐棚若拆毁了，必得神所造……在天上永存的房屋」；我们「行事为人是凭着信心，不是凭着眼见」，「更愿意离开身体与主同住」；但「我们众人必要在基督台前显露出来」。基督的爱激励我们（11-17节）：「一人既替众人死，众人就都死了」；所以我们「不再为自己活」，也「不凭着外貌认人」；「若有人在基督里，他就是新造的人」。与神和好（18-21节）：神「藉着基督使我们与他和好」，又把和好的职分交给我们；「神使那无罪的，替我们成为罪，好叫我们在他里面成为神的义」。

这一章从将来的盼望讲起，再讲到今天的生活和使命，最后落在全本圣经中最精简的福音宣告之一：林后5:21。

深读 5:1-10 帐棚、房屋与基督的审判台

1. 帐棚与房屋。 「我们原知道，我们这地上的帐棚若拆毁了，必得神所造，不是人手所造，在天上永存的房屋。」（林后5:1）保罗自己是织帐棚的（徒18:3）。帐棚是暂时的，会旧、会破、会被拆下；神所造的房屋却是永存的。多数解经家认为，「房屋」是指信徒将来复活的身体（参林前15:42-44）。「必得」原文直译是我们现在就有；许多人认为，这表示这事确定到好像已经拿在手里。也有学者（如默里·哈里斯）认为，这表示信徒死的时候就得着这房屋；还有人认为「房屋」是指天上的居所。无论哪种理解，保罗都确信：帐棚拆毁不是结局。

2. 不愿赤身，愿意穿上。 「我们在这帐棚里叹息劳苦，并非愿意脱下这个，乃是愿意穿上那个，好叫这必死的被生命吞灭了。」（林后5:4）有些希腊哲学认为身体是灵魂的监牢，死亡就是灵魂得释放。保罗却不是这样盼望。他叹息，不是因为想摆脱身体，而是渴望得着复活的身体；「赤身」（林后5:3）很可能是指死后、复活前灵魂离开身体的状态。保罗最大的盼望是复活，不只是灵魂得释放。

3. 圣灵作凭据。 「为此，培植我们的就是神，他又赐给我们圣灵作凭据。」（林后5:5）这里又用了林后1:22的「凭据」一词。今天住在我们里面的圣灵，是神给我们的定金，保证将来复活的荣耀一定会来。

4. 离开身体与主同住。 「我们坦然无惧，是更愿意离开身体与主同住。」（林后5:8）在复活以前，信徒死了，就「与主同住」（参腓1:23；路23:43）。这是安慰，因为信徒死后不是进入虚无，也不是成为无处可归、要靠后人祭拜供养的亡魂，而是与主同在。但这还不是最后的结局；最后的结局是身体的复活（林后4:14）。

5. 基督台前。 「因为我们众人必要在基督台前显露出来，叫各人按着本身所行的，或善或恶受报。」（林后5:10）「台」原文是审判官的座位。哥林多城的广场上就有这样一个台，保罗曾经被人拉到那里，站在迦流面前（徒18:12，「公堂」）。这节经文是对信徒说的。它不是说信徒要在那里重新被审，看能不能得救：「在基督耶稣里的就不定罪了」（罗8:1）。它是说，信徒的一生要在主面前显露出来，按着所行的得赏赐，或者受亏损（林前3:13-15）。改革宗传统（参《威斯敏斯德信条》第33章）也强调，按行为审判会显明一个人的信心是否真实：行为是真信心的果子和凭据，却不是我们被神接纳的根据；我们被接纳的唯一根据，是基督替我们成为罪，我们在他里面成为神的义（林后5:21）。因信称义不会叫人轻看今生怎样活，反而叫人「立了志向，要得主的喜悦」（林后5:9）。

要点：我们的盼望不是脱离身体，而是复活的身体；圣灵就是这盼望的凭据。在基督里，我们不再被定罪，我们仍要在主面前交账；但因为已经在基督里蒙悦纳，我们乐意立志要得主的喜悦。
深读 5:11-17 基督的爱激励我们

1. 劝人。 「我们既知道主是可畏的，所以劝人。」（林后5:11）保罗知道人人都要站在基督台前，所以他劝人。敬畏神和爱人，在他身上是连在一起的。

2. 颠狂与谨守。 「我们若果颠狂，是为神；若果谨守，是为你们。」（林后5:13）可能有人说保罗疯了，或者说他的属灵经历太狂热（「颠狂」也可能指他的异象和启示，参林后12:1-4）；也有人嫌他太平凡，不够属灵。保罗说，无论别人怎么看，他做的一切，不是为自己，而是为神、为人。

3. 基督的爱。 「原来基督的爱激励我们；因我们想，一人既替众人死，众人就都死了。」（林后5:14）「基督的爱」主要是指基督对我们的爱。「激励」原文有紧紧抓住、催逼的意思：基督的爱像一股力量，抓住保罗，推动他的一生。

4. 「替众人死」。 「一人既替众人死」说的是代替：基督替我们死。「众人就都死了」说的是联合：我们在他里面也死了（罗6:6）。「众人」指的是谁？福音派有不同的理解：

  • 改革宗传统（如约翰·欧文）认为，这是指所有在基督里的人：凡基督替他死的，也都在他里面死了，这些人就是15节「活着的人」、17节「在基督里」的人；
  • 卫斯理宗传统（如约翰·卫斯理）和路德宗认为，这是指世上所有的人：「众人」与19节的「世人」相应，基督为所有人死，但只有信的人得着救恩。

两方都同意：基督的死是代替的死，人必须信靠他才能得救，而福音要向所有人传扬（林后5:20）。

5. 不再为自己活。 「并且他替众人死，是叫那些活着的人不再为自己活，乃为替他们死而复活的主活。」（林后5:15）基督的死不只是要免去我们的刑罚，也要改变我们活着的方向：从「为自己活」转向「为主活」。

6. 不凭着外貌认人。 「所以，我们从今以后，不凭着外貌认人了。虽然凭着外貌认过基督，如今却不再这样认他了。」（林后5:16）「凭着外貌」原文直译是照着肉体，就是照着世人的标准：出身、学历、财富、口才、外表。保罗信主以前，也是这样看基督的：一个被钉十字架的人，怎么可能是弥赛亚？现在他不再这样看基督，也不再这样看人。

7. 新造的人。 「若有人在基督里，他就是新造的人，旧事已过，都变成新的了。」（林后5:17）原文很简短，可以直译为：若有人在基督里，就有新的创造！这句话让人想起以赛亚的应许：「看哪，我要做一件新事」（赛43:19）；「看哪！我造新天新地」（赛65:17）。神在末日要更新万有，这新创造已经在基督里开始了，每一个在基督里的人，都是这新创造的一部分。

要点：基督替我们死，我们也在他里面死了，所以我们不再为自己活。在基督里的人是新造的人：神要更新万有的工作，已经在他身上开始了；我们也不再按世人的标准看人。
深读 5:18-21 与神和好

1. 一切都是出于神。 「一切都是出于神；他藉着基督使我们与他和好，又将劝人与他和好的职分赐给我们。」（林后5:18）是人得罪了神，却是神主动寻求和好。在人间，通常是犯错的一方要先去道歉；在福音里，却是被得罪的神先来找我们（参罗5:10）。

2. 不将过犯归到他们身上。 「这就是神在基督里，叫世人与自己和好，不将他们的过犯归到他们身上，并且将这和好的道理托付了我们。」（林后5:19）神怎能不把罪算在人身上？不是因为他不在乎罪，而是因为他把罪归到了基督身上（林后5:21）。和好是神在十字架上成就的：不只除去了我们对神的敌意，也平息了神因罪而发的公义忿怒。但这不等于人不信也已经得救。人要藉着信才得着这和好，拒绝的人仍在神的震怒之下（约3:36）；所以保罗恳求人「与神和好」（林后5:20）。

3. 基督的使者。 「所以，我们作基督的使者，就好像神藉我们劝你们一般。我们替基督求你们与神和好。」（林后5:20）使者代表君王说话，自己没有权力改动信息。保罗用的词却很温柔：「劝」「求」。和好的工作在基督里已经完成，人却必须接受；所以福音的使者恳求人：「与神和好！」如果你还没有与神和好，神今天就藉着他的话恳求你。

4. 伟大的交换。 「神使那无罪的，替我们成为罪，好叫我们在他里面成为神的义。」（林后5:21）

  • 「那无罪的」： 基督完全没有罪（来4:15）。他不是为自己的罪死。
  • 「替我们成为罪」： 不是说基督自己变成了罪人，而是说神把我们的罪归在他身上，使他承受罪的刑罚（赛53:6；加3:13）。也有解经家认为，「罪」在这里也带有赎罪祭的意思，因为希腊文旧约常用同一个词指赎罪祭（参罗8:3；赛53:10）。两种理解都说明：基督代替我们受了罪的审判。
  • 「在他里面成为神的义」： 宗教改革以来，路德宗和改革宗的解经家多认为，这是指信的人与基督联合，神就把那从神而来的义算为他们的（参腓3:9）；改教家称之为基督的义归算给信徒。也有学者（如汤姆·赖特）认为，「神的义」在这里是指神守约的信实；因为上下文讲的是和好的职分（林后5:18–6:2），他认为「我们」主要指使徒，意思是他们在服事中成了神守约信实的活见证。前一种理解与上文「不将他们的过犯归到他们身上」（林后5:19）的对比最为吻合，也是本书采取的看法。
要点：是被得罪的神主动与我们和好。他把我们的罪归在无罪的基督身上，又把基督的义归给我们。教会的使命，就是作基督的使者，恳求人与神和好。
默想

默想： 「若有人在基督里，他就是新造的人，旧事已过，都变成新的了。」（林后5:17）我是否一直活在别人给我贴的标签底下：从小被说「没出息」，被拿来和兄弟姊妹比较，被说「你就是这种人」；或者因为坐过牢、得过某种病、做过某件错事，就觉得自己一辈子都只能是那样的人？我是否也这样看别人，凭着他的过去、学历、收入或口音，就给他下了定论？有些标签是别人强加在我身上的谎言，有些却说中了我真实的罪。前一种，我不必再背。后一种，神没有假装看不见：在神面前，我真实的光景是一个被定罪的罪人。但神把我的罪归在无罪的基督身上：「神使那无罪的，替我们成为罪，好叫我们在他里面成为神的义。」（林后5:21）这个最重的判决，主耶稣已经替我承担了（西2:14）。凡悔改、信靠基督的人，神现在看他，是看他在基督里，是一个「新造的人」。如果我还不在基督里，今天就可以悔改，信靠这位替我成为罪的主（林后6:2）。这不是说过去的伤痛和后果都会立刻消失，而是说，过去不再能定义我是谁。我能不能把一个压在我身上多年的标签告诉神，然后读出这句话：「旧事已过，都变成新的了」？我能不能也求神叫我不再凭着外貌认人，用新的眼光看一位我早已给他定了论的人？我能这样看别人，是因为神先这样看了我：他在基督里给我的新名字，比任何人贴给我的标签都更真。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 5 has three parts. Tent and building (vv. 1–10): "if the tent, which is our earthly home, is destroyed, we have a building from God... eternal in the heavens"; "we walk by faith, not by sight," and "would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord"; yet "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ." The love of Christ controls us (vv. 11–17): "one has died for all, therefore all have died"; so we "no longer live for ourselves," and "regard no one according to the flesh"; "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." Reconciled to God (vv. 18–21): God "through Christ reconciled us to himself" and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God."

The chapter moves from future hope to present life and mission, and ends on one of the most compact statements of the gospel in all Scripture: 2 Corinthians 5:21.

Going Deeper 5:1–10 Tent, Building and the Judgment Seat of Christ

1. Tent and building. "For we know that if the tent, which is our earthly home, is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens" (2 Corinthians 5:1). Paul was himself a tentmaker (Acts 18:3). A tent is temporary; it wears out, tears and is taken down. The building God makes lasts forever. Most interpreters take the "building" to be the believer's future resurrection body (cf. 1 Cor 15:42–44). Paul says "we have," which many take to mean it is as good as in hand, so certain is it. Some (e.g. Murray J. Harris) read "we have" as receiving this building at death; others take the "building" as a heavenly dwelling. On any reading, Paul is sure that the tent's destruction is not the end.

2. Not unclothed, but further clothed. "For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened--not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life" (2 Corinthians 5:4). Some Greek philosophy saw the body as the soul's prison and death as the soul's release. Paul's hope is different. He groans not to be rid of the body but for the resurrection body. "Unclothed" (and "naked," 2 Corinthians 5:3) probably refers to the state after death and before the resurrection, when the soul is apart from the body. Paul's highest hope is resurrection, not merely the soul set free.

3. The Spirit as guarantee. "He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee" (2 Corinthians 5:5). Here again is the "guarantee" of 2 Corinthians 1:22. The Spirit who lives in us now is God's down payment, guaranteeing that the glory of the resurrection will surely come.

4. At home with the Lord. "Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). Before the resurrection, believers who die are "at home with the Lord" (cf. Phil 1:23; Luke 23:43). This is comfort: at death believers do not pass into nothingness, nor become wandering spirits dependent on their descendants' offerings, but are with the Lord. Yet this is not the final end; the final end is the resurrection of the body (2 Corinthians 4:14).

5. The judgment seat of Christ. "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil" (2 Corinthians 5:10). The "judgment seat" (bēma) was a judge's tribunal. The forum at Corinth had one, and Paul had once been dragged there before Gallio (Acts 18:12, "the tribunal"). This verse is addressed to believers. It does not mean believers will be tried again to see whether they are saved: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Rom 8:1). It means a believer's life will be laid open before the Lord, to receive reward or suffer loss according to what he has done (1 Cor 3:13–15). The Reformed tradition (cf. Westminster Confession 33) also stresses that judgment according to works reveals whether faith was genuine: works are the fruit and evidence of true faith, never the ground of our acceptance. That ground is Christ alone, who was made sin for us so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). Justification by faith does not make us careless about how we live; it makes us "aim to please him" (2 Corinthians 5:9).

The point: Our hope is not escape from the body but the resurrection body, and the Spirit is its guarantee. In Christ we are no longer condemned, we will still give account before the Lord; but because we are already accepted in Christ, we gladly make it our aim to please him.
Going Deeper 5:11–17 The Love of Christ Controls Us

1. Persuading others. "Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others" (2 Corinthians 5:11). Paul knew that everyone will stand before Christ's judgment seat, so he persuaded people. In him, fearing God and loving people went together.

2. Beside ourselves, or in our right mind. "For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you" (2 Corinthians 5:13). Perhaps some said Paul was mad, or that his spiritual experiences were extreme ("beside ourselves" may refer to his visions and revelations, cf. 2 Corinthians 12:1–4); others found him too ordinary, not spiritual enough. Paul says that whatever others think, all he does is not for himself but for God and for others.

3. The love of Christ. "For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died" (2 Corinthians 5:14). "The love of Christ" here is mainly Christ's love for us. "Controls" carries the sense of gripping and pressing on: Christ's love is a force that has hold of Paul and drives his whole life.

4. "Died for all." "One has died for all" speaks of substitution: Christ died in our place. "Therefore all have died" speaks of union: in him we died too (Rom 6:6). Evangelicals differ over whom "all" means:

  • the Reformed tradition (e.g. John Owen) takes it as all who are in Christ: those for whom he died also died in him, and they are "those who live" (v. 15), those "in Christ" (v. 17);
  • the Wesleyan tradition (e.g. John Wesley) and Lutherans take it as everyone in the world: "all" matches "the world" in v. 19; Christ died for all, but only those who believe receive salvation.

Both agree that Christ's death was substitutionary, that people must trust him to be saved, and that the gospel is to be preached to all (2 Corinthians 5:20).

5. No longer living for ourselves. "...and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised" (2 Corinthians 5:15). Christ's death does not only remove our penalty. It changes the direction of our lives, from living for ourselves to living for the Lord.

6. Regarding no one according to the flesh. "From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer" (2 Corinthians 5:16). "According to the flesh" means by worldly standards: family background, education, wealth, eloquence, looks. Before his conversion Paul saw Christ that way: how could a crucified man be the Messiah? Now he no longer sees Christ that way, nor anyone else.

7. A new creation. "Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come" (2 Corinthians 5:17). The Greek is very terse and can be rendered, "If anyone is in Christ: new creation!" It recalls Isaiah's promises: "Behold, I am doing a new thing" (Isa 43:19); "For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth" (Isa 65:17). The renewal of all things that God will bring at the end has already begun in Christ, and everyone in Christ is part of that new creation.

The point: Christ died for us, and we died in him, so we no longer live for ourselves. Whoever is in Christ is a new creation: God's work of making all things new has already begun in him, and we no longer judge people by worldly standards.
Going Deeper 5:18–21 Reconciled to God

1. All this is from God. "All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation" (2 Corinthians 5:18). It was we who offended God, yet God took the initiative to make peace. Among people, the one in the wrong usually has to apologize first; in the gospel, the God who was wronged comes to us first (cf. Rom 5:10).

2. Not counting their trespasses. "...that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation" (2 Corinthians 5:19). How can God not count sins against people? Not because he does not care about sin, but because he counted it against Christ (2 Corinthians 5:21). Reconciliation was accomplished by God at the cross. It removed not only our hostility to God but the just wrath of God against sin. Yet this does not mean people are saved without believing; that is exactly why Paul pleads, "be reconciled to God" (2 Corinthians 5:20). It becomes ours through faith, and those who refuse it remain under God's wrath (John 3:36).

3. Ambassadors for Christ. "Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God" (2 Corinthians 5:20). An ambassador speaks for the king and has no authority to change the message. Yet Paul's words are tender: "appeal," "implore." The work of reconciliation is finished in Christ, but people must receive it, so the gospel's ambassadors plead: "be reconciled to God!" If you are not yet reconciled to God, he is pleading with you today through his word.

4. The great exchange. "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21).

  • "Who knew no sin": Christ was entirely without sin (Heb 4:15). He did not die for sins of his own.
  • "Made him to be sin": not that Christ himself became a sinner, but that God laid our sin on him, so that he bore its penalty (Isa 53:6; Gal 3:13). Some interpreters think "sin" here also carries the sense of "sin offering," since the Greek Old Testament often uses the same word for the sin offering (cf. Rom 8:3; Isa 53:10). Either way, Christ bore the judgment of sin in our place.
  • "Become the righteousness of God in him": since the Reformation, Lutheran and Reformed interpreters have mostly taken this to mean that believers, united to Christ, are counted righteous with the righteousness that comes from God (cf. Phil 3:9), what the Reformers called Christ's righteousness credited to us. Some scholars (such as N. T. Wright) take "the righteousness of God" here as God's covenant faithfulness. Because the context is the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18–6:2), they read "we" as chiefly the apostles, who in their ministry become the embodiment of God's covenant faithfulness. The first reading fits best with the contrast to "not counting their trespasses against them" (2 Corinthians 5:19), and it is the view taken here.
The point: The God we wronged took the initiative to reconcile us to himself. He laid our sin on the sinless Christ and credits Christ's righteousness to us. The church's mission is to be Christ's ambassadors, pleading with people to be reconciled to God.
Meditation

Reflect: "Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come" (2 Corinthians 5:17). Have I lived for years under labels others put on me: told from childhood that I would never amount to anything, compared with my brothers and sisters, told "you're just that kind of person"? Or because I went to prison, or have a certain illness, or did a certain wrong, do I feel I can only ever be that person? Do I label others the same way, judging someone by his past, his education, his income or his accent? Some labels are lies others have put on me; some name sins I really committed. The first kind I no longer have to carry. The second kind God does not pretend not to see: before God, my true condition is that of a condemned sinner. But God laid my sin on the sinless Christ: "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). That heaviest verdict the Lord Jesus has borne for me (Col 2:14). Whoever repents and trusts Christ, God now sees in Christ, as "a new creation." If I am not yet in Christ, I can repent today and trust the Lord who was made sin for me (2 Corinthians 6:2). This does not mean past wounds and consequences vanish at once. It means the past no longer defines who I am. Can I tell God about one label that has weighed on me for years, and then read aloud, "The old has passed away; behold, the new has come"? And can I ask God to stop me regarding people according to the flesh, and to give me new eyes for someone I settled my verdict on long ago? I can see others this way only because God first saw me this way: the new name he gives me in Christ is truer than any label anyone has put on me.

本章脉络

第六章有三段。不可徒受神的恩典（1-2节）：「现在正是悦纳的时候！现在正是拯救的日子。」神的用人（3-13节）：保罗列出他在「许多的忍耐、患难、穷乏、困苦」中怎样表明自己是神的用人；他「似乎一无所有，却是样样都有的」。然后他向哥林多人敞开心：「我们向你们，口是张开的，心是宽宏的」，也求他们「照样用宽宏的心」回报。不要同负一轭（林后6:14–7:1）：「你们和不信的原不相配，不要同负一轭」，「因为我们是永生神的殿」。

这一章一方面叫教会把心打开，接纳保罗；另一方面叫教会在拜偶像的事上分别出来。宽宏和分别，看起来方向相反，其实都出于同一位神：他接纳我们作他的儿女，也要我们单单属于他。

深读 6:1-2 现在正是拯救的日子

1. 不可徒受恩典。 「我们与神同工的，也劝你们不可徒受他的恩典。」（林后6:1）保罗刚刚说完「你们与神和好」（林后5:20），现在接着劝：不要让神的恩典在你们身上落空。这不是说恩典要靠人的努力才有效，而是说，领受恩典的人若不让恩典改变他的生活，反而去追随另一个福音（林后11:4），这恩典在他身上就落空了，这就是「徒受」了恩典。

2. 悦纳的时候。 「因为他说：『在悦纳的时候，我应允了你；在拯救的日子，我搭救了你。』看哪，现在正是悦纳的时候！现在正是拯救的日子。」（林后6:2）这句话引自赛49:8，原来是神对他的仆人所说的话；这位仆人要作「外邦人的光」（赛49:6）。保罗说，以赛亚所应许的那个日子，现在已经来到了：基督已经来了，死了，又复活了。

3. 「现在」。 保罗连说了两次「现在」。福音的邀请不是「等你准备好了再来」，也不是「等退休了再说」「等家里人同意了再说」。神的恩典今天就在这里。对还没有信主的人，这是呼召：不要再拖延。对已经信主的人，这是提醒：不要以为恩典是以后的事，今天就活在其中。

要点：以赛亚所应许的拯救之日，已经在基督里来到了。神的恩典今天就向人敞开，不要把它推到明天，也不要让它在我们身上落空。
深读 6:3-10 似乎一无所有，却是样样都有

1. 不叫人有妨碍。 「我们凡事都不叫人有妨碍，免得这职分被人毁谤。」（林后6:3）保罗知道，传道人的生活可以帮助人信福音，也可以成为人信福音的绊脚石。

2. 一份不寻常的履历。 「反倒在各样的事上表明自己是神的用人，就如在许多的忍耐、患难、穷乏、困苦、鞭打、监禁、扰乱、勤劳、警醒、不食。」（林后6:4-5）假使徒用荐信、口才和成功来证明自己；保罗用来证明自己的，却是他受的苦。这份履历在世人看来是失败的记录，在神看来却是忠心的记号。

3. 内在的品格。 「廉洁、知识、恒忍、恩慈、圣灵的感化、无伪的爱心、真实的道理、神的大能。」（林后6:6-7）保罗表明自己是神的用人，不只靠忍受苦难，也靠圣灵结出的品格。「圣灵的感化」原文只是「圣灵」一词，多数解经家认为这里指的就是圣灵自己：在一连串的美德中间，保罗提到圣灵自己，因为这一切都是从他而来的。

4. 左右手的兵器。 「仁义的兵器在左在右。」（林后6:7）古时的士兵右手拿刀，左手拿盾。保罗的意思可能是，他无论进攻还是防守，都只用公义的方法，不用诡诈和手段（参林后4:2）。

5. 七个「似乎……却是」。 「似乎是诱惑人的，却是诚实的；似乎不为人所知，却是人所共知的；似乎要死，却是活着的；似乎受责罚，却是不至丧命的；似乎忧愁，却是常常快乐的；似乎贫穷，却是叫许多人富足的；似乎一无所有，却是样样都有的。」（林后6:8-10）别人怎么看保罗是一回事，在神面前的真实又是另一回事。他「似乎贫穷，却是叫许多人富足」，这正是基督的样式：「他本来富足，却为你们成了贫穷，叫你们因他的贫穷，可以成为富足」（林后8:9）。

要点：神的用人在基督里样样都有，所以不必靠成功的履历证明自己，可以在苦难中忍耐，在圣灵里活出真实的品格。
深读 6:11-13 心是宽宏的

1. 张开的口，宽宏的心。 「哥林多人哪，我们向你们，口是张开的，心是宽宏的。」（林后6:11）保罗在书信中很少这样直呼收信人（另见加3:1「无知的加拉太人哪」；腓4:15「腓立比人哪」）。他说他已经把话都说出来了，心也向他们完全打开。

2. 你们的心肠狭窄。 「你们狭窄，原不在乎我们，是在乎自己的心肠狭窄。」（林后6:12）「心肠」原文指人的内脏，古人认为那是感情所在的地方。保罗的意思是：我们之间的距离，不是因为我关上了门，而是因为你们的心冷了、窄了。也许是因为那次痛苦的探访，也许是因为假使徒的挑拨，哥林多人对保罗有了戒心。

3. 像父亲对孩子说话。 「你们也要照样用宽宏的心报答我。我这话正像对自己的孩子说的。」（林后6:13）保罗是哥林多教会属灵的父亲（林前4:15）。父母被儿女误解的时候，心里的痛常常比被外人误解更深。保罗没有用权柄压他们，而是像父亲一样恳求：请把你们的心也向我打开。

要点：保罗向一个曾经伤害他的教会敞开自己的心，并且恳求他们也敞开心；他能这样，是因为基督先向他敞开了心。关系冷淡的时候，我们可以诚实地问：是不是有时候，是我自己的心肠变窄了？
深读 6:14–7:1 不要同负一轭

1. 不相配的轭。 「你们和不信的原不相配，不要同负一轭。」（林后6:14）「同负一轭」这个词，在希腊文旧约中出现在利19:19（不可叫牲畜与异类配合）；画面则让人想起「不可并用牛、驴耕地」（申22:10）。牛和驴力气不同、步伐不同，套在同一个轭下，就无法同心耕地。

2. 五个问题。 「义和不义有什么相交呢？光明和黑暗有什么相通呢？基督和彼列有什么相和呢？信主的和不信主的有什么相干呢？神的殿和偶像有什么相同呢？」（林后6:14-16）「彼列」在希伯来文旧约中是无用、邪恶的意思（撒上2:12的「恶人」，原文就是彼列的儿子），后来在犹太文献（如死海古卷）中成了撒但的一个名字。这五个问题的答案都是：没有。

3. 这里指的是什么？ 从上下文看，保罗最直接关心的，是哥林多人与拜偶像的事（林后6:16；参林前10:14-22），也可能包括那些叫人「另得一个福音」的假使徒（林后11:4、13-15）。但这个原则也适用于别的关系：凡会把信徒和不信的人在属灵方向上绑在一起的，都要留意。教会很早就把它用在婚姻上，因为保罗在别处也说信徒「只是要嫁这在主里面的人」（林前7:39）。同时要留意三件事：

  • 这不是叫信徒离开世界，不与不信的人来往（林前5:10）；
  • 这也不是叫已经和不信主的配偶结婚的信徒离婚（林前7:12-13），因为「不信的丈夫就因着妻子成了圣洁」（林前7:14）；当然，这也不是要受虐待的一方留在危险中；
  • 这是关于属灵方向上的捆绑，例如在婚姻、宗教活动（像家族祭拜祖先、庙会、生意开张拜神），或要违背良心的合伙生意中，和不信的人绑在同一条路上。

4. 永生神的殿。 「因为我们是永生神的殿，就如神曾说：我要在他们中间居住，在他们中间来往；我要作他们的神；他们要作我的子民。」（林后6:16）保罗把几处旧约经文合在一起（利26:11-12；结37:27；赛52:11；结20:34；撒下7:8、14）。神在旧约应许要住在他百姓中间，这应许今天在教会身上成就了：教会就是神的殿。

5. 作神的儿女。 「我要作你们的父；你们要作我的儿女。这是全能的主说的。」（林后6:18）神原本对大卫的后裔说「我要作他的父，他要作我的子」（撒下7:14），保罗在这里把它扩大为「儿女」（参赛43:6「我的众子」「我的众女」）。分别出来，不是为了失去什么，而是因为我们已经属于一位父亲。

6. 洁净自己。 「亲爱的弟兄啊，我们既有这等应许，就当洁净自己，除去身体、灵魂一切的污秽，敬畏神，得以成圣。」（林后7:1）次序很重要：先有应许，后有洁净。我们不是为了成为神的儿女才洁净自己；我们已经是他的儿女，所以要活得像他的儿女。

有些学者认为林后6:14–7:1这一段和上下文接得不顺，可能是后来放进来的。不过，现存所有希腊文抄本都有这一段，而且都在这个位置。今天多数解经家，包括福音派解经家，都认为它与上下文是连在一起的：保罗要哥林多人向他敞开心（林后6:13；林后7:2），同时也要他们向偶像和假使徒关上门。

要点：信徒是永生神的殿、全能者的儿女，所以不可与拜偶像和不信的事同负一轭。这不是叫我们离开世界，而是因为我们已经属于神，要单单属于他。
默想

默想： 「哥林多人哪，我们向你们，口是张开的，心是宽宏的。你们狭窄，原不在乎我们，是在乎自己的心肠狭窄。你们也要照样用宽宏的心报答我。」（林后6:11-13）我的心是否因为过去的伤害，对教会、对某位牧者、对某些弟兄姊妹关上了？也许我曾经被误会、被冷落，或者在一次教会纷争中受了伤；从那以后，我虽然还来聚会，却总是站在边上，不再信任任何人，不再投入。或者，我是否也曾因为几句闲话，就对一位忠心的牧者起了戒心？保罗被这个教会伤得很深，他的心却仍然向他们敞开。他能这样，是因为基督先向他敞开了心：主耶稣被他自己的人拒绝，被门徒离弃，在十字架上仍然为钉他的人祷告（路23:34）；他张开双臂，接纳了我这个曾经与他为敌的人（林后5:18；罗5:10）。当然，如果我受的伤害是性侵、暴力、属灵操控或其他不安全的事，宽宏不等于要我回到危险里，不等于要我重新信任那个伤害我的人，更不等于要我为了教会的面子保持沉默。向警方或有关部门报案是正当的（罗13:4），教会也不可以用「家丑不可外扬」为理由把事情压下去。我可以寻求帮助、讲出真相，在一个安全的地方（也可以是另一间教会）重新学习信任。如果伤害是真实的，只是不涉及安全，主也不要我假装没事；我可以先在他面前哀哭，宽宏的心常常是慢慢打开的。但如果我发现，我的心变窄，更多是因为失望、骄傲，或者听信了别人背后的话，我能不能今天向神承认，求他用基督宽宏的爱，把我的心重新打开一点？在我的心还没有打开以前，他的心早已向我敞开；他不会因为我打开得慢，就向我关上门。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 6 has three parts. Do not receive God's grace in vain (vv. 1–2): "Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation." Servants of God (vv. 3–13): Paul lists how he commends himself as God's servant "by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities," "as having nothing, yet possessing everything." Then he opens his heart to the Corinthians: "We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open," and asks them in return to "widen your hearts also." Do not be unequally yoked (2 Corinthians 6:14–7:1): "Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers... For we are the temple of the living God."

This chapter calls the church to open its heart and welcome Paul, and also to come out and be separate from idolatry. Widening and separating seem to pull in opposite directions, but both come from the same God: he welcomes us as his children, and he wants us to belong to him alone.

Going Deeper 6:1–2 Now Is the Day of Salvation

1. Not in vain. "Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain" (2 Corinthians 6:1). Paul has just said "be reconciled to God" (2 Corinthians 5:20), and now he urges: do not let God's grace come to nothing in you. This does not mean grace depends on human effort to work. It means that someone who receives grace but does not let it change his life, and instead follows "a different gospel" (2 Corinthians 11:4), has in effect received it for nothing.

2. The favorable time. "For he says, 'In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.' Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Corinthians 6:2). Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8, where God speaks to his Servant, who will be "a light for the nations" (Isa 49:6). Paul says the day Isaiah promised has now come: Christ has come, died and risen.

3. "Now." Paul says "now" twice. The gospel's invitation is not "come when you're ready," nor "wait until you retire" or "wait until your family agrees." God's grace is here today. For those who do not yet believe, this is a call: don't put it off any longer. For believers, it is a reminder: grace is not for later; live in it today.

The point: The day of salvation Isaiah promised has come in Christ. God's grace is open to us today; do not put it off until tomorrow, and do not let it come to nothing in us.
Going Deeper 6:3–10 Having Nothing, Yet Possessing Everything

1. No obstacle. "We put no obstacle in anyone's way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry" (2 Corinthians 6:3). Paul knew that a preacher's life can help people believe the gospel, or become a stumbling block to it.

2. An unusual résumé. "...but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger" (2 Corinthians 6:4–5). The false apostles proved themselves by letters, eloquence and success. Paul proves himself by what he has suffered. To the world this résumé looks like a record of failure; to God it is the mark of faithfulness.

3. Character within. "...by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love, by truthful speech, and the power of God" (2 Corinthians 6:6–7). Paul relies not only on enduring hardship but on the character the Spirit produces. In the middle of a list of virtues the Greek simply says "holy spirit"; most take it as the Holy Spirit himself, because all of them come from him.

4. Weapons for right hand and left. "...with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left" (2 Corinthians 6:7). An ancient soldier held a sword in his right hand and a shield in his left. Paul may mean that in attack and defense alike he uses only righteous means, never cunning or manipulation (cf. 2 Corinthians 4:2).

5. Seven "as... yet"s. "We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything" (2 Corinthians 6:8–10). How others see Paul is one thing; the truth before God is another. "As poor, yet making many rich" is the very pattern of Christ: "though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9).

The point: Because God's servants possess everything in Christ, they need no résumé of success; they can endure hardship and live out the genuine character the Spirit forms.
Going Deeper 6:11–13 Our Heart Is Wide Open

1. An open mouth, a wide heart. "We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open" (2 Corinthians 6:11). Paul rarely addresses a church directly by name like this (cf. Gal 3:1; Phil 4:15). He has said everything, and his heart is fully open to them.

2. Restricted affections. "You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections" (2 Corinthians 6:12). "Affections" is literally the inner organs, which the ancients saw as the seat of feeling. Paul means: the distance between us is not because I have shut the door, but because your affection has shrunk. Perhaps because of the painful visit, perhaps because the false apostles stirred them up, the Corinthians had grown guarded toward Paul.

3. As a father to his children. "In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also" (2 Corinthians 6:13). Paul is the Corinthian church's spiritual father (1 Cor 4:15). When parents are misunderstood by their children, the pain is often deeper than being misunderstood by strangers. Paul does not press them with his authority; like a father he pleads: open your hearts to me too.

The point: Paul opens his heart to a church that had hurt him, and pleads with them to open theirs. He could, because Christ had first opened his heart to him. When a relationship grows cold, we can honestly ask whether, at times, it is our own heart that has narrowed.
Going Deeper 6:14–7:1 Do Not Be Unequally Yoked

1. A mismatched yoke. "Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers" (2 Corinthians 6:14). The related word appears in the Greek Old Testament at Lev 19:19 (not letting cattle breed with a different kind), and the image recalls "You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together" (Deut 22:10). An ox and a donkey differ in strength and stride; yoked together they cannot plow as one.

2. Five questions. "For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols?" (2 Corinthians 6:14–16). "Belial" in the Hebrew Old Testament means "worthlessness" (e.g. 1 Sam 2:12, "worthless men," literally "sons of Belial"), and in later Jewish writings such as the Dead Sea Scrolls it became a name for Satan. The answer to all five questions is: none.

3. What is in view? From the context, Paul's most immediate concern is the Corinthians' involvement with idolatry (2 Corinthians 6:16; cf. 1 Cor 10:14–22), and possibly the false apostles who preached "a different gospel" (2 Corinthians 11:4, 13–15). But the principle also applies to other relationships that bind a believer to an unbeliever in spiritual direction. The church has long applied it to marriage, since Paul elsewhere says a believer may marry "only in the Lord" (1 Cor 7:39). At the same time, note three things:

  • this does not tell believers to leave the world and avoid unbelievers (1 Cor 5:10);
  • it does not tell believers already married to an unbelieving spouse to divorce (1 Cor 7:12–13), for "the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife" (1 Cor 7:14); nor does it require anyone to remain in danger from an abusive spouse;
  • it concerns being bound in spiritual direction, for example in marriage, in religious practice (such as ancestral rites, temple festivals, or worshiping idols at a business opening), or in a partnership that would require going against conscience, binding one to an unbeliever's road.

4. The temple of the living God. "For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, 'I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people'" (2 Corinthians 6:16). Paul weaves together several Old Testament texts (Lev 26:11–12; Ezek 37:27; Isa 52:11; Ezek 20:34; 2 Sam 7:8, 14). God promised in the Old Testament to dwell among his people; that promise is fulfilled today in the church, which is God's temple.

5. Sons and daughters. "...and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty" (2 Corinthians 6:18). God originally said of David's offspring, "I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son" (2 Sam 7:14). Paul widens it to "sons and daughters" (cf. Isa 43:6, "my sons... my daughters"). Being separate is not about losing something; it is because we already belong to a Father.

6. Cleansing ourselves. "Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God" (2 Corinthians 7:1). The order matters: the promises first, then the cleansing. We do not cleanse ourselves to become God's children; we are already his children, so we live like his children.

Some scholars think 2 Corinthians 6:14–7:1 fits awkwardly in its context and may have been inserted later. Yet every surviving Greek manuscript contains the passage, and in this place. Most commentators today, including evangelical ones, think it belongs where it is: Paul wants the Corinthians to open their hearts to him (2 Corinthians 6:13; 2 Corinthians 7:2) and at the same time to shut the door on idols and false apostles.

The point: Believers are the temple of the living God and children of the Almighty, so they must not be yoked with idolatry and unbelief. This is not a call to leave the world; it is because we already belong to God and are to belong to him alone.
Meditation

Reflect: "We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also" (2 Corinthians 6:11–13). Has past hurt closed my heart toward the church, toward a pastor, toward certain brothers and sisters? Perhaps I was misunderstood or ignored, or wounded in a church conflict. Since then I still come to services, but I stay on the edge, trust no one and hold back. Or have I grown guarded toward a faithful pastor because of a few rumors? Paul had been deeply hurt by this church, yet his heart stayed open to them. He could do this because Christ first opened his heart to him. The Lord Jesus was rejected by his own people and deserted by his disciples, and on the cross he still prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34). He opened his arms and welcomed me, who was once his enemy (2 Corinthians 5:18; Rom 5:10). Of course, if what I suffered was sexual abuse, violence, spiritual manipulation or anything unsafe, widening my heart does not mean going back into danger, or trusting again the person who harmed me, or keeping quiet to protect the church's reputation. Reporting it to the police or the proper authorities is right (Rom 13:4), and a church must never hush it up to save face. I can seek help, tell the truth, and learn to trust again in a safe place, which may be a different church. If the hurt was real but not a matter of safety, the Lord does not ask me to pretend it did not happen; I can first lament before him, and a heart usually widens slowly. But if I see that my heart has narrowed more through disappointment, pride, or listening to talk behind someone's back, can I confess it to God today, and ask him to open my heart a little again with the wide love of Christ? Before my heart is open, his is already open to me, and he will not shut his door on me because mine opens slowly.

entries.day_label: 哥林多后书 · 第 7 / 13 章
entries.title: 依着神的意思忧愁
entries.title_en: Godly Grief That Leads to Repentance

verse_parts.text: 因为依着神的意思忧愁，就生出没有后悔的懊悔来，以致得救；但世俗的忧愁是叫人死。

entries.verse_text: 因为依着神的意思忧愁，就生出没有后悔的懊悔来，以致得救；但世俗的忧愁是叫人死。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第七章接着第六章的劝勉，然后回到林后2:13中断的故事。心地宽大收纳我们（2-4节）：保罗再次请哥林多人向他敞开心，「你们常在我们心里，情愿与你们同生同死」。提多带来的安慰（5-7节）：保罗到了马其顿，「外有争战，内有惧怕」；「但那安慰丧气之人的神藉着提多来安慰了我们」。两种忧愁（8-13节上）：那封严厉的信叫哥林多人忧愁，但他们是「依着神的意思忧愁」，生出了悔改。提多的喜乐（13节下-16节）：哥林多人怎样接待提多，保罗就「能在凡事上为你们放心」。

第1节「我们既有这等应许，就当洁净自己」是上一章的总结，已在第六章讲过。这一章的中心是林后7:10：「依着神的意思忧愁，就生出没有后悔的懊悔来，以致得救；但世俗的忧愁是叫人死。」

深读 7:2-4 你们常在我们心里

1. 收纳我们。 「你们要心地宽大收纳我们。我们未曾亏负谁，未曾败坏谁，未曾占谁的便宜。」（林后7:2）这里接着林后6:13「你们也要照样用宽宏的心报答我」。保罗为自己辩护，大概是因为有人指控他在钱财上有问题。「占便宜」这个词在林后12:17-18又出现，那里保罗问：「提多占过你们的便宜吗？」

2. 同生同死。 「我说这话，不是要定你们的罪。我已经说过，你们常在我们心里，情愿与你们同生同死。」（林后7:3）这是至死忠诚的话，像以太对大卫说的「无论生死」（撒下15:21）：生也好，死也好，都不分离。一位使徒对一个曾经伤害他的教会这样说，可见他的爱是真实的。

3. 在患难中快乐。 「我们在一切患难中分外的快乐。」（林后7:4）保罗的快乐不是因为没有患难，而是因为神在患难中安慰他，也因为他看见哥林多人的回转。

要点：保罗的爱不是有条件的；即使受了伤害，他仍然说：「你们常在我们心里。」他的爱反映了基督的爱：主爱我们，在我们还作罪人的时候就为我们死（罗5:8）。
深读 7:5-7 安慰丧气之人的神

1. 外有争战，内有惧怕。 「我们从前就是到了马其顿的时候，身体也不得安宁，周围遭患难，外有争战，内有惧怕。」（林后7:5）保罗没有把自己说成一位从不害怕的英雄。他身体疲倦，外面有冲突，里面有惧怕：他担心哥林多教会会怎样回应那封信，担心提多的安全。

2. 那安慰丧气之人的神。 「但那安慰丧气之人的神藉着提多来安慰了我们。」（林后7:6）「丧气之人」原文是指卑微、低落、被压下去的人。以赛亚书说：「耶和华已经安慰他的百姓，也要怜恤他困苦之民。」（赛49:13）这节经文在七十士译本（旧约希腊文译本）里说，神安慰他百姓中卑微的人，用的正是保罗这里的词。保罗在林后6:2刚刚引过同一章（赛49:8）。神特别靠近这样的人。

3. 神藉着人安慰人。 「不但藉着他来，也藉着他从你们所得的安慰，安慰了我们；因他把你们的想念、哀恸，和向我的热心，都告诉了我，叫我更加欢喜。」（林后7:7）神的安慰常常藉着人而来：一位朋友的到来，一个好消息，一句真心的话。保罗在第一章说他要「用神所赐的安慰去安慰」人（林后1:4）；在这里，他自己也被人安慰了。在教会里，安慰是彼此传递的。

要点：神是「安慰丧气之人的神」。保罗不以「内有惧怕」为耻；神偏偏靠近被压下去的人，常常藉着一位弟兄的到来、一个好消息，把安慰带给他们。
深读 7:8-13上 两种忧愁

1. 叫人忧愁的信。 「我先前写信叫你们忧愁，我后来虽然懊悔，如今却不懊悔；因我知道，那信叫你们忧愁不过是暂时的。」（林后7:8）保罗写了那封信以后，也曾后悔，担心自己说得太重。这让我们看见一位牧者的挣扎：说真话是对的，但说完以后，心里也不好受。

2. 不是因为你们忧愁而欢喜。 「如今我欢喜，不是因你们忧愁，是因你们从忧愁中生出懊悔来。」（林后7:9）保罗不是喜欢看别人难过。他欢喜，是因为忧愁结出了果子：悔改。「懊悔」在这里就是悔改；这个词在新约里指整个人转离罪、归向神。

3. 两种忧愁。 「因为依着神的意思忧愁，就生出没有后悔的懊悔来，以致得救；但世俗的忧愁是叫人死。」（林后7:10）

  • 依着神的意思忧愁： 是因为得罪了神而忧伤，这忧伤把人带到神面前，生出悔改，以致得救。多数解经家认为「没有后悔」是形容这悔改：这样的悔改，人永远不会后悔。
  • 世俗的忧愁： 是因为罪的后果、因为被人发现、因为丢了面子而难过。这种忧愁只看自己，不看神，可能叫人自怨自艾、自我厌恶、自暴自弃，却不会把人带到神面前，最后「叫人死」。

新约中有两个人，都在主受难的那一夜犯了大罪。彼得三次不认主，「主转过身来看彼得……他就出去痛哭」（路22:61-62）；后来复活的主三次问他「你爱我吗」，把他挽回过来（约21:15-17）。犹大卖了主，后来也「后悔」，承认「我卖了无辜之人的血是有罪了」（太27:3-4），可是他没有回到主那里去。两个人都很痛苦，但一个人的痛苦把他带回到主面前，另一个人的痛苦却叫他离开了主。（马太在这里用的「后悔」，和保罗在林后7:8说自己「懊悔」是同一个词。可见分别不在用词，而在于这忧愁有没有把人带回主那里。）

4. 悔改的果子。 「你看，你们依着神的意思忧愁，从此就生出何等的殷勤、自诉、自恨、恐惧、想念、热心、责罚。」（林后7:11）真实的悔改不只是心里难过，也会结出行动：认真处理罪（殷勤），愿意澄清（自诉），对罪的愤恨（自恨；这里不是厌弃自己这个人，而是对那件罪的义愤），存敬畏的心（恐惧，可能是怕保罗带着刑杖来，参林前4:21，也是敬畏神），想念和热心（都是向着保罗，参林后7:7），以及按公义处理犯错的人（责罚，参林后2:6）。

5. 信的目的。 「我虽然从前写信给你们，却不是为那亏负人的，也不是为那受人亏负的，乃要在神面前把你们顾念我们的热心表明出来。」（林后7:12）保罗写信最终的目的，不是只为处理一个人的问题，而是要整个教会在神面前看清楚自己的心。

要点：世俗的忧愁只为后果和面子难过，最后叫人离开神；依着神的意思忧愁，却把人带到神面前，生出悔改，以致得救。真实的悔改不只是难过，也会结出行动的果子；而领我们走上这条路的，是神的恩慈，不是我们对自己的惩罚。
深读 7:13下-16 提多的喜乐

1. 提多心里畅快。 「并且在安慰之中，因你们众人使提多心里畅快欢喜，我们就更加欢喜了。」（林后7:13）提多大概带着那封严厉的信去了哥林多，心里很可能也很紧张。结果哥林多人接待了他，提多的心「畅快」了，原文是得了安息、重新得力的意思。

2. 夸奖的话成了真的。 「我若对提多夸奖了你们什么，也觉得没有惭愧；因我对提多夸奖你们的话成了真的，正如我对你们所说的话也都是真的。」（林后7:14）保罗在提多面前曾经称赞哥林多人。在他们最糟糕的时候，保罗仍然看见神在他们身上的工作。

3. 恐惧战兢地接待他。 「并且提多想起你们众人的顺服，是怎样恐惧战兢地接待他，他爱你们的心肠就越发热了。」（林后7:15）「恐惧战兢」不是害怕提多会伤害他们，而是在神面前认真、谦卑的态度（参腓2:12）。

4. 放心。 「我如今欢喜，能在凡事上为你们放心。」（林后7:16）第一至七章的主线到这里告一段落：关系恢复了。接下来，保罗可以放心地谈到下一个题目：为耶路撒冷圣徒的捐献。

要点：保罗在教会最糟糕的时候，仍然看见神在他们身上的工作，也敢在别人面前称赞他们。悔改带来关系的恢复，也带来彼此的喜乐。
默想

默想： 「因为依着神的意思忧愁，就生出没有后悔的懊悔来，以致得救；但世俗的忧愁是叫人死。」（林后7:10）当我犯了罪，我心里的难过是哪一种？我是否主要是因为被人发现、怕丢面子、怕承担后果而难过？我是否一遍又一遍地责备自己、讨厌自己，以为这样难过就是悔改，却始终不敢来到神面前？这样的忧愁只会叫我越陷越深。神给我的不是一条靠自我惩罚来赎罪的路，因为主耶稣已经在十字架上为我的罪受了刑罚。彼得三次不认主，复活的主却在海边为他预备了早饭，三次问他「你爱我吗」，把他挽回过来（约21:9-17）。神「丰富的恩慈」原是「领你悔改」的（罗2:4）。今天，我能不能停止在自责中打转，把那件事直接告诉神，具体地承认它，相信「我们若认自己的罪，神是信实的，是公义的，必要赦免我们的罪」（约一1:9），然后问他：主啊，我当怎样纠正、怎样修复？如果这件事伤害了别人，甚至触犯了法律，依着神的意思忧愁不会躲开后果，而会诚实地承担；但我不可以要求受伤的人马上原谅我，或者再与我亲近。彼得出去痛哭，可是眼泪不是他故事的结局；结局是岸上那堆炭火和主的呼唤。我回到主面前的时候，迎接我的不是一份罪状，而是那位已经替我受了刑罚的主。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 7 continues the appeal of chapter 6 and then picks up the story broken off at 2 Corinthians 2:13. Make room for us (vv. 2–4): Paul again asks the Corinthians to open their hearts: "you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together." Comfort through Titus (vv. 5–7): in Macedonia there was "fighting without and fear within," "but God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus." Two kinds of grief (vv. 8–13a): the severe letter grieved the Corinthians, but they "felt a godly grief" that led to repentance. Titus's joy (vv. 13b–16): because of how the Corinthians received Titus, Paul has "perfect confidence in you."

Verse 1, "Since we have these promises... let us cleanse ourselves," sums up the previous chapter and was treated there. The center of this chapter is 2 Corinthians 7:10: "For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death."

Going Deeper 7:2–4 You Are in Our Hearts

1. Make room for us. "Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one" (2 Corinthians 7:2). This picks up 2 Corinthians 6:13, "widen your hearts also." Paul defends himself, probably because some had accused him of misconduct with money. The verb "take advantage" recurs in 2 Corinthians 12:17–18: "Did Titus take advantage of you?"

2. To die together and to live together. "I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together" (2 Corinthians 7:3). This is the language of loyalty to death (cf. Ittai to David, 2 Sam 15:21, "whether for death or for life"): in life or death, never parted. That an apostle says this to a church that had hurt him shows his love is real.

3. Joy in affliction. "In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy" (2 Corinthians 7:4). Paul's joy is not the absence of affliction. It comes because God comforts him in it, and because he has seen the Corinthians turn back.

The point: Paul's love was not conditional; even after being hurt he could say, "you are in our hearts." His love reflects Christ's, who loved us and died for us while we were still sinners (Rom 5:8).
Going Deeper 7:5–7 God Who Comforts the Downcast

1. Fighting without, fear within. "For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn- fighting without and fear within" (2 Corinthians 7:5). Paul does not present himself as a hero who is never afraid. His body was tired, there was conflict outside and fear inside: fear about how the Corinthians would answer the letter, fear for Titus's safety.

2. God who comforts the downcast. "But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus" (2 Corinthians 7:6). "The downcast" means the lowly, the low in spirit, those pressed down. Isaiah says, "the LORD has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted" (Isa 49:13). In the Greek version Isaiah 49:13 says God "comforted the lowly of his people," the very word Paul uses here; Paul has just quoted the same chapter (Isa 49:8) in 2 Corinthians 6:2. God draws especially near to such people.

3. God comforts through people. "...and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more" (2 Corinthians 7:7). God's comfort often comes through people: a friend's arrival, good news, a sincere word. In chapter 1 Paul said he would comfort others "with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God" (2 Corinthians 1:4); here he himself is comforted by others. In the church, comfort is passed back and forth.

The point: God is the God "who comforts the downcast." Paul was not ashamed to admit "fear within"; God draws near precisely to those pressed down, often through a brother's arrival or a piece of good news.
Going Deeper 7:8–13a Two Kinds of Grief

1. A letter that grieved. "For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it- though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while" (2 Corinthians 7:8). After writing the letter, Paul too had regrets, worried he had said too much. Here we see a pastor's struggle: speaking the truth was right, but afterwards it still hurt.

2. Not glad that you grieved. "As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting" (2 Corinthians 7:9). Paul did not enjoy seeing others hurt. He rejoiced because the grief bore fruit: repentance. In the New Testament the word means a whole-person turning from sin to God.

3. Two kinds of grief. "For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death" (2 Corinthians 7:10).

  • Godly grief: sorrow for having sinned against God. It brings a person to God, produces repentance and leads to salvation. Most take "without regret" with repentance: no one ever regrets that kind of repentance.
  • Worldly grief: sorrow over sin's consequences, over being found out, over losing face. It looks only at oneself, not at God. It can lead to self-hatred, self-blame and giving up, but it does not bring a person to God, and in the end it "produces death."

The New Testament tells of two men who both sinned greatly on the night of the Lord's suffering. Peter denied the Lord three times, "and the Lord turned and looked at Peter... And he went out and wept bitterly" (Luke 22:61–62); later the risen Lord asked him three times, "Do you love me?" and restored him (John 21:15–17). Judas betrayed the Lord and afterwards also "changed his mind," confessing, "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood" (Matt 27:3–4), but he did not go back to the Lord. Both men were in anguish; one man's anguish brought him back to the Lord, the other's took him away from him. (Matthew's word for Judas's remorse is the same verb Paul uses of his own regret in 2 Corinthians 7:8, so the difference is not in the word but in whether the grief turned the man back to the Lord.)

4. The fruit of repentance. "For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment!" (2 Corinthians 7:11). Real repentance is not only feeling bad; it bears fruit in action: dealing with sin seriously (earnestness), willingness to set things straight (eagerness to clear yourselves), anger at sin (indignation; not loathing oneself, but being angry at the sin itself), fear (perhaps of Paul's coming "with a rod," and of God; cf. 1 Cor 4:21), longing and zeal (both directed toward Paul, cf. 2 Corinthians 7:7), and punishment, that is, justice carried out on the offender (cf. 2 Corinthians 2:6).

5. The letter's purpose. "So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God" (2 Corinthians 7:12). Paul's ultimate aim was not only to deal with one man's problem but for the whole church to see its own heart clearly before God.

The point: Worldly grief mourns only consequences and lost face, and in the end draws us away from God. Godly grief brings us to God and produces repentance that leads to salvation. Real repentance is more than sorrow; it bears fruit in action, and what leads us there is God's kindness, not our punishing ourselves.
Going Deeper 7:13b–16 Titus's Joy

1. Titus refreshed. "And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all" (2 Corinthians 7:13). Titus had probably carried the severe letter to Corinth, and was likely anxious. In the end the Corinthians received him, and his spirit was "refreshed," given rest and renewed strength.

2. Boasting proved true. "For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true" (2 Corinthians 7:14). Paul had praised the Corinthians to Titus. Even at their worst, Paul could still see God's work in them.

3. Received with fear and trembling. "And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling" (2 Corinthians 7:15). "Fear and trembling" does not mean they were afraid Titus would harm them. It describes a serious and humble attitude before God (cf. Phil 2:12).

4. Confidence. "I rejoice, because I have perfect confidence in you" (2 Corinthians 7:16). This sentence closes the main thread of chapters 1–7: the relationship has been restored. Next Paul can turn with confidence to his next subject, the collection for the saints in Jerusalem.

The point: At the church's worst, Paul could still see God's work in them and dared to praise them to others. Repentance brings restored relationships and shared joy.
Meditation

Reflect: "For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death" (2 Corinthians 7:10). When I have sinned, which kind of grief do I feel? Am I sorry mainly because I was found out, because I am afraid of losing face or of facing the consequences? Do I blame and despise myself again and again, thinking that feeling bad is the same as repenting, yet never dare to come to God? That kind of grief only pulls me deeper. God has not given me a way of paying for sin by punishing myself, because the Lord Jesus has already borne the punishment for my sin on the cross. Peter denied the Lord three times, yet the risen Lord made him breakfast by the shore, asked him three times, "Do you love me?" and restored him (John 21:9–17). "God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance" (Rom 2:4). Today, can I stop going round in circles of self-blame, tell God plainly about that thing, confess it specifically, believe that "if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins" (1 John 1:9), and then ask him: Lord, how should I put it right, and what needs repairing? If what I did has hurt someone, or even broken the law, godly grief does not dodge the consequences; it owns them honestly. But I may not demand that the person I hurt forgive me at once or let me close again. Peter went out and wept, but his tears were not the end of his story; the end was a charcoal fire on the shore and the Lord calling him. When I come back to the Lord, what meets me is not a charge sheet but the Lord who has already borne my punishment.

entries.day_label: 哥林多后书 · 第 8 / 13 章
entries.title: 他本来富足，却为你们成了贫穷
entries.title_en: Though He Was Rich, He Became Poor for Your Sake

verse_parts.text: 你们知道我们主耶稣基督的恩典：他本来富足，却为你们成了贫穷，叫你们因他的贫穷，可以成为富足。

entries.verse_text: 你们知道我们主耶稣基督的恩典：他本来富足，却为你们成了贫穷，叫你们因他的贫穷，可以成为富足。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第八、九两章讲的是同一件事：为耶路撒冷穷困的圣徒捐钱。第八章有三段。马其顿众教会的榜样（1-7节）：他们「在极穷之间还格外显出他们乐捐的厚恩」，因为他们「先把自己献给主」。基督的恩典与均平的原则（8-15节）：「他本来富足，却为你们成了贫穷」；捐献要照「所有的」，不是照「所无的」；「多收的也没有余；少收的也没有缺」。诚实地处理钱财（16-24节）：保罗派提多和两位弟兄一同去办这事，「免得有人因我们收的捐银很多，就挑我们的不是」。

保罗在这一章里很少直接提「钱」，却一再用「恩」这个词（林后8:1、4、6、7、9、16、19，和合本译作「恩」「恩情」「慈惠的事」「恩典」「多谢」「捐资」；第九章8、14、15节又出现，连最后一句「感谢神」也是这个词）。在保罗看来，捐献不是筹款，而是恩典在人身上流动的结果。

深读 8:1-7 先把自己献给主

1. 这次捐献的背景。 耶路撒冷的信徒很穷，原因可能有几个：早年的饥荒带来长期的困难（徒11:28-30，那时安提阿教会已经送过一次救济）；信徒受逼迫；许多人被家人和社会排斥。耶路撒冷的使徒曾嘱咐保罗「记念穷人」（加2:10）。保罗多年来在外邦教会中为这事募捐（林前16:1-4；罗15:25-27；参徒24:17）。这不只是救济，也是外邦教会与犹太信徒彼此相连的记号：「外邦人既然在他们属灵的好处上有分，就当把养身之物供给他们。」（罗15:27）

2. 神赐的恩。 「弟兄们，我把神赐给马其顿众教会的恩告诉你们。」（林后8:1）马其顿的教会包括腓立比、帖撒罗尼迦和庇哩亚。保罗没有说「马其顿人很慷慨」，而是说这是「神赐给」他们的恩。慷慨本身就是恩典的果子。

3. 极穷之中的厚恩。 「就是他们在患难中受大试炼的时候，仍有满足的快乐，在极穷之间还格外显出他们乐捐的厚恩。」（林后8:2）这些教会自己正在受逼迫（帖前1:6；腓1:29-30），而且非常穷。按常理，患难加上贫穷，只会叫人抓紧手里的东西；可是再加上喜乐，结果竟是慷慨。

4. 再三地求我们。 「我可以证明，他们是按着力量，而且也过了力量，自己甘心乐意地捐助，再三地求我们，准他们在这供给圣徒的恩情上有分。」（林后8:3-4）保罗原本大概不好意思向这么穷的教会募捐，反倒是他们「再三地求」保罗，让他们有份。

5. 先把自己献给主。 「并且他们所做的，不但照我们所想望的，更照神的旨意先把自己献给主，又归附了我们。」（林后8:5）这是一切慷慨的根源：先把自己献给主。人若先把自己交给主，钱财就不再是他的主人。

要点：慷慨是神赐的恩典，不是人天生的美德。马其顿的信徒在患难和极穷之中仍然乐意捐献，因为他们先把自己献给了主。
深读 8:8-15 基督的恩典与均平

1. 不是吩咐。 「我说这话，不是吩咐你们，乃是藉着别人的热心试验你们爱心的实在。」（林后8:8）保罗是使徒，本可以下命令，但他不这样做。被强迫的捐献不是爱。

2. 基督的恩典。 「你们知道我们主耶稣基督的恩典：他本来富足，却为你们成了贫穷，叫你们因他的贫穷，可以成为富足。」（林后8:9）这是全章的中心，也是保罗劝人捐献的真正理由。

  • 「本来富足」： 指基督在成为人以前与父同享的荣耀（约17:5；腓2:6）。
  • 「成了贫穷」： 指他道成肉身（他成了人，却没有停止作神），生在马槽，一生「没有枕头的地方」（太8:20），最后在十字架上替我们的罪受死（林后5:21；腓2:7-8）。
  • 「可以成为富足」： 这里的富足不是指钱财，而是指罪得赦免、与神和好、作神的儿女、得着永远的产业。有人用这节经文说信耶稣一定会发财，这完全误解了保罗（参林后9:11）：保罗自己「似乎贫穷，却是叫许多人富足」（林后6:10）。

保罗不是用罪疚感，也不是用别人的眼光来推动捐献，而是用基督的恩典：你们已经从他的贫穷中得着了这么大的富足，现在也可以让别人从你们的富余中得着帮助。

3. 照你们所有的。 「如今就当办成这事。既有愿做的心，也当照你们所有的去办成。因为人若有愿做的心，必蒙悦纳，乃是照他所有的，并不是照他所无的。」（林后8:11-12）哥林多人一年前就开始了，后来停了下来，大概是因为与保罗的关系出了问题。保罗劝他们完成。同时他说得很清楚：神看的是愿意的心，不是数目。教会不可以要人借钱奉献，不可以叫穷人觉得自己捐得少就低人一等，也不可以用「奉献越多，神越祝福」的话给人压力，也不宜在周报上公布奉献芳名和数目，叫人彼此比较。

4. 均平。 「我原不是要别人轻省，你们受累，乃要均平，就是要你们的富余，现在可以补他们的不足，使他们的富余，将来也可以补你们的不足，这就均平了。」（林后8:13-14）「均平」不是要所有人的财产都一样，也不是强制的平均分配，而是彼此补足：今天你有余，就补别人的不足；明天别人有余，也会补你的不足。「他们的富余，将来也可以补你们的不足」，有人理解为将来物质上的回报，也有人照罗15:27理解为外邦人从耶路撒冷得着的属灵好处；无论哪一种，原则都是彼此补足。

5. 吗哪。 「如经上所记：多收的也没有余；少收的也没有缺。」（林后8:15）这句话引自出16:18。以色列人在旷野收吗哪，神叫每个人都够用，多收的没有余，少收的也不缺；想留到第二天的，就生虫变臭了（出16:16-20）。神是供应的神；他的百姓也要彼此分享，像同一家人一样。

要点：捐献的真正动力是基督的恩典：他本来富足，却为我们成了贫穷。神看的是愿意的心，不是数目；信徒彼此补足，就像旷野中人人都有吗哪。
深读 8:16-24 在人面前也行光明的事

1. 提多。 「多谢神，感动提多的心，叫他待你们殷勤，像我一样。」（林后8:16）提多刚从哥林多回来，现在又自愿回去办这事。

2. 一位有名的弟兄。 「我们还打发一位兄弟和他同去，这人在福音上得了众教会的称赞。不但这样，他也被众教会挑选，和我们同行。」（林后8:18-19）这位弟兄是谁，保罗没有说。有些早期教父猜测是路加（如俄利根、耶柔米），屈梭多模提到路加或巴拿巴，但都只是推测。重要的是，他是「被众教会挑选」的，不是保罗自己指定的。

3. 免得有人挑我们的不是。 「这就免得有人因我们收的捐银很多，就挑我们的不是。我们留心行光明的事，不但在主面前，就在人面前也是这样。」（林后8:20-21）保罗知道，钱是最容易引起怀疑的地方，所以他刻意让几个人一起经手，而且其中有教会选出来的代表。保罗这句话几乎逐字取自箴3:4的七十士译本（旧约希腊文译本），那里说要在主和人面前留心行美善的事（和合本照希伯来文译作「在神和世人眼前蒙恩宠」）。他在罗12:17也说：「众人以为美的事要留心去做。」对神诚实是根本，但在人面前也要做到清清楚楚。

4. 今天的提醒。 教会处理钱财，也应当：

  • 由多人共同经手，不由一个人独自管理；
  • 账目公开、定期查核；
  • 让会众知道钱用在哪里。

华人教会常碍于人情和面子，不好意思查账、不好意思过问。其实这样做不是不信任同工，而是保护同工，也免得神的名受羞辱。这也适用于小组、团契的经费，或者替人代收的钱：再小的数目，也找另一个人一同点算、留下记录，叫人在钱上看见的是基督的诚实，不是我们的精明。

要点：保罗处理钱财时，不但在主面前，也在人面前行光明的事。教会今天也要用透明、多人经手和公开查账来保护同工，并且荣耀主的名。
默想

默想： 「你们知道我们主耶稣基督的恩典：他本来富足，却为你们成了贫穷，叫你们因他的贫穷，可以成为富足。」（林后8:9）我是否常常觉得「等我有余了再说」：等房贷还完、孩子读完书、生意稳定、退休金存够了，才谈得上慷慨？我心底是不是总怕钱不够用，好像只要一松手，生活就会垮掉？马其顿的信徒在极穷之间仍然乐意捐献，不是因为他们不怕穷，而是因为他们「先把自己献给主」，相信神是那位叫旷野中「少收的也没有缺」的神。主耶稣也不是从他的富余里分一点给我；他为我放下天上的荣耀，成了贫穷，甚至舍了自己的性命。神不是看数目，而是看「愿做的心」（林后8:12）。今天，我能不能把我对钱的惧怕带到神面前，向他承认我常常靠钱、不靠他，然后先把自己重新献给主？然后，我可以安静地问他：我所有的，有哪些是他要我拿出来，与有需要的人分享的？如果我现在真的入不敷出、背着债，神并不要我照「所无的」去给（林后8:12）；我可以先把这份窘迫老实告诉他。无论我能给多少，我都已经因主的贫穷成了富足：罪得赦免，作了神的儿女。这份富足，没有人能从我手里拿走。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapters 8 and 9 deal with one subject: the collection for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem. Chapter 8 has three parts. The example of the Macedonian churches (vv. 1–7): "their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity," because "they gave themselves first to the Lord." The grace of Christ and the principle of fairness (vv. 8–15): "though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor"; giving is "according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have"; "Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack." Handling money with integrity (vv. 16–24): Paul sends Titus and two brothers to handle it, "so that no one should blame us about this generous gift."

In this chapter Paul hardly uses the word "money," but again and again uses the word "grace" (charis, 2 Corinthians 8:1, 4, 6, 7, 9, 16, 19; the ESV renders it "grace," "favor," "act of grace," "thanks"; it returns in 2 Corinthians 9:8, 14, 15, where even "Thanks be to God" is charis). For him giving is not fundraising but the result of grace flowing through people.

Going Deeper 8:1–7 They Gave Themselves First to the Lord

1. The background of the collection. The believers in Jerusalem were poor, probably because of lasting hardship after the earlier famine (Acts 11:28–30, when Antioch had already sent relief), persecution, and the rejection many faced from family and society. The Jerusalem apostles had asked Paul to "remember the poor" (Gal 2:10). For years Paul gathered this collection in the Gentile churches (1 Cor 16:1–4; Rom 15:25–27; cf. Acts 24:17). It was more than relief; it was a sign binding the Gentile churches to Jewish believers: "For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings" (Rom 15:27).

2. The grace of God given. "We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia" (2 Corinthians 8:1). The Macedonian churches included Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. Paul does not say "the Macedonians are generous." He says it is "the grace of God... given" to them. Generosity itself is the fruit of grace.

3. Generosity in extreme poverty. "...for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part" (2 Corinthians 8:2). These churches were themselves being persecuted (1 Thess 1:6; Phil 1:29–30), and they were very poor. Yet affliction plus poverty, with joy, overflowed in generosity.

4. Begging us earnestly. "For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own free will, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints" (2 Corinthians 8:3–4). Paul was probably reluctant to ask such poor churches. It was they who begged him to let them take part.

5. Themselves first to the Lord. "...and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us" (2 Corinthians 8:5). This is the root of all generosity: giving ourselves first to the Lord. When people give themselves to the Lord first, money is no longer their master.

The point: Generosity is a gift of God's grace, not a natural virtue. The Macedonian believers gave gladly in affliction and extreme poverty because they had first given themselves to the Lord.
Going Deeper 8:8–15 The Grace of Christ and Fairness

1. Not a command. "I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine" (2 Corinthians 8:8). Paul was an apostle and could have commanded, but he did not. Forced giving is not love.

2. The grace of Christ. "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). This is the center of the chapter and Paul's real reason for urging generosity.

  • "Though he was rich": the glory Christ shared with the Father before he became man (John 17:5; Phil 2:6).
  • "He became poor": his incarnation (he became man without ceasing to be God), his birth in a manger, a life with "nowhere to lay his head" (Matt 8:20), and finally his death on the cross in our place (2 Corinthians 5:21; Phil 2:7–8).
  • "That you... might become rich": not riches of money, but forgiveness of sins, reconciliation with God, adoption as God's children and an eternal inheritance. Some use this verse to claim that believing in Jesus will make you wealthy, which completely misreads Paul. Paul himself was "poor, yet making many rich" (2 Corinthians 6:10).

Paul does not motivate giving by guilt or by what others will think, but by the grace of Christ: you have received such wealth from his poverty; now others can receive help from your abundance.

3. According to what you have. "So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have. For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have" (2 Corinthians 8:11–12). The Corinthians had begun a year earlier, then stopped, probably because of the trouble with Paul. Paul urges them to finish. At the same time he is clear: God looks at a willing heart, not at the amount. A church must not ask people to borrow in order to give, must not make the poor feel inferior because they give little, must not pressure people with "the more you give, the more God will bless you," and should not publish donors' names and amounts in the bulletin for people to compare.

4. Fairness. "I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness" (2 Corinthians 8:13–14). "Fairness" does not mean everyone must own the same, nor enforced redistribution. It means mutual supply: today you have more and supply another's need; tomorrow others may have more and supply yours. "Their abundance may supply your need" is read by some as future material help, by others (cf. Rom 15:27) as the spiritual riches Jerusalem has already given the Gentiles; either way the principle is mutual supply.

5. Manna. "As it is written, 'Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack'" (2 Corinthians 8:15). This is from Exodus 16:18. When Israel gathered manna in the wilderness, God made sure everyone had enough: those who gathered much had nothing left over, those who gathered little did not go short, and what was kept till morning bred worms (Exod 16:16–20). God is the God who provides, and his people are to share with one another like one family.

The point: The real motive for giving is the grace of Christ: though he was rich, he became poor for us. God looks at a willing heart, not the amount; believers supply one another's needs, as everyone in the wilderness had manna.
Going Deeper 8:16–24 Honorable in the Sight of Man Too

1. Titus. "But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you" (2 Corinthians 8:16). Titus had just returned from Corinth and now volunteered to go back for this.

2. A famous brother. "With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us" (2 Corinthians 8:18–19). Paul does not say who this brother was. Some early church fathers guessed Luke (Origen, Jerome); Chrysostom mentions Luke or Barnabas; but these are only guesses. What matters is that he was "appointed by the churches," not chosen by Paul himself.

3. So that no one should blame us. "We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord's sight but also in the sight of man" (2 Corinthians 8:20–21). Paul knew that money is where suspicion arises most easily, so he deliberately had several people handle it together, including representatives chosen by the churches. Paul's wording is almost exactly the Greek version of Proverbs 3:4: "take thought for what is honorable before the Lord and before men" (the Hebrew, followed by the ESV, reads "find favor... in the sight of God and man"). He uses the same phrase in Rom 12:17. Honesty before God is the root, but before people too things must be plain.

4. A word for today. A church handling money should also:

  • have several people handle it together, not one person alone;
  • keep accounts open and audit them regularly;
  • let the congregation know where the money goes.

Chinese churches often hesitate to audit or ask questions out of relational obligation and face; but this is not distrust of the workers. It protects them, and it protects God's name from dishonor. The same applies to a small-group or fellowship fund, or money collected on someone's behalf: however small the sum, count it with someone else and keep a record, so that what people see in our handling of money is Christ's honesty, not our cleverness.

The point: In handling money Paul did what was honorable not only before the Lord but before people. The church today, too, should protect its workers and honor the Lord's name by transparency, shared handling and open accounts.
Meditation

Reflect: "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). Do I often think, "I'll be generous once I have more": once the mortgage is paid off, the children have finished school, the business is stable, the retirement fund is big enough? Is there, deep down, a fear of not having enough, as though if I loosen my grip my life will fall apart? The Macedonian believers gave gladly in their extreme poverty, not because they had no fear of being poor, but because "they gave themselves first to the Lord," trusting the God by whom, in the wilderness, "whoever gathered little had no lack." The Lord Jesus did not give me a little out of his surplus. He laid aside the glory of heaven, became poor and gave up his very life. God does not look at the amount but at "the readiness" (2 Corinthians 8:12). Today, can I bring my fear about money to God, confess that I often trust money rather than him, and give myself afresh to the Lord first? After that, I can quietly ask him what, out of what I have, he wants me to share with someone in need. If I am in fact not making ends meet, or am in debt, God accepts what is given "according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have" (2 Corinthians 8:12); I can tell him honestly how tight things are. However much or little I can give, I have already become rich through the Lord's poverty: forgiven, and made a child of God. No one can take that wealth out of my hands.

entries.content:
本章脉络

第九章继续讲为耶路撒冷圣徒的捐献，有三段。预备妥当（1-5节）：保罗曾向马其顿人夸奖哥林多人「预备好了」，现在他先派弟兄们去，好叫他们所捐的「是出于乐意，不是出于勉强」。撒种与收割（6-11节）：「少种的少收，多种的多收」；「捐得乐意的人是神所喜爱的」；「神能将各样的恩惠多多地加给你们」。感谢归于神（12-15节）：这捐献不但补足圣徒的缺乏，更叫许多人感谢神、为他们祷告。全章以一句赞美结束：「感谢神，因他有说不尽的恩赐！」

第八章的中心是基督的恩典（林后8:9），第九章的结尾是神说不尽的恩赐（林后9:15）。保罗讲钱，从头到尾都在讲恩典。

深读 9:1-5 出于乐意，不是出于勉强

1. 不必写信。 「论到供给圣徒的事，我不必写信给你们；因为我知道你们乐意的心，常对马其顿人夸奖你们，说亚该亚人预备好了，已经有一年了。」（林后9:1-2）哥林多人一开始很热心，他们的热心「激动了许多人」，这里指的就是马其顿人。可是后来他们停了下来。保罗一面用哥林多人激励马其顿人（林后9:2），一面又用马其顿人激励哥林多人（林后8:1-5）。

2. 免得夸奖落空。 「万一有马其顿人与我同去，见你们没有预备，就叫我们所确信的，反成了羞愧；你们羞愧，更不用说了。」（林后9:4）保罗说得很坦白，还带点幽默。他提到羞愧，却点到为止，只是提醒他们兑现当初的承诺；他先派弟兄去，正是不想让捐献变成当众的压力。

3. 不是勒索。 「因此，我想不得不求那几位弟兄先到你们那里去，把从前所应许的捐资预备妥当，就显出你们所捐的是出于乐意，不是出于勉强。」（林后9:5）这里的「勉强」，原文是「贪心」这个词（和林后9:7的「勉强」不是同一个词），与林后7:2、林后12:17-18的「占便宜」同一个字根。有人理解为被人硬要、勒索出来的捐款，也有人理解为捐的人因为贪心舍不得而勉强给的。与它相对的「乐意」，原文是「祝福」。保罗先派人去，是为了让他们有时间安静地预备，免得他到了，大家才被迫当众凑钱。

要点：保罗要捐献出于乐意，不是出于勉强；这份礼物原文叫作祝福，是恩典的流露，不是被挤出来的钱。所以他提醒哥林多人兑现承诺，提到羞愧也只是点到为止，并且刻意避免用当众的场面去逼人。
深读 9:6-11 撒种与收割

1. 少种少收，多种多收。 「「少种的少收，多种的多收」，这话是真的。」（林后9:6）这是农夫都懂的道理（参箴11:24-25）。但保罗不是在说「奉献是一种投资，捐得越多，赚得越多」。他接下来说明，收成是什么，又是为了什么。

2. 随本心所酌定的。 「各人要随本心所酌定的，不要作难，不要勉强，因为捐得乐意的人是神所喜爱的。」（林后9:7）

  • 「随本心所酌定的」： 是在神面前想清楚、自己决定的，不是被情绪煽动，不是看别人捐多少，也不是像包红包、随礼那样，按人情和场面定一个体面的数目。
  • 「不要作难」： 不是心里难过、舍不得地捐。
  • 「不要勉强」： 不是因为压力、面子或罪疚感。
  • 「捐得乐意的人」： 这句话来自箴22:8。七十士译本（旧约希腊文译本）在这一节多了一句（希伯来原文和和合本都没有），说神赐福给乐意施舍的人；保罗把这里换成了「喜爱」。神喜爱的不是数目，而是一颗因恩典而喜乐的心。这不是说神只爱乐意捐的人；在我们还舍不得、还是罪人的时候，他已经爱了我们。「我们爱，因为神先爱我们」（约一4:19）；乐意是他的爱在我们心里结的果子，不是换取他的爱的条件。

3. 神能。 「神能将各样的恩惠多多地加给你们，使你们凡事常常充足，能多行各样善事。」（林后9:8）这一节里有一连串的「各样」「凡事」「常常」。神不是吝啬的神。「充足」原文是哲学家常用的词，意思是自给自足、不需要依靠别人；保罗却说，真正的充足是从神来的，而且是为了「多行各样善事」，不是为了囤积。

4. 他的仁义存到永远。 「如经上所记：他施舍钱财，周济贫穷；他的仁义存到永远。」（林后9:9）这是诗112:9。那篇诗描写一个敬畏神的人：他慷慨施舍，他的义行会长存。多数解经家认为这里的「他」是慷慨的信徒；也有人认为保罗指的是神自己（林后9:8、10的主语都是神，参诗111:3）。这里的「仁义」是指义的行为，不是叫人称义的义；我们因信基督白白称义，慷慨是这恩典结出的果子。

5. 那赐种给撒种的。 「那赐种给撒种的，赐粮给人吃的，必多多加给你们种地的种子，又增添你们仁义的果子。」（林后9:10）这句话来自赛55:10（「使撒种的有种，使要吃的有粮」），「仁义的果子」也让人想起何10:12（七十士译本）。是神给种子，也是神叫它生长。我们所施舍的，原本就是从神来的。

6. 富足是为了施舍。 「叫你们凡事富足，可以多多施舍，就藉着我们使感谢归于神。」（林后9:11）神叫人富足的目的，是「可以多多施舍」，最后「使感谢归于神」。今天有些教导说，你捐钱给教会（或给某位传道人），神就会叫你发大财，这就是所谓的成功神学：把神当作投资的工具，和庙里烧香许愿、求财还愿的心态没有两样，完全违背了保罗的意思。神所应许的收成，首先是「仁义的果子」，是使人有能力继续行善，而不是让人满足贪心。

要点：神喜爱捐得乐意的人。他先爱了我们；我们所给的，原本就是神所赐的；神叫我们充足，是为了让我们多行善事，使感谢归于神，而不是为了让我们囤积或发财。
深读 9:12-15 感谢归于神

1. 不只是补足缺乏。 「因为办这供给的事，不但补圣徒的缺乏，而且叫许多人越发感谢神。」（林后9:12）捐献有两个果效：一个是实际的帮助，一个是属灵的果子，叫许多人感谢神。

2. 顺服福音的凭据。 「他们从这供给的事上得了凭据，知道你们承认基督顺服他的福音，多多地捐钱给他们和众人，便将荣耀归与神。」（林后9:13）耶路撒冷的犹太信徒中，有些人可能怀疑外邦信徒是否真的信了主；保罗也请罗马的信徒为他祷告，叫这捐项「可蒙圣徒悦纳」（罗15:31）。这份捐献会成为一个凭据：这些外邦人真是「承认基督」的人。慷慨是福音真实的见证。

3. 彼此想念，彼此代祷。 「他们也因神极大的恩赐显在你们心里，就切切地想念你们，为你们祈祷。」（林后9:14）犹太信徒和外邦信徒，过去彼此隔阂，保罗盼望他们因为这份捐献而彼此想念、彼此代祷。钱财在这里成了合一的桥梁。基督「拆毁了中间隔断的墙」（弗2:14），这份捐献，就是这道墙被拆毁的一个具体见证。

4. 说不尽的恩赐。 「感谢神，因他有说不尽的恩赐！」（林后9:15）保罗讲了两章的捐献，最后却不是讲人的慷慨，而是讲神的恩赐。这「说不尽的恩赐」，最自然的理解是神赐下他的儿子（参林后8:9；约3:16；罗8:32）。我们一切的施舍，都只是对这恩赐小小的回应。

要点：捐献不只补足人的缺乏，也叫人感谢神，使不同背景的信徒在基督里合一。一切的起点和终点，都是神那说不尽的恩赐：他的儿子。
默想

默想： 「各人要随本心所酌定的，不要作难，不要勉强，因为捐得乐意的人是神所喜爱的。」（林后9:7）当我奉献的时候，推动我的是什么？是怕别人看见我捐得少而没有面子？是怕神不祝福我，好像在跟神做交易？是一种「我欠了」的罪疚感？还是因为我又想起，神为我所做的，说也说不尽？也许我曾在教会里感到奉献的压力，或者曾经因为面子捐了超过自己能力的钱，后来心里很不平安；也许我一直捐得很少，因为心里舍不得。无论是哪一种，背后常常是把面子或钱财看得比神更重，这需要在神面前承认。神的心意不是要我被逼，而是要我被恩典打动。神把他的独生子赐给了我，「岂不也把万物和他一同白白地赐给我们吗？」（罗8:32）今天，我能不能先不想数目，在神面前问他，我当怎样回应，再「随本心所酌定的」去行：也许是通过可靠、账目清楚的渠道，为一个远方、贫穷或受逼迫的教会献上一份心意，也为他们祷告？如果我曾经为了面子捐过了头，神并没有因此记我的账，我也不必再用钱向人证明什么。我给得多，他的恩赐不会因此变大；我给得少，也不会因此变小。保罗讲了两章的钱，最后一句却不是讲我们给了什么，而是讲神给了什么：「感谢神，因他有说不尽的恩赐！」
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 9 continues the subject of the collection for the saints in Jerusalem, in three parts. Be ready (vv. 1–5): Paul had boasted to the Macedonians that the Corinthians were ready; now he sends the brothers ahead "so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction." Sowing and reaping (vv. 6–11): "whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly"; "God loves a cheerful giver"; "God is able to make all grace abound to you." Thanksgiving to God (vv. 12–15): the gift not only supplies the saints' needs but makes many give thanks to God and pray for the givers. The chapter ends with praise: "Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!"

The center of chapter 8 is the grace of Christ (2 Corinthians 8:9); the end of chapter 9 is God's inexpressible gift (2 Corinthians 9:15). When Paul talks about money, he is talking about grace from beginning to end.

Going Deeper 9:1–5 A Willing Gift, Not an Exaction

1. No need to write. "Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year" (2 Corinthians 9:1–2). The Corinthians had begun with great zeal, and their zeal "stirred up most of them," that is, the Macedonians. But then they stopped. Paul spurs the Macedonians with the Corinthians' example (2 Corinthians 9:2) and the Corinthians with the Macedonians' (2 Corinthians 8:1–5).

2. So that our boasting is not in vain. "Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated- to say nothing of you- for being so confident" (2 Corinthians 9:4). Paul is frank here, with a touch of humor. Paul does name the prospect of shame, but lightly, reminding them to keep the commitment they made; and he sends the brothers ahead precisely so that the gift will not be wrung out under public pressure.

3. Not an exaction. "So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction" (2 Corinthians 9:5). The word behind "exaction" is the noun for greed, related to the verb "take advantage" in 2 Corinthians 7:2 and 2 Corinthians 12:17–18. Some read it as a gift squeezed out of the givers (ESV, NRSV); others as a gift given grudgingly out of the givers' own covetousness (KJV, NIV). Its opposite, "willing gift," is literally "blessing." Paul sends people ahead so they can prepare quietly, rather than being forced to scrape money together in front of everyone when he arrives.

The point: Paul wants giving to be willing, not forced; the gift is literally called a blessing, an overflow of grace, not money squeezed out. So he reminds the Corinthians to keep their promise, names shame only lightly, and deliberately avoids public pressure.
Going Deeper 9:6–11 Sowing and Reaping

1. Sow sparingly, reap sparingly. "The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully" (2 Corinthians 9:6). Every farmer knows this (cf. Prov 11:24–25). But Paul is not saying, "Giving is an investment: the more you give, the more you'll earn." He goes on to explain what the harvest is, and what it is for.

2. As he has made up his mind. "Each one must give as he has made up his mind, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7).

  • "As he has made up his mind": thought through before God and decided for oneself, not stirred up by emotion or by watching what others give, nor, as with a wedding red envelope, setting a "respectable" amount by social obligation.
  • "Not reluctantly": not giving with a sorrowful, reluctant heart.
  • "Not under compulsion": not from pressure, face or guilt.
  • "A cheerful giver": from a line the Greek version adds after Proverbs 22:8 (absent from the Hebrew and the ESV): "God blesses a cheerful and giving man." Paul changes "blesses" to "loves." God loves not the amount but a heart made glad by grace. This does not mean God loves only cheerful givers; he loved us while we were still grudging and still sinners. "We love because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19); cheerfulness is the fruit of his love in us, not the price of it.

3. God is able. "And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work" (2 Corinthians 9:8). This verse piles up "all," "all things," "at all times." God is not stingy. "Sufficiency" was a word philosophers used for self-sufficiency, not needing anyone else. Paul says true sufficiency comes from God, and it is so that we "may abound in every good work," not so that we can hoard.

4. His righteousness endures forever. "As it is written, 'He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever'" (2 Corinthians 9:9). This is Psalm 112:9, a psalm describing a man who fears God: he gives generously, and his righteous deeds endure. Most take "he" to be the generous believer; some think Paul applies it to God, the subject of 2 Corinthians 9:8 and 2 Corinthians 9:10 (cf. Ps 111:3). Either way, "righteousness" here is righteous conduct, not the righteousness by which we are justified; we are justified freely through faith in Christ, and generosity is the fruit of that grace.

5. He who supplies seed to the sower. "He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness" (2 Corinthians 9:10). This echoes Isaiah 55:10 ("giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater"), and "the harvest of your righteousness" recalls Hosea 10:12 (in the Greek version). God gives the seed and God makes it grow. What we give away came from God in the first place.

6. Enriched in order to give. "You will be enriched in every way for all your generosity, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God" (2 Corinthians 9:11). God enriches people "for all your generosity," and in the end "thanksgiving to God." Some teach today that if you give to the church (or to a certain preacher), God will make you rich. This is the so-called prosperity gospel: it treats God as an investment vehicle, no different from offering incense at a temple for wealth and repaying the vow, and it flatly contradicts Paul. The harvest God promises is first "the harvest of your righteousness," the means to keep doing good, not the satisfaction of greed.

The point: God loves a cheerful giver. He loved us first; what we give came from God; he makes us sufficient so that we can abound in good works and bring thanks to God, not so that we can hoard or get rich.
Going Deeper 9:12–15 Thanksgiving to God

1. More than meeting needs. "For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints, but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God" (2 Corinthians 9:12). The gift has two effects: practical help, and spiritual fruit, making many give thanks to God.

2. Proof of submission to the gospel. "By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission flowing from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others" (2 Corinthians 9:13). Some Jewish believers in Jerusalem may have doubted whether Gentile believers had truly come to faith; Paul asked the Romans to pray that the gift "may be acceptable to the saints" (Rom 15:31). This gift would be evidence that these Gentiles really confessed the gospel of Christ. Generosity is a witness to the reality of the gospel.

3. Longing for one another, praying for one another. "...while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you" (2 Corinthians 9:14). Jewish and Gentile believers, once divided, Paul expects that because of this gift they will long for each other and pray for each other. Money here becomes a bridge of unity. Christ "has broken down... the dividing wall" (Eph 2:14), and this gift is one concrete expression of that in daily life.

4. The inexpressible gift. "Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!" (2 Corinthians 9:15). After two chapters on giving, Paul ends not with human generosity but with God's gift. The most natural reading of this "inexpressible gift" is God's giving of his Son (cf. 2 Corinthians 8:9; John 3:16; Rom 8:32). All our giving is only a small response to this gift.

The point: Giving not only meets needs but leads people to thank God and unites believers of different backgrounds in Christ. The beginning and end of it all is God's inexpressible gift: his Son.
Meditation

Reflect: "Each one must give as he has made up his mind, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7). When I give, what moves me? Fear of losing face if others see I gave little? Fear that God won't bless me, as if I were bargaining with him? A sense of guilt, that "I owe"? Or because I have remembered once again that what God has done for me is beyond words? Perhaps I have felt pressure to give at church, or once gave more than I could afford for the sake of face, and had no peace afterwards. Perhaps I have always given very little, because I could not bear to let go. Behind either one, there is often a heart that values face or money above God, and that needs to be confessed. God's desire is not that I be forced but that I be moved by grace. God gave me his only Son; "how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?" (Rom 8:32). Today, can I set aside the question of how much and, before God, as I have made up my mind, ask him how he wants me to respond: perhaps, through a trustworthy and accountable channel, with a gift for a distant, poor or persecuted church, and with prayer for them? If I once gave beyond my means for the sake of face, God is not holding it against me, and I no longer need money to prove anything to anyone. If I give much, his gift does not grow larger; if I give little, it does not grow smaller. Paul spent two chapters on money, but his last sentence is not about what we give. It is about what God has given: "Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!"
