entries.content:
本章脉络

第四章是全信的结尾，有四段。在主里同心（2-3节）：保罗劝友阿蝶和循都基两位姊妹在主里同心（她们曾在福音上与他一同劳苦），也请一位同工帮助她们。喜乐、平安和思念（4-9节）：要靠主常常喜乐；当叫众人知道你们谦让的心；应当一无挂虑，凡事藉着祷告、祈求和感谢告诉神，神的平安必保守你们；凡是真实的、可敬的……都要思念，并且去行。知足的秘诀（10-20节）：保罗为腓立比人的馈送感谢神，他已经学会了无论在什么景况都可以知足，因为「我靠着那加给我力量的，凡事都能做」；神必照他荣耀的丰富，使他们一切所需用的都充足。问安和祝福（21-23节）：连凯撒家里的人也问他们安。

全章贯穿着两个词：「主」和「平安」。在主里同心，靠主喜乐，主已经近了；神的平安保守我们，赐平安的神与我们同在。

深读 4:2-3 要在主里同心

1. 点名劝勉。 「我劝友阿蝶和循都基，要在主里同心」（腓4:2）。保罗在一封要公开宣读的信里点了两个人的名字，可见她们的不和已经影响到教会。但原文里保罗对两个人各说了一次「我劝」，没有偏袒哪一方，也没有说谁对谁错。

2. 她们是同工。 「因为她们在福音上曾与我一同劳苦」（腓4:3）。「一同劳苦」和腓1:27「齐心努力」是同一个词，有并肩作战的意思。这两位姊妹不是爱闹事的人，而是曾和保罗一起为福音拼搏的同工。腓立比的教会是从河边一群妇女开始的（徒16:13-15），妇女在这个教会里一直有重要的服事。忠心的同工也可能闹不和；不和不能抹去她们过去的劳苦，但也不能放着不管。

3. 「在主里」同心。 和合本译作「同心」的这个词，就是腓2:2、腓2:5的「心」（思念、存心）。保罗不是只要她们表面上握手言和，而是要她们一同「以基督耶稣的心为心」（腓2:5）。合一的根基不是谁让步了，而是她们都在主里。

4. 「真实同负一轭的」。 「我也求你这真实同负一轭的，帮助这两个女人」（腓4:3）。这个人是谁，解经家有不同看法：有人认为是路加，有人认为是以巴弗提或西拉，也有人认为「同负一轭的」原文是一个人名（叙西古）。无论是谁，保罗都请第三个人来帮助她们和好。弟兄姊妹之间的冲突，有时需要一个可信、成熟的人在中间帮助。

5. 名字都在生命册上。 「他们的名字都在生命册上」（腓4:3；参启3:5；出32:32-33；诗69:28；但12:1）。这话直接说的是腓4:3提到的革利免和其余同工，但这两位姊妹既然和他们一同劳苦，自然也包括在内。她们在神面前的身份，比她们之间的分歧更深、更确实。

6. 和好不等于掩盖伤害。 这两位姊妹的不和，看起来是同工之间的分歧。但如果冲突牵涉到虐待、欺压或犯罪，教会就不可只是叫双方「在主里同心」。向警方或法庭举报是对的（罗13:4）；受害的人不必留在危险中，也不必和仍不安全的人和好；饶恕不等于恢复犯错者的职分，也不等于让他再接近受害者或孩子；教会更不可为了「家丑不可外扬」而遮掩。

要点：教会里忠心的同工也会不和。保罗不偏袒，也不放任，而是提醒她们：你们都在主里，和众同工一样名字都在生命册上，所以要以基督的心为心。
深读 4:4-7 靠主喜乐，一无挂虑

1. 靠主常常喜乐。 「你们要靠主常常喜乐。我再说，你们要喜乐」（腓4:4）。保罗说「常常」，又说「我再说」，也许是因为他知道这不容易。这里的关键是「靠主」：不是靠环境喜乐，而是在主里喜乐。环境会变，主不变。喜乐可以被吩咐，因为它不只是一种情绪，更是把眼光转向主的结果；但这不是说信徒不可以忧伤（参腓2:27；罗12:15）。

2. 谦让的心。 「当叫众人知道你们谦让的心。主已经近了」（腓4:5）。「谦让」这个词很难翻译，可以指宽容、温和、通情达理、不坚持自己的权利。信徒为什么能不坚持自己的权利？因为「主已经近了」。

  • 「主已经近了」的两种理解： 一种是时间上的近，主快要再来了（参腓3:20）；一种是空间上的近，主就在我们身边（参诗145:18）。两种意思都合乎圣经，保罗可能有意兼含这两层意思。
  • 为什么不必争： 如果主快要来，一切都要在他面前显明，我就不必现在拼命为自己争；如果主就在身边，我就不必怕被人占便宜。（这不是叫受虐待或被欺压的人放弃保护自己；寻求法律和教会的帮助，正是把案子交给公义的主。）

3. 应当一无挂虑。 「应当一无挂虑，只要凡事藉着祷告、祈求，和感谢，将你们所要的告诉神」（腓4:6）。

  • 「一无挂虑」： 这和耶稣说的「不要为生命忧虑」（太6:25）是同一个词。这不是叫我们不负责任、不去计划，而是不让忧虑掌管我们的心。
  • 「凡事」： 挂虑的反面不是什么都不想，而是把「凡事」都带到神面前。没有一件事太小，也没有一件事太大。
  • 「和感谢」： 一边把需要告诉神，一边感谢他，就是提醒自己：这位神过去是信实的，他现在也在听。
  • 焦虑症不是信心小： 有些人的焦虑是一种需要医治的病。这节经文不是说他们灵性不好；寻求医生和专业辅导的帮助，和祷告并不冲突。

4. 神的平安必保守。 「神所赐、出人意外的平安必在基督耶稣里保守你们的心怀意念」（腓4:7）。

  • 「出人意外」： 这平安超过人的理解。也就是说，问题也许还没有解决，人看不出你为什么能平安，但神的平安已经在那里。
  • 「保守」： 这是一个军事用语，意思是驻军看守。腓立比是罗马安置退伍军人的殖民地，城里的人很熟悉士兵站岗守卫的景象。神的平安就像一支驻军，守住我们的心和思想，不让忧虑攻进来。
  • 「在基督耶稣里」： 这平安不是一种心理技巧，而是因为我们在基督里，已经与神和好（罗5:1）。
要点：信徒可以不被忧虑掌管，不是因为问题都解决了，而是因为主已经近了。我们把凡事带着感谢告诉神，神的平安就在基督里守住我们的心。
深读 4:8-9 这些事你们都要思念

1. 八样美好的事。 「凡是真实的、可敬的、公义的、清洁的、可爱的、有美名的，若有什么德行，若有什么称赞，这些事你们都要思念」（腓4:8）。

  • 用了当时人熟悉的词： 其中好几个词是当时希腊哲学家讲道德时常用的。保罗的意思不是说，外邦人的道德就等于福音，而是说：凡是真正美好的东西，都是从神来的，信徒都可以欣赏、可以思想。华人文化也看重德行，儒家讲修身、讲仁义；凡是真实的美德都可以欣赏，但人不能靠修身成为义人，只有在基督里才有从神而来的义（腓3:9）。
  • 「思念」： 这不只是想一想，而是反复思想，让这些事在心里扎根。我们心里常想什么，慢慢就会成为什么样的人。
  • 真实、可爱最完全的体现，就是基督自己： 我们思念这些美好的事，最终会被带到那位一切美善的源头面前。

2. 去行出来。 「你们在我身上所学习的，所领受的，所听见的，所看见的，这些事你们都要去行，赐平安的神就必与你们同在」（腓4:9）。思念要带出行动。腓4:7说神所赐的平安，腓4:9说「赐平安的神」：我们不只是得着平安，更有赐平安的神亲自与我们同在。

要点：基督是一切真实、可爱之事的源头；我们越思念他所造的美好，就越被他吸引，越像他。赐平安的神也必与我们同在。
深读 4:10-20 我已经学会了知足

1. 不是因为缺乏。 「我并不是因缺乏说这话；我无论在什么景况都可以知足，这是我已经学会了」（腓4:11）。保罗感谢腓立比人的馈送，却很小心，不让他们以为他在暗示要他们再送。

  • 「知足」： 这个词是当时斯多亚派哲学家常用的，意思是不受外在环境左右，靠自己就够了。保罗用了这个词，却改变了它的意思：他的知足不是靠自己，而是靠基督（腓4:13）。
  • 「学会了」： 知足不是天生的，而是学来的，而且是在「处卑贱」和「处丰富」两种景况里都学（腓4:12）。丰富的时候也需要学知足，因为富足同样会叫人忘记神（箴30:8-9）。
  • 「秘诀」： 这个词原本用于当时神秘宗教的入门礼，指被引进、得知奥秘。保罗说，他已经得知了知足的秘诀，下一节就告诉我们这秘诀是什么。

2. 凡事都能做。 「我靠着那加给我力量的，凡事都能做」（腓4:13）。

  • 上下文： 这句话常被人用在考试、比赛、做生意上，好像是说信主的人想做什么都能成功。但从上下文看，「凡事」是指腓4:12的各种景况：饱足或饥饿，有余或缺乏。保罗的意思是：无论在什么景况中，我都能靠基督知足、忠心地活着。
  • 「那加给我力量的」： 秘诀不在于保罗自己有多坚强，而在于基督不断地加给他力量（参林后12:9）。

3. 同受患难原是美事。 「然而，你们和我同受患难原是美事」（腓4:14）。保罗虽然知足，却没有因此轻看别人的爱心。他说「你们和我同受患难」，用的是腓1:5「同心合意」的那个字根（腓4:15「授受的事」也是）：腓立比人送钱，就是和保罗同担他的患难。

4. 极美的香气。 「我已经充足，因我从以巴弗提受了你们的馈送，当作极美的香气，为神所收纳、所喜悦的祭物」（腓4:18）。

  • 馈送是献给神的： 腓立比人是在帮助保罗，保罗却说，这同时是献给神的「祭物」（参腓2:17；来13:16）。
  • 「归在你们的帐上」： 「我并不求什么馈送，所求的就是你们的果子渐渐增多，归在你们的帐上」（腓4:17）。保罗又用了记账的词（参腓3:7-8）。他高兴的不是自己得了什么，而是腓立比人在神面前的果子增多了。
  • 腓立比人自己并不富裕： 保罗在别处说，马其顿众教会「在极穷之间还格外显出他们乐捐的厚恩」（林后8:2）。

5. 神必使你们充足。 「我的神必照他荣耀的丰富，在基督耶稣里，使你们一切所需用的都充足」（腓4:19）。

  • 「我的神」： 保罗用的是很个人的称呼：供应过我的那位神，也会供应你们。
  • 「所需用的」： 是「需用的」，不是「想要的」。这不是成功神学（富足福音）所应许的那种保证，保罗自己也经历过饥饿和缺乏（腓4:12）。
  • 「照他荣耀的丰富」： 不是「从」他的丰富中拿一点出来，而是「照着」他的丰富，按他丰富的尺度来供应。
  • 「在基督耶稣里」： 神最大的供应，就是基督自己。

6. 愿荣耀归给父神。 「愿荣耀归给我们的父神，直到永永远远。阿们！」（腓4:20）。一段关于钱的话，结尾却是颂赞。一切的供应，最终都是为了神的荣耀。

要点：知足的秘诀不在于环境，也不在于自己有多坚强，而在于基督不断加给我们力量。神必照他荣耀的丰富，在基督里供应我们一切所需用的。
深读 4:21-23 凯撒家里的人

1. 凯撒家里的人。 「众圣徒都问你们安。在凯撒家里的人特特地问你们安」（腓4:22）。「凯撒家里的人」多半不是指皇帝的亲属，而是为皇帝服务的奴隶和获释的奴隶，有的在皇宫里，有的在各地的官署里。在罗马权力的中心，福音已经生了根（参腓1:13）。腓立比人知道这件事，就会得到很大的鼓励。

2. 以恩典结束。 「愿主耶稣基督的恩常在你们心里！」（腓4:23）。这封信从「恩惠、平安」开始（腓1:2），也以「恩」结束。信徒的喜乐、合一、知足，都是从基督的恩典开始，也靠基督的恩典完成。

要点：福音能进到凯撒的家里，也能进到我们的家里。这封信从恩典开始，也以恩典结束。
默想

默想： 「应当一无挂虑，只要凡事藉着祷告、祈求，和感谢，将你们所要的告诉神。神所赐、出人意外的平安必在基督耶稣里保守你们的心怀意念」（腓4:6-7）。最近让我睡不着的是什么？也许是每个月的房贷，也许是公司在裁员，也许是孩子不肯和我说话，也许是一个必须做、却不知道怎样选的决定。我常常在心里一遍又一遍地想这些事，好像想得越多，就越能控制。可是我越想越乱，越乱越怕。保罗写这句话的时候，他自己可能也面对着死刑的判决（腓1:20）。他没有说「不要想了，没事的」，而是说「凡事……告诉神」：把那些在心里打转的事，一件一件说出来，交给那位听祷告的神。（如果我的焦虑已经重到影响吃饭、睡觉和工作，寻求医生或辅导的帮助，也是神给我的恩典。）今天，我能不能拿一张纸，把挂虑的事写下来，每一件都变成一句向神的祈求？然后在每一句旁边，写下神过去曾怎样向我显出信实（不论是在这件事上，还是在别的事上），并为此感谢他。也许问题明天还在，但我不是一个人面对它。基督已经为我死了、复活了，他在父面前为我代求；在他里面，神的平安就像驻军一样守着我的心。主已经近了。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 4 closes the letter and has four parts. Agreeing in the Lord (vv. 2–3): Paul urges Euodia and Syntyche, two women who had labored with him in the gospel, to agree in the Lord, and asks a co-worker to help them. Joy, peace and right thinking (vv. 4–9): rejoice in the Lord always; let your reasonableness be known to everyone; do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God, and the peace of God will guard you; whatever is true, honorable… think about these things and practice them. The secret of contentment (vv. 10–20): Paul thanks God for the Philippians' gift; he has learned to be content in whatever situation, for "I can do all things through him who strengthens me"; God will supply every need of theirs according to his riches in glory. Greetings and blessing (vv. 21–23): even those of Caesar's household send greetings.

Two words run through the chapter: "Lord" and "peace." Agree in the Lord, rejoice in the Lord, the Lord is at hand; the peace of God will guard us, and the God of peace will be with us.

Going Deeper: 4:2–3 Agree in the Lord

1. Named in public. "I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord" (Philippians 4:2). Paul names two people in a letter to be read aloud to the church, which shows their disagreement was already affecting the church. But he uses the same verb, "I entreat," for each of them; he takes no side and does not say who is right.

2. They were co-workers. "Who have labored side by side with me in the gospel" (Philippians 4:3). "Labored side by side" is the same word as "striving side by side" in Philippians 1:27, a picture of fighting shoulder to shoulder. These two women were not troublemakers but co-workers who had contended alongside Paul for the gospel. The Philippian church began with a group of women by the river (Acts 16:13–15), and women had important ministries in this church from the start. Faithful co-workers can fall out; their quarrel does not erase their past labor, but it cannot be left alone either.

3. Agree "in the Lord." The verb translated "agree" is the same "mind" word as in Philippians 2:2 and Philippians 2:5. Paul does not want them merely to shake hands outwardly, but to share together "this mind… which is yours in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 2:5). The ground of their unity is not that one of them gives way, but that both are in the Lord.

4. "True companion." "Yes, I ask you also, true companion, help these women" (Philippians 4:3). Interpreters differ on who this is: some suggest Luke, others Epaphroditus or Silas, and some think the Greek word for "companion" (syzygos) is a proper name, Syzygus. Whoever it was, Paul asks a third person to help them be reconciled. Conflict between brothers and sisters sometimes needs a trusted, mature person to help in the middle.

5. Names in the book of life. "Whose names are in the book of life" (Philippians 4:3; see Rev 3:5; Exod 32:32–33; Ps 69:28; Dan 12:1). In the same breath, Paul says that his fellow workers' names "are in the book of life." The words refer most directly to Clement and the rest, but since these two women labored alongside them, they are surely included. Their standing before God is deeper and surer than their disagreement.

6. Reconciliation is not covering up harm. The quarrel between these two women seems to be a disagreement between co-workers. But if a conflict involves abuse, oppression or crime, the church must not simply tell both sides to "agree in the Lord." Reporting abuse or crime to the police or courts is right (Rom 13:4). Victims need not stay in danger or reconcile with someone still unsafe. Forgiveness does not restore an offender's office or give him access to victims or children. And the church must never hide abuse to save face.

The point: Faithful co-workers in a church can fall out. Paul neither takes sides nor lets it go; he reminds them that both are in the Lord, and with their fellow workers their names are in the book of life, so they are to share the mind of Christ.
Going Deeper: 4:4–7 Rejoice in the Lord, Do Not Be Anxious

1. Rejoice in the Lord always. "Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, Rejoice" (Philippians 4:4). Paul says "always" and then "again I will say," perhaps because he knows this is not easy. The key is "in the Lord": not joy in circumstances but joy in the Lord. Circumstances change; the Lord does not. Joy can be commanded because it is not merely a mood but what happens when we turn our eyes to the Lord; yet this does not mean believers may not grieve (see Philippians 2:27; Rom 12:15).

2. Reasonableness. "Let your reasonableness be known to everyone. The Lord is at hand" (Philippians 4:5). The word translated "reasonableness" is hard to render; it can mean forbearance, gentleness, not insisting on one's rights. Why can believers let go of insisting on their rights? Because "the Lord is at hand."

  • Two readings of "the Lord is at hand": near in time, soon to return (see Philippians 3:20); or near in space, beside us (see Ps 145:18). Both are biblical, and Paul may intend both.
  • Why we need not fight: if the Lord is coming soon and everything will be laid bare before him, I need not fight for myself so hard now; if the Lord is beside me, I need not fear being taken advantage of. (This does not ask anyone who is abused or oppressed to give up protecting themselves; seeking help from the law and the church is itself a way of entrusting the case to the just Lord.)

3. Do not be anxious about anything. "Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God" (Philippians 4:6).

  • "Do not be anxious": the same word Jesus used in "do not be anxious about your life" (Matt 6:25). This does not mean being irresponsible or refusing to plan, but not letting worry rule our hearts.
  • "In everything": the opposite of anxiety is not thinking about nothing, but bringing "everything" to God. Nothing is too small, and nothing too large.
  • "With thanksgiving": to thank God while telling him our needs is to remind ourselves that this God has been faithful before and is listening now.
  • An anxiety disorder is not small faith: some people's anxiety is an illness that needs treatment. This verse does not say their spiritual life is poor; seeking a doctor's and a counselor's help does not conflict with prayer.

4. The peace of God will guard you. "And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:7).

  • "Surpasses all understanding": this peace goes beyond human understanding. The problem may not be solved yet, and others may not see why you can be at peace, but God's peace is already there.
  • "Guard": a military word, meaning to keep watch as a garrison. Philippi was a Roman colony settled by army veterans, so its people knew well the picture of soldiers standing guard. God's peace is like a garrison stationed around our hearts and minds, keeping anxiety from breaking in.
  • "In Christ Jesus": this peace is not a mental technique; it comes because in Christ we are already at peace with God (Rom 5:1).
The point: Believers need not be ruled by anxiety, not because every problem has been solved, but because the Lord is at hand. When we bring everything to God with thanksgiving, his peace guards our hearts in Christ.
Going Deeper: 4:8–9 Think About These Things

1. Eight good things. "Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things" (Philippians 4:8).

  • Words people of his day knew: several of these words were common in Greek philosophers' teaching on virtue. Paul does not mean that pagan morality equals the gospel, but that everything truly good comes from God, and believers may value it and think about it. Chinese culture also prizes virtue, and Confucian teaching speaks of self-cultivation, humaneness and righteousness; every true virtue may be valued, but no one becomes righteous by self-cultivation; righteousness from God is found only in Christ (Philippians 3:9).
  • "Think about": not just a passing thought, but careful consideration that lets it shape us. What we dwell on slowly shapes who we become.
  • What is most fully true and lovely is Christ himself: as we think about these good things, they lead us in the end to the source of all goodness.

2. Practice them. "What you have learned and received and heard and seen in me—practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you" (Philippians 4:9). Thinking must lead to doing. Verse 7 speaks of "the peace of God"; verse 9 of "the God of peace." We receive not only peace but the presence of the God who gives it.

The point: Christ is the source of all that is true and lovely; the more we dwell on the good he has made, the more we are drawn to him and made like him. And the God of peace will be with us.
Going Deeper: 4:10–20 I Have Learned to Be Content

1. Not from need. "Not that I am speaking of being in need, for I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content" (Philippians 4:11). Paul thanks the Philippians for their gift but takes care that they do not think he is hinting for more.

  • "Content": the word was a favorite of the Stoic philosophers, meaning self-sufficient, untouched by outward circumstances. Paul uses the word but changes its meaning: his contentment comes not from himself but from Christ (Philippians 4:13).
  • "I have learned": contentment is not inborn but learned, and learned both when he was "brought low" and when he would "abound" (Philippians 4:12). Abundance also needs contentment to be learned, for riches can equally make us forget God (Prov 30:8–9).
  • "The secret": the Greek word was used in the religions of the day for being initiated into a mystery. Paul says he has learned the secret of contentment, and the next verse tells us what it is.

2. All things through him. "I can do all things through him who strengthens me" (Philippians 4:13).

  • The context: this verse is often applied to exams, sports or business, as if believers can succeed at whatever they attempt. But in context, "all things" means the situations of Philippians 4:12: plenty and hunger, abundance and need. Paul means that in any situation he can live content and faithful through Christ.
  • "Him who strengthens me": the secret is not how strong Paul is but that Christ keeps giving him strength (see 2 Cor 12:9).

3. Kind to share my trouble. "Yet it was kind of you to share my trouble" (Philippians 4:14). Though Paul is content, he does not make light of others' love. "Share" uses the same root as "partnership" in Philippians 1:5 (as does "entered into partnership" in Philippians 4:15): by sending money, the Philippians shared in Paul's affliction.

4. A fragrant offering. "I am well supplied, having received from Epaphroditus the gifts you sent, a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God" (Philippians 4:18).

  • The gift was given to God: the Philippians were helping Paul, and Paul says their gift was also a "sacrifice" to God (see Philippians 2:17; Heb 13:16).
  • "To your credit": "Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit that increases to your credit" (Philippians 4:17). Paul uses bookkeeping words again (see Philippians 3:7–8). He is glad not for what he has received but because the Philippians' fruit before God has increased.
  • The Philippians were not rich: elsewhere Paul says of the Macedonian churches that "in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part" (2 Cor 8:2).

5. God will supply. "And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:19).

  • "My God": Paul speaks personally: the God who has supplied me will supply you.
  • "Every need": needs, not wants. This is not a guarantee of the prosperity gospel; Paul himself knew hunger and need (Philippians 4:12).
  • "According to his riches in glory": not a little taken "from" his riches, but "according to" them, in a measure that matches his wealth.
  • "In Christ Jesus": God's greatest provision is Christ himself.

6. Glory to the Father. "To our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen" (Philippians 4:20). A passage about money ends in praise. Every provision is in the end for the glory of God.

The point: The secret of contentment is not in circumstances or in our own strength, but in Christ who keeps strengthening us. God will supply every need of ours in Christ, according to his riches in glory.
Going Deeper: 4:21–23 Caesar's Household

1. Those of Caesar's household. "All the saints greet you, especially those of Caesar's household" (Philippians 4:22). "Caesar's household" does not necessarily mean the emperor's relatives; it refers to the slaves and freedmen who served the emperor, some in the palace and some in government offices across the empire. At the center of Roman power the gospel had taken root (see Philippians 1:13). Knowing this would greatly encourage the Philippians.

2. Ending with grace. "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit" (Philippians 4:23). The letter begins with "grace… and peace" (Philippians 1:2) and ends with "grace." Believers' joy, unity and contentment all begin with the grace of Christ and are completed by it.

The point: The gospel can enter Caesar's household, and it can enter ours. This letter begins with grace and ends with grace.
Meditation

Reflect: "Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:6–7). What has been keeping me awake lately? Perhaps the monthly mortgage, perhaps layoffs at work, perhaps a child who will not talk to me, perhaps a decision I must make and do not know how to choose. I go over these things in my mind again and again, as if thinking about them more would let me control them. But the more I think, the more confused I get, and the more confused, the more afraid. When Paul wrote these words, he himself may have been facing a death sentence (Philippians 1:20). He did not say, "Stop thinking about it, it'll be fine," but "in everything… let your requests be made known to God": say aloud, one by one, the things circling in your mind, and hand them to the God who hears prayer. (If my anxiety has become heavy enough to affect my eating, sleeping and work, seeking a doctor's or counselor's help is also God's grace to me.) Today, can I take a sheet of paper, write down my worries, and turn each one into a request to God? Then beside each request, can I write one way God has shown me his faithfulness, in this matter or another, and thank him for it? The problem may still be there tomorrow, but I will not face it alone. Christ has died and risen for me and intercedes for me before the Father; in him, God's peace stands guard over my heart like a garrison. The Lord is at hand.

entries.content:
这卷书在讲什么

歌罗西书是保罗写的一封信，收信的教会他从来没有见过面（西2:1）。这个教会在一个不起眼的小城里，人数大概不多，却面对一种听起来很属灵、很有智慧的教导。那种教导没有叫人离开基督，只是暗示：单有基督还不够，你还需要更深的经历、更严的规条、更高的知识，才能得着真正的丰盛。

保罗的回答贯穿全信：基督已经是一切。「爱子是那不能看见之神的像」，「万有都是靠他造的」，「他也是教会全体之首」（西1:15-18）；「因为神本性一切的丰盛都有形有体地居住在基督里面，你们在他里面也得了丰盛」（西2:9-10）。信徒不是缺了什么，要到基督以外去补，而是要在已经得着的基督里面「生根建造」（西2:7）。

这封信有几条线交织在一起：

  • 基督超乎万有： 他是创造的主，也是新创造的头；万有藉着他造，也藉着他十字架的血与神和好（西1:15-20）。
  • 基督足够： 一切智慧知识都在他里面藏着（西2:3）；神赦免了我们一切过犯，把攻击我们的字据钉在十字架上，因为基督在那里替我们担当了罪的刑罚（西2:13-14）。所以信徒不必被「理学和虚空的妄言」掳去（西2:8），也不必让人在饮食、节期上论断自己（西2:16）。
  • 与基督同死同复活： 信徒已经与基督一同埋葬、一同复活（西2:12；西3:1），所以要「求在上面的事」，脱去旧人，穿上新人（西3:1-10）。
  • 在家里和日常中活出来： 夫妻、父母儿女、主人和奴隶，都在主面前生活：「无论做什么……都要奉主耶稣的名」（西3:17–4:1）。

保罗在西3:11用一句话总结：「惟有基督是包括一切，又住在各人之内。」

作者与写作背景

1. 城市和教会。 歌罗西在小亚细亚西部的吕卡斯河谷，离老底嘉和希拉坡里不远（西4:13）。这个城在早期曾经兴旺，到了保罗的时候已经远远比不上它的两个邻城。十九世纪的英国学者莱特福特说，在保罗写信去的城市当中，歌罗西是最不重要的一个。可是，新约里一些最崇高的基督论，正是写给这个小城的。罗马史家塔西佗记载老底嘉在主后60年左右遭遇大地震；有学者认为歌罗西也在那段时期受到重创，但具体年份和受灾程度，古代资料说法不一。

2. 教会是怎样开始的。 保罗没有亲自到过歌罗西（西2:1）。歌罗西人是从以巴弗学到福音的（西1:7）。以巴弗是「你们那里的人」（西4:12），可能是在保罗住在以弗所的那两年多里信了主，然后把福音带回自己的家乡（参徒19:10，「叫一切住在亚细亚的……都听见主的道」）。这是推断，但很合理。后来以巴弗来到保罗那里，报告了歌罗西人的信心和爱心（西1:8），大概也报告了那种新教导带来的困扰。保罗就写了这封信，由推基古和阿尼西谋送去（西4:7-9）。

3. 作者。 书信开头写着「奉神旨意，作基督耶稣使徒的保罗和兄弟提摩太」（西1:1），结尾又说「我－保罗亲笔问你们安」（西4:18）。初期教会一致接受这是保罗的书信，今天许多学者（如弗雷德里克·布鲁斯、道格拉斯·穆尔、汤姆·赖特）也这样认为。另有一些学者（如爱德华·洛泽）认为这是保罗去世后，他的门徒用他的名义写的。他们的理由主要有三点：句子长而繁复，和保罗其他书信的文风不同；基督论更宏大，特别是论到基督和万有的关系；而且信徒已经与基督一同复活（西2:12；西3:1），似乎比保罗其他书信更强调「已经」。詹姆斯·邓恩提出一个居中的看法：这封信也许是提摩太在保罗还活着的时候、经保罗同意写成的。

  • 主张保罗所写的学者回应说： 文风会随着题目和代笔的人而改变；这样崇高的基督论，在腓2:6-11和林前8:6里已经可以看到；罗马书虽然把身体的复活留在将来，却也说信徒如今就要「一举一动有新生的样式」，「向神……当看自己是活的」（罗6:4、11）；歌罗西书更强调「已经」，是因为要回应那种「还不够」的教导。
  • 歌罗西书和腓利门书： 这两封信提到的人名几乎完全相同（亚里达古、马可、以巴弗、路加、底马、亚基布；参门2、23-24），阿尼西谋也同时出现（西4:9；门10）。若说这封信是后人托名写的，就很难解释这么多细节为什么会和腓利门书吻合。这套研读按书信自己的说法（西1:1；西4:18），以保罗为作者。

4. 写作地点和时间。 保罗写信时正在坐监（西4:3、10、18）。传统认为是在罗马的监禁（徒28:16、30），大约在主后60-62年，许多学者（如道格拉斯·穆尔）仍持这个看法。也有学者（如汤姆·赖特）认为是在以弗所，大约在主后50年代中期，理由是以弗所离歌罗西只有约两百公里，阿尼西谋去那里比去罗马容易，保罗也在腓利门书里请腓利门给他预备住处（门22）。不过，使徒行传没有记载保罗在以弗所坐监，这只是推断（参林后11:23）。还有少数学者（如博·赖克）认为是在该撒利亚（徒23:35；徒24:27）。这几种看法都有一定的理由，问题没有定论。

5. 和以弗所书的关系。 歌罗西书和以弗所书有许多相似的句子，例如论到推基古的话几乎一字不差（西4:7-8；参弗6:21-22），讲家庭的部分也很接近（西3:18–4:1；参弗5:22–6:9）。许多人认为这两封信是在同一段时期写成，由推基古一同带去。西4:16提到「从老底嘉来的书信」，有人认为是一封已经失传的信，也有人认为就是以弗所书（它可能是一封在亚细亚各教会传阅的信）。

6. 那种「理学」是什么？ 保罗没有把那种教导的内容完整地写出来，我们只能从他的回应里拼凑。信中提到：饮食、节期、月朔、安息日（西2:16）；「故意谦虚和敬拜天使」，「拘泥在所见过的」（西2:18）；「不可拿、不可尝、不可摸」的规条（西2:20-21）；「世上的小学」（西2:8、20）；也许还有割礼（西2:11）。学者的看法大致有三种：

  • 犹太教的神秘主义和禁欲操练： 有人（如弗雷德·弗朗西斯）认为这是一种犹太人的属灵操练，靠禁食和守节期预备自己，好在异象中升到天上，与天使一同敬拜（「敬拜天使」也可以理解为参与天使所献上的敬拜）。
  • 希腊哲学的影响： 有人（如爱德华·施魏策尔）认为它带着希腊哲学的色彩，例如新毕达哥拉斯派那种追求脱离物质、苦待身体的学说。
  • 混合的民间宗教： 也有人（如克林顿·阿诺德）认为它把当地弗吕家的民间信仰、犹太教的成分和求天使保护的巫术混在一起，人求告天使或灵界的势力，好得着保护。

也有学者（如詹姆斯·邓恩）认为它纯粹是犹太教的教导。这些看法不必互相排斥。可以确定的是：这种教导不照着基督（西2:8），并且暗示信徒还不够「丰盛」。保罗的回答不是逐条辩论，而是把基督高举出来。

钥匙经文：2:9-10

1. 「神本性一切的丰盛」「有形有体地」住在基督里。 不是一部分神性，也不是神的能力暂时住在他身上：基督是完完全全的神，又真是成了肉身的人。这不是说有两位神：父、子、圣灵是三个位格，每一位都是完全的神，却只有一位神。（详见第二章。）

2. 「你们在他里面也得了丰盛」。 这话的意思不是信徒也变成了神，或者得着了神自己的本体，而是：信徒在基督里面，在得救和敬虔的事上一无所缺。这是神已经做成的事，不是信徒要努力去达到的目标。信徒仍要长进（西1:10、28），但那是在已经得着的丰盛里长进，不是为了得着它。

3. 「他是各样执政掌权者的元首」。 那些叫人惧怕的灵界势力，都是基督所造的（西1:16），又被他在十字架上胜过（西2:15）。基督是这些势力的元首；属于他的人，就不必再惧怕它们。

全书结构

歌罗西书是一封书信，大致可以这样分：

  • 问安、感谢和祷告（西1:1-14）：保罗为歌罗西人的信心、爱心和盼望感谢神，又求神叫他们满心知道神的旨意，行事为人对得起主。
  • 基督超乎万有（西1:15-23）：爱子是神的像，是创造的主，是教会的头；神藉着他十字架的血叫万有与自己和好，也叫从前与神隔绝的歌罗西人与神和好。
  • 保罗的劳苦（西1:24–2:5）：保罗为教会受苦，传扬那「历世历代所隐藏的奥秘」，就是「基督在你们心里成了有荣耀的盼望」（西1:26-27）。
  • 在基督里生根，不被掳去（西2:6-23）：信徒在基督里已经得了丰盛，受了割礼，与他同埋葬、同复活；所以不要被人间的遗传、规条和自高的「谦虚」夺去奖赏。
  • 新的生命（西3:1-17）：求在上面的事；治死地上的肢体；脱去旧人，穿上新人；彼此包容、饶恕；凡事奉主耶稣的名感谢父神。
  • 家庭和工作（西3:18–4:1）：妻子、丈夫、儿女、父亲、仆人、主人，各人都在主面前生活。
  • 祷告、见证和问安（西4:2-18）：恒切祷告，向外人有智慧；一长串同工的名字；「你们要记念我的捆锁。愿恩惠常与你们同在」（西4:18）。

全信可以分成两大部分：前两章讲基督是谁、他为我们做了什么；后两章讲在基督里的人怎样生活。两部分之间的枢纽是西2:6-7：「你们既然接受了主基督耶稣，就当遵他而行，在他里面生根建造。」

怎样读这卷书

1. 留意「丰盛」。 「一切的丰盛在他里面居住」（西1:19）、「神本性一切的丰盛」（西2:9）、「你们在他里面也得了丰盛」（西2:10）。保罗求神叫歌罗西人「满心知道神的旨意」（西1:9），他自己也要「把神的道理传得全备」（西1:25）。这几处原文用的是同一个词根。歌罗西书一再告诉我们：丰盛在基督里面，不在基督以外。

2. 留意「在他里面」和「与基督一同」。 信徒「在爱子里得蒙救赎」（西1:13-14），在他里面生根建造（西2:7），与他「一同埋葬」「一同复活」（西2:12），生命「与基督一同藏在神里面」（西3:3）。读的时候，可以把这些短语画出来，看看自己在基督里已经得着了什么。

3. 留意「上面」和「地上」。 「你们要思念上面的事，不要思念地上的事」（西3:2）。这不是叫人轻看身体和日常生活；西3:18–4:1讲的都是家里和工作上最平常的事。「上面的事」是指基督坐在神右边所掌管的一切，信徒要从那里出发来过地上的日子。

4. 读的时候想想今天的「理学」。 今天的教会里，也会有人说：信了耶稣还要加上一点什么，才算真属灵。也许是一套更严的饮食和节期的规条，也许是某种特别的经历或异象，也许是一种「秘诀」或操练方法，也许是在信耶稣之外，还偷偷戴着护身符、求签问卦，好多一层保险。歌罗西书没有轻看操练和敬虔，却一再问：这是照着基督，还是在基督以外另找丰盛？

5. 和腓利门书一起读。 送这封信的阿尼西谋，就是腓利门书里那个奴隶（西4:9；门10-16）。传统认为他是逃走的；也有人认为他是特意去找保罗，请保罗为他向主人说情。读西3:11「为奴的、自主的」和西4:1论主人的话时，可以想到他和腓利门在同一个聚会里坐在一起的情景。

默想

默想： 「正如你们从我们所亲爱、一同作仆人的以巴弗所学的」（西1:7）。歌罗西人信主，不是因为一位著名的使徒来布道，而是因为一个本地人以巴弗把福音带了回来。后来他离开家乡，到了保罗那里，仍然「在祷告之间，常为你们竭力地祈求」（西4:12）。「竭力」这个词，和保罗说自己为教会「尽心竭力」（西1:29；西2:1）是同一个词根，原指运动员在赛场上竭力拼搏。我是从谁那里第一次听到福音的？也许是一位同学、一位邻居、一位亲戚，名字也许没有人记得。也许他后来自己也软弱了，甚至离开了教会；可是他带给我的福音不是他的，是基督的，所以不会因为他跌倒就失效。如果那个人后来伤害过我，我不必假装感激他，也不必再走近他；我可以单单为福音本身感谢神。今天，有没有人一直在为我竭力地祈求？也许是一位年长的姊妹，也许是远方的父母，也许有我根本不知道的人。如果我想不起有谁在为我祷告，我也不是孤单的：「有基督耶稣已经死了，而且从死里复活，现今在神的右边，也替我们祈求」（罗8:34）。他「是长远活着，替他们祈求」（来7:25）。今天，让我安静下来想一想：基督此刻正在父的右边为我祈求，他比以巴弗更可靠，他记得我的名字。我得着福音不是靠自己，持守信心也不是只靠自己；我在他里面，已经得了丰盛。
entries.content_en:
What This Book Is About

Colossians is Paul's letter to a church he had never seen face to face (Colossians 2:1). The church was in an unremarkable small town, probably not large, and it faced a teaching that sounded very spiritual and very wise. That teaching did not tell people to leave Christ. It only hinted that Christ alone was not enough: you also needed deeper experiences, stricter rules and higher knowledge before you could be "complete."

Paul's answer runs through the whole letter: Christ is already everything. "He is the image of the invisible God… by him all things were created… he is the head of the body, the church" (Colossians 1:15–18); "For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him" (Colossians 2:9–10). Believers are not lacking something that they must go outside Christ to supply. They are to be "rooted and built up in him" (Colossians 2:7), the Christ they have already received.

Several threads run through the letter:

  • Christ above all: he is the Lord of creation and the head of the new creation; all things were made through him, and through the blood of his cross all things are reconciled to God (Colossians 1:15–20).
  • Christ is enough: all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him (Colossians 2:3); God forgave all our trespasses and nailed the record of debt to the cross, where Christ bore sin's penalty in our place (Colossians 2:13–14). So believers need not be taken captive "by philosophy and empty deceit" (Colossians 2:8), and need not let anyone pass judgment on them over food or festivals (Colossians 2:16).
  • Died and raised with Christ: believers have been buried and raised with Christ (Colossians 2:12; Colossians 3:1), so they are to "seek the things that are above," putting off the old self and putting on the new (Colossians 3:1–10).
  • Lived out at home and in daily life: wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters are to do "whatever you do… in the name of the Lord Jesus" (Colossians 3:17–4:1).

Paul sums it up in a single line in Colossians 3:11: "Christ is all, and in all."

Author and Setting

1. The city and the church. Colossae lay in the Lycus valley in the west of Asia Minor, not far from Laodicea and Hierapolis (Colossians 4:13). The town had once prospered, but by Paul's day it was far behind its two neighbors. The nineteenth-century English scholar J. B. Lightfoot called Colossae the least important town to which Paul ever wrote a letter. Yet some of the most exalted teaching about Christ in the New Testament was written to this small town. The Roman historian Tacitus records a great earthquake at Laodicea around AD 60. Some scholars think Colossae was badly damaged in the same period, but ancient sources differ on the exact year and how much damage was done.

2. How the church began. Paul had never visited Colossae (Colossians 2:1). The Colossians learned the gospel from Epaphras (Colossians 1:7), who was "one of you" (Colossians 4:12). He may have come to faith during Paul's two-plus years in Ephesus and then carried the gospel back to his hometown (see Acts 19:10, "all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord"). This is an inference, but a reasonable one. Later Epaphras came to Paul and reported the Colossians' faith and love (Colossians 1:8), and probably also the trouble the new teaching was causing. So Paul wrote this letter and sent it with Tychicus and Onesimus (Colossians 4:7–9).

3. Author. The letter opens, "Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother" (Colossians 1:1), and closes, "I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand" (Colossians 4:18). The early church received it unanimously as Paul's letter, and many scholars today (such as F. F. Bruce, Douglas Moo and N. T. Wright) agree. Other scholars (such as Eduard Lohse) think a disciple of Paul wrote it in his name after his death. They give three main reasons: the sentences are long and elaborate, unlike the style of Paul's other letters; the teaching about Christ is grander, especially about Christ's relation to all things; and believers have "already" been raised with Christ (Colossians 2:12; Colossians 3:1), which seems to stress the "already" more than Paul's other letters do. James Dunn proposed a middle view: Timothy may have written the letter while Paul was still alive, with Paul's approval.

  • Those who hold that Paul wrote it reply: style changes with the subject and with the secretary who writes it down; the high view of Christ is already present in Phil 2:6–11 and 1 Cor 8:6; Romans already calls believers to "walk in newness of life" and to be "alive to God" now (Rom 6:4, 11), though it keeps the bodily resurrection future; Colossians presses the "already" because it is answering a "not yet enough" teaching.
  • Colossians and Philemon: the two letters name almost exactly the same people (Aristarchus, Mark, Epaphras, Luke, Demas, Archippus; see Phlm 23–24; Phlm 2), and Onesimus appears in both (Colossians 4:9; Phlm 10). If Colossians were written later under Paul's name, it would be hard to explain why so many details fit Philemon. This study, following the letter's own claim (Colossians 1:1; Colossians 4:18), takes Paul as the author.

4. Place and date. Paul wrote while in prison (Colossians 4:3, 10, 18). Tradition places the letter in his Roman imprisonment (Acts 28:16, 30), around AD 60–62, and many scholars (such as Douglas Moo) still hold this view. Others (such as N. T. Wright) suggest Ephesus in the mid-50s: Ephesus is only about 120 miles (some 190 km) from Colossae, Onesimus could reach it more easily than Rome, and in Philemon Paul asks for a guest room to be prepared for him (Phlm 22). Acts, however, records no imprisonment in Ephesus; it is inferred (see 2 Cor 11:23). A few scholars (such as Bo Reicke) suggest Caesarea (Acts 23:35; Acts 24:27). Each view has some support, and the question remains open.

5. Relation to Ephesians. Colossians and Ephesians share many similar sentences. What they say about Tychicus is almost word for word the same (Colossians 4:7–8; see Eph 6:21–22), and the sections on the household are very close (Colossians 3:18–4:1; see Eph 5:22–6:9). Many think the two letters were written in the same period and carried together by Tychicus. "The letter from Laodicea" in Colossians 4:16 may be a letter now lost, or it may be Ephesians itself (which may have been a letter circulated among the churches of Asia).

6. What was the "philosophy"? Paul never sets out the teaching in full; we can only piece it together from his answer. The letter mentions food and drink, festivals, new moons and Sabbaths (Colossians 2:16); "asceticism and worship of angels," "going on in detail about visions" (Colossians 2:18); rules such as "Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch" (Colossians 2:21); "the elemental spirits of the world" (Colossians 2:8, 20); and perhaps circumcision (Colossians 2:11). Scholars' views fall roughly into three groups:

  • Jewish mysticism and ascetic practice: some (e.g. Fred Francis) think it was a Jewish spiritual discipline that used fasting and the keeping of holy days to prepare for visionary ascent to heaven, to join the angels in worship ("worship of angels" can also be read as "the worship the angels offer").
  • Greek philosophy: some (e.g. Eduard Schweizer) see in it the color of Greek philosophy, such as the Neo-Pythagorean teaching that sought escape from the material world and harsh treatment of the body.
  • A mixed folk religion: others (e.g. Clinton Arnold) think it blended local Phrygian folk belief, Jewish elements and magic that called on angels for protection, so that people invoked angels or spiritual powers to keep themselves safe.

Some (e.g. James Dunn) think it was a purely Jewish teaching. These views need not exclude one another. What is clear is that this teaching was "not according to Christ" (Colossians 2:8) and implied that believers were not yet "filled." Paul does not answer it point by point. He lifts up Christ.

Key Verse: 2:9–10

1. "The whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" in Christ. Not part of deity, nor God's power resting on him for a time: Christ is fully God, and truly became man in the flesh. This does not mean there are two gods: Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three persons, each fully God, and there is only one God. (See chapter 2 for more.)

2. "You have been filled in him." This does not mean believers become God or receive God's own being. It means that in Christ believers lack nothing for salvation and godliness. This is something God has already done, not a goal believers must strive to reach. Believers still grow (Colossians 1:10, 28), but they grow within a fullness already given, not in order to obtain it.

3. "The head of all rule and authority." The spiritual powers people feared were created by Christ (Colossians 1:16) and defeated by him at the cross (Colossians 2:15). Believers belong to their head, so they need not fear them any longer.

The Shape of the Book

Colossians is a letter, and it can be roughly divided like this:

  • Greeting, thanksgiving and prayer (Colossians 1:1–14): Paul thanks God for the Colossians' faith, love and hope, and prays that they may be filled with the knowledge of God's will and walk in a manner worthy of the Lord.
  • Christ above all (Colossians 1:15–23): the Son is the image of God, the Lord of creation and the head of the church; through the blood of his cross God reconciles all things to himself, including the Colossians, who were once alienated.
  • Paul's labor (Colossians 1:24–2:5): Paul suffers for the church and proclaims "the mystery hidden for ages and generations," which is "Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:26–27).
  • Rooted in Christ, not taken captive (Colossians 2:6–23): in Christ believers have been filled, circumcised, buried and raised with him, so they must not let human traditions, rules and puffed-up "humility" disqualify them.
  • The new life (Colossians 3:1–17): seek the things above; put to death what is earthly; put off the old self and put on the new; bear with and forgive one another; do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father.
  • Home and work (Colossians 3:18–4:1): wives, husbands, children, fathers, slaves and masters all live before the Lord.
  • Prayer, witness and greetings (Colossians 4:2–18): continue steadfastly in prayer, walk in wisdom toward outsiders; a long list of fellow workers; "Remember my chains. Grace be with you" (Colossians 4:18).

The letter falls into two main parts: the first two chapters tell who Christ is and what he has done for us, and the last two tell how those in Christ are to live. The hinge between them is Colossians 2:6–7: "Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him."

How to Read This Book

1. Watch for "fullness." "In him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell" (Colossians 1:19); "the whole fullness of deity" (Colossians 2:9); "you have been filled in him" (Colossians 2:10). Paul prays that the Colossians "may be filled with the knowledge of his will" (Colossians 1:9), and his own task is "to make the word of God fully known" (Colossians 1:25). In Greek these all come from the same root. Colossians tells us again and again that fullness is in Christ, not outside him.

2. Watch for "in him" and "with Christ." Believers have redemption in the beloved Son (Colossians 1:13–14), are rooted and built up in him (Colossians 2:7), were "buried with him" and "raised with him" (Colossians 2:12), and their life "is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3). As you read, you might underline these phrases and see what you already have in Christ.

3. Watch for "above" and "on earth." "Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth" (Colossians 3:2). This does not tell us to despise the body or ordinary life; Colossians 3:18–4:1 is all about the most ordinary things at home and at work. "The things above" are everything Christ rules as he sits at God's right hand, and believers are to live their days on earth from there.

4. Think about today's "philosophy." In today's church, too, some say that after believing in Jesus you must add something more before you are truly spiritual. It may be a stricter set of rules about food and holy days; it may be a special experience or vision; it may be a "secret" or a technique of practice; or it may be quietly keeping an amulet or consulting fortune-telling sticks on the side, as extra insurance alongside faith in Jesus. Colossians does not despise spiritual discipline or godliness, but it keeps asking: is this according to Christ, or is it seeking fullness somewhere outside him?

5. Read it with Philemon. Onesimus, who carried this letter, is the slave of the letter to Philemon (Colossians 4:9; Phlm 10–16). He is traditionally understood to have run away; some think he went to Paul to ask him to plead his case. When you read "slave, free" in Colossians 3:11 and Paul's word to masters in Colossians 4:1, you can picture Onesimus and Philemon sitting in the same meeting.

Meditation

Reflect: "Just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant" (Colossians 1:7). The Colossians did not believe because a famous apostle came to preach, but because a local man, Epaphras, brought the gospel home. Later he left his hometown to be with Paul, and he was still "always struggling on your behalf in his prayers" (Colossians 4:12). The word "struggling" shares its root with Paul's own "struggling" for the church (Colossians 1:29; Colossians 2:1); it first meant straining every muscle in a contest. From whom did I first hear the gospel? Perhaps a classmate, a neighbor or a relative whose name no one else will remember. Perhaps that person later grew weak, or even left the church; yet the gospel they brought me was not theirs but Christ's, so it does not lose its power because they fell. If that person later harmed me, I do not have to pretend gratitude toward them or go near them again; I can thank God for the gospel itself. Is anyone struggling in prayer for me today? Perhaps an older sister in the church, parents far away, or people I know nothing about. And if I cannot think of anyone praying for me, I am still not alone: "Christ Jesus is the one who died—more than that, who was raised—who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us" (Rom 8:34). "He always lives to make intercession for them" (Heb 7:25). Today, let me be still and remember that Christ is at the Father's right hand interceding for me right now; he is more sure than Epaphras ever could be, and he remembers my name. I did not receive the gospel by myself, and I do not hold on to faith by myself alone; in him I have already been filled.

entries.title_en: Preeminent in Everything

verse_parts.text: 爱子是那不能看见之神的像，是首生的，在一切被造的以先。因为万有都是靠他造的，无论是天上的，地上的；能看见的，不能看见的；或是有位的，主治的，执政的，掌权的；一概都是藉着他造的，又是为他造的。他在万有之先；万有也靠他而立。他也是教会全体之首。他是元始，是从死里首先复生的，使他可以在凡事上居首位。

entries.content:
本章脉络

第一章有五段。感谢（3-8节）：保罗为歌罗西人的信心、爱心和盼望感谢神，他们是从以巴弗那里学到福音的。祷告（9-14节）：保罗求神叫他们满心知道神的旨意，行事为人对得起主，并且感谢父救他们脱离黑暗的权势，把他们迁到爱子的国里。基督的颂歌（15-20节）：爱子是那不能看见之神的像，万有都是靠他造的，也靠他而立；他是教会的首，藉着十字架的血叫万有与神和好。你们也与神和好了（21-23节）：从前与神为敌的人，如今藉着基督的肉身受死与神和好，只要在所信的道上恒心。保罗的劳苦（24-29节）：保罗为教会受苦，传扬那历世历代所隐藏的奥秘，就是「基督在你们心里成了有荣耀的盼望」。

15-20节是全章，也是全书的中心。歌罗西教会受到一种「理学」（西2:8）的搅扰，叫人以为单有基督还不够。保罗的回答不是先列出一套规条，而是先把基督高举出来：他创造万有，托住万有，又叫万有与神和好。认识了这位基督，就知道在他以外不需要再加什么。

深读 1:3-8 信心、爱心和盼望

1. 先感谢，后劝勉。 「我们感谢神我们主耶稣基督的父，常常为你们祷告」（西1:3）。保罗没有见过歌罗西的信徒（参西2:1），信中也有警告，但他先为他们感谢神。他在别人身上先看见神的工作，然后才指出问题。

2. 三样恩典连在一起。 「因听见你们在基督耶稣里的信心，并向众圣徒的爱心，是为那给你们存在天上的盼望」（西1:4-5）。信心、爱心、盼望在保罗的书信里常常一同出现（参林前13:13；帖前1:3）。这里值得留意的是次序：他们爱众圣徒，是「为」那存在天上的盼望。盼望已经稳稳地存在天上，所以他们不必在地上抓紧一切，可以放手去爱人。

  • 信心的对象： 保罗说的是「在基督耶稣里的信心」。救人的不是信心有多强，而是所信的那一位。

3. 福音在结果子。 「这福音传到你们那里，也传到普天之下，并且结果，增长」（西1:6）。许多人认为这里呼应了创世记的「要生养众多」（创1:28）：福音像一粒种子，在世界各地长出新的生命。歌罗西只是吕卡斯河谷里一座不大的城，但神的工作在那里和在全世界一样真实。

  • 「真知道神恩惠」： 他们不只是听过一些宗教道理，而是「真知道神恩惠」（西1:6）。后来的假教师要给他们加上更高的「知识」，保罗却提醒他们：你们从一开始所领受的，就是真正的恩典。

4. 以巴弗：忠心的执事。 「正如你们从我们所亲爱、一同作仆人的以巴弗所学的。他为我们作了基督忠心的执事」（西1:7）。（「执事」在这里是服事的人，不是指教会里的执事职分。）歌罗西教会多半不是保罗亲自建立的。以巴弗是本地人（西4:12），可能在保罗住在以弗所的那段时间信了主（参徒19:10），然后回到家乡传福音。（许多早期古卷作「为我们」，和合本也这样译，意思是以巴弗代表保罗；也有古卷作「为你们」，有些英文译本这样译，强调他为歌罗西人服事。无论哪一种，他都忠心服事了他们。）保罗称他为「一同作仆人的」，把他放在和自己同等的地位上。神常常用一个不出名的人，把福音带到一座城。

要点：福音不是一套需要不断升级的道理，而是神的恩惠本身。信徒能够爱人，是因为他们的盼望已经稳稳地存在天上。
深读 1:9-14 迁到他爱子的国里

1. 祷告求什么。 「愿你们在一切属灵的智慧悟性上，满心知道神的旨意」（西1:9）。保罗求的不是一种神秘的特别知识，而是知道神的旨意。而且这知识是要落实在生活里的：「好叫你们行事为人对得起主，凡事蒙他喜悦，在一切善事上结果子，渐渐地多知道神」（西1:10）。

  • 知道与行事连在一起： 认识神叫人结果子，结果子又叫人更认识神。属灵的知识若不改变生活，就不是保罗所说的知识。

2. 力上加力，为了忍耐。 「照他荣耀的权能，得以在各样的力上加力，好叫你们凡事欢欢喜喜地忍耐宽容」（西1:11）。神的大能在这里不是叫人行奇事，而是叫人能「忍耐宽容」。我们常以为神的能力是用来改变环境的，保罗却说，神的能力常常是叫我们在没有改变的环境中站立得住，而且「欢欢喜喜地」。

3. 感谢父的三件事。 「又感谢父，叫我们能与众圣徒在光明中同得基业。他救了我们脱离黑暗的权势，把我们迁到他爱子的国里」（西1:12-13）。

  • 「叫我们能」： 原文的意思是使我们有资格。这资格不是我们挣来的，而是父给的。
  • 「救了我们脱离」： 这让人想起出埃及：神救以色列脱离法老的权势，又带他们进入应许之地的基业。如今神救我们脱离的是「黑暗的权势」。
  • 「迁到」： 这个词在古代可以指一国的人被整批迁到另一国去。信徒不是在黑暗的国里慢慢变好，而是已经被迁到另一个国度，换了主人。这几个动词在原文都表示已经完成的动作：这不是我们还在努力的目标，而是神已经做成的事。

4. 在爱子里得蒙救赎。 「我们在爱子里得蒙救赎，罪过得以赦免」（西1:14）。「救赎」原指付代价把人赎回来。保罗紧接着说明救赎的内容：「罪过得以赦免」。我们最大的问题不是缺少知识，也不是缺少灵性的经历，而是罪。这一句也为后面的颂歌铺路：那位赦免我们罪的爱子，就是创造万有的主。

要点：保罗为信徒求的，是认识神并且活出来。但这一切的根基，是父已经做成的事：他救了我们，迁了我们，在爱子里赦免了我们。
深读 1:15-20 爱子是那不能看见之神的像

1. 一首关于基督的颂歌。 西1:15-20的句子很有节奏，许多人把它分成两段：15-17节讲基督与创造，18-20节讲基督与新的创造（教会、复活、和好）；也有人把18节上半节归在第一段。许多学者（如拉尔夫·马丁）认为这是早期教会的一首诗歌，保罗引用并加以补充；也有学者（如道格拉斯·穆尔）认为这可能就是保罗自己写的。无论来源如何，这都是新约论到基督最高的经文之一。

2. 「不能看见之神的像」。 「爱子是那不能看见之神的像」（西1:15）。神是不能看见的（约1:18），但神在爱子身上显明出来。耶稣说：「人看见了我，就是看见了父。」（约14:9）

  • 不只是相像： 这里的「像」不是一张不完全的照片，而是把神本身完全显明出来（参林后4:4；来1:3「是神本体的真像」）。
  • 和人的「形象」： 人是照着神的形象造的（创1:27），但人犯罪，使这形象受了亏损。基督是神真正的像，他来，要把我们更新，「渐渐更新，正如造他主的形象」（西3:10）。

3. 「首生的」是什么意思。 「是首生的，在一切被造的以先」（西1:15）。有人根据这句话说，基督是神所造的第一个受造物。古代的亚流派这样说，今天耶和华见证人也这样教导。我们可以尊重他们认真读经，但这种理解违背经文，也否认了基督是神。亚流的教导在主后325年的尼西亚会议上已经被教会判为异端。

  • 下一句就是答案： 「因为万有都是靠他造的」（西1:16）。如果他自己是被造的，他就不能造「万有」。约翰福音也说：「凡被造的，没有一样不是藉着他造的。」（约1:3）
  • 「首生的」常指地位： 在旧约里，「长子」可以指地位和继承权，不一定指先出生。神说以色列是「我的长子」（出4:22）；诗篇论到耶西最小的儿子大卫说：「我也要立他为长子，为世上最高的君王。」（诗89:20、27）大卫本来不是长子，这里「长子」是一个地位，而不是出生的次序。
  • 「在一切被造的以先」： 和合本这样翻译，强调他在时间上先于万有（参西1:17「他在万有之先」）；原文直译是一切被造之物的首生者，也可以强调他在万有之上的地位。保罗并没有说他是首先被造的。两种重点都对：他在万有之先，也在万有之上，好像承受产业的长子一样。
  • 他是神： 西2:9说：「神本性一切的丰盛都有形有体地居住在基督里面。」爱子不是被造的，他与父同是独一的神，本质相同；尼西亚信经说他是「受生而非受造」。
  • 旧约智慧的背景： 许多解经家认为，这首颂歌带着旧约智慧文学的背景（箴8:22-31；参创1:1的「起初」与本章18节的「元始」）。古代亚流派正是用箴8:22说基督是被造的；但保罗把创造之功完全归给爱子：他不是被造的智慧，而是造万有的主。

4. 万有是「为他」造的。 「无论是天上的，地上的；能看见的，不能看见的；或是有位的，主治的，执政的，掌权的；一概都是藉着他造的，又是为他造的」（西1:16）。

  • 连属灵的势力也在其中： 歌罗西人可能很怕天使和看不见的权势（参西2:18）。保罗说，无论是什么样的权势，都是基督造的，都在他以下。今天许多华人信徒也会怕鬼神、风水、冲煞；保罗的话同样是对他们说的：没有一样不是爱子所造的。
  • 「为他造的」： 万有存在的目的就是基督。不是基督为我的人生服务，而是我的人生、连整个宇宙，都是为他而有的。

5. 万有靠他而立。 「他在万有之先；万有也靠他而立」（西1:17）。「而立」的意思是被维系、被托住，不至散开。宇宙不是一部上好了发条就自己运转的机器，而是每一刻都靠着基督托住（参来1:3）。

6. 教会的首，从死里首先复生的。 「他也是教会全体之首。他是元始，是从死里首先复生的，使他可以在凡事上居首位」（西1:18）。颂歌的第二段从创造转到新的创造。基督是创造的首生者，也是复活的首生者：他第一个从死里复活，而且不再死，跟着他的还有许多人（参林前15:20）。所以「在凡事上」，旧的创造和新的创造，他都居首位。

7. 一切的丰盛在他里面。 「因为父喜欢叫一切的丰盛在他里面居住」（西1:19）。原文没有「父」字，和合本是按意思补上的；也有人把「一切的丰盛」本身当作主语，意思是：神一切的丰盛乐意住在他里面。西2:9说得更清楚：「神本性一切的丰盛」都住在基督里面。这表明基督不是众多神明中的一个，也不是通往神的许多台阶之一，神的一切都在他里面。

8. 藉着十字架的血叫万有和好。 「既然藉着他在十字架上所流的血成就了和平，便藉着他叫万有……都与自己和好了」（西1:20）。

  • 和好的代价： 和好不是靠一个宣告，而是靠「十字架上所流的血」。人与神为敌（西1:21），人的罪当受神的忿怒（西3:6）；基督在十字架上替我们承担了这罪的刑罚（参赛53:5；林后5:21）。和平是用他的血换来的。
  • 「万有」和好，是否表示人人都得救： 有人从这一节推论出普救论，认为最后所有的人都会得救。改革宗、循道宗和天主教的传统大多不这样理解。原因有三：21-23节说和好要藉着信心领受；保罗也说不信福音的人「要受刑罚，就是永远沉沦」（帖后1:9）；西2:15也不是说执政掌权的与神和好，而是说基督把它们「掳来」。所以许多人认为，信靠基督的人真正与神和好；抵挡神的势力则被制伏，整个宇宙要重新归在基督的主权之下（参弗1:10）。
要点：爱子是神的像，是万有的创造者、托住者和目的；他也是从死里首先复生的，藉着十字架的血使人与神和好。在他以外，不需要再加什么，因为神一切的丰盛都在他里面。这首颂歌不只要我们明白，更要我们敬拜：他配得我们一切的敬拜和喜乐。
深读 1:21-23 如今他叫你们与自己和好

1. 从前：与神为敌。 「你们从前与神隔绝，因着恶行，心里与他为敌」（西1:21）。保罗的描写很直接：我们不只是迷路的人，而是神的「仇敌」（参罗5:10）。这敌意在「心里」，又显在「恶行」上。

2. 如今：藉着他的肉身受死。 「但如今他藉着基督的肉身受死，叫你们与自己和好」（西1:22）。和好的方法很具体：是「肉身」，是「受死」。歌罗西的假教导可能轻看身体和物质，保罗却强调，救恩是在一个真实的身体里，藉着一次真实的死成就的。

3. 和好的目的。 「都成了圣洁，没有瑕疵，无可责备，把你们引到自己面前」（西1:22）。「没有瑕疵」是旧约献祭用的词，指献给神的祭物要完全。我们本来有瑕疵，配不上站在神面前；基督自己成了那无瑕疵的祭物（参彼前1:19）；我们如今在基督里被算为义，到那日也要完全圣洁，被带到神面前。这不是靠我们越来越好，而是靠基督替我们所做的。

4. 「只要你们在所信的道上恒心」。 「只要你们在所信的道上恒心，根基稳固，坚定不移，不至被引动失去福音的盼望」（西1:23）。这句话怎样理解，不同传统有不同的看法。

  • 改革宗的理解： 加尔文和许多改革宗解经家认为，真正与神和好的人，神必保守他们恒心到底（参约10:28-29；腓1:6）。这里的「只要」是一个真实的警告，神用这警告来保守他的百姓；而最后离开福音的人，显明他们本来就不属基督（参约一2:19）。
  • 循道宗与阿民念派的理解： 约翰·卫斯理和阿民念派的解经家认为，真正的信徒若离开信仰，有可能失去救恩（参来3:14）。所以这里的「只要」表示，持守是得救的真实条件。
  • 「只要」的语气： 许多人（如莱特福特）指出，原文这个「只要」常带着有把握的语气，意思接近：我相信你们是会恒心的。
  • 双方都同意的： 无论哪一种理解，双方都认为这是严肃的劝勉，不可轻看；双方也都认为恒心不是靠自己的力量，而是靠住在基督里（参约15:5）。保罗在这里也不是要叫信徒活在怀疑中，而是叫他们不要被假教导「引动」，离开起初所听的福音。
要点：我们曾是神的仇敌，基督却藉着自己的身体和死，叫我们与神和好，要把我们没有瑕疵地带到神面前。恒心持守的人，不是靠自己站稳，而是一直站在这福音上。
深读 1:24-29 基督在你们心里成了有荣耀的盼望

1. 为你们受苦倒觉欢乐。 「现在我为你们受苦，倒觉欢乐」（西1:24）。保罗写这封信时正在坐监（西4:3、18）。他受苦不是为了自己的功劳，而是「为你们」，为了外邦人能听到福音。

2. 「补满基督患难的缺欠」：不是说救恩不够。 「并且为基督的身体，就是为教会，要在我肉身上补满基督患难的缺欠」（西1:24）。这句话很不容易明白。首先要说清楚：这不是说基督在十字架上的救赎还不够。许多人指出，这里的「患难」一词，在新约里从来没有用在基督赎罪的死上。保罗在同一章说，我们「在爱子里得蒙救赎，罪过得以赦免」（西1:14），又说和平是藉着「十字架上所流的血」成就的（西1:20）。耶稣说：「成了！」（约19:30）「他一次献祭，便叫那得以成圣的人永远完全。」（来10:14）

3. 几种理解。

  • 弥赛亚的患难： 许多学者（如道格拉斯·穆尔）认为，犹太人相信在新时代来到以前，神的百姓要受一定量的患难（参太24:8）。基督已经受了最重要的苦，教会还要在这段时间里经历其余的患难。有人进一步认为，保罗愿意自己多担一些，好叫别人少担一些。
  • 与基督联合： 也有许多人强调，教会是基督的身体，教会受苦，基督也一同感受。复活的主问扫罗：「你为什么逼迫我？」（徒9:4）保罗为教会受的苦，也可以称为基督的患难（参林后1:5；腓3:10）。
  • 天主教的理解： 天主教的教导（如《天主教教理》1508条引用这节经文，1476-1477条论教会的宝库）说，信徒可以把自己的苦难与基督的苦难联合，为教会献上，同时也承认基督的献祭是独一的。这个传统也用这节经文支持功德库的教导，认为圣徒的功德可以帮助别人减免罪罚。改革宗和信义宗的传统不接受后面这种读法，因为保罗在这里说的是为传福音、建立教会而受苦，不是为别人赎罪；赎罪的工作只有基督完成，而且已经完成了。

4. 历世历代所隐藏的奥秘。 「这道理就是历世历代所隐藏的奥秘；但如今向他的圣徒显明了」（西1:26）。在保罗的书信里，「奥秘」不是只有少数人才知道的秘密，而是神从前没有完全显明、如今藉着福音公开了的计划（参弗3:6）。歌罗西的假教导可能自称有更深的秘密，保罗却说，真正的奥秘已经公开向所有圣徒显明了。

5. 基督在你们心里。 「神愿意叫他们知道，这奥秘在外邦人中有何等丰盛的荣耀，就是基督在你们心里成了有荣耀的盼望」（西1:27）。奥秘的内容就是一个人：基督。而且这位基督住在外邦人中间，住在从前「与神隔绝」的人心里（西1:21）。（「在你们心里」也可以译作「在你们中间」，两种意思都合乎经文：基督住在每个信徒心里，也住在他的教会中间。）我们的盼望不是靠自己将来能变成什么样，而是已经在我们里面的基督。

6. 传扬他，为了把各人完全地带到神面前。 「我们传扬他，是用诸般的智慧，劝戒各人，教导各人，要把各人在基督里完完全全地引到神面前」（西1:28）。保罗传的不是一套方法，而是「他」，就是基督。「各人」出现了三次：福音不是只给属灵精英的，每一个人都可以在基督里成熟。

  • 靠着他的大能劳苦： 「我也为此劳苦，照着他在我里面运用的大能尽心竭力」（西1:29）。保罗很努力，但他知道，叫他能这样努力的，是基督在他里面运行的大能。
要点：保罗甘心受苦，不是为了补足基督的救恩，而是为了让外邦人也听见这奥秘：基督住在你们心里，就是你们得荣耀的盼望。
默想

默想： 「一概都是藉着他造的，又是为他造的……万有也靠他而立」（西1:16-17）。在我心里，耶稣有多大？也许我很自然地把他和主日、灵修、教会的事连在一起；可是一进实验室、写字楼、工地或厨房，一碰到我读的专业、我每天看的新闻，我就把他忘了，好像世界上有一大片地方与他无关。保罗却说，「天上的，地上的；能看见的，不能看见的」，一概都是他造的，又是为他造的。我算的账、写的程序、种的菜、窗外那棵树，都在他手里，也都是为荣耀他而存在。这不是要给我再加一副担子，叫我把每件事都做得更「属灵」，而是要打开我的眼睛，在平常的工作和神所造的美物里看见他的智慧，为他欢喜。我承认，我常常活得好像他很小，只占我一周里的两个钟头。可是这位托住万有的主，并没有因为我把他看小了就丢下我。他反倒为我这个曾经与神隔绝、「心里与他为敌」的人，在十字架上流血，好叫我「圣洁，没有瑕疵，无可责备」地站在神面前（西1:21-22）。今天，让我在一个以为与他无关的地方停一停，对他说：「主啊，这也是你造的，也是为你造的。」然后感谢他，因为他已经叫我与神和好。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 1 has five sections. Thanksgiving (vv. 3–8): Paul thanks God for the Colossians' faith, love and hope; they learned this gospel from Epaphras. Prayer (vv. 9–14): Paul asks that they be filled with the knowledge of God's will and walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, giving thanks to the Father, who delivered them from the domain of darkness and transferred them to the kingdom of his beloved Son. The hymn to Christ (vv. 15–20): the Son is the image of the invisible God; all things were created by him and hold together in him; he is the head of the church and reconciles all things to God by the blood of his cross. You too are reconciled (vv. 21–23): those who were once hostile are now reconciled by Christ's death in his body of flesh, if indeed they continue in the faith. Paul's labor (vv. 24–29): Paul suffers for the church and proclaims the mystery hidden for ages, "Christ in you, the hope of glory."

Verses 15–20 are the center of the chapter and of the whole letter. The Colossian church was being troubled by a "philosophy" (Colossians 2:8) that told them Christ alone was not enough. Paul's answer does not begin with a list of rules. He begins by lifting up Christ: he created all things, holds all things together and reconciles all things to God. Once you know this Christ, you know nothing needs to be added to him.

Going Deeper: 1:3–8 Faith, Love and Hope

1. Thanks first, then exhortation. "We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you" (Colossians 1:3). Paul had never met the Colossian believers (see Colossians 2:1), and the letter contains warnings, yet he begins by thanking God for them. He sees God's work in others first, and only then names the problems.

2. Three graces held together. "Since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints, because of the hope laid up for you in heaven" (Colossians 1:4–5). Faith, love and hope often appear together in Paul (see 1 Cor 13:13; 1 Thess 1:3). Notice the order here: they love the saints because of the hope laid up in heaven. Their hope is already secure in heaven, so they do not need to clutch at everything on earth. They are free to give themselves in love.

  • The object of faith: Paul speaks of "faith in Christ Jesus." What saves is not how strong the faith is but the one in whom we believe.

3. The gospel bearing fruit. "Which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and growing" (Colossians 1:6). Many hear an echo of "be fruitful and multiply" (Gen 1:28): the gospel is like a seed, bringing new life up all over the world. Colossae was a modest town in the Lycus Valley, but God's work there was as real as anywhere in the world.

  • "Understood the grace of God in truth": They had not merely heard some religious ideas; they had "understood the grace of God in truth" (Colossians 1:6). The false teachers would offer them a higher "knowledge." Paul reminds them that what they received at the very start was the real grace of God.

4. Epaphras, a faithful minister. "Just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf" (Colossians 1:7). Paul probably did not found the Colossian church himself. Epaphras was a local man (Colossians 4:12) who may have come to faith while Paul was living in Ephesus (see Acts 19:10) and then carried the gospel back home. (Many early manuscripts read "on our behalf," as the Chinese Union Version does, making Epaphras Paul's representative; others read "on your behalf," as the ESV does, stressing his service to the Colossians. Either way he served them faithfully.) Paul calls him a "fellow servant," putting him on the same level as himself. God often uses someone little known to bring the gospel to a whole town.

The point: The gospel is not a set of teachings that keeps needing an upgrade. It is the grace of God itself. Believers are free to love because their hope is already secure in heaven.
Going Deeper: 1:9–14 Transferred to the Kingdom of His Beloved Son

1. What Paul prays for. "Asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding" (Colossians 1:9). Paul does not ask for some special, mystical knowledge. He asks that they know God's will, and that this knowledge show up in their lives: "so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him, bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God" (Colossians 1:10).

  • Knowing and walking go together: Knowing God makes us bear fruit, and bearing fruit makes us know God more. Spiritual knowledge that does not change a life is not what Paul means by knowledge.

2. Strength for endurance. "May you be strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy" (Colossians 1:11). God's power here is not given to work wonders but for "endurance and patience." We often think God's power is for changing our circumstances. Paul says God's power often holds us up in circumstances that do not change, and does so "with joy."

3. Three things to thank the Father for. "Giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light. He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son" (Colossians 1:12–13).

  • "Qualified you": The inheritance is not something we qualify for by our own effort. The Father makes us fit for it.
  • "Delivered us from": This recalls the exodus. God rescued Israel from Pharaoh's power and brought them into the inheritance of the promised land. Now he rescues us from "the domain of darkness."
  • "Transferred": In the ancient world this word could describe a whole people being moved from one country to another. Believers are not slowly improving inside the kingdom of darkness. They have been moved into another kingdom and now belong to another Lord. These verbs are in the past tense: this is not a goal we are still working toward but something God has already done.

4. Redemption in the beloved Son. "In whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins" (Colossians 1:14). "Redemption" means buying someone back at a price. Paul immediately says what that redemption is: "the forgiveness of sins." Our deepest problem is not a lack of knowledge or of spiritual experience but sin. This sentence also prepares for the hymn that follows: the beloved Son who forgives our sins is the Lord who created all things.

The point: Paul prays that believers would know God and live it out. But the ground of it all is what the Father has already done: he delivered us, transferred us, and forgave us in his beloved Son.
Going Deeper: 1:15–20 The Image of the Invisible God

1. A hymn about Christ. The lines of Colossians 1:15–20 are rhythmic, and many divide them into two stanzas: verses 15–17 are about Christ and creation; verses 18–20 are about Christ and the new creation (the church, the resurrection, reconciliation). Others place 18a with the first stanza. Many scholars (e.g. Ralph Martin) think this is an early Christian hymn that Paul quotes and expands; others (e.g. Douglas Moo) think Paul may have written it himself. Wherever it came from, it is one of the highest passages about Christ in the New Testament.

2. "The image of the invisible God." "He is the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). God cannot be seen (John 1:18), but in the Son, God is made known. Jesus said, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9).

  • More than a likeness: "Image" here is not an imperfect photograph but the full revealing of God himself (see 2 Cor 4:4; Heb 1:3, "the exact imprint of his nature").
  • Our image: Human beings were made in the image of God (Gen 1:27), but sin defaced that image. Christ is the true image of God, and he comes to renew us "after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10).

3. What "firstborn" means. "The firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15). Some have read this to mean that Christ is the first thing God created. The ancient Arians taught this, and Jehovah's Witnesses teach it today. We can respect their seriousness about Scripture, but this reading contradicts the text and denies that Christ is God; the church condemned Arius's teaching as heresy at the Council of Nicaea (AD 325).

  • The next sentence answers it: "For by him all things were created" (Colossians 1:16). If he were created, he could not be the creator of "all things." John says the same: "without him was not any thing made that was made" (John 1:3).
  • "Firstborn" often means rank: In the Old Testament, "firstborn" can mean status and the right of inheritance, not birth order. God calls Israel "my firstborn son" (Exod 4:22), and the psalm says of David, the youngest of Jesse's sons, "I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth" (Ps 89:20, 27). David was not the eldest; there "firstborn" is a position, not the order of birth.
  • "Before all creation": The Chinese Union Version renders the phrase "firstborn, before all that was created," stressing that he comes before all things in time (see Colossians 1:17, "he is before all things"). The ESV keeps the literal "firstborn of all creation"; the NIV's "firstborn over all creation" brings out rank. Paul did not say "first-created." Both are true: he is before all things and over all things, like the firstborn son who inherits the estate.
  • He is God: "For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:9). The Son is not created. With the Father he is the one God, of the same nature; the Nicene Creed confesses him "begotten, not made."
  • The wisdom background: Many interpreters read the hymn against the Old Testament wisdom literature (Prov 8:22–31; compare "in the beginning" in Gen 1:1 with "the beginning" in Col 1:18). The ancient Arians used Prov 8:22 to argue that Christ was created; but Paul gives the whole work of creation to the Son. He is not created wisdom but the Lord who made all things.

4. All things were created "for him." "In heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him" (Colossians 1:16).

  • Even spiritual powers: The Colossians may well have feared angels and unseen powers (see Colossians 2:18). Paul says that whatever power there is, Christ made it, and it is under him. Many Chinese believers still fear spirits, feng shui and inauspicious days; Paul's words are for them too: nothing exists that the Son did not make.
  • "For him": Christ is the purpose of everything that exists. Christ does not exist to serve my life; my life, and the whole universe, exist for him.

5. All things hold together in him. "And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:17). To "hold together" is to be held in place and kept from falling apart. The universe is not a machine wound up once and left to run. Every moment, Christ upholds it (see Heb 1:3).

6. Head of the church, firstborn from the dead. "And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent" (Colossians 1:18). The second stanza moves from creation to new creation. Christ is firstborn over creation and firstborn from the dead: he is the first to rise never to die again, and many will follow him (see 1 Cor 15:20). So "in everything," the old creation and the new, he is preeminent.

7. All the fullness in him. "For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell" (Colossians 1:19). The Greek has no word for "God" or "Father" here; translations supply it from the sense (the ESV "God," the Chinese Union Version "the Father"). Paul says it even more plainly in Colossians 2:9: "the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" in Christ. Christ is not one divine being among many, or one rung on a ladder up to God. All that God is, is in him.

8. Reconciled by the blood of the cross. "And through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross" (Colossians 1:20).

  • The cost of peace: Peace was not made by a declaration but "by the blood of his cross." We were God's enemies (Colossians 1:21), and our sin deserved God's wrath (Colossians 3:6). On the cross Christ bore the penalty of that sin in our place (see Isa 53:5; 2 Cor 5:21). Peace was bought with his blood.
  • Does "all things" mean everyone will be saved? Some have drawn universalism from this verse: in the end every person will be saved. Reformed, Wesleyan and Catholic traditions mostly do not read it this way, because Colossians 1:21–23 says reconciliation is received by faith; Paul says those who reject the gospel "will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction" (2 Thess 1:9); and Colossians 2:15 says Christ "disarmed" the rulers and authorities, not that they were reconciled. So many conclude that those who trust Christ are truly reconciled to God, while the hostile powers are subdued, and the whole universe is brought back under the rule of Christ (see Eph 1:10).
The point: The Son is the image of God, the creator, sustainer and goal of all things. He is also the firstborn from the dead, who makes peace with God by the blood of his cross. Nothing needs to be added to him, because all the fullness of God dwells in him. This hymn asks not only to be understood but to be sung: he is worthy of all our worship and joy.
Going Deeper: 1:21–23 Now He Has Reconciled You

1. Once: hostile to God. "And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds" (Colossians 1:21). Paul is blunt. We were not merely lost; we were God's "enemies" (see Rom 5:10). The hostility was in the mind and showed itself in evil deeds.

2. Now: by his death in the body. "He has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death" (Colossians 1:22). The means of reconciliation is concrete: a "body of flesh," a "death." The false teaching at Colossae may have looked down on the body and the material world. Paul insists that salvation was won in a real body, through a real death.

3. The goal of reconciliation. "In order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him" (Colossians 1:22). "Blameless" is a sacrificial word: what was offered to God had to be without defect. We had defects and were not fit to stand before God. Christ himself became the spotless sacrifice (see 1 Pet 1:19); in him we are counted righteous now, and at the last we will be made wholly holy and brought before God. This does not rest on our getting better and better but on what Christ has done for us.

4. "If indeed you continue in the faith." "If indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard" (Colossians 1:23). Different traditions read this condition differently.

  • The Reformed reading: Calvin and many Reformed interpreters hold that those who are truly reconciled to God will be kept by God to the end (see John 10:28–29; Phil 1:6). The "if" is a real warning, and God uses such warnings to keep his people; those who finally abandon the gospel show that they never truly belonged to Christ (see 1 John 2:19).
  • The Wesleyan and Arminian reading: John Wesley and Arminian interpreters hold that a true believer who abandons the faith can lose salvation (see Heb 3:14). So the "if" states a real condition of final salvation.
  • The tone of "if indeed": Many (e.g. J. B. Lightfoot) note that the Greek "if indeed" often carries a confident tone, close to "assuming, as I do, that you continue."
  • What both agree on: On either reading, this is a serious exhortation not to be taken lightly; and on either reading, perseverance does not come from our own strength but from abiding in Christ (see John 15:5). Paul is not trying to make believers live in doubt. He is urging them not to be "shifted" by false teaching away from the gospel they first heard.
The point: We were God's enemies, yet Christ reconciled us through his own body and death, to bring us before God without blemish. Those who continue do not stand by their own strength; they keep standing on this gospel.
Going Deeper: 1:24–29 Christ in You, the Hope of Glory

1. Rejoicing in suffering for others. "Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake" (Colossians 1:24). Paul was in prison as he wrote (Colossians 4:3, 18). He did not suffer to earn merit but "for your sake," so that the Gentiles could hear the gospel.

2. What "filling up what is lacking" does not mean. "And in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church" (Colossians 1:24). This is a hard sentence. First, it does not mean that Christ's redeeming work on the cross was not enough. Many note that the word for "afflictions" here is never used in the New Testament for Christ's atoning death. In this same chapter Paul says we "have redemption, the forgiveness of sins" in the Son (Colossians 1:14), and that peace was made "by the blood of his cross" (Colossians 1:20). Jesus said, "It is finished" (John 19:30). "By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified" (Heb 10:14).

3. Several readings.

  • The messianic woes: Many scholars (e.g. Douglas Moo) note a Jewish expectation that God's people would pass through a set measure of suffering before the new age fully came (see Matt 24:8). Christ has borne the decisive suffering; the church still shares in the rest during this age. Some add that Paul is glad to take more of it on himself so that others may bear less.
  • Union with Christ: Many others stress that the church is Christ's body, so when the church suffers, Christ shares in it. The risen Lord asked Saul, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" (Acts 9:4). The sufferings Paul bears for the church can be called Christ's afflictions (see 2 Cor 1:5; Phil 3:10).
  • The Catholic reading: Catholic teaching (e.g. Catechism 1508, which cites this verse, and 1476–77 on the "treasury of the Church") speaks of believers uniting their sufferings to Christ's for the church, while holding that his sacrifice is unique. The same tradition also uses the verse in support of the treasury of merit, in which the saints' merits help others have the temporal punishment for sin remitted. Reformed and Lutheran traditions reject this last reading, because Paul is speaking of suffering in order to spread the gospel and build the church, not to atone for others. Atonement is Christ's work alone, and it is finished.

4. The mystery hidden for ages. "The mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints" (Colossians 1:26). In Paul's letters a "mystery" is not a secret kept for a few insiders. It is God's plan, not fully shown before, that has now been made public through the gospel (see Eph 3:6). The false teaching at Colossae may have claimed deeper secrets. Paul says the true mystery has already been openly revealed to all the saints.

5. Christ in you. "To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:27). The content of the mystery is a person: Christ. And this Christ lives among the Gentiles, in people who were once "alienated" from God (Colossians 1:21). ("In you" can also mean "among you." Both fit: Christ lives in each believer and among his church.) Our hope does not rest on what we might become one day but on the Christ who is already in us.

6. Proclaiming him, to present everyone mature. "Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ" (Colossians 1:28). Paul does not proclaim a method but "him," Christ. "Everyone" appears three times: the gospel is not for a spiritual elite; every person can grow to maturity in Christ.

  • Laboring by his power: "For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me" (Colossians 1:29). Paul works hard, but he knows that what enables him to work this way is Christ's power at work in him.
The point: Paul gladly suffers, not to complete Christ's salvation but so that the Gentiles too may hear the mystery: Christ lives in you, and he is your hope of glory.
Meditation

Reflect: "All things were created through him and for him... and in him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:16–17). How large is Jesus in my mind? I easily connect him with Sunday, devotions and church. But in the lab, the office, the building site or the kitchen, in my field of study or in the news I read each day, I seldom think of him at all, as if most of the world had nothing to do with him. Paul says that all things "in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible" were created through him and for him. The accounts I balance, the code I write, the vegetables I grow and the tree outside my window are in his hands and exist for his glory. This is not one more burden, as if I had to make every task more "spiritual." It opens my eyes to see his wisdom in ordinary work and in the good things he made, and to delight in him there. I admit that I often live as if he were small, worth two hours of my week. Yet the one who holds all things together has not let go of me for thinking him small. Instead he shed his blood on the cross for me, who was once alienated from God and "hostile in mind," so that I could stand before God "holy and blameless and above reproach" (Colossians 1:21–22). Today, let me stop in one place I thought had nothing to do with him and say, "Lord, this too was made by you and for you." And then let me thank him, because he has already reconciled me to God.
