entries.title: 在他里面得了丰盛
entries.title_en: Filled in Him

verse_parts.text: 因为神本性一切的丰盛都有形有体地居住在基督里面，你们在他里面也得了丰盛。他是各样执政掌权者的元首。

entries.verse_text: 因为神本性一切的丰盛都有形有体地居住在基督里面，你们在他里面也得了丰盛。他是各样执政掌权者的元首。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第二章有四段。保罗的竭力（1-5节）：保罗为歌罗西人、老底嘉人和一切没有见过他面的信徒尽心竭力，要他们的心得安慰，因爱心互相联络，真知神的奥秘，就是基督；「所积蓄的一切智慧知识，都在他里面藏着」。在他里面生根（6-7节）：「你们既然接受了主基督耶稣，就当遵他而行」。这两节承上启下，是全信的转折点。在基督里的丰盛（8-15节）：要谨慎，不要被「理学和虚空的妄言」掳去，因为神本性一切的丰盛都有形有体地居住在基督里面，「你们在他里面也得了丰盛」；神赦免了我们一切过犯，把攻击我们的字据钉在十字架上，又仗着十字架胜过了一切执政的、掌权的。不要再服从人的规条（16-23节）：饮食、节期、安息日原是影儿，形体却是基督；不可让人因着故意谦虚和敬拜天使夺去你们的奖赏；既然已经与基督同死，为什么还要服从「不可拿、不可尝、不可摸」的规条呢？

全章反复出现「在他里面」：一切智慧知识在他里面藏着（3节），信徒要在他里面生根建造（7节），神本性一切的丰盛在他里面居住（9节），信徒在他里面得了丰盛，也在他里面受了割礼（10-11节）。保罗的论证很简单：既然一切都在基督里面，信徒就不需要在基督以外再找什么。

深读 2:1-5 一切智慧知识都在他里面藏着

1. 为没见过面的人竭力。 「我愿意你们晓得，我为你们和老底嘉人，并一切没有与我亲自见面的人，是何等地尽心竭力」（西2:1）。歌罗西教会不是保罗亲自建立的，而是以巴弗把福音传给他们的（西1:7；西4:12-13）。保罗从来没有见过他们，却为他们「尽心竭力」。这个词和西1:29的「尽心竭力」是同一个词根，原文有角力、奋斗的意思；以巴弗也是这样在祷告中为他们「竭力地祈求」（西4:12）。保罗当时被捆锁（西4:3、18），他能为他们做的，主要是祷告和写信。

2. 保罗竭力的目标。 「要叫他们的心得安慰，因爱心互相联络，以致丰丰足足在悟性中有充足的信心，使他们真知神的奥秘，就是基督」（西2:2）。

  • 心得安慰： 「安慰」在这里也有鼓励、坚固的意思。保罗不是只想让他们心里好受，而是要他们站稳。
  • 因爱心互相联络： 「联络」这个词在西2:19又出现，指身体的筋节把肢体连在一起。真理不是各人关起门来研究的，而是在彼此相爱的群体里一同明白的。
  • 神的奥秘就是基督： 神的奥秘就是基督（见西1:26-27）：不是一套知识，而是一位。

3. 一切宝藏都在他里面。 「所积蓄的一切智慧知识，都在他里面藏着」（西2:3）。「积蓄」原文就是宝藏。注意保罗说「一切」。歌罗西人可能听到有人说：基督是好的，但要有更深的智慧，还要加上别的东西。保罗回答：一切智慧和知识的宝藏都在基督里面，不在基督以外。「藏着」不是说神不让人找到这些宝藏，而是说它们只能在基督里面找到（参林前1:24、30；参箴2:4「隐藏的珍宝」）。

4. 花言巧语。 「我说这话，免得有人用花言巧语迷惑你们」（西2:4）。「花言巧语」指听起来很有道理、很能说服人的话。错误的教导很少一开始就否认基督，常常是用动听的话告诉人：你还缺一点东西。保罗先把基督的丰富讲清楚，再揭露那些说法，这是他保护教会的方法。

5. 保罗为他们欢喜。 「我身子虽与你们相离，心却与你们同在，见你们循规蹈矩，信基督的心也坚固，我就欢喜了」（西2:5）。「循规蹈矩」和「坚固」可能都是军队的用语，指队伍整齐、阵线稳固。保罗不是在责备一个已经跌倒的教会，而是在提醒一个还站得稳的教会，要防备将来的危险。

要点：人心常常以为，真正的智慧和属灵的深度藏在基督以外的某个地方。保罗说，一切智慧知识的宝藏都在基督里面；人越认识他，就越丰富。
深读 2:6-7 既然接受了主，就当遵他而行

1. 怎样开始，就怎样走下去。 「你们既然接受了主基督耶稣，就当遵他而行」（西2:6）。「接受」这个词常用来指领受传下来的教导（参林前15:3「我当日所领受」）。歌罗西人从以巴弗那里领受的，不只是一些关于基督的教导，而是「主基督耶稣」自己。他们怎样开始，就要怎样走下去：开始是靠基督，往前走也是靠基督，不是开始靠恩典，后来换成靠别的方法（参加3:3）。

2. 「主」基督耶稣。 保罗特别称他为「主」。歌罗西人接受的不只是一位帮助他们的老师，而是那位「万有都是靠他造的」主（西1:16）。所以「遵他而行」，就是在生活的每一部分都让他作主。

3. 生根、建造、坚固。 「在他里面生根建造，信心坚固，正如你们所领的教训」（西2:7）。保罗在这里用了几幅图画：

  • 生根： 像一棵树把根扎在土里。许多解经家指出，「生根」原文的时态表示根已经扎下，并且一直扎在那里；「建造」和「坚固」则表示仍在进行。
  • 建造： 像一座房子在根基上一层一层地建起来。
  • 坚固： 在所领受的信仰上站稳，「正如你们所领的教训」。

这几个词在原文都是被动的。许多人认为这暗示：使我们扎根、建造、坚固的，首先是神。我们的责任是留在基督里面，不离开这根基。

4. 感谢的心也更增长。 「感谢的心也更增长了」（西2:7）。感谢在歌罗西书里出现了好几次（西1:3、12；西3:15、17；西4:2）。一个知道自己在基督里已经得着一切的人，常常会感谢。反过来，一个总觉得自己还缺这缺那、需要在基督以外再找东西的人，心里就很难有感谢。

要点：我们怎样领受了基督，就要怎样在他里面行。开始是靠恩典，往前走也靠恩典；感谢是在基督里扎根的人自然结出的果子。
深读 2:8-15 你们在他里面也得了丰盛

1. 不要被掳去。 「你们要谨慎，恐怕有人用他的理学和虚空的妄言，不照着基督，乃照人间的遗传和世上的小学就把你们掳去」（西2:8）。

  • 「掳去」： 这个词有掳掠的意思，好像把战俘带走。错误的教导不是给人更多自由，而是叫人失去在基督里的自由。
  • 「理学」： 和合本的「理学」就是哲学，与中国的宋明理学不是一回事。保罗不是反对一切思考和学问，而是反对「不照着基督」的哲学。这里的「理学」可能是当时人对一套宗教思想的称呼，不一定是指希腊哲学家的学说。
  • 歌罗西的错误教导是什么： 信里没有直接说明，几种主要看法见导读。无论是哪一种，它都叫人觉得单有基督还不够。
  • 「世上的小学」： 和加4:3、9一样，原文是基本的元素：有人认为指初阶的宗教规条，有人认为指当时人以为掌管世界的灵界势力，也有人认为两层意思都有。上下文两边都连得上（西2:15「执政的、掌权的」；西2:20-21的规条）。

2. 神本性一切的丰盛。 「因为神本性一切的丰盛都有形有体地居住在基督里面」（西2:9）。这是新约里宣告基督神性最清楚的经文之一。

  • 「神本性」： 原文这个词指神之所以为神的本质，不只是神的某些属性或能力。基督不是半神，也不是神和人之间众多中保里的一位；神本性「一切」的丰盛都在他里面。
  • 「居住」： 指长久的居住，不是暂时寄居。这呼应西1:19：「父喜欢叫一切的丰盛在他里面居住」。
  • 「有形有体地」： 就是在身体里。永恒的神子取了真实的人性，有真实的身体（约1:14）；他复活升天以后，仍然是神，也仍然是人。这不是说神性变成了人性，也不是说人性被神性吞没。正如迦克墩会议（451年）所表达的：基督是一个位格，有完全的神性，也有完全的人性，两性不相混合，也不分离。
  • 为什么重要： 如果有人说，要亲近神，还需要天使或别的灵界中保，保罗的回答是：神的一切丰盛已经在基督里面，而且是在一个人的身体里，就是那位为我们死而复活的主。我们不需要越过他，去找一条更接近神的路。

3. 你们在他里面也得了丰盛。 「你们在他里面也得了丰盛。他是各样执政掌权者的元首」（西2:10）。

  • 同一个词根： 「丰盛」（西2:9）和「得了丰盛」（西2:10）在原文是同一个词根。丰盛在基督里面，信徒也在基督里面，所以信徒也得了丰盛。这不是说信徒变成了神，而是说，信徒在基督里已经有了与神相交所需要的一切。保罗在弗3:19甚至求神「叫神一切所充满的，充满了你们」，那也不是说人成了神。
  • 「得了」： 原文的时态指已经成就、现在仍然有效的事。保罗不是说你们将来才会得着，也不是说你们再加上什么才能得着，而是说你们已经得了。
  • 各样执政掌权者的元首： 这些「执政的、掌权的」都是藉着基督造的（西1:16），他也是它们的元首。人在基督里面，就不必惧怕这些势力，更不可敬拜它们。

4. 不是人手所行的割礼。 「你们在他里面也受了不是人手所行的割礼，乃是基督使你们脱去肉体情欲的割礼」（西2:11）。

  • 心里的割礼： 旧约已经应许，神要给人心里的割礼（申30:6；参耶4:4）。歌罗西信徒大多是外邦人，没有受过肉身的割礼，却在基督里受了真正的割礼。
  • 「脱去肉体情欲」： 原文直译是脱去肉体的身体。和合本理解为脱去旧的罪性，这和西3:9的「脱去旧人」相合。
  • 「基督……的割礼」： 解经家有两种主要理解。一种（如莱特福特）认为是基督所施行的割礼，就是他在我们身上所做的工作，使我们脱去旧的罪性。另一种（如弗雷德里克·布鲁斯）认为是指基督自己所受的割礼，就是他在十字架上的死：他的身体被脱去，我们在他里面也一同死了（参西2:12、20）；西1:22正是用「肉身」这个词说基督的身体受死。两种理解都把重点放在基督身上：我们真正的割礼，是在基督里面成就的。

5. 与他一同埋葬，一同复活。 「你们既受洗与他一同埋葬，也就在此与他一同复活，都因信那叫他从死里复活神的功用」（西2:12）。

  • 洗礼表明与基督联合： 和罗6:3-4一样，洗礼表明信徒与基督一同死、一同埋葬、一同复活。（和合本的「在此」可以指洗礼，也可以指基督，和西2:11「在他里面」平行。）
  • 割礼和洗礼的关系： 保罗在这里把割礼和洗礼放在一起，不同的传统有不同的理解。主张婴儿洗礼的改革宗传统（如加尔文《基督教要义》4.16；《威斯敏斯德信条》第28章）认为，洗礼在新约里取代了割礼，是神立约的记号，所以信徒的儿女也应当受洗，正如旧约里以色列的男孩受割礼（创17:10-11）。浸信会的传统（如1689年《伦敦浸信会信条》第29章）则认为，「不是人手所行的割礼」指的是重生；保罗又把洗礼和「因信」连在一起，所以只有能够自己表明信心的人才受洗。
  • 两个传统都同意的： 洗礼本身不是我们得救的根基。（信义宗和天主教对洗礼的功效另有更强的理解，这里不详论。）我们与基督一同复活，是「因信那叫他从死里复活神的功用」：大能是神的，根基是基督，信心是领受的途径。

6. 神叫我们活过来。 「你们从前在过犯和未受割礼的肉体中死了，神赦免了你们一切过犯，便叫你们与基督一同活过来」（西2:13）。注意这句话的主语是「神」。死人不能叫自己活过来（参弗2:5）。神赦免的不是一部分过犯，而是「一切过犯」。

7. 字据钉在十字架上。 「又涂抹了在律例上所写、攻击我们、有碍于我们的字据，把它撤去，钉在十字架上」（西2:14）。

  • 「字据」： 原文指亲笔写的欠条，欠债的人签了名，承认自己欠了多少。
  • 这字据是什么： 解经家有几种理解。多数人认为，这是我们在神面前欠下的罪债，因为我们没有遵守神的「律例」（参罗3:19-20）；有人认为这字据就是摩西的律法本身，因为律法定了人的罪；也有人联系到犹太文献里天上记录人罪行的册子。无论哪一种，这字据都是「攻击我们」的：它证明我们有罪，该受刑罚。
  • 钉在十字架上： 罗马人钉死犯人的时候，有时会把罪状写在牌子上，安在十字架上（参约19:19）。有些解经家认为保罗可能借用了这个画面：基督的十字架上，钉的是我们的罪状。基督在十字架上代替我们担当了罪的刑罚（参加3:13；林后5:21；彼前2:24），所以神可以公义地涂抹这字据。罪债不是被当作没有发生，而是由基督付清了。

8. 仗着十字架夸胜。 「既将一切执政的、掌权的掳来，明显给众人看，就仗着十字架夸胜」（西2:15）。

  • 「掳来」： 原文这个词的意思是剥去。多数解经家理解为：神解除了这些势力的武装，剥夺了它们的权势。也有人（如莱特福特）理解为：基督把这些攻击他的势力从自己身上脱下来，好像脱下衣服一样。
  • 「明显给众人看」： 这是罗马凯旋游行的图画：得胜的将军带着被掳的敌人游街示众（参林后2:14）。十字架在人看来是耶稣最大的失败和羞辱，在神看来却是他胜过一切黑暗权势的时候。
  • 「仗着十字架」： 原文这里可以指基督，也可以指十字架；和合本译作十字架。无论哪一种，得胜都是在十字架上成就的。
  • 今天的意义： 这些势力已经被解除武装。信徒仍然要警醒（参弗6:12），但不必活在惧怕里，好像还要靠什么方法才能保护自己。
要点：神本性一切的丰盛都在基督里面，信徒在基督里面也得了丰盛。我们的罪债已经被钉在十字架上，攻击我们的权势已经被解除武装；在基督以外，我们不需要再找什么；我们可以不再惧怕，只管在他里面欢喜。
深读 2:16-19 影儿与形体

1. 不可让人论断你们。 「所以，不拘在饮食上，或节期、月朔、安息日都不可让人论断你们」（西2:16）。「所以」把这段和上文连起来：既然基督已经成就了一切，就不要让人用这些事来论断你们。「节期、月朔、安息日」是旧约常见的说法（代上23:31；何2:11；结45:17），许多人认为是指以色列人每年、每月、每周的圣日（另一种看法见下文）。

2. 影儿和形体。 「这些原是后事的影儿；那形体却是基督」（西2:17）。影儿是真的，却不是本体。人看见影子，就知道有一个实体要来了；实体来了，就不必再抓着影子不放（参来8:5；来10:1）。旧约的饮食条例和节期是神亲自设立的，本身不是坏的，但它们都指向基督。「形体」原文是身体：真正的实体是基督。

3. 安息日的问题。 这节经文常常引起讨论：信徒今天怎样看安息日？

  • 威斯敏斯德和清教徒的传统（如《威斯敏斯德信条》21.7-8）认为，十诫的第四条是道德律，根于创造（创2:3；出20:11）；到了新约，安息日改为七日的第一日，就是主日，是「基督徒的安息日」。按照这个看法，保罗在这里说的是犹太历法里礼仪性的安息日，所以和节期、月朔连在一起。这个传统里也有人承认这里包括犹太人每周的安息日，但认为过去的只是它礼仪的部分，七日中有一日归给神的原则仍然存在。
  • 另一些福音派学者（如道格拉斯·穆尔，以及卡森所编《从安息日到主日》一书的几位作者）认为，安息日本身也是影儿，在基督里得着成全（参太11:28；来4:9）；信徒在七日的第一日聚会（徒20:7；林前16:2；启1:10），是因为主在这一天复活，而不是因为第四条诫命移到了这一天。
  • 基督复临安息日会的信徒守星期六为安息日。他们认为这里所说的只是礼仪性的安息日（参利23章），不是十诫的第四条。
  • 保罗的重点： 无论怎样理解，保罗都不是要人轻看敬拜和安息，而是说：守日子不是得神接纳的条件，也不可用来论断别人（参罗14:5-6）。主耶稣说：「安息日是为人设立的，人不是为安息日设立的」（可2:27）；他自己就是「安息日的主」（太12:8）。

4. 夺去奖赏的人。 「不可让人因着故意谦虚和敬拜天使，就夺去你们的奖赏。这等人拘泥在所见过的，随着自己的欲心，无故地自高自大」（西2:18）。

  • 「夺去你们的奖赏」： 这个词原是运动场上裁判的用语，指判人失去资格。那些人好像自封的裁判，说你不够资格，因为你没有他们那样的操练和经历。
  • 「故意谦虚」： 这里和西2:23的「谦卑」是同一个词，很可能是指禁食和苦待己身一类的操练。这种谦虚是故意做出来的，可以拿来比较，也可以拿来炫耀。
  • 「敬拜天使」： 解经家有两种主要理解。一种（如克林顿·阿诺德）认为是向天使敬拜、求告天使：当时小亚细亚一带的民间宗教，有人求天使保护、驱邪。另一种（如弗雷德·弗朗西斯）认为是天使所献上的敬拜：有人以为，经过禁食和苦修，就可以在异象中上到天上，和天使一同敬拜神。无论哪一种，都是把某种特别的属灵经历放在基督之上。圣经里的天使自己也不许人拜他（启22:8-9）。
  • 「拘泥在所见过的」： 这句话原文很难翻译，可能是指人沉浸在自己见过的异象里，以此为凭据，自高自大。
  • 「随着自己的欲心」： 原文直译是肉体的心思。讽刺的是，这些人自以为最属灵，保罗却说他们的心思是属肉体的。

5. 不持定元首。 「不持定元首。全身既然靠着他，筋节得以相助联络，就因神大得长进」（西2:19）。这才是问题的根：他们看起来很属灵，却没有持定基督。一个人可以有许多操练和经历，却离开了元首。教会的长进不是靠少数自以为属灵的精英，而是全身都靠着元首，彼此联络（参弗4:15-16）。长进是「因神」而来的。

要点：旧约的饮食和节期是影儿，真正的实体是基督。没有人有权因为你缺少某种操练或经历，就判你不够资格；你的奖赏在基督手里，不在自封的裁判手里。
深读 2:20-23 「不可拿、不可尝、不可摸」

1. 你们已经与基督同死。 「你们若是与基督同死，脱离了世上的小学，为什么仍像在世俗中活着、服从那『不可拿、不可尝、不可摸』等类的规条呢？」（西2:20）。这里的「若是」不是表示怀疑，而是「既然」的意思。信徒已经与基督同死（西2:12），就脱离了「世上的小学」的辖制。人死了，就不再受从前那个国度的法律管辖。

2. 规条的问题。

  • 「不可拿、不可尝、不可摸」： 这些规条一条比一条严。有人以为，规条越多越严，人就越属灵。
  • 「正用的时候就都败坏了」： 这些规条管的多半是食物一类的东西，吃下去就没有了（西2:22）。主耶稣说，从外面进去的不能污秽人（可7:15、19）；保罗也说：「凡神所造的物都是好的，若感谢着领受，就没有一样可弃的」（提前4:4）。
  • 「照人所吩咐、所教导的」： 这些规条不是从神来的，而是从人来的（西2:22；参赛29:13；可7:7）。

3. 看起来有智慧，其实没有功效。 「这些规条使人徒有智慧之名，用私意崇拜，自表谦卑，苦待己身，其实在克制肉体的情欲上是毫无功效」（西2:23）。保罗承认，这些规条看起来很有智慧，很有敬虔的样子。但它们有一个致命的问题：不能改变人心。规条可以管住人的手，却管不住人的心；它甚至会让人更骄傲，因为人会拿自己守得多好去和别人比。真正能胜过肉体情欲的，是保罗在西3:1以下所说的：与基督一同复活，思念上面的事。

4. 今天的规条。 在华人教会里，这样的规条可能有不同的样子：

  • 有人认为，信徒一定要每天清早几点起来晨祷、禁食多少天、每年读经多少遍，才算属灵；
  • 有人把某些属灵经历（比如说方言、见异象、做异梦）当作信徒的等级，没有这些经历的，就好像是二等信徒；
  • 有些从民间宗教背景信主的人，仍然带着从前守禁忌的心态，只是把初一十五吃素一类的禁忌，换成了一套教会里的规矩，在穿着、饮食、娱乐上用它来衡量人的属灵程度。

这些事未必都错。禁食、晨祷、读经都是好的操练（参太6:16-18）；有人为了良心的缘故不喝酒，也是可以的（参罗14:21-22）。神今天也可以赐人特别的经历（各教会对属灵恩赐的看法不同，参林前12章）。问题在于把这些当作在神面前的资格，或者拿来论断别人。属灵操练是领受恩典的途径，不是挣得恩典的手段。

要点：规条可以让人看起来很属灵，却不能改变人心。信徒已经与基督同死、同复活，不必再受人的规条辖制；属灵操练是领受恩典的途径，不是挣得恩典的手段。
默想

默想： 「所积蓄的一切智慧知识，都在他里面藏着」（西2:3）；「你们在他里面也得了丰盛」（西2:10）。我是不是常常觉得，属灵生命还差一点什么？也许是下一个特会、下一本书、一套新的灵修方法，或者一次「突破性」的经历。我一样一样地去试，起初很火热，过几个月又淡了，就再去找下一个。也许小组里有人分享，他每天清早五点起来祷告两个钟头，或者讲起自己见过的异象，我心里羡慕，又觉得自己像个二等信徒。又或者，我自己就是那个暗暗给别人打分、看谁不如我属灵的人。那位弟兄的操练，也许正是神给他的恩典；问题不在他，而在我心里那个念头：基督只是起点，真正的丰盛要到别处去找。父已经「叫我们能与众圣徒在光明中同得基业」（西1:12）；神本性一切的丰盛都在基督里面，而我在基督里面，也「得了丰盛」。这不是我修来的，而是因为神「赦免了你们一切过犯」（西2:13），基督把我的罪债钉在十字架上（西2:14）。我最好的操练不能给这丰盛加添什么，我最失败的日子也不能使它减少什么。今天，我能不能把这份不停的寻找，连同我暗暗给人打过的分，一起带到主面前认罪，然后对他说：「主啊，在你里面，我已经得了丰盛；我不需要在你以外再找什么。」这样，祷告、读经、禁食都可以是我来到他面前的路，而不是我拿来给人看的证明。基督已经在十字架上为我得胜（西2:15）；我的奖赏不在任何裁判手里，而在他手里。他说，属他的人，「谁也不能从我手里把他们夺去」（约10:28）。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 2 has four parts. Paul's struggle (vv. 1–5): Paul struggles for the Colossians, the Laodiceans and all who have not seen him face to face, that their hearts may be encouraged, knit together in love, and reach the knowledge of God's mystery, which is Christ, "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." Rooted in him (vv. 6–7): "As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him." These two verses look back and forward; they are the hinge of the letter. Fullness in Christ (vv. 8–15): see to it that no one takes you captive "by philosophy and empty deceit," for in Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, "and you have been filled in him"; God has forgiven all our trespasses, nailed the record of debt that stood against us to the cross, and triumphed over the rulers and authorities. No longer under human regulations (vv. 16–23): food, festivals and Sabbaths are a shadow, but the substance belongs to Christ; let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and the worship of angels; since you died with Christ, why submit to "Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch"?

The phrase "in him" runs through the chapter: all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him (v. 3), believers are rooted and built up in him (v. 7), the whole fullness of deity dwells in him (v. 9), and believers have been filled in him and circumcised in him (vv. 10–11). Paul's argument is simple: since everything is in Christ, believers need not look for anything outside him.

Going Deeper: 2:1–5 All the Treasures Hidden in Him

1. Struggling for people he has never met. "For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face" (Colossians 2:1). Paul did not plant the church in Colossae; Epaphras brought them the gospel (Colossians 1:7; Colossians 4:12–13). Paul had never seen them, yet he "struggles" for them. It shares its root with "struggling" in Colossians 1:29, a word for wrestling and contending; Epaphras too is "always struggling on your behalf in his prayers" (Colossians 4:12). Paul was in chains (Colossians 4:3, 18), and what he could do for them was chiefly to pray and to write.

2. The aim of his struggle. "That their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God's mystery, which is Christ" (Colossians 2:2).

  • Hearts encouraged: the word also carries the sense of strengthening. Paul does not only want them to feel better; he wants them to stand firm.
  • Knit together in love: the same word appears in Colossians 2:19 for the ligaments that hold a body together. Truth is not studied by each person alone behind closed doors; it is understood together in a community that loves one another.
  • God's mystery is Christ: in Paul's letters a "mystery" is not a secret only a few may know, but God's plan once hidden and now revealed (Colossians 1:26–27). This mystery is not a body of knowledge but a person: Christ.

3. Every treasure is in him. "In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). Notice the word "all." The Colossians may have been told that Christ is good, but deeper wisdom requires something more. Paul answers that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are in Christ, not outside him. "Hidden" does not mean God keeps them from being found, but that they can be found only in Christ (see 1 Cor 1:24, 30; compare "hidden treasures" in Prov 2:4).

4. Plausible arguments. "I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments" (Colossians 2:4). "Plausible arguments" are words that sound reasonable and persuasive. False teaching seldom begins by denying Christ; it more often tells people in attractive words that they are still missing something. Paul first sets out the riches of Christ and only then exposes those claims; this is how he protects the church.

5. Paul rejoices over them. "For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ" (Colossians 2:5). "Good order" and "firmness" may both be military terms, for ranks in order and a battle line holding. Paul is not rebuking a church that has already fallen, but warning a church still standing firm about a danger ahead.

The point: The human heart often imagines that true wisdom and spiritual depth are hidden somewhere outside Christ. Paul says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are in Christ; the more we know him, the richer we are.
Going Deeper: 2:6–7 As You Received Christ, So Walk in Him

1. Go on as you began. "Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him" (Colossians 2:6). "Received" is often used of receiving teaching that has been handed down (see 1 Cor 15:3, "what I also received"). What the Colossians received from Epaphras was not only teaching about Christ but "Christ Jesus the Lord" himself. As they began, so they are to go on: they began by Christ and go on by Christ; they did not begin by grace in order to switch later to some other method (see Gal 3:3).

2. Christ Jesus "the Lord." Paul deliberately calls him "the Lord." The Colossians received not merely a teacher who helps them, but the Lord by whom "all things were created" (Colossians 1:16). To "walk in him" is to let him be Lord over every part of life.

3. Rooted, built up, established. "Rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught" (Colossians 2:7). Paul uses several pictures here:

  • Rooted: like a tree sending its roots into the soil. Many interpreters note that the tense of "rooted" points to roots already put down and still holding, while "built up" and "established" describe something still going on.
  • Built up: like a house rising floor by floor on its foundation.
  • Established: standing firm in the faith received, "just as you were taught."

All these verbs are passive in Greek. Many take this to suggest that it is first of all God who roots, builds and establishes us. Our part is to remain in Christ and not leave this foundation.

4. Abounding in thanksgiving. "Abounding in thanksgiving" (Colossians 2:7). Thanksgiving comes up again and again in Colossians (Colossians 1:3, 12; Colossians 3:15, 17; Colossians 4:2). Someone who knows he already has everything in Christ will often give thanks. By contrast, someone who always feels he is missing this or that, and must look outside Christ for more, will find thanks hard to come by.

The point: As we received Christ, so we walk in him. We began by grace and we go on by grace; thanksgiving is the natural fruit of a life rooted in Christ.
Going Deeper: 2:8–15 You Have Been Filled in Him

1. Do not be taken captive. "See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ" (Colossians 2:8).

  • "Takes you captive": a word for carrying off plunder or leading away captives of war. False teaching does not give people more freedom; it robs them of their freedom in Christ.
  • "Philosophy": (The Chinese Union Version's word here, 理学, simply means "philosophy"; it is unrelated to Chinese Neo-Confucianism.) Paul is not against all thinking and learning, but against philosophy "not according to Christ." The word may be how people then named a body of religious ideas, not necessarily the schools of the Greek philosophers.
  • What was the Colossian error? The letter never states it directly; for the main proposals see the Introduction. Whatever it was exactly, it left people feeling that Christ alone was not enough.
  • "The elemental spirits of the world": as in Galatians 4:3, 9, the Greek word means basic elements: some take it as elementary religious rules, some as the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world (the ESV's "elemental spirits"), others as both. The context fits both (the "rulers and authorities" of Colossians 2:15; the rules of Colossians 2:20–21).

2. The whole fullness of deity. "For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:9). This is one of the clearest statements of Christ's deity in the New Testament.

  • "Deity": the Greek word means the very being of God, what makes God God, not merely some of his attributes or powers. Christ is not a demigod, nor one of many intermediaries between God and humanity; the "whole" fullness of deity is in him.
  • "Dwells": a lasting dwelling, not a temporary stay. It echoes Colossians 1:19: "For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell."
  • "Bodily": in a body. The eternal Son took a true human nature, with a real body (John 1:14); after his resurrection and ascension he remains God and remains man. This does not mean deity turned into humanity, or that his humanity was swallowed up by his deity. As the Council of Chalcedon (451) put it, Christ is one person, fully God and fully man, his two natures neither mixed nor separated.
  • Why it matters: if anyone says that to draw near to God we also need angels or other spiritual intermediaries, Paul's answer is that all God's fullness is already in Christ, and in a human body, the body of the Lord who died and rose for us. We do not need to go past him to find a road closer to God.

3. You have been filled in him. "And you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority" (Colossians 2:10).

  • The same root: "fullness" (Colossians 2:9) and "filled" (Colossians 2:10) come from the same Greek root. The fullness is in Christ, believers are in Christ, so believers have been filled. This does not mean believers become God (Eph 3:19 even prays that we be "filled with all the fullness of God," and that too does not mean we become God), but that in Christ they already have everything they need for fellowship with God.
  • "Have been filled": the tense describes something already accomplished and still in effect. Paul does not say you will be filled one day, or that you will be filled once you add something more, but that you have been filled.
  • Head of all rule and authority: these "rulers and authorities" were created through Christ (Colossians 1:16), and he is their head. Those who are in Christ need not fear these powers, and must not worship them.

4. A circumcision made without hands. "In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ" (Colossians 2:11).

  • Circumcision of the heart: the Old Testament had already promised that God would circumcise the heart (Deut 30:6; see Jer 4:4). Most of the Colossian believers were Gentiles who had never been circumcised in the body, yet in Christ they had received the true circumcision.
  • "Putting off the body of the flesh": the CUV renders it "putting off the sinful desires of the flesh," taking it as putting off the old sinful nature, which fits "you have put off the old self" in Colossians 3:9.
  • "The circumcision of Christ": interpreters hold two main views. One (for example, J. B. Lightfoot) takes it as the circumcision Christ performs, his work in us by which we put off the old sinful nature. The other (for example, F. F. Bruce) takes it as the "circumcision" Christ himself underwent, his death on the cross: his body was "put off," and we died with him in him (see Colossians 2:12, 20); Colossians 1:22 uses the same phrase, "body of flesh," for Christ's own body in death. Both readings put the weight on Christ: our true circumcision was accomplished in Christ.

5. Buried with him, raised with him. "Having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead" (Colossians 2:12).

  • Baptism shows union with Christ: as in Romans 6:3–4, baptism shows that the believer has died, been buried and been raised with Christ. (The ESV's "in which" may refer to baptism, or to Christ, "in whom," parallel to "in him" in Colossians 2:11.)
  • How circumcision and baptism relate: Paul sets circumcision and baptism side by side here, and traditions understand this differently. The Reformed tradition that baptizes infants (for example, Calvin, Institutes 4.16; the Westminster Confession, ch. 28) holds that in the new covenant baptism takes the place of circumcision as the sign of God's covenant, so believers' children should be baptized, as Israelite boys were circumcised under the old covenant (Gen 17:10–11). The Baptist tradition (for example, the 1689 London Baptist Confession, ch. 29) holds that Paul here ties baptism to "faith," and that the circumcision made without hands is the new birth, so baptism is for those who can profess faith for themselves.
  • What both traditions agree on: baptism itself is not the ground of our salvation. (Lutheran and Catholic traditions hold a stronger view of baptism's efficacy, which we do not take up here.) We are raised with Christ "through faith in the powerful working of God": the power is God's, the ground is Christ, and faith is the means by which we receive it.

6. God made us alive. "And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). Notice that the subject of the sentence is "God." The dead cannot make themselves alive (see Eph 2:5). God forgave not some of our trespasses but "all our trespasses."

7. The record of debt nailed to the cross. "By canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross" (Colossians 2:14).

  • "Record of debt": the Greek word means a handwritten IOU, signed by the debtor, acknowledging how much he owed.
  • What the record is: interpreters offer several readings. Most take it as the debt of sin we owe God because we have not kept his "legal demands" (see Rom 3:19–20); some take it as the law of Moses itself, since the law condemns sinners; others connect it with a heavenly book of misdeeds found in Jewish writings. On every reading, the record "stood against us": it proved us guilty and deserving of punishment.
  • Nailed to the cross: when the Romans crucified someone, they sometimes wrote the charge on a placard and fixed it to the cross (see John 19:19). Some interpreters think Paul may be drawing on that picture: on Christ's cross hung the charge against us. Christ bore the penalty of sin in our place on the cross (see Gal 3:13; 2 Cor 5:21; 1 Pet 2:24), so God can justly cancel the record. The debt was not treated as though it had never existed; Christ paid it.

8. Triumph through the cross. "He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him" (Colossians 2:15).

  • "Disarmed": the Greek word means stripped. Most interpreters understand it as God disarming these powers and stripping them of their authority. Some (for example, J. B. Lightfoot) understand it as Christ stripping off from himself the powers that assailed him, as one takes off a garment.
  • "Put them to open shame": the picture is a Roman triumph, in which a victorious general led his captured enemies through the streets on display (see 2 Cor 2:14). In human eyes the cross was Jesus' greatest defeat and shame; in God's eyes it was the moment he triumphed over all the powers of darkness.
  • "In him": the Greek can refer to Christ or to the cross; the CUV translates "by the cross." Either way, the victory was won at the cross.
  • What it means today: these powers have been disarmed. Believers must still be watchful (see Eph 6:12), but they need not live in fear, as though they still had to find some method to protect themselves.
The point: The whole fullness of deity is in Christ, and in Christ believers have been filled. Our debt has been nailed to the cross, and the powers that stood against us have been disarmed; outside Christ we need look for nothing more. We need not fear; we may simply rejoice in him.
Going Deeper: 2:16–19 Shadow and Substance

1. Let no one pass judgment on you. "Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath" (Colossians 2:16). "Therefore" links this paragraph to what came before: since Christ has accomplished everything, do not let anyone judge you over these things. "Festival, new moon and Sabbath" is a common Old Testament grouping (1 Chr 23:31; Hos 2:11; Ezek 45:17). Many take it as Israel's yearly, monthly and weekly holy days; for another view, see below.

2. Shadow and substance. "These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ" (Colossians 2:17). A shadow is real, but it is not the thing itself. When we see a shadow, we know that something real is coming; once it has come, there is no need to keep clutching the shadow (see Heb 8:5; Heb 10:1). The Old Testament food laws and festivals were given by God himself and were not bad in themselves, but they pointed to Christ. The Greek word for "substance" is "body": the reality is Christ.

3. The question of the Sabbath. This verse often raises the question of how believers today should think about the Sabbath.

  • The Westminster and Puritan tradition (for example, the Westminster Confession 21.7–8) holds that the fourth commandment is moral law rooted in creation (Gen 2:3; Exod 20:11), and that in the new covenant the Sabbath moved to the first day of the week, the Lord's Day, which is "the Christian Sabbath." On this view Paul is speaking of the ceremonial sabbaths of the Jewish calendar, which is why they stand alongside festivals and new moons. Some in this tradition grant that the weekly Jewish Sabbath is meant, but hold that only its ceremonial form has passed away, while the principle of one day in seven given to God remains.
  • Other evangelical scholars (for example, Douglas Moo and the contributors to From Sabbath to Lord's Day, edited by D. A. Carson) hold that the Sabbath itself is also a shadow fulfilled in Christ (see Matt 11:28; Heb 4:9), and that believers gather on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2; Rev 1:10) because the Lord rose on that day, not because the fourth commandment moved to it.
  • Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday as the Sabbath. They hold that this verse speaks only of ceremonial sabbaths (see Lev 23), not of the fourth commandment.
  • Paul's point: however this is understood, Paul is not telling anyone to think lightly of worship or rest. He is saying that keeping days is not a condition of God's acceptance, and must not be used to judge others (see Rom 14:5–6). The Lord Jesus said, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27), and he himself is "lord of the Sabbath" (Matt 12:8).

4. Those who would disqualify you. "Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind" (Colossians 2:18).

  • "Disqualify": the word was used of an umpire at the games ruling a competitor out. These people acted like self-appointed umpires, declaring you unqualified because you lacked their disciplines and experiences.
  • "Asceticism": the Greek word is "humility," the same word as in Colossians 2:23 (the CUV has "deliberate humility"). It most likely refers to fasting and harsh treatment of the body. This kind of humility is put on deliberately; it can be compared and it can be displayed.
  • "Worship of angels": interpreters hold two main views. One (for example, Clinton Arnold) takes it as worship directed to angels, calling on them: in the popular religion of Asia Minor, people invoked angels for protection and to ward off evil. The other (for example, Fred Francis) takes it as the worship that angels offer: some believed that through fasting and severe discipline they could ascend in visions to heaven and join the angels in worshiping God. On either view, a special spiritual experience is being set above Christ. In Scripture the angels themselves refuse worship (Rev 22:8–9).
  • "Going on in detail about visions": the Greek phrase is hard to translate. It may mean dwelling on visions one has seen and using them as credentials, puffed up.
  • "His sensuous mind": literally "the mind of the flesh." The irony is that those who thought themselves most spiritual had, Paul says, a fleshly mind.

5. Not holding fast to the Head. "And not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God" (Colossians 2:19). Here is the root of the problem: they looked very spiritual, but they did not hold fast to Christ. A person can have many disciplines and experiences and still let go of the Head. The church does not grow by a few who think themselves a spiritual elite, but by the whole body depending on the Head and being knit together (see Eph 4:15–16). Its growth is "from God."

The point: The Old Testament food laws and festivals were a shadow; the reality is Christ. No one has the right to rule you unqualified because you lack some discipline or experience; your prize is in Christ's hands, not in the hands of a self-appointed umpire.
Going Deeper: 2:20–23 "Do Not Handle, Do Not Taste, Do Not Touch"

1. You died with Christ. "If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations—'Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch'" (Colossians 2:20–21). "If" here expresses no doubt; it means "since." Believers have already died with Christ (Colossians 2:12) and so have been released from the rule of "the elemental spirits of the world." The dead are no longer under the laws of the realm they once lived in.

2. The trouble with regulations.

  • "Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch": each rule is stricter than the last. Some imagine that the more and stricter the rules, the more spiritual a person is.
  • "Things that all perish as they are used": these rules mostly concern things like food, which are gone once eaten (Colossians 2:22). The Lord Jesus said that nothing outside a person can defile him by going into him (Mark 7:15, 19), and Paul says, "For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving" (1 Tim 4:4).
  • "According to human precepts and teachings": these rules come not from God but from people (Colossians 2:22; see Isa 29:13; Mark 7:7).

3. An appearance of wisdom, but no value. "These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh" (Colossians 2:23). Paul grants that these rules look wise and devout. But they have a fatal flaw: they cannot change the heart. Rules can restrain the hand but not the heart; they can even make a person prouder, as he compares how well he keeps them with how others do. What truly overcomes the indulgence of the flesh is what Paul describes from Colossians 3:1 on: being raised with Christ and setting the mind on things above.

4. Regulations today. In Chinese churches such rules can take various forms:

  • some believe a Christian must rise at a set early hour for morning prayer, fast so many days, or read the Bible through so many times a year to count as spiritual;
  • some treat certain spiritual experiences (speaking in tongues, seeing visions, receiving dreams) as ranks among believers, so that those without them seem second-class Christians;
  • some who come to faith from a folk-religion background carry over the old mindset of keeping taboos, simply exchanging vegetarian days on the first and fifteenth of the lunar month for a set of church rules about dress, food and entertainment, used to measure how spiritual people are.

Not all of these things are wrong. Fasting, morning prayer and Bible reading are good disciplines (see Matt 6:16–18); someone who abstains from alcohol for conscience' sake may do so (see Rom 14:21–22). God can also give special experiences today (churches differ in their view of spiritual gifts; see 1 Cor 12). The problem comes when these are treated as qualifications before God, or used to judge others. Spiritual disciplines are means of receiving grace, not ways of earning it.

The point: Regulations can make people look spiritual, but they cannot change the heart. Believers have died and been raised with Christ and need not be ruled by human regulations; spiritual disciplines are means of receiving grace, not ways of earning it.
Meditation

Reflect: "In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3); "and you have been filled in him" (Colossians 2:10). Do I often feel that my spiritual life is still missing something? Perhaps it is the next conference, the next book, a new method of devotion or a "breakthrough" experience. I try them one after another, eager at first, flat a few months later, and then I go looking for the next. Perhaps someone in my small group shared that he rises at five to pray for two hours, or told of visions he had seen, and I admired him and felt like a second-class Christian. Or perhaps I am the one quietly scoring others, noting who is less spiritual than I am. That brother's discipline may well be God's gift to him. The problem is not him but the thought in my own heart that Christ is only the starting point and real fullness lies somewhere else. The Father "has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light" (Colossians 1:12); the whole fullness of deity is in Christ, and in Christ I too "have been filled." I did not attain this by discipline; God has forgiven "us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13), and Christ nailed my record of debt to the cross (Colossians 2:14). My best disciplines cannot add anything to this fullness, and my worst failures cannot take anything from it. Today, can I bring this restless searching, along with any scores I have quietly kept on others, to the Lord in confession, and say to him, "Lord, in you I have been filled; I need nothing outside you"? Then prayer, Bible reading and fasting can be roads by which I come to him, not proofs I hold up to others. Christ has already triumphed for me at the cross (Colossians 2:15); my prize is not in any umpire's hands but in his, and he says of those who are his, "no one will snatch them out of my hand" (John 10:28).

entries.verse_text: 因为你们已经死了，你们的生命与基督一同藏在神里面。基督是我们的生命，他显现的时候，你们也要与他一同显现在荣耀里。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第二章揭露了歌罗西那些「不可拿、不可尝、不可摸」的规条（西2:20-23），第三章就正面说明：真正的圣洁生活是从哪里来的。本章可以分为五段：与基督一同复活（1-4节）；治死与脱去（5-11节）；穿上基督的样式（12-17节）；家中的关系（18-21节）；仆人与主人（西3:22-4:1）。西4:1和上文是同一段，所以放在本章一起读。

全章的次序很重要：先说「你们已经……」，再说「所以要……」。先有神在基督里为我们做成的事，然后才有我们的顺服。本章最常出现的名字是「基督」和「主」：基督坐在神的右边，基督是我们的生命，基督是包括一切，基督的平安，基督的道理，事奉主基督。

深读 3:1-4 求在上面的事

1. 「你们若真与基督一同复活」。 「所以，你们若真与基督一同复活，就当求在上面的事；那里有基督坐在神的右边」（西3:1）。这里的「若」不是怀疑，而是「既然」的意思：保罗在西2:12已经说过，「你们既受洗与他一同埋葬，也就在此与他一同复活」。信徒与基督联合，所以基督的死就是我们的死，基督的复活就是我们的复活（参罗6:4-11）。保罗先说我们是谁，再说我们该怎样活。

2. 那里有基督。 「上面的事」不是叫人脱离现实、空想天堂，而是指基督所在的地方，和他所看重的事。「坐在神的右边」引自诗篇第一百一十篇第1节，表示基督已经得胜，正在掌权。歌罗西的假教师要人靠规条、节期和天使的异象去「往上爬」（西2:16-18）；保罗却说，不必爬，因为你们已经在基督里，而基督已经在上面了。

3. 思念上面的事。 「你们要思念上面的事，不要思念地上的事」（西3:2）。「思念」是指一个人心思的方向，就是他常常想什么、看重什么、追求什么。「地上的事」不是说吃饭、工作、成家这些事本身不好；下面保罗就要谈家庭和工作。「地上的事」是指那些属于旧人、与基督无关的心思和欲望（西3:5）。

4. 已经死了，生命藏着。 「因为你们已经死了，你们的生命与基督一同藏在神里面」（西3:3）。「已经死了」是指那个属于旧世界的我已经与基督同死了（西2:20）。「藏」是隐藏，现在还看不出来；而藏在神里面，也就是被安稳地保守着（参西2:3）。我们真正的生命不在别人的评价里，也不在自己的成就里，而是在基督里，并且「在神里面」，没有人能夺走（参约10:28-29）。

5. 他显现的时候。 「基督是我们的生命，他显现的时候，你们也要与他一同显现在荣耀里」（西3:4）。保罗不只说基督「给」我们生命，而是说基督「是」我们的生命。现在这生命是藏着的，将来基督再来的时候，神要把他在基督里为我们所做的，完全显明出来（参约一3:2；罗8:18-19）。

要点：信徒已经与基督同死、同复活，真正的生命与基督一同藏在神里面。所以我们思念上面的事，不是要逃离地上的生活，而是因为我们的生命就在那位坐在神右边的基督那里。
深读 3:5-11 治死与脱去

1. 「所以，要治死」。 「所以，要治死你们在地上的肢体，就如淫乱、污秽、邪情、恶欲，和贪婪（贪婪就与拜偶像一样）」（西3:5）。注意开头的「所以」：因为你们已经死了（西3:3），所以要治死。这听起来好像矛盾，其实不然：神已经使我们与基督一同死了，旧人确实已经死了（罗6:6），我们现在就照着这个事实去活，不再顺从那些属于旧人的欲望（参罗6:11）。清教徒约翰·欧文在《论治死罪》里说：「你若不治死罪，罪就要治死你。」但他也强调，治死罪是靠着圣灵（罗8:13）、仰望基督的十字架；我们治死罪，是因为已经被神接纳，而不是为了被神接纳。

「在地上的肢体」不是叫人伤害自己的身体；保罗刚刚说过，「苦待己身」的规条对克制肉体的情欲毫无功效（西2:23）。他说的是在我们里面那些还属于地上的欲望和行为。

2. 贪婪就是拜偶像。 保罗列出的五样罪，前四样多半和性方面的罪有关，最后一样是贪婪。他特别说「贪婪就与拜偶像一样」（参太6:24）。拜偶像的本质，就是把神以外的东西当作安全、满足和意义的来源。在一个常常说「有钱才有安全感」的文化里，我们很可能一面在教会里事奉，一面心里真正倚靠的却是存款和房子。我们很少把贪婪当作罪来认，所以更需要把它点明，在神面前悔改。

3. 神的忿怒。 「因这些事，神的忿怒必临到那悖逆之子」（西3:6）。（「那悖逆之子」这几个字，有几份很早的抄本没有，但大多数抄本都有；和合本有，有些英文译本没有。）保罗提到忿怒，不是要叫信徒活在惧怕中，而是要我们看清罪有多严重。基督已经为这些罪承受了神的忿怒，我们就不能再把它们当作小事。一个人若安心继续活在这些罪中，就不可自欺，以为自己属于基督（参弗5:5-6；林前6:9-11）。「当你们在这些事中活着的时候，也曾这样行过」（西3:7）：「曾」字说明，那是从前的事，不是现在的身份。

4. 口中的罪。 「但现在你们要弃绝这一切的事，以及恼恨、忿怒、恶毒、毁谤，并口中污秽的言语。不要彼此说谎」（西3:8-9）。第二组罪多半和话语有关。教会里更常见的罪不是淫乱，而是闲话、讽刺、背后批评和不诚实。这些罪拆毁的，正是基督的身体。

5. 已经脱去旧人，穿上新人。 「因你们已经脱去旧人和旧人的行为，穿上了新人。这新人在知识上渐渐更新，正如造他主的形象」（西3:9-10）。这里的「脱去」「穿上」，原文是过去时态的分词。许多解经家（如约翰·默里）认为这是说明原因：信徒归信、与基督联合的时候，已经脱去旧人、穿上新人，所以和合本译作「已经」。也有人认为这里同时带着劝勉的意思，因为西3:12紧接着就吩咐「就要存」（原文是穿上），弗4:22-24也是劝勉。无论哪一种，新人都在「渐渐更新」：新人已经穿上，但还在成长。神起初照着自己的形象造人（创1:27），罪使这形象受了亏损；而基督就是「那不能看见之神的像」（西1:15），神要使我们「效法他儿子的模样」（罗8:29）。

6. 惟有基督是包括一切。 「在此并不分希腊人、犹太人，受割礼的、未受割礼的，化外人、西古提人，为奴的、自主的，惟有基督是包括一切，又住在各人之内」（西3:11）。「化外人」是希腊人对不讲希腊话的人的称呼；「西古提人」住在黑海北边，在当时被看作最野蛮的民族。在新人里面，这些分别不再决定一个人的价值和地位（参加3:28）。今天的教会里，也可能有看不起人的分别：早来的移民和新来的移民，讲粤语的和讲国语的，学历高的和学历低的。这些不同不会消失，但在基督里，没有一样可以叫人高人一等，因为「基督是包括一切」。

要点：治死罪和脱去旧人，不是叫人靠自己的努力变好，而是照着神在基督里已经做成的事去活。新人正在照着基督的形象更新，在新人里面，惟有基督是一切。
深读 3:12-17 穿上基督的样式

1. 先是身份，再是衣服。 「所以，你们既是神的选民，圣洁蒙爱的人，就要存怜悯、恩慈、谦虚、温柔、忍耐的心」（西3:12）。在保罗吩咐我们「穿上」什么之前，他先说我们是谁：「神的选民，圣洁蒙爱的人」。这三个称呼原本是用在以色列身上的（参申7:6-8），现在用在歌罗西这些外邦信徒身上。我们不是为了被拣选、被爱而去存怜悯的心；我们是因为已经蒙拣选、蒙爱，才能这样待人。这五样美德，每一样都可以在耶稣身上看见（参太11:29）。

2. 主怎样饶恕了你们。 「倘若这人与那人有嫌隙，总要彼此包容，彼此饶恕；主怎样饶恕了你们，你们也要怎样饶恕人」（西3:13）。保罗很实际：教会里一定会有「嫌隙」。他没有说「没关系，忘了吧」，而是把饶恕建立在主的饶恕上（参弗4:32；太18:33）。主饶恕我们，不是因为我们的罪不严重，而是因为他自己担当了这罪。我们饶恕人，也不是说那件事不严重，而是把讨债的权利交给神（罗12:19）。

3. 饶恕不等于掩盖伤害。 这节经文常常被误用来叫受伤的人沉默，所以必须说清楚。如果伤害牵涉到家暴、性侵、虐待儿童或其他犯罪，向警察或法院举报是对的（罗13:4）；受害的人不必留在危险中，也不必和仍然不安全的人和好；饶恕一个人，不等于恢复他在教会里的职分，也不等于让他重新接近受害者或孩子；教会更不可为了「家丑不可外扬」而劝人忍耐、替伤害人的人遮掩。饶恕是在神面前放下报复，不是叫受害的人再一次受害。

4. 爱心和平安。 「在这一切之外，要存着爱心，爱心就是联络全德的」（西3:14）。前面的美德像一件件衣服，爱心就像把它们束在一起的带子。「又要叫基督的平安在你们心里作主」（西3:15）：「作主」这个词，许多解经家认为原本是指比赛中的裁判。当教会里意见不合的时候，最后作决定的，不是谁的声音大，而是基督所赐的平安。这平安也是肢体之间的和睦，因为「你们也为此蒙召，归为一体」。

5. 基督的道理丰丰富富地存在心里。 「当用各样的智慧，把基督的道理丰丰富富地存在心里，用诗章、颂词、灵歌，彼此教导，互相劝戒，心被恩感，歌颂神」（西3:16）。「基督的道理」可以指基督所说的话，也可以指关于基督的信息；这两层意思在这里分不开。这道理不只要住在每一个人心里，也要住在会众中间，因为下面说的是「彼此」教导。「诗章、颂词、灵歌」很难截然分开，但可以看出教会的诗歌是教导的一部分：我们唱的，就是我们所信的。

6. 无论做什么。 「无论做什么，或说话或行事，都要奉主耶稣的名，藉着他感谢父神」（西3:17）。这节经文打破了属灵的事和属世的事之间的界限。家里和工作上的平常事，都可以「奉主耶稣的名」来做；这句话也是下面家庭和工作那一段的总纲。这一段三次提到感恩：西3:15「存感谢的心」，西3:16「心被恩感」（也可以理解为心存感恩），西3:17「藉着他感谢父神」。穿上新人的人，感恩就像呼吸一样自然。

要点：我们是神所拣选、所爱的人，所以能穿上基督的样式，彼此包容、饶恕，像主饶恕我们一样。基督的平安作主，基督的道理住在会众中间，生活的每一件事都可以奉主的名、带着感恩去做。
深读 3:18-21 家中的关系

1. 「在主里面」的家。 从西3:18到西4:1，保罗对家中的六种人说话：妻子和丈夫，儿女和父亲，仆人和主人。当时希腊罗马社会的治家守则通常只对一家之主说话；保罗却直接对妻子、儿女和仆人说话，把他们当作在神面前有责任的人，并把每一对关系都放在「主」面前（参弗5:22-6:9）。

2. 妻子顺服，「这在主里面是相宜的」。 「你们作妻子的，当顺服自己的丈夫，这在主里面是相宜的」（西3:18）。对这节经文，福音派里有不同的理解：

  • 互补派（如韦恩·古德恩）认为，丈夫在家中有带领的责任，妻子在主里自愿顺服；他们常把这个次序追溯到创造（参创2:18-23；林前11:8-9；提前2:13；弗5:23）。
  • 平等派（如克雷格·基纳）认为，保罗是在当时的社会结构里教导信徒怎样活出见证；「在主里面是相宜的」表示这教导要按主的标准来衡量，原则在于彼此顺服（参弗5:21），而不是永远固定的等级。

无论哪一种理解，顺服都是「在主里面」的：妻子是向主负责，不是向丈夫交出良心；顺服也绝不包括顺从丈夫去犯罪，或忍受虐待。

3. 丈夫要爱，不可苦待。 「你们作丈夫的，要爱你们的妻子，不可苦待她们」（西3:19）。这里的「爱」，是像基督那样舍己的爱（弗5:25）；「苦待」原文的意思是使人苦毒、对人尖刻。保罗点出丈夫常犯的罪：冷言冷语，在别人面前贬低妻子。彼得也说，丈夫要敬重妻子，因为她们是「与你一同承受生命之恩的」（彼前3:7）。一个丈夫若用这段经文来控制、恐吓或伤害妻子，就完全违背了经文的意思。

4. 安全的提醒。 如果婚姻中有家暴、性暴力、经济控制或其他虐待，向警察或法院求助是对的（罗13:4）；受害的人可以离开，到安全的地方去，不必为了「顺服」而留在危险中，也不必与仍然不安全的人和好或复合；教会的责任是保护受害者，不是劝她回去忍耐，更不可为了「家丑不可外扬」而替施暴者遮掩。施暴的人即使后来悔改、蒙了饶恕，也不等于他就可以恢复教会里的职分，或重新接近受害者和孩子。丈夫也可能是受害者，同样应当得到保护。

5. 儿女听从，父亲不要惹儿女的气。 「你们作儿女的，要凡事听从父母，因为这是主所喜悦的。你们作父亲的，不要惹儿女的气，恐怕他们失了志气」（西3:20-21）。「这是主所喜悦的」原文直译是在主里可喜悦的：儿女的听从，也是放在主面前的。所以「凡事」不包括听从父母去犯罪，也不包括默默忍受殴打或性侵；孩子若在家中受到伤害，告诉老师、可信的大人或警察是对的（罗13:4）。保罗在这里说的，是还在父母家中的儿女；成年以后，我们仍要孝敬父母（弗6:2），却不等于在一切事上都要听从父母，特别是在信仰和婚姻的事上，最终是向主负责（参太10:37）。「父亲」这个词有时也泛指父母（参来11:23），所以作母亲的也要听。保罗对父亲只说一件事：不要惹他们，免得他们「失了志气」，就是灰心、放弃，觉得怎么做都不够好。在一个讲究严父的文化里，许多孩子从来没有听过父亲说一句「你做得很好」，只听过「为什么不是第一名」。作父亲的若在这件事上已经失败，福音给他的不是更重的定罪，而是回头的路：天父已经在基督里饶恕了他，他也可以向孩子认错，重新开始。若你自己就是在这样的家里长大的，神在基督里称你为「圣洁蒙爱的人」（西3:12）。

要点：保罗把家中的每一个人都放在主面前：妻子在主里顺服，丈夫像基督一样爱、不可苦待，儿女在主里听从，父亲不可叫儿女灰心。「在主里」既是动机，也是界限，绝不是任何人欺压人的借口。
深读 3:22-4:1 仆人与主人

1. 当时的奴隶制度。 保罗对仆人说的话，比对其他人都长。当时的奴隶制度和后来建立在拐卖人口之上的种族奴隶制度不完全一样，但仍然是不公义的制度：奴隶在法律上是主人的财产。保罗在这里没有直接呼吁废除奴隶制度，可是他说「若能以自由，就求自由更好」（林前7:21；许多译本，包括和合本，这样理解），又把拐卖人口的人列在罪人当中（提前1:10；参出21:16）。后世有奴隶主拿这段经文为奴隶制度辩护，这是严重的误用。今天，这段经文也不是叫人默默忍受拖欠工资、强迫劳动、人口贩卖，或职场上的欺凌和性骚扰。向劳动部门、警察或法院求助是对的（罗13:4）。

2. 阿尼西谋在场。 腓利门的奴隶阿尼西谋离开了主人（是逃跑还是特意来找保罗求情，学者看法不一；见下一章），信主以后要回到他那里去（西4:9；门10-16）。这段话在教会里宣读的时候，腓利门和阿尼西谋可能都坐在会众当中。

3. 凡事听从，却有界限。 「你们作仆人的，要凡事听从你们肉身的主人」（西3:22）：「肉身的」主人只有暂时、有限的权柄，在他之上还有「主」；所以「凡事」和西3:20一样，不包括听从人去犯罪（参徒5:29），也不是叫人默默忍受虐待。

4. 像是给主做的。 「不要只在眼前事奉，像是讨人喜欢的，总要存心诚实敬畏主。无论做什么，都要从心里做，像是给主做的，不是给人做的」（西3:22-23）。今天我们大多数人不是奴隶，但这原则可以用在工作上。「只在眼前事奉」就是做给人看；而信徒知道，自己真正服事的是「主基督」（西3:24）。这样，就是一份在人眼中卑微的工作，例如洗碗、送货、清洁、看护，都有了尊贵的意义，因为是为主做的。为主做工，也不是要把自己累垮来证明什么；我们服事的这位主，已经把基业当作恩典赐给我们（西3:24）。

5. 奴隶也得基业。 「因你们知道从主那里必得着基业为赏赐；你们所事奉的乃是主基督」（西3:24）。按罗马法，奴隶通常不能继承产业（除非在同一份遗嘱里被释放）。保罗却说，这些奴隶要从主那里得着「基业」，就是神为他儿女所预备的产业（参西1:12）。这是真实的赏赐，却是恩典的赏赐：不是工钱，而是儿女的身份所带来的。

6. 主并不偏待人。 「那行不义的必受不义的报应；主并不偏待人」（西3:25）。这句话是对谁说的？有人认为是警告仆人，不要以为可以偷懒或欺骗（这节以「因为」接上文，又在对仆人说的话里面；参门18）；也有人认为是安慰受欺压的仆人：欺负他们的主人也逃不过神的审判，因为弗6:9正是对主人说「他并不偏待人」。保罗也许有意两边都包括：在主面前，不论地位高低，谁都不能靠身份免责。

7. 主人也有一位主。 「你们作主人的，要公公平平地待仆人，因为知道你们也有一位主在天上」（西4:1）。今天作老板、主管、家里请了保姆或工人的人，也要记住：我也是仆人，我也有一位主在天上。这位主就是那位「取了奴仆的形象」（腓2:7），为门徒洗脚的基督（约13:5）。

要点：保罗在一个不公义的制度里，把仆人和主人都放在同一位主面前：仆人从心里做工，像是给主做的，并要从主那里得着基业；主人要公平待人，因为自己也是仆人。在基督里，谁都不是别人的工具。
默想

默想： 「你们的生命与基督一同藏在神里面。基督是我们的生命，他显现的时候，你们也要与他一同显现在荣耀里」（西3:3-4）。我的生活，有没有一部分是没有人看见的？也许我每天下班后照顾一个有特殊需要的孩子，许多年来没有一个晚上是自己的；也许我在餐馆后厨或工厂的流水线上做了二十年，客人吃完就走，没有人知道这道菜是谁做的。更难承认的是，在这些看不见的日子里，我也常常不耐烦、发怨言，甚至心里苦毒，只是没有人知道。又或者，我最怕的正是不被看见：做了事，总想知道有没有人注意到，有没有人记得我的功劳。保罗说，我的生命「藏」着，不是丢了，也不是白费了，而是与基督一同被珍藏在神里面。我那些没有人看见的罪，基督已经在十字架上担当了，旧的我已经与他同死（西3:3）；我那些没有人看见的日子，也没有一天是在神眼前漏掉的。我的生命不是我做了多少、别人怎样看我，而是基督自己。有一天他要显现，那时我不必再证明什么，因为我要与他「一同」显现在荣耀里。今天，当我又一次在没有人看见的地方做那件平凡的事，或者又一次因为自己的软弱而灰心的时候，我能不能对主说：主啊，我的生命藏在你里面；你看见，你记得，你就是我的生命？那位坐在神右边的基督，不会忘记任何一个属于他的人。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 2 exposed the "Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch" regulations of the false teaching at Colossae (Colossians 2:20–23). Chapter 3 now shows where a truly holy life comes from. It falls into five parts: Raised with Christ (vv. 1–4); Putting to death and putting off (vv. 5–11); Putting on the likeness of Christ (vv. 12–17); Relationships at home (vv. 18–21); Slaves and masters (Colossians 3:22–4:1). Since Colossians 4:1 belongs to the same paragraph, we read it with this chapter.

The order of the chapter matters. First Paul says, "you have…", then, "therefore…". What God has done for us in Christ comes first, and our obedience follows. The names that recur most often are "Christ" and "the Lord": Christ seated at God's right hand, Christ who is our life, Christ who is all, the peace of Christ, the word of Christ, serving the Lord Christ.

Going Deeper: 3:1–4 Seek the Things That Are Above

1. "If then you have been raised with Christ." "If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God" (Colossians 3:1). The "if" expresses no doubt; it means "since." Paul has already said in Colossians 2:12 that you were "buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him." Believers are united to Christ, so his death is our death and his resurrection our resurrection (cf. Rom 6:4–11). Paul first tells us who we are, then how to live.

2. Where Christ is. "The things that are above" do not mean otherworldly daydreams detached from life. They mean the place where Christ is and the things he values. "Seated at the right hand of God" echoes Psalm 110:1 and means that Christ has won and now reigns. The false teachers at Colossae wanted people to "climb up" by rules, festivals and visions of angels (Colossians 2:16–18). Paul says there is no need to climb: you are already in Christ, and Christ is already above.

3. Set your minds above. "Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth" (Colossians 3:2). To "set the mind" is the direction of a person's thoughts: what he keeps thinking about, values and pursues. "Things that are on earth" does not mean that eating, working or raising a family are bad in themselves; Paul is about to speak of home and work. It means the thoughts and desires that belong to the old self and have nothing to do with Christ (Colossians 3:5).

4. Dead, and hidden. "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3). The self that belonged to the old world has died with Christ (Colossians 2:20). "Hidden" means concealed, not yet visible; and hidden in God, it is also kept safe (cf. Colossians 2:3). Our true life does not lie in others' opinions or our own achievements. It is in Christ, and "in God," where no one can snatch it away (cf. John 10:28–29).

5. When he appears. "When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory" (Colossians 3:4). Paul does not only say that Christ "gives" us life. He says Christ "is" our life. That life is hidden now; when Christ returns, God will display in full what he has done for us in Christ (cf. 1 John 3:2; Rom 8:18–19).

The point: Believers have died and been raised with Christ, and their true life is hidden with Christ in God. We set our minds above not to escape life on earth, but because our life is with Christ, seated at God's right hand.
Going Deeper: 3:5–11 Put to Death, Put Off

1. "Put to death therefore." "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry" (Colossians 3:5). Notice the "therefore": because you have died (Colossians 3:3), put to death. That sounds like a contradiction, but it is not. God has joined us to Christ in his death, so the old self really has died (Rom 6:6), and now we live in line with that fact, no longer obeying the desires that belong to the old self (cf. Rom 6:11). The Puritan John Owen, in Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, wrote: "Be killing sin or it will be killing you." Yet he insisted that sin is put to death by the Spirit (Rom 8:13), looking to the cross of Christ; we put sin to death because we have already been accepted by God, not in order to be accepted. "What is earthly in you" (literally "your members that are on earth") is not a call to harm the body. Paul has just said that "severity to the body" is of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:23). He means the desires and deeds within us that still belong to the earth.

2. Covetousness is idolatry. Of the five sins Paul lists, the first four mostly concern sexual sin; the last is covetousness. He adds that covetousness "is idolatry" (cf. Matt 6:24). Idolatry at its core is treating something other than God as the source of security, satisfaction and meaning. In a culture that often says "money is what makes you feel safe," we may well serve in church while what we truly rely on is savings and property. Covetousness is rarely confessed as sin, which is why it needs to be named, and repented of before God.

3. The wrath of God. "On account of these the wrath of God is coming" (Colossians 3:6). (The words "upon the sons of disobedience" are absent from a few very early manuscripts but present in most; the CUV includes them, the ESV leaves them out.) Paul mentions wrath not to make believers live in fear, but so that we see how serious sin is: Christ bore wrath for these sins, so we cannot treat them as small. And anyone content to go on living in them must not deceive himself that he belongs to Christ (cf. Eph 5:5–6; 1 Cor 6:9–11). "In these you too once walked" (Colossians 3:7): "once" marks this as the past, not their present identity.

4. Sins of the mouth. "But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth. Do not lie to one another" (Colossians 3:8–9). The second list is mostly about speech. Sin in the church is often not sexual immorality but gossip, sarcasm, criticism behind someone's back and dishonesty. These are the sins that tear down the body of Christ.

5. You have put off the old, put on the new. "Seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:9–10). The verbs are aorist participles. Many interpreters (e.g., John Murray) take them as giving the reason, meaning something done at conversion and union with Christ (ESV "seeing that"; CUV 「已经」). Others, noting the command "put on" in Colossians 3:12 and Eph 4:22–24, hear a note of exhortation here too. Either way, the new self "is being renewed": it has been put on, but it is still growing. God first made humankind in his own image (Gen 1:27); sin marred that image; Christ is "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15), and God means for us "to be conformed to the image of his Son" (Rom 8:29).

6. Christ is all. "Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all" (Colossians 3:11). "Barbarian" was the Greek word for anyone who did not speak Greek; the Scythians lived north of the Black Sea and were thought of as the most savage of peoples. In the new self these distinctions no longer decide a person's worth or standing (cf. Gal 3:28). Churches today can have their own looking-down: earlier immigrants and newcomers, Cantonese and Mandarin speakers, the highly educated and the less educated. These differences do not disappear, but in Christ none of them can make anyone superior, because "Christ is all."

The point: Putting sin to death and putting off the old self do not mean making ourselves better by our own effort. They mean living out what God has already done in Christ. The new self is being renewed after Christ's image, and in it Christ is everything.
Going Deeper: 3:12–17 Putting On the Likeness of Christ

1. Identity first, then clothing. "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience" (Colossians 3:12). Before Paul tells us what to "put on," he says who we are: "God's chosen ones, holy and beloved." These titles once belonged to Israel (cf. Deut 7:6–8); now they are given to these Gentile believers at Colossae. We do not show compassion in order to be chosen and loved. We are able to treat others this way because we already are chosen and loved. Each of these five qualities can be seen in Jesus (cf. Matt 11:29).

2. As the Lord has forgiven you. "Bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive" (Colossians 3:13). Paul is realistic: there will be "complaints" in the church. He does not say, "Never mind, just forget it." He builds forgiveness on the Lord's forgiveness (cf. Eph 4:32; Matt 18:33). The Lord forgives us not because our sin was not serious, but because he himself bore it. When we forgive, we are not saying the wrong was not serious; we are handing the right to repayment over to God (Rom 12:19).

3. Forgiveness does not cover up harm. This verse is often misused to silence the wounded, so it must be said plainly. Where harm involves domestic violence, sexual assault, child abuse or other crime, reporting it to the police or courts is right (Rom 13:4). Victims need not stay in danger, nor reconcile with someone who is still unsafe. Forgiving someone does not restore his office in the church or give him access again to victims or children. And the church must never urge victims to endure, or cover for the one who did harm, in order to keep "family shame" from getting out (家丑不可外扬). Forgiveness lets go of revenge before God; it does not make the victim a victim again.

4. Love and peace. "And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony" (Colossians 3:14). If the earlier qualities are garments, love is the belt that holds them together. "And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts" (Colossians 3:15). Many interpreters note that the word for "rule" was used of an umpire at the games. When the church disagrees, the final decision belongs not to whoever is loudest but to the peace Christ gives. This peace is also harmony between members, "to which indeed you were called in one body."

5. The word of Christ dwelling richly. "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God" (Colossians 3:16). "The word of Christ" may mean the words Christ spoke or the message about Christ; here the two cannot be separated. This word is to dwell not only in each heart but among the congregation, since Paul speaks of teaching "one another." "Psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" are hard to tell apart, but it is clear that the church's singing is part of its teaching: what we sing is what we believe.

6. Whatever you do. "And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him" (Colossians 3:17). This verse breaks down the line between "spiritual" and "secular" things. The ordinary tasks of home and work can all be done "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; the verse also heads the section on home and work that follows. Thanksgiving appears three times in this passage (Colossians 3:15, 16, 17): it is the natural breathing of those who have put on the new self.

The point: We are chosen and loved by God, so we can put on the likeness of Christ, bearing with and forgiving one another as the Lord forgave us. Christ's peace rules, Christ's word dwells among the congregation, and every part of life can be done in the Lord's name and with thanksgiving.
Going Deeper: 3:18–21 Relationships at Home

1. A home "in the Lord." From Colossians 3:18 to Colossians 4:1 Paul addresses six kinds of people in the household: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. Greco-Roman household codes of the day usually spoke only to the head of the house; Paul speaks directly to wives, children and slaves, treating them as people responsible before God, and sets every relationship before "the Lord" (cf. Eph 5:22–6:9).

2. Wives submit, "as is fitting in the Lord." "Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord" (Colossians 3:18). Evangelicals read this verse in different ways:

  • Complementarians (e.g., Wayne Grudem) hold that husbands bear a responsibility to lead at home and wives submit willingly in the Lord; they often trace this order back to creation (cf. Gen 2:18–23; 1 Cor 11:8–9; 1 Tim 2:13; Eph 5:23).
  • Egalitarians (e.g., Craig Keener) hold that Paul is teaching believers how to bear witness within the social structures of their day; "as is fitting in the Lord" means the teaching is measured by the Lord's standard, and the principle is mutual submission (cf. Eph 5:21) rather than a permanent hierarchy.

On either reading, submission is "in the Lord": a wife answers to the Lord and does not hand her conscience over to her husband; submission never includes following a husband into sin or enduring abuse.

3. Husbands love and are not harsh. "Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them" (Colossians 3:19). The love is Christ's self-giving love (Eph 5:25). "Be harsh" means to embitter, to be sharp with someone. Paul knows the sins husbands often commit: cold words, belittling a wife in front of others. Peter too tells husbands to honor their wives, "since they are heirs with you of the grace of life" (1 Pet 3:7). A husband who uses this passage to control, intimidate or harm his wife has completely violated its meaning.

4. A word on safety. If a marriage involves domestic violence, sexual violence, financial control or other abuse, seeking help from the police or courts is right (Rom 13:4). The victim may leave and go somewhere safe, and need not stay in danger for the sake of "submission," nor reconcile with someone who is still unsafe. The church's duty is to protect the victim, not to urge her to go back and endure, and never to cover for the abuser in order to keep "family shame" from getting out. Even if an abuser later repents and is forgiven, that does not restore him to office in the church or give him access again to the victim or the children. Husbands can be victims too, and they also deserve protection.

5. Children obey; fathers do not provoke. "Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Colossians 3:20–21). "This pleases the Lord" is literally "this is pleasing in the Lord": children's obedience is also set before the Lord, so "everything" does not include obeying parents into sin, nor silently enduring beatings or sexual abuse. A child harmed at home is right to tell a teacher, a trusted adult or the police (Rom 13:4). Paul is speaking to children still in their parents' home. Honoring parents continues into adulthood (Eph 6:2), but it does not mean obeying them in everything, especially in matters of faith and marriage, where adult children answer finally to the Lord (cf. Matt 10:37). The word "fathers" can sometimes mean parents (cf. Heb 11:23), so mothers should hear this too. To fathers Paul says one thing: do not provoke your children, lest they "become discouraged," lose heart, give up, feel that nothing they do is ever enough. In a culture that prizes the "strict father," many children have never heard their father say, "Well done," only, "Why weren't you first?" A father who has already failed here is offered by the gospel not heavier condemnation but a way back: the Father has forgiven him in Christ, and he can confess his wrong to his child and begin again. If you grew up in such a home, God in Christ calls you "holy and beloved" (Colossians 3:12).

The point: Paul sets everyone in the home before the Lord. Wives submit in the Lord; husbands love as Christ loves and are never harsh; children obey in the Lord; fathers must not discourage their children. "In the Lord" is both the motive and the limit, never an excuse for anyone to oppress another.
Going Deeper: 3:22–4:1 Slaves and Masters

1. Slavery in that day. Paul says more to slaves than to anyone else. Slavery then was not identical to the later race-based slavery built on kidnapping, but it was still an unjust system: in law a slave was the master's property. Paul does not directly call here for slavery to be abolished, but he says, "if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity" (1 Cor 7:21, as most translations, including the ESV and CUV, take it), and he lists "enslavers" among sinners (1 Tim 1:10; cf. Exod 21:16). Slaveholders in later centuries used these verses to defend slavery, a grave misuse. Nor does this passage ask anyone today to endure wage theft, forced labor, trafficking, or bullying and sexual harassment at work; seeking help from labor authorities, the police or the courts is right (Rom 13:4).

2. Onesimus in the room. Philemon's slave Onesimus, who had left him (whether as a runaway or to seek Paul's intercession is debated; see the next chapter), was now a believer and returning to him (Colossians 4:9; Phlm 10–16). When these words were read aloud to the church, Philemon and Onesimus may both have been sitting in the congregation.

3. Obey in everything, within limits. "Slaves, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters" (Colossians 3:22): an "earthly" master (literally "according to the flesh") holds a temporary, limited authority under the Lord. So "everything" here, as in Colossians 3:20, never includes obeying into sin (cf. Acts 5:29) or silently enduring abuse.

4. As for the Lord. "Not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men" (Colossians 3:22–23). Most of us today are not slaves, but the principle applies to work. "Eye-service" is work done for show; believers know that the one they truly serve is "the Lord Christ" (Colossians 3:24). So even work that people regard as lowly, such as washing dishes, making deliveries, cleaning or caring for the sick, has dignity, because it is done for the Lord. Working for the Lord does not mean wearing ourselves out to prove something; the Lord we serve has already given us the inheritance as a gift of grace (Colossians 3:24).

5. Slaves receive the inheritance. "Knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ" (Colossians 3:24). Under Roman law, slaves generally could not inherit (unless freed in the same will). Yet Paul says these slaves will receive from the Lord "the inheritance," the portion God has prepared for his children (cf. Colossians 1:12). It is a real reward, yet a reward of grace: not a wage, but what comes with being a child.

6. No partiality. "For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality" (Colossians 3:25). To whom is this said? Some take it as a warning to slaves not to think they can shirk or cheat (it is joined to v. 24 by "for" and stands in the slaves' paragraph; cf. Phlm 18); others as comfort to oppressed slaves, since in Eph 6:9 "no partiality" is said directly to masters, and masters who mistreat slaves will not escape God's judgment. Paul may intend both: before the Lord no one, high or low, can rely on status to escape accountability.

7. Masters have a Master. "Masters, treat your slaves justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven" (Colossians 4:1). Bosses and managers today, and anyone who employs a nanny or a worker at home, should remember: I am a servant too; I too have a Master in heaven. That Master is the Christ who took "the form of a servant" (Phil 2:7) and washed his disciples' feet (John 13:5).

The point: Within an unjust system Paul sets slaves and masters before the same Lord. Slaves work heartily, as for the Lord, and will receive the inheritance from him; masters treat others fairly, because they too are servants. In Christ no one is merely a tool for someone else.
Meditation

Reflect: "Your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory" (Colossians 3:3–4). Is there a part of my life that no one sees? Perhaps every evening after work I care for a child with special needs, and for years not one evening has been my own. Perhaps I have worked for twenty years in a restaurant kitchen or on a factory line; customers eat and leave, and no one knows who made the meal. Harder to admit, in these unseen days I am often impatient, I complain, my heart even turns bitter, and no one knows. Or perhaps what I fear most is exactly this, not being seen: when I do something, I need to know whether anyone noticed, whether anyone will remember what I did. Paul says my life is "hidden": not lost, not wasted, but treasured with Christ in God. The sins no one saw, Christ has already borne on the cross, and the old me has died with him (Colossians 3:3). And the days no one saw, not one of them has slipped past God's eyes. My life is not how much I accomplish or what others think of me; my life is Christ himself. One day he will appear, and then I will have nothing left to prove, because I will appear "with him" in glory. Today, when once again I do that ordinary thing where no one sees, or once again lose heart over my own weakness, can I say to the Lord: Lord, my life is hidden in you; you see, you remember, you are my life? The Christ seated at the right hand of God will not forget a single one who belongs to him.
