entries.title: 言语要常常带着和气
entries.title_en: Let Your Speech Always Be Gracious

verse_parts.text: 你们要爱惜光阴，用智慧与外人交往。你们的言语要常常带着和气，好像用盐调和，就可知道该怎样回答各人。

entries.verse_text: 你们要爱惜光阴，用智慧与外人交往。你们的言语要常常带着和气，好像用盐调和，就可知道该怎样回答各人。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第四章是歌罗西书的结尾。第1节「你们作主人的，要公公平平地待仆人」属于西3:18起的治家守则，上一章已经讲过。从第2节起，全章有三段。

  • 祷告和言语（2-6节）。要恒切祷告，警醒感恩，也为保罗祷告，求神给他开传道的门。对外人要用智慧，言语要常常带着和气，好像用盐调和。
  • 两位送信的人（7-9节）。推基古和阿尼西谋要把保罗的景况告诉他们，安慰他们的心。
  • 问安和嘱咐（10-18节）。六位同工问安，其中有犹太人，也有外邦人。保罗请他们问候老底嘉的弟兄和宁法家里的教会，嘱咐他们交换书信，又嘱咐亚基布尽他的职分。最后保罗亲笔问安：「你们要记念我的捆锁。愿恩惠常与你们同在！」

这一章看起来像一串名单，却让我们看见，前三章所讲的「基督是包括一切，又住在各人之内」（西3:11），怎样落实在一个个真实的人身上：一个曾经半途离开宣教队伍的马可，一个从前「没有益处」的奴隶阿尼西谋，一位很可能是外邦人的医生，一位打开自己的家让教会聚会的姊妹。保罗被捆锁，福音却藉着这些人继续传开。

深读 4:2-4 恒切祷告，求神开门

1. 恒切祷告。 「你们要恒切祷告，在此警醒感恩」（西4:2）。「恒切」这个词也用在初期教会「同心合意地恒切祷告」（徒1:14；参罗12:12），有坚持、专心、不放手的意思。祷告不像民间信仰那样有求才拜、临急才烧香，而是生活的常态。耶稣也设比喻，「是要人常常祷告，不可灰心」（路18:1）。

2. 警醒。 「警醒」原文的意思是保持清醒、不睡觉。耶稣在客西马尼园对门徒说：「总要警醒祷告，免得入了迷惑」（太26:41）；他也吩咐门徒为他的再来警醒：「要警醒！」（可13:37）。所以许多解经家认为，这里的警醒有两层意思：一是留心试探，也留心身边人的需要；二是记得主必再来。

3. 感恩。 歌罗西书常常提到感谢（西1:3、12；西2:7；西3:15、17）。保罗把感恩放在祷告里，不是叫人假装一切都好，而是提醒我们：我们所求的这位神，已经「救了我们脱离黑暗的权势，把我们迁到他爱子的国里」（西1:13）。祈求是因为我们有需要，感恩是因为神已经成就了救恩。

4. 不只求出监，更求开门。 「也要为我们祷告，求神给我们开传道的门，能以讲基督的奥秘（我为此被捆锁）」（西4:3）。保罗被捆锁，但在这封信里，他请人祷告的重点不是早日获释（虽然他在门22也盼望「藉着你们的祷告」得释放），而是有传道的「门」。「开门」是保罗常用的说法，指传福音的机会（林前16:9；林后2:12；参徒14:27）。门是神开的；保罗的责任是在门开的时候讲。「基督的奥秘」就是从前隐藏、如今显明的福音：连外邦人也因基督在他们心里，得着荣耀的盼望（西1:26-27；西2:2）。

5. 连保罗也需要人代祷。 「叫我按着所该说的话将这奥秘发明出来」（西4:4）。和合本的「发明」是显明、讲清楚的意思。保罗是大使徒，却请歌罗西教会为他祷告，求神帮助他把福音讲清楚，而那里大多数人从没见过他的面（西2:1）。传福音需要胆量（弗6:19-20），也需要清楚。能把福音讲清楚，本身就是神的恩赐，要靠祷告求来。

要点：我们向那位已经救我们脱离黑暗权势的神祷告，所以祷告可以持续、清醒，并且带着感恩。我们为传福音的人求的，不只是平安顺利，更是求神开门，叫福音被讲清楚；连使徒保罗也靠着弟兄姊妹的代祷开口。
深读 4:5-6 用智慧与外人交往

1. 谁是「外人」。 「你们要爱惜光阴，用智慧与外人交往」（西4:5）。「外人」指教会以外、还没有信主的人（参林前5:12-13；帖前4:12）。和合本译作「交往」的这个词，原文是「行」，和西1:10「行事为人对得起主」、西2:6「就当遵他而行」的「行」是同一个词。保罗关心的不只是信徒怎样说话，也是他们怎样在邻居、同事和家人面前过日子。

2. 爱惜光阴。 「爱惜光阴」原文可以直译为买回时机（参弗5:16）。这里的「光阴」是时机、机会的意思。这不是叫信徒把每一分钟都排满，而是说：神放在我们身边的机会不会一直在那里，要珍惜。保罗在第3节求神开门，在这里吩咐信徒把握门开的时候。

3. 言语带着和气。 「你们的言语要常常带着和气」（西4:6）。和合本译作「和气」的，原文就是「恩典」这个词。信徒的话不只是要客气、有礼貌，更要流露出自己所领受的恩典。众人曾希奇耶稣「口中所出的恩言」（路4:22）；道成肉身的主「充充满满地有恩典有真理」（约1:14）。这里的「和气」不是华人常说的以和为贵、息事宁人，而是基督的恩典。有恩典的话并非不讲真理；讲真理，也不可没有恩典。「带着和气」也不等于凡事附和，或对罪恶和欺压闭口不言。

4. 好像用盐调和。 「好像用盐调和」是什么意思？解经家有几种看法。有人认为盐使食物有味道，指说话要有分量、不乏味（古希腊文学里，「盐」有时指机智风趣的话）；有人认为盐能防止腐坏，指话语要纯净，不说污秽的话（参弗4:29）；也有人联系到耶稣说的「你们里头应当有盐，彼此和睦」（可9:50；参太5:13）。这几层意思可以并存：信徒的话既要有恩典，也要有味道、有内容，不是空洞的套话。

5. 知道该怎样回答各人。 「就可知道该怎样回答各人」（西4:6）。每个人的问题不同，处境也不同：有人真心想知道，有人带着嘲笑，有人在悲伤中发问。有智慧的回答，先要听清楚对方在问什么。彼得也说：「有人问你们心中盼望的缘由，就要常作准备，以温柔、敬畏的心回答各人」（彼前3:15）。回答不是为了辩赢，而是为了让对方看见基督。

6. 在华人家庭和职场里。 过年回家，长辈也许会问：「你信了洋教，以后还拜不拜祖先？」同事也许会笑你：「周末不加班，跑去教会干什么？」有人因为怕伤和气、怕没面子，就一句话也不说；有人一开口就是争论，把亲人当成要驳倒的对手。保罗指出了另一条路：不躲避，也不攻击；带着恩典，也带着真理。长辈这样问，心里常常是在问：你还是不是这家的人？我们走了以后，还有没有人记得我们？信徒可以坚持不祭拜祖先、不拜偶像，同时更加孝敬父母（参出20:12）：父母在世时多陪伴、多照顾；先人离世后，用追思礼拜、清明扫墓献花、讲述他们的生平来纪念他们。也要在合适的时候用话说明：我们敬拜的是创造天地、赐人生命的神，祖先也是他所造的人，所以我们纪念祖先，却不敬拜他们（本计划在哥林多前书第八章和第十章有较详细的讨论）。这样，家人可以从我们的行动和话语中看见，信耶稣的人没有忘本。

要点：我们对外人说的话，应当流露出我们自己领受的恩典：先听清楚，再温柔、诚实地回答。开门是神的事，回答是我们服事人的方式。
深读 4:7-9 推基古和阿尼西谋

1. 推基古。 「有我亲爱的兄弟推基古要将我一切的事都告诉你们。他是忠心的执事，和我一同作主的仆人」（西4:7）。推基古是亚细亚人（徒20:4），也替保罗把以弗所书带到收信的教会（弗6:21-22）。保罗用三个称呼形容他：亲爱的兄弟、忠心的执事、一同作主的仆人。送信要走很远的路，这样的服事并不显眼，保罗却很看重。

2. 安慰人心。 「我特意打发他到你们那里去，好叫你们知道我们的光景，又叫他安慰你们的心」（西4:8）。保罗在监里，却打发人去安慰歌罗西人。他不只盼望别人关心他，也关心别人听到他坐监的消息后会怎样。

3. 阿尼西谋。 「我又打发一位亲爱忠心的兄弟阿尼西谋同去；他也是你们那里的人」（西4:9）。从腓利门书看，阿尼西谋原是歌罗西信徒腓利门的奴隶，离开了主人，后来在保罗那里信了主（门10）。他为什么离开，学者看法不一：有人认为他是逃跑的奴隶，也有人认为他得罪了主人之后，特意去找主人的朋友保罗代为求情。保罗说他「从前与你没有益处，但如今与你我都有益处」（门11）。

4. 「亲爱忠心的兄弟」。 保罗称推基古为「亲爱的兄弟」「忠心的执事」，也称阿尼西谋为「亲爱忠心的兄弟」。在罗马的法律里，奴隶是主人的财产；但在教会里，奴隶阿尼西谋和使徒的同工推基古，得着同样的称呼：「亲爱的兄弟」。这就是西3:11「为奴的、自主的……惟有基督是包括一切」落实在一个人身上。歌罗西的教会要接待的，不是一个闯过祸的奴隶，而是「你们那里的人」，一位弟兄。

5. 保罗与奴隶制度。 上一章已经谈过保罗怎样看奴隶制度（西3:22-4:1）。这里只要留意：保罗请腓利门接待阿尼西谋，「不再是奴仆，乃是高过奴仆，是亲爱的兄弟」（门16）。福音里的弟兄关系，从根本上否定了把人当作财产的制度。

要点：在基督里，一个从前「没有益处」的奴隶，成了「亲爱忠心的兄弟」。福音改变的不只是人的心，也改变人与人之间的关系。
深读 4:10-14 六位同工

1. 亚里达古。 「与我一同坐监的亚里达古问你们安」（西4:10）。亚里达古是马其顿的帖撒罗尼迦人，曾在以弗所的暴动中被众人拿住（徒19:29），后来又陪保罗坐船往罗马去（徒27:2）。「一同坐监」原文直译是一同被掳的战俘，可能是他也被拘禁，也可能是他自愿陪着保罗受囚。在腓利门书里，「与我同坐监的」是以巴弗（门23），亚里达古则被称为同工（门24），所以也有人认为同工们是轮流陪伴保罗的。

2. 马可。 「巴拿巴的表弟马可也问你们安。（说到这马可，你们已经受了吩咐；他若到了你们那里，你们就接待他。）」（西4:10）。马可曾在第一次宣教旅程中途离开（徒13:13），后来保罗不肯再带他同去，甚至和巴拿巴「起了争论，甚至彼此分开」（徒15:39）。圣经没有告诉我们当时谁对谁错。如今马可在保罗身边作同工；在保罗最后的一封信里，他还说「他在传道的事上于我有益处」（提后4:11）。彼得也称他为「我儿子马可」（彼前5:13），教会历来的传统认为马可福音就是他写的。一个曾经半途而废的人，没有被永远定型；保罗特别嘱咐歌罗西人接待他，也许正是因为有人还记得他过去的事。

3. 耶数又称为犹士都。 「耶数又称为犹士都，也问你们安」（西4:11）。「耶数」在原文和「耶稣」是同一个名字（相当于希伯来文的约书亚），当时是很普通的犹太名字；和合本译作「耶数」，与主的名字区分开来。保罗接着说：「奉割礼的人中，只有这三个人是为神的国与我一同做工的，也是叫我心里得安慰的」（西4:11）。保罗自己是犹太人，可是此时在他身边、奉割礼的同工，只有这三位。这句话里有孤单，也有感谢。

4. 以巴弗。 以巴弗是歌罗西人，很可能是最早把福音带到歌罗西的人（西1:7）。他「在祷告之间，常为你们竭力地祈求，愿你们在神一切的旨意上得以完全，信心充足，能站立得稳」（西4:12）。和合本译作「竭力」的这个词，和西1:29保罗「尽心竭力」、西2:1「何等地尽心竭力」是同一个词根，原意是在竞技场上拼搏（参罗15:30）。祷告是真实的劳苦。以巴弗为他们求的，不是生意兴隆，而是在神的旨意上成熟、确信、站立得稳，正好针对那些要把他们「掳去」的假教训（西2:8）。他不只为歌罗西劳苦，也为附近老底嘉和希拉坡里的弟兄劳苦（西4:13）。

5. 路加。 「所亲爱的医生路加和底马问你们安」（西4:14）。保罗在第11节列完「奉割礼的人」，才提到以巴弗、路加和底马，所以许多学者推断路加是外邦人；也有学者（如埃利斯）认为，「奉割礼的人」在这里可能指一群较严格的犹太信徒，所以路加也可能是讲希腊话的犹太人。如果路加是外邦人，那么占新约很大篇幅的路加福音和使徒行传，就是出自一位外邦信徒的手。保罗称他为「所亲爱的医生」；在保罗最后的日子，「独有路加在我这里」（提后4:11）。

6. 底马。 底马在这里只提了名字，没有任何称赞（在门24他被称为同工）。后来保罗写道：「底马贪爱现今的世界，就离弃我往帖撒罗尼迦去了」（提后4:10）。他后来有没有回转，圣经没有说，我们也不必猜测。马可和底马的名字放在一起，是一个提醒：曾经跌倒的人可以被恢复；「自己以为站得稳的，须要谨慎，免得跌倒」（林前10:12）。我们的盼望不在自己过去的服事，而在「那能保守你们不失脚」的神（犹24）。

要点：保罗身边是一群有名有姓、各有故事的同工：有一同坐监的，有被恢复的，有竭力祷告的，有默默陪伴的，也有后来离开的。福音的工作从来不是一个人的事，而是神用一群软弱的人一同做成的。
深读 4:15-18 家里的教会，亲笔的问安

1. 宁法家里的教会。 「请问老底嘉的弟兄和宁法，并她家里的教会安」（西4:15）。初期教会没有礼拜堂，常在信徒家里聚会（罗16:5；林前16:19；门2）。有些抄本把「她家里」写成「他家里」，这样宁法就成了男子；但多数学者根据梵蒂冈抄本等重要抄本。他们又考虑到抄写的人比较可能把女名改成男名，而不是反过来，认为宁法是一位姊妹，和合本也这样翻译。她打开自己的家，让教会在那里聚会。

2. 交换书信。 「你们念了这书信，便交给老底嘉的教会，叫他们也念；你们也要念从老底嘉来的书信」（西4:16）。保罗的信是要在教会中公开宣读的（参帖前5:27），也要在教会之间传阅。「从老底嘉来的书信」是哪一封，有几种看法：

  • 一封失传的信： 保罗另外写给老底嘉教会的信，没有保存下来。
  • 以弗所书： 以弗所书的导论提过，以弗所书可能原是一封在亚细亚众教会中传阅的信；持这个看法的人认为，它是经过老底嘉再传到歌罗西的。据特土良记载，二世纪的马吉安就称以弗所书为《致老底嘉人书》。莱特福特等学者持这个看法。但有些学者（如霍纳；见以弗所书导论）认为弗1:1的「在以弗所」是原文，他们多半认为这是一封失传的信。
  • 腓利门书： 也有人这样认为，但接受的人较少。

后来流传的一封拉丁文《致老底嘉人书》，内容大多是从腓立比书拼凑而成；中世纪许多拉丁文圣经抄本收了它，但教会从来没有把它列为正典。无论是哪一封，神已经把他要教会领受的话保守在圣经里（参彼前1:25；提后3:16-17）。

3. 亚基布。 「要对亚基布说：『务要谨慎，尽你从主所受的职分。』」（西4:17）。亚基布也出现在腓利门书，被称为「与我们同当兵的」（门2）；有人推测他是腓利门的儿子，但圣经没有说。他的职分是什么，我们也不知道；有人认为在以巴弗不在的时候，他在歌罗西承担服事。这句嘱咐要在全教会面前念出来，带着鼓励，也带着提醒。职分是「从主所受」的，所以要向主交账，也可以靠主完成（参西1:25、29）。

4. 亲笔问安。 「我－保罗亲笔问你们安」（西4:18）。保罗的信常常由别人代笔（参罗16:22），他在信末亲手写几句，证明这封信确实出于他（帖后3:17；参林前16:21；加6:11）。

5. 「你们要记念我的捆锁」。 保罗最后的请求，不是要人同情他，而是要他们记得为他祷告（参西4:3），也记得这位福音的使者是戴着锁链的（参弗6:20）。然而，「神的道却不被捆绑」（提后2:9）。

6. 「愿恩惠常与你们同在！」 这封信以恩惠开始：「愿恩惠、平安从神我们的父归与你们！」（西1:2）；也以恩惠结束。保罗讲了基督的超越，揭穿了假教师的规条，描绘了新人的生活和家中的关系，最后一句话却不是叫人更加努力，而是「恩惠」。信徒的整个生活，从起头到末了，都活在神的恩典里。

要点：福音在家里的聚会中传开，在教会之间被传阅，由一群同工带到各处；而这一切的起头和结尾，都是神的恩惠。
默想

默想： 「你们的言语要常常带着和气，好像用盐调和」（西4:6）。想一位你常见面、却还没有信主的人：同事、同学，或者过年才见面的亲戚。回想你们上一次谈到信仰的时候：你是怕气氛尴尬，什么都没说？还是急着说服他，越说越大声？还是根本没有听清楚他在问什么？若我不开口是因为怕人、爱面子，就要先向主认这个罪。保罗在锁链中，最先请人代求的不是早日出狱，而是能把福音讲清楚（西4:3-4）。你可以把这个人的名字告诉一位弟兄姊妹，请他为你，也为这个人祷告。门是神开的，人心也是神改变的；你不必靠自己的口才赢得一个人，也不必因为上次说错了话或者没有开口，就以为门永远关上了。

再想一想：你自己还是「外人」的时候（西4:5），基督是怎样待你的？就算你从小在教会长大，也曾经是那个需要恩典、需要被等候的人（参弗2:12）。他没有用一句话把你驳倒，而是一次又一次地忍耐你、等候你，藉着别人，也藉着他的话，向你说恩典的话。你今天能说出的每一句带着和气的话，都是先从他那里领受的恩典。所以保罗在信的最后没有再加上一条吩咐，只说：「愿恩惠常与你们同在！」（西4:18）。下一次开口的时候，这恩惠也与你同在。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 4 brings Colossians to a close. Verse 1, "Masters, treat your slaves justly and fairly," belongs to the household code that began at Colossians 3:18 and was covered in the last chapter. From verse 2 the chapter has three parts.

  • Prayer and speech (vv. 2–6). Continue steadfastly in prayer, watchful and thankful, and pray for Paul too, that God would open a door for the word. Walk wisely toward outsiders, and let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt.
  • Two messengers (vv. 7–9). Tychicus and Onesimus will tell them how Paul is and encourage their hearts.
  • Greetings and charges (vv. 10–18). Six co-workers send greetings, some Jewish and some Gentile. Paul greets the brothers at Laodicea and the church in Nympha's house, asks the churches to exchange letters, and gives Archippus a charge to fulfill his ministry. Finally Paul writes with his own hand: "Remember my chains. Grace be with you."

The chapter can look like a list of names, but it shows how the claim of the first three chapters, "Christ is all, and in all" (Colossians 3:11), takes shape in real people: Mark, who once left the mission halfway; Onesimus, a slave who was once "useless"; a physician who was very likely a Gentile; a woman who opened her home to the church. Paul is in chains, yet through these people the gospel keeps moving.

Going Deeper: 4:2–4 Continue in Prayer, Pray for an Open Door

1. Continue steadfastly. "Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving" (Colossians 4:2). The same verb describes the early church, who "with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer" (Acts 1:14; see Rom 12:12). It means persisting, giving close attention, not letting go. Prayer is not like folk religion's burning incense only in a crisis; it is the steady texture of life. Jesus told a parable "to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart" (Luke 18:1).

2. Watchful. The word means to stay awake and alert. In Gethsemane Jesus told his disciples, "Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation" (Matt 26:41), and he told them to watch for his return: "Stay awake" (Mark 13:37). So many interpreters hear two things here: alertness to temptation and to the needs of those around us, and remembering that the Lord will come again.

3. With thanksgiving. Colossians speaks of thanks again and again (Colossians 1:3, 12; Colossians 2:7; Colossians 3:15, 17). Paul puts thanksgiving inside prayer, not to make us pretend that all is well, but to remind us that the God we ask "has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son" (Colossians 1:13). We ask because we are needy; we give thanks because God has already accomplished our salvation.

4. Not only release, but a door. "At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison" (Colossians 4:3). Paul is in chains, but in this letter the prayer he asks for is not chiefly release (though he hopes for that "through your prayers" in Phlm 22). It is a "door." An open door is Paul's way of speaking about an opportunity for the gospel (1 Cor 16:9; 2 Cor 2:12; see Acts 14:27). God opens the door; Paul's part is to speak when it opens. "The mystery of Christ" is the gospel once hidden and now revealed: that even Gentiles have "Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Col 1:26–27; Col 2:2).

5. Even Paul needed prayer. "That I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak" (Colossians 4:4). Paul the apostle asks a church most of whose members had never seen him (Colossians 2:1) to pray that God would help him make the gospel clear. Gospel speech needs boldness (Eph 6:19–20), and it also needs clarity. Being able to make the gospel plain is itself a gift of God, and it is sought in prayer.

The point: We pray to the God who has already rescued us from the domain of darkness, so our prayer can be persistent, alert and full of thanks. For those who preach the gospel we ask not only for safety and success, but for God to open doors and to make the message clear. Even the apostle Paul opened his mouth leaning on the prayers of the saints.
Going Deeper: 4:5–6 Wisdom Toward Outsiders

1. Who are "outsiders"? "Conduct yourselves wisely toward outsiders, making the best use of the time" (Colossians 4:5). Outsiders are those outside the church who do not yet believe (see 1 Cor 5:12–13; 1 Thess 4:12). The verb behind "conduct yourselves" is "walk," the same word as in Colossians 1:10, "walk in a manner worthy of the Lord," and Colossians 2:6, "so walk in him." Paul cares not only about how believers talk but about how they live before neighbors, colleagues and family.

2. Making the best use of the time. The phrase can be rendered "buying up the opportunity" (see Eph 5:16). The word for "time" here means a season or opportunity. Paul is not telling believers to fill every minute. He is saying that the openings God places around us will not stay open forever, so treasure them. In verse 3 Paul asked God to open a door; here he tells believers to walk through it while it is open.

3. Gracious speech. "Let your speech always be gracious" (Colossians 4:6). Literally, "let your speech always be with grace." Believers are to be more than polite; their words should carry something of the grace they have received. People marveled at "the gracious words that were coming from [Jesus'] mouth" (Luke 4:22); the Word made flesh was "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). This "grace" is not the Chinese ideal of keeping the peace at any cost, but Christ's grace. Gracious words are not empty of truth, and truthful words must not be empty of grace. Gracious speech also does not mean agreeing with everything, or keeping silent about sin and oppression.

4. Seasoned with salt. What does "seasoned with salt" mean? Interpreters offer several readings. Some say salt gives food flavor, so speech should be interesting and substantial, not dull (in Greek writers "salt" could mean wit). Some say salt preserves from decay, so speech should be clean, free of corrupting talk (see Eph 4:29). Others connect it with Jesus' words, "Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another" (Mark 9:50; see Matt 5:13). These can stand together: a believer's words should carry grace, and also flavor and weight, not stock phrases.

5. Knowing how to answer each person. "So that you may know how you ought to answer each person" (Colossians 4:6). People's questions differ, and so do their situations. One person truly wants to know, another is mocking, another asks out of grief. A wise answer begins by hearing what is actually being asked. Peter says the same: "always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you" (1 Pet 3:15), and he goes on to say it should be done with gentleness and respect. The aim of an answer is not to win but to let the other person see Christ.

6. In Chinese families and workplaces. At New Year an older relative may ask, "You've joined a foreign religion. Will you still worship the ancestors?" A colleague may tease, "You won't work weekends because you go to church?" Some of us say nothing, afraid of spoiling the peace or losing face. Others argue at once and treat relatives as opponents to be defeated. Paul shows another way: neither hiding nor attacking, carrying both grace and truth. Behind an elder's question there is often another one: are you still one of this family, and will anyone remember us when we are gone? A believer can decline to worship the ancestors or any idol and still honor parents all the more (see Exod 20:12): spending time with them and caring for them while they live, and after they die remembering them through a memorial service, by tending the grave and laying flowers at Qingming, and by telling their stories. When the time is right, we also explain in words: we worship the God who made heaven and earth and gives life, and our ancestors too were people he made, so we remember them but do not worship them (this plan discusses these questions more fully in 1 Corinthians, chapters 8 and 10). In this way the family can see from what we do and say that following Jesus does not mean forgetting one's roots.

The point: Our words to outsiders should carry the grace we ourselves have received: listen first, then answer gently and honestly. Opening the door is God's work; answering is one way we serve people.
Going Deeper: 4:7–9 Tychicus and Onesimus

1. Tychicus. "Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord" (Colossians 4:7). Tychicus came from Asia (Acts 20:4) and also carried Ephesians to the churches it was written for (Eph 6:21–22). Paul gives him three titles: beloved brother, faithful minister, fellow servant. Carrying letters meant long journeys and little notice, but Paul valued that service highly.

2. Encouraging hearts. "I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts" (Colossians 4:8). Paul, in prison, sends someone to comfort the Colossians. He does not only want others to care about him; he cares how they will take the news of his imprisonment.

3. Onesimus. "And with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you" (Colossians 4:9). From Philemon we learn that Onesimus was the slave of Philemon, a believer in Colossae. He had left his master and later came to faith through Paul (Phlm 10). Why he left is debated: some think he was a runaway; others think that, having wronged his master, he went to Paul, his master's friend, to ask him to intercede. Paul writes, "Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me" (Phlm 11).

4. "Faithful and beloved brother." Paul calls Tychicus "a beloved brother and faithful minister," and he calls Onesimus "our faithful and beloved brother." In Roman law a slave was his master's property; in the church the slave Onesimus and the apostle's co-worker Tychicus are given the same title, "beloved brother." This is Colossians 3:11, "slave, free; but Christ is all," lived out in one man. The church in Colossae was to welcome not a slave who had caused trouble, but "one of you," a brother.

5. Paul and slavery. The previous chapter has already looked at how Paul treats slavery (Colossians 3:22–4:1). Here we need only notice that Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother" (Phlm 16). The brotherhood of the gospel undercuts at the root any system that treats people as property.

The point: In Christ a slave once "useless" became a "faithful and beloved brother." The gospel changes not only hearts but the relationships between people.
Going Deeper: 4:10–14 Six Co-workers

1. Aristarchus. "Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you" (Colossians 4:10). Aristarchus was a Macedonian from Thessalonica. He was seized by the mob in the Ephesian riot (Acts 19:29) and later sailed with Paul toward Rome (Acts 27:2). "Fellow prisoner" (literally "fellow prisoner of war") may mean he too was detained, or that he chose to share Paul's confinement. In Philemon it is Epaphras who is called "my fellow prisoner" (Phlm 23) and Aristarchus a fellow worker (Phlm 24), so some think the co-workers took turns staying with Paul.

2. Mark. "And Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him)" (Colossians 4:10). Mark had left partway through the first missionary journey (Acts 13:13). Later Paul refused to take him again, and "there arose a sharp disagreement" between Paul and Barnabas, "so that they separated from each other" (Acts 15:39). Scripture does not tell us who was right. Now Mark is with Paul as a co-worker, and in his last letter Paul says, "he is very useful to me for ministry" (2 Tim 4:11). Peter calls him "Mark, my son" (1 Pet 5:13), and the church's long tradition holds that he wrote the Gospel of Mark. A man who once quit halfway was not fixed forever by that failure; Paul's instruction to welcome him may be because some still remembered his past.

3. Jesus called Justus. "And Jesus who is called Justus" (Colossians 4:11). "Jesus" (the Greek form of the Hebrew name Joshua) was a common Jewish name; the Chinese Union Version spells his name differently to distinguish him from the Lord. Paul adds, "These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me" (Colossians 4:11). Paul was a Jew himself, yet of the men of the circumcision with him at this time, only these three were his fellow workers. There is loneliness in that sentence, and gratitude too.

4. Epaphras. Epaphras was from Colossae and was very likely the one who first brought the gospel there (Colossians 1:7). He is "always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God" (Colossians 4:12). "Struggling" shares its root with Paul's "struggling" in Colossians 1:29 and his "great struggle" in Colossians 2:1; it was used of an athlete's contest (see Rom 15:30). Prayer is real labor. Epaphras did not pray for their business to prosper but for them to stand mature and fully assured in God's will, which is exactly what the false teaching that would "take [them] captive" threatened (Colossians 2:8). He worked hard not only for Colossae but for nearby Laodicea and Hierapolis (Colossians 4:13).

5. Luke. "Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas" (Colossians 4:14). Paul finishes listing "the men of the circumcision" in verse 11 before naming Epaphras, Luke and Demas, so many scholars infer that Luke was a Gentile. Others (e.g., E. Earle Ellis) argue that "the men of the circumcision" may denote a narrower group of strict Jewish believers, so Luke may have been a Greek-speaking Jew. If Luke was a Gentile, then Luke and Acts, a large share of the New Testament, came from a Gentile believer's hand. Paul calls him "the beloved physician," and in Paul's last days, "Luke alone is with me" (2 Tim 4:11).

6. Demas. Demas is simply named here, with no word of praise (in Phlm 24 he is called a fellow worker). Later Paul writes, "Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me" (2 Tim 4:10). Whether he ever returned, Scripture does not say, and we need not guess. Mark and Demas side by side are a reminder: one who has fallen can be restored, and "let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall" (1 Cor 10:12). Our hope is not in our past service but in "him who is able to keep you from stumbling" (Jude 24).

The point: Around Paul was a group of named co-workers, each with a story: one shared his imprisonment, one had been restored, one wrestled in prayer, one quietly stayed, and one later left. Gospel work is never one person's work; God accomplishes it through a company of weak people together.
Going Deeper: 4:15–18 A Church in a House, a Greeting in Paul's Hand

1. The church in Nympha's house. "Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house" (Colossians 4:15). The early church had no church buildings and often met in believers' homes (Rom 16:5; 1 Cor 16:19; Phlm 2). Some manuscripts read "his house," which makes the name masculine (Nymphas). But most scholars, following Codex Vaticanus and judging that scribes were likelier to turn a woman's name into a man's than the reverse, take Nympha to be a woman, as the CUV and ESV do. She opened her home for the church to meet there.

2. Exchanging letters. "And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea" (Colossians 4:16). Paul's letters were meant to be read aloud in the church (see 1 Thess 5:27) and passed between churches. Which letter is "the letter from Laodicea"? There are several views:

  • A lost letter: another letter Paul wrote to the Laodicean church, which has not survived.
  • Ephesians: as the introduction to Ephesians noted, Ephesians may first have been a circular letter for the churches of Asia; on this view it reached Colossae by way of Laodicea. According to Tertullian, Marcion in the second century called Ephesians the letter "to the Laodiceans." Lightfoot and others held this view; scholars who take "in Ephesus" in Eph 1:1 as original (e.g., Hoehner; see the Ephesians introduction) generally favor a lost letter.
  • Philemon: some have suggested this, but few accept it.

A Latin "Epistle to the Laodiceans" that circulated later is made up largely of phrases from Philippians; many medieval Latin Bibles copied it, but the church never received it as canonical. Whichever letter Paul meant, God has kept in Scripture the words he meant his church to receive (see 1 Pet 1:25; 2 Tim 3:16–17).

3. Archippus. "And say to Archippus, 'See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord'" (Colossians 4:17). Archippus also appears in Philemon as "our fellow soldier" (Phlm 2). Some guess he was Philemon's son, but Scripture does not say. Nor do we know what his ministry was; some think he served the church in Colossae while Epaphras was away. The charge was to be read before the whole church, as both encouragement and reminder. The ministry was "received in the Lord," so it is answerable to the Lord and can be fulfilled in his strength (see Colossians 1:25, 29).

4. In Paul's own hand. "I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand" (Colossians 4:18). Paul's letters were often written down by someone else (cf. Rom 16:22); he added a few lines in his own hand at the end as a mark that the letter was genuine (2 Thess 3:17; see 1 Cor 16:21; Gal 6:11).

5. "Remember my chains." Paul's last request is not for pity. He wants them to keep praying for him (see Colossians 4:3) and to remember that the gospel's ambassador is in chains (see Eph 6:20). Yet "the word of God is not bound!" (2 Tim 2:9).

6. "Grace be with you." The letter opened with grace: "Grace to you and peace from God our Father" (Colossians 1:2), and it closes with grace. Paul has spoken of Christ's supremacy, exposed the false teachers' rules, and described the new self and the life of the household, and his last word is not "try harder" but "grace." The whole Christian life, from first to last, is lived in the grace of God.

The point: The gospel spread through gatherings in homes, letters passed from church to church, and a company of co-workers carrying it from place to place; and all of it begins and ends with the grace of God.
Meditation

Reflect: "Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt" (Colossians 4:6). Think of someone you see often who does not yet believe: a colleague, a classmate, or a relative you see only at New Year. Recall the last time faith came up between you. Did you say nothing because it felt awkward? Did you rush to convince them, getting louder as you went? Or did you never quite hear what they were asking? If I kept silent out of fear of people or of losing face, I confess that to the Lord first. Paul in chains asked first not for an early release but that he could make the gospel clear (Colossians 4:3–4). You might tell a brother or sister this person's name and ask them to pray for you and for them. God opens the door, and God changes hearts. You do not have to win this person by your own eloquence, and you need not think the door is shut forever because last time you said the wrong thing, or nothing at all.

Then think again: when you yourself were an "outsider" (Colossians 4:5), how did Christ treat you? Even if you grew up in church, you too were once someone who needed grace and needed to be waited for (see Eph 2:12). He did not defeat you with one sharp sentence. He was patient with you and waited for you, again and again, and spoke words of grace to you through other people and through his word. Every gracious word you can say today is grace you first received from him. That is why Paul ends the letter without one more command, only this: "Grace be with you" (Colossians 4:18). The next time you open your mouth, that grace is with you too.

这卷书在讲什么

帖撒罗尼迦前书是保罗写给一个新生教会的信。保罗在那里传福音的时间不长，就被逼离开了（徒17:1-10）。他走的时候，这群信徒信主才几个月，有的也许只有几个星期，却已经在「大难之中」（帖前1:6），受着「本地人的苦害」（帖前2:14）。保罗放心不下，像父母被迫离开年幼的孩子一样，「极力地想法子」要回去看他们（帖前2:17）。去不成，就打发提摩太去；提摩太带回了好消息，保罗就写了这封信。

所以这封信读起来特别温暖。保罗一再说「你们自己知道」，提醒他们当初怎样领受福音；他说自己在他们中间，「如同母亲乳养自己的孩子」（帖前2:7），又「好像父亲待自己的儿女一样」（帖前2:11）。信中有感谢，有思念，有劝勉，也回答了他们心里的几个问题：信主的亲人死了怎么办？主什么时候再来？

这封信有几条线交织在一起：

  • 福音改变了一群人： 「你们是怎样离弃偶像，归向神，要服事那又真又活的神，等候他儿子从天降临」（帖前1:9-10）。福音不只是一套新的想法，而是叫人掉转方向。
  • 神的道在受苦的人心里运行： 他们领受这道，「不以为是人的道，乃以为是神的道」，这道「运行在你们信主的人心中」（帖前2:13）。患难没有把他们冲走，反倒叫他们的信心传遍各处（帖前1:8）。
  • 在神面前过圣洁的生活： 「神的旨意就是要你们成为圣洁」（帖前4:3）。这包括身体和性的事，也包括彼此相爱、安静做工（帖前4:3-12）。
  • 主必再来： 每一章都以主的再来作结（帖前1:10；帖前2:19；帖前3:13；帖前4:17；帖前5:23）。这盼望安慰丧亲的人（帖前4:18），也叫人警醒谨守（帖前5:6）。

保罗在帖前5:9-10把全信的根基说了出来：「因为神不是预定我们受刑，乃是预定我们藉着我们主耶稣基督得救。他替我们死，叫我们无论醒着，睡着，都与他同活。」

作者与写作背景

1. 城市。 帖撒罗尼迦是罗马马其顿省的省会，也是一个港口城市，横贯东西的埃格那提亚大道就从城中穿过。主前42年，这城因为在罗马内战中站在胜利者一边，得了自由城的地位，由本地的官员管理。使徒行传称这些官员为「地方官」（徒17:6），原文是一个很少见的词，后来出土的帖撒罗尼迦碑文正好用了这个词，印证了路加记载的准确。城里有许多神庙，也敬拜罗马皇帝；尊荣凯撒，关系到全城的荣耀和安危。难怪有人控告信徒「违背凯撒的命令，说另有一个王耶稣」（徒17:7）。

2. 教会是怎样开始的。 保罗、西拉和提摩太在第二次宣教旅程中，离开腓立比来到这里；他们在腓立比刚刚「被害受辱」（帖前2:2；参徒16:19-24）。保罗照常先到会堂，「一连三个安息日」本着圣经辩论，讲解基督必须受害、从死里复活（徒17:2-3）。有些犹太人信了，「并有许多虔敬的希腊人，尊贵的妇女也不少」（徒17:4）。但从这封信看，教会里多数人原是拜偶像的外邦人（帖前1:9）。

  • 住了多久？ 使徒行传只提到三个安息日。但保罗在那里「昼夜做工」（帖前2:9），腓立比教会也「一次两次地」送钱给他（腓4:16），所以许多解经家认为他在城里前后住了几个月，三个安息日只是在会堂里辩论的时间。无论多长，都不算久。
  • 被逼离开： 不信的犹太人「招聚了些市井匪类」闯进耶孙的家（徒17:5-9），弟兄们只好连夜送走保罗和西拉。保罗后来说，他们是「暂时与你们离别」（帖前2:17），许多解经家认为，原文带着成了孤儿的意思：被硬生生拆开。

3. 写信的经过。 保罗到了庇哩亚，又被追赶，就到了雅典（徒17:10-15）。他「既不能再忍」，就打发提摩太回帖撒罗尼迦去坚固他们（帖前3:1-2）。后来保罗到了哥林多，提摩太从马其顿回来（徒18:5），带来了好消息：他们的信心和爱心都站立得稳，也很想见保罗（帖前3:6）。保罗大喜，就写了这封信。

  • 提摩太的行程： 使徒行传说西拉和提摩太留在庇哩亚，后来在哥林多与保罗会合（徒18:5）；这封信却说提摩太是从雅典被打发回去的。保罗到雅典后曾叫他们「速速」来（徒17:15），所以最简单的理解是，提摩太先到雅典见了保罗，又被差回帖撒罗尼迦，路加没有记下这一段。帖前3:1说保罗「独自」留在雅典，也许西拉也被差往别处，例如腓立比。

4. 写作时间。 保罗在哥林多住了一年零六个月（徒18:11）。在希腊的德尔斐出土了一块碑文，可以推算出亚该亚方伯迦流（徒18:12）的任期大约是主后51-52年。所以这封信大约写于主后50-51年，离耶稣受死复活只有二十年左右。这若不是保罗现存最早的一封信，也是最早的几封之一；在新约各卷中，它也是很早写成的。许多持南加拉太说的学者（如弗雷德里克·布鲁斯、理查德·朗格内克）认为加拉太书写于主后48-49年，比本书更早；持北加拉太说的学者（如莱特福特、汉斯·贝茨）和部分持南加拉太说的学者，则把加拉太书定在本书之后（参本研读加拉太书导读）。

5. 作者。 信的开头写着「保罗、西拉、提摩太」（帖前1:1），信中多数地方用「我们」，有时保罗也单独说「我」（帖前2:18；帖前3:5；帖前5:27）。初期教会一致接受这是保罗的书信，今天几乎所有学者也这样看。

  • 帖前2:14-16的问题： 少数学者（如伯格·皮尔逊）认为帖前2:14-16论到犹太人的几句话太严厉，不像保罗写的，也似乎与罗马书9-11章不合，可能是后人在主后70年耶路撒冷被毁以后加进去的。但现存所有的抄本都有这几句，大多数学者（如杰弗里·韦玛、吉恩·格林）认为这是保罗自己写的。这段话要怎样理解，留到第二章再谈。
钥匙经文：1:9-10

1. 「离弃偶像，归向神」。 原文先说「归向神」，再说「离弃偶像」。这是同一个转身，不是先后两步；但保罗把重点放在神身上。福音不是先叫人努力丢掉什么，而是叫人看见那「又真又活的神」，偶像就失去了吸引力。第一世纪的帖撒罗尼迦人，要为此付上很大的代价：家族的祭祀、行会的宴席、城市的节庆，都和拜偶像连在一起。离弃偶像，常常就是离开原来的整个圈子。

2. 「服事」和「等候」。 这两个动词说出了信徒的整个生活：现在服事又真又活的神，同时等候他儿子从天降临。服事不是为了赚取救恩，因为后面马上说，救我们的是耶稣；等候也不是闲坐，而是在盼望中服事。

3. 「救我们脱离将来忿怒的耶稣」。 神的忿怒是真实的，是神因人的罪而发的公义审判（参帖前5:3、9）。但这里的重点是：耶稣「救我们脱离」。他怎样救？帖前5:10说：「他替我们死。」他担当了我们当受的刑罚，所以信靠他的人可以安心等候他来，不必惧怕。这位要从天降临的，就是神「从死里复活」的那一位。

全书结构

帖撒罗尼迦前书是一封书信，大致可以这样分：

  • 问安和感谢（帖前1:1-10）：保罗为他们因信心所做的工夫、因爱心所受的劳苦、因盼望所存的忍耐感谢神；他们离弃偶像归向神，成了各处信徒的榜样。
  • 保罗怎样在他们中间（帖前2:1-12）：不是讨人喜欢，也没有贪心；存心温柔，像母亲，又像父亲。
  • 神的道与患难（帖前2:13-16）：他们领受神的道，也像犹太的教会一样受苦。
  • 思念、打发提摩太和祷告（帖前2:17–3:13）：保罗想回去，却被撒但阻挡；提摩太带回好消息；保罗为他们祷告，愿他们在主来的时候心里坚固，成为圣洁。
  • 圣洁和相爱（帖前4:1-12）：远避淫行，用圣洁、尊贵守着自己的身体；弟兄相爱，安静做工。
  • 睡了的人（帖前4:13-18）：信主的人死了不是没有指望；主必降临，死了的人必先复活，我们要和主永远同在。
  • 主的日子（帖前5:1-11）：那日子像夜间的贼一样来到；信徒是光明之子，要警醒谨守。
  • 教会生活和结语（帖前5:12-28）：敬重劳苦的人，彼此和睦；常常喜乐，不住地祷告，凡事谢恩；「那召你们的本是信实的，他必成就这事」（帖前5:24）。

全信可以分成两大部分：前三章多是回顾和感谢，讲神已经在他们中间做了什么；后两章多是劝勉，讲他们要怎样继续走下去。两部分之间的枢纽是帖前4:1：「你们既然受了我们的教训，知道该怎样行可以讨神的喜悦，就要照你们现在所行的更加勉励。」

怎样读这卷书

1. 留意信心、爱心、盼望。 保罗一开头就提到「因信心所做的工夫，因爱心所受的劳苦，因盼望我们主耶稣基督所存的忍耐」（帖前1:3），快结束时又说「把信和爱当作护心镜遮胸，把得救的盼望当作头盔戴上」（帖前5:8）。读的时候，可以留意这三样在信中怎样一再出现。

2. 留意主的再来。 每一章都以主的再来作结（帖前1:10；帖前2:19；帖前3:13；帖前4:17；帖前5:23）。保罗讲主的再来，不是为了满足好奇心，也不是为了排出时间表，而是为了安慰（帖前4:18）、坚固（帖前3:13）、劝人圣洁（帖前5:23）。读的时候可以问：这个盼望怎样改变今天的生活？

3. 留意「你们自己知道」。 保罗一再说「你们知道」「你们自己原晓得」（帖前1:5；帖前2:1、2、5、11；帖前3:3、4；帖前4:2；帖前5:2）。他没有给他们新的东西，而是叫他们记得已经领受的。信徒在患难中，常常需要的不是新的道理，而是重新想起自己所信的。

4. 留意家人的语言。 保罗称他们为「弟兄」十几次，又说自己像母亲、像父亲，离开他们像成了孤儿。教会不是一个机构，而是神的家。今天许多华人信徒因为信主，在家里受压力，甚至被家人排斥。这封信告诉你：在神的家里，你有弟兄姊妹。

5. 和使徒行传17章、帖撒罗尼迦后书一起读。 徒17:1-10记载了教会怎样开始；帖撒罗尼迦后书大概是不久以后写的，继续讨论主的日子和那些不肯做工的人。

默想

默想： 「我们也不住地感谢神，因你们听见我们所传神的道就领受了；不以为是人的道，乃以为是神的道。这道实在是神的，并且运行在你们信主的人心中。」（帖前2:13）帖撒罗尼迦人听到的，是几个刚从别的城被赶出来、在他们城里辛苦做工的外地人讲的话。可是他们听出来，这是神的道。我还记得神的话第一次对我说话的时候吗？也许是一节经文忽然叫我流泪，也许是一篇讲道正好说中了我的心事；也许我想不起有哪一次特别的时刻，只记得神的话一点一点地变得真实。可是今天，读经可能已经变成了一件例行公事：读完一章，合上圣经，什么也没有留下，好像只是读了一些古人的话。有时我甚至不敢承认，自己已经很久没有被神的话感动了。保罗并没有说，这道只在信徒热心的时候才运行；他说这道「实在是神的」，并且「运行在你们信主的人心中」。神的话不靠我的感觉才有能力。在我觉得最干涩的日子，它仍然在做工，像种子在土里，看不见，却在长。今天，我不必等到有了感觉才打开圣经，也不必在合上圣经的时候检查自己被感动了多少。我可以照样读，像帖撒罗尼迦人一样，把它当作神的话来领受；因为在这些字句背后的，是那位「道成了肉身」（约1:14）、为我舍命的耶稣。我对他的话冷淡的日子，他从来没有对我冷淡过；他的话也决不会徒然返回（赛55:11）。
entries.content_en:
What This Book Is About

1 Thessalonians is Paul's letter to a newborn church. Paul had not been preaching there long before he was forced to leave (Acts 17:1–10). When he left, these believers had been Christians for only a few months, some perhaps only a few weeks, and they were already "in much affliction" (1 Thessalonians 1:6), suffering "from your own countrymen" (1 Thessalonians 2:14). Paul could not stop worrying about them. Like a parent forced to leave young children, he "endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face" (1 Thessalonians 2:17). When he could not go, he sent Timothy; Timothy came back with good news, and Paul wrote this letter.

So the letter reads with unusual warmth. Paul keeps saying "you yourselves know," reminding them how they first received the gospel. He says that among them he was "like a nursing mother taking care of her own children" (1 Thessalonians 2:7), and "like a father with his children" (1 Thessalonians 2:11). The letter holds thanksgiving, longing and exhortation, and it answers some questions on their minds: what about believing loved ones who have died? When will the Lord come?

Several threads run through the letter:

  • The gospel changed a group of people: "how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven" (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). The gospel is not just a new set of ideas; it turns people around.
  • God's word at work in suffering people: they received the word "not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers" (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Affliction did not sweep them away; instead their faith became known everywhere (1 Thessalonians 1:8).
  • A holy life before God: "this is the will of God, your sanctification" (1 Thessalonians 4:3). That covers the body and sexual life, and also loving one another and working quietly (1 Thessalonians 4:3–12).
  • The Lord will come: every chapter ends with the Lord's coming (1 Thessalonians 1:10; 1 Thessalonians 2:19; 1 Thessalonians 3:13; 1 Thessalonians 4:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:23). This hope comforts the grieving (1 Thessalonians 4:18) and calls people to stay awake and sober (1 Thessalonians 5:6).

In 1 Thessalonians 5:9–10 Paul states the foundation of the whole letter: "For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him."

Author and Setting

1. The city. Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia and a port city, and the Via Egnatia, the great east–west highway, ran right through it. In 42 BC, because it had backed the winning side in Rome's civil war, it was made a free city, governed by its own local officials. Acts calls these officials "city authorities" (Acts 17:6). Luke's Greek word, politarchēs, is rare, and inscriptions later found in Thessalonica use exactly this title, supporting his accuracy. The city had many temples and also honored the Roman emperor; honoring Caesar was part of the city's glory and security. No wonder the believers were accused of "acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus" (Acts 17:7).

2. How the church began. On the second missionary journey, Paul, Silas and Timothy came here from Philippi, where they had just "suffered and been shamefully treated" (1 Thessalonians 2:2; see Acts 16:19–24). As usual, Paul went first to the synagogue, and "on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures," explaining that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead (Acts 17:2–3). Some Jews believed, "as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women" (Acts 17:4). But this letter suggests that most of the church had been Gentile idol-worshipers (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

  • How long did he stay? Acts mentions only three Sabbaths. But Paul "worked night and day" there (1 Thessalonians 2:9), and the Philippian church sent him help "once and again" (Phil 4:16), so many commentators think he stayed in the city for some months, with the three Sabbaths being the time of debate in the synagogue. Either way, it was not long.
  • Forced out: unbelieving Jews gathered "some wicked men of the rabble" and attacked Jason's house (Acts 17:5–9), and the brothers had to send Paul and Silas away by night. Paul later says they were "torn away from you" (1 Thessalonians 2:17); many take his Greek word to carry the sense of being orphaned, wrenched apart.

3. How the letter came to be written. Paul went on to Berea, was pursued again, and reached Athens (Acts 17:10–15). "When we could bear it no longer," he sent Timothy back to Thessalonica to strengthen them (1 Thessalonians 3:1–2). Later, when Paul was in Corinth, Timothy came back from Macedonia (Acts 18:5) with good news: their faith and love were standing firm, and they longed to see Paul (1 Thessalonians 3:6). Overjoyed, Paul wrote this letter.

  • Timothy's movements: Acts says Silas and Timothy stayed in Berea and later joined Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:5); this letter, however, says Timothy was sent back from Athens. Paul had asked them to come to him "as soon as possible" (Acts 17:15), so the simplest explanation is that Timothy first came to Paul in Athens and was then sent back to Thessalonica, a round trip Luke does not record. Since 1 Thessalonians 3:1 says Paul was left "alone" at Athens, Silas too may have been sent elsewhere, perhaps to Philippi.

4. Date. Paul stayed in Corinth a year and six months (Acts 18:11). An inscription found at Delphi in Greece lets us date the proconsulship of Gallio in Achaia (Acts 18:12) to about AD 51–52. So the letter was probably written around AD 50–51, only about twenty years after Jesus' death and resurrection. It is either Paul's earliest surviving letter or one of the earliest, and one of the earliest books of the New Testament. Many South Galatian scholars (such as F. F. Bruce and Richard Longenecker) date Galatians to AD 48–49, before this letter; North Galatian scholars (such as J. B. Lightfoot and Hans Dieter Betz) and some South Galatian scholars place Galatians later (see this study's Galatians introduction).

5. Author. The letter opens with "Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy" (1 Thessalonians 1:1). Most of it uses "we," though Paul sometimes says "I" (1 Thessalonians 2:18; 1 Thessalonians 3:5; 1 Thessalonians 5:27). The early church received it unanimously as Paul's, and almost all scholars today agree.

  • The question of 1 Thessalonians 2:14–16: a few scholars (such as Birger Pearson) think the words about the Jews in 1 Thessalonians 2:14–16 are too harsh to be Paul's and seem to conflict with Romans 9–11, and may have been added after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. But every surviving manuscript contains these verses, and most scholars (such as Jeffrey Weima and Gene Green) hold that Paul wrote them. How to understand the passage is left for chapter 2.
Key Verse: 1:9–10

1. "Turned to God from idols." The Greek names God first: "to God from idols." This is one turning, not two steps, but the weight falls on God. The gospel does not begin by telling people to strain to throw things away; it shows them "the living and true God," and the idols lose their pull. For first-century Thessalonians the cost was high: family rites, trade-guild banquets and city festivals were all bound up with idol worship. Leaving idols often meant leaving one's whole network of relationships.

2. "Serve" and "wait." These two verbs describe the whole of the believer's life: serving the living and true God now, while waiting for his Son from heaven. The serving does not earn salvation, for the very next words say that Jesus is the one who delivers us; and the waiting is not idleness, but service in hope.

3. "Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come." God's wrath is real; it is his righteous judgment on sin (see 1 Thessalonians 5:3, 9). But the stress here is that Jesus "delivers us." How? 1 Thessalonians 5:10 says he "died for us." He bore the penalty we deserved, so those who trust him can wait for his coming in peace, without dread. The one coming from heaven is the one God "raised from the dead."

The Shape of the Book

1 Thessalonians is a letter, and it can be roughly divided like this:

  • Greeting and thanksgiving (1 Thessalonians 1:1–10): Paul thanks God for their work of faith, labor of love and steadfastness of hope; they turned from idols to God and became an example to believers everywhere.
  • How Paul lived among them (1 Thessalonians 2:1–12): not to please people, with no greed; gentle like a mother, and like a father.
  • The word of God and affliction (1 Thessalonians 2:13–16): they received God's word, and suffered as the churches in Judea did.
  • Longing, sending Timothy, and prayer (1 Thessalonians 2:17–3:13): Paul wanted to return but Satan hindered him; Timothy brought good news; Paul prays that their hearts be established blameless in holiness at the Lord's coming.
  • Holiness and love (1 Thessalonians 4:1–12): abstain from sexual immorality, control one's own body in holiness and honor; love one another, live quietly and work.
  • Those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18): believers who die are not without hope; the Lord will descend, the dead in Christ will rise first, and we will always be with the Lord.
  • The day of the Lord (1 Thessalonians 5:1–11): that day will come like a thief in the night; believers are children of light and must stay awake and sober.
  • Church life and closing (1 Thessalonians 5:12–28): respect those who labor among you, be at peace; rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; "He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it" (1 Thessalonians 5:24).

The letter falls into two main parts: the first three chapters mostly look back and give thanks for what God has already done among them; the last two mostly exhort them how to keep going. The hinge is 1 Thessalonians 4:1: "as you received from us how you ought to live and to please God, just as you are doing, that you do so more and more."

How to Read This Book

1. Watch for faith, love and hope. Paul begins with "your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Thessalonians 1:3), and near the end says, "having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation" (1 Thessalonians 5:8). As you read, notice how these three keep coming back.

2. Watch for the Lord's coming. Every chapter ends with the Lord's coming (1 Thessalonians 1:10; 1 Thessalonians 2:19; 1 Thessalonians 3:13; 1 Thessalonians 4:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:23). Paul does not speak of it to satisfy curiosity or to draw up a timetable, but to comfort (1 Thessalonians 4:18), to strengthen (1 Thessalonians 3:13) and to call to holiness (1 Thessalonians 5:23). As you read, ask: how does this hope change today?

3. Watch for "you yourselves know." Paul keeps saying "you know," "you yourselves know" (1 Thessalonians 1:5; 1 Thessalonians 2:1, 2, 5, 11; 1 Thessalonians 3:3, 4; 1 Thessalonians 4:2; 1 Thessalonians 5:2). He is not giving them something new; he is calling them to remember what they already received. In affliction, believers often need not new teaching but to recall what they believe.

4. Watch for family language. Paul calls them "brothers" more than a dozen times, and says he was like a mother and a father to them, and that leaving them was like being orphaned. The church is not an institution but God's household. For many Chinese believers today who face pressure at home for their faith, or are even shut out by their families, this letter says: you have brothers and sisters in God's family.

5. Read it with Acts 17 and 2 Thessalonians. Acts 17:1–10 tells how the church began; 2 Thessalonians, probably written soon afterward, continues the discussion of the day of the Lord and of those who refuse to work.

Meditation

Reflect: "And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers" (1 Thessalonians 2:13). What the Thessalonians heard came from a few outsiders who had just been driven out of another city and were working hard at a trade in theirs. Yet they heard in it the word of God. Do I remember the first time God's word spoke to me? Perhaps a single verse suddenly brought me to tears, or a sermon named exactly what was on my heart; or perhaps I can recall no single moment, only that God's word slowly became real to me. But today, Bible reading may have become routine: I finish a chapter, close the book, and nothing remains, as if I had only read some old human words. Sometimes I hardly dare admit how long it has been since God's word moved me. Paul does not say this word works only when believers are fervent. He says it "really is" the word of God and that it "is at work in you believers." God's word does not depend on my feelings for its power. On my driest days it is still at work, like a seed in the soil, unseen but growing. Today I need not wait to feel something before I open the Bible, nor check, when I close it, how much I was moved. I can simply read and receive it, as the Thessalonians did, as the word of God; for behind these words stands Jesus, "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14), who gave himself for me. On the days I am cold toward his word, he has never once been cold toward me, and his word will not return empty (Isa 55:11).

verse_parts.text: 因为他们自己已经报明我们是怎样进到你们那里，你们是怎样离弃偶像，归向神，要服事那又真又活的神，等候他儿子从天降临，就是他从死里复活的－那位救我们脱离将来忿怒的耶稣。

entries.content:
本章脉络

第一章是一段很长的感谢，可以分成三部分。问安（1节）：保罗、西拉、提摩太写信给「在父神和主耶稣基督里的教会」。感谢神的工作（2-5节）：保罗为他们的信心、爱心和盼望感谢神，并且知道他们是蒙拣选的，因为福音传到他们那里，「不独在乎言语，也在乎权能和圣灵」。他们成了榜样（6-10节）：他们在大难之中仍有圣灵所赐的喜乐，信心传遍各处；各地的人都在讲，他们怎样「离弃偶像，归向神，要服事那又真又活的神，等候他儿子从天降临」。

整章的焦点不在帖撒罗尼迦人有多好，而在神在他们身上做了什么：神爱他们，拣选他们，用福音的大能改变他们。所以保罗是为这一切感谢神。

深读 1:1 在父神和主耶稣基督里的教会

1. 三个写信的人。 「保罗、西拉、提摩太写信给……」（帖前1:1）西拉就是使徒行传里与保罗同行的那一位（徒15:40；徒17:4），原文这里用的是他的拉丁名字。提摩太是保罗的年轻同工，刚刚被打发回帖撒罗尼迦（帖前3:2）。保罗在这里没有称自己为「使徒」（比较加1:1；林前1:1）。一个可能的原因是，他和这个教会的关系很亲密，不需要先确立自己的权柄。

2. 「在父神和主耶稣基督里」。 保罗说这个教会是「在父神和主耶稣基督里」的。这封信写在耶稣复活以后大约二十年，保罗已经把「主耶稣基督」和「父神」并列，用同一个介词连在一起，说教会同时活在父和子里面。许多学者认为，一个严守独一真神信仰的犹太人竟这样说话，可见在最早的教会里，耶稣已经被尊为主，与父同享神的尊荣（参帖前3:11：保罗求「神－我们的父和我们的主耶稣」引领他们，原文的动词却是单数）。

  • 教会是谁的？ 帖撒罗尼迦城里有许多团体：行会、宗教社团、城里的公民大会。「教会」这个词在希腊城市里指公民大会；在希腊文旧约里，它常指以色列的会众，就是神召聚到他面前的百姓（参申4:10）。保罗说，这群人的身份不在于他们属于哪一个城、哪一个行会，而在于他们在父神和主耶稣基督里。

3. 「愿恩惠、平安归与你们」。 这是保罗书信中常见的问安，把希腊人的问候（恩惠）和犹太人的问候（平安）合在一起。但在保罗笔下，这不只是客套话：恩惠是神白白的爱，平安是因这爱与神和好。整封信都建立在这两样上面。

深读 1:2-5 信心、爱心、盼望和神的拣选

1. 三样恩典，三种表现。 「不住地记念你们因信心所做的工夫，因爱心所受的劳苦，因盼望我们主耶稣基督所存的忍耐」（帖前1:3）。新约中把信心、爱心、盼望连在一起说的，这里很可能是最早的几处之一（参加5:5-6；林前13:13；西1:4-5）。保罗注意的不只是这三样本身，而是它们在生活中结出的果子：

  • 信心做工： 真信心不是闲着的，它会动起来（参加5:6）。这不是靠行为得救，而是得救的信心必然会活出来。
  • 爱心受劳苦： 「劳苦」这个词指做到筋疲力尽的辛劳。爱不只是一种感觉，而是愿意为人累着。
  • 盼望存忍耐： 「忍耐」不是消极地忍受，而是在压力下站立得稳、不肯放弃。他们能这样，是因为盼望的是「我们主耶稣基督」，盼望有一个确实的对象。

2. 「我知道你们是蒙拣选的」。 「被神所爱的弟兄啊，我知道你们是蒙拣选的」（帖前1:4）。保罗怎么知道？他并没有偷看神的生命册，而是看见了神的工作：「因为我们的福音传到你们那里，不独在乎言语，也在乎权能和圣灵，并充足的信心」（帖前1:5）。他们的改变，就是神拣选的记号。

  • 拣选是出于爱： 保罗先说「被神所爱的」，再说「蒙拣选的」。拣选不是冷冰冰的宿命，而是神的爱在创立世界以前就定意要得着他们（参申7:7-8）。
  • 不同的理解： 神的拣选怎样与人的回应相连，教会历史上有不同的看法。改革宗传统（如加尔文，以及今天的巴刻）认为，神在创世以前，在基督里无条件地拣选了一些人（弗1:4），他们必然会信。阿民念和卫斯理传统（如霍华德·马歇尔）认为，神预先知道谁会信，就拣选了他们；也有学者（如威廉·克莱因）强调，神拣选的首先是在基督里的群体，人藉着信加入这群体。这几种看法都同意：人得救全是出于神的恩典；福音要传给所有人；没有人能拿拣选作借口不信或不传福音。
  • 这节经文的用处： 保罗讲拣选，不是为了叫人猜测自己是不是在名单上，而是为了叫受苦的信徒有把握：你们信主不是偶然的，是神的手在做工。如果我看自己身上的改变还很少，也不必因此怀疑；保罗先看的是福音怎样带着圣灵的能力临到他们，叫他们领受了（帖前1:5-6）。

3. 「不独在乎言语」。 保罗不是说言语不重要；福音本身就是要用言语讲明的。他是说，言语以外还有「权能和圣灵」。圣灵叫人听见的不只是一番道理，而是神亲自的呼召。

  • 「充足的信心」： 这可能指传福音的人满有把握地讲，也可能指听的人被说服，深信不疑。从上下文看，两种都说得通。不过紧接着讲的是传道人「是怎样为人」，所以许多解经家（如杰弗里·韦玛）比较倾向前一种。
  • 「我们……是怎样为人」： 紧接着，保罗提到自己的生活（帖前1:5下）。福音的能力也显在传福音的人身上。第二章会详细讲这一点。
要点：信徒能确知自己蒙神拣选，不是靠窥探神隐秘的旨意，而是因为神的福音真的临到了自己：我听见了基督，也投靠了他。生命的改变会随之而来，但拣选的根源是神的爱，不是我们的好，也不在于我们改变得够不够快。
深读 1:6-8 在大难之中有圣灵的喜乐

1. 患难和喜乐同时存在。 「你们在大难之中，蒙了圣灵所赐的喜乐，领受真道」（帖前1:6）。「大难」原文指压力、逼迫。他们一信主就受苦：家人的反对、邻舍的排斥，可能还有失去生计（参帖前2:14；徒17:5-9）。可是他们同时有喜乐。这喜乐不是从环境来的，是「圣灵所赐的」。

  • 不是假装不痛： 圣经里的喜乐并不要求人否认痛苦。保罗自己在受苦的时候也忧伤（帖前3:7「在一切困苦患难之中」）。圣灵的喜乐，是在痛苦里面仍然知道：神是我的，我是神的。

2. 效法我们，也效法了主。 「领受真道就效法我们，也效法了主」（帖前1:6）。他们效法的，不是保罗的口才，而是他在患难中仍然传福音的样式（帖前2:2）；而这样式又是从主耶稣来的，他「因那摆在前面的喜乐，就轻看羞辱，忍受了十字架的苦难」（来12:2）。

  • 一条效法的链子： 主→保罗→帖撒罗尼迦人→马其顿和亚该亚的信徒（帖前1:7）。福音常常不是靠书本传下去，而是靠一个人的生命影响另一个人。

3. 主的道从你们那里传扬出来。 「因为主的道从你们那里已经传扬出来」（帖前1:8）。「传扬出来」这个词在新约里只出现在这里，许多人认为它带着声音响亮、四处回荡的意思，像号角或雷声一样。帖撒罗尼迦位于大道旁，又是港口，来往的人很多，这群信徒的故事就这样传开了。

  • 不是靠宣传： 保罗说「所以不用我们说什么话」（帖前1:8）。一群普通人在受苦中仍然喜乐地信靠神，这本身就是最响亮的见证。
要点：福音最有力的见证，常常不是一场精彩的布道会，而是一群受苦的普通人，因圣灵所赐的喜乐仍然站立得住。
深读 1:9-10 离弃偶像，等候他儿子

1. 掉转方向。 「你们是怎样离弃偶像，归向神」（帖前1:9）。「归向」原文就是转身、回头的意思，旧约先知常用它呼召以色列回转（参耶3:12-14）。信主不只是在原有的生活上加一点宗教，而是转过身来：脸向着神，背向着偶像。这就是圣经所说的悔改。

  • 重点在神： 原文先说「归向神」，再说「离弃偶像」。这是同一个转身，不是先后两步，但重点在神身上。人不是先靠自己丢掉偶像，才配来到神面前；而是看见了神，偶像就不再有那么大的吸引力。

2. 「又真又活的神」。 偶像是死的、假的：「有口却不能言，有眼却不能看」（诗115:5）。神是「又真又活的」。他是真的，不是人手所造的；他是活的，会说话，会行事，会救人。

  • 今天的偶像： 对许多华人家庭来说，偶像是很具体的：家里的神台、祖先牌位、观音像、财神，还有逢年过节的拜祭。离弃这些，往往会带来家人的误会和压力。信徒不可焚香、跪拜祖先牌位或神明（林前10:20-21），但仍要用敬重和温柔对待家人，可以用别的方式表达孝敬和怀念，例如追思礼拜、扫墓献花、讲述先人的生平（参本研读林前第八章、第十章关于祭祀和祭物的讨论）。不过，偶像也可以是看不见的：我们若指望神以外的东西给我们安全感、人生的意义和自己的价值，那东西就成了偶像，例如金钱、事业、别人的认可，甚至一段感情。

3. 服事和等候。 「要服事那又真又活的神，等候他儿子从天降临」（帖前1:9-10）。离开偶像不是留下一片空白，而是有了新的主人和新的盼望。

  • 服事： 原文是作奴仆的意思。从前是偶像的奴仆，如今是神的仆人。但这位主人不像偶像那样要人用祭物去讨好他，他自己先爱了我们。
  • 等候： 信徒的生活有一个方向：主要来。这等候不是坐着看天，而是在盼望中忠心地生活（参帖前4:11-12；帖前5:6）。

4. 「救我们脱离将来忿怒的耶稣」。 这一节浓缩了福音的要点：他是神的儿子；神叫他从死里复活；他要从天降临；他救我们脱离将来的忿怒。

  • 将来的忿怒： 神的忿怒不是喜怒无常的情绪，而是他对罪公义、圣洁的审判。保罗毫不避讳地说，这忿怒是「将来」必有的。
  • 他怎样救： 保罗在帖前5:9-10说：「神不是预定我们受刑，乃是预定我们藉着我们主耶稣基督得救。他替我们死」。耶稣代替我们承受了罪的刑罚，所以信他的人不必再承受。
  • 「救我们」： 原文用的是现在分词。有人认为这是一个称号，意思是那拯救我们的一位，正像以赛亚书说「必有一位救赎主来到锡安」（赛59:20；参罗11:26）；也有人认为这里的现在式指向将来那日的拯救。无论哪一种，他都是我们的拯救者。
要点：福音叫人从偶像转向又真又活的神，现在服事他，将来等候他的儿子。我们敢等候那审判的日子，是因为来的那一位，正是替我们死、救我们脱离忿怒的耶稣。
默想

默想： 「你们是怎样离弃偶像，归向神，要服事那又真又活的神，等候他儿子从天降临」（帖前1:9-10）。有人信主的时候，真的把家里的神像搬了出去；有人从小在教会长大，从来没有拜过什么偶像，就以为这句话和自己没有关系。可是偶像不一定摆在神台上。我最怕失去的是什么？当一切都不顺的时候，我第一个想抓住的是什么？是存款，是一个人的认可，还是我的健康和能干？也许我早已归向了神，却在一些日子里又悄悄转过身去，向这些东西要平安。偶像总是要我先付出，才肯给我一点安全感：多加一点班，多存一点钱，多讨好一个人；而且给了也不长久。帖撒罗尼迦人的转身并不轻松，他们为此受了苦；我也不必假装自己的心已经完全转过来了。但保罗说，他们等候的那一位，是「救我们脱离将来忿怒的耶稣」。他不是等我把偶像全清干净了才来救我；他在我还背着脸的时候，就已经为我死了。今天，我可以把那个最想抓住的东西说出来，告诉他：「主啊，这不是我的神，你才是。」然后转过身来，不是因为我有力量转，而是因为他一直在那里，又真又活，并且要来接我。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 1 is one long thanksgiving, in three parts. Greeting (v. 1): Paul, Silvanus and Timothy write "to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." Thanks for God's work (vv. 2–5): Paul thanks God for their faith, love and hope, and knows they are chosen, because the gospel came to them "not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit." They became an example (vv. 6–10): in much affliction they still had the joy of the Holy Spirit, and their faith became known everywhere; people all over are telling how they "turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven."

The focus of the whole chapter is not how good the Thessalonians were but what God did in them: God loved them, chose them, and changed them by the power of the gospel. So it is God whom Paul thanks for all of it.

Going Deeper: 1:1 The Church in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ

1. Three writers. "Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church..." (1 Thessalonians 1:1). Silvanus is the Silas who travels with Paul in Acts (Acts 15:40; Acts 17:4); Silvanus is his Roman name. Timothy is Paul's young co-worker, recently sent back to Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 3:2). Here Paul does not call himself an "apostle" (compare Gal 1:1; 1 Cor 1:1). One likely reason is that his relationship with this church is close, and he has no need to establish his authority first.

2. "In God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." Paul says this church is "in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." Writing about twenty years after Jesus' resurrection, Paul already sets "the Lord Jesus Christ" alongside "God the Father," joined by a single preposition, saying the church lives in both the Father and the Son. When a strictly monotheistic Jew speaks this way, many take this to show that in the earliest church Jesus was already honored as Lord, sharing the honor that belongs to God (see 1 Thessalonians 3:11, where "our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus" together direct Paul's way, and the verb there is singular).

  • Whose church? Thessalonica had many groups: trade guilds, religious associations, the citizens' assembly. In Greek cities the word for "church" meant the citizens' assembly; in the Greek Old Testament it often translates the "assembly" of Israel gathered before God (see Deut 4:10). Paul says this group's identity lies not in which city or guild they belong to but in being in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

3. "Grace to you and peace." This is Paul's usual greeting, joining a Greek greeting (grace) with a Jewish one (peace). But in Paul's hands it is not mere politeness: grace is God's free love, and peace is being reconciled to God through that love. The whole letter rests on these two.

Going Deeper: 1:2–5 Faith, Love, Hope and God's Choosing

1. Three graces, three outworkings. "Remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Thessalonians 1:3). This is probably among the earliest places where faith, love and hope appear together (see Gal 5:5–6; 1 Cor 13:13; Col 1:4–5). Paul notices not only the three themselves but the fruit they bear in life:

  • Faith works: true faith is not idle; it moves (see Gal 5:6). This is not salvation by works; saving faith will always show itself.
  • Love labors: the word "labor" means toil to the point of exhaustion. Love is not only a feeling but a willingness to be worn out for others.
  • Hope endures: "steadfastness" is not passive putting up with things but standing firm under pressure and refusing to give up. They could do this because their hope was "in our Lord Jesus Christ"; their hope had a sure object.

2. "We know... that he has chosen you." "For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you" (1 Thessalonians 1:4). How did Paul know? He had not seen God's book; he had seen God's work: "because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction" (1 Thessalonians 1:5). Their transformation was the mark of God's choosing.

  • Choosing comes from love: Paul first says "loved by God," then "chosen." Election is not cold fatalism but God's love resolving before the foundation of the world to have them as his own (see Deut 7:7–8).
  • Different understandings: Church history holds different views of how God's choosing relates to human response. The Reformed tradition (Calvin, and today J. I. Packer) holds that before creation God chose some in Christ unconditionally (Eph 1:4), and they will surely believe. The Arminian and Wesleyan traditions (such as I. Howard Marshall) hold that God chose those he foreknew would believe; others (such as William W. Klein) stress that God chose first a people in Christ, which individuals join by faith. All these views agree that salvation is wholly by God's grace, that the gospel is to be preached to all, and that no one may use election as an excuse not to believe or not to evangelize.
  • What this verse is for: Paul speaks of election not to make people guess whether they are on the list but to give suffering believers assurance: your faith is no accident; God's hand has been at work. If I see little change in myself yet, I need not doubt on that account; Paul looks first at how the gospel came to them in the Spirit's power and how they received it (1 Thessalonians 1:5–6).

3. "Not only in word." Paul is not saying words do not matter; the gospel must be put into words. He is saying that beyond the words it came "in power and in the Holy Spirit." The Spirit makes people hear not just an argument but God's own call.

  • "Full conviction": this may mean that the preachers spoke with full assurance, or that the hearers were persuaded and convinced. In context both fit; since 1 Thessalonians 1:5b goes on to "what kind of men we proved to be," many (such as Jeffrey Weima) lean toward the preachers' assurance.
  • "What kind of men we proved to be": Paul at once mentions his own conduct (1 Thessalonians 1:5b). The power of the gospel also showed in those who preached it. Chapter 2 develops this.
The point: Believers can know they are chosen by God, not by prying into his hidden will, but because his gospel has truly come to them: they have heard Christ and taken refuge in him. Change will follow, but the root of election is God's love, not our goodness, and not how fast we are changing.
Going Deeper: 1:6–8 The Joy of the Spirit in Much Affliction

1. Affliction and joy together. "You received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit" (1 Thessalonians 1:6). "Affliction" means pressure, persecution. They suffered as soon as they believed: opposition from family, rejection by neighbors, perhaps the loss of a livelihood (see 1 Thessalonians 2:14; Acts 17:5–9). Yet at the same time they had joy. This joy did not come from their circumstances; it was the joy "of the Holy Spirit."

  • Not pretending it doesn't hurt: joy in Scripture does not require denying pain. Paul himself was distressed in his own suffering (1 Thessalonians 3:7, "in all our distress and affliction"). The Spirit's joy is knowing, even in pain, that God is mine and I am his.

2. Imitators of us and of the Lord. "You became imitators of us and of the Lord" (1 Thessalonians 1:6). What they imitated was not Paul's eloquence but his way of preaching the gospel even in affliction (1 Thessalonians 2:2); and that way came from the Lord Jesus, "who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame" (Heb 12:2).

  • A chain of imitation: the Lord → Paul → the Thessalonians → the believers in Macedonia and Achaia (1 Thessalonians 1:7). The gospel is often passed on not by books but by one life shaping another.

3. The word sounded forth from you. "For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you" (1 Thessalonians 1:8). The Greek verb behind "sounded forth" appears only here in the New Testament, and many take it to suggest a loud, echoing sound, like a trumpet or thunder. Thessalonica sat on the highway and was a port, with many travelers, and the story of these believers spread that way.

  • Not by publicity: Paul says, "so that we need not say anything" (1 Thessalonians 1:8). A group of ordinary people still trusting God with joy in suffering is itself the loudest testimony.
The point: The most powerful witness to the gospel is often not a brilliant evangelistic rally but a group of ordinary people who suffer and still stand, held up by the joy the Holy Spirit gives.
Going Deeper: 1:9–10 Turned from Idols, Waiting for His Son

1. Turning around. "How you turned to God from idols" (1 Thessalonians 1:9). "Turned" means to turn around, to come back; the Old Testament prophets often used it to call Israel to return (see Jer 3:12–14). Coming to faith is not adding a little religion to the life one already has; it is turning around: face toward God, back toward the idols. This is what Scripture calls repentance.

  • The weight on God: the Greek names God first, "to God from idols." This is one turning, not two steps, but the weight falls on God. People do not first get rid of their idols by their own strength and so become fit to come to God; they see God, and the idols lose much of their pull.

2. "The living and true God." Idols are dead and false: "They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see" (Ps 115:5). God is "living and true." He is true, not made by human hands; he is living: he speaks, acts and saves.

  • Idols today: for many Chinese families, idols are very concrete: the family altar and ancestor tablets, a statue of Guanyin or the god of wealth, and offerings at festivals. Leaving these often brings misunderstanding and pressure from family. Believers must not burn incense or bow to ancestor tablets or deities (1 Cor 10:20–21), yet they should still treat their families with respect and gentleness, and may honor and remember them in other ways, such as a memorial service, tending graves with flowers, or telling the family's story (see this study's discussion of offerings and sacrificial food in 1 Corinthians chapters 8 and 10). But idols can also be invisible: anything we look to for security, meaning and worth that is not God can become an idol, such as money, career, others' approval, even a relationship.

3. Serving and waiting. "To serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven" (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). Leaving idols does not leave an empty space; it brings a new master and a new hope.

  • Serving: the word means to serve as a slave. Once slaves of idols, they are now God's servants. But this master is not like the idols, who must be appeased with offerings; he loved us first.
  • Waiting: the believer's life has a direction: the Lord is coming. This waiting is not sitting and staring at the sky but living faithfully in hope (see 1 Thessalonians 4:11–12; 1 Thessalonians 5:6).

4. "Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come." This verse condenses the heart of the gospel: he is God's Son; God raised him from the dead; he will come from heaven; he delivers us from the wrath to come.

  • The wrath to come: God's wrath is not a moody outburst but his righteous and holy judgment on sin. Paul says plainly that this wrath is surely "to come."
  • How he delivers: in 1 Thessalonians 5:9–10 Paul says, "God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us." Jesus bore sin's penalty in our place, so those who trust him need not bear it.
  • "Who delivers us": the Greek is a present participle. Some read it as a title, our Deliverer, like the Redeemer who "will come to Zion" (Isa 59:20; see Rom 11:26, "the Deliverer"); others read the present as pointing to the rescue on that coming day. Either way, he is our rescuer.
The point: The gospel turns people from idols to the living and true God, to serve him now and wait for his Son. We dare to await the day of judgment because the one who is coming is Jesus, who died for us and delivers us from wrath.
Meditation

Reflect: "How you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven" (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). Some people, when they came to faith, really did carry the idols out of their homes. Others grew up in church, never bowed to anything, and assume this verse has nothing to do with them. But idols are not always on an altar. What am I most afraid of losing? When everything goes wrong, what is the first thing I reach for? Savings, someone's approval, my health and competence? Perhaps I turned to God long ago, yet on some days I quietly turn back around and ask these things for peace. Idols always demand that I pay first before they hand me a little security: one more late night at work, a bit more in the account, one more person to keep happy; and what they give never lasts. The Thessalonians' turning was not easy; they suffered for it. I need not pretend my heart has fully turned either. But Paul says the one they were waiting for is "Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come." He did not wait until I had cleared out every idol before he came to save me; while my back was still turned, he had already died for me. Today I can name the thing I most want to cling to and tell him, "Lord, this is not my God; you are." Then turn around, not because I have the strength to turn, but because he has been there all along, living and true, and he is coming for me.

verse_parts.text: 我们既是这样爱你们，不但愿意将神的福音给你们，连自己的性命也愿意给你们，因你们是我们所疼爱的。
为此，我们也不住地感谢神，因你们听见我们所传神的道就领受了；不以为是人的道，乃以为是神的道。这道实在是神的，并且运行在你们信主的人心中。
