entries.content:
本章脉络

第二章有四段。保罗怎样传福音（1-6节）：他在腓立比受了害，仍放胆传讲；他不是要讨人喜欢，没有用谄媚的话，也没有藏着贪心。像母亲，又像父亲（7-12节）：他在他们中间存心温柔，「如同母亲乳养自己的孩子」；又昼夜做工，免得叫人受累；他劝勉他们，「好像父亲待自己的儿女一样」。领受神的道，也为它受苦（13-16节）：他们领受神的道，就像犹太的教会一样，受了同胞的苦害。被迫离别的思念（17-20节）：保罗很想回去，却被撒但阻挡；到主来的时候，他们就是保罗的盼望、喜乐和冠冕。

保罗为什么要花这么长的篇幅讲自己当初的为人？许多解经家（如杰弗里·韦玛）认为，他走得匆忙，城里有人趁机说他的坏话：这些人不过是到处骗钱、骗人追随的江湖客，一遇到麻烦就溜了。当时的希腊城市里确实有不少这样的游方讲师。也有学者（如亚伯拉罕·马勒布）认为，保罗未必是在回应具体的指控，而是用当时的人熟悉的对比，把自己的为人摆出来作榜样。无论哪一种，保罗都是为福音说话：如果传福音的人是骗子，福音也就站不住了。

深读 2:1-6 不是要讨人喜欢

1. 受了害仍放胆。 「我们从前在腓立比被害受辱……然而还是靠我们的神放开胆量，在大争战中把神的福音传给你们」（帖前2:2）。在腓立比，保罗和西拉被剥了衣服，用棍打，下在监里（徒16:22-24）。一个只为名利的人，不会刚被打完就到下一个城去讲同样的话。

  • 胆量从哪里来： 保罗说是「靠我们的神」。勇气不是天生的性格，而是信靠神的结果。

2. 三个「不是」。 「我们的劝勉不是出于错误，不是出于污秽，也不是用诡诈」（帖前2:3）。「错误」指所传的是假道理；「污秽」可能指动机不纯（保罗在帖前4:7用同一个词指性方面的不洁，所以也有人认为，他是在否认借传道之便满足情欲）；「诡诈」指用手段骗人上钩。保罗说，这三样都没有。

3. 讨神喜欢，不是讨人喜欢。 「神既然验中了我们，把福音托付我们，我们就照样讲，不是要讨人喜欢，乃是要讨那察验我们心的神喜欢」（帖前2:4）。「验中」和「察验」出自同一个词根，原指试验金属，看它是不是真的。神先察验了保罗，把福音托付他；神也一直在察验他的心。

  • 福音是托付的： 保罗不是福音的主人，只是受托的管家（参林前4:1-2）。管家不能按客人的口味改动主人的东西。
  • 今天的试探： 传道人和信徒都会面对这个试探：讲人爱听的，避开人不爱听的；或者为了被接纳，把福音说得软一点。保罗的答案是：我要向那察验人心的神交账。

4. 没有谄媚，没有贪心，不求荣耀。 「我们从来没有用过谄媚的话……也没有藏着贪心，这是神可以作见证的。我们作基督的使徒，虽然可以叫人尊重，却没有向你们或向别人求荣耀」（帖前2:5-6）。

  • 谄媚： 说好听的话，为的是得到好处。
  • 贪心的幌子： 原文指用好听的理由来掩饰贪心。保罗说这件事人看不见，所以他请神作见证。
  • 「可以叫人尊重」： 原文直译是可以成为重担，可以理解为使徒有权要求供养（参林前9:4-6），也可以理解为可以摆出使徒的威严。两种意思都通：保罗本可以要，却选择不要。保罗在帖前2:9说「免得叫你们一人受累」，用的是相关的词，这比较支持前一种理解。
要点：福音是神托付的，我们没有权柄按自己的方便去改它。传福音的人能不看听众的掌声，是因为在基督里，我们已经被那察验人心的神接纳；有了他的接纳，就不必再向人讨。
深读 2:7-12 像母亲，又像父亲

1. 「如同母亲乳养自己的孩子」。 「只在你们中间存心温柔，如同母亲乳养自己的孩子」（帖前2:7）。这里的「母亲」原文是乳母，但保罗特别加上「自己的」孩子：不是受雇的乳母照顾别人的孩子，而是母亲亲自喂养自己的骨肉。在一个男性领袖常以威严为美的文化里，一位使徒说自己像喂奶的母亲，是很惊人的。

  • 一个抄本问题： 「温柔」和「婴孩」在原文只差一个字母，而经文中紧挨在它前面的那个词，正好以这个字母结尾，抄写时很容易多抄或漏抄。较早、较多的抄本作「婴孩」，意思是保罗在他们中间像婴孩一样，没有心机、不摆架子；现在通行的希腊文新约校勘本也采用这个读法，许多学者（如杰弗里·韦玛、戈登·费依）认为这是原文。但和合本和多数英文译本照另一些抄本译作「温柔」，也有学者认为「婴孩」和紧接着的母亲比喻不太协调。无论哪一种，意思都相近：保罗不用权势压人。

2. 连自己的性命也给你们。 「我们既是这样爱你们，不但愿意将神的福音给你们，连自己的性命也愿意给你们，因你们是我们所疼爱的」（帖前2:8）。「性命」原文也可以译作「自己」：保罗给他们的不只是一篇讲道，而是他自己，他的时间、他的心、他的生活。

  • 福音和生命连在一起： 有些人传福音像推销员发传单；保罗却像父母一样，把自己的生活向他们敞开。这正是基督的样式：他「为我舍己」（加2:20）。

3. 昼夜做工。 「你们记念我们的辛苦劳碌，昼夜做工，传神的福音给你们，免得叫你们一人受累」（帖前2:9）。保罗是制造帐棚的（徒18:3），可能是做皮革活。这种手艺人每天从天亮做到天黑，社会地位不高。许多学者认为，保罗白天在作坊里做工，边做工边和来往的人谈福音，晚上很可能还要教导他们。

  • 为什么不收钱： 保罗并不反对传道人受供养（林前9:14；加6:6）；只是在这样一个新建立的教会里，他不愿给人任何借口，说他是为钱来的。

4. 「好像父亲待自己的儿女一样」。 「我们怎样劝勉你们，安慰你们，嘱咐你们各人，好像父亲待自己的儿女一样，要叫你们行事对得起那召你们进他国、得他荣耀的神」（帖前2:11-12）。母亲的形象说的是温柔和舍己，父亲的形象说的是教导和引导。在古代，父亲有责任教导儿女怎样做人。

  • 「各人」： 保罗不是只对着人群讲道，而是一个一个地关心。
  • 三个动词： 劝勉、安慰、嘱咐。有时要推一把，有时要扶一把，有时要郑重地提醒。
  • 目标： 「行事对得起……神」。不是为了讨保罗喜欢，而是因为神已经召他们进入他的国和荣耀。先有神的呼召，然后才有这样的生活。

5. 属灵的父母不是控制人的理由。 保罗用母亲和父亲的比喻，是为了说明他怎样温柔、舍己地爱他们，不是为了说明他有权控制他们。今天有些教会领袖也喜欢自称「属灵父亲」「属灵母亲」，却用这个称呼要求别人绝对顺服、不许质疑，甚至在钱财、婚姻或性方面利用别人。这正是保罗在帖前2:3-6所拒绝的：「污秽」「诡诈」「谄媚」「贪心」。如果有人以属灵权柄为名伤害了你，那不是你的错；你可以离开，可以向可靠的人求助；如果涉及侵犯和犯罪，应当报警，交给执法和司法机关处理（罗13:4）。受害的人不必和不安全的人和好；就算施害的人认罪、得了饶恕，也不表示他可以恢复职分，或再接触受害人和孩子。教会不可以为了「家丑不可外扬」而遮掩。主耶稣是「为羊舍命」的好牧人（约10:11）；神自己也严厉责备那些「只知牧养自己」、「用强暴严严地辖制」羊群的牧人（结34:2-4）。

要点：保罗像母亲一样温柔，像父亲一样引导，把自己的生命和福音一起给了人。这样的爱是从基督来的：他不但把真理告诉我们，更把自己给了我们。
深读 2:13-16 领受神的道，也为它受苦

1. 不是人的道，乃是神的道。 「因你们听见我们所传神的道就领受了；不以为是人的道，乃以为是神的道。这道实在是神的，并且运行在你们信主的人心中」（帖前2:13）。原文有两个动词：一个是领受传下来的道，保罗常用这个词指领受使徒传下来的福音（参林前15:1-3）；一个是心里接纳，像欢迎一位客人进门一样。他们听的是保罗的声音，却认出了神的话。

  • 神的道在做工： 「运行」这个词在保罗书信中常用来指神的大能在做工（参腓2:13）。神的道不是写在纸上就停在那里，而是活的，会改变人（参来4:12）。

2. 受同胞的苦害。 「你们也受了本地人的苦害，像他们受了犹太人的苦害一样」（帖前2:14）。帖撒罗尼迦的信徒多半是外邦人，逼迫他们的也是他们自己城里的人，包括亲戚、邻舍、同行。犹太地的基督徒也受过自己同胞的逼迫（参徒8:1-3；保罗自己从前就是逼迫的人）。

  • 今天的「本地人」： 许多华人信徒最深的压力，不是来自陌生人，而是来自家里：父母说你背祖忘宗，亲戚说你不孝，同事说你古怪。保罗告诉帖撒罗尼迦人：你们不是第一批这样受苦的人，在你们以前，神的众教会都走过这条路。

3. 这几句严厉的话怎样理解？ 「这犹太人杀了主耶稣和先知，又把我们赶出去。他们不得神的喜悦，且与众人为敌，不许我们传道给外邦人使外邦人得救，常常充满自己的罪恶。」（帖前2:15-16）这几句话在历史上曾被人用来仇视犹太人，所以要仔细读。许多解经家认为，这里指的是犹太地那些反对福音的人；使徒行传也记载，帖撒罗尼迦的风波是会堂里不信的人鼓动起来的（徒17:5）。

  • 保罗自己是犹太人： 他说的不是犹太民族本身，而是那些拒绝耶稣、并且阻挡福音传给外邦人的人。他在罗马书中为自己的骨肉之亲「大有忧愁，心里时常伤痛」（罗9:2），又说神并没有弃绝他的百姓（罗11:1-2）。
  • 先知式的责备： 这样的话是以色列内部的先知传统，正像耶稣自己责备耶路撒冷「杀害先知」（太23:37），司提反说「哪一个先知不是你们祖宗逼迫呢？」（徒7:52）。这是家里人在说家里的事，不是外人在辱骂一个民族。
  • 「充满自己的罪恶」： 这是旧约的说法，参创15:16「亚摩利人的罪孽还没有满盈」；耶稣也说「你们去充满你们祖宗的恶贯吧！」（太23:32）。罪积满了，审判就要来到。
  • 谁杀了耶稣？ 新约说，希律、彼拉多、外邦人和以色列民都参与了（徒4:27）。但耶稣是「按着神的定旨先见被交与人」（徒2:23）；他「被交给人，是为我们的过犯」（罗4:25）。说到底，是我们的罪把他钉上了十字架。
  • 教会的悔改： 历史上，一些自称基督徒的人曾拿这样的经文逼迫犹太人，这是极大的罪，与福音完全相反，教会应当为此认罪悔改。

4. 「神的忿怒临在他们身上已经到了极处」。 这句话（帖前2:16）怎样理解，解经家有几种看法：

  • 指已经发生的事： 有人认为指当时临到犹太人的灾难，例如克劳第皇帝把犹太人赶出罗马（徒18:2，一般定在主后49年），或者同一时期耶路撒冷圣殿里的屠杀和饥荒。也有人认为这句话是在主后70年以后加进去的（参导读）。
  • 指必然的结局： 有人认为保罗用过去式，是要说明神的审判已经确定，像先知讲将来的事常用过去式一样。
  • 「到了极处」： 这个短语也可以译作「终于」或「直到末了」。

无论哪一种，保罗都没有说以色列被永远弃绝；他在罗马书11章盼望「以色列全家都要得救」（罗11:26）。

要点：神的道在领受它的人心里有能力，这能力也常常带来苦难。但受苦的信徒并不孤单，在他们以前，神的众教会都走过这条路；而那位被杀的主耶稣，正是为我们受死的。
深读 2:17-20 我们的盼望和喜乐

1. 被硬生生拆开。 「弟兄们，我们暂时与你们离别，是面目离别，心里却不离别」（帖前2:17）。「离别」原文的意思是像孤儿一样被拆开。我们通常说孩子失去父母是孤儿，但许多解经家认为，保罗在这里反过来用这个词，形容父母失去孩子。他走得太突然，这群信徒信主的日子又太短，他心里非常牵挂。

  • 「极力地想法子」： 保罗不是说说而已，他真的一再想办法回去。

2. 「只是撒但阻挡了我们」。 「我－保罗有一两次要去，只是撒但阻挡了我们」（帖前2:18）。保罗没有说是怎样阻挡的。有人推测可能和耶孙交的保状有关（徒17:9），城里的官员也许不许保罗再回来；也有人推测是疾病或其他逼迫。

  • 属灵的争战是真实的： 保罗不把一切都看成单纯的环境。在神主权的掌管下，撒但确实在抵挡福音。但撒但不是最后的赢家：保罗去不成，就写了这封信，今天全世界的教会都在读它。
  • 不必凡事都怪撒但： 使徒行传记载，圣灵（也就是耶稣的灵）曾禁止他们去某些地方（徒16:6-7）。保罗也没有教我们把每一次不顺都归给魔鬼；分辨的时候需要谦卑和祷告。

3. 「所夸的冠冕」。 「我们的盼望和喜乐，并所夸的冠冕是什么呢？岂不是我们主耶稣来的时候、你们在他面前站立得住吗？因为你们就是我们的荣耀，我们的喜乐」（帖前2:19-20）。「冠冕」原文是花冠，可以指古代竞技会上得胜者的花冠，也可以指节庆或尊荣的花冠；「所夸的冠冕」这个说法，在希腊文旧约中也出现过（参箴16:31）。

  • 「来的时候」： 这个词原文常用来指君王或大官正式到访一座城。耶稣自己也用这个词指他的降临（太24:27），保罗用它来指主耶稣的再来。
  • 人就是冠冕： 保罗在主面前最想夸的，不是自己建了多少教会、讲了多少道，而是这些人自己。传福音的人最大的赏赐，是看见他所爱的人站在主面前。如果我所爱的人现在离开了主，这并不是我的冠冕被夺走了；保罗也为他们的信心担过心（帖前3:5），却把他们交托给那位信实的神（帖前5:24）。
要点：保罗最深的盼望和喜乐，不是他自己的成就，而是在主耶稣面前看见他所爱的人。这冠冕本身也是神的工作，所以他把感谢归给神（帖前3:9）；而那一天最大的喜乐，是主耶稣自己来了。
默想

默想： 「我们既是这样爱你们，不但愿意将神的福音给你们，连自己的性命也愿意给你们，因你们是我们所疼爱的。」（帖前2:8）有时我很愿意给人一些东西：一本书、一段经文、一句劝勉，甚至一次很用心的查经。可是我不太愿意给出我自己。我不想让别人看见我的软弱，不想让他们走进我的家、我的时间、我的生活，因为那样太累，也太危险，我可能会被看穿，也可能会被辜负。也许更老实地说，我太忙了：给人一段经文只要一分钟，陪一个人吃一顿饭、听他把话说完，却要一个晚上。保罗不是不知道这代价，他「辛苦劳碌，昼夜做工」，后来又和他们被硬生生拆开，心里痛了很久。可是他仍然说：你们是我们所疼爱的。他这样爱，是因为他自己先被这样爱过。耶稣没有只从天上把真理丢下来给我，他亲自来了，住在我们中间，「为我舍己」（加2:20）。在我还作罪人、还不可爱的时候（罗5:8），他就把自己给了我。今天，我不必一下子向所有人敞开；但我可以想一想，有没有一个人（不是曾经伤害我、对我不安全的人），神放在我身边，需要的不只是我的话，而是我这个人？我可以带着基督给我的爱，向那个人走近一步。就算我走得很笨拙，就算我仍有惧怕，他已经把他自己给了我，这就够了。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 2 has four parts. How Paul preached the gospel (vv. 1–6): after suffering at Philippi he still spoke boldly; he did not seek to please people, used no flattery and hid no greed. Like a mother, and like a father (vv. 7–12): he was gentle among them, "like a nursing mother taking care of her own children"; he worked night and day so as not to be a burden; he exhorted them "like a father with his children." Receiving God's word and suffering for it (vv. 13–16): they received the word of God and, like the churches in Judea, suffered from their own countrymen. Longing after being torn away (vv. 17–20): Paul longed to come back but Satan hindered him; they are his hope, joy and crown at the Lord's coming.

Why does Paul spend so long on how he lived among them? Many commentators (such as Jeffrey Weima) think that he left in a hurry, and some in the city used it to slander him: these men are just wandering con artists after money and followers, who slip away at the first sign of trouble. Greek cities of the day did have many such traveling teachers. Others (such as Abraham Malherbe) think Paul is not answering specific charges but presenting his conduct as a model, using a contrast his hearers knew well. Either way, Paul is speaking for the gospel: if those who preached it were frauds, the gospel itself would fall.

Going Deeper: 2:1–6 Not to Please People

1. Bold after suffering. "Though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi... we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict" (1 Thessalonians 2:2). At Philippi Paul and Silas were stripped, beaten with rods and thrown into prison (Acts 16:22–24). A man seeking only fame and money would not go straight on to the next city to say the same thing.

  • Where the boldness came from: Paul says it was "in our God." Courage is not an inborn temperament but the fruit of trusting God.

2. Three "nots." "For our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive" (1 Thessalonians 2:3). "Error" means the message was false; "impurity" may mean impure motives; Paul uses the word for sexual impurity in 1 Thessalonians 4:7, so some think he is also denying any sexual motive; "deceive" means using tricks to hook people. Paul says none of these was true of him.

3. Pleasing God, not people. "But just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts" (1 Thessalonians 2:4). "Approved" and "tests" share a root that originally meant testing metal to see whether it was genuine. God first tested Paul and entrusted him with the gospel, and God keeps testing his heart.

  • The gospel is a trust: Paul is not the owner of the gospel, only a steward entrusted with it (see 1 Cor 4:1–2). A steward may not alter the master's goods to suit the guests' taste.
  • Today's temptation: preachers and ordinary believers alike face this temptation: say what people like to hear and avoid what they don't, or soften the gospel to be accepted. Paul's answer is: I must give account to God, who tests the heart.

4. No flattery, no greed, no seeking glory. "For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness. Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others, though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ" (1 Thessalonians 2:5–6).

  • Flattery: saying pleasant things in order to get something.
  • A pretext for greed: a fine-sounding reason used to cover greed. Paul says people cannot see this, so he calls God as witness.
  • "Could have made demands": the Greek is literally that they could have been a weight. It may mean apostles had a right to be supported (see 1 Cor 9:4–6), or that they could have stood on apostolic dignity. Both fit: Paul could have claimed it and chose not to. In 1 Thessalonians 2:9 he uses a related word ("that we might not be a burden"), which leans toward the first reading.
The point: The gospel is entrusted to us by God; we have no right to alter it for our convenience. Those who speak it can let go of the audience's applause because in Christ we are already accepted by the God who tests the heart; having his acceptance, we need not beg for anyone else's.
Going Deeper: 2:7–12 Like a Mother, and Like a Father

1. "Like a nursing mother taking care of her own children." "But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children" (1 Thessalonians 2:7). The word can mean a wet nurse, but Paul adds "her own" children: not a hired nurse caring for someone else's child, but a mother nursing her own. In a culture where male leaders prized dignity and severity, an apostle comparing himself to a nursing mother was startling.

  • A manuscript question: in Greek, "gentle" and "infants" differ by a single letter, and the preceding word in the verse ends in that letter, so a scribe could easily add or drop it. The earlier and broader manuscript evidence reads "infants," meaning Paul was like a little child among them, without guile or pretension; the standard critical Greek text prints it, and many scholars (such as Jeffrey Weima and Gordon Fee) accept it. The CUV and most English versions follow other manuscripts in reading "gentle," and some scholars think "infants" sits awkwardly beside the nursing-mother image that follows. Either way the sense is close: Paul did not throw his weight around.

2. Our own selves as well. "So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us" (1 Thessalonians 2:8). Paul gave them not just a sermon but himself: his time, his heart, his life.

  • The gospel and a life together: some people share the gospel like a salesman handing out flyers; Paul, like a parent, opened his life to them. This is Christ's own way: he "gave himself for me" (Gal 2:20).

3. Working night and day. "For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God" (1 Thessalonians 2:9). Paul was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), likely a leatherworker. Such craftsmen worked from dawn to dusk and had low social standing. Many scholars think Paul worked in the shop by day, talking about the gospel with whoever came by, and probably taught them in the evenings as well.

  • Why he took no money: Paul did not think preachers should not be supported (1 Cor 9:14; Gal 6:6), but in a brand-new church like this he would not give anyone an excuse to say he had come for money.

4. "Like a father with his children." "For you know how, like a father with his children, we exhorted each one of you and encouraged you and charged you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory" (1 Thessalonians 2:11–12). The mother image speaks of gentleness and self-giving; the father image speaks of teaching and guiding. In the ancient world a father was responsible for teaching his children how to live.

  • "Each one of you": Paul did not only preach to a crowd; he cared for them one by one.
  • Three verbs: exhorted, encouraged, charged. Sometimes a push, sometimes a hand to steady, sometimes a solemn reminder.
  • The goal: "to walk in a manner worthy of God." Not to please Paul, but because God has already called them into his kingdom and glory. God's call comes first; this life follows.

5. Spiritual parents are no license for control. Paul uses mother and father images to show how gently and self-givingly he loved them, not to claim a right to control them. Today some church leaders like to call themselves "spiritual fathers" or "spiritual mothers," yet use the title to demand absolute obedience, forbid questions, or even exploit others financially, in marriage, or sexually. This is exactly what Paul rejects in 1 Thessalonians 2:3–6: "impurity," "deceive," "flattery," "greed." If someone has harmed you in the name of spiritual authority, it is not your fault. You may leave, and you may seek help from someone trustworthy; where there is abuse or crime, it should be reported to the police and dealt with by the authorities and courts (Rom 13:4). Victims need not reconcile with someone unsafe; even if the offender confesses and is forgiven, that does not restore his office or give him access to victims or children. The church must not cover it up to keep "family shame" from getting out. Jesus is the good shepherd who "lays down his life for the sheep" (John 10:11), and God himself condemns shepherds "who have been feeding yourselves" and rule the flock "with force and harshness" (Ezek 34:2–4).

The point: Paul was gentle like a mother and guiding like a father, giving people his own life together with the gospel. Such love comes from Christ: he did not only tell us the truth; he gave us himself.
Going Deeper: 2:13–16 Receiving God's Word and Suffering for It

1. Not the word of men but the word of God. "When you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers" (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Paul uses two verbs here. The first ("received") is the word for receiving a handed-on message (see 1 Cor 15:1–3); the second ("accepted") means welcoming it in the heart, as one welcomes a guest in at the door. They heard Paul's voice, yet recognized God's word.

  • God's word at work: the verb "at work" is often used in Paul for God's power working (see Phil 2:13). God's word does not stay put once written on paper; it is living and changes people (see Heb 4:12).

2. Suffering from their own countrymen. "For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews" (1 Thessalonians 2:14). The Thessalonian believers were mostly Gentiles, and those persecuting them were people of their own city: relatives, neighbors, people in the same trade. The Christians in Judea had also been persecuted by their own people (see Acts 8:1–3; Paul himself had been one of the persecutors).

  • Today's "countrymen": for many Chinese believers, the deepest pressure comes not from strangers but from home: parents who say you have abandoned your ancestors, relatives who call you unfilial, coworkers who find you strange. Paul tells the Thessalonians: you are not the first to suffer like this; God's churches have walked this road before you.

3. How to read these harsh words? "The Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out, and displease God and oppose all mankind by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved—so as always to fill up the measure of their sins" (1 Thessalonians 2:15–16). These words have been used in history to fuel hatred of Jews, so they must be read carefully. Many take Paul to mean the Judean opponents of the gospel; Acts also records that the trouble in Thessalonica was stirred up by unbelievers from the synagogue (Acts 17:5).

  • Paul himself was a Jew: he is speaking not of the Jewish people as such but of those who rejected Jesus and blocked the gospel from going to the Gentiles. In Romans he has "great sorrow and unceasing anguish" for his kinsmen (Rom 9:2), and says God has not rejected his people (Rom 11:1–2).
  • Prophetic rebuke: such words belong to Israel's own prophetic tradition, just as Jesus rebuked Jerusalem as the city "that kills the prophets" (Matt 23:37), and Stephen asked, "Which of the prophets did not your fathers persecute?" (Acts 7:52). It is one of the family speaking about the family, not an outsider abusing a people.
  • "To fill up the measure of their sins": this is Old Testament language; see Genesis 15:16, "the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete," and Jesus' words, "Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers" (Matt 23:32). When sin is full, judgment comes.
  • Who killed Jesus? The New Testament says Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel were all involved (Acts 4:27). Yet Jesus was "delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God" (Acts 2:23); he "was delivered up for our trespasses" (Rom 4:25): our sins nailed him to the cross.
  • The church's repentance: in history, some who called themselves Christians used passages like this to persecute Jews. This was a grievous sin, utterly contrary to the gospel. The church must confess and repent of it.

4. "God's wrath has come upon them at last." Commentators read this line (1 Thessalonians 2:16) in several ways:

  • An event already past: some think it refers to a disaster then befalling the Jews, such as Claudius' expulsion of Jews from Rome, usually dated AD 49 (see Acts 18:2), or the massacre in the temple courts and the famine of the same period. Some think the line was added after AD 70 (see the introduction).
  • A certain outcome: some think Paul uses the past tense to show that God's judgment is settled, as the prophets often spoke of future things in the past tense.
  • "At last": the phrase can also be rendered "fully" or "to the end."

Whichever is right, Paul does not say Israel is rejected forever; in Romans 11 he hopes that "all Israel will be saved" (Rom 11:26).

The point: God's word has power in those who receive it, and that power often brings suffering. But suffering believers are not alone; God's churches have walked this road before them, and the Lord Jesus who was killed is the one who died for us.
Going Deeper: 2:17–20 Our Hope and Joy

1. Torn apart. "But since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart" (1 Thessalonians 2:17). Paul's word means to be torn apart like an orphan. We usually call a child who loses its parents an orphan, but many take Paul to use the word here for parents who lose their children. He left too suddenly, the believers were so new in the faith, and his heart was full of worry.

  • "Endeavored the more eagerly": this was not mere talk; he really tried again and again to return.

2. "But Satan hindered us." "Because we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, again and again—but Satan hindered us" (1 Thessalonians 2:18). Paul does not say how. Some guess it was connected with the security Jason had posted (Acts 17:9), so that the city officials would not let Paul return; others guess illness or other persecution.

  • Spiritual warfare is real: Paul does not treat everything as mere circumstance. Under God's sovereign rule, Satan really does oppose the gospel. But Satan does not have the last word: Paul could not go, so he wrote this letter, and churches around the world read it today.
  • Not blaming Satan for everything: Acts records that the Holy Spirit (the Spirit of Jesus) kept them from going to certain places (Acts 16:6–7). Paul does not teach us to blame the devil for every setback; discerning takes humility and prayer.

3. "Crown of boasting." "For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you? For you are our glory and joy" (1 Thessalonians 2:19–20). The Greek word for "crown" is a wreath, given to victors at the games or as a festal or civic honor; the phrase "crown of boasting" also appears in the Greek Old Testament (see Prov 16:31).

  • "At his coming": the Greek word was often used for the official visit of a king or high official to a city. Jesus used the same word for his own coming (Matt 24:27), and Paul uses it for the Lord Jesus' return.
  • People are the crown: what Paul most wants to boast of before the Lord is not how many churches he planted or sermons he preached, but these people themselves. The greatest reward of one who shares the gospel is to see those he loves standing before the Lord. If someone I love has now walked away from the Lord, my crown has not been taken from me; Paul too feared for their faith (1 Thessalonians 3:5), and entrusted them to the God who is faithful (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
The point: Paul's deepest hope and joy was not his own achievement but seeing those he loved before the Lord Jesus. Even this crown is God's work, so he gives the thanks to God (1 Thessalonians 3:9); and the great joy of that day is that the Lord Jesus himself has come.
Meditation

Reflect: "So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us" (1 Thessalonians 2:8). Sometimes I am glad to give people things: a book, a verse, a word of encouragement, even a carefully prepared Bible study. But I am less willing to give myself. I don't want others to see my weakness; I don't want them coming into my home, my time, my life, because it is tiring and risky: I might be seen through, or let down. Or, more honestly, I am too busy: giving someone a verse takes a minute; sharing a meal and hearing them out takes an evening. Paul knew the cost. He "worked night and day," and later, torn away from these people, his heart ached for a long time. Yet he still said, you had become very dear to us. He loved like this because he had first been loved like this. Jesus did not just drop truth down to me from heaven; he came himself, lived among us, and "gave himself for me" (Gal 2:20). While I was still a sinner and unlovely (Rom 5:8), he gave himself to me. Today I need not open my life to everyone at once. But I can think: is there one person (not someone who has harmed me or is unsafe) God has placed near me who needs not only my words but me? I can take one step toward that person, carrying the love Christ has given me. Even if I step clumsily, even if I am still afraid, he has already given himself to me, and that is enough.

entries.title_en: Now We Live, if You Are Standing Fast in the Lord
entries.verse: 帖撒罗尼迦前书 3:8，帖撒罗尼迦前书 3:12-13

verse_parts.text: 你们若靠主站立得稳，我们就活了。
又愿主叫你们彼此相爱的心，并爱众人的心都能增长，充足，如同我们爱你们一样，好使你们当我们主耶稣同他众圣徒来的时候，在我们父神面前，心里坚固，成为圣洁，无可责备。

entries.content:
本章脉络

第三章接着第二章末了的思念，分成三段。打发提摩太（1-5节）：保罗「既不能再忍」，宁可自己独自留在雅典，也要打发提摩太回去坚固他们，免得他们被患难摇动。好消息来了（6-10节）：提摩太带回他们信心和爱心的好消息，保罗说：「你们若靠主站立得稳，我们就活了。」保罗的祷告（11-13节）：愿神开路让他回去，愿主叫他们的爱心增长，并在主耶稣同他众圣徒来的时候，心里坚固，成为圣洁。

这一章让我们看见一位牧者的心。保罗担心的不是自己的事工做得好不好，而是这群年轻的信徒会不会在患难中倒下。他的忧虑最后化成了祷告，而祷告的终点，又是主的再来。

深读 3:1-5 患难原是命定的

1. 宁可独自留下。 「我们既不能再忍，就愿意独自等在雅典，打发我们的兄弟在基督福音上作神执事的提摩太前去」（帖前3:1-2）。在雅典，保罗是一个外地人（参徒17:16-34）；把提摩太打发回去以后，他身边就没有同工了。他「愿意」孤单，也要把最得力的帮手送回去。

  • 提摩太的称呼： 有些抄本称提摩太为神的同工，有些抄本作神的执事，和合本照后者翻译。称一个人为神的同工，说法很大胆，有些抄写的人也许因此改了字；多数经文鉴别学者认为，同工是原来的读法（参林前3:9「我们是与神同工的」）。无论哪一种，保罗都是在告诉帖撒罗尼迦人：我差来的不是一个小助手，而是在福音上为神做工的人。

2. 去做什么？ 「坚固你们，并在你们所信的道上劝慰你们，免得有人被诸般患难摇动」（帖前3:2-3）。「坚固」原指用支柱把东西撑稳；「摇动」这个词在古希腊文中可以形容狗摇尾巴讨好人，所以有人认为这里带着被花言巧语引离的意思。不过多数解经家认为，这里只是被摇动、不安。患难可以把人吓走，也可以用温和的方式把人慢慢拉走。

  • 劝慰： 这个词兼有劝勉和安慰两层意思。软弱的人需要人在身边，不只是听一篇道理。

3. 「我们受患难原是命定的」。 「因为你们自己知道，我们受患难原是命定的。我们在你们那里的时候，预先告诉你们，我们必受患难，以后果然应验了」（帖前3:3-4）。「命定」是说这是神所定的道路，不是意外，也不是神失去了掌管。

  • 保罗早就说过： 他在传福音的时候，并没有应许他们信主以后一帆风顺。他「预先告诉」他们会受苦（参徒14:22「我们进入神的国，必须经历许多艰难」）。
  • 对今天的意义： 有些传福音的方式会让人以为，信了耶稣就会平安、健康、发达。当苦难来了，这样的人就会以为神不在了，或者自己信错了。保罗说：患难不是神离开的记号，而是跟随一位被钉十字架的主必走的路（参彼前4:12-13）。这不是说每一样苦难都是逼迫，也不是说要去找苦吃；而是说，苦难临到的时候，不必以为奇怪。

4. 「恐怕那诱惑人的」。 「我既不能再忍，就打发人去，要晓得你们的信心如何，恐怕那诱惑人的到底诱惑了你们，叫我们的劳苦归于徒然」（帖前3:5）。「那诱惑人的」就是撒但（参帖前2:18）。他利用患难，引诱人怀疑神、离开神。

  • 保罗也会担心： 一个伟大的使徒，也会担心自己的劳苦是不是白费了。他没有假装刚强，坦白承认「不能再忍」；但他也没有被忧虑压垮，而是采取行动：差人去，然后祷告。
要点：苦难不是神离开的证据；跟随被钉十字架的主，本来就要走这条路，主早已说明了。神没有应许我们不受苦，却应许在苦难中坚固我们。
深读 3:6-10 好消息：我们就活了

1. 「好消息」。 「但提摩太刚才从你们那里回来，将你们信心和爱心的好消息报给我们」（帖前3:6）。「报好消息」这个动词在保罗书信别处都是指传福音，这是唯一一处用来说别的事。保罗用这个词，也许是要表明：他们站立得稳的消息，本身就是福音结出的果子，叫他大大喜乐。

  • 他们也想念保罗： 「又说你们常常记念我们，切切地想见我们，如同我们想见你们一样」（帖前3:6）。城里那些说保罗坏话的人（参第二章）没有离间他们。

2. 「你们若靠主站立得稳，我们就活了」。 「所以，弟兄们，我们在一切困苦患难之中，因着你们的信心就得了安慰。你们若靠主站立得稳，我们就活了」（帖前3:7-8）。保罗自己也在患难中（参徒18:5-6；林前2:3），而他得到的安慰，是从这群年轻信徒来的。

  • 安慰是双向的： 保罗打发提摩太去安慰他们，结果是他们的信心安慰了保罗。在神的家里，没有人永远只是给的人，或永远只是受的人。
  • 「靠主」： 原文是在主里。他们能站稳，不是靠自己的毅力，而是因为他们在主里。

3. 感谢和喜乐。 「我们在神面前，因着你们甚是喜乐；为这一切喜乐，可用何等的感谢为你们报答神呢？」（帖前3:9）保罗没有把他们站稳的功劳归给自己或提摩太，也没有归给他们自己，而是感谢神。他们站稳，是神的作为。

4. 「补满你们信心的不足」。 「我们昼夜切切地祈求，要见你们的面，补满你们信心的不足」（帖前3:10）。保罗刚说完他们信心的好消息，紧接着就说他们的信心还有「不足」。

  • 不是矛盾： 他们的信心是真的，却还年轻、还不完整。他们需要更多的教导（例如第四、五章讲的圣洁、睡了的人和主的日子），需要在认识上、生活上更成熟。
  • 「补满」和「不足」： 「补满」这个动词有修补、使之完全的意思，太4:21「补网」用的就是这个动词；「不足」这个名词，也用在别处指缺少的部分（参腓2:30「不及之处」）。信心有缺口并不可耻，这正是教会彼此教导、彼此扶持的原因。
要点：真实的信心也可能还有缺欠。神用患难试验信心，用弟兄姊妹的扶持坚固信心，用他的话补满信心的缺口。我们若能站稳，是因为我们在主里站立。
深读 3:11-13 保罗的祷告

1. 父和子一同引领。 「愿神－我们的父和我们的主耶稣一直引领我们到你们那里去」（帖前3:11）。这里有两个主语：「神我们的父」和「我们的主耶稣」，但「引领」这个动词在原文是单数。许多解经家认为，保罗很自然地让父与子共用一个单数动词，把他们看作一同行事。单数动词本身不足以证明什么，但帖后2:16-17先提主耶稣，动词仍是单数，这个看法就更有根据了。这不是说父和子是同一个位格，而是说，保罗把耶稣放在只属于神的位置上：在祷告中把他与父并列呼求，求他引领。

  • 祷告蒙了应允，只是来得晚一些： 保罗后来确实回到了马其顿（徒20:1-2）。神的引领有他的时候。

2. 爱心增长、充足。 「又愿主叫你们彼此相爱的心，并爱众人的心都能增长，充足，如同我们爱你们一样」（帖前3:12）。保罗没有求主除掉他们的患难，而是求主叫他们的爱心增长。

  • 「彼此」和「众人」： 爱不只在教会里面，也要临到「众人」，包括那些正在逼迫他们的同胞（参帖前5:15）。
  • 爱是主赐的： 「愿主叫你们……增长」。爱心的增长不是我们自己拼命挤出来的，而是主的工作。我们可以求他。

3. 心里坚固，成为圣洁。 「好使你们当我们主耶稣同他众圣徒来的时候，在我们父神面前，心里坚固，成为圣洁，无可责备」（帖前3:13）。这是保罗祷告的目标：在主再来的那一天，他们能站在神面前，无可责备。

  • 从爱到圣洁： 保罗先求爱心增长，然后说「好使」他们心里坚固、成为圣洁。圣洁不是冷冰冰地守规条，而是在爱中长大。
  • 「无可责备」： 不是说信徒在今生已经完全无罪，而是说神要坚固他们，叫他们在那日能站立得住。这是神的工作：「愿主……好使你们」。保罗在帖前5:23-24也这样说：「愿赐平安的神亲自使你们全然成圣……那召你们的本是信实的，他必成就这事。」
  • 「众圣徒」是谁？ 「圣徒」原文也可以译作「圣者」。有人认为指天使，因为撒迦利亚书说「耶和华－我的神必降临，有一切圣者同来」（亚14:5），耶稣也说人子要「同圣天使降临」（可8:38）；有人认为指已经离世的信徒（参帖前4:14「神也必将他们与耶稣一同带来」）；也有人认为天使和信徒都包括在内。
要点：保罗在忧虑中祷告，求的不是患难快快过去，而是主叫他们的爱心增长，并且坚固他们，在主来的时候能站立得住。这是主自己的工作。
默想

默想： 「免得有人被诸般患难摇动。因为你们自己知道，我们受患难原是命定的。」（帖前3:3）也许当初带我信主的人，没有告诉我会受苦；也许有人告诉过我，我却没有放在心上。后来苦难真的来了：一场病、一次失业、一段关系的破裂，或者因为信主在家里受了冷落。我的信心被摇动了。我心里问过：神是不是不在了？我是不是信错了？我甚至不敢告诉别人，因为我觉得一个好基督徒不应该这样。保罗没有因为帖撒罗尼迦人的信心有「不足」就看不起他们；他昼夜为他们祈求，要来「补满」那些缺口。他也没有假装自己从不担心；他说他「不能再忍」。耶稣对快要跌倒的彼得说：「我已经为你祈求，叫你不至于失了信心。」（路22:32）彼得后来还是跌倒了，但他的信心没有完全失去，因为有一位为他祈求的主。今天，我可以把那个被摇动的地方老老实实地告诉主，也可以告诉一位可靠的弟兄姊妹，让他们为我祷告。我能站稳，不是靠我的信心有多坚强，而是因为主「坚固」我的心。保罗的祷告不是求他们自己坚固起来，而是「愿主……好使你们……心里坚固」。那位曾为彼得祈求的主耶稣，现今在神的右边，也替我祈求（罗8:34）。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 3 continues the longing at the end of chapter 2, in three parts. Sending Timothy (vv. 1–5): "when we could bear it no longer," Paul chose to be left alone in Athens so that he could send Timothy back to strengthen them, so that no one would be moved by afflictions. Good news arrives (vv. 6–10): Timothy brings good news of their faith and love, and Paul says, "For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord." Paul's prayer (vv. 11–13): may God open the way for him to return, may the Lord make their love increase, and may their hearts be established blameless in holiness at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

This chapter shows us a pastor's heart. Paul's worry is not whether his ministry is going well, but whether these young believers will fall in affliction. His anxiety becomes prayer in the end, and the prayer ends, again, at the Lord's coming.

Going Deeper: 3:1–5 Destined for Affliction

1. Willing to be left alone. "Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ" (1 Thessalonians 3:1–2). In Athens Paul was a stranger (see Acts 17:16–34); once he had sent Timothy back, he had no co-worker beside him. He was "willing" to be alone in order to send back his best helper.

  • What Timothy is called: some manuscripts call Timothy God's coworker, others God's minister; the CUV follows the latter. Calling someone God's coworker is a bold phrase, and some copyists may have found it too bold and changed it; most textual critics judge "coworker" original (cf. 1 Cor 3:9). Either way, Paul is telling the Thessalonians: the one I sent is not a minor assistant but someone working for God in the gospel.

2. Sent to do what? "To establish and exhort you in your faith, that no one be moved by these afflictions" (1 Thessalonians 3:2–3). "Establish" originally meant to prop something up with a support; the word for "moved" could describe a dog wagging its tail to fawn on someone, so some think it carries the idea of being coaxed away, though most take it here simply as "shaken" or "unsettled." Affliction can frighten people off, or it can draw them away gently, little by little.

  • Exhort: this word carries both urging and comforting. Weak believers need someone beside them, not just a lecture.

3. "We are destined for this." "For you yourselves know that we are destined for this. For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass" (1 Thessalonians 3:3–4). "Destined" means this is the road God has appointed, not an accident, nor a sign that God has lost control.

  • Paul had said so already: when he preached the gospel, he did not promise them smooth sailing after conversion. He "kept telling you beforehand" that they would suffer (see Acts 14:22, "through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God").
  • For today: some ways of preaching the gospel leave people thinking that believing in Jesus will bring safety, health and prosperity. When suffering comes, such people think God has gone, or that they believed wrongly. Paul says: affliction is not a sign that God has left; it is the road that following a crucified Lord must take (see 1 Pet 4:12–13). This does not mean every hardship is persecution, nor that we should go looking for suffering; it means that when suffering comes, we need not be surprised.

4. "For fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you." "For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain" (1 Thessalonians 3:5). "The tempter" is Satan (see 1 Thessalonians 2:18). He uses affliction to tempt people to doubt God and leave him.

  • Paul worried too: a great apostle could worry that his labor had been wasted. He did not pretend to be strong; he admitted he "could bear it no longer." But he was not crushed by worry; he acted: he sent someone, and he prayed.
The point: Suffering is not evidence that God has left but the road that following a crucified Lord was always said to involve. God has not promised that we will not suffer, but he has promised to strengthen us in suffering.
Going Deeper: 3:6–10 Good News: Now We Live

1. "Good news." "But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love" (1 Thessalonians 3:6). Elsewhere in Paul's letters the verb "bring good news" always refers to preaching the gospel; this is the only place he uses it for something else. His choice may suggest that news of their standing firm was itself the fruit of the gospel, and a great joy to him.

  • They missed Paul too: "and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you" (1 Thessalonians 3:6). The people slandering Paul in the city (see chapter 2) had not turned them against him.

2. "For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord." "For this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith. For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord" (1 Thessalonians 3:7–8). Paul himself was in affliction (see Acts 18:5–6; cf. 1 Cor 2:3), and his comfort came from these young believers.

  • Comfort flows both ways: Paul sent Timothy to comfort them, and their faith ended up comforting Paul. In God's household no one is always only the giver or always only the receiver.
  • "In the Lord": they stood firm not by their own willpower but "in the Lord."

3. Thanks and joy. "For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God" (1 Thessalonians 3:9). Paul gives the credit for their standing firm not to himself or Timothy, nor even to them, but thanks God. That they stood was God's doing.

4. "Supply what is lacking in your faith." "As we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith" (1 Thessalonians 3:10). Right after the good news about their faith, Paul says their faith still "lacks" something.

  • No contradiction: their faith was real, but still young and incomplete. They needed more teaching (such as chapters 4–5 give on holiness, those who have fallen asleep, and the day of the Lord), and they needed to mature in understanding and in life.
  • The word "supply": the Greek verb can mean to mend or restore, and is used of mending nets (Matt 4:21); the noun "what is lacking" is used elsewhere for what is missing (see Phil 2:30). A gap in faith is nothing to be ashamed of; it is the very reason the church teaches and supports one another.
The point: Real faith can still have gaps. God tests it through affliction, strengthens it through others' support, and fills it out with his word. If we stand firm at all, it is because we stand in the Lord.
Going Deeper: 3:11–13 Paul's Prayer

1. Father and Son direct together. "Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you" (1 Thessalonians 3:11). There are two subjects here, "our God and Father" and "our Lord Jesus," but the verb "direct" is singular in Greek. Many commentators think Paul, without stopping to explain, treats the Father and the Son as acting together as one. A singular verb alone proves little, but 2 Thess 2:16–17, which names Jesus first and again uses singular verbs, strengthens the point. This does not mean the Father and the Son are the same person; it means Paul places Jesus where only God belongs: invoking him alongside the Father in prayer and asking him to guide.

  • A prayer answered, though later: Paul did eventually return to Macedonia (Acts 20:1–2). God's guidance has its own timing.

2. Love increasing and abounding. "And may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you" (1 Thessalonians 3:12). Paul does not ask the Lord to remove their afflictions, but to make their love grow.

  • "One another" and "all": love is not only for those inside the church; it reaches "all," including the countrymen who were persecuting them (see 1 Thessalonians 5:15).
  • Love is the Lord's gift: "May the Lord make you increase." Growth in love is not squeezed out by our own effort; it is the Lord's work, and we may ask him for it.

3. Hearts established in holiness. "So that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints" (1 Thessalonians 3:13). This is the aim of Paul's prayer: that on the day the Lord returns they may stand before God blameless.

  • From love to holiness: Paul first asks for love to grow, then says "so that" their hearts may be established in holiness. Holiness is not cold rule-keeping; it is growing up in love.
  • "Blameless": not that believers are already sinless in this life, but that God will establish them so they can stand on that day. This is God's work: "may the Lord... so that he may establish." Paul says the same in 1 Thessalonians 5:23–24: "Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely... He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it."
  • Who are "all his saints"? "Saints" can also be rendered "holy ones." Some think it means angels, since Zechariah says "the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him" (Zech 14:5), and Jesus says the Son of Man will come "with the holy angels" (Mark 8:38); some think it means believers who have died (see 1 Thessalonians 4:14, "God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep"); others think both are included.
The point: In his anxiety Paul prays, not that the affliction pass quickly, but that the Lord make their love grow and establish them to stand at his coming. This is the Lord's own work.
Meditation

Reflect: "That no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this" (1 Thessalonians 3:3). Perhaps the person who led me to faith never told me I would suffer; or perhaps someone did, and I did not take it to heart. Then suffering really came: an illness, a lost job, a broken relationship, or coldness at home because of my faith. My faith was shaken. I asked in my heart: has God gone? Did I believe wrongly? I did not even dare tell anyone, because I felt a good Christian should not be like this. Paul did not look down on the Thessalonians because their faith had gaps; he prayed night and day to come and "supply what is lacking." Nor did he pretend he never worried; he said he "could bear it no longer." Jesus said to Peter, who was about to fall, "I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail" (Luke 22:32). Peter still fell, but his faith did not fail completely, because he had a Lord who prayed for him. Today I can tell the Lord honestly where I have been shaken, and I can tell a trustworthy brother or sister and let them pray for me. I stand firm not because my faith is strong, but because the Lord "establishes" my heart. Paul's prayer is not that they would establish themselves, but "may the Lord... establish your hearts." The Lord Jesus who prayed for Peter is now at the right hand of God, interceding for me too (Rom 8:34).

verse_parts.text: 神的旨意就是要你们成为圣洁，远避淫行；
因为主必亲自从天降临，有呼叫的声音和天使长的声音，又有神的号吹响；那在基督里死了的人必先复活。以后我们这活着还存留的人必和他们一同被提到云里，在空中与主相遇。这样，我们就要和主永远同在。所以，你们当用这些话彼此劝慰。

entries.verse_text: 神的旨意就是要你们成为圣洁，远避淫行；因为主必亲自从天降临，有呼叫的声音和天使长的声音，又有神的号吹响；那在基督里死了的人必先复活。以后我们这活着还存留的人必和他们一同被提到云里，在空中与主相遇。这样，我们就要和主永远同在。所以，你们当用这些话彼此劝慰。
entries.content:
本章脉络

从第四章开始，保罗由回顾转向劝勉。本章分成四段。更加勉励（1-2节）：他们已经知道怎样讨神喜悦，现在要「更加勉励」。成为圣洁（3-8节）：「神的旨意就是要你们成为圣洁，远避淫行」，用圣洁、尊贵守着自己的身体。相爱和做工（9-12节）：他们蒙了神的教训彼此相爱，要更加相爱，并且立志作安静人，亲手做工。睡了的人（13-18节）：信主的人死了，活着的人不要像没有指望的人那样忧伤；主必降临，在基督里死了的人必先复活，我们要和主永远同在。

这几个题目看起来各不相同，其实都和提摩太带回来的消息有关（帖前3:6、10）。他们的信心是真的，但还有「不足」：在性的事上，外邦的旧习惯还拉扯着他们；有些人可能不肯安分做工；还有人为死去的弟兄姊妹忧伤，不知道他们在主来的时候会怎样。保罗一样一样地回答，最后都回到同一个盼望：「我们就要和主永远同在。」

深读 4:1-2 更加勉励

1. 不是从头开始，而是继续向前。 「你们既然受了我们的教训，知道该怎样行可以讨神的喜悦，就要照你们现在所行的更加勉励」（帖前4:1）。保罗先肯定他们已经在走（「照你们现在所行的」），然后才鼓励他们「更加」。

  • 「讨神的喜悦」： 这不是靠行为赚得神的爱。他们已经是「被神所爱」的（帖前1:4）。就像儿女已经被父母爱着，仍然愿意叫父母欢喜一样，信徒是因为蒙了爱，才愿意讨神喜悦。许多人从小觉得父母的爱要靠成绩去换；在神的家里，次序正好相反。

2. 「凭主耶稣」。 「你们原晓得，我们凭主耶稣传给你们什么命令」（帖前4:2）。保罗的教导不是他个人的意见，而是凭主耶稣的权柄。这为下面关于性的教导定了调：这不是保守的文化习惯，而是主的命令。

深读 4:3-8 神的旨意就是要你们成为圣洁

1. 「神的旨意」。 「神的旨意就是要你们成为圣洁，远避淫行」（帖前4:3）。许多信徒常常为「神的旨意是什么」烦恼：该读哪个专业、做哪份工作、和谁结婚。保罗在这里很直接地说出神的一个旨意：你们要成为圣洁。

  • 「成为圣洁」： 这个词指一个过程：神动工，使人越来越像他（参帖前5:23）。它在本段出现了三次（帖前4:3、4、7）。
  • 「淫行」： 原文是一个含义很广的词，包括婚姻以外的一切性行为：婚前的、婚外的、嫖妓等等。

2. 外邦的习惯。 「不放纵私欲的邪情，像那不认识神的外邦人」（帖前4:5）。在希腊罗马的城市里，男人在婚外和奴隶、妓女发生关系，常常被视为平常的事，只要不碰别人的妻子就可以了。城里有些宗教节庆（例如敬拜酒神的）也带着性的象征和放纵，有学者认为这是背景的一部分。帖撒罗尼迦的信徒是从这样的文化里出来的。

  • 今天的处境： 今天的文化也有它的「平常」：婚前同居、色情影片、网上的暧昧关系、应酬场所里的种种安排。有些华人信徒在生意或工作上，会被要求陪客户去一些地方；也有人出差在外，没有人看见。保罗的话今天同样清楚：这不只是「不认识神的」人的问题，也是我们自己的问题。

3. 「守着自己的身体」。 「要你们各人晓得怎样用圣洁、尊贵守着自己的身体」（帖前4:4）。「身体」原文是「器皿」，这个词怎样理解，解经家有不同的看法：

  • 指自己的身体： 和合本和许多英文译本这样理解，意思是要学会管住自己的身体（参林前6:18-20）。
  • 指妻子： 有些解经家认为意思是「娶妻」，也就是在婚姻里，以圣洁、尊重的态度对待妻子（参彼前3:7，原文称妻子为较软弱的器皿）。
  • 委婉的说法： 也有人认为这个词在这里委婉地指性器官，意思是要控制自己的性欲。

这几种看法的重点都一样：性是神所赐的好东西，要在圣洁和尊重中，在一男一女的婚姻里享受（创2:24；来13:4），而不是任凭私欲放纵。

4. 不要欺负弟兄。 「不要一个人在这事上越分，欺负他的弟兄；因为这一类的事，主必报应」（帖前4:6）。大多数解经家认为「这事」仍然指性的事：淫乱不只是个人的私事，它会伤害别人，例如破坏另一个人的婚姻，或者占另一个人的便宜。也有少数人认为这里转到了生意上的欺骗。

  • 「主必报应」： 神看见一切，也会为受害的人伸冤。这句话对受害的人是安慰：你所受的伤害，神没有忽略。
  • 关于性侵犯： 如果有人在教会、家里或工作中受到性侵犯或性骚扰，那不是受害人的错，也不是受害人的「不洁」。神的审判是对着施害的人说的。这样的事应当报警，交给执法和司法机关处理（罗13:4）；受害人不必和不安全的人和好，也不必留在危险中。饶恕不等于恢复施害者的职分，也不等于让他再接近受害人或孩子。教会绝不可以为了「家丑不可外扬」而遮掩。

5. 神召我们，是要我们圣洁。 「神召我们，本不是要我们沾染污秽，乃是要我们成为圣洁。所以，那弃绝的，不是弃绝人，乃是弃绝那赐圣灵给你们的神」（帖前4:7-8）。

  • 呼召在先： 圣洁不是我们要先跨过、才能被神接纳的门槛；正因为神已经召了我们，我们才要过圣洁的生活。
  • 神赐圣灵： 「赐」在原文多数抄本是现在式，许多人认为这强调神是那位不断赐圣灵的神。「赐圣灵给你们」这句话，也几乎是照着以西结书的应许说的：神要把他的灵放在他百姓里面，使他们能遵行他的律例，并且活过来（结36:27；结37:14）。神没有只给我们一条命令，就让我们自己去拼；他把能力也赐给了我们。

6. 给已经跌倒的人。 这段话很清楚，也很严肃。读到这里，有些人心里会很沉重，因为他们在这件事上已经失败过，也许不止一次。保罗写信给哥林多教会时，列出了淫乱的人，接着说：「你们中间也有人从前是这样；但如今你们奉主耶稣基督的名，并藉着我们神的灵，已经洗净，成圣，称义了。」（林前6:11）基督的血足以洗净这样的罪。圣洁的道路，是从十字架开始的。「如今，那些在基督耶稣里的就不定罪了。」（罗8:1）先有不定罪，然后才有新的生活。不论你跌倒过多少次，今天都可以回到主面前，认罪，离弃这罪，倚靠他的赦免（约一1:9）。

  • 不必独自挣扎： 如果你正在色情或其他性的罪中挣扎，可以找一位可靠的肢体坦白：弟兄找弟兄，姊妹找姊妹，请他们为你祷告，也陪你走。坦白也许会让你觉得羞愧，但这正是在光明中行（约一1:7）；基督已经为我们「轻看羞辱，忍受了十字架的苦难」（来12:2）。如果这已经成了长期的捆绑，也可以寻求牧者或专业辅导的帮助。
要点：神的旨意是要我们成为圣洁，这包括我们的身体和性。这不是冷冰冰的禁令；召我们的神把圣灵赐给我们，要我们活出他的样式。对已经跌倒的人，失败不是最后的结论；在十字架那里有洗净，也有重新开始，而且每一次跌倒都可以再回到那里。
深读 4:9-12 彼此相爱，安静做工

1. 「蒙了神的教训」。 「论到弟兄们相爱，不用人写信给你们；因为你们自己蒙了神的教训，叫你们彼此相爱」（帖前4:9）。「蒙了神的教训」原文是一个词，很可能是保罗自己造的。它让人想起以赛亚书的应许：「你的儿女都要受耶和华的教训」（赛54:13；参约6:45）。新约的信徒有圣灵在心里，神亲自教他们怎样爱。

  • 「弟兄相爱」： 原文这个词本来是指亲兄弟姊妹之间的爱。家人也许已经和他们断绝来往，教会就成了他们的新家。

2. 更加勉励。 「你们向马其顿全地的众弟兄固然是这样行，但我劝弟兄们要更加勉励」（帖前4:10）。他们的爱已经越过自己的城，临到整个马其顿的信徒，可能包括接待来往的弟兄、彼此帮助。保罗还是说：「更加」。爱总还可以更多，因为神向我们的爱从来没有用尽。

3. 立志作安静人。 「又要立志作安静人，办自己的事，亲手做工」（帖前4:11）。「立志」这个词原指追求名声、争取荣誉。保罗把它和「安静」放在一起，几乎是一种幽默：你们要拼命追求的，是安安静静地过日子。

  • 为什么要这样说？ 可能有几个原因：有些人以为主快要来了，就不再做工（参帖后3:10-12）；也有学者认为，当时有些穷人依靠有钱的「恩主」生活，要为恩主四处奔走，替他争面子；也可能有人因为热心，到处插手别人的事。保罗说：好好做自己的工，不要成为别人的负担。
  • 亲手做工： 在希腊罗马文化里，有地位的人看不起用手做工的人。保罗自己就是用手做工的（帖前2:9），他要信徒看见：平凡的劳动是尊贵的（参弗4:28）。

4. 「向外人行事端正」。 「叫你们可以向外人行事端正，自己也就没有什么缺乏了」（帖前4:12）。信徒在城里本来就被人议论，如果再有人游手好闲，靠人接济，就会让福音受羞辱。

  • 不是看不起不能工作的人： 保罗在这里批评的是「不肯」做工的人（参帖后3:10），不是因为疾病、残障、年老或失业而不能工作的人。对这些人，教会要「扶助软弱的人」（帖前5:14）。
要点：神亲自教我们彼此相爱。爱有时是大大的牺牲，有时只是安静、忠心地做好每天的工作；不能工作的人，也在这份爱里被扶持。我们能这样爱，是因为神先这样爱了我们。
深读 4:13-14 不像那些没有指望的人

1. 为什么有这个问题？ 「论到睡了的人，我们不愿意弟兄们不知道，恐怕你们忧伤，像那些没有指望的人一样」（帖前4:13）。保罗离开以后，教会里有人去世了，也许是因为逼迫，也许是生病。活着的人很困惑：他们会不会错过主的再来？保罗在那里的时间很短，也许还没有详细教导身体复活的事，或者他们还没有明白复活和主再来的关系。

2. 忧伤是可以的。 保罗没有说不要忧伤，而是说不要「像那些没有指望的人一样」忧伤。耶稣自己在拉撒路的坟前也「哭了」（约11:35）。信徒失去亲人，同样会心痛、会流泪。这不是信心不够。

  • 没有指望的忧伤： 古代希腊罗马的墓碑上，常常刻着「我曾经不存在，后来存在，如今不再存在」这类的话，表达对死亡的无奈。古希腊诗人忒奥克里托斯也写过：「活人才有盼望，死人没有盼望。」保罗说，信徒的忧伤不一样，因为有指望。

3. 「睡了」。 保罗把信徒的死称为「睡了」（帖前4:13、14、15）。这不是说死后灵魂就失去知觉；保罗在别处说，离世是「与基督同在」，「这是好得无比的」（腓1:23；参林后5:8）。「睡」是一个充满盼望的说法：睡觉的人还要醒来。他们的身体在等候复活。

  • 耶稣是「死」了： 许多解经家注意到，保罗说「耶稣死而复活了」（帖前4:14），说到耶稣，他没有用「睡」这个词。耶稣承受了死亡全部的重量，所以属他的人死了，只是睡了。

4. 「神也必将他们与耶稣一同带来」。 「我们若信耶稣死而复活了，那已经在耶稣里睡了的人，神也必将他们与耶稣一同带来」（帖前4:14）。信徒的盼望不是建立在一种模糊的乐观上，而是建立在一件历史事实上：耶稣死了，又复活了。他的复活是保证，属他的人也必复活（参林前15:20）。

  • 华人的丧礼： 信徒在丧礼上，可以哀哭，可以怀念，可以讲述逝者的生平，也可以唱诗、读经、祷告，把盼望讲出来。这里说的盼望，属于「在耶稣里睡了的人」。至于没有信主就去世的亲人，圣经清楚地说，人得救只有靠着基督（徒4:12）。我们不知道每个人临终时在神面前的光景，也不必猜测，可以把他们交托给那位审判全地、必行公义、又满有怜悯的神（创18:25）。追思礼拜也常是许多未信的亲友第一次听见复活盼望的时候。（另参本研读林前第十五章。）
深读 4:15-18 主必亲自从天降临

1. 「照主的话」。 「我们现在照主的话告诉你们一件事」（帖前4:15）。这「主的话」是什么，有不同看法：可能是耶稣在世时的教训，只是福音书没有一字一句地记下来（参太24:30-31）；也可能是复活的主启示给保罗自己或其他先知的话。无论哪一种，保罗都表明：这不是他自己的推测。

2. 主再来的情景。 「因为主必亲自从天降临，有呼叫的声音和天使长的声音，又有神的号吹响；那在基督里死了的人必先复活」（帖前4:16）。

  • 「亲自」： 不是差一位天使，而是主自己来。
  • 呼叫、天使长的声音、号： 这些都是旧约里神显现、召聚他百姓时常用的意象（参出19:16；赛27:13；亚9:14），耶稣也说过，「他要差遣使者，用号筒的大声，将他的选民……都招聚了来」（太24:31）。
  • 死了的人必先复活： 这正好回答了帖撒罗尼迦人所担心的事。死去的信徒不但不会错过，反而要「先」复活。

3. 「被提」和「相遇」。 「以后我们这活着还存留的人必和他们一同被提到云里，在空中与主相遇」（帖前4:17）。「被提」原文的意思是被突然、有力地抓去。拉丁文武加大译本在这里用了一个意思是我们要被提的词，西方教会讲被提的那个术语，就是从这个拉丁词来的。

  • 「相遇」这个词： 在当时，这个词常常用来指城里的人出城去迎接来访的君王或大官，然后陪着他一同进城（参徒28:15，罗马的弟兄「出来」迎接保罗；太25:6「新郎来了，你们出来迎接他」）。许多解经家（如弗雷德里克·布鲁斯、吉恩·格林）因此认为，信徒在空中与主相遇以后，会陪着主一同回到地上；但也有人认为这个词在这里不一定带着这样的含义。

4. 不同的看法。 关于被提和主再来的次序，基督徒有几种主要看法；在福音派中，每一种看法都有认真读经的人持守。华人教会受时代论影响很深，许多信徒只听过灾前被提一种看法。

  • 灾前被提： 时代论者（如约翰·沃尔沃德）认为，主会先在空中接走教会，然后地上有一段大灾难，最后主再与圣徒一同降临地上。
  • 灾后被提： 一些前千禧年派学者（如乔治·赖德、道格拉斯·穆尔）认为，教会要经过末后的大灾难，而被提和主降临是同一件事。信徒被提到空中迎接主，随即与他一同降临。（此外还有灾中被提等看法，同样以末后有一段大灾难为前提。）
  • 不分阶段的一次再来： 改革宗和路德宗的主流（例如无千禧年派的安东尼·胡克玛），以及天主教和东正教的传统，也认为被提就是主再来的一部分。他们一般不用七年大灾难的框架来解释末世。
  • 千禧年的问题： 至于主再来和启示录20章的「一千年」怎样连在一起（前千禧年派、无千禧年派、后千禧年派），这段经文没有讨论。

这些看法在细节上不同，但都同意最重要的几件事：主耶稣必亲自、有形有体地再来；在基督里死了的人必复活；活着的信徒也必改变（林前15:51-52）；我们要和主永远同在。

5. 「这样，我们就要和主永远同在」。 这是整段的高峰。保罗没有详细描写天上的样子，也没有排时间表。他只说：我们要和主在一起，而且是永远。基督徒的盼望，中心不是一个地方，而是一个人。

6. 「你们当用这些话彼此劝慰」。 「所以，你们当用这些话彼此劝慰」（帖前4:18）。保罗讲末世的事，目的不是叫人争论、害怕，而是叫人彼此安慰。如果我们讲主的再来，结果只是叫人惧怕，或者在教会里分党，那就偏离了保罗的用意。

  • 「我们这活着还存留的人」： 保罗把自己放在「活着」的人中间，有人据此说保罗以为主一定会在他有生之年再来，结果错了。保罗也许盼望自己能活到主来，但他从没有定下日子；他在别处也把自己算在将来要复活的人中间（林后4:14），也认真考虑过自己会死（腓1:20-23）。那日子来到「好像夜间的贼一样」（帖前5:2），耶稣也说没有人知道（太24:36）。保罗是以每一代信徒都应有的盼望说话：主随时可能来。
要点：信徒的忧伤是有指望的忧伤，因为耶稣死而复活了。主必亲自降临，死了的人必先复活，我们要和主永远同在。关于时间和次序，信徒有不同的看法；但这盼望的目的，是叫我们彼此安慰。
默想

默想： 「所以，你们当用这些话彼此劝慰。」（帖前4:18）当身边有人失去亲人的时候，我常常不知道该说什么。有时我说「节哀顺变」，有时说「他去了更好的地方」，有时什么也说不出来，只好站得远一点，怕说错话。保罗给了我们「这些话」，但他并没有叫我们一见面就讲一篇末世论。拉撒路死了以后，耶稣对马大说：「复活在我，生命也在我」（约11:25）；到了马利亚面前，他没有再讲道理，只是「哭了」（约11:35）；然后他走到坟前，「大声呼叫说：『拉撒路出来！』」（约11:43）同一位主，对这个人说话，陪那个人流泪，最后亲自叫死人复活。今天，也许有一位弟兄姊妹正在为离世的父母、配偶，甚至孩子忧伤。我可以先去坐在他旁边，求主给我智慧：这个人此刻需要的是一句话，还是有人陪他流泪？等到合适的时候，我可以轻轻地说：「主必亲自从天降临……我们就要和主永远同在。」也许我自己就是那个正在忧伤的人；那么，我也可以让弟兄姊妹用这些话来安慰我，不必一个人硬撑。那位在拉撒路坟前呼叫的主，有一天也要用同样的声音，叫醒一切在他里面睡了的人，也必亲自来接我。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

From chapter 4 Paul turns from looking back to exhortation. The chapter has four parts. More and more (vv. 1–2): they already know how to please God, and now they are to do so "more and more." Holiness (vv. 3–8): "this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality," controlling one's own body in holiness and honor. Love and work (vv. 9–12): they have been taught by God to love one another, and are to love more, and to aspire to live quietly and work with their hands. Those who have fallen asleep (vv. 13–18): when believers die, the living are not to grieve like those without hope; the Lord will descend, the dead in Christ will rise first, and we will always be with the Lord.

These topics look unrelated, but all of them connect with the news Timothy brought (1 Thessalonians 3:6, 10). Their faith was real but still "lacking": in sexual matters, old pagan habits still pulled at them; some may have been unwilling to work steadily; others grieved for brothers and sisters who had died and did not know what would happen to them at the Lord's coming. Paul answers each in turn, and all of them come back to the same hope: "we will always be with the Lord."

Going Deeper: 4:1–2 More and More

1. Not starting over, but going further. "As you received from us how you ought to live and to please God, just as you are doing, that you do so more and more" (1 Thessalonians 4:1). Paul first affirms that they are already on the road ("just as you are doing"), and only then urges them on "more and more."

  • "To please God": this is not earning God's love by works. They are already "loved by God" (1 Thessalonians 1:4). Just as children who are already loved still want to make their parents glad, believers want to please God because they are loved. Many grew up feeling that a parent's love had to be earned with good grades; in God's household the order is the reverse.

2. "Through the Lord Jesus." "For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus" (1 Thessalonians 4:2). Paul's teaching is not his personal opinion but comes with the authority of the Lord Jesus. This sets the tone for what follows on sex: it is not conservative cultural habit but the Lord's command.

Going Deeper: 4:3–8 This Is the Will of God, Your Sanctification

1. "The will of God." "For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality" (1 Thessalonians 4:3). Many believers agonize over "what God's will is": which subject to study, which job to take, whom to marry. Here Paul states one part of God's will directly: that you be holy.

  • "Sanctification": this word describes a process, God's work of making people more and more like himself (see 1 Thessalonians 5:23). It appears three times in this passage (1 Thessalonians 4:3, 4, 7).
  • "Sexual immorality": the Greek word is broad, covering all sexual activity outside marriage: before marriage, outside marriage, with prostitutes, and so on.

2. Pagan habits. "Not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God" (1 Thessalonians 4:5). In Greek and Roman cities, it was often considered normal for men to have sex outside marriage with slaves or prostitutes, so long as they did not touch another man's wife. Some cults and festivals in the city (for example, of Dionysus) carried sexual symbolism and license, which some scholars see as part of the background. The Thessalonian believers had come out of such a culture.

  • Today: today's culture has its own "normal": living together before marriage, pornography, flirtatious relationships online, and the arrangements of certain entertainment venues. Some Chinese believers in business or work are expected to take clients to such places; others travel for work where no one sees. Paul's words are just as clear today: this is not only a problem for "those who do not know God," but our own.

3. "Control his own body." "That each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor" (1 Thessalonians 4:4). The Greek word for "body" is literally "vessel," and commentators understand it in different ways:

  • One's own body: the CUV and many English versions take it this way, meaning learning to master one's own body (see 1 Cor 6:18–20).
  • A wife: some commentators think it means "take a wife," that is, treating one's wife within marriage in holiness and honor (see 1 Pet 3:7, which calls the wife "the weaker vessel").
  • A euphemism: others think the word here politely refers to the sexual organ, meaning controlling one's sexual desire.

All these views make the same point: sex is God's good gift, to be enjoyed in holiness and honor within the marriage of one man and one woman (Gen 2:24; Heb 13:4), not handed over to lust.

4. Do not wrong your brother. "That no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things" (1 Thessalonians 4:6). Most commentators think "this matter" still refers to sex: sexual immorality is not a private matter; it harms others, for example by breaking up another person's marriage or taking advantage of someone. A few think Paul has turned to cheating in business.

  • "The Lord is an avenger": God sees everything and will vindicate those who have been wronged. For victims this is comfort: God has not overlooked the harm done to you.
  • On sexual abuse: if someone has suffered sexual assault or harassment in church, at home or at work, it is not the victim's fault, nor the victim's "impurity." God's judgment is spoken against the one who did the harm. Such things should be reported to the police and dealt with by the authorities and courts (Rom 13:4). Victims need not reconcile with someone unsafe or remain in danger. Forgiveness does not restore an abuser's office or give him access to victims or children. The church must never cover it up to keep "family shame" from getting out.

5. God called us to holiness. "For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness. Therefore whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you" (1 Thessalonians 4:7–8).

  • The call comes first: holiness is not a threshold we must reach to be accepted by God; we are called to a holy life because God has already called us.
  • God gives the Spirit: most manuscripts have a present participle, which many take to stress that God is the one who gives his Spirit. The phrase "gives his Holy Spirit to you" also closely echoes Ezekiel's promise that God would put his Spirit within his people, cause them to walk in his statutes, and make them live (Ezek 36:27; Ezek 37:14). God has not just handed us a command and left us to struggle alone; he gives us the power as well.

6. For those who have already fallen. This passage is clear and serious. Reading it, some will feel heavy, because they have already failed in this area, perhaps more than once. When Paul wrote to the Corinthians, he listed the sexually immoral and then said, "And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God" (1 Cor 6:11). The blood of Christ is enough to wash such sin. The road of holiness begins at the cross. "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Rom 8:1). First comes "no condemnation," then the new life. However many times you have fallen, you can come back to the Lord today, confess, turn from this sin, and rest on his forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

  • No need to struggle alone: if you are struggling with pornography or other sexual sin, you can confess to a trustworthy brother or sister of the same sex and ask them to pray for you and walk with you. Confessing may feel shameful, but it is walking in the light (1 John 1:7), and Christ has already endured the cross, "despising the shame" (Heb 12:2). If this has become a long-standing bondage, seek help from a pastor or a trained counselor too.
The point: God's will is that we be holy, and that includes our bodies and our sexuality. This is not a cold prohibition but the God who called us and gives us his Spirit, wanting us to live out his likeness. For those who have fallen, failure is not the final word; at the cross there is washing and a new start, and we may come back there every time we fall.
Going Deeper: 4:9–12 Love One Another, Live Quietly

1. "Taught by God." "Now concerning brotherly love you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another" (1 Thessalonians 4:9). "Taught by God" is a single word in Greek, very likely coined by Paul. It recalls Isaiah's promise, "All your children shall be taught by the LORD" (Isa 54:13; see John 6:45). New covenant believers have the Spirit in their hearts, and God himself teaches them how to love.

  • "Brotherly love": the Greek word originally meant the love between siblings. At a time when their own families may have cut them off, the church became their new family.

2. More and more. "For that indeed is what you are doing to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers, to do this more and more" (1 Thessalonians 4:10). Their love already reached beyond their own city to believers throughout Macedonia, perhaps by hosting traveling brothers and helping one another. Still Paul says, "more and more." Love can always grow, because God's love for us never runs out.

3. Aspire to live quietly. "And to aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands" (1 Thessalonians 4:11). The word "aspire" originally meant to seek honor and pursue a reputation. Putting it next to "quietly" is almost humorous: what you should strive for with all your might is a quiet life.

  • Why say this? There may be several reasons. Some may have thought the Lord was coming so soon that they stopped working (see 2 Thess 3:10–12). Some scholars think that poorer people at the time lived off wealthy patrons and had to run around on their errands and enhance their standing. Others may simply, out of zeal, have been meddling everywhere. Paul says: do your own work well, and do not become a burden on others.
  • Working with your hands: in Greek and Roman culture, people of status looked down on manual labor. Paul himself worked with his hands (1 Thessalonians 2:9), and wanted believers to see that ordinary labor is honorable (see Eph 4:28).

4. "Live properly before outsiders." "So that you may live properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one" (1 Thessalonians 4:12). The believers were already talked about in the city; if some were idle and living off others, the gospel would be put to shame.

  • Not looking down on those who cannot work: Paul is criticizing those who are "not willing" to work (see 2 Thess 3:10), not those who cannot work because of illness, disability, age or unemployment. For them the church is to "help the weak" (1 Thessalonians 5:14).
The point: God himself teaches us to love one another. Sometimes love is great sacrifice; sometimes it is simply doing our daily work quietly and faithfully; and those who cannot work are carried by the same love. We can love like this because God loved us first.
Going Deeper: 4:13–14 Not Like Those Who Have No Hope

1. Why the question? "But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). After Paul left, some in the church had died, perhaps through persecution, perhaps through illness. The living were confused: would the dead miss the Lord's coming? Paul's time with them had been short; perhaps he had not yet taught them in detail about bodily resurrection, or they had not yet grasped how resurrection relates to the Lord's coming.

2. Grief is allowed. Paul does not say "do not grieve," but do not grieve "as others do who have no hope." Jesus himself "wept" at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35). Believers who lose loved ones also ache and weep. This is not a lack of faith.

  • Grief without hope: ancient Greek and Roman gravestones often bore lines like "I was not, I was, I am not," expressing resignation before death. The Greek poet Theocritus wrote, "There is hope for the living, but the dead have none." Paul says the believer's grief is different, because it has hope.

3. "Asleep." Paul calls the death of believers "sleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13, 14, 15). This does not mean the soul loses consciousness after death; elsewhere Paul says that to depart is to "be with Christ, for that is far better" (Phil 1:23; see 2 Cor 5:8). "Sleep" is a word full of hope: those who sleep will wake. Their bodies await the resurrection.

  • Jesus "died": many have noticed that Paul says "Jesus died and rose again" (1 Thessalonians 4:14); for Jesus he does not use the word "sleep." Jesus bore the full weight of death, so that for those who belong to him death becomes "sleep."

4. "God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep." "For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:14). The believer's hope does not rest on vague optimism but on a fact of history: Jesus died and rose again. His resurrection is the guarantee that those who are his will also rise (see 1 Cor 15:20).

  • Chinese funerals: at a funeral, believers may weep, remember, tell the story of the one who has died, sing, read Scripture and pray, and speak the hope aloud. The hope spoken of here is for "those who have fallen asleep" through Jesus. For relatives who died without believing, Scripture is clear that salvation is in Christ alone (Acts 4:12); but we do not know how each stood before God at the end, and we need not speculate; we entrust them to the Judge of all the earth, who will do right and is merciful (Gen 18:25). A memorial service is often the first time unbelieving relatives hear the hope of resurrection. (See also this study's chapter on 1 Corinthians 15.)
Going Deeper: 4:15–18 The Lord Himself Will Descend from Heaven

1. "By a word from the Lord." "For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord" (1 Thessalonians 4:15). Views differ on what this "word from the Lord" is: it may be teaching Jesus gave during his earthly life, though not recorded word for word in the Gospels (see Matt 24:30–31); or it may be a word revealed by the risen Lord to Paul himself or to another prophet. Either way, Paul makes clear that this is not his own speculation.

2. The scene of the Lord's coming. "For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first" (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

  • "Himself": not sending an angel, but the Lord coming in person.
  • Cry, archangel's voice, trumpet: these are all images the Old Testament uses when God appears and gathers his people (see Exod 19:16; Isa 27:13; Zech 9:14), and Jesus said, "he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect" (Matt 24:31).
  • The dead will rise first: this is precisely the answer to the Thessalonians' worry. The believers who have died will not miss out; they will rise "first."

3. "Caught up" and "meet." "Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air" (1 Thessalonians 4:17). "Caught up" means to be seized suddenly and forcefully. The Latin Vulgate rendered this with a word meaning "we shall be caught up," from which the English word "rapture" comes.

  • The word "meet": at the time this word was often used for the citizens of a city going out to meet a visiting king or official and then escorting him back into the city (see Acts 28:15, where the brothers from Rome "came... to meet" Paul; Matt 25:6, "Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him"). So many commentators (such as F. F. Bruce and Gene Green) think that believers, after meeting the Lord in the air, will accompany him back to earth; others think the word need not carry that sense here.

4. Different views. On the rapture and the order of events at the Lord's return, Christians hold several main views; among evangelicals, each is held by people who read Scripture carefully. Chinese churches have been strongly shaped by dispensationalism, and many believers have heard only the pretribulational view.

  • Pretribulational rapture: the dispensational tradition (such as John Walvoord) holds that the Lord will first take the church away in the air, then there will be a period of great tribulation on earth, and finally the Lord will descend to earth with his saints.
  • Posttribulational rapture: some premillennial scholars (such as George Ladd and Douglas Moo) hold that the church will go through the final tribulation, and that the rapture and the Lord's descent are one event: believers are caught up to meet the Lord and at once come down with him. (Other views, such as a midtribulational rapture, are also argued within this tribulation framework.)
  • One undivided coming: mainstream Reformed and Lutheran teaching (e.g. the amillennialist Anthony Hoekema), and Catholic and Orthodox tradition, likewise see the catching up as part of the one return of Christ, and generally do not read the end within a seven-year tribulation framework.
  • The millennium: how the Lord's return relates to the "thousand years" of Revelation 20 (premillennial, amillennial, postmillennial) is not discussed in this passage.

These views differ in detail but agree on what matters most: the Lord Jesus will return personally and bodily; the dead in Christ will rise; living believers will be changed (1 Cor 15:51–52); and we will always be with the Lord.

5. "And so we will always be with the Lord." This is the summit of the passage. Paul does not describe heaven in detail or give a timetable. He says only that we will be with the Lord, and forever. The center of Christian hope is not a place but a person.

6. "Encourage one another with these words." "Therefore encourage one another with these words" (1 Thessalonians 4:18). Paul speaks of the last things not to start arguments or spread fear, but so that people may comfort one another. If our talk about the Lord's return only makes people afraid, or divides the church into parties, we have missed Paul's purpose.

  • "We who are alive, who are left": Paul places himself among "the living," and some say this shows he was sure the Lord would come in his lifetime, and was wrong. Paul may well have hoped to be alive at the Lord's coming, but he never set a date; elsewhere he counts himself among those who will be raised (2 Cor 4:14) and weighs his own death (Phil 1:20–23). The day comes "like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2), and Jesus said no one knows it (Matt 24:36). Paul speaks with the hope every generation of believers should have: the Lord may come at any time.
The point: The believer's grief is grief with hope, because Jesus died and rose again. The Lord will descend in person, the dead will rise first, and we will always be with the Lord. Believers hold different views on timing and order, but the purpose of this hope is that we comfort one another.
Meditation

Reflect: "Therefore encourage one another with these words" (1 Thessalonians 4:18). When someone near me loses a loved one, I often do not know what to say. Sometimes I say "be strong and accept it," sometimes "they've gone to a better place," and sometimes I can't say anything, so I keep my distance for fear of saying the wrong thing. Paul has given us "these words," but he does not tell us to deliver a lecture on the end times the moment we meet. When Lazarus died, Jesus said to Martha, "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25); with Mary he gave no explanation but "wept" (John 11:35); then he went to the tomb and "cried out with a loud voice, 'Lazarus, come out'" (John 11:43). The same Lord gave one grieving sister words and wept with the other, and in the end he raised the dead himself. Today perhaps a brother or sister is grieving a parent, a spouse, even a child. I can go and sit beside them first, asking the Lord for wisdom: does this person need a word right now, or someone to weep with them? When the time is right, I can say gently, "The Lord himself will descend from heaven... and so we will always be with the Lord." Perhaps I am the one grieving; then I too may let brothers and sisters comfort me with these words, instead of holding up alone. The Lord who cried out at Lazarus's tomb will one day call, with that same voice, all who have fallen asleep in him, and he will come for me himself.
