verse_parts.text: 因为神不是预定我们受刑，乃是预定我们藉着我们主耶稣基督得救。他替我们死，叫我们无论醒着，睡着，都与他同活。
愿赐平安的神亲自使你们全然成圣！又愿你们的灵与魂与身子得蒙保守，在我们主耶稣基督降临的时候，完全无可指摘！那召你们的本是信实的，他必成就这事。

entries.verse_text: 因为神不是预定我们受刑，乃是预定我们藉着我们主耶稣基督得救。他替我们死，叫我们无论醒着，睡着，都与他同活。愿赐平安的神亲自使你们全然成圣！又愿你们的灵与魂与身子得蒙保守，在我们主耶稣基督降临的时候，完全无可指摘！那召你们的本是信实的，他必成就这事。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第五章是全信的结尾，分成三大段。主的日子（1-11节）：主的日子要像夜间的贼一样来到，但信徒是光明之子，要警醒谨守；「神不是预定我们受刑，乃是预定我们藉着我们主耶稣基督得救」。教会的生活（12-22节）：敬重劳苦的人，彼此和睦；警戒、勉励、扶助、忍耐；常常喜乐，不住地祷告，凡事谢恩；不要消灭圣灵的感动，但要凡事察验。祝福和结语（23-28节）：愿神亲自使他们全然成圣；「那召你们的本是信实的，他必成就这事」；请他们为保罗祷告，把信念给众人听，愿主的恩常与他们同在。

第四章回答的是「死了的人怎么办」，第五章回答的是「活着的人怎么办」。保罗不给时间表，而是告诉他们怎样在等候中生活：警醒、谨守，彼此建立。全信的最后，焦点又回到神身上：叫人成圣的是神，召人的是神，成就这事的也是神。

深读 5:1-3 好像夜间的贼

1. 「时候、日期」。 「弟兄们，论到时候、日期，不用写信给你们」（帖前5:1）。这个说法也见于但以理书（但2:21），耶稣复活以后也对门徒说：「父凭着自己的权柄所定的时候、日期，不是你们可以知道的。」（徒1:7）帖撒罗尼迦人很可能想知道主到底什么时候来。保罗说，这件事你们已经知道了，就是：没有人知道。

2. 「好像夜间的贼一样」。 「因为你们自己明明晓得，主的日子来到，好像夜间的贼一样」（帖前5:2）。这个比喻是耶稣自己用过的：「家主若知道几更天有贼来，就必警醒」（太24:43）。贼不会预先通知，所以重点不是猜什么时候，而是随时预备好。

  • 「主的日子」： 这是旧约先知常用的说法，指神介入历史、施行审判和拯救的日子（参摩5:18；珥2:31）。新约把这一天和主耶稣的再来连在一起。
  • 关于预言日期： 教会历史上，不断有人宣称算出了主再来的确切日子，吸引许多人变卖家产等候，结果一次又一次落空，也叫许多人跌倒。保罗和耶稣的教导都很清楚：任何人宣称知道日子，都不必相信（参太24:36）。

3. 「平安稳妥」。 「人正说『平安稳妥』的时候，灾祸忽然临到他们，如同产难临到怀胎的妇人一样，他们绝不能逃脱」（帖前5:3）。许多学者指出，「平安稳妥」很像罗马帝国宣传自己的口号：罗马带来了和平与安全。也有学者认为这里主要是呼应旧约假先知的话：「平安了！平安了！其实没有平安。」（耶6:14）耶利米书接着也说「疼痛仿佛产难的妇人」（耶6:24）。两种背景可以同时存在：人以为靠自己的制度和力量就可以安全，却不知道审判近了。这也是对还没有信主的人的警告：那日子来到，人的制度、财富和功德都靠不住。「现在正是拯救的日子」（林后6:2），要悔改，投靠那位替我们死的主。

  • 产难的比喻： 产难有两个特点：来得突然，却也一定会来。怀孕的妇人不知道确切的时刻，却知道那一天一定会到。
深读 5:4-11 光明之子，警醒谨守

1. 「你们却不在黑暗里」。 「弟兄们，你们却不在黑暗里，叫那日子临到你们像贼一样。你们都是光明之子，都是白昼之子」（帖前5:4-5）。保罗不是要吓唬信徒，而是要提醒他们自己是谁。那日子临到不信的人，像贼一样；对信徒，却是他们所盼望的日子。

  • 「之子」： 这是希伯来式的说法，「光明之子」就是属于光明、带着光明特征的人。信徒有这样的身份，不是自己挣来的，而是因为神把他们从黑暗中迁了出来（参西1:13）。

2. 不要睡觉。 「所以，我们不要睡觉像别人一样，总要警醒谨守」（帖前5:6）。这里的「睡觉」和帖前4:13的「睡了」意思不同：那里是指死亡，这里是指属灵上的麻木、不在意。

  • 「谨守」： 原文的意思是清醒、不醉。保罗紧接着说「醉了的人是在夜间醉」（帖前5:7）。这不只是说不要喝醉酒，而是说不要让任何东西麻醉我们的心，叫我们忘记主要来。

3. 信、爱、望的军装。 「但我们既然属乎白昼，就应当谨守，把信和爱当作护心镜遮胸，把得救的盼望当作头盔戴上」（帖前5:8）。这个意象来自以赛亚书：神自己「以公义为铠甲，以拯救为头盔」（赛59:17），出来为他的百姓争战。保罗后来在以弗所书6章把这个意象展开得更完整。

  • 又是信、爱、望： 保罗在帖前1:3提过这三样，现在又把它们当作军装。在等候主来的时候，保护我们的不是自己的聪明，而是信靠神、彼此相爱，以及得救的确实盼望。
  • 得救的盼望： 「盼望」在圣经里不是一厢情愿地希望会这样，而是对神所应许之事的确实期待。

4. 「他替我们死」。 「因为神不是预定我们受刑，乃是预定我们藉着我们主耶稣基督得救。他替我们死，叫我们无论醒着，睡着，都与他同活」（帖前5:9-10）。这是全信最清楚的福音宣告。

  • 「受刑」： 原文就是「忿怒」，和帖前1:10的「将来忿怒」是同一个词。神的忿怒是真实的，但神对信徒的定意，不是忿怒，而是拯救。（持灾前被提看法的人也常引用这一节，认为信徒不必经历大灾难。）
  • 「替我们」： 耶稣的死是为了我们、代替我们。他承受了我们当受的忿怒，好叫我们得着他的生命（参林后5:21）。我们能够不惧怕主的日子，根基不在于我们警醒得够不够，而在于他已经替我们死了。
  • 「无论醒着，睡着」： 保罗在这里又回到了第四章的问题。「醒着」指活着的人，「睡着」指已经死去的人。无论主来的时候我们是活着还是已经死了，都要「与他同活」。这是对帖撒罗尼迦人最后的安慰。

5. 彼此劝慰，互相建立。 「所以，你们该彼此劝慰，互相建立，正如你们素常所行的」（帖前5:11）。这句话和帖前4:18几乎一样。末世的教导，最后落在教会彼此之间的关系上。

  • 「建立」： 原文是盖房子的意思。信徒彼此的话语和关心，就像一块一块的砖，把对方建造起来。
要点：主的日子会突然来到，但信徒不必惧怕，因为神预定我们得救，不是受刑；耶稣已经替我们死了。我们等候他的方式，是清醒地活着，穿戴信、爱、望，彼此建立。
深读 5:12-15 在教会里彼此相待

1. 敬重劳苦的人。 「弟兄们，我们劝你们敬重那在你们中间劳苦的人，就是在主里面治理你们、劝戒你们的；又因他们所做的工，用爱心格外尊重他们」（帖前5:12-13）。这个教会刚成立不久，大概还没有正式的「长老」称号，但已经有一些人在带领、照顾和劝戒其他人。

  • 三件事： 他们「劳苦」（做得筋疲力尽）、「治理」（原文有带领和照顾的意思）、「劝戒」（警告、纠正）。
  • 「因他们所做的工」： 尊重的理由不是头衔或地位，而是他们的工作。保罗要信徒「用爱心」尊重，不是因为惧怕。
  • 尊重不等于不受监督： 华人教会尊重传道人是好的；但尊重带领的人，不等于他们说什么都不能质疑，更不等于他们犯了罪也要掩盖。新约同样要求，对长老的指控要有见证人，犯罪的要在众人面前受责备（提前5:19-20）。如果带领的人有欺压、性侵犯或其他违法的事，应当按程序处理，涉及犯罪的应当报警（罗13:4）。受害的人不必留在危险中，也不必和不安全的人和好；施害的人即使认罪悔改，也不能因此恢复职分，或再接近受害人和孩子。教会绝不可以为了「家丑不可外扬」而替带领的人遮掩。

2. 「你们也要彼此和睦」。 「你们也要彼此和睦」（帖前5:13）。一个受外面逼迫的教会，最怕的就是里面不和。和睦不是不讲真话、把问题压下去，而是在真理和爱中一同生活。

3. 不同的人，不同的帮助。 「我们又劝弟兄们，要警戒不守规矩的人，勉励灰心的人，扶助软弱的人，也要向众人忍耐」（帖前5:14）。这句话不是只对领袖说的，而是对「弟兄们」，也就是全教会说的。

  • 不守规矩的人： 原文指像士兵离开队伍一样，不守秩序；在这封信里很可能是指不肯做工的人（参帖前4:11-12；帖后3:6-12）。这样的人需要「警戒」。
  • 灰心的人： 原文直译是心小的人，也就是胆怯、容易沮丧的人。这样的人需要「勉励」，而不是责备。
  • 软弱的人： 可能指信心软弱的，也可能指身体或生活上软弱的。这样的人需要有人「扶助」，就是在旁边扶着他。
  • 向众人忍耐： 不同的人需要不同的对待，但对所有的人，都要有耐心。神对我们也是这样忍耐（参彼后3:9）。

4. 不可以恶报恶。 「你们要谨慎，无论是谁都不可以恶报恶；或是彼此相待，或是待众人，常要追求良善」（帖前5:15）。这个教会正受着「本地人的苦害」，要做到这句话很不容易。这是耶稣自己的教导（太5:44），也是他自己的样式：「他被骂不还口」（彼前2:23）。彼得接着说：「他被挂在木头上，亲身担当了我们的罪」（彼前2:24）。他不但没有以恶报恶，反而亲身承受了我们的恶；我们能不以恶报恶，是因为我们自己先蒙了这样的恩。

  • 不报复不等于不求公义： 不以恶报恶，不是说受害的人不可以报警、不可以寻求法律的保护，也不是说他们必须继续留在危险之中。把事情交给神和他所设立的权柄（罗12:19；罗13:4），正是不自己报复的方式。
要点：教会是一个家：带领的人劳苦服事，其他人用爱尊重他们；软弱的、灰心的、走偏的，各人都得到合适的帮助。这一切都源于神先向我们忍耐。
深读 5:16-18 常常喜乐，不住地祷告，凡事谢恩

1. 三个很短的命令。 「要常常喜乐，不住地祷告，凡事谢恩；因为这是神在基督耶稣里向你们所定的旨意」（帖前5:16-18）。这三句话在原文都很短，很容易背，也很难做到。

  • 常常喜乐： 这不是要人永远面带笑容。保罗自己也有眼泪（参林后2:4）。这喜乐的根基是神，不是环境；所以在患难中也可能有喜乐（参帖前1:6）。
  • 不住地祷告： 不是说一天二十四小时都跪着，而是像呼吸一样，生活中随时转向神。保罗自己就是这样，他说自己「昼夜切切地祈求」（帖前3:10）。
  • 凡事谢恩： 原文的意思是在一切的事上谢恩，不是为一切的事谢恩。我们不必为罪恶、虐待或灾难本身感谢神；但在任何处境中，我们都能找到可以感谢神的地方，因为他仍然与我们同在。（弗5:20说「凡事要……常常感谢父神」，那是为神一切的恩赐和他美好的旨意感谢，不是为罪恶本身感谢。）

2. 「神……所定的旨意」。 第四章已经说过，神清楚的旨意是叫我们成圣（帖前4:3）；这里保罗又加上喜乐、祷告、谢恩。

  • 「在基督耶稣里」： 这是神「在基督耶稣里」向我们所定的。我们能喜乐、祷告、谢恩，是因为在基督里，神已经成为我们的父。

3. 不是不许哀伤。 诗篇里有许多哀歌，耶稣在客西马尼园也「忧愁起来，极其难过」（太26:37）。「常常喜乐」不是要我们压抑痛苦，而是在痛苦中仍然向神说话。保罗和西拉在腓立比的监里，背上还带着伤，「约在半夜……祷告，唱诗赞美神」（徒16:25）。

深读 5:19-22 不要消灭圣灵的感动

1. 「不要消灭」。 「不要消灭圣灵的感动；不要藐视先知的讲论」（帖前5:19-20）。「消灭」原文是用来指扑灭火的。圣灵在圣经里常常和火连在一起（参徒2:3）。信徒可以用冷淡、怀疑或刻意的压制，扑灭圣灵在教会中的工作。

  • 先知的讲论： 早期教会里，有人会说出圣灵感动的话，用来劝勉、安慰、造就人（林前14:3）。帖撒罗尼迦教会可能因为有人滥用，就开始看不起这样的讲论。
  • 不同的看法： 今天福音派对「先知的讲论」有不同的理解。终止论（如加芬）认为，带着启示性质的先知恩赐在使徒时代以后已经停止，今天相应的是根据圣经的讲道和劝勉；延续论（如古德恩）认为，这种恩赐今天仍然存在，但它的权威低于圣经，必须经过察验。（另参本研读林前第十二至十四章。）

2. 「但要凡事察验」。 「但要凡事察验；善美的要持守，各样的恶事要禁戒不做」（帖前5:21-22）。保罗没有叫人全盘接受，也没有叫人全盘拒绝，而是要察验（参约一4:1；林前14:29）。

  • 用什么察验： 用圣经，用福音的核心（基督是谁、他做了什么），也看说话的人的生命和果子。
  • 「各样的恶事」： 有些旧译本（如英文钦定本）把这句译成各样恶的外表，有人就理解为凡事都要避嫌、怕别人误会。「瓜田李下」式的避嫌自有它的智慧，但这节经文讲的不是这个。和合本译作「各样的恶事」，更接近原文。保罗是说，察验之后发现是恶的，就要远离，不管它以什么面貌出现。
要点：圣灵在教会里做工，我们不可以扑灭他；但不是每一句自称出于圣灵的话都是真的，所以要用神的话凡事察验，持守善美的，远离一切的恶。
深读 5:23-28 他必成就这事

1. 「赐平安的神亲自」。 「愿赐平安的神亲自使你们全然成圣！」（帖前5:23）保罗在全信讲了许多劝勉，最后却不是说你们要努力成圣，而是祷告：愿神亲自使你们成圣。成圣是神的工作。

  • 「全然」： 原文的意思是完全、彻底，不留下任何一部分。神不是只要我们的一部分，而是要使我们整个人都圣洁。

2. 灵、魂、身子。 「又愿你们的灵与魂与身子得蒙保守，在我们主耶稣基督降临的时候，完全无可指摘！」（帖前5:23）人常用这句话来讨论人的构成：

  • 三分说： 有些人认为人由灵、魂、体三部分组成（如十九世纪的德里慈，以及《司可福串注圣经》），这种看法对华人教会影响很深（例如倪柝声的《属灵人》）。
  • 二分说： 更多的改革宗和福音派神学家（如加尔文、伯克富、古德恩）认为，人由物质的身体和非物质的灵魂组成，「灵」和「魂」是从不同角度描述同一个内在的人（参太10:28只提「身体」和「灵魂」；可12:30也连用心、性、意、力来说整个人）。

无论哪一种，保罗在这里的重点都不是给人的构成画图，而是说：神要保守整个人，里里外外，直到主来。

3. 「那召你们的本是信实的」。 「那召你们的本是信实的，他必成就这事。」（帖前5:24）这是全信最安慰人的一句话。

  • 我们的成圣，靠的是神的信实： 帖撒罗尼迦人的信心还有「不足」（帖前3:10），在性的事上还在挣扎（帖前4:3-8），有人灰心，有人软弱（帖前5:14）。可是保罗的盼望不是建立在他们身上，而是建立在神身上。神开始了这工作，他也必完成（参腓1:6）。
  • 「召」： 神的呼召贯穿全信：他召他们进他的国、得他的荣耀（帖前2:12），召他们成为圣洁（帖前4:7），现在又说，那召他们的是信实的。

4. 结语。 「请弟兄们为我们祷告。与众弟兄亲嘴问安，务要圣洁。我指着主嘱咐你们，要把这信念给众弟兄听。愿我主耶稣基督的恩常与你们同在！」（帖前5:25-28）

  • 使徒也需要祷告： 保罗不是高高在上的属灵伟人，他也请这些年轻的信徒为他祷告。
  • 圣洁的亲嘴： 在当时，亲吻是家人和朋友之间常见的问安方式。保罗说「务要圣洁」，是要他们像神家里的人那样，用圣洁的心彼此问安。华人教会今天多用握手、点头，或一声「平安」，表达的是同样的意思。
  • 「念给众弟兄听」： 如果这是保罗现存最早的书信（参导读），这也是新约里最早明文吩咐把书信念给全教会听的地方（参西4:16）。保罗为什么要起誓嘱咐，经文没有说；也许是要确保每一个人，包括不识字的人，都听到这些话。
  • 恩典开始，恩典结束： 这封信以「愿恩惠、平安归与你们」开始（帖前1:1），以「愿我主耶稣基督的恩常与你们同在」结束。
要点：保罗把所有的劝勉都交在神手中：叫人成圣的是神，召人的是神，成就这事的也是神。我们的盼望不在于自己有多坚强，而在于那召我们的本是信实的。
默想

默想： 「因为神不是预定我们受刑，乃是预定我们藉着我们主耶稣基督得救。他替我们死，叫我们无论醒着，睡着，都与他同活。」（帖前5:9-10）有些人一想到主的日子，心里就紧张。也许是小时候听过的讲道，讲到末日的灾难，讲到有人被提、有人被留下；也许是看了一部电影，或者听人说主再来的日子已经被算出来了。我曾经害怕：如果主今天来，我是不是准备好了？我是不是够警醒？那种害怕，有时让我更努力地读经祷告，有时却让我干脆不去想。保罗写这一段，不是为了叫帖撒罗尼迦人害怕，而是叫他们「彼此劝慰」。他说，那日子对不信的人像贼，对信的人却不是这样，因为神对我们的定意不是忿怒，而是拯救；而这拯救的根据，是耶稣「替我们死」。到那日我能站立得住，不是因为我警醒得够，而是因为他替我承受了忿怒。如果我连自己是不是属他的人都不确定，这句话也是向我发出的邀请：他是「替我们死」的，替罪人死的；今天我就可以投靠他，不必等到自己觉得够好。今天，我可以把心里对那日子的恐惧说出来，然后读这一句：「那召你们的本是信实的，他必成就这事。」（帖前5:24）他召了我，他必保守我，直到他来；那一天，将是我见他面的日子。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 5 closes the letter in three main parts. The day of the Lord (vv. 1–11): the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, but believers are children of light and must stay awake and sober; "God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ." Church life (vv. 12–22): respect those who labor among you and be at peace; admonish, encourage, help, be patient; rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; do not quench the Spirit, but test everything. Blessing and closing (vv. 23–28): may God himself sanctify them completely; "He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it"; pray for us, read this letter to all, and the grace of the Lord be with you.

Chapter 4 answered "what about the dead?"; chapter 5 answers "what about the living?" Paul gives no timetable; instead he tells them how to live while they wait: awake, sober, building one another up. At the very end the focus returns to God: it is God who sanctifies, God who calls, and God who will do it.

Going Deeper: 5:1–3 Like a Thief in the Night

1. "The times and the seasons." "Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you" (1 Thessalonians 5:1). The pairing appears in Daniel (Dan 2:21), and after his resurrection Jesus told the disciples, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority" (Acts 1:7). The Thessalonians very likely wanted to know when the Lord would come. Paul says: you already know this, namely, that no one knows.

2. "Like a thief in the night." "For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2). Jesus himself used this picture: "if the master of the house had known in what part of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake" (Matt 24:43). A thief gives no notice, so the point is not to guess the time but to be ready at any time.

  • "The day of the Lord": a phrase the Old Testament prophets often used for the day God steps into history to judge and to save (see Amos 5:18; Joel 2:31). The New Testament links that day with the return of the Lord Jesus.
  • On predicting dates: throughout church history, people have claimed to have calculated the exact day of the Lord's return, drawing many to sell their possessions and wait, only to be disappointed again and again, and causing many to stumble. Paul's teaching and Jesus' are clear: no one who claims to know the day is to be believed (see Matt 24:36).

3. "Peace and security." "While people are saying, 'There is peace and security,' then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape" (1 Thessalonians 5:3). Many scholars note that "peace and security" sounds very like the Roman Empire's own propaganda: Rome had brought peace and safety. Others think the main echo is the Old Testament false prophets, "saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace" (Jer 6:14). Jeremiah goes on to speak of "pain as of a woman in labor" (Jer 6:24). Both backgrounds can stand together: people think their own systems and strength make them safe, unaware that judgment is near. This is also a warning to those who have not yet believed: when that day comes, no system, wealth or merit will hold. "Now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor 6:2); repent and take refuge in the Lord who died for us.

  • The picture of labor pains: labor has two features: it comes suddenly, and it surely comes. A pregnant woman does not know the exact moment, but she knows the day will come.
Going Deeper: 5:4–11 Children of Light, Awake and Sober

1. "But you are not in darkness." "But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief. For you are all children of light, children of the day" (1 Thessalonians 5:4–5). Paul is not trying to frighten believers but to remind them who they are. To unbelievers that day comes like a thief; to believers it is the day they long for.

  • "Children of": this is a Hebrew way of speaking; "children of light" are people who belong to the light and bear its marks. Believers did not earn this identity; God brought them out of darkness (see Col 1:13).

2. Do not sleep. "So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober" (1 Thessalonians 5:6). "Sleep" here differs from "asleep" in 1 Thessalonians 4:13: there it meant death; here it means spiritual numbness and indifference.

  • "Be sober": the word means clear-headed, not drunk. Paul goes on, "those who get drunk, are drunk at night" (1 Thessalonians 5:7). This is not only about not getting drunk on wine; it means not letting anything dull our hearts until we forget that the Lord is coming.

3. The armor of faith, love and hope. "But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation" (1 Thessalonians 5:8). The image comes from Isaiah, where God himself "put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head" (Isa 59:17) and went out to fight for his people. Paul later develops the image more fully in Ephesians 6.

  • Faith, love and hope again: Paul mentioned these three in 1 Thessalonians 1:3, and now makes them armor. While we wait for the Lord, what protects us is not our own cleverness but trust in God, love for one another, and a sure hope of salvation.
  • The hope of salvation: "hope" in Scripture is not wishful thinking but confident expectation of what God has promised.

4. "Who died for us." "For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him" (1 Thessalonians 5:9–10). This is the letter's clearest statement of the gospel.

  • "Wrath": the same word as "the wrath to come" in 1 Thessalonians 1:10. God's wrath is real, but God's purpose for believers is not wrath but salvation. (Pretribulationists often cite this verse for the church's exemption from the tribulation.)
  • "For us": Jesus died for us and in our place. He bore the wrath we deserved so that we might have his life (see 2 Cor 5:21). We need not fear the day of the Lord, not because we are watchful enough, but because he has already died for us.
  • "Whether we are awake or asleep": here Paul returns to the question of chapter 4. "Awake" means those still alive; "asleep" means those who have died. Whether we are alive or already dead when the Lord comes, we will "live with him." This is Paul's final comfort to the Thessalonians.

5. Encourage and build up one another. "Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing" (1 Thessalonians 5:11). This is almost the same as 1 Thessalonians 4:18. Teaching about the end lands, in the end, on how the church treats one another.

  • "Build up": the word means to build a house. Believers' words and care for one another are like bricks, building each other up.
The point: The day of the Lord will come suddenly, but believers need not fear, because God has destined us for salvation, not wrath; Jesus has already died for us. We wait for him by living awake, wearing faith, love and hope, and building one another up.
Going Deeper: 5:12–15 How to Treat One Another in the Church

1. Respect those who labor. "We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work" (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13). This young church probably had no formal title of "elder" yet, but some were already leading, caring for and admonishing others.

  • Three things: they "labor" (to the point of exhaustion), are "over you" (the word carries the sense of leading and caring for), and "admonish" (warn and correct).
  • "Because of their work": the reason for respect is not title or status but their work. Paul wants believers to esteem them "in love," not out of fear.
  • Respect is not freedom from accountability: Respecting pastors, as Chinese churches do, is good; but respecting leaders does not mean they can never be questioned, still less that their sin should be covered up. The New Testament also requires that charges against an elder be supported by witnesses and that those who persist in sin be rebuked publicly (1 Tim 5:19–20). If a leader is guilty of oppression, abuse or crime, it should be dealt with through proper process, and crimes should be reported to the police (Rom 13:4). Victims need not remain in danger or reconcile with someone unsafe; even genuine repentance does not restore an abuser's office or give him access to victims or children. The church must never cover up a leader's abuse to save face.

2. "Be at peace among yourselves." "Be at peace among yourselves" (1 Thessalonians 5:13). A church under persecution from outside has most to fear from discord within. Peace does not mean avoiding the truth and pushing problems down; it means living together in truth and love.

3. Different people, different help. "And we urge you, brothers, admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all" (1 Thessalonians 5:14). These words are addressed not only to leaders but to "brothers," the whole church.

  • The idle: the word describes a soldier out of rank, disorderly; in this letter it very likely means those who will not work (see 1 Thessalonians 4:11–12; 2 Thess 3:6–12). Such people need to be "admonished."
  • The fainthearted: literally "small-souled," that is, timid and easily discouraged. Such people need encouragement, not rebuke.
  • The weak: this may mean weak in faith, or weak in body or circumstances. Such people need someone to "help," to come alongside and hold them up.
  • Patient with all: different people need different treatment, but all need patience. God is patient with us like this (see 2 Pet 3:9).

4. Do not repay evil for evil. "See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to everyone" (1 Thessalonians 5:15). For a church suffering "from your own countrymen," this was hard to do. It is Jesus' own teaching (Matt 5:44), and his own way: "When he was reviled, he did not revile in return" (1 Pet 2:23). Peter goes on, "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree" (1 Pet 2:24). Far from repaying evil, he bore ours in his own body; we can refuse to repay evil because we ourselves have first received such grace.

  • Not taking revenge is not giving up on justice: not repaying evil for evil does not mean victims may not report to the police or seek the protection of the law, nor that they must remain in danger. Handing the matter to God and to the authorities he has appointed (Rom 12:19; Rom 13:4) is the very way not to take revenge oneself.
The point: The church is a family: leaders labor to serve and others esteem them in love; the weak, the fainthearted and those who stray each receive the help they need. All of this flows from God's patience with us first.
Going Deeper: 5:16–18 Rejoice Always, Pray Without Ceasing, Give Thanks

1. Three short commands. "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18). In Greek these three lines are very short, easy to memorize and hard to live.

  • Rejoice always: this does not mean wearing a permanent smile. Paul himself had tears (see 2 Cor 2:4). This joy rests on God, not circumstances, so it is possible even in affliction (see 1 Thessalonians 1:6).
  • Pray without ceasing: not kneeling twenty-four hours a day, but turning to God throughout life, like breathing. Paul himself did this; he says he prayed "most earnestly night and day" (1 Thessalonians 3:10).
  • Give thanks in all circumstances: the Greek means giving thanks "in everything," not "for everything." We need not thank God for sin, abuse or disaster themselves; but in any situation we can find something to thank God for, because he is still with us. (Eph 5:20 does say "giving thanks always and for everything"; that is thanks for all God's gifts and his good purposes, not thanks for evil itself.)

2. "The will of God." Chapter 4 already showed that God's clear will is our sanctification (1 Thessalonians 4:3); here Paul adds joy, prayer and thanksgiving.

  • "In Christ Jesus": this is God's will for us "in Christ Jesus." We can rejoice, pray and give thanks because in Christ God has become our Father.

3. Not a ban on lament. The Psalms are full of laments, and in Gethsemane Jesus "began to be sorrowful and troubled" (Matt 26:37). "Rejoice always" does not ask us to suppress pain but to keep speaking to God in it. Paul and Silas, in prison at Philippi still wounded from the beating, were "about midnight... praying and singing hymns to God" (Acts 16:25).

Going Deeper: 5:19–22 Do Not Quench the Spirit

1. "Do not quench." "Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies" (1 Thessalonians 5:19–20). "Quench" is the word for putting out a fire. In Scripture the Holy Spirit is often linked with fire (see Acts 2:3). Believers can put out the Spirit's work in the church through coldness, suspicion or deliberate suppression.

  • Prophecies: in the early church some would speak words prompted by the Spirit, for upbuilding, encouragement and consolation (1 Cor 14:3). The Thessalonian church may have begun to despise such words because some had misused them.
  • Different views: evangelicals today understand "prophecy" differently. Cessationists (such as Richard Gaffin) hold that the revelatory gift of prophecy ceased after the apostolic age, and that its counterpart today is preaching and exhortation grounded in Scripture. Continuationists (such as Wayne Grudem) hold that the gift continues today, but with authority lower than Scripture, and must always be tested. (See also this study's chapters on 1 Corinthians 12–14.)

2. "But test everything." "But test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil" (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22). Paul tells them neither to accept everything nor to reject everything, but to test (see 1 John 4:1; 1 Cor 14:29).

  • Test by what: by Scripture, by the heart of the gospel (who Christ is and what he has done), and by the life and fruit of the one speaking.
  • "Every form of evil": an old English translation rendered this "all appearance of evil," and some took it to mean always avoiding anything that might look bad to others. But the Greek means "every kind of evil": once testing shows something to be evil, stay away from it, whatever form it takes. Care about appearances has its own wisdom, but this verse is not about that; the CUV's "every form of evil" is closer to the Greek.
The point: The Holy Spirit works in the church, and we must not quench him; but not every word claiming to come from the Spirit is true, so we test everything by God's word, hold fast what is good, and keep away from every evil.
Going Deeper: 5:23–28 He Will Surely Do It

1. "The God of peace himself." "Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely" (1 Thessalonians 5:23). After all his exhortations, Paul does not end by telling them to work hard at being holy, but with a prayer that God himself would sanctify them. Sanctification is God's work.

  • "Completely": the word means wholly, through and through, leaving no part out. God does not want only part of us; he means to make the whole person holy.

2. Spirit, soul and body. "And may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Thessalonians 5:23). This verse is often used in discussions of human nature:

  • Trichotomy: some hold that humans have three parts, spirit, soul and body (such as Franz Delitzsch in the nineteenth century, and the Scofield Reference Bible); this view has also been very influential in Chinese churches (for example, Watchman Nee's The Spiritual Man).
  • Dichotomy: more Reformed and evangelical theologians (such as Calvin, Louis Berkhof and Wayne Grudem) hold that humans consist of a material body and an immaterial soul, and that "spirit" and "soul" describe the same inner person from different angles (see Matt 10:28, which mentions only "body" and "soul"; Mark 12:30 likewise piles up heart, soul, mind and strength for the whole person).

Either way, Paul's point here is not to draw a diagram of human nature, but to say that God will keep the whole person, inside and out, until the Lord comes.

3. "He who calls you is faithful." "He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it" (1 Thessalonians 5:24). This is the most comforting sentence in the letter.

  • Our sanctification rests on God's faithfulness: the Thessalonians' faith still had gaps (1 Thessalonians 3:10); they were still struggling in sexual matters (1 Thessalonians 4:3–8); some were fainthearted, some weak (1 Thessalonians 5:14). But Paul's hope did not rest on them; it rested on God. God began this work, and he will complete it (see Phil 1:6).
  • "Calls": God's call runs through the whole letter: he calls them into his own kingdom and glory (1 Thessalonians 2:12), calls them to holiness (1 Thessalonians 4:7), and now Paul says the one who calls them is faithful.

4. Closing. "Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you" (1 Thessalonians 5:25–28).

  • Apostles need prayer too: Paul is no spiritual giant on a pedestal; he asks these young believers to pray for him.
  • A holy kiss: a kiss was a common greeting among family and friends at the time. Paul says "holy": greet one another as members of God's household. In many cultures today a handshake, an embrace or a greeting expresses the same thing; Chinese churches often use a handshake, a nod or a word of "peace."
  • "Read to all the brothers": if this is Paul's earliest surviving letter (see the introduction), this is the earliest written instruction in the New Testament for a letter to be read to the whole church (cf. Col 4:16). The text does not say why Paul puts them under oath; perhaps to make sure everyone, including those who could not read, heard it.
  • Beginning and ending in grace: the letter begins with "Grace to you and peace" (1 Thessalonians 1:1) and ends with "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you."
The point: Paul places all his exhortations in God's hands: it is God who sanctifies, God who calls, and God who will do it. Our hope does not lie in how strong we are, but in the faithfulness of the one who calls us.
Meditation

Reflect: "For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him" (1 Thessalonians 5:9–10). Some people tense up whenever they think about the day of the Lord. Perhaps it was sermons heard in childhood about end-time disasters, about some taken and some left behind; perhaps a film, or someone claiming the date of the Lord's return had been calculated. I have been afraid: if the Lord came today, would I be ready? Am I watchful enough? That fear has sometimes made me read and pray harder, and sometimes made me stop thinking about it at all. Paul did not write this passage to frighten the Thessalonians but so that they could "encourage one another." He says that to unbelievers that day comes like a thief, but not so for believers, because God's purpose for us is not wrath but salvation; and the ground of that salvation is that Jesus "died for us." I can stand before that day not because I have been watchful enough, but because he bore the wrath in my place. And if I am not even sure that I belong to him, these words are an invitation to me as well: he "died for us," for sinners; I can take refuge in him today, without waiting until I feel good enough. Today I can name my fear of that day before him, and then read this line: "He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it" (1 Thessalonians 5:24). He called me, he will keep me until he comes; and that day will be the day I see his face.

entries.content:
这卷书在讲什么

帖撒罗尼迦后书是保罗写给同一个年轻教会的第二封信，大概在第一封信之后不久写成。教会的处境并没有好转：他们仍在「所受的一切逼迫患难中」（帖后1:4）。不但如此，又有新的问题出现了。有人说「主的日子现在到了」（帖后2:2），叫信徒心里动摇惊慌；教会中也有人「什么工都不做，反倒专管闲事」（帖后3:11）。

这封信很短，只有三章，却回答了三个很实际的问题：

  • 受苦的时候，神公义吗？ 保罗说，神必在主耶稣显现的时候施行公义的审判：加患难给信徒的人要受报应，受患难的人要得平安（帖后1:5-10）。苦难不是神忘记了他们，他们的忍耐反倒是神公义判断的「明证」（帖后1:5）。
  • 主的日子已经到了吗？ 没有。在那日子以前，「必有离道反教的事，并有那大罪人，就是沉沦之子，显露出来」（帖后2:3）。主耶稣必胜过他，「用口中的气灭绝他」（帖后2:8）。所以信徒「不要轻易动心，也不要惊慌」（帖后2:2）。
  • 等候主来的时候，该怎样生活？ 不是放下工作、等着别人养活，而是「安静做工，吃自己的饭」（帖后3:12）；「行善不可丧志」（帖后3:13）。

整封信的根基不是信徒的刚强，而是神的信实：「但主是信实的，要坚固你们，保护你们脱离那恶者。」（帖后3:3）

作者与写作背景

1. 写信的人和时间。 信的开头和第一封信几乎一样：「保罗、西拉、提摩太写信给帖撒罗尼迦……的教会」（帖后1:1）。三位同工仍在一起，这与徒18:5记载他们同在哥林多相合。所以多数学者认为，这封信也是在哥林多写的，大约在主后50-51年，离第一封信只有几个月。

  • 先后次序： 少数学者（如查尔斯·瓦纳梅克）认为这封信其实比前书更早。但多数人认为，本书2:15提到「信上写的」，很可能就是指前书；而且本书讲主的日子，像是在澄清前书4-5章引起的误会。本研读采用通常的次序。

2. 作者问题。 初期教会一致接受这封信是保罗写的。信中也两次提到保罗的书信：一次警告有人「冒我名」写信（帖后2:2），一次说保罗亲笔问安，「凡我的信都以此为记」（帖后3:17）。

  • 怀疑的看法： 从十九世纪初起（最早是1801年的施密特），有些学者（如威廉·弗雷德、沃尔夫冈·特里林）认为这是保罗死后有人托名写的。他们的理由主要有三：这封信和前书的用词、结构太相像，像是照着前书模仿的；语气比前书冷淡、正式；讲末世的方式似乎和前书不同，前书说主来得像贼一样突然（帖前5:2），这封信却列出主的日子以前必有的事。
  • 支持保罗为作者的看法： 多数福音派学者和不少其他学者（如亚伯拉罕·马勒布、戈登·费依、杰弗里·韦玛）认为是保罗写的。他们回答说：同一个人在几个月之内写信给同一个教会，用词相像是很自然的；语气比较严肃，是因为有人在传错误的教训，又有人不肯做工；至于末世的说法，耶稣自己也同时讲过「那日子，那时辰，没有人知道」（太24:36），又讲过在那以前必有的事（太24:4-28）。两种说法本来就并存。
  • 本研读的立场： 照信本身所说的（帖后1:1；帖后3:17），把它当作保罗的书信来读。

3. 教会遇到的问题。

  • 逼迫： 和前书一样，信徒因为信主受苦（帖后1:4-7）。
  • 错误的末世教训： 有人宣称「主的日子现在到了」。这话可能来自自称从灵来的启示，可能来自某人的讲论，也可能来自一封「冒我名的书信」（帖后2:2）。有人认为，这些人以为主的日子已经在属灵上来到了，或者把眼前的逼迫当作末日大灾难已经开始；保罗没有细说，只是说：那日子还没有到。
  • 不肯做工的人： 有人「不按规矩而行，什么工都不做」（帖后3:11）。许多解经家认为，这和错误的末世热潮有关：既然主的日子到了，何必还要工作？也有学者（如布鲁斯·温特）认为，背后是当时恩主与门客的社会制度：一些人宁可作有钱人的门客，也不愿亲手做工。两种原因也可能同时存在。
钥匙经文：2:1-2；3:3

1. 「论到我们主耶稣基督降临和我们到他那里聚集」。 保罗没有否认主要再来，也没有否认信徒要「到他那里聚集」（参帖前4:17）。他所纠正的，不是盼望本身，而是对时间的错误说法。盼望是真的；只是那日子还没有到。

2. 「不要轻易动心，也不要惊慌」。 「动心」原文是摇动、被摇松的意思，有解经家比作船被冲离了停泊的地方；「惊慌」是心里起了骚乱。错误的末世教训常常不是叫人更爱主，而是叫人惧怕、焦虑，甚至放下日常的责任。保罗说：不要被这样的话摇动。

3. 「但主是信实的」。 在帖后3:2保罗刚说「人不都是有信心」，接着就说「但主是信实的」。人的信心会有不足，人的话也会骗人；但主是信实的。他「要坚固你们，保护你们脱离那恶者」。信徒能站稳，最终是因为主的信实，不是因为自己算准了日子，或分辨得比别人更精明。

全书结构

帖撒罗尼迦后书是一封书信，大致可以这样分：

  • 问安（帖后1:1-2）。
  • 在患难中感谢，神公义的审判（帖后1:3-12）：他们的信心增长，爱心充足；神必报应加患难给他们的人，使受患难的人得平安；主耶稣显现的日子，要在圣徒身上得荣耀。保罗为他们祷告，愿神看他们配得过所蒙的召。
  • 主的日子还没有到（帖后2:1-12）：先有离道反教的事和那大罪人显露；现在有一个拦阻的；主耶稣必用口中的气灭绝那不法的人。
  • 感谢和坚固（帖后2:13-17）：神从起初拣选了他们，召他们得着主耶稣基督的荣光；要站立得稳，坚守所领受的教训。
  • 请他们代祷，主是信实的（帖后3:1-5）。
  • 不按规矩而行的人（帖后3:6-15）：效法保罗亲手做工的榜样；不肯做工的就不可吃饭；不要以他为仇人，要劝他如弟兄。
  • 祝福和亲笔问安（帖后3:16-18）。
怎样读这卷书

1. 和前书一起读。 前书安慰丧亲的人，说主必再来；后书提醒那些以为主的日子已经到了的人，说那日子还没有到。两封信合起来，帮助我们既热切地盼望，又安静地生活。

2. 读帖后2:1-12时要谦卑。 这段是新约中最难解的经文之一。「那大罪人」是谁？「那拦阻的」是什么？保罗说他在帖撒罗尼迦的时候已经讲过（帖后2:5），帖撒罗尼迦人「知道」（帖后2:6），我们却没有听到那些口头的教导。奥古斯丁在《上帝之城》里坦白说，他不知道保罗所说的「拦阻的」是指什么（第二十卷第十九章）。历世历代，忠心的信徒对这些问题有不同的看法；我们可以讨论，却不必把自己的看法当作唯一的答案，更不要用它来推算日期，或把它套在某个政治人物身上。

3. 留意经文的目的。 保罗讲末世，不是为了让人画出时间表，而是为了叫人「不要轻易动心」（帖后2:2），叫人「站立得稳」（帖后2:15），叫人在患难中仍有「永远的安慰并美好的盼望」（帖后2:16）。读的时候，可以问：这段经文要我怎样信靠主、怎样生活？

4. 留意神的公义和神的恩典。 第一章讲神公义的审判，说得很严肃；但同一章也说，一切都是「照着我们的神并主耶稣基督的恩」（帖后1:12）。第二章讲那些「不领受爱真理的心」的人被定罪，紧接着就说「主所爱的弟兄们哪……他从起初拣选了你们」（帖后2:13）。信徒得救，不是因为比别人好，而是因为神的爱和拣选。

5. 留意工作和教会生活。 第三章看起来很平常：做工、吃饭、不要管闲事。但这正是保罗对末世热潮的回答。盼望主来的人，不是不食人间烟火，而是在平凡的工作中忠心，在教会里彼此劝勉。

默想

默想： 「论到我们主耶稣基督降临和我们到他那里聚集……不要轻易动心，也不要惊慌。」（帖后2:1-2）帖撒罗尼迦的信徒听到的话，好像有属灵的来源，甚至好像出自使徒本人。今天也常有这样的说法传到我耳边：某件时事被说成应验了启示录的某段经文，某位传道人排出了末日的时间表。老实说，吸引我的有时不是主自己，而是那种我比别人先知道的感觉；我花在谈论「那大罪人」是谁的时间，也许比我和那位要来的主说话的时间还多。这些说法叫我兴奋一阵，过一段时间又叫我失望，有的甚至叫我觉得眼前的工作、学业和家人都不那么要紧了。保罗没有给帖撒罗尼迦人一个更准确的时间表。他提醒他们，盼望的中心不是什么时候，而是「到他那里」（帖后2:1）：我们等候的是一位主，不是一个日期。这位主不是靠我解开记号来讨他喜悦的。他为我死而复活；那「爱我们、开恩将永远的安慰并美好的盼望赐给我们的父神」（帖后2:16），已经藉着他把这盼望白白给了我。所以，即使我曾被这些说法推着走，把心思放错了地方，也不必再被它们摇动。我所等候的，是那位已经爱了我的主。
entries.content_en:
What This Book Is About

2 Thessalonians is Paul's second letter to the same young church, probably written not long after the first. Their situation had not improved: they were still enduring "all your persecutions and... the afflictions" (2 Thessalonians 1:4). And new problems had appeared. Some were saying that "the day of the Lord has come" (2 Thessalonians 2:2), leaving believers shaken and alarmed; and some in the church were "not busy at work, but busybodies" (2 Thessalonians 3:11).

The letter is short, only three chapters, but it answers three very practical questions:

  • When we suffer, is God just? Paul says God will bring righteous judgment when the Lord Jesus is revealed: those who afflict believers will be repaid, and the afflicted will receive relief (2 Thessalonians 1:5–10). Suffering does not mean God has forgotten them; their endurance is in fact "evidence of the righteous judgment of God" (2 Thessalonians 1:5).
  • Has the day of the Lord already come? No. Before that day, "the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction" (2 Thessalonians 2:3). The Lord Jesus will overcome him and "kill with the breath of his mouth" (2 Thessalonians 2:8). So believers are "not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed" (2 Thessalonians 2:2).
  • How should we live while we wait for the Lord? Not by laying down our work and waiting for others to support us, but by doing our "work quietly" and earning our "own living" (2 Thessalonians 3:12), and by not growing "weary in doing good" (2 Thessalonians 3:13).

The foundation of the whole letter is not the believers' strength but God's faithfulness: "But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one" (2 Thessalonians 3:3).

Author and Setting

1. Writers and date. The opening is almost identical to the first letter: "Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians" (2 Thessalonians 1:1). The three co-workers are still together, which fits Acts 18:5, where they are together in Corinth. So most scholars think this letter too was written from Corinth, around AD 50–51, only a few months after the first.

  • Which came first? A few scholars (such as Charles Wanamaker) think this letter was actually written before "1 Thessalonians." But most hold that when 2 Thessalonians 2:15 mentions "our letter" it very likely means 1 Thessalonians, and that this letter's teaching on the day of the Lord reads like a correction of misunderstandings that grew out of 1 Thessalonians 4–5. This study follows the usual order.

2. The question of authorship. The early church received this letter unanimously as Paul's. The letter itself twice refers to Paul's letters: once warning about "a letter seeming to be from us" (2 Thessalonians 2:2), and once saying Paul writes the greeting with his own hand, "the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine" (2 Thessalonians 3:17).

  • The doubting view: since the early nineteenth century (beginning with J. E. C. Schmidt in 1801), some scholars (such as William Wrede and Wolfgang Trilling) have argued that someone wrote it in Paul's name after his death. Their main reasons are three: its wording and structure are so close to 1 Thessalonians that it looks like an imitation; its tone is cooler and more formal; and its way of speaking about the end seems different, since 1 Thessalonians says the Lord comes suddenly, like a thief (1 Thess 5:2), while this letter lists things that must happen before the day of the Lord.
  • The view that Paul wrote it: most evangelical scholars and many others (such as Abraham Malherbe, Gordon Fee and Jeffrey Weima) hold that Paul wrote it. They reply that one person writing to the same church within a few months would naturally use similar wording; that the more serious tone fits a church where false teaching was spreading and some refused to work; and that on the end, Jesus himself said both that "concerning that day and hour no one knows" (Matt 24:36) and that certain things must come first (Matt 24:4–28). The two kinds of statement stand side by side.
  • This study's position: we read it as Paul's letter, as it presents itself (2 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 3:17).

3. The church's problems.

  • Persecution: as in the first letter, believers were suffering for their faith (2 Thessalonians 1:4–7).
  • False teaching about the end: some were claiming that "the day of the Lord has come." This may have come from a claimed revelation "by a spirit," from someone's "spoken word," or from "a letter seeming to be from us" (2 Thessalonians 2:2). Some think these people understood the day of the Lord as having already come in a spiritual sense, or took the persecution they faced as the start of the final tribulation. Paul does not explain in detail; he simply says the day has not yet come.
  • Those who would not work: some "walk in idleness, not busy at work" (2 Thessalonians 3:11). Many commentators link this with the mistaken end-time excitement: if the day of the Lord has come, why keep working? Some scholars (such as Bruce Winter) point instead to the patron–client customs of the time, in which some preferred to attach themselves to a wealthy patron rather than work with their own hands. Both causes may have been at work together.
Key Verses: 2:1–2; 3:3

1. "Concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him." Paul does not deny that the Lord will come, or that believers will be "gathered together to him" (see 1 Thess 4:17). What he corrects is not the hope itself but a false claim about its timing. The hope is true; that day simply has not come yet.

2. "Not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed." The word for "shaken" means shaken loose; some commentators compare a ship driven from its mooring; "alarmed" means inner turmoil. False teaching about the end often does not make people love the Lord more; it makes them afraid and anxious, and can even lead them to drop their daily responsibilities. Paul says: do not be shaken by such words.

3. "But the Lord is faithful." In 2 Thessalonians 3:2 Paul has just said, "not all have faith," and at once he adds, "But the Lord is faithful." Human faith can fall short, and human words can deceive, but the Lord is faithful. He "will establish you and guard you against the evil one." In the end, believers stand firm because of the Lord's faithfulness, not because they have calculated the date correctly or are shrewder at discernment than others.

The Shape of the Book

2 Thessalonians is a letter, and it can be roughly divided like this:

  • Greeting (2 Thessalonians 1:1–2).
  • Thanksgiving in affliction; God's righteous judgment (2 Thessalonians 1:3–12): their faith is growing and their love increasing; God will repay those who afflict them and grant relief to the afflicted; on the day the Lord Jesus is revealed he will be glorified in his saints. Paul prays that God will make them worthy of his calling.
  • The day of the Lord has not come (2 Thessalonians 2:1–12): first the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness; something now restrains; the Lord Jesus will kill the lawless one with the breath of his mouth.
  • Thanksgiving and strengthening (2 Thessalonians 2:13–17): God chose them to be saved and called them to obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ; they are to stand firm and hold to the traditions they were taught.
  • A request for prayer; the Lord is faithful (2 Thessalonians 3:1–5).
  • Those walking in idleness (2 Thessalonians 3:6–15): imitate Paul's example of working with his own hands; anyone not willing to work should not eat; do not regard such a person as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.
  • Blessing and greeting in Paul's own hand (2 Thessalonians 3:16–18).
How to Read This Book

1. Read it with 1 Thessalonians. The first letter comforts the grieving with the promise that the Lord will come; the second warns those who think the day of the Lord has already come that the day has not yet arrived. Together the two letters help us hope eagerly and live quietly.

2. Read 2 Thessalonians 2:1–12 humbly. This is one of the hardest passages in the New Testament. Who is "the man of lawlessness"? What is "restraining"? Paul says he told them these things while he was with them (2 Thessalonians 2:5), and the Thessalonians "know" (2 Thessalonians 2:6), but we did not hear that spoken teaching. Augustine admitted frankly in The City of God that he did not know what Paul meant by what restrains (book 20, chapter 19). Faithful believers through the centuries have held different views on these questions. We can discuss them, but we need not treat our own view as the only answer, and we must not use it to calculate dates or fit it onto some political figure.

3. Notice the purpose of the passage. Paul speaks of the end not so that people can draw up a timetable, but so that they will "not be quickly shaken" (2 Thessalonians 2:2), will "stand firm" (2 Thessalonians 2:15), and will have "eternal comfort and good hope" even in affliction (2 Thessalonians 2:16). As you read, ask: how does this passage call me to trust the Lord and to live?

4. Notice both God's justice and God's grace. Chapter 1 speaks very seriously of God's righteous judgment, yet the same chapter says all is "according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ" (2 Thessalonians 1:12). Chapter 2 speaks of the condemnation of those who "refused to love the truth," and at once says, "brothers beloved by the Lord... God chose you" (2 Thessalonians 2:13). Believers are saved not because they are better than others, but because of God's love and choosing.

5. Notice work and church life. Chapter 3 seems very ordinary: work, eat, do not meddle. But this is exactly Paul's answer to end-time excitement. People who hope for the Lord's coming do not float above ordinary life; they are faithful in ordinary work and warn and encourage one another in the church.

Meditation

Reflect: "Concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we ask you, brothers, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed" (2 Thessalonians 2:1–2). What the Thessalonians heard seemed to have a spiritual source, even to come from the apostle himself. Claims like that still reach me: some news event is said to fulfill a passage in Revelation, a preacher lays out a timetable for the end. If I am honest, what draws me is sometimes not the Lord himself but the feeling of knowing before others do; I may have spent more time discussing who "the man of lawlessness" is than talking with the Lord who is coming. These claims excite me for a season and then leave me let down, and some even make my work, my studies and my family seem not to matter much. Paul did not give the Thessalonians a better timetable. He reminded them that the center of their hope was not "when" but "to him" (2 Thessalonians 2:1): we are waiting for a person, not a date. And this person is not someone I please by decoding signs. He died and rose for me; and through him God our Father, "who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace" (2 Thessalonians 2:16), has already given me this hope as a gift. So even if I have been pushed along by such claims and set my heart on the wrong thing, I do not have to be shaken by them again. The one I am waiting for is the Lord who has already loved me.

entries.content:
本章脉络

第一章分成三段。问安（1-2节）：和前书几乎一样，只是加上恩惠、平安「从父神和主耶稣基督」而来。感谢和神公义的审判（3-10节）：保罗为他们增长的信心和充足的爱心感谢神；他们在逼迫中的忍耐，正是神公义判断的明证；主耶稣从天上显现的时候，神要报应加患难给他们的人，叫受患难的人得平安。祷告（11-12节）：愿神看他们配得过所蒙的召，用大能成就他们一切的善工，叫主耶稣的名在他们身上得荣耀。

这一章说到神的审判，说得很重；但它是写给受苦的信徒的。保罗不是要他们幸灾乐祸，而是要他们知道：神看见了，神是公义的，历史最后由主耶稣来定案。

深读 1:3-5 在逼迫中增长的信心

1. 「我们该为你们常常感谢神，这本是合宜的」。 「该」在原文这个词里带着欠债、有义务的意思。保罗不是说感谢是勉强的，而是说，看见神在他们身上的工作，不感谢就不对了。

  • 有人认为这是回应： 有些较早的解经家（如米利根、弗雷姆）认为，帖撒罗尼迦人也许谦虚地说过，自己不配得保罗在前书中那样的称赞。保罗回答说：为你们感谢神，是「合宜的」。不过这只是推测。

2. 信心增长，爱心充足。 「因你们的信心格外增长，并且你们众人彼此相爱的心也都充足」（帖后1:3）。保罗在前书曾求主叫他们的爱心「增长，充足」（帖前3:12），又想要「补满你们信心的不足」（帖前3:10）。现在他看见，神应允了那些祷告。

  • 「众人」： 不只是几个热心的人，而是「你们众人」。爱心在整个教会里充足起来。
  • 没有提盼望： 前书的开头提到信心、爱心和盼望（帖前1:3），这里只提信心和爱心。有人认为，这正是因为他们的盼望被错误的末世教训搅乱了，所以保罗在第二章要处理这个问题。不过也有许多解经家指出，第4节的「忍耐」，正和前书1:3「因盼望……所存的忍耐」相呼应，所以盼望其实也在其中。

3. 「仍旧存忍耐和信心」。 「甚至我们在神的各教会里为你们夸口，都因你们在所受的一切逼迫患难中，仍旧存忍耐和信心」（帖后1:4）。保罗不夸自己的事工，却在别的教会里夸他们。

  • 忍耐： 不是消极地咬牙忍受，而是在压力下站住、不放弃。
  • 「仍旧」： 逼迫没有停，他们的信心也没有停。

4. 「这正是神公义判断的明证」。 「这正是神公义判断的明证，叫你们可算配得神的国；你们就是为这国受苦」（帖后1:5）。「这」指什么？多数解经家认为，指他们在逼迫中的忍耐和信心。

  • 怎样是「明证」？ 有两种主要理解。一种认为，神现在藉着苦难炼净他们，这就显出神的判断是公义的：他正在预备他们进入他的国（参彼前4:17）。另一种认为，他们在苦难中仍有信心，这本身就是神工作的记号，证明将来神在审判的日子会判他们为义、接纳他们（参腓1:28）。两种理解都把重点放在神身上，不是放在他们的功劳上。
  • 「可算配得」： 不是说他们靠受苦赚到了神的国，而是说神「算」他们为配得。神的国是白白赐的恩典，受苦是往这国去的人必经的路（参徒14:22）。
要点：信徒在逼迫中仍旧存着信心，不是因为自己特别刚强，而是神在他们里面做工。这样的忍耐本身就在宣告：神是公义的，神没有忘记他们。
深读 1:6-10 神公义的审判

1. 「神既是公义的」。 「神既是公义的，就必将患难报应那加患难给你们的人，也必使你们这受患难的人与我们同得平安」（帖后1:6-7）。这里讲的是公义的报应：叫加患难的人受患难，叫受患难的人得安息。

  • 「平安」： 原文是放松、解脱的意思，好像弓弦松开，或者重担卸下。
  • 「与我们同得」： 保罗自己也在患难中。他不是站在远处安慰人，而是和他们一同等候。

2. 伸冤在神。 这段经文不是叫信徒自己报复，而是叫他们把伸冤的事交给神。保罗在罗马书说：「亲爱的弟兄，不要自己伸冤，宁可让步，听凭主怒」，因为主说：「伸冤在我，我必报应。」（罗12:19；参申32:35）正因为神必定公义地审判，信徒才可以不自己报仇，还可以为逼迫他们的人祷告（参太5:44）。

  • 这不是叫人沉默： 把最终的伸冤交给神，不是说受了欺压、虐待或犯罪伤害的人不可以报警，或不可以寻求法律的保护。保罗在罗13:4说，在上掌权的是「神的用人，是伸冤的，刑罚那作恶的」。向警察和法庭举报罪行是对的；受害的人不必留在危险中，也不必勉强和仍然不安全的人和好；饶恕也不等于让加害的人恢复原有的职分，或让他再接近受害人和孩子；教会更不可以为了面子，把这样的事压下来（「家丑不可外扬」）。

3. 「主耶稣……从天上在火焰中显现」。 「那时，主耶稣同他有能力的天使从天上在火焰中显现，要报应那不认识神和那不听从我主耶稣福音的人」（帖后1:7-8）。这里的描写，用的是旧约描写耶和华降临的语言：「看哪，耶和华必在火中降临……以火焰施行责罚」（赛66:15）。保罗把旧约里耶和华的作为，直接归给主耶稣。

  • 耶稣是审判的主： 那位曾经被人审判、被钉十字架的耶稣，将来要作审判全地的主（参徒17:31；约5:22）。
  • 两种人还是一种人？ 「不认识神的」和「不听从……福音的」，有人认为是两种人：前者指外邦人，后者指犹太人。但多数解经家认为，这是希伯来诗歌常用的平行句，说的是同一群人：拒绝神、不肯顺服福音的人。
  • 「不认识神」： 这是旧约描写列国的说法（参耶10:25「愿你将忿怒倾在不认识你的列国中」；帖前4:5）。这不是说人因为无知就无罪，而是说人压抑了对神的认识，不肯归荣耀给他（罗1:20-21、28）。这里首先是指那些听过福音却敌挡福音、逼迫信徒的人，但不只限于他们。

4. 「永远沉沦，离开主的面」。 「他们要受刑罚，就是永远沉沦，离开主的面和他权能的荣光」（帖后1:9）。这是新约中论到最后审判最严肃的经文之一。

  • 「永远沉沦」： 多数解经家认为，「沉沦」（原文的意思是毁灭、败坏）在这里不是指不再存在，而是指彻底的毁坏和失丧；保罗用同一个词时，也不是指人不再存在（参帖前5:3；林前5:5）。「永远」和太25:46的「永刑」相对照（「这些人要往永刑里去」），说明这刑罚没有尽头。教会历来的主流教导（如奥古斯丁、加尔文、乔纳森·爱德华兹，今天的巴刻、卡森），都认为不信的人要永远清醒地承受神的刑罚。也有少数福音派学者（如爱德华·富奇；约翰·斯托得也曾有保留地提出）主张有条件不朽论（又称灭绝论），认为不信的人最后会被灭绝，「永远」是指结果永远不能挽回。多数福音派神学家认为，这种看法很难与太25:46等经文相合。
  • 「离开主的面」： 这句话几乎是逐字引用赛2:10、19、21的希腊文译本。原文的介词可以理解为离开，也可以理解为从……而来。若是前者，地狱的可怕在于永远与主恩惠的同在和荣光隔绝（参太7:23「你们这些作恶的人，离开我去吧」），这不是说神不在那里（参启14:10）；若是后者，刑罚是从主的面前、从他权能的荣光发出来的（参赛2:10）。和合本和多数英文译本采取前一种理解。
  • 为什么要这样说？ 不是为了吓唬人，而是因为这是真的。保罗说这话，是要信徒知道罪恶不会得胜，也要我们看见拒绝福音的人面对的是什么。我们能免去这审判，不是因为我们比逼迫信徒的人好，而是因为主耶稣在十字架上替我们承受了神的忿怒（帖前1:10；帖前5:9-10；加3:13）。如果你读到这里，知道自己还没有投靠基督，这段话不是要把你推开，而是一个出于爱的警告。那位将来「在火焰中显现」的主，就是曾经为罪人被审判、被钉十字架的耶稣；他今天仍然说：「凡劳苦担重担的人可以到我这里来。」（太11:28）你不必等到自己变好了才来。「看哪，现在正是悦纳的时候！现在正是拯救的日子」（林后6:2）。

5. 「在他圣徒的身上得荣耀」。 「这正是主降临、要在他圣徒的身上得荣耀、又在一切信的人身上显为希奇的那日子」（帖后1:10）。同一日，对不信的人是审判，对信徒却是荣耀的日子。

  • 耶稣在圣徒身上得荣耀： 主来的那一天，最奇妙的不是信徒自己有多好。一切信的人看着这群曾经软弱、受苦、跌倒的人，都要惊叹：主耶稣做了何等的事！
  • 「我们对你们作的见证，你们也信了」： 帖撒罗尼迦人能在那日站在主的一边，原因很简单：他们信了福音。不是因为他们的功劳，而是因为他们领受了关于耶稣的见证。
要点：神必公义地审判，罪恶和逼迫不会得到最后的胜利。所以信徒可以把伸冤交给神，也可以寻求正当的保护。对不信的人，这是严肃的警告，也是今天仍然敞开的邀请；对信的人，那日子是主耶稣在他们身上得荣耀的日子。
深读 1:11-12 配得过所蒙的召

1. 「因此，我们常为你们祷告」。 保罗讲完将来的日子，立刻回到现在：为他们祷告。他不是只叫他们等候，而是求神在等候的日子里在他们身上做工。

2. 「愿我们的神看你们配得过所蒙的召」。 「配得过」的意思，和第5节一样，不是说他们要靠自己的表现赚得神的召，而是求神「看」他们配得，也可以理解为求神使他们配得（原文这个词两种意思都可以）。神召了他们，神也要成全他们（参腓1:6「那在你们心里动了善工的，必成全这工」）。

3. 「用大能成就你们一切所羡慕的良善」。 「又用大能成就你们一切所羡慕的良善和一切因信心所做的工夫」（帖后1:11）。

  • 「所羡慕的良善」： 原文指心里的立志、渴望。信徒心里想要行善，这本身就是神的工作；但光有心愿还不够，保罗求神「用大能成就」。
  • 「因信心所做的工夫」： 和帖前1:3是同一个说法。信心不是空的，会做出工夫来；但这工夫也要靠神的大能。
  • 神的大能： 我们想做的善事常常做不成，或者半途而废。保罗不是叫他们更加努力，而是为他们祷告：愿神用他的大能完成他们所不能完成的。

4. 「都照着我们的神并主耶稣基督的恩」。 「叫我们主耶稣的名在你们身上得荣耀，你们也在他身上得荣耀，都照着我们的神并主耶稣基督的恩」（帖后1:12）。

  • 彼此得荣耀： 主耶稣在信徒身上得荣耀，信徒也在他身上得荣耀。这荣耀今天已经开始，到主来的那日要完全显明（帖后1:10）。
  • 「照着……恩」： 整个祷告的根基是恩典。被召、配得、行善、得荣耀，没有一样是靠人自己的。
  • 一个原文的问题： 「我们的神并主耶稣基督」在原文中，有人认为可以读成我们的神和主，就是耶稣基督，指同一位（参多2:13；彼后1:1）。但多数解经家（如丹尼尔·华莱士、默里·哈里斯）认为，保罗书信里「主耶稣基督」常常连成一个固定的称号，所以仍是指父和子两位。无论哪一种，保罗都把父和子并列为恩典的源头。
要点：神召我们，也要成全我们。我们心里向善的渴望，和因信心所做的工夫，都要靠神的大能才能完成；这一切都是照着恩典，为要叫主耶稣的名得荣耀。
默想

默想： 「愿我们的神看你们配得过所蒙的召，又用大能成就你们一切所羡慕的良善和一切因信心所做的工夫。」（帖后1:11）我心里曾经有过一些向善的心愿：想和一位疏远的家人重新说话，想每个星期陪孩子读一段圣经，想去探望一位长期卧病的弟兄，想在教会里接下一件一直没有人做的小服事。有些我开始过，后来停了；有些我连开始都没有。时间久了，这些心愿就变成了心里的一份清单，每次想起来都觉得惭愧，最后干脆不去想了。我以为，问题只在于我不够努力。可是保罗没有叫帖撒罗尼迦人更努力，而是为他们祷告：愿神「用大能成就」他们所羡慕的良善。这些心愿里凡是真正向善的，本来就是神放在我心里的；那位把心愿放进我心里的，也能用他的大能把它成全。今天，我可以把那份清单拿出来，不是为了再一次责备自己，而是把它带到神面前，求他照他的恩典做成。保罗这样求，目的也不只是叫我不再惭愧，而是「叫我们主耶稣的名在你们身上得荣耀」（帖后1:12）：主要在我这个常常半途而废的人身上，显出他的恩典有多大。我也不必等到这些都做好了，才相信自己「配得过」神的召；配得过的原因不在我，而在那位为我舍命、如今在父面前为我代求的主耶稣。保罗说，这一切「都照着我们的神并主耶稣基督的恩」（帖后1:12）。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 1 falls into three parts. Greeting (vv. 1–2): almost the same as in the first letter, except that grace and peace now come "from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." Thanksgiving and God's righteous judgment (vv. 3–10): Paul thanks God for their growing faith and increasing love; their endurance under persecution is evidence of God's righteous judgment; when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven, God will repay those who afflict them and grant relief to the afflicted. Prayer (vv. 11–12): may God make them worthy of his calling, fulfill every work of faith by his power, and glorify the name of the Lord Jesus in them.

This chapter speaks heavily of God's judgment, but it is written to suffering believers. Paul does not want them to gloat; he wants them to know that God has seen, that God is just, and that the last word in history belongs to the Lord Jesus.

Going Deeper: 1:3–5 Faith That Grows Under Persecution

1. "We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right." "Ought" carries the sense of a debt or obligation. Paul does not mean that thanksgiving is grudging; he means that, having seen God's work in them, it would be wrong not to give thanks.

  • Perhaps a reply: some older commentators (such as Milligan and Frame) suggested the Thessalonians may have humbly said they did not deserve the praise Paul gave them in the first letter, and Paul answers that giving thanks for them is "right." But this is only a guess.

2. Faith growing, love increasing. "Because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing" (2 Thessalonians 1:3). In the first letter Paul prayed that the Lord would make their love "increase and abound" (1 Thess 3:12), and longed to "supply what is lacking in your faith" (1 Thess 3:10). Now he sees that God has answered those prayers.

  • "Every one of you": not just a few zealous members, but "every one of you." Love is increasing throughout the church.
  • Hope not mentioned: the first letter opens with faith, love and hope (1 Thess 1:3); here only faith and love are named. Some think this is because their hope had been unsettled by false teaching about the end, which Paul takes up in chapter 2. But many commentators note that "steadfastness" in verse 4 echoes the "steadfastness of hope" of 1 Thessalonians 1:3, so hope is not wholly absent.

3. "Your steadfastness and faith." "Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring" (2 Thessalonians 1:4). Paul does not boast about his own ministry; he boasts about them to other churches.

  • Steadfastness: not passive teeth-gritting, but standing firm under pressure and not giving up.
  • "That you are enduring": the persecution had not stopped, and neither had their faith.

4. "This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God." "This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering" (2 Thessalonians 1:5). What does "this" refer to? Most commentators take it as their steadfastness and faith under persecution.

  • Evidence in what sense? There are two main readings. One holds that God is now refining them through suffering, which shows that his judgment is right: he is preparing them for his kingdom (see 1 Pet 4:17). The other holds that their faith in suffering is itself a sign of God's work, proving that on the day of judgment God will vindicate and welcome them (see Phil 1:28). Both readings put the weight on God, not on their merit.
  • "Considered worthy": this does not mean they earned the kingdom by suffering, but that God "considers" them worthy. The kingdom of God is a free gift of grace; suffering is what those on the road to that kingdom will meet (see Acts 14:22).
The point: Believers keep their faith under persecution not because they are especially strong, but because God is at work in them. Such endurance itself declares that God is just and has not forgotten them.
Going Deeper: 1:6–10 God's Righteous Judgment

1. "God considers it just." "Since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us" (2 Thessalonians 1:6–7). This is just recompense: affliction for those who afflict, rest for the afflicted.

  • "Relief": the word means loosening, release, like a bowstring slackened or a heavy load set down.
  • "As well as to us": Paul too is suffering. He does not comfort them from a distance; he waits with them.

2. Vengeance belongs to God. This passage does not tell believers to take revenge themselves; it tells them to leave vengeance to God. As Paul writes in Romans: "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord'" (Rom 12:19; see Deut 32:35). Precisely because God will surely judge justly, believers can refrain from revenge, and can even pray for those who persecute them (see Matt 5:44).

  • This is not a call to silence: leaving final vengeance to God does not mean that people who suffer oppression, abuse or criminal harm may not go to the police or seek the protection of the law. In Romans 13:4 Paul says the governing authority is "the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer." Reporting crime to the police and the courts is right; victims need not stay in danger, nor force themselves to reconcile with someone who is still unsafe; forgiveness does not restore an offender's office or give him access again to victims or children; and the church must never hush such things up to save face (「家丑不可外扬」, "do not air the family's dirty laundry").

3. "The Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven... in flaming fire." "When the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus" (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). The description uses the Old Testament language for the LORD's coming: "For behold, the LORD will come in fire... and his rebuke with flames of fire" (Isa 66:15). Paul assigns directly to the Lord Jesus what the Old Testament says of the LORD.

  • Jesus is the Lord who judges: the Jesus who was once judged by men and crucified will judge the whole earth (see Acts 17:31; John 5:22).
  • Two groups or one? Some take "those who do not know God" and "those who do not obey the gospel" as two groups, Gentiles and Jews. But most commentators see a Hebrew-style parallelism describing one group: those who reject God and refuse to obey the gospel.
  • "Do not know God": this is an Old Testament phrase for the nations (see Jer 10:25, "Pour out your wrath on the nations that know you not"; 1 Thess 4:5). It does not mean that ignorance makes people innocent, but that people suppress what they know of God and refuse to give him glory (Rom 1:20–21, 28). Here those who persecute believers, who have heard the gospel and opposed it, are first in view, but the phrase is not limited to them.

4. "Eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord." "They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might" (2 Thessalonians 1:9). This is one of the most solemn statements about final judgment in the New Testament.

  • "Eternal destruction": most interpreters take "destruction" (olethros) here not as ceasing to exist but as utter ruin and loss, since Paul uses the same word elsewhere without that sense (1 Thess 5:3; 1 Cor 5:5); and "eternal," read alongside Matthew 25:46 ("these will go away into eternal punishment"), means the punishment has no end. The church's mainstream teaching through history (Augustine, Calvin, Jonathan Edwards, and today J. I. Packer and D. A. Carson) has understood this as people remaining consciously under God's judgment forever. A minority of evangelical scholars (John Stott, tentatively, and Edward Fudge) hold to "conditional immortality," the view that unbelievers will in the end be destroyed, with "eternal" meaning the result can never be reversed. Most evangelical theologians judge that this view is hard to square with texts such as Matthew 25:46.
  • "Away from the presence": this phrase almost word for word echoes the Greek of Isaiah 2:10, 19, 21. The Greek preposition can mean "away from" or "from" in the sense of "coming from." On the first reading, the horror of hell is being shut out forever from the Lord's gracious presence and glory (not that God is absent there; see Rev 14:10) (see Matt 7:23, "depart from me, you workers of lawlessness"); on the second, the punishment goes out from the Lord's presence, from the glory of his might (see Isa 2:10). The CUV and most English versions take the first reading.
  • Why say this? Not to frighten people, but because it is true. Paul says it so that believers know evil will not win, and so that we see what those who reject the gospel face. We escape this judgment not because we are better than those who persecute believers, but because on the cross the Lord Jesus bore God's wrath in our place (1 Thess 1:10; 1 Thess 5:9–10; Gal 3:13). If you are reading this and know that you have not yet put your trust in Christ, these words are not meant to push you away; they are a warning given in love. The Lord who will be "revealed... in flaming fire" is the same Jesus who was judged and crucified for sinners, and today he still says, "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden" (Matt 11:28). You do not need to become better first: "Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor 6:2).

5. "To be glorified in his saints." "When he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed" (2 Thessalonians 1:10). The same day is judgment for unbelievers and glory for believers.

  • Jesus glorified in his saints: the wonder of that day will not be how good believers are, but that, looking at these once-weak, suffering, stumbling people, all who have believed will marvel at what the Lord Jesus has done.
  • "Because our testimony to you was believed": the Thessalonians will stand on the Lord's side on that day for a simple reason: they believed the gospel. Not because of their merit, but because they received the testimony about Jesus.
The point: God will judge justly; evil and persecution will not have the last word. So believers can leave vengeance to God, and can also seek rightful protection. For unbelievers this is a solemn warning, and an invitation still open today; for believers that day is the day the Lord Jesus is glorified in them.
Going Deeper: 1:11–12 Worthy of His Calling

1. "To this end we always pray for you." Having spoken of the coming day, Paul turns at once to the present: he prays for them. He does not simply tell them to wait; he asks God to work in them while they wait.

2. "That our God may make you worthy of his calling." "Worthy," as in verse 5, does not mean they must earn God's call by their performance; Paul asks God to "make" them worthy (the word can mean "count worthy" or "make worthy"). God called them, and God will complete them (see Phil 1:6, "he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion").

3. "May fulfill every resolve for good." "And may fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power" (2 Thessalonians 1:11).

  • "Resolve for good": the word means a desire or purpose of the heart. That believers want to do good is itself God's work; but desire alone is not enough, so Paul asks God to "fulfill" it "by his power."
  • "Work of faith": the same phrase as 1 Thessalonians 1:3. Faith is not empty; it produces work. But this work too depends on God's power.
  • God's power: the good we want to do often goes undone, or is abandoned halfway. Paul does not tell them to try harder; he prays that God by his power will complete what they cannot.

4. "According to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ." "So that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ" (2 Thessalonians 1:12).

  • Glory both ways: the Lord Jesus is glorified in believers, and believers in him. This exchange of glory begins today and is completed on the day the Lord comes (2 Thessalonians 1:10).
  • "According to... grace": the whole prayer rests on grace. Being called, being made worthy, doing good, being glorified: none of it rests on us.
  • A question in the Greek: some think "our God and the Lord Jesus Christ" could be read as "our God and Lord, Jesus Christ," referring to one person (compare Titus 2:13; 2 Pet 1:1). But most commentators (such as Daniel Wallace and Murray Harris) think that "Lord Jesus Christ" works here as a proper name, so that the phrase still refers to two persons, Father and Son. Either way, Paul names Father and Son together as the source of grace.
The point: God calls us, and God will complete us. Our heart's desire for good, and the work that faith produces, can be completed only by God's power; all of it is according to grace, so that the name of the Lord Jesus may be glorified.
Meditation

Reflect: "That our God may make you worthy of his calling and may fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power" (2 Thessalonians 1:11). There have been good desires in my heart: to start speaking again with a family member I have drifted from, to read a passage of Scripture with my children every week, to visit a brother who has been ill for a long time, to take up some small task at church that no one has done for a long time. Some of these I started and then stopped; some I never started at all. Over time they have become a list in my heart, and every time I think of it I feel ashamed, until in the end I stop thinking about it. I assumed the only problem was that I had not tried hard enough. But Paul did not tell the Thessalonians to try harder. He prayed for them, that God would "fulfill" their resolves for good "by his power." Whatever in these desires is truly good was put in my heart by God in the first place, and the one who put it there can complete it by his power. Today I can take out that list, not to accuse myself once more, but to bring it before God and ask him to accomplish it according to his grace. And Paul's aim in praying this is not only that I stop feeling ashamed, but "that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you" (2 Thessalonians 1:12): the Lord means to show, in someone who so often gives up halfway, how great his grace is. Nor do I have to wait until all of it is done before I believe I am "worthy" of God's calling. The reason I am made worthy is not in me, but in the Lord Jesus, who gave his life for me and now intercedes for me before the Father. All of this, Paul says, is "according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ" (2 Thessalonians 1:12).

verse_parts.text: 我劝你们：无论有灵、有言语、有冒我名的书信，说主的日子现在到了，不要轻易动心，也不要惊慌。
主所爱的弟兄们哪，我们本该常为你们感谢神；因为他从起初拣选了你们，叫你们因信真道，又被圣灵感动，成为圣洁，能以得救。神藉我们所传的福音召你们到这地步，好得着我们主耶稣基督的荣光。
但愿我们主耶稣基督和那爱我们、开恩将永远的安慰并美好的盼望赐给我们的父神，安慰你们的心，并且在一切善行善言上坚固你们。
