本章脉络

第二章是全封信的中心，分成两大段。主的日子还没有到（1-12节）：有人说主的日子现在到了，保罗劝他们不要动心惊慌；那日子以前，必有离道反教的事，并有那大罪人显露；现在有一个拦阻的，等到拦阻的被除去，那不法的人才显露；主耶稣必用口中的气灭绝他；那些不领受爱真理之心的人，要被虚谎迷惑。感谢、劝勉和祷告（13-17节）：神从起初拣选了他们，藉福音召他们得着基督的荣光；所以要站立得稳，坚守所领受的教训；愿主耶稣基督和父神安慰他们的心，在一切善行善言上坚固他们。

这一章的前半段很难，历代解经家有许多不同的看法。但它的后半段很清楚：无论末世的细节怎样，信徒的安稳在于神的拣选、神的呼召和神的安慰。读这一章，要像保罗一样，从「不法的隐意」转到「主所爱的弟兄们」。

深读 2:1-3上 不要被诱惑

1. 保罗纠正的是什么？ 「弟兄们，论到我们主耶稣基督降临和我们到他那里聚集，我劝你们：无论有灵、有言语、有冒我名的书信，说主的日子现在到了，不要轻易动心，也不要惊慌」（帖后2:1-2）。

  • 「降临」： 原文就是前书多次用的那个词（帖前2:19；帖前3:13；帖前4:15；帖前5:23），当时用来指君王驾临一座城。
  • 「聚集」： 指信徒被聚集到主那里，和帖前4:17「被提到云里，在空中与主相遇」说的是同一件事。
  • 「现在到了」： 原文的意思不是快要到了，而是已经来到、已经在这里了。

2. 错误的教训从哪里来？ 保罗列了三个可能的来源：「灵」，就是自称从圣灵来的预言；「言语」，就是某人的讲论或教导；「冒我名的书信」，就是假托保罗写的信，或者有人歪曲了保罗写过的信（参彼后3:16）。保罗不确定是哪一种，但他说，不管从哪里来，都不要相信。

  • 试验预言： 保罗在前书说：「不要藐视先知的讲论」，「但要凡事察验」（帖前5:20-21）。这里正是一个例子：一个自称是从灵来的信息，若与使徒的教训不合，就要拒绝。

3. 「人不拘用什么法子，你们总不要被他诱惑」。 「诱惑」是欺骗、引人走错路。耶稣自己也这样警告过：「你们要谨慎，免得有人迷惑你们。因为将来有好些人冒我的名来……并且要迷惑许多人」（太24:4-5）。

  • 为什么说主的日子已经到了是错的？ 这话会叫人以为，眼前的苦难就是最后的审判，主已经来了，自己却没有被聚集；也可能叫人以为，从此不必再工作，不必再过平常的生活（参帖后3:6-12）。无论哪一种，都会叫信徒失去平安，离开正路。
要点：属灵的话也要试验。凡是叫人惊慌、离开使徒教训的末世信息，不管说得多么属灵，都不要轻易相信。
深读 2:3下-8 那大罪人和那拦阻的

1. 「离道反教的事」。 「因为那日子以前，必有离道反教的事，并有那大罪人，就是沉沦之子，显露出来」（帖后2:3）。「离道反教」原文是一个词，常指背叛、叛乱。

  • 背叛谁？ 有人认为指教会中大规模的背道，许多自称信主的人离弃真道（参太24:10-12）；也有人认为指整个世界公开起来反叛神。也可能两种意思都有。
  • 和被提的次序： 这段经文也是关于被提时间争论的重要经文（参帖前4章的讨论）。持灾后被提看法的人（如乔治·赖德、道格拉斯·穆尔）和主张只有一次再来的人（如安东尼·胡克玛）指出，第1节的「聚集」和第2节的「主的日子」说的是同一件事，所以信徒被聚集到主那里，是在离道反教和那大罪人显露之后。持灾前被提看法的人（如约翰·沃尔沃德）则把第1节的「聚集」和第2-3节的「主的日子」分开，认为信徒在那日子以前已经被提。有些时代论作者（如肯尼斯·伍斯特）甚至把「离道反教」解作离开，指教会被提；但多数解经家，包括许多时代论者，都不接受这种解释，因为这个词在旧约希腊文译本和新约里都是指宗教上的背叛（参书22:22；徒21:21）。这段经文的重点不是排出时间表，而是说那日子还没有到。
  • 「那日子以前」： 原文这句话没有说完，意思是：若不先有这些事，那日子不会来到。保罗的意思很清楚：这些事还没有发生，所以主的日子还没有到。

2. 「那大罪人，就是沉沦之子」。 和合本作「大罪人」，所根据的抄本作罪的人（如亚历山大抄本和多数拜占庭抄本）。较早的抄本（如西乃抄本、梵蒂冈抄本）作不法的人，现代多数译本采用这个读法，和第7-8节的「不法的隐意」「不法的人」一致。「沉沦之子」是说他注定灭亡（参约17:12）。

  • 他的样子： 「他是抵挡主，高抬自己，超过一切称为神的和一切受人敬拜的，甚至坐在神的殿里，自称是神」（帖后2:4）。这话很像但以理书描写那位王：「王必任意而行，自高自大，超过所有的神」（但11:36）；也像以西结书对推罗王说的：「因你心里高傲，说：我是神」（结28:2）。
  • 历史的影子： 主前167年，安提阿古四世在耶路撒冷的圣殿里设立偶像的坛；主后40年，罗马皇帝卡利古拉曾下令把自己的像立在圣殿里，后来没有成功。帖撒罗尼迦人也许听说过这类事（参但9:27；但11:31；可13:14「那行毁坏可憎的」）。保罗所说的，是这种狂傲最后、最彻底的表现。

3. 「那大罪人」是谁？ 历代信徒有几种主要看法。

  • 将来的一个人： 初期教会许多教父（如爱任纽）和今天许多福音派学者认为，这是在主再来之前要出现的一个具体的人，就是约翰书信所说「那敌基督的」（约一2:18）。持这种看法的人当中，又有人认为他会在一座重建的耶路撒冷圣殿里坐下（如时代论者），有人认为「坐在神的殿里」是借用旧约的说法，表示他狂妄地自居神的地位。
  • 教会历史中的一种制度： 宗教改革时期，马丁·路德、加尔文和许多改革宗信条（如1646年的《威斯敏斯德信条》第二十五章第6节）认为，这是指罗马教皇制度，因为它坐在「神的殿」，也就是教会中，自称拥有属于神的权柄。今天大多数改革宗学者已不这样确指。美国北长老会在1903年修订信条时删去了这句话；今天美国的正统长老会和美洲长老会所用的版本也没有这句话。
  • 已经过去的人物： 过去论者认为，这是指主后70年以前的人物或势力，比如攻陷耶路撒冷、毁灭圣殿的罗马人。但保罗说主耶稣要「用降临的荣光废掉他」（帖后2:8），这很难与主后70年的事件相合，所以多数学者不接受这种看法。
  • 共同之处： 无论哪一种看法，都同意几件事：邪恶会在历史的最后集中地显露；它的本质是人想坐在神的位置上；它最后必被主耶稣毁灭。约翰也说「现在已经有好些敌基督的出来了」（约一2:18），所以这种狂傲的灵今天已经在运行。

4. 「那拦阻的」。 「现在你们也知道，那拦阻他的是什么，是叫他到了的时候才可以显露。因为那不法的隐意已经发动，只是现在有一个拦阻的，等到那拦阻的被除去，那时这不法的人必显露出来」（帖后2:6-8）。保罗在第6节用中性（「那拦阻……的是什么」），在第7节用阳性（「有一个拦阻的」），所以拦阻的可能既是一种力量，又与一个位格有关。

  • 罗马帝国和法律秩序： 初期教会许多人（如特土良、屈梭多模）认为，这是指罗马帝国，或者更广地说，指政府和法律维持的秩序（参罗13:1-4）。只要还有秩序，不法就不能完全显露。
  • 圣灵或教会： 许多时代论者（如约翰·沃尔沃德）认为，这是指圣灵藉着教会在世上的工作；「被除去」就是教会被提，然后不法的人才显露。这种看法常常与灾前被提的看法连在一起。批评的人指出，很难说圣灵会「被除去」；持这看法的人回答说，被除去的不是无所不在的圣灵，而是他住在教会里、藉着教会所做的拦阻工作。
  • 福音的传扬： 有些学者（如奥斯卡·库尔曼）认为，这是指福音的传扬，甚至指保罗本人的宣教，因为耶稣说「这天国的福音要传遍天下……然后末期才来到」（太24:14）。
  • 天使长米迦勒： 也有学者（如科林·尼科尔）根据但以理书10章和12章，认为这是指保护神子民的天使长米迦勒。
  • 神自己： 也有人认为，拦阻的就是神，或者神的旨意；无论用什么方法，都是神在掌管时间。
  • 奥古斯丁的谦卑： 奥古斯丁坦白承认他不知道保罗指的是什么。帖撒罗尼迦人「知道」，因为保罗口头讲过（帖后2:5）；我们没有听到，所以要谦卑。最重要的一点却很清楚：那不法的人要等到「到了的时候」才可以显露，而这时候是神所定的。

5. 「主耶稣要用口中的气灭绝他」。 「那时这不法的人必显露出来。主耶稣要用口中的气灭绝他，用降临的荣光废掉他」（帖后2:8）。保罗用很长的篇幅描写那不法的人，却只用一句话写他的结局：主耶稣只要一口气，就把他灭绝了。

  • 旧约的背景： 以赛亚论到大卫的后裔说：「以口中的杖击打世界，以嘴里的气杀戮恶人。」（赛11:4）主耶稣就是那位弥赛亚王（参启19:15）。
  • 不是两个势均力敌的对手： 那不法的人虽然狂傲，却不是神的对手。主耶稣「降临的荣光」一显现，他就被废掉了。
要点：保罗讲那大罪人，不是为了叫我们惧怕，也不是为了叫我们去猜他是谁，而是为了告诉我们：主的日子还没有到；邪恶什么时候显露，在神手中；主耶稣一口气就能灭绝那不法的人。
深读 2:9-12 不领受爱真理的心

1. 撒但的运动。 「这不法的人来，是照撒但的运动，行各样的异能、神迹，和一切虚假的奇事，并且在那沉沦的人身上行各样出于不义的诡诈」（帖后2:9-10）。

  • 「来」： 原文和第8节主耶稣的「降临」是同一个词。那不法的人有他自己的「降临」，是假冒的、模仿的。
  • 虚假的神迹： 神迹本身不能证明信息是真的。耶稣也说：「假基督、假先知将要起来，显大神迹、大奇事，倘若能行，连选民也就迷惑了」（太24:24）。撒但也会「装作光明的天使」（林后11:14）。

2. 「因他们不领受爱真理的心」。 「因他们不领受爱真理的心，使他们得救。」（帖后2:10）意思是：他们不肯领受那能叫他们得救的、爱真理的心。他们沉沦的原因，不是没有机会认识真理，而是不肯爱真理。

  • 爱真理： 保罗说的不只是知道真理，而是爱真理。人可以知道很多关于神的事，心里却不爱他，宁可相信自己想听的话（参提后4:3-4）。
  • 真理就是一位主： 耶稣说：「我就是道路、真理、生命。」（约14:6）爱真理，归根到底就是爱耶稣。

3. 「神就给他们一个生发错误的心」。 「故此，神就给他们一个生发错误的心，叫他们信从虚谎，使一切不信真理、倒喜爱不义的人都被定罪」（帖后2:11-12）。这是很严肃的话。

  • 先后次序： 「故此」很重要。不是神先叫人信谎言，叫无辜的人沉沦；而是他们先「不领受爱真理的心」，「喜爱不义」，然后神把他们交给他们自己所选择的。这和罗马书第一章所说的「神任凭他们」（罗1:24、26、28）是一样的道理：神的审判，有时就是让人得到他们坚持要的东西。
  • 神仍然掌管： 「神就给他们」是神主动的审判，不只是任凭；但神不是罪的源头（参《威斯敏斯德信条》5.4）。连欺骗的工作也在神的主权之下，撒但不能越过神所定的界限。
  • 一个安慰： 你若心里害怕，担心自己是不是已经被神交给了谎言，这害怕本身就说明你还在乎真理。保罗在这里描写的人，不是那些为自己的软弱忧伤的人，而是「喜爱不义」、不愿意得救的人。今天，你仍可以来到那位「就是真理」的耶稣面前（约6:37「到我这里来的，我总不丢弃他」）。
要点：人沉沦，是因为不肯爱真理。神没有欺骗任何寻求他的人；他把那些坚持拒绝真理的人交给他们自己所选的谎言。保护我们的不是聪明，而是那位就是真理的主先爱了我们，叫我们也能爱他。
深读 2:13-17 主所爱的弟兄们

1. 「但」。 「主所爱的弟兄们哪，我们本该常为你们感谢神」（帖后2:13）。在讲完那些沉沦的人之后，保罗立刻转向帖撒罗尼迦人，语气完全不同。「主所爱的」：世界再可怕，他们仍是主所爱的人。

2. 「他从起初拣选了你们」。 这里原文有两种读法：一种读作「从起初」，和合本照这个读法翻译；一种读作初熟的果子，不少现代译本照这个读法翻译。两种读法的抄本证据都很强，学者意见不一（如莱昂·莫里斯取前者；杰弗里·韦玛、查尔斯·瓦纳梅克取后者，联合圣经公会希腊文新约的编委会也采用后者）。若是「从起初」，就和弗1:4「从创立世界以前……拣选了我们」相近；若是初熟的果子，就是说他们好像庄稼中最先献给神的那一份，后面还有更多的人要被收进来（参雅1:18；启14:4）。无论哪一种，重点都是：救恩出于神的拣选。

  • 拣选的理解： 改革宗传统（如加尔文）认为，神的拣选是无条件的，不是因为预见人会信，而是出于神的怜悯（参罗9:16）；阿民念传统和卫斯理宗传统认为，神是照着他预知谁会信而拣选（参罗8:29）。两方面都同意：得救的人要因信而得救，也都同意得救的荣耀归于神。

3. 拣选的方法和目标。 「叫你们因信真道，又被圣灵感动，成为圣洁，能以得救。神藉我们所传的福音召你们到这地步，好得着我们主耶稣基督的荣光」（帖后2:13-14）。

  • 方法： 有两方面：圣灵使人成为圣洁，人信真道。神的拣选不是叫人坐着不动，而是藉着圣灵的工作和人的信心实现。
  • 对比： 第10-12节的人「不信真理」，这里的人「信真道」；那些人被「虚谎」迷惑，这些人被「福音」呼召。
  • 目标： 「得着我们主耶稣基督的荣光」。那不法的人想要自己的荣耀（帖后2:4），信徒却要分享基督的荣耀。

4. 「站立得稳」，「都要坚守」。 「所以，弟兄们，你们要站立得稳，凡所领受的教训，不拘是我们口传的，是信上写的，都要坚守」（帖后2:15）。「教训」原文指传下来的东西，就是使徒所传、他们所领受的福音和教导（参林前11:2；林前15:1-3）。

  • 不同的理解： 天主教认为这节经文支持圣经和圣传并重（参梵蒂冈第二次大公会议《启示宪章》8；《天主教教理》78、80-82条）：使徒的教导有一部分是口传的，由教会的传统保存下来。按照新教唯独圣经的原则，使徒口传的教导就是他们所传的福音；这福音已经在圣灵的引导下写成新约圣经（参《威斯敏斯德信条》1.1、1.6。1.6还说，不可在圣经以外加上所谓圣灵的新启示或人的传统，正可对照帖后2:2的「有灵」）；所以今天我们是藉着圣经来坚守使徒的教训。
  • 对抗错误的方法： 保罗没有给他们一个新的时间表，而是叫他们回到当初领受的教训。面对新奇的说法，最好的保护是牢牢守住已经领受的福音。

5. 保罗的祷告。 「但愿我们主耶稣基督和那爱我们、开恩将永远的安慰并美好的盼望赐给我们的父神，安慰你们的心，并且在一切善行善言上坚固你们」（帖后2:16-17）。

  • 先提主耶稣基督： 保罗这里把主耶稣放在父神前面；后面的动词（第17节）和分词（第16节）都用单数（参帖前3:11）。许多解经家认为，这显出父与子在作为上的合一；至少，保罗把子放在父前面，一同作祷告的对象，若子不与父同等，这样祷告就说不通了。
  • 「永远的安慰并美好的盼望」： 这是「开恩」赐的，是已经给了的。人的安慰会过去，神的安慰是「永远的」。错误的教训叫人惊慌，福音却给人盼望。
  • 「善行善言」： 安慰不是叫人安静地坐着，而是叫人在言语和行为上被坚固，继续行善（参帖后3:13）。
要点：在一个充满欺骗的世界里，信徒的安稳不在于自己看透一切，而在于神的爱、神的拣选和神的呼召。所以我们可以站立得稳，守住福音，安心地行善。
默想

默想： 「因他们不领受爱真理的心，使他们得救。」（帖后2:10）保罗说那些人沉沦，不是因为他们不够聪明，而是因为他们不爱真理。读到这里，我要老实问自己：我爱真理，还是爱我想听的话？我会转发那些证明我对、别人错的文章，却很少去查证；我喜欢听叫我舒服的讲道，听到说中我的罪的地方，就想换一个话题；在家人和弟兄姊妹面前，我常常只说对自己有利的那一半事实。也许有一句关于我自己的实话，朋友、配偶或某一篇讲道已经不止一次想告诉我，我却每次都找到理由不去听。保罗说那些人「喜爱不义」；我不敢说自己和他们毫无关系。可是保罗接着说：「主所爱的弟兄们哪……他从起初拣选了你们。」（帖后2:13）我能爱真理，不是因为我比那些人更诚实，而是因为那位就是真理的主（约14:6）「爱我，为我舍己」（加2:20）。他知道关于我、我最不想听的那句实话，仍然为我舍命。今天，我可以把那句我一直不肯听的实话带到他面前，在他面前听，不必害怕。耶稣说：「天父的儿子若叫你们自由，你们就真自由了。」（约8:36）叫我自由的，不是我终于诚实了，而是那位就是真理的主自己。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 2 is the center of the letter, in two main sections. The day of the Lord has not come (vv. 1–12): some are saying the day of the Lord has come, and Paul urges them not to be shaken or alarmed; before that day the rebellion must come and the man of lawlessness be revealed; something now restrains him, and when it is removed the lawless one will be revealed; the Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth; those who refused to love the truth will be deceived by what is false. Thanksgiving, exhortation and prayer (vv. 13–17): God chose them to be saved and called them through the gospel to obtain Christ's glory; so they are to stand firm and hold to the traditions they were taught; may our Lord Jesus Christ and God our Father comfort their hearts and establish them in every good work and word.

The first half of this chapter is hard, and interpreters through the centuries have held many different views. But the second half is clear: whatever the details of the end, believers' security lies in God's choosing, God's calling and God's comfort. To read this chapter well we must move, as Paul does, from "the mystery of lawlessness" to "brothers beloved by the Lord."

Going Deeper: 2:1–3a Let No One Deceive You

1. What is Paul correcting? "Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we ask you, brothers, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come" (2 Thessalonians 2:1–2).

  • "Coming": the same word the first letter uses many times (1 Thess 2:19; 1 Thess 3:13; 1 Thess 4:15; 1 Thess 5:23), used at the time for a ruler's arrival at a city.
  • "Being gathered": believers being gathered to the Lord, the same event as 1 Thessalonians 4:17, "caught up together... in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air."
  • "Has come": the Greek means not "is about to come" but "has arrived," "is here."

2. Where did the false teaching come from? Paul lists three possible sources: "a spirit," that is, a prophecy claimed to come from the Holy Spirit; "a spoken word," someone's message or teaching; or "a letter seeming to be from us," a forged letter in Paul's name, or a distortion of a letter Paul had written (see 2 Pet 3:16). Paul is not sure which, but whatever the source, they are not to believe it.

  • Testing prophecy: in the first letter Paul said, "Do not despise prophecies, but test everything" (1 Thess 5:20–21). Here is a case in point: a message claimed to come from the Spirit must be rejected if it contradicts the apostolic teaching.

3. "Let no one deceive you in any way." To deceive is to mislead, to lead someone down the wrong path. Jesus himself warned, "See that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name... and they will lead many astray" (Matt 24:4–5).

  • Why is "the day has come" wrong? It could make people think their present suffering was the final judgment, that the Lord had come and they had not been gathered; or it could make them think they no longer needed to work or live ordinary lives (see 2 Thessalonians 3:6–12). Either way, believers would lose their peace and leave the right path.
The point: Even spiritual-sounding words must be tested. Any message about the end that spreads alarm and leads away from the apostles' teaching, however spiritual it sounds, should not be believed lightly.
Going Deeper: 2:3b–8 The Man of Lawlessness and the Restrainer

1. "The rebellion." "For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction" (2 Thessalonians 2:3). "Rebellion" (apostasia) usually means revolt or defection.

  • Rebellion against whom? Some take it as a large-scale apostasy within the church, many professing believers abandoning the faith (see Matt 24:10–12); others as an open revolt of the whole world against God. Both may be in view.
  • And the timing of the rapture: this passage is also central in the debate over the timing of the rapture (see the discussion at 1 Thessalonians 4). Posttribulationists (such as George Ladd and Douglas Moo) and those who hold one undivided coming (such as Anthony Hoekema) argue that "our being gathered" in verse 1 and "the day of the Lord" in verse 2 are one event, so that believers are gathered to the Lord after the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness. Pretribulationists (such as John Walvoord) distinguish the gathering in verse 1 from the day of the Lord in verses 2–3, holding that believers are caught up before that day. Some dispensational writers (such as Kenneth Wuest) even read apostasia as "departure," meaning the rapture; but most interpreters, including many dispensationalists, reject this, because the word means religious rebellion in the Greek Old Testament and the New Testament (see Josh 22:22; Acts 21:21). The point of the passage is not to draw up a timetable but to say that the day has not yet come.
  • "That day will not come": the Greek sentence breaks off, and English versions supply "that day will not come, unless..." Paul's meaning is clear: these things have not yet happened, so the day of the Lord has not yet come.

2. "The man of lawlessness... the son of destruction." The CUV's "great sinner" follows later manuscripts that read "man of sin" (such as Alexandrinus and the Byzantine majority); earlier manuscripts (such as Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) read "man of lawlessness," which most modern versions follow, matching "the mystery of lawlessness" and "the lawless one" in verses 7–8. "Son of destruction" means he is destined for ruin (see John 17:12).

  • What he is like: he "opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God" (2 Thessalonians 2:4). This echoes Daniel's description of the king who "shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god" (Dan 11:36), and Ezekiel's word to the prince of Tyre: "Because your heart is proud, and you have said, 'I am a god'" (Ezek 28:2).
  • Shadows in history: in 167 BC Antiochus IV set up an idolatrous altar in the Jerusalem temple; in AD 40 the emperor Caligula ordered his own statue placed in the temple, though the plan failed. The Thessalonians may well have heard of such things (see Dan 9:27; Dan 11:31; Mark 13:14, "the abomination of desolation"). Paul is describing the final and fullest form of this arrogance.

3. Who is the man of lawlessness? Believers through the ages have held several main views.

  • A future individual: many early church fathers (such as Irenaeus) and many evangelical scholars today hold that this is a specific person who will appear before the Lord's return, the one John calls "antichrist" (1 John 2:18). Among those who hold this view, some think he will sit in a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem (such as dispensationalists), while others take "takes his seat in the temple of God" as Old Testament language for arrogantly claiming God's place.
  • An institution in church history: at the Reformation, Martin Luther, Calvin and many Reformed confessions (such as the Westminster Confession of 1646, chapter 25, section 6) identified this with the papacy, which sits in "the temple of God," the church, claiming authority that belongs to God. Most Reformed scholars today no longer make this identification. Later American Presbyterian revisions removed the clause: the Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. removed it from 25.6 in 1903, and it is also absent from the texts used today by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church and the Presbyterian Church in America.
  • A past figure: preterists hold that this refers to a person or power before AD 70, such as the Romans who captured Jerusalem and destroyed the temple. But Paul says the Lord Jesus will "bring to nothing" this figure "by the appearance of his coming" (2 Thessalonians 2:8), which is hard to fit with the events of AD 70, so most scholars do not accept this view.
  • Common ground: all these views agree on several things: evil will show itself in concentrated form at the end of history; its essence is a human being seeking to sit in God's place; and it will finally be destroyed by the Lord Jesus. John also says that "now many antichrists have come" (1 John 2:18), so this spirit of arrogance is already at work today.

4. "What is restraining." "And you know what is restraining him now so that he may be revealed in his time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way" (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7). In verse 6 Paul uses the neuter ("what is restraining"); in verse 7 the masculine ("he who now restrains"). So the restrainer may be both a force and connected with a person.

  • The Roman Empire and legal order: many in the early church (such as Tertullian and Chrysostom) took this as the Roman Empire, or more broadly the order upheld by government and law (see Rom 13:1–4). As long as order remains, lawlessness cannot fully show itself.
  • The Holy Spirit or the church: many dispensationalists (such as John Walvoord) take this as the Holy Spirit working through the church in the world; "out of the way" is the rapture of the church, after which the lawless one is revealed. This view is often tied to a pretribulational rapture. Critics point out that it is hard to speak of the Holy Spirit being "out of the way"; proponents reply that what is removed is not the omnipresent Spirit but his restraining ministry through the indwelt church.
  • The preaching of the gospel: some scholars (such as Oscar Cullmann) take it as the preaching of the gospel, even Paul's own mission, since Jesus said, "this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world... and then the end will come" (Matt 24:14).
  • The archangel Michael: some scholars (such as Colin Nicholl), drawing on Daniel 10 and 12, take it as Michael, the archangel who protects God's people.
  • God himself: others think the restrainer is God, or God's will; by whatever means, God governs the timing.
  • Augustine's humility: Augustine admitted frankly that he did not know what Paul meant. The Thessalonians "know," because Paul had told them in person (2 Thessalonians 2:5); we did not hear it, so we must be humble. Yet the most important point is clear: the lawless one can be revealed only "in his time," and that time is set by God.

5. "The Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth." "And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming" (2 Thessalonians 2:8). Paul spends many words describing the lawless one, but only one sentence on his end: with a single breath the Lord Jesus destroys him.

  • Old Testament background: Isaiah says of David's descendant, "he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked" (Isa 11:4). The Lord Jesus is that messianic king (see Rev 19:15).
  • Not two equal opponents: for all his arrogance, the lawless one is no match for God. When "the appearance of his coming" shines out, he is brought to nothing.
The point: Paul speaks of the man of lawlessness not to make us afraid or to set us guessing who he is, but to tell us that the day of the Lord has not yet come, that the time of evil is in God's hands, and that the Lord Jesus can destroy the lawless one with a breath.
Going Deeper: 2:9–12 Refusing to Love the Truth

1. The activity of Satan. "The coming of the lawless one is by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders, and with all wicked deception for those who are perishing" (2 Thessalonians 2:9–10).

  • "Coming": the same word as the Lord Jesus' "coming" in verse 8. The lawless one has his own "coming," a counterfeit and an imitation.
  • False signs: miracles by themselves do not prove a message true. Jesus said, "false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect" (Matt 24:24). Satan too "disguises himself as an angel of light" (2 Cor 11:14).

2. "Because they refused to love the truth." "And so be saved" (2 Thessalonians 2:10). They perish not because they had no chance to know the truth, but because they would not love it.

  • Loving the truth: Paul speaks not only of knowing the truth, but of loving it. A person can know much about God and yet not love him, preferring to believe what he wants to hear (see 2 Tim 4:3–4).
  • The truth is a person: Jesus said, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). To love the truth is, in the end, to love Jesus.

3. "God sends them a strong delusion." "Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false, in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness" (2 Thessalonians 2:11–12). These are solemn words.

  • The order matters: "Therefore" is important. It is not that God first makes people believe a lie and sends innocent people to ruin; rather, they first "refused to love the truth" and "had pleasure in unrighteousness," and then God gave them over to what they had chosen. This is the same principle as "God gave them up" in Romans 1 (Rom 1:24, 26, 28): God's judgment sometimes means letting people have what they insist on.
  • God is still in control: "God sends" is an active act of judgment, not mere permission; yet God is not the author of sin (see Westminster Confession 5.4). Even the work of deception is under God's sovereignty; Satan cannot go beyond the limits God has set.
  • A comfort: if a reader is afraid that God has already handed them over to a lie, that very fear shows that they still care about the truth. The people Paul describes here are not those grieving over their weakness, but those who "had pleasure in unrighteousness" and did not want to be saved. Today you may still come to Jesus, who is the truth (John 6:37, "whoever comes to me I will never cast out").
The point: People perish because they will not love the truth. God deceives no one who seeks him; he gives those who persist in rejecting the truth over to the lie they have chosen. What protects us is not cleverness, but the Lord who is the truth, who loved us first and so teaches us to love him.
Going Deeper: 2:13–17 Brothers Beloved by the Lord

1. "But." "But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord" (2 Thessalonians 2:13). Having spoken of those who are perishing, Paul turns at once to the Thessalonians, and his tone changes completely. "Beloved by the Lord": in a frightening world, they are people the Lord loves.

2. "God chose you as the first fruits." The manuscripts differ here: some read "from the beginning," which the CUV follows; others read "as first fruits," which the ESV follows. Both readings have strong manuscript support, and scholars are divided (Leon Morris prefers the first; Jeffrey Weima and Charles Wanamaker the second, which the editorial committee of the UBS Greek New Testament also printed). If "from the beginning," it is close to Ephesians 1:4, "he chose us in him before the foundation of the world"; if "first fruits," they are like the first portion of the harvest offered to God, a pledge of more to come (see Jas 1:18; Rev 14:4). Either way, the point is that salvation comes from God's choosing.

  • How election is understood: the Reformed tradition (such as Calvin) holds that God's election is unconditional, not based on foreseen faith but flowing from God's mercy (see Rom 9:16); the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions hold that God chose according to his foreknowledge of who would believe (see Rom 8:29). Both agree that those who are saved are saved through faith, and both give the glory of salvation to God.

3. The means and the goal of election. "Through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth. To this he called you through our gospel, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ" (2 Thessalonians 2:13–14).

  • The means: sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth. God's choosing does not leave people passive; it is carried out through the Spirit's work and human faith.
  • The contrast: the people in verses 10–12 "did not believe the truth"; these "believe the truth." Those were deceived by "what is false"; these are called by "the gospel."
  • The goal: "that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ." The lawless one seeks his own glory (2 Thessalonians 2:4); believers will share in Christ's glory.

4. "Stand firm and hold to the traditions." "So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter" (2 Thessalonians 2:15). "Traditions" means what has been handed on, the gospel and teaching the apostles passed on and the Thessalonians received (see 1 Cor 11:2; 1 Cor 15:1–3).

  • Different understandings: Catholic teaching sees this verse as supporting Scripture and Sacred Tradition together (see Vatican II, Dei Verbum 8; Catechism of the Catholic Church 78, 80–82): part of the apostles' teaching was oral, and is preserved in the church's tradition. The Protestant principle of sola Scriptura holds that the apostles' oral teaching was the gospel they preached, and that this gospel has been written down in the New Testament under the Spirit's guidance (see Westminster Confession 1.1, 1.6; 1.6 also rules out adding "new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men," which bears directly on "by a spirit" in 2 Thessalonians 2:2); so today we hold to the apostles' teaching through Scripture.
  • How to resist error: Paul does not give them a new timetable; he calls them back to the teaching they first received. Faced with novel claims, the best protection is to hold fast to the gospel already received.

5. Paul's prayer. "Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word" (2 Thessalonians 2:16–17).

  • The Lord Jesus Christ named first: here Paul puts the Lord Jesus before God the Father, and the verbs (v. 17) and participles (v. 16) that follow are singular (see 1 Thess 3:11). Many commentators see in this the unity of Father and Son in their action; at the least, Paul names the Son before the Father as one addressed together with him in prayer, which makes sense only if the Son is equal with the Father.
  • "Eternal comfort and good hope": this is given "through grace," and has already been given. Human comfort passes; God's comfort is "eternal." False teaching brings alarm; the gospel brings hope.
  • "Every good work and word": comfort does not leave people sitting still; it strengthens them in word and deed to keep doing good (see 2 Thessalonians 3:13).
The point: In a world full of deception, believers' security does not lie in seeing through everything themselves, but in God's love, God's choosing and God's calling. So we can stand firm, hold to the gospel, and do good with quiet hearts.
Meditation

Reflect: "Because they refused to love the truth and so be saved" (2 Thessalonians 2:10). Paul says these people perish not because they are not clever enough, but because they do not love the truth. Reading this, I have to ask myself honestly: do I love the truth, or what I want to hear? I pass along articles that prove I am right and others wrong, and rarely check them; I like sermons that make me comfortable, and when one names my sin I want to change the subject; before my family and fellow believers I often tell only the half of the facts that favors me. Perhaps there is one truth about myself that a friend, my spouse or a sermon has tried to tell me more than once, and each time I have found a reason not to hear it. Paul says these people "had pleasure in unrighteousness"; I dare not say I have nothing in common with them. But Paul goes on: "brothers beloved by the Lord... God chose you" (2 Thessalonians 2:13). I can love the truth not because I am more honest than they are, but because the Lord who is the truth (John 14:6) "loved me and gave himself for me" (Gal 2:20). He knows the truth about me that I least want to hear, and still gave his life for me. Today I can bring him that one truth I have refused to hear, and listen to it in his presence without fear. Jesus said, "So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed" (John 8:36). What sets me free is not that I have finally become honest, but the Lord who is himself the truth.

entries.content:
本章脉络

第三章分成三段。请为我们祷告，主是信实的（1-5节）：保罗请他们为福音的传扬和自己的安全祷告；人不都有信心，但主是信实的，要坚固他们，保护他们脱离那恶者。不按规矩而行的人（6-15节）：有人不肯做工，反倒专管闲事；保罗以自己亲手做工为榜样，吩咐他们安静做工、吃自己的饭；对不听从的人，教会要远离他，叫他自觉羞愧，但不要以他为仇人，要劝他如弟兄。祝福和亲笔问安（16-18节）：愿赐平安的主随时随事亲自给他们平安；保罗亲笔写下问安，作为这封信的记号。

这一章看起来很平常，讲的是工作、吃饭和教会纪律。但保罗在讲完主的再来之后才讲这些，正是要告诉我们：盼望主来的人，要在平常的日子里忠心。

深读 3:1-5 主是信实的

1. 「请你们为我们祷告」。 「弟兄们，我还有话说：请你们为我们祷告，好叫主的道理快快行开，得着荣耀，正如在你们中间一样，也叫我们脱离无理之恶人的手」（帖后3:1-2）。保罗是使徒，却请这个年轻的教会为他祷告（参罗15:30；西4:3）。

  • 「快快行开」： 原文是奔跑的意思，好像赛跑的人跑向终点（参诗147:15）。保罗先求的不是自己的安全，而是神的道能畅通无阻，并且「得着荣耀」，就是被人尊重、接受。
  • 「正如在你们中间一样」： 帖撒罗尼迦人自己就是神的道奔跑的见证（参帖前1:8）。
  • 「无理之恶人」： 保罗写这封信的时候在哥林多，那里也有犹太人敌挡他（徒18:6）。

2. 「人不都是有信心」。 原文直译是信心不是众人都有的，也可以理解为那（福音的）信仰不是众人都有的。这话说得很平实：福音不会被所有人接受，有些人还会敌挡。保罗不惊讶，也不灰心。

3. 「但主是信实的」。 「但主是信实的，要坚固你们，保护你们脱离那恶者」（帖后3:3）。原文里「信心」和「信实」是同一个词根，保罗在这里用了一个文字上的对比：人不都有信心，但主是信实的。

  • 「那恶者」： 可以指恶事，也可以指撒但。多数解经家认为指撒但（参帖后2:9；帖前3:5），和主祷文「救我们脱离凶恶」相近（参太6:13）。
  • 保罗请他们为自己代祷，转过来却安慰他们： 他说完自己的危险，立刻转过来安慰他们。他的眼光不是停在自己身上。

4. 「我们靠主深信」。 「我们靠主深信，你们现在是遵行我们所吩咐的，后来也必要遵行」（帖后3:4）。保罗对他们的信心，不是建立在他们自己的能力上，而是「靠主」。他相信主会继续在他们身上做工。

5. 「叫你们爱神，并学基督的忍耐」。 「愿主引导你们的心，叫你们爱神，并学基督的忍耐！」（帖后3:5）

  • 「引导」： 原文是修直道路、除去障碍的意思（帖前3:11「引领」是同一个词）。
  • 「爱神」： 原文可以指我们对神的爱，也可以指神对我们的爱。许多解经家认为，这里可能两层意思都有：主引导我们的心进入神的爱里，叫我们因被爱而爱他。
  • 「基督的忍耐」： 可以指基督自己忍受苦难的那种忍耐（参来12:2-3），也可以指等候基督再来的忍耐（英文钦定本这样译）。和合本作「学基督的忍耐」，采取前一种理解。
要点：神的道要奔跑，靠的不是我们的力量，而是信实的主。人会不信，也会敌挡，但主要坚固我们，保护我们，引导我们的心进入神的爱里。
深读 3:6-12 安静做工，吃自己的饭

1. 「不按规矩而行」。 「弟兄们，我们奉主耶稣基督的名吩咐你们，凡有弟兄不按规矩而行，不遵守从我们所受的教训，就当远离他」（帖后3:6）。「不按规矩」原文指士兵离开队伍、不守秩序；有些蒲草纸文献用它指旷工、不尽本分。在这一章，这种不守秩序具体表现为不肯做工（帖后3:10-11）。前书已经劝过他们（帖前4:11-12；帖前5:14），现在保罗的语气更重了：「奉主耶稣基督的名吩咐」。

  • 为什么不做工？ 第11节说他们「什么工都不做，反倒专管闲事」。原文是一个双关语：不做工，却在别人的工作上忙。许多解经家认为，这与第二章错误的末世教训有关：既然主的日子到了，何必还要工作？也有学者（如布鲁斯·温特）认为，背后是当时恩主与门客的社会制度。也可能有人觉得，教会的弟兄姊妹既然彼此相爱，就可以一直靠别人的爱心生活。

2. 保罗的榜样。 「你们自己原知道应当怎样效法我们。因为我们在你们中间，未尝不按规矩而行，也未尝白吃人的饭，倒是辛苦劳碌，昼夜做工，免得叫你们一人受累」（帖后3:7-8）。保罗在帖撒罗尼迦的时候，一边传福音，一边亲手做工（参帖前2:9；徒18:3「他们本是制造帐棚为业」）。

  • 「这并不是因我们没有权柄」： 保罗在别处说，传福音的人有权柄「靠着福音养生」（林前9:14）。他不用这权柄，「乃是要给你们作榜样，叫你们效法我们」（帖后3:9）。
  • 劳动的尊严： 在当时的希腊罗马社会，有地位的人常常看不起手工劳动。保罗却甘心做一个手艺人。他让信徒看见，平凡的工作是可以荣耀神的（参西3:23；弗4:28）。

3. 「若有人不肯做工，就不可吃饭」。 「我们在你们那里的时候，曾吩咐你们说，若有人不肯做工，就不可吃饭」（帖后3:10）。

  • 关键在「不肯」： 保罗说的是不愿意工作的人，不是因为疾病、残障、年老、照顾家人或失业而不能工作的人。对那些人，教会要「扶助软弱的人」（帖前5:14），要像早期教会照顾寡妇一样照顾他们（参提前5:16；徒6:1）。
  • 是对教会说的，不是政治口号： 这句话后来被人拿去作社会口号，例如列宁和1936年的苏联宪法都引用过类似的话，用来要求人民为国家劳动，却去掉了保罗所说的「不肯」。但保罗是在对教会说话：教会的爱心和饭桌，不应该被那些能工作却不肯工作的人利用。这不是叫我们对穷人冷漠，而是叫我们的爱心有智慧。
  • 今天的应用： 这也提醒那些可以工作、却长期依赖家人或教会的人，也提醒那些总是替别人收拾残局、使对方永远学不会负责的人。爱有时需要说「不」。

4. 「要安静做工，吃自己的饭」。 「我们靠主耶稣基督吩咐、劝戒这样的人，要安静做工，吃自己的饭」（帖后3:12）。

  • 「靠主耶稣基督」： 保罗不是用自己的权威压人，而是在主里劝勉他们。这是吩咐，也是劝戒。
  • 「安静」： 和「专管闲事」相对。不是到处奔走、插手别人的事，而是专心做自己该做的事（参帖前4:11「立志作安静人」）。
  • 工作是爱邻舍的一种方式： 自己做工，就不叫人受累（帖后3:8）；还能有余分给缺乏的人（弗4:28；徒20:35「施比受更为有福」）。
要点：等候主来，不是放下工作，而是在平凡的工作中忠心。保罗不是看不起不能工作的人，而是劝那些能工作却不肯工作的人：安静做工，吃自己的饭，这也是爱人的方式。我们不是靠工作在神面前站立；正因为已经蒙恩，才能把平凡的工作当作献给主的事奉。
深读 3:13-15 不要以他为仇人

1. 「行善不可丧志」。 「弟兄们，你们行善不可丧志」（帖后3:13）。这话是对那些忠心做工、又一直帮助人的信徒说的。有人利用你的爱心，你很容易灰心，想从此不再帮助任何人。保罗说：不要因此停止行善（参加6:9）。

  • 疲倦是真实的： 长期照顾人、帮助人，会叫人疲倦。保罗没有责备疲倦的人，而是劝他们继续，并且要有智慧地分辨，谁真需要帮助，谁是不肯做工。保罗刚刚为他们祷告，愿主「引导你们的心，叫你们爱神，并学基督的忍耐」（帖后3:5）；能继续行善的力量，不是来自对方的回报，而是来自那位先为我们忍受苦难的基督（来12:2-3）。

2. 「要记下他，不和他交往」。 「若有人不听从我们这信上的话，要记下他，不和他交往，叫他自觉羞愧」（帖后3:14）。

  • 「记下」： 意思是留意、认出这个人，不是公开羞辱他。
  • 「不和他交往」： 原文是不要和他混在一起。许多解经家认为，这可能包括不让他在教会的饭桌上白吃（参帖后3:10），或者不让他像平常一样参与教会的团契。保罗在这里用的「交往」，和林前5:9、11是同一个词；不同之处在于罪的性质，以及第15节「不要以他为仇人，要劝他如弟兄」。哥林多前书5章是严重的罪，要把人赶出去（林前5:11-13）；这里的语气比较轻，目的是叫他回转。这里是正式的教会处分，还是较轻的疏远，解经家看法不一。
  • 「叫他自觉羞愧」： 羞愧在这里不是为了惩罚，而是为了叫他醒悟。教会的疏远是众人看得见的，但目的是叫他自己知耻回转，不是叫他当众丢脸。华人文化看重面子，教会更要小心，不可把纪律变成羞辱。这和耶稣在太18:15-17所说的步骤相近：先私下劝，再带人同去，最后告诉教会，目的都是「得了你的弟兄」。

3. 「但不要以他为仇人，要劝他如弟兄」。 「但不要以他为仇人，要劝他如弟兄」（帖后3:15）。这是全段的关键。教会的纪律不是为了赶走敌人，而是为了挽回弟兄。

  • 他仍是弟兄： 即使他犯了错，不肯听从，他仍是「弟兄」。教会对他的态度，不是厌恶，而是忧伤和盼望（参加6:1「用温柔的心把他挽回过来」）。
  • 华人教会的处境： 有些教会对不守规矩的人睁一只眼闭一只眼，怕伤了和气，怕得罪人；也有些教会一旦有人犯错，就在背后议论，叫他再也抬不起头来，甚至从此离开。保罗两样都不赞成：要劝戒，不要放任；要挽回，不要排斥。
  • 纪律的界限： 这段经文讲的是不肯做工、不听劝的弟兄。若是牵涉到虐待、性侵犯、诈骗等罪行，就不只是教会内部劝戒的事，应当向警察或法庭举报（参罗13:4）。受害的人不必留在危险中，也不必勉强和仍然不安全的人和好。挽回一个犯罪的人，不等于让他恢复原有的职分，或让他再接近受害人和孩子。教会也绝不可以为了面子，把这样的事压下来（「家丑不可外扬」）。
要点：教会的纪律要有爱，也要有真理。对不肯悔改的人要认真处理，目的却是挽回，不是排斥；他仍是弟兄，我们要像对待弟兄一样劝他。
深读 3:16-18 赐平安的主

1. 「愿赐平安的主随时随事亲自给你们平安」。 「愿赐平安的主随时随事亲自给你们平安！愿主常与你们众人同在！」（帖后3:16）这封信处理了人心的惊慌（帖后2:2），最后以平安作结。

  • 「亲自」： 平安不是靠我们把所有问题都处理好才得到的，而是主「亲自」赐的。
  • 「随时随事」： 不是只在顺境中，而是在逼迫中、在错误教训的混乱中、在教会处理纪律的难处中。耶稣说：「在世上，你们有苦难；但你们可以放心，我已经胜了世界。」（约16:33）
  • 「众人」： 包括那些忠心做工的人，也包括那些需要被劝戒的人。保罗的祝福没有把任何人排除在外。

2. 「我－保罗亲笔问你们安」。 「我－保罗亲笔问你们安。凡我的信都以此为记，我的笔迹就是这样」（帖后3:17）。保罗常请人代笔（参罗16:22），到最后亲笔写下问安（参林前16:21；加6:11；西4:18；门19）。

  • 为什么特别提这一点？ 因为帖后2:2提到有「冒我名的书信」。保罗的亲笔，是这封信真实的记号。
  • 怀疑作者的人怎样看？ 主张托名说的学者认为，这句话正是托名的作者故意加上去的，好叫人相信这是保罗写的信。支持保罗为作者的学者回答说，这句话最自然的理解，就是保罗本人对假信的回应（参导读）。

3. 「愿我们主耶稣基督的恩常与你们众人同在」。 「愿我们主耶稣基督的恩常与你们众人同在！」（帖后3:18）这和前书的最后一句几乎一样（帖前5:28），只是加上了「众人」。整封信讲了审判、讲了那不法的人、讲了教会纪律，最后一句话却是恩典。

要点：信徒的平安不是从环境来的，而是赐平安的主亲自赐的。这封信处理了惊慌，最后以恩典作结；凡属主的人，一生的故事也必这样结束。
默想

默想： 「但不要以他为仇人，要劝他如弟兄。」（帖后3:15）也许在我的教会里，或者在信主的亲戚中间，有一个人让我失望透了：他借了钱不还，承诺的事从来不做，或者总是让别人替他收拾残局。我帮过他好几次，后来就放弃了。现在我不再和他说话，提起他的时候，口气里只有冷淡和讽刺。我心里已经把他当作一个仇人，或者至少当作一个不值得再费心的人。保罗没有叫帖撒罗尼迦人假装没事，他叫他们认真处理；但他也说：不要以他为仇人。我想起耶稣复活的那个早晨。在他最需要的时候，「门徒都离开他，逃走了」（可14:50）；可是复活的主托人带给他们的话是：「你们去告诉我的弟兄」（太28:10）。他为他们死，也为他们复活，没有把他们记成仇人。他「称他们为弟兄也不以为耻」（来2:11），而这些弟兄里面也有我，一个常常辜负主的人。今天，我不必勉强自己去信任一个仍然不可靠的人，也不必回到一个不安全的关系里；但我可以求主除去我心里的那份敌意，在适当的时候、用适当的方式，再一次像对弟兄一样对他说话；在那以前，至少先在心里、在祷告中，重新称他为弟兄。保罗这封信的最后一句是：「愿我们主耶稣基督的恩常与你们众人同在！」（帖后3:18）这「众人」里面有他，也有我。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 3 falls into three parts. Pray for us; the Lord is faithful (vv. 1–5): Paul asks them to pray for the spread of the gospel and for his safety; not all have faith, but the Lord is faithful, and he will establish them and guard them against the evil one. Those walking in idleness (vv. 6–15): some will not work and are busybodies instead; Paul points to his own example of working with his hands and commands them to work quietly and earn their own living; the church is to keep away from anyone who will not obey, so that he may be ashamed, yet not regard him as an enemy but warn him as a brother. Blessing and greeting in Paul's own hand (vv. 16–18): may the Lord of peace himself give them peace at all times in every way; Paul writes the greeting himself as the sign of the letter's genuineness.

This chapter looks ordinary: work, food, church discipline. But Paul places these things right after the Lord's coming to show us that people who hope for the Lord's coming are faithful in ordinary days.

Going Deeper: 3:1–5 The Lord Is Faithful

1. "Pray for us." "Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as happened among you, and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men" (2 Thessalonians 3:1–2). Paul is an apostle, yet he asks this young church to pray for him (see Rom 15:30; Col 4:3).

  • "Speed ahead": the Greek means "run," like a runner racing toward the finish (see Ps 147:15). What Paul asks first is not his own safety but that God's word may run unhindered and "be honored," that is, be respected and received.
  • "As happened among you": the Thessalonians themselves are evidence of God's word running (see 1 Thess 1:8).
  • "Wicked and evil men": Paul was in Corinth when he wrote, and Jews there opposed him too (Acts 18:6).

2. "Not all have faith." The Greek could also be read "not all have the faith." It is a plain statement: the gospel will not be received by everyone, and some will oppose it. Paul is neither surprised nor discouraged.

3. "But the Lord is faithful." "But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one" (2 Thessalonians 3:3). In Greek "faith" and "faithful" share a root, and Paul plays on the words: not all have faith, but the Lord is faithful.

  • "The evil one": this could mean evil in general or Satan. Most commentators take it as Satan (see 2 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Thess 3:5), close to the Lord's Prayer, "deliver us from evil" (see Matt 6:13).
  • Paul asks prayer for his own needs, yet turns to comfort them: having spoken of his own danger, he turns at once to comfort them. His eyes do not stay on himself.

4. "We have confidence in the Lord about you." "And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will do the things that we command" (2 Thessalonians 3:4). Paul's confidence in them does not rest on their own ability but is "in the Lord." He trusts that the Lord will go on working in them.

5. "To the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ." "May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ" (2 Thessalonians 3:5).

  • "Direct": the word means to make a road straight, to clear obstacles (the same word as "direct" in 1 Thess 3:11).
  • "The love of God": this could mean our love for God or God's love for us. Many commentators think both may be in view: the Lord directs our hearts into God's love, so that, being loved, we love him.
  • "The steadfastness of Christ": this could mean the steadfastness Christ himself showed in suffering (see Heb 12:2–3), or patient waiting for Christ's return (as the King James Version translates it). The CUV, "learn the steadfastness of Christ," takes the first view.
The point: God's word runs not by our strength but by the faithful Lord. People will disbelieve and oppose, but the Lord will establish us, guard us, and direct our hearts into God's love.
Going Deeper: 3:6–12 Work Quietly and Earn Your Own Living

1. "Walking in idleness." "Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us" (2 Thessalonians 3:6). The word for "idleness" describes a soldier out of rank, disorderly; some papyri use it of skipping work or neglecting one's duty. In this chapter the disorder shows itself concretely as refusing to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10–11). The first letter had already urged them (1 Thess 4:11–12; 1 Thess 5:14); now Paul's tone is stronger: "we command you... in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ."

  • Why were they not working? Verse 11 says they were "not busy at work, but busybodies," a wordplay in Greek: "not working, but working around" in others' business. Many commentators link this with the false teaching about the end in chapter 2: if the day of the Lord has come, why work? Some scholars (such as Bruce Winter) point to the patron–client customs of the time. Others may have felt that, since church members loved one another, they could simply live on that love indefinitely.

2. Paul's example. "For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone's bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you" (2 Thessalonians 3:7–8). In Thessalonica Paul preached the gospel while working with his own hands (see 1 Thess 2:9; Acts 18:3, "they were tentmakers by trade").

  • "Not because we do not have that right": elsewhere Paul says those who preach the gospel have the right to "get their living by the gospel" (1 Cor 9:14). He did not use this right, "but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate" (2 Thessalonians 3:9).
  • The dignity of labor: in Greco-Roman society people of standing often looked down on manual work. Paul willingly worked as a craftsman. He showed believers that ordinary work can glorify God (see Col 3:23; Eph 4:28).

3. "If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat." "For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

  • The key is "not willing": Paul is speaking of those who will not work, not those who cannot work because of illness, disability, age, caring for family, or unemployment. For them the church is to "help the weak" (1 Thess 5:14), and to care for them as the early church cared for widows (see 1 Tim 5:16; Acts 6:1).
  • For the church, not a political slogan: this saying was later taken up as a social slogan; Lenin and the 1936 Soviet constitution, for example, used similar words to demand that people labor for the state, dropping Paul's "not willing." But Paul is speaking to the church: the church's love and its table should not be exploited by those who can work and will not. This does not make us cold toward the poor; it makes our love wise.
  • Today: this also speaks to those who could work but rely long-term on family or church, and to those who always clean up after others so that the other person never learns responsibility. Love sometimes has to say "no."

4. "Do their work quietly and earn their own living." "Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ to do their work quietly and to earn their own living" (2 Thessalonians 3:12).

  • "In the Lord Jesus Christ": Paul does not press them with his own authority, but exhorts them in the Lord. It is a command, and also an appeal.
  • "Quietly": the opposite of being a busybody. Not running around meddling in others' affairs, but attending to one's own work (see 1 Thess 4:11, "aspire to live quietly").
  • Work as a way of loving one's neighbor: working for one's own living means not being a burden (2 Thessalonians 3:8), and even having something to share with those in need (Eph 4:28; Acts 20:35, "It is more blessed to give than to receive").
The point: Waiting for the Lord does not mean laying down our work but being faithful in ordinary work. Paul does not look down on those who cannot work; he urges those who can work but will not: work quietly and earn your own living. This too is a way of loving others. We do not stand before God by our work; because we have already received grace, we can offer our ordinary work to the Lord.
Going Deeper: 3:13–15 Do Not Regard Him as an Enemy

1. "Do not grow weary in doing good." "As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good" (2 Thessalonians 3:13). This is said to believers who work faithfully and keep helping others. When someone exploits your kindness, it is easy to become discouraged and decide never to help anyone again. Paul says: do not stop doing good because of it (see Gal 6:9).

  • Weariness is real: long years of caring for and helping others make people tired. Paul does not rebuke the weary; he urges them to keep going, and to discern wisely who truly needs help and who will not work. Paul has just prayed that the Lord would "direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ" (2 Thessalonians 3:5); the strength to keep doing good comes not from being repaid, but from Christ, who first endured for us (Heb 12:2–3).

2. "Take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him." "If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed" (2 Thessalonians 3:14).

  • "Take note": to mark or recognize the person, not to humiliate him publicly.
  • "Have nothing to do with him": the Greek means "do not mix with him." Many commentators think this may include not letting him eat freely at the church's table (see 2 Thessalonians 3:10), or not letting him take part in fellowship as usual. Paul uses the same verb in 1 Corinthians 5:9 and 11; the difference lies in the nature of the offense and in verse 15, "Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother." In 1 Corinthians 5 the sin is serious and the person is to be put out (1 Cor 5:11–13); here the tone is milder, and the aim is his return. Whether this means formal church discipline or a lighter social distance, commentators differ.
  • "That he may be ashamed": shame here is not punishment for its own sake but a means of waking him up; the church's withdrawal is visible, but its aim is inner conviction, not humiliation, and in a culture that prizes face the church must take special care that discipline never becomes humiliation. This is close to the steps Jesus gives in Matthew 18:15–17: speak privately first, then take others along, and finally tell the church; the aim throughout is that "you have gained your brother" (Matt 18:15).

3. "Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother." "Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:15). This is the key to the passage. Church discipline is not for driving out enemies but for winning back brothers.

  • He is still a brother: even when he is in the wrong and will not listen, he is still a "brother." The church's attitude toward him is not disgust but grief and hope (see Gal 6:1, "restore him in a spirit of gentleness").
  • In Chinese churches: some churches turn a blind eye to those who will not be corrected, for fear of spoiling the peace or offending people; others, once someone has done wrong, talk behind his back until he can never hold his head up again, and he leaves for good. Paul approves of neither: admonish rather than tolerate; restore rather than shut out.
  • The limits of this discipline: this passage concerns a brother who will not work and will not be corrected. Where abuse, sexual assault, fraud or other crimes are involved, it is no longer only a matter for church admonition; it should be reported to the police or the courts (see Rom 13:4). Victims need not stay in danger, nor force themselves to reconcile with someone who is still unsafe. Restoring someone who has sinned does not mean returning him to his former office or giving him access again to victims or children. And the church must never hush such things up to save face (「家丑不可外扬」).
The point: Church discipline must have both love and truth. It deals seriously with those who will not repent, but its aim is restoration, not exclusion; such a person is still a brother, and we warn him as a brother.
Going Deeper: 3:16–18 The Lord of Peace

1. "May the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way." "Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way. The Lord be with you all" (2 Thessalonians 3:16). The letter deals with alarm (2 Thessalonians 2:2) and ends with peace.

  • "Himself": peace does not come because we have sorted out every problem; the Lord gives it "himself."
  • "At all times in every way": not only in good times, but in persecution, in the confusion of false teaching, in the difficulty of church discipline. Jesus said, "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33).
  • "All": including those who work faithfully and those who need to be warned. Paul's blessing leaves no one out.

2. "I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand." "I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write" (2 Thessalonians 3:17). Paul often had someone else write for him (see Rom 16:22), and then wrote the closing greeting himself (see 1 Cor 16:21; Gal 6:11; Col 4:18; Phlm 19).

  • Why point this out? Because 2 Thessalonians 2:2 mentioned "a letter seeming to be from us." Paul's own hand is the sign that this letter is genuine.
  • How do those who doubt the authorship see it? Scholars who think the letter was written in Paul's name see this sentence as exactly what such a writer would add to make it believable. Scholars who hold that Paul wrote it reply that the most natural reading is Paul's own response to forged letters (see the introduction).

3. "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all." "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all" (2 Thessalonians 3:18). This is almost the same as the last line of the first letter (1 Thess 5:28), with "all" added. The letter has spoken of judgment, of the lawless one and of church discipline, but its last word is grace.

The point: Believers' peace does not come from their circumstances; the Lord of peace gives it himself. This letter deals with alarm and ends with grace; so will the story of everyone who belongs to him.
Meditation

Reflect: "Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Perhaps in my church, or among my believing relatives, there is someone who has thoroughly disappointed me: he borrowed money and never repaid it, never did what he promised, or always left others to clean up after him. I helped him several times, and then I gave up. Now I no longer speak to him, and when his name comes up my voice holds only coldness and sarcasm. In my heart I have already made him an enemy, or at least someone not worth any more effort. Paul did not tell the Thessalonians to pretend nothing was wrong; he told them to deal with it seriously. But he also said: do not regard him as an enemy. I think of the morning Jesus rose. When he needed them most, his disciples "all left him and fled" (Mark 14:50); yet the message the risen Lord sent them was, "go and tell my brothers" (Matt 28:10). He had died for them and risen for them, and he did not mark them down as enemies. He "is not ashamed to call them brothers" (Heb 2:11), and among those brothers is me, someone who has often failed the Lord. Today I do not have to force myself to trust someone who is still unreliable, nor go back into a relationship that is unsafe. But I can ask the Lord to take away the hostility in my heart, and at a fitting time and in a fitting way to speak to him once more as a brother; and until then, at least begin calling him brother again, in my heart and in my prayers. The last line of Paul's letter is, "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all" (2 Thessalonians 3:18). That "all" includes him, and it includes me.

entries.content:
这卷书在讲什么

提摩太前书是保罗写给一位同工的信。保罗往马其顿去，把提摩太留在以弗所，「好嘱咐那几个人不可传异教」（提前1:3）。以弗所的教会已经有长老（参徒20:17），却出了问题：有人讲「荒渺无凭的话语和无穷的家谱」（提前1:4），有人「想要作教法师，却不明白自己所讲说的」（提前1:7），有人禁止嫁娶、禁戒食物（提前4:3），有人以敬虔为得利的门路（提前6:5）。提摩太要在这样的处境中坚守真道，也要整顿神的家。

保罗自己说明了写信的目的：「倘若我耽延日久，你也可以知道在神的家中当怎样行。这家就是永生神的教会，真理的柱石和根基。」（提前3:15）

所以这封信讲了很多教会生活的实际问题：

  • 教导： 要抵挡异教和一切「敌正道的事」（提前1:10），持守「纯正的话」（提前6:3）。
  • 祷告和敬拜： 要为万人祷告，为君王和一切在位的祷告（提前2:1-2）；男人、女人在聚会中当怎样行（提前2:8-15）。
  • 带领的人： 监督和执事要有怎样的品格（提前3:1-13）；怎样对待长老，包括对长老的控告（提前5:17-25）。
  • 教会里的各种人： 老年人和少年人（提前5:1-2）、寡妇（提前5:3-16）、作仆人的（提前6:1-2）、富足的人（提前6:17-19）。
  • 提摩太自己： 要操练敬虔（提前4:7）、不可叫人小看他年轻（提前4:12）、要谨慎自己和自己的教训（提前4:16）、要逃避贪财（提前6:10-11）、要为真道打那美好的仗（提前6:12）。

但这封信不只是一本教会手册。在讲规矩以前，保罗先讲福音：「『基督耶稣降世，为要拯救罪人。』这话是可信的，是十分可佩服的。在罪人中我是个罪魁。」（提前1:15）在讲完监督和执事以后，他又唱出一首颂赞基督的诗：「大哉，敬虔的奥秘……」（提前3:16）。教会的秩序，是从福音来的；神的家，是建立在基督身上的。

作者与写作背景

1. 提摩太是谁。 提摩太很可能是路司得人，母亲是「信主之犹太妇人」，父亲是希腊人（徒16:1）。他从小就从外祖母罗以和母亲友妮基那里认识圣经（提后1:5；提后3:15）。保罗第二次旅行布道时带他同去（徒16:3），此后他一直是保罗最亲近的同工之一。保罗称他为「我所亲爱、有忠心的儿子」（林前4:17），又说：「我没有别人与我同心」（腓2:20）。保罗也常常派他去处理棘手的教会问题（帖前3:2；林前4:17；腓2:19）。

  • 他的为人： 从保罗的话看，提摩太可能比较年轻（提前4:12），身体也不太好（提前5:23），有时显得胆怯（参林前16:10-11；提后1:7）。保罗却把这样一个人留在一个艰难的地方。

2. 以弗所。 以弗所是罗马亚细亚省最重要的城市之一，有著名的亚底米神庙（参徒19:27、35）。保罗在那里住了将近三年（徒19:10；徒20:31），福音从那里传遍亚细亚。保罗与以弗所长老告别时曾警告说：「就是你们中间，也必有人起来说悖谬的话，要引诱门徒跟从他们。」（徒20:30）提摩太前书显示，这话已经应验了。

3. 作者问题。 提摩太前书、提摩太后书和提多书常被合称为教牧书信。从爱任纽（约主后180年）起，教会普遍接受这三封信是保罗写的；只有马吉安的正典没有收入这三封信，据说他提安也不接受提摩太前后书。

  • 怀疑的看法： 十九世纪初，施莱尔马赫在1807年撰文质疑提摩太前书，后来艾希霍恩把质疑扩大到三封信。此后许多学者（如哈里森、马丁·狄比留斯）认为，教牧书信是保罗死后有人托名写的。他们的理由主要是：用词和文风与保罗其他书信不同（如「敬虔」、「纯正的道理」、「可信的话」这些词很常见）；教会的组织似乎比保罗在世时更完备；信中提到的保罗行踪，很难放进使徒行传的记载里。
  • 折中的看法： 也有福音派学者（如霍华德·马歇尔）认为，可能是保罗的门生在他死后不久，根据他的教导和材料写成的，而不是刻意冒名。
  • 支持保罗为作者的看法： 许多福音派学者（如乔治·奈特、威廉·孟恩斯、菲利普·汤纳），以及一些非福音派学者（如路加·提摩太·约翰逊）认为是保罗写的。他们回答说：主题不同，用词自然不同；保罗可能用了代笔的人（参罗16:22），文风也会受影响；长老（监督）和执事在保罗早期的书信和使徒行传中已经出现（徒14:23；徒20:17；腓1:1）；至于行踪：使徒行传写到保罗在罗马被软禁两年就结束了（徒28:30-31）。许多人认为保罗后来获释，再次出外旅行，这几封信就写在那段时间。
  • 本研读的立场： 照信本身所说的（提前1:1），把它当作保罗的书信来读。

4. 写作时间。 如果保罗在罗马第一次被囚后获释，提摩太前书大约写于主后62-64年，在他再次被捕、殉道（提后4:6）以前。也有少数学者（如约翰·罗宾逊）认为可以放在使徒行传的时期之内，例如保罗离开以弗所往马其顿去的时候（徒20:1）。本研读采用前一种看法，这也是主张保罗为作者的学者中较普遍的看法。罗马的革利免在主后一世纪末说，保罗到了西方的尽头（《革利免一书》5.7）；许多人认为，这是保罗获释后再出外旅行的线索。

5. 异教是什么。 保罗没有系统地描述以弗所的错误教训，我们只能从信中的零星线索来推想：

  • 有犹太的色彩：「无穷的家谱」、「想要作教法师」（提前1:4、7）。
  • 有禁欲的色彩：「禁止嫁娶，又禁戒食物」（提前4:3）。
  • 自以为有特别的知识：保罗称之为「似是而非的学问」（提前6:20），原文就是「知识」这个词。
  • 和争论、钱财有关：「专好问难，争辩言词」，「以敬虔为得利的门路」（提前6:4-5）。

许多学者认为，这种教训混合了犹太传统和禁欲主义，也带有一些后来发展成诺斯底主义的早期倾向；提摩太后书还提到许米乃等人说「复活的事已过」（提后2:17-18）。保罗的回应不是只辩倒对方，而是把人带回福音：命令的总归就是爱（提前1:5），律法要用得合宜（提前1:8），神所造的物都是好的（提前4:4），敬虔加上知足的心便是大利（提前6:6）。

钥匙经文：1:15；3:15-16

1. 「基督耶稣降世，为要拯救罪人」。 这是教牧书信五句「可信的话」中的第一句（提前1:15；提前3:1；提前4:9；提后2:11；多3:8）。保罗在整封信的开头，先说出自己是怎样一个人：「在罪人中我是个罪魁。」提摩太要整顿教会，但教会不是一群好人的俱乐部，而是蒙了怜悯的罪人组成的家。

2. 「在神的家中当怎样行」。 保罗用「家」来形容教会。所以他教导提摩太，对老年人要「劝他如同父亲；劝少年人如同弟兄；劝老年妇女如同母亲；劝少年妇女如同姊妹」（提前5:1-2）。教会的秩序不是公司的规章，也不是论资排辈的宗族，而是一个家的秩序；家里有父亲，就是永生的神。

3. 「真理的柱石和根基」。 教会不是真理的来源，而是支撑、高举真理的柱子和根基。有学者认为，这可能会叫以弗所人想起亚底米神庙那许多高大的柱子。神的教会也是一座殿，但它所高举的，是关于基督的真理。

4. 「大哉，敬虔的奥秘」。 提前3:16很可能是初期教会的一首诗歌，或一段认信的话。敬虔的奥秘不是一套方法，而是一个人：「神在肉身显现……被接在荣耀里。」和合本这里作「神」，跟随的是较晚的抄本；较早的抄本作那一位，英文标准译本就是这样译的。无论哪一种读法，所说的都是道成肉身的基督（详见第三章）。教会要怎样行，最终在于教会认识谁。

全书结构

提摩太前书是一封书信，大致可以这样分：

  • 问安（提前1:1-2）。
  • 抵挡异教，持守福音（提前1:3-20）：命令的总归就是爱；律法要用得合宜；保罗自己是蒙怜悯的罪魁；要打那美好的仗。
  • 敬拜和祷告（提前2:1-15）：为万人祷告，因为神愿意万人得救，只有一位中保；男人、女人在聚会中当怎样行。
  • 监督和执事（提前3:1-13）。
  • 神的家与敬虔的奥秘（提前3:14-16）。
  • 作基督耶稣的好执事（提前4:1-16）：后来必有人离弃真道；神所造的物都是好的；操练敬虔；不可叫人小看你年轻。
  • 怎样对待教会中的各种人（提前5:1-6:2）：老年人和少年人、寡妇、长老、作仆人的。
  • 敬虔与钱财，最后的嘱咐（提前6:3-21）：敬虔加上知足的心便是大利；贪财是万恶之根；要打那美好的仗；嘱咐富足的人；要保守所托付的。
怎样读这卷书

1. 先看福音，再看规矩。 这封信有许多关于教会秩序的教导，但保罗每讲一段规矩，就会回到福音（提前1:15-16；提前2:5-6；提前3:16；提前6:13-16）。读的时候，要问：这条教导和基督所做的有什么关系？

2. 留意「敬虔」。 「敬虔」在这封信中出现了很多次（提前2:2；提前3:16；提前4:7-8；提前6:3、5-6、11）。保罗所说的敬虔，不只是宗教的外表，而是在生活中敬畏神、顺服神。敬虔的根，是「敬虔的奥秘」，就是基督自己。这不是靠自己修身养性修出来的，而是从认识基督生出来的。

3. 读难解的经文时要谦卑。 这封信有几处经文，历代忠心的信徒有不同的理解：女人在聚会中的角色（提前2:11-15）、「只作一个妇人的丈夫」（提前3:2）、提前3:11说的是执事的妻子还是女执事、寡妇的名册（提前5:9）。我们要认真查考经文，把不同的看法公平地摆出来，也要在意见不同时彼此尊重。

4. 留意保罗对一个人的爱。 这是一位年长的使徒写给「因信主作我真儿子」（提前1:2）的信。保罗叮嘱他，也关心他的身体（提前5:23），为他打气（提前4:12），把重担交给他，又把他交托给神。读这封信，也可以留意神怎样用一个人去坚固另一个人。

默想

默想： 「我往马其顿去的时候，曾劝你仍住在以弗所。」（提前1:3）保罗离开了，提摩太却要留下来。留在一个有人反对、有人背后说话、问题又多的地方，不是一件容易的事。我也可能正在一个想离开的地方：带我信主的牧者调走了，同工一个个离开，只剩下我；或者是一个艰难的教会，一个总是有难处的家。我要先分辨：如果那里有人在伤害我，有人用权柄压制、欺负人，主没有要我留在危险里，我可以寻求帮助、向警方或相关机构举报（罗13:4），也可以离开。可是如果只是辛苦，只是看不到成果，只是没有人感谢，我就要在主面前安静下来，问他是否要我留下来。留下或离开，本身都不是属灵高低的记号；保罗自己也离开了以弗所，往马其顿去作主的工。如果我已经离开了，也不必一直背着这件事；若有亏欠，可以带到主面前，他是赦免人的主；他在我现在所在的地方与我同在。我想起耶稣。他「定意向耶路撒冷去」（路9:51），因为他知道那是父差他去的地方。后来他被钉在十字架上，人在底下讥诮他说：「你如果是神的儿子，就从十字架上下来吧！」（太27:40）他本来可以下来，却没有下来。他留在那里，是为了担当我的罪。我留下来，不是要靠自己咬紧牙关撑下去；乃是因为那位为我留在十字架上的主，也与我同在这里。今天我可以对他说：主啊，我在这里，求你在这里坚固我。
entries.content_en:
What This Book Is About

1 Timothy is a letter Paul wrote to a coworker. Paul had gone on to Macedonia and left Timothy in Ephesus "that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine" (1 Timothy 1:3). The church in Ephesus already had elders (see Acts 20:17), but trouble had come: some devoted themselves "to myths and endless genealogies" (1 Timothy 1:4); some desired "to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying" (1 Timothy 1:7); some forbade marriage and required abstinence from foods (1 Timothy 4:3); some imagined "that godliness is a means of gain" (1 Timothy 6:5). In this setting Timothy was to hold fast to the truth and set God's household in order.

Paul himself states why he is writing: "if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of truth" (1 Timothy 3:15).

So the letter deals with many practical questions of church life:

  • Teaching: resisting false teaching and holding to "sound words" (1 Timothy 6:3) and resisting "whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine" (1 Timothy 1:10).
  • Prayer and worship: praying for all people, for kings and all in high positions (1 Timothy 2:1–2); how men and women are to conduct themselves in the gathering (1 Timothy 2:8–15).
  • Leaders: the character of overseers and deacons (1 Timothy 3:1–13); how to treat elders, including accusations against them (1 Timothy 5:17–25).
  • Different people in the church: older and younger people (1 Timothy 5:1–2), widows (1 Timothy 5:3–16), slaves (1 Timothy 6:1–2), the rich (1 Timothy 6:17–19).
  • Timothy himself: train yourself for godliness (1 Timothy 4:7); let no one despise you for your youth (1 Timothy 4:12); keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching (1 Timothy 4:16); flee the love of money (1 Timothy 6:10–11); fight the good fight of the faith (1 Timothy 6:12).

But the letter is more than a church manual. Before giving any instructions, Paul speaks of the gospel: "The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost" (1 Timothy 1:15). After describing overseers and deacons, he breaks into a hymn in praise of Christ: "Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness..." (1 Timothy 3:16). The order of the church comes from the gospel; God's household is built on Christ.

Author and Setting

1. Who Timothy was. Timothy was probably from Lystra; his mother was "a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek" (Acts 16:1). From childhood he had known the Scriptures through his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Tim 1:5; 2 Tim 3:15). Paul took him along on his second missionary journey (Acts 16:3), and from then on he was one of Paul's closest coworkers. Paul calls him "my beloved and faithful child in the Lord" (1 Cor 4:17) and says, "I have no one like him" (Phil 2:20). Paul often sent him to deal with hard church situations (1 Thess 3:2; 1 Cor 4:17; Phil 2:19).

  • His temperament: from Paul's words, Timothy may have been relatively young (1 Timothy 4:12) and not in good health (1 Timothy 5:23), and at times he seems to have been timid (see 1 Cor 16:10–11; 2 Tim 1:7). Paul left someone like this in a hard place.

2. Ephesus. Ephesus was one of the most important cities in the Roman province of Asia, home to the famous temple of Artemis (see Acts 19:27, 35). Paul stayed there nearly three years (Acts 19:10; Acts 20:31), and from there the gospel spread through Asia. When Paul said farewell to the Ephesian elders, he warned them: "from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them" (Acts 20:30). 1 Timothy shows that this had come true.

3. Authorship. 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus are often called the "Pastoral Letters." From Irenaeus (c. AD 180) on, the church broadly received all three as Paul's; only Marcion's canon left them out, and Tatian is reported to have rejected 1 and 2 Timothy.

  • The doubting view: since the early nineteenth century (Schleiermacher's 1807 study questioned 1 Timothy, and Eichhorn soon extended the doubt to all three), many scholars (such as P. N. Harrison and Martin Dibelius) have held that the Pastoral Letters were written in Paul's name after his death. Their main reasons: the vocabulary and style differ from Paul's other letters (words such as "godliness," "sound doctrine" and "trustworthy saying" are common here); church organization seems more developed than in Paul's day; and the movements of Paul mentioned in the letters are hard to fit into the account in Acts.
  • A middle view: some evangelical scholars (such as I. Howard Marshall) suggest a disciple of Paul wrote them soon after his death, from his teaching and materials, without intent to deceive.
  • The view that Paul wrote it: many evangelical scholars (such as George Knight, William Mounce, Philip Towner), and some scholars outside evangelicalism (such as Luke Timothy Johnson), hold that Paul wrote it. They answer that different subjects naturally call for different vocabulary; Paul may have used a secretary (see Rom 16:22), which would affect the style; elders/overseers and deacons already appear in Paul's earlier letters and in Acts (Acts 14:23; Acts 20:17; Phil 1:1); and as for Paul's movements, Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years (Acts 28:30–31). Many believe Paul was later released and traveled again, and that these letters were written in that period.
  • This study's position: following the letter's own claim (1 Timothy 1:1), we read it as Paul's letter.

4. Date. If Paul was released after his first Roman imprisonment, 1 Timothy was written around AD 62–64, before he was arrested again and martyred (2 Tim 4:6). A few scholars (such as John A. T. Robinson) place it within the period covered by Acts, for example when Paul left Ephesus for Macedonia (Acts 20:1). This study follows the first view, the usual one among those who hold Pauline authorship (late in the first century Clement of Rome says Paul reached "the limits of the west," which many take as a hint of travels after his release; 1 Clement 5.7).

5. What the false teaching was. Paul does not describe the Ephesian error systematically; we can only infer it from scattered clues in the letter:

  • It had a Jewish coloring: "endless genealogies," "desiring to be teachers of the law" (1 Timothy 1:4, 7).
  • It had an ascetic coloring: those who "forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods" (1 Timothy 4:3).
  • It claimed special knowledge: Paul calls it "what is falsely called 'knowledge'" (1 Timothy 6:20).
  • It was tied to quarrels and money: "an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words," "imagining that godliness is a means of gain" (1 Timothy 6:4–5).

Many scholars think this was a mixture of Jewish tradition, asceticism and some early tendencies of what later became Gnosticism; 2 Timothy also mentions Hymenaeus and others "saying that the resurrection has already happened" (2 Tim 2:17–18). Paul's response is not only to refute them but to bring people back to the gospel: the aim of our charge is love (1 Timothy 1:5); the law is good if used lawfully (1 Timothy 1:8); everything created by God is good (1 Timothy 4:4); godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6:6).

Key Verses: 1:15; 3:15–16

1. "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." This is the first of the five "trustworthy sayings" in the Pastoral Letters (1 Timothy 1:15; 1 Timothy 3:1; 1 Timothy 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Titus 3:8). At the very start of the letter Paul says what kind of man he is: "of whom I am the foremost." Timothy is to set the church in order, but the church is not a club of good people; it is the household of sinners who have received mercy.

2. "How one ought to behave in the household of God." Paul calls the church a household. So he tells Timothy to "encourage him as you would a father. Treat younger men like brothers, older women like mothers, younger women like sisters" (1 Timothy 5:1–2). The order of the church is not a company's regulations, nor a clan ranked by seniority, but the order of a family, and the Father of this family is the living God.

3. "A pillar and buttress of truth." The church is not the source of truth; it is the pillar and foundation that holds the truth up. Some scholars suggest this may have reminded the Ephesians of the many tall columns of the temple of Artemis. God's church is a temple too, but what it holds up is the truth about Christ.

4. "Great indeed... is the mystery of godliness." Verse 1 Timothy 3:16 is very likely an early Christian hymn or confession. The mystery of godliness is not a method but a person: "He was manifested in the flesh... taken up in glory." The CUV reads "God" here, following later manuscripts; the earliest manuscripts read "who" (ESV "He"). Either way the subject is the incarnate Christ (see chapter 3). How the church is to behave depends, in the end, on whom the church knows.

Structure of the Book

1 Timothy is a letter and can be outlined roughly as follows:

  • Greeting (1 Timothy 1:1–2).
  • Resisting false teaching, holding to the gospel (1 Timothy 1:3–20): the aim of our charge is love; the law is good if used lawfully; Paul himself is the foremost of sinners who received mercy; wage the good warfare.
  • Worship and prayer (1 Timothy 2:1–15): pray for all people, because God desires all people to be saved and there is one mediator; how men and women are to conduct themselves in the gathering.
  • Overseers and deacons (1 Timothy 3:1–13).
  • The household of God and the mystery of godliness (1 Timothy 3:14–16).
  • A good servant of Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 4:1–16): some will depart from the faith; everything created by God is good; train yourself for godliness; let no one despise you for your youth.
  • How to treat different people in the church (1 Timothy 5:1–6:2): older and younger people, widows, elders, slaves.
  • Godliness and money; final charge (1 Timothy 6:3–21): godliness with contentment is great gain; the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils; fight the good fight; a charge to the rich; guard the deposit.
How to Read This Book

1. Look first at the gospel, then at the instructions. The letter has much teaching on church order, but each time Paul gives instructions he returns to the gospel (1 Timothy 1:15–16; 1 Timothy 2:5–6; 1 Timothy 3:16; 1 Timothy 6:13–16). As you read, ask: how does this instruction relate to what Christ has done?

2. Notice "godliness." The word "godliness" appears many times in this letter (1 Timothy 2:2; 1 Timothy 3:16; 1 Timothy 4:7–8; 1 Timothy 6:3, 5–6, 11). As Paul uses it, it is not merely a religious exterior but reverence for God and obedience to him in daily life, rooted in "the mystery of godliness," Christ himself. It is not self-cultivation but the fruit of knowing Christ.

3. Read the hard passages with humility. In several passages faithful believers through the centuries have understood the text differently: women's role in the gathering (1 Timothy 2:11–15); "the husband of one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2); whether 1 Timothy 3:11 speaks of deacons' wives or women deacons; the list of widows (1 Timothy 5:9). We should study the text carefully, set out the different views fairly, and respect one another where we differ.

4. Notice Paul's love for one man. This is a letter from an aging apostle to "my true child in the faith" (1 Timothy 1:2). Paul charges him, cares about his health (1 Timothy 5:23), encourages him (1 Timothy 4:12), lays a burden on him and commits him to God. As you read, notice how God uses one person to strengthen another.

Meditation

Reflect: "As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus" (1 Timothy 1:3). Paul left; Timothy had to stay. Staying in a place where people oppose you, talk behind your back and the problems never end is not easy. I may be in a place I want to leave: the pastor who led me to faith has moved on, coworkers have left one by one, and I am the one still here; or a difficult church, a home where there is always trouble. First I need to discern: if someone there is harming me, if someone is using authority to crush or bully others, the Lord has not asked me to stay in danger; I can seek help, report it to the police or the proper authorities (Rom 13:4), and I can leave. But if it is only hard, only fruitless to my eyes, only unthanked, then I need to grow quiet before the Lord and ask whether he wants me to stay. Staying or leaving is not in itself a measure of spirituality; Paul himself left Ephesus for the Lord's work in Macedonia. If I have already left, I need not keep carrying it; if I failed in leaving, I can bring that to the Lord, who forgives; he is with me where I am now. I think of Jesus. He "set his face to go to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51), because he knew that was where the Father had sent him. Later, when he hung on the cross, people below mocked him: "If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross" (Matt 27:40). He could have come down, and he did not. He stayed there to bear my sin. If I stay, it is not by gritting my teeth and holding on in my own strength; it is because the Lord who stayed on the cross for me is here with me too. Today I can say to him: Lord, here I am; strengthen me here.
