entries.content:
本章脉络

第一章分成五段。问安（1-2节）：保罗称提摩太为「因信主作我真儿子」，愿恩惠、怜悯、平安归与他。命令的总归就是爱（3-7节）：提摩太要嘱咐那几个人不可传异教，不可听从荒渺的话语和无穷的家谱；这些人偏离了爱，就是从清洁的心、无亏的良心、无伪的信心生出来的爱。律法要用得合宜（8-11节）：律法是好的，是为不法和不服的人设立的，与那荣耀的福音相合。我是罪人中的罪魁（12-17节）：保罗从前是亵渎神、逼迫人的，却蒙了怜悯；基督耶稣降世，为要拯救罪人；基督在他身上显明一切的忍耐，给后来信他的人作榜样。打那美好的仗（18-20节）：提摩太要常存信心和无亏的良心；有人丢弃良心，在真道上如同船破坏了一般。

这一章的中心是第15节。保罗要提摩太去纠正别人的错误，却也要他记住：我自己是罪魁，我是蒙了怜悯的人。这是一切服事的起点。

深读 1:3-7 命令的总归就是爱

1. 「荒渺无凭的话语和无穷的家谱」。 「我往马其顿去的时候，曾劝你仍住在以弗所，好嘱咐那几个人不可传异教，也不可听从荒渺无凭的话语和无穷的家谱」（提前1:3-4）。

  • 「异教」： 原文的意思是传别的道理。这里不是指教会外面的其他宗教，而是在教会里面传与使徒教训不同的道理（参提前6:3；加1:6-7）。
  • 「荒渺无凭的话语和无穷的家谱」： 保罗没有细说内容。许多解经家认为，这可能是根据旧约人物的家谱，编出许多传说和猜测，这在当时一些犹太著作中很常见（参多1:14「犹太人荒谬的言语」）。
  • 「只生辩论」： 这些事叫人争辩不休，「并不发明神在信上所立的章程」。这里的「发明」是阐明、彰显的意思。「章程」这个词原文与管家有关，指管家治理一个家的安排；在这里是指神安排救恩、治理他家的计划。这计划是在信心里领受的，不是靠猜测找出来的。

2. 「命令的总归就是爱」。 「但命令的总归就是爱；这爱是从清洁的心和无亏的良心，无伪的信心生出来的。」（提前1:5）

  • 「命令」： 这里指保罗交给提摩太的嘱咐（提前1:3、18），不是指摩西的律法。提摩太去纠正错误的目的，不是要赢得辩论，而是要叫人生出爱来。
  • 爱的三个源头： 清洁的心（内心不被污秽搅乱，参太5:8）、无亏的良心（在神面前没有隐藏的罪）、无伪的信心（不是表演给人看的信心）。这三样是内里的，爱是从里面流出来的。
  • 对照： 那些传异教的人追求知识和辩论，结果是争竞；福音的教导追求的是爱。

3. 「想要作教法师」。 「有人偏离这些，反去讲虚浮的话，想要作教法师，却不明白自己所讲说的所论定的。」（提前1:6-7）这些人很有把握，「所论定的」原文是很肯定地断言；可是保罗说，他们其实不明白。在教会里，讲得最肯定的人，不一定是最明白的人。

要点：教导真理的目的不是赢得辩论，而是生出爱来；这爱从一颗被福音洁净的心、一个在神面前无亏的良心、一份不虚假的信心中流出来。
深读 1:8-11 律法原是好的

1. 「律法原是好的，只要人用得合宜」。 「我们知道律法原是好的，只要人用得合宜」（提前1:8；参罗7:12）。保罗不反对律法，他反对的是错用律法：在以弗所，是把律法当作猜测和争论的材料（提前1:4、7）；更普遍的危险，是把律法当作叫人自以为义的阶梯。

2. 「律法不是为义人设立的」。 「因为律法不是为义人设立的，乃是为不法和不服的，不虔诚和犯罪的……设立的」（提前1:9）。

  • 这是什么意思？ 保罗不是说义人可以不顾律法，而是说律法的定罪功用是对着罪人的。律法像一面镜子，叫人看见自己的罪（参罗3:20）。
  • 清单的次序： 许多解经家注意到，从「弑父母」开始，这清单大致跟着十诫的后半部：孝敬父母（第五诫，参出21:15）、不可杀人（第六诫）、不可奸淫（第七诫）、不可偷盗（第八诫）、不可作假见证（第九诫，「说谎话的，并起假誓的」）。前面的「不虔诚」、「不圣洁」等，大致可以对应十诫前半部得罪神的罪。
  • 「抢人口」： 就是拐卖人口，对应第八诫。摩西律法把这罪定为死罪（出21:16；申24:7），一些犹太解经者（如斐洛）称之为最严重的偷窃。今天拐卖妇女儿童的事仍然存在，神看这是极重的罪。
  • 「亲男色的」： 保罗在这里和林前6:9用的是同一个词。这个词很可能是从七十士译本利18:22、提前20:13「与男人苟合」的用语组合而成的，在清单中也正放在第七诫的位置上。历代教会普遍认为，这是指男人之间的性行为；近代有学者（如博斯韦尔）提出不同的理解，也有学者（如赖特、盖格农）作了回应，但多数解经家（包括许多非福音派学者）仍然这样理解。保罗在这里说的是行为，不是一个人所经历的试探。我们也要留意：保罗把这罪和说谎、起假誓放在同一张清单里，清单上的每一种罪都需要福音。保罗在林前6:11也说：「你们中间也有人从前是这样；但如今……已经洗净，成圣，称义了。」福音呼召每一个罪人悔改，包括我自己；也应许每一个悔改信靠的人得着完全的洗净。在同性吸引中挣扎的人，教会不可推开，也不可轻看；我们每一个人都是靠同一位救主得救的。

3. 「照着可称颂之神交托我荣耀福音」。 律法所定罪的，是一切「敌正道的事」（提前1:10）；而这正道是「照着可称颂之神交托我荣耀福音说的」（提前1:11）。律法叫人看见罪，福音叫人看见救主。律法用得合宜，就会把人带到福音面前。

要点：律法是好的，能照出我们的罪，却不是给我们夸口的阶梯；律法用得合宜，就会把罪人带到那荣耀的福音面前。
深读 1:12-17 在罪人中我是个罪魁

1. 「我感谢那给我力量的」。 「我感谢那给我力量的我们主基督耶稣，因他以我有忠心，派我服事他。」（提前1:12）保罗服事主，不是因为他先有力量，而是基督「给我力量」。「以我有忠心」不是说保罗先证明了自己可靠，然后才被选上；下一节立刻说明，他被派的时候是怎样的一个人。

2. 「我从前是亵渎神的，逼迫人的，侮慢人的」。 「我从前是亵渎神的，逼迫人的，侮慢人的；然而我还蒙了怜悯」（提前1:13）。

  • 三个词： 「亵渎神的」是用言语攻击神；「逼迫人的」是用行动迫害教会（参徒26:9-11）；「侮慢人的」原文指傲慢、施暴的人。保罗没有把自己的过去说得轻描淡写。
  • 「因我是不信不明白的时候而做的」： 这不是说保罗因为不明白就不算有罪，也不是说他配得怜悯。旧约区分误犯的罪和擅敢行的罪（民15:27-31）；彼得也对耶路撒冷的人说：「你们做这事是出于不知」（徒3:17；参路23:34，有些古抄本没有这句）。许多解经家认为，保罗的意思是：他的罪虽然可怕，却不是民数记所说「擅敢行」、明知故犯地抵挡真理的罪（民15:30；对照本章20节）。他蒙怜悯的真正原因在第16节：基督要显明他的忍耐。所以保罗仍然说「我还蒙了怜悯」，因为怜悯从来都是不配得的。

3. 「我主的恩是格外丰盛」。 「并且我主的恩是格外丰盛，使我在基督耶稣里有信心和爱心。」（提前1:14）「格外丰盛」原文是满溢出来的意思（参罗5:20「恩典就更显多了」）。保罗从前满了亵渎和暴力，现在恩典满溢，带来信心和爱心，正是第5节所说的：从无伪的信心生出来的爱。

4. 「基督耶稣降世，为要拯救罪人」。 「『基督耶稣降世，为要拯救罪人。』这话是可信的，是十分可佩服的。在罪人中我是个罪魁。」（提前1:15）

  • 「这话是可信的」： 这是教牧书信中五句「可信的话」的第一句（参提前3:1；提前4:9；提后2:11；多3:8），很可能是当时教会中流传的一句话，保罗加以认可。和合本「十分可佩服的」是旧时的说法，意思是值得人完全接受、诚心信服。
  • 「降世」： 这句话包含了基督先存的意思：他本来在父那里，然后来到世上（参约1:9；约3:17）。
  • 「为要拯救罪人」： 许多华人认为宗教都是劝人为善；但基督来，不是为了帮助好人变得更好，而是为了拯救罪人（参路5:32；路19:10）。他拯救罪人，是藉着舍自己，代替罪人受死：「他舍自己作万人的赎价」（提前2:6）。罪人得救，不是靠把自己改好，乃是靠信他得永生（提前1:16）。
  • 「我是个罪魁」： 注意保罗用的是现在式：「我是」，不是「我从前是」。他得救多年以后，仍然这样看自己。这不是假谦虚，也不是华人习惯的客套自谦。一个人越认识神，就越看见自己的罪，也越看见恩典之大；保罗说的，正是这样的人的话（参林前15:9-10）。

5. 「显明他一切的忍耐」。 「然而，我蒙了怜悯，是因耶稣基督要在我这罪魁身上显明他一切的忍耐，给后来信他得永生的人作榜样。」（提前1:16）

  • 「一切的忍耐」： 基督对保罗的忍耐是完全的。在大马士革的路上，主没有对扫罗说要惩罚他，而是说：「扫罗！扫罗！你为什么逼迫我？」（徒9:4）
  • 「作榜样」： 原文可以指样本、草图，就是给后来的人看的样式。神救了保罗，好像是要告诉后来每一个人：如果连他都能得救，你也能，只要你信靠他。没有人罪大到基督的忍耐够不着。

6. 「但愿尊贵、荣耀归与……独一的神」。 「但愿尊贵、荣耀归与那不能朽坏、不能看见、永世的君王、独一的神，直到永永远远。阿们！」（提前1:17）保罗讲到自己的得救，就忍不住赞美。这颂赞的话出自旧约：「惟耶和华是真神，是活神，是永远的王」（耶10:10；参申6:4）。在拜亚底米、也尊奉罗马皇帝的以弗所，保罗宣告只有一位「永世的君王、独一的神」。真正认识恩典的人，最后不是夸自己，而是敬拜神。

要点：基督耶稣降世，为要拯救罪人，这是可信的话。没有人好到不需要他，也没有人坏到他救不了；他在罪魁身上显明的忍耐，今天仍在等候每一个人回转归向他。
深读 1:18-20 打那美好的仗

1. 「照从前指着你的预言」。 「我儿提摩太啊，我照从前指着你的预言，将这命令交托你，叫你因此可以打那美好的仗」（提前1:18）。提摩太被按立的时候，曾有指着他的预言（参提前4:14）。保罗提醒他：你的服事不是你自己选的，是神呼召的。在困难的时候，这呼召可以坚固他。

2. 「常存信心和无亏的良心」。 「常存信心和无亏的良心。有人丢弃良心，就在真道上如同船破坏了一般。」（提前1:19）

  • 良心和真道连在一起： 一个人若长期违背良心，在生活中容让罪，最后往往会改变自己的信仰来配合自己的生活。错误的道理常常不是从头脑开始的，而是从被丢弃的良心开始的。这不是说每一个有疑问的人都在隐藏罪；诚实的疑问可以带到神面前。
  • 「如同船破坏了一般」： 以弗所是港口城市，读信的人都知道船破是什么样子。船破常常是先偏离了航道（参提前1:6「偏离」）。

3. 「把他们交给撒但」。 「其中有许米乃和亚历山大；我已经把他们交给撒但，使他们受责罚就不再谤渎了。」（提前1:20）

  • 这是什么意思？ 多数解经家认为，这是指把他们赶出教会的团契（参林前5:5、13），使他们回到撒但掌权的世界里。
  • 目的是挽回： 「使他们受责罚」原文是受管教、受训练的意思。教会施行纪律，目的不是报复，而是叫人悔改。华人教会有时为了顾全情面不肯管教，有时又把管教变成整人；这两样都不合圣经。
  • 这两个人： 许米乃后来又出现在提后2:17-18，说「复活的事已过」；亚历山大可能就是提后4:14的「铜匠亚历山大」，但不能确定。
要点：服事是一场美好的仗；打这仗，是出于神的呼召（提前1:18），力量是基督所赐的（提前1:12），我们靠着他常存信心和无亏的良心。良心被丢弃，信仰的船就会偏离航道；但教会的管教仍以挽回为目的。
默想

默想： 「然而，我蒙了怜悯，是因耶稣基督要在我这罪魁身上显明他一切的忍耐，给后来信他得永生的人作榜样。」（提前1:16）如果有人请我讲讲自己信主的见证，我会怎样讲？我可能会讲我从前怎样，后来怎样改变，现在生活怎样好起来。这些都可能是真的。可是保罗讲自己的见证，重点不在他变得多好，而在基督多么忍耐。也许我觉得自己的见证太平淡：从小在教会长大，没有做过什么大坏事。可是保罗说的「罪魁」，不是要我比较谁的罪更大，而是要我看见：我和保罗一样，都需要基督的怜悯，也都是靠他的忍耐活到今天的。也许正相反，我觉得自己的过去太黑暗，不敢说出来，怕别人知道了会看不起我。可是保罗把自己最不堪的过去写在信里，因为那正是基督忍耐的证据。我不必把每一件事都告诉每一个人，有些事只适合对一两位可信的人说；如果那黑暗是别人加在我身上的，那不是我的罪。可是在主面前，我什么都不必再藏，因为他早已知道，也没有放弃我。今天我可以这样回想：主在哪些时候忍耐了我？在我还不信的时候，在我信了却又跌倒的时候，在我一次又一次犯同样的罪的时候，他都没有放弃我。我的见证，最后要讲的不是我，而是他。然后，我也可以像保罗一样，用这句话结束：「但愿尊贵、荣耀归与那不能朽坏、不能看见、永世的君王、独一的神，直到永永远远。阿们！」（提前1:17）
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 1 falls into five parts. Greeting (vv. 1–2): Paul calls Timothy "my true child in the faith" and wishes him grace, mercy and peace. The aim of our charge is love (vv. 3–7): Timothy is to charge certain persons not to teach a different doctrine or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies; these people have swerved from the love that comes from a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith. Using the law lawfully (vv. 8–11): the law is good; it is laid down for the lawless and disobedient, in keeping with the glorious gospel. I am the foremost of sinners (vv. 12–17): Paul was once a blasphemer and persecutor, yet he received mercy; Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; in Paul Christ displayed his perfect patience as an example to those who would believe. Wage the good warfare (vv. 18–20): Timothy is to hold faith and a good conscience; some have rejected conscience and made shipwreck of their faith.

The center of the chapter is verse 15. Paul is sending Timothy to correct others' errors, but he also reminds him: I myself am the foremost of sinners; I am a man who has received mercy. That is where all ministry begins.

Going Deeper: 1:3–7 The Aim of Our Charge Is Love

1. "Myths and endless genealogies." "As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies" (1 Timothy 1:3–4).

  • "A different doctrine": the Greek means "to teach otherwise." It does not refer to other religions outside, but to teaching inside the church that differs from the apostles' teaching (see 1 Timothy 6:3; Gal 1:6–7).
  • "Myths and endless genealogies": Paul does not describe their content. Many commentators think these may have been legends and speculations built on the genealogies of Old Testament figures, something common in some Jewish writings of the time (see Titus 1:14, "Jewish myths").
  • "Which promote speculations": these things lead to endless argument, "rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith." "Stewardship" is the word for a household manager's office: God's plan for arranging salvation and ordering his household. That plan is received by faith, not discovered by speculation.

2. "The aim of our charge is love." "The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith" (1 Timothy 1:5).

  • "Our charge": this refers to the instruction Paul gave Timothy (1 Timothy 1:3, 18), not to the law of Moses. The purpose of Timothy's correcting error is not to win an argument but to produce love.
  • Three sources of love: a pure heart (an inner life not muddied by defilement, see Matt 5:8), a good conscience (no hidden sin before God), and a sincere faith (not a faith performed for others). All three are inward; love flows out from within.
  • The contrast: the false teachers pursue knowledge and debate, and the result is quarreling; the gospel's teaching aims at love.

3. "Desiring to be teachers of the law." "Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions" (1 Timothy 1:6–7). These people are very sure of themselves; "make confident assertions" means to state something emphatically. Yet Paul says they do not actually understand. In the church, the one who speaks most confidently is not necessarily the one who understands most.

The point: The aim of teaching the truth is not to win arguments but to produce love, love that flows from a heart cleansed by the gospel, a conscience clear before God and a faith that is not pretended.
Going Deeper: 1:8–11 The Law Is Good

1. "The law is good, if one uses it lawfully." "Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully" (1 Timothy 1:8; see Rom 7:12). Paul is not against the law; he is against its misuse: in Ephesus, as material for speculation and argument (1 Timothy 1:4, 7); and, more generally, as a ladder for self-righteousness.

2. "The law is not laid down for the just." "Understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners..." (1 Timothy 1:9).

  • What does this mean? Paul is not saying the righteous may ignore the law, but that the law's condemning work is aimed at sinners. The law is like a mirror that shows people their sin (see Rom 3:20).
  • The order of the list: many commentators notice that from "those who strike their fathers and mothers" onward, the list roughly follows the second half of the Ten Commandments: honor your father and mother (fifth; see Exod 21:15), you shall not murder (sixth), you shall not commit adultery (seventh), you shall not steal (eighth; "enslavers" are kidnappers and traffickers, a capital crime in the law of Moses [Exod 21:16; Deut 24:7], which some Jewish interpreters [such as Philo] called the worst form of theft), you shall not bear false witness (ninth; "liars, perjurers"). The earlier words, "ungodly," "unholy" and so on, may correspond broadly to sins against God in the first half. Trafficking of women and children still happens today; God counts it a grave sin.
  • "Men who practice homosexuality": Paul uses the same word here as in 1 Cor 6:9. The word appears to be formed from the Septuagint wording of Lev 18:22; 1 Timothy 20:13 ("lie with a male"), and in the list it stands in the place of the seventh commandment. The church through the centuries has generally understood it to refer to sexual relations between men; some modern scholars (such as John Boswell) have proposed other readings, others (such as David F. Wright and Robert Gagnon) have replied, but most commentators (including many who are not evangelical) still hold that this is its meaning. Notice that Paul puts this sin in the same list as lying and perjury; every sin on the list needs the gospel. In 1 Cor 6:11 Paul also says, "And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified." Paul names a practice, not the experience of temptation; the gospel calls every sinner, me included, to repentance, and promises complete washing to everyone who repents and trusts in Christ. The church must not push away or look down on those who struggle with same-sex attraction; every one of us is saved by the same Savior.

3. "In accordance with the glorious gospel of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted." The law is laid down against "whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine" (1 Timothy 1:10), and that sound doctrine is "in accordance with the glorious gospel of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted" (1 Timothy 1:11). The law shows people their sin; the gospel shows them their Savior. Used lawfully, the law brings people to the gospel.

The point: The law is good. It exposes our sin; it is not a ladder for boasting. Used lawfully, it brings sinners to the glorious gospel.
Going Deeper: 1:12–17 Of Whom I Am the Foremost

1. "I thank him who has given me strength." "I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service" (1 Timothy 1:12). Paul serves the Lord not because he first had strength, but because Christ "has given me strength." "Judged me faithful" does not mean Paul first proved himself reliable and was then chosen; the next verse immediately says what kind of man he was when he was appointed.

2. "Formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent." "Though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy" (1 Timothy 1:13).

  • Three words: a "blasphemer" attacks God with words; a "persecutor" attacks the church with deeds (see Acts 26:9–11); an "insolent opponent" is an arrogant, violent man. Paul does not soften his past.
  • "Because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief": this does not mean that Paul's ignorance made him guiltless, or that he deserved mercy. The Old Testament distinguishes unintentional sins from sins done "with a high hand" (Num 15:27–31); Peter too told the people of Jerusalem, "you acted in ignorance" (Acts 3:17; see Luke 23:34, a line some early manuscripts lack). Many take the clause to explain not why Paul deserved mercy but why his sin was not the defiant, "high-handed" sin of Num 15:30, the knowing rejection of the truth (contrast v. 20). The real reason for the mercy is given in verse 16: Christ meant to display his patience. He still says "I received mercy"; mercy is never deserved.

3. "The grace of our Lord overflowed for me." "And the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 1:14). "Overflowed" means to abound beyond measure (see Rom 5:20, "grace abounded all the more"). Paul was once full of blasphemy and violence; now grace overflows, bringing faith and love, the very faith and love of verse 5.

4. "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." "The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost" (1 Timothy 1:15).

  • "The saying is trustworthy": this is the first of the five "trustworthy sayings" in the Pastoral Letters (see 1 Timothy 3:1; 1 Timothy 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Titus 3:8), probably a saying that circulated in the churches, which Paul endorses.
  • "Came into the world": the phrase implies Christ's preexistence: he was with the Father and then came into the world (see John 1:9; John 3:17).
  • "To save sinners": Many assume all religions just teach people to be good; but Christ did not come to help good people become better but to save sinners (see Luke 5:32; Luke 19:10). He saves sinners by giving himself in their place: he "gave himself as a ransom for all" (1 Timothy 2:6). Sinners are saved not by improving themselves but by believing in him for eternal life (1 Timothy 1:16).
  • "Of whom I am the foremost": notice that Paul uses the present tense: "I am," not "I was." Many years after his conversion he still sees himself this way. This is not false modesty, nor polite self-deprecation; it is the voice of a man who, the more he knows God, sees more of his own sin and more of the greatness of grace (see 1 Cor 15:9–10).

5. "To display his perfect patience." "But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life" (1 Timothy 1:16).

  • "Perfect patience": Christ's patience toward Paul was complete. On the Damascus road the Lord did not say, "Saul, I will punish you," but, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" (Acts 9:4).
  • "As an example": the word can mean a sample or an outline sketch, a pattern for those who come later. In saving Paul, God seems to say to everyone after him: if even he could be saved, so can you, if you trust in him. No one's sin is so great that Christ's patience cannot reach it.

6. "To the King of ages... the only God, be honor and glory." "To the King of ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen" (1 Timothy 1:17). When Paul speaks of his own salvation, he cannot help praising God. The doxology comes from the Old Testament: "the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King" (Jer 10:10; see Deut 6:4). In an Ephesus that worshiped Artemis and honored the emperors, Paul declares there is only one "King of ages... the only God." Those who truly know grace end not by boasting in themselves but by worshiping God.

The point: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; the saying is trustworthy. No one is good enough not to need him, and no one is too far gone for him to save. The patience he displayed in the foremost of sinners still waits today for everyone to turn to him.
Going Deeper: 1:18–20 Wage the Good Warfare

1. "In accordance with the prophecies previously made about you." "This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare" (1 Timothy 1:18). When Timothy was set apart for ministry, there had been prophecies about him (see 1 Timothy 4:14). Paul reminds him: your ministry is not something you chose for yourself; God called you to it. In hard times that call can steady him.

2. "Holding faith and a good conscience." "Holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith" (1 Timothy 1:19).

  • Conscience and faith go together: if someone goes on violating conscience and tolerating sin in daily life, he will often end by changing his beliefs to fit his life. False teaching often begins not in the head but in a conscience that has been thrown overboard. This does not mean every honest question hides a sin; honest questions can be brought to God.
  • "Made shipwreck": Ephesus was a port city; its readers knew what a shipwreck looked like. A wreck often begins with drifting off course (see 1 Timothy 1:6, "swerving").

3. "Whom I have handed over to Satan." "Among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme" (1 Timothy 1:20).

  • What does this mean? Most commentators take it to mean putting them out of the church's fellowship (see 1 Cor 5:5, 13), returning them to the world where Satan rules.
  • The aim is restoration: "that they may learn" means to be disciplined or trained. Church discipline aims not at revenge but at repentance. Churches sometimes avoid discipline to save face, and sometimes turn discipline into a way of punishing a person; neither is biblical.
  • These two men: Hymenaeus appears again in 2 Tim 2:17–18, "saying that the resurrection has already happened"; Alexander may be "Alexander the coppersmith" of 2 Tim 4:14, but this is not certain.
The point: Ministry is a good warfare, fought under God's call (1 Timothy 1:18) and in the strength Christ gives (1 Timothy 1:12); leaning on him, we hold faith and a good conscience. When conscience is thrown away, the ship of faith drifts off course; yet the church's discipline still aims to restore.
Meditation

Reflect: "But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life" (1 Timothy 1:16). If someone asked me to share my testimony, how would I tell it? I might talk about what I used to be like, how I changed, and how much better my life is now. All of that may be true. But when Paul tells his testimony, the focus is not on how good he became but on how patient Christ was. Perhaps I feel my testimony is too ordinary: I grew up in church and never did anything very bad. But when Paul says "the foremost," he is not asking me to compare whose sins are bigger; he wants me to see that I, like Paul, need Christ's mercy, and that I too have lived to this day by his patience. Or perhaps it is the opposite: my past feels too dark to tell, and I am afraid that if people knew they would look down on me. Yet Paul wrote the worst of his past into his letter, because that was exactly the evidence of Christ's patience. I do not have to tell everyone everything; some things are for one or two trusted people. And if the darkness was done to me, it is not my sin. But before the Lord I need hide nothing, for he already knows, and he has not given up on me. Today I can look back and ask: when has the Lord been patient with me? When I did not yet believe, when I believed and then fell, when I committed the same sin again and again, he did not give up on me. In the end my testimony is not about me but about him. And then, like Paul, I can end with these words: "To the King of ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen" (1 Timothy 1:17).

verse_parts.text: 我劝你，第一要为万人恳求、祷告、代求、祝谢；为君王和一切在位的，也该如此，使我们可以敬虔、端正、平安无事地度日。
因为只有一位神，在神和人中间，只有一位中保，乃是降世为人的基督耶稣；他舍自己作万人的赎价，到了时候，这事必证明出来。

entries.verse_text: 我劝你，第一要为万人恳求、祷告、代求、祝谢；为君王和一切在位的，也该如此，使我们可以敬虔、端正、平安无事地度日。因为只有一位神，在神和人中间，只有一位中保，乃是降世为人的基督耶稣；他舍自己作万人的赎价，到了时候，这事必证明出来。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第二章分成三段。为万人祷告（1-7节）：要为万人恳求、祷告、代求、祝谢，也为君王和一切在位的祷告；因为神愿意万人得救，只有一位神，在神和人中间只有一位中保，就是降世为人的基督耶稣，他舍自己作万人的赎价。男人在祷告中当怎样（8节）：男人要无忿怒，无争论，举起圣洁的手，随处祷告。女人在聚会中当怎样（9-15节）：女人要以善行为妆饰，不以炫耀的打扮为妆饰；要沉静学道；保罗不许女人讲道，也不许她辖管男人，并举出创造的次序和始祖堕落的经过为理由；女人若常存信心、爱心，又圣洁自守，就必在生产上得救。

这一章从祷告讲起，整章都围绕着敬拜。保罗关心的是：神的百姓聚集的时候，应当是一个怎样的群体？他的答案从福音开始：神愿意万人得救，所以教会要为万人祷告。

深读 2:1-4 为万人祷告

1. 「第一要为万人……」。 「我劝你，第一要为万人恳求、祷告、代求、祝谢」（提前2:1）。「第一」不只是次序上的第一，也是最重要的事。整顿教会，保罗从祷告开始。

  • 四个词： 「恳求」是为具体的需要向神祈求；「祷告」泛指向神说话；「代求」是为别人向神请求；「祝谢」是感谢。这四个词不必严格区分，合起来是说：要为万人献上各样的祷告。
  • 「为万人」： 那些传异教的人可能把得救的范围缩小到少数有特别知识的人。保罗说：要为所有的人祷告，没有一个人在我们的祷告之外。

2. 「为君王和一切在位的」。 「为君王和一切在位的，也该如此，使我们可以敬虔、端正、平安无事地度日。」（提前2:2）

  • 当时的君王是谁？ 写这封信的时候，罗马皇帝很可能是尼禄。后来正是他在罗马逼迫基督徒。保罗没有说只为好的君王祷告，而是为「一切在位的」祷告。这延续了旧约的教导：被掳的人要为巴比伦城「求平安，为那城祷告耶和华」（耶29:7）。
  • 为什么要为他们祷告？ 「使我们可以敬虔、端正、平安无事地度日」。保罗不是求教会得到特权，而是求一个可以安静地敬畏神、过正直生活的环境；在这样的环境里，福音也更容易传开（参提前2:4）。
  • 为他们祷告，不等于赞同他们的一切作为： 我们为在位的人祷告，因为他们也是需要救恩的人，也因为神掌管万有（参罗13:1）。为他们祷告，是把他们带到神面前，不是把他们当作神。初期教会为皇帝祷告，却不肯向皇帝的像献香。

3. 「他愿意万人得救，明白真道」。 「这是好的，在神我们救主面前可蒙悦纳。他愿意万人得救，明白真道。」（提前2:3-4）

  • 神的心意： 神不喜悦恶人死亡（结18:23、32），「不愿有一人沉沦，乃愿人人都悔改」（彼后3:9）。神对失丧的人有真实的怜悯，这是我们为万人祷告的根据。
  • 「万人」是什么意思？ 这一节在历史上有不同的理解。改革宗传统（如加尔文）常认为，「万人」在这里指各种各样的人，包括第2节所说的君王和在位的，就是不分身份、种族。也有改革宗神学家（如约翰·派博）说，神有他启示出来的心意（他真实地愿意人得救），也有他隐秘的旨意（他按着主权拣选人），这两方面在神里面并不矛盾。阿民念和卫斯理传统（如约翰·卫斯理；解经家如霍华德·马歇尔）则认为，神真实地愿意每一个人得救，并藉着先行的恩典使人都能回应，但人仍可能拒绝。两种传统都同意：并不是每一个人最后都会得救（参太7:13-14），也都同意：教会要为所有人祷告、向所有人传福音。
  • 「明白真道」： 得救和明白真理是连在一起的。那些人传的是「似是而非的学问」（提前6:20）；神要人认识的真理，却是下面第5-6节所讲的福音。
要点：神愿意万人得救，所以教会要为万人祷告，包括那些我们不喜欢、甚至敌对我们的掌权者。没有一个人在神的怜悯之外，也不应该有一个人在我们的祷告之外。
深读 2:5-7 只有一位中保

1. 「只有一位神」。 「因为只有一位神」（提前2:5）。这是以色列人每天背诵的认信：「以色列啊，你要听！耶和华－我们神是独一的主。」（申6:4）因为只有一位神，他就是万人的神，不只是某一个民族、某一群人的神（参罗3:29-30）。这正是要为万人祷告的理由。

2. 「在神和人中间，只有一位中保」。 「在神和人中间，只有一位中保，乃是降世为人的基督耶稣」（提前2:5）。

  • 「中保」： 就是站在两方中间、使两方和好的人。约伯曾经叹息：「我们中间没有听讼的人可以向我们两造按手。」（伯9:33）现在，这样一位中保来了。
  • 「只有一位」： 没有别的中间人能把我们带到神面前：不是天使，不是圣徒，不是有特别属灵知识的人，也不是神职人员，也不是祖先，或庙里任何的菩萨神明（参约14:6；徒4:12）。宗教改革强调这一点：信徒可以藉着基督直接来到神面前（来4:16）。天主教传统也认信基督是唯一的中保，但认为马利亚和圣徒的代求，是在基督中保职分之下的一种参与（《天主教教理》第956、969-970条）。改教家特别反对向马利亚和已故圣徒祈求，认为这模糊了基督的独一性；请弟兄姊妹为我们代祷则是另一回事（提前2:1）。
  • 「降世为人的」： 原文直译是：人基督耶稣。中保必须是人，才能代表人；他也必须是神，才能把神带到人面前（参来2:17；论他的神性，参约1:1、14；来1:3）。保罗在这里特别强调他的人性：他是真正的人，懂得我们的软弱（来4:15），今天，这位成为人的基督仍在父面前为我们代求（罗8:34；来7:25）。

3. 「他舍自己作万人的赎价」。 「他舍自己作万人的赎价，到了时候，这事必证明出来。」（提前2:6）

  • 「赎价」： 这话很接近耶稣自己说的：「人子来……要舍命作多人的赎价。」（可10:45）赎价是赎回奴隶或俘虏所付的代价。保罗用的词，比耶稣所用的多了一个表示代替的前缀。许多人认为，这是强调替代：基督舍自己，代替我们，付了我们付不起的代价。
  • 「舍自己」： 不是神从基督身上夺去生命，而是基督自己甘心舍命（参约10:18；加2:20）。
  • 「万人」： 这里和第4节一样，在历史上有不同的理解。改革宗传统（如加尔文和《多特信经》）认为，基督的死足够为所有人赎罪，但它的目的和实际的果效是救赎所有属他的人，「万人」指各样的人，不分种族和身份（参启5:9）；也有一些改革宗神学家（如达文南特）认为，基督为每一个人死，条件是人要信，同时神又特别定意要拯救选民；阿民念和卫斯理传统（如约翰·卫斯理；解经家如霍华德·马歇尔）认为，基督为每一个人死，为所有人预备了救恩，要藉着信才能领受。这三种看法都相信：基督的死是真实的代赎，凡信的人都必得救，教会要向所有人传这个好消息。

4. 「我为此奉派作传道的」。 「我为此奉派作传道的，作使徒，作外邦人的师傅，教导他们相信，学习真道。」（提前2:7）保罗的整个人生，都是为了这一位中保和这一个赎价。他从前逼迫信徒，现在被派去把这个好消息传给外邦人。

要点：在神和人中间只有一位中保，就是降世为人的基督耶稣；他舍自己作了赎价。我们来到神面前，不需要别的关系，也不需要先献上什么，只需要他。
深读 2:8-10 举起圣洁的手，只要有善行

1. 「我愿男人……随处祷告」。 「我愿男人无忿怒，无争论，举起圣洁的手，随处祷告」（提前2:8）。

  • 「举起圣洁的手」： 举手祷告是旧约和初期教会常见的姿势（参诗141:2；诗28:2）。重点不在姿势，而在「圣洁的手」，也就是祷告的人生活要清洁。
  • 「无忿怒，无争论」： 以弗所的教会有争论（提前1:4；提前6:4-5），男人很可能也卷入其中。保罗是说：一边和弟兄争吵、怀恨，一边举手祷告，是自相矛盾的（参太5:23-24；彼前3:7）。这不是说心里有怒气的人就不能来到神面前；诗篇里有不少祷告，就是把心中的苦情和怒气倾倒在神面前，交给他去审判。我们可以把怒气带到神面前、交给他，却不可怀着它不放，一边举手祷告，一边与弟兄相争（参弗4:26）。
  • 「随处」： 可能指以弗所各处的家庭教会。无论在哪里聚会，都要这样祷告。

2. 「又愿女人……以正派衣裳为妆饰」。 「又愿女人廉耻、自守，以正派衣裳为妆饰，不以编发、黄金、珍珠，和贵价的衣裳为妆饰，只要有善行，这才与自称是敬神的女人相宜。」（提前2:9-10）

  • 保罗反对的是什么？ 在当时，精致的编发配上黄金和珍珠，是富有妇女显示身份和财富的方式，有时也带有性的诱惑。保罗不是禁止女人编头发，而是反对在敬拜中炫耀自己、吸引人注意自己（参彼前3:3-4）。
  • 「只要有善行」： 保罗把重点从外面转到里面，从炫耀转到服事。这不只是对女人的要求：男人也不应该在教会里炫耀财富和地位（参雅2:1-4）。
要点：敬拜的时候，男人要放下怒气和争论，女人要放下炫耀。我们放得下，是因为来到神面前只靠那一位中保，不必再靠争赢或打扮来证明自己。
深读 2:11-15 沉静学道

这一段是新约中争议最多的经文之一。历代忠心的信徒对它有不同的理解，下面把主要的看法放在一起，请读者自己查考。

1. 「女人要沉静学道」。 「女人要沉静学道，一味地顺服。」（提前2:11）

  • 「学道」： 在保罗的时代，一些拉比的话反对教导女人律法（如《密西拿·疑妻篇》3.4），希腊罗马社会也很少让女人受教育。保罗却说，女人要学道。这在当时是一个积极的教导（参路10:39，马利亚坐在耶稣脚前听道）。
  • 「沉静」： 原文和第2节的「平安无事」是同一个词根，意思是安静、不吵闹，不一定是完全不说话。

2. 「我不许女人讲道，也不许她辖管男人」。 「我不许女人讲道，也不许她辖管男人，只要沉静。」（提前2:12）这是争议的中心。

  • 「辖管」： 这个词在新约中只出现在这里，在当时的希腊文中也不常见。有学者认为这是个中性的词，就是行使权柄；也有学者认为带有负面的意思，如专横、操控。有学者（如寇斯坦伯格）从「不许……也不许……」的句法认为，讲道和辖管应同属正面或同属负面；另一些学者（如佩恩、贝尔维尔）不同意。这个问题至今仍有讨论。
  • 认为教会某些职分男女有别的看法（常称为互补派）： 许多学者（如乔治·奈特、威廉·孟恩斯、托马斯·施莱纳、道格拉斯·穆尔，以及古德恩、派博）认为，保罗在这里不许女人在教会聚集中担任教导男人、带领全教会的职分，就是长老或监督的职分（参提前3:2「善于教导」）。他们认为第13节诉诸神创造的次序，所以这教导不只适用于以弗所，而是适用于各时代的教会。他们也强调：这不是说女人的价值比较低，男女都照神的形象被造（创1:27），在基督里都是一（加3:28）；女人在教会中有许多教导和服事的机会，例如教导其他妇女（多2:3-5）和孩子（参提后1:5；提后3:15）、在私下讲解神的道（徒18:26）、祷告和说预言（林前11:5，和合本译作「讲道」，原文是说预言）。
  • 认为教会职分不分男女的看法（常称为平等派）： 另一些学者（如戈登·费依、克雷格·基纳、菲利普·佩恩）认为，保罗是针对以弗所当时的问题：一些女人被异教迷惑（参提前5:13；提后3:6-7），又缺少受教育的机会，所以保罗暂时不许她们教导，先叫她们「学道」。他们认为第13-14节是举例说明受迷惑的后果，不是一条永久的原则；他们也指出，保罗在别处称赞女同工，例如女执事非比（罗16:1）、百基拉（罗16:3），以及在聚会中祷告、说预言的女人（林前11:5）。
  • 双方都同意的： 男女都是照神形象造的，都同样蒙恩；女人在神的国中有尊贵、不可缺少的服事；任何人都不可藉着这段经文轻看、压制或伤害女人。

3. 「因为先造的是亚当，后造的是夏娃」。 「因为先造的是亚当，后造的是夏娃，且不是亚当被引诱，乃是女人被引诱，陷在罪里。」（提前2:13-14）

  • 第13节： 保罗引用创世记第2章的次序（创2:7、22）。互补派认为，这表明神在创造中设立的次序；平等派认为，这可能是针对以弗所传异教的人对创世记的误用。
  • 第14节： 保罗暗指创3:13「那蛇引诱我，我就吃了」。对这一节主要有两种理解：许多互补派学者（如施莱纳、穆尔）认为，这是支持第12节的第二个理由：在堕落的事上，创造的次序被颠倒了，夏娃领头，亚当跟从，结果带来了祸患；许多平等派学者和另一些人认为，保罗提到夏娃，是因为以弗所的一些女人正在被假教师引诱，就像夏娃从前一样。
  • 不是说女人天生容易受骗： 历史上有些解经家认为，这表示女人天生比较容易受骗；今天两派的多数学者都不接受这种理解。保罗在罗马书说罪是从「一人」亚当入了世界（罗5:12），亚当虽然没有被引诱，罪责却不因此减轻；他是明知故犯。

4. 「就必在生产上得救」。 「然而，女人若常存信心、爱心，又圣洁自守，就必在生产上得救。」（提前2:15）这节也很难解，主要有三种理解：

  • 因那「生产」得救： 有学者（如乔治·奈特）认为，「生产」指的是那一次独特的生产，就是「女人的后裔」（创3:15）基督的降生。女人虽然先被引诱，救主却是藉着一个女人降生的（参加4:4）。
  • 在生产中蒙保守： 有人认为「得救」在这里是身体上的保守，就是女人在生产时蒙神保护。
  • 在神所给的呼召中活出救恩： 许多学者（如施莱纳、穆尔、汤纳）认为，以弗所的假教师「禁止嫁娶」（提前4:3），保罗在这里说：女人不必放弃婚姻、不必拒绝作母亲，才能得救；她们是在神所给的生活中，常存信心、爱心、圣洁，活出她们的救恩。
  • 这节绝不是说： 保罗绝不是说女人要靠生孩子才能得救。这句话本身就说要「常存信心」；整封信也说救恩是因基督的赎价（提前2:6），也是因信（提前1:16）。没有结婚的女人、不能生育的女人、失去孩子的母亲（在看重传宗接代的家庭里，她们常常背着羞耻），和其他人一样，都是藉着信基督得救的。

5. 一个必要的提醒。 无论我们采取哪一种看法，谁都不可用这段经文为家庭暴力或教会中的欺压辩护。「顺服」从来不是要人忍受虐待；遭受家暴或性侵的人，可以而且应当寻求帮助，向警察和法院报案也是正当的（罗13:4）；受害者不必留在危险之中，也不必与不安全的人和好；饶恕不等于恢复施暴者的职分，也不等于让他再接近受害者或孩子；教会不可为了「家丑不可外扬」而劝受害者沉默。保罗在这封信中也吩咐提摩太，要「劝少年妇女如同姊妹；总要清清洁洁的」（提前5:2）。

要点：这段经文有真实的难处，忠心的信徒有不同的理解；但无论哪一种看法，男女都是照神形象造的，都是因信基督得救，都要在神的家中彼此尊重，一同事奉那位舍己作赎价的主。
默想

默想： 「因为只有一位神，在神和人中间，只有一位中保，乃是降世为人的基督耶稣；他舍自己作万人的赎价。」（提前2:5-6）在我们的社会里，很多事都要「找关系」：看病要托人认识医生，孩子上学要找人说情，办事要先送礼。久而久之，我面对神的时候，可能也不知不觉用同样的方法：觉得自己的祷告分量不够，要找一个「更属灵」的人替我祷告，神才会听；或者觉得要先送上点什么，神才肯接纳我。请别人为我代祷是好的，圣经也这样教导我们（提前2:1）；但他们不是我的中保。保罗说，在神和人中间，只有一位中保。他不是一个需要我先打点、先送礼的人；他自己就是那份礼物，「他舍自己作万人的赎价」。他也不是一个高高在上、不认识我的人；他是「降世为人的基督耶稣」，懂得我的软弱，现在就在父面前为我祈求（罗8:34）。而且，门那边坐着的，也不是一位要人打点才肯开门的官。保罗称他为「神我们救主」，是他自己「愿意万人得救」（提前2:3-4），是他差了这位中保来。今天，我不需要先找到对的人，也不需要先准备好什么，就可以藉着他来到神面前。我可以直接对父说：我是藉着耶稣来的，他已经替我付清了。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 2 falls into three parts. Prayer for all people (vv. 1–7): supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings are to be made for all people, including kings and all in high positions, because God desires all people to be saved; there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all. How men are to pray (v. 8): men are to pray in every place, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling. How women are to conduct themselves in the gathering (vv. 9–15): women are to adorn themselves with good works, not with showy display; they are to learn quietly; Paul does not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man, giving the order of creation and the fall as his reason; she will be saved through childbearing if they continue in faith, love and holiness, with self-control.

The chapter begins with prayer and centers on worship. Paul's concern is: when God's people gather, what kind of community should they be? His answer begins with the gospel: God desires all people to be saved, so the church prays for all people.

Going Deeper: 2:1–4 Prayer for All People

1. "First of all... for all people." "First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people" (1 Timothy 2:1). "First of all" means not only first in sequence but first in importance. To set the church in order, Paul begins with prayer.

  • Four words: "supplications" are requests for specific needs; "prayers" is the general word for speaking to God; "intercessions" are requests on behalf of others; "thanksgivings" are expressions of gratitude. The four need not be sharply distinguished; together they mean that every kind of prayer is to be offered for all people.
  • "For all people": the false teachers may have narrowed salvation to a few people with special knowledge. Paul says: pray for everyone; no one is outside our prayers.

2. "For kings and all who are in high positions." "For kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way" (1 Timothy 2:2).

  • Who was the emperor? When this letter was written, the Roman emperor was most likely Nero, the very man who later persecuted Christians in Rome. Paul does not say "pray for good kings," but for "all who are in high positions." This continues the Old Testament teaching that the exiles were to "seek the welfare of the city... and pray to the LORD on its behalf" (Jer 29:7).
  • Why pray for them? "That we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way." Paul is not asking privileges for the church but a setting in which people can quietly fear God and live upright lives; in such a setting the gospel also spreads more freely (see 1 Timothy 2:4).
  • Praying for them is not approving all they do: we pray for those in authority because they too need salvation, and because God rules over all (see Rom 13:1). But such prayer does not treat them as gods. The early church prayed for the emperor but refused to offer incense to his image.

3. "Who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth." "This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:3–4).

  • God's heart: God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 18:23, 32); he is "not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance" (2 Pet 3:9). God has real compassion for the lost, and this is the ground of our praying for all people.
  • What does "all people" mean? This verse has been understood in different ways. The Reformed tradition (for example Calvin) has often taken "all people" here to mean all kinds of people, including the kings and officials of verse 2, regardless of status or race. Some Reformed theologians (such as John Piper) also say that God has a revealed will (he truly desires people to be saved) and a hidden will (he elects in sovereign freedom), and that the two do not contradict each other in God. The Arminian and Wesleyan traditions (for example John Wesley; among commentators, I. Howard Marshall) hold that God truly desires every single person to be saved and by his prevenient grace enables all to respond, though people may refuse. Both traditions agree that not everyone will finally be saved (see Matt 7:13–14), and both agree that the church must pray for all people and preach the gospel to all.
  • "The knowledge of the truth": salvation and knowing the truth go together. Unlike those who teach "what is falsely called 'knowledge,'" the truth God wants people to know is what verses 5–6 go on to say.
The point: God desires all people to be saved, so the church prays for all people, including rulers we dislike or who oppose us. No one is outside God's compassion, and no one should be outside our prayers.
Going Deeper: 2:5–7 One Mediator

1. "There is one God." "For there is one God" (1 Timothy 2:5). This is the confession Israel recited every day: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one" (Deut 6:4). Because there is only one God, he is the God of all people, not of one nation or group alone (see Rom 3:29–30). This is exactly why we pray for all people.

2. "One mediator between God and men." "And there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5).

  • "Mediator": one who stands between two parties to reconcile them. Job once lamented, "There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both" (Job 9:33). Now such a mediator has come.
  • "One": there is no other go-between who can bring us to God: not angels, not saints, not people with special spiritual knowledge, not clergy, nor ancestors, nor any deity or bodhisattva in a temple (see John 14:6; Acts 4:12). The Reformation stressed this: believers may come directly to God through Christ (Heb 4:16). Catholic teaching also confesses Christ as the one mediator, but holds that the intercession of Mary and the saints shares in Christ's mediation under him (Catechism of the Catholic Church 956, 969–970). The Reformers objected especially to calling on Mary and the departed saints, which they held blurs Christ's uniqueness; asking fellow believers to pray for us is another matter (1 Timothy 2:1).
  • "The man": the Greek reads literally "the man Christ Jesus." A mediator must be human to represent humans; he must also be God to bring God to us (see Heb 2:17; for his deity, John 1:1, 14; Heb 1:3). Here Paul stresses his humanity: he is truly human, sympathizes with our weaknesses (Heb 4:15), and even now, as a man, intercedes for us before the Father (Rom 8:34; Heb 7:25).

3. "Who gave himself as a ransom for all." "Who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time" (1 Timothy 2:6).

  • "Ransom": this is very close to Jesus' own words: "the Son of Man came... to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). A ransom is the price paid to free a slave or captive. Paul's word, antilytron, adds the prefix anti ("in place of") to Jesus' word; many take it to stress substitution: Christ gave himself in our place and paid the price we could not pay.
  • "Gave himself": God did not take Christ's life from him against his will; Christ laid down his life willingly (see John 10:18; Gal 2:20).
  • "For all": as with verse 4, this has been understood in different ways. The Reformed tradition (for example Calvin and the Canons of Dort) holds that Christ's death is sufficient for all but was intended to redeem, and actually redeems, all who belong to him, "all" meaning all kinds of people regardless of race or status (see Rev 5:9). Some Reformed theologians (the hypothetical universalists, such as John Davenant) hold that Christ died for every person on condition of faith, while God specially purposed to save the elect. The Arminian and Wesleyan traditions (for example John Wesley; among commentators, I. Howard Marshall) hold that Christ died for every person and made salvation available to all, received through faith. All three views hold that Christ's death was a real substitution, that all who believe will be saved, and that the church must announce this good news to everyone.

4. "For this I was appointed a preacher." "For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth" (1 Timothy 2:7). Paul's whole life is given to this one mediator and this one ransom. Once he persecuted believers; now he is sent to bring this good news to the Gentiles.

The point: There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom. To come to God we need no other connection and nothing to offer first; we need only him.
Going Deeper: 2:8–10 Holy Hands and Good Works

1. "I desire then that in every place the men should pray." "I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1 Timothy 2:8).

  • "Lifting holy hands": lifting the hands in prayer was a common posture in the Old Testament and the early church (see Ps 141:2; Ps 28:2). The point is not the posture but "holy hands," a clean life.
  • "Without anger or quarreling": the church in Ephesus had quarrels (1 Timothy 1:4; 1 Timothy 6:4–5), and the men were likely in the middle of them. Paul is saying that lifting hands in prayer while quarreling with and resenting a brother is a contradiction (see Matt 5:23–24; 1 Pet 3:7). This does not mean an angry heart cannot come to God; many psalms pour out grief and anger before him and leave judgment to him. We may bring our anger to God and hand it over to him; what we may not do is keep holding it, lifting our hands in prayer while quarrelling with a brother (see Eph 4:26).
  • "In every place": probably the various house churches around Ephesus. Wherever they gather, they are to pray this way.

2. "Likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel." "Likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness, with good works" (1 Timothy 2:9–10).

  • What is Paul opposing? In that culture, elaborate braided hairstyles with gold and pearls were a way for wealthy women to display status and wealth, sometimes with sexual allure. Paul is not forbidding braids; he is opposing self-display, drawing attention to oneself in worship (see 1 Pet 3:3–4).
  • "With good works": Paul moves the focus from outside to inside, from display to service. This is not a demand on women only: men too should not display wealth and status in the church (see Jas 2:1–4).
The point: In worship, men are to lay down anger and quarrels, women to lay down display. We can let them go because we come to God through the one Mediator alone; we no longer need to prove ourselves by winning arguments or by how we look.
Going Deeper: 2:11–15 Learning Quietly

This is one of the most debated passages in the New Testament. Faithful believers through the centuries have understood it differently; the main views are set out side by side below for readers to weigh.

1. "Let a woman learn quietly." "Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness" (1 Timothy 2:11).

  • "Learn": in Paul's day some rabbinic sayings discouraged teaching women the law (e.g. Mishnah Sotah 3.4), and Greco-Roman society seldom educated women. Paul says women are to learn. In that setting this was a positive instruction (see Luke 10:39, Mary sitting at Jesus' feet listening to his teaching).
  • "Quietly": the Greek word shares a root with "quiet" in verse 2 ("a peaceful and quiet life"). It means calm, not disruptive, not necessarily total silence.

2. "I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man." "I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet" (1 Timothy 2:12). This is the heart of the debate.

  • "Exercise authority": this word occurs only here in the New Testament and is uncommon in Greek of the period. Some scholars think it is neutral, "to exercise authority"; others think it is negative, such as "to domineer" or "to usurp." Some (such as Andreas Köstenberger) argue from the "neither... nor" construction that "teach" and "exercise authority" must both be positive or both negative; others (such as Philip Payne and Linda Belleville) dispute this. Study of the word is still debated.
  • The view that certain church offices are distinguished by sex (often called complementarian): many scholars (such as George Knight, William Mounce, Thomas Schreiner and Douglas Moo, as well as Wayne Grudem and John Piper) hold that Paul here does not permit women, in the church's gathering, to hold the office of teaching men and leading the whole church, that is, the office of elder or overseer (see 1 Timothy 3:2, "able to teach"). Because verse 13 appeals to the order of creation, they hold that this teaching applies not only to Ephesus but to the church in every age. They also stress that this does not mean women are of lesser worth: men and women alike are made in God's image (Gen 1:27) and are one in Christ (Gal 3:28); women have many opportunities to teach and serve in the church, such as teaching other women (Titus 2:3–5) and children (see 2 Tim 1:5; 2 Tim 3:15), explaining God's word privately (Acts 18:26), and praying and prophesying (1 Cor 11:5).
  • The view that church offices are open to both sexes (often called egalitarian): other scholars (such as Gordon Fee, Craig Keener and Philip Payne) hold that Paul is addressing a specific problem in Ephesus: some women had been led astray by false teaching (see 1 Timothy 5:13; 2 Tim 3:6–7) and lacked education, so Paul temporarily forbade them to teach and first told them to "learn." They see verses 13–14 as an illustration of the consequences of deception, not a permanent principle, and they point out that Paul elsewhere commends women coworkers, such as Phoebe, a deacon (Rom 16:1), Prisca (Rom 16:3), and women who pray and prophesy in the gathering (1 Cor 11:5).
  • What both sides agree on: men and women are both made in God's image and receive the same grace; women have honored and indispensable service in God's kingdom; no one may use this passage to belittle, suppress or harm women.

3. "For Adam was formed first, then Eve." "For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor" (1 Timothy 2:13–14).

  • Verse 13: Paul cites the order of Genesis 2 (Gen 2:7, 22). Complementarians see here an order God established in creation; egalitarians think Paul may be answering the Ephesian false teachers' misuse of Genesis.
  • Verse 14: Paul alludes to Gen 3:13, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate." Interpreters read this verse in two main ways. Many complementarians (such as Schreiner and Moo) take it as a second reason supporting verse 12: at the fall the order of creation was reversed, with Eve taking the lead and Adam following, and harm followed. Many egalitarians, and some others, think Paul mentions Eve because some women in Ephesus were being deceived by false teachers, as Eve once was.
  • Not that women are by nature easily deceived: many older interpreters took the verse to mean women are by nature more easily deceived; most modern interpreters on both sides reject that reading. In Romans Paul says sin entered the world through "one man," Adam (Rom 5:12); Adam's guilt was not lessened because he was not deceived; he sinned knowingly.

4. "She will be saved through childbearing." "Yet she will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control" (1 Timothy 2:15). This verse is also hard; there are three main readings:

  • Saved through "the childbearing": some scholars (such as George Knight) think "childbearing" refers to the birth of the Child, the "offspring" of the woman (Gen 3:15), Christ. Though the woman was deceived first, it was through a woman that the Savior was born (see Gal 4:4).
  • Kept safe in childbirth: some take "saved" here as physical preservation, God protecting women through childbirth.
  • Living out salvation in God's calling: many scholars (such as Schreiner, Moo and Towner) note that the Ephesian false teachers "forbid marriage" (1 Timothy 4:3). Paul is saying that women do not need to abandon marriage and motherhood in order to be saved; in the life God has given them, continuing in faith, love and holiness, they live out their salvation.
  • What it certainly does not mean: Paul is not saying women are saved by having children. The verse itself says "if they continue in faith"; the whole letter says salvation comes through Christ's ransom (1 Timothy 2:6) and through faith (1 Timothy 1:16). Unmarried women, women who cannot have children, and mothers who have lost children (who in families that prize carrying on the family line often bear shame) are saved, like everyone else, through faith in Christ.

5. A necessary word. Whichever view we take, this passage can never be used to justify domestic violence or abuse in the church. "Submission" never means enduring abuse; those who suffer domestic violence or sexual abuse can and should seek help, and reporting to the police and courts is right (Rom 13:4); victims need not remain in danger or reconcile with someone unsafe; forgiveness does not restore an abuser's office or give him access to victims or children; the church must not urge victims to keep silent to protect its reputation (the Chinese saying 家丑不可外扬, "don't air the family's shame outside"). In this same letter Paul tells Timothy to treat "younger women as sisters, in all purity" (1 Timothy 5:2).

The point: This passage has real difficulties, and faithful believers understand it differently; but on every view, men and women are made in God's image, are saved through faith in Christ, and are to honor one another in God's household as they serve together the Lord who gave himself as a ransom.
Meditation

Reflect: "For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all" (1 Timothy 2:5–6). In our society many things depend on "finding a connection" (找关系): to see a good doctor you need someone who knows him; to get a child into a school you need someone to put in a word; to get something done you first bring a gift. Over time I may come to God the same way without noticing: feeling that my own prayers do not carry enough weight, so I need someone "more spiritual" to pray for me before God will listen; or feeling that I must bring something first before God will accept me. Asking others to pray for me is good; Scripture teaches it (1 Timothy 2:1). But they are not my mediator. Paul says there is only one mediator between God and men. He is not someone I must first win over with a gift; he himself is the gift: "who gave himself as a ransom for all." Nor is he someone high above who does not know me; he is "the man Christ Jesus," who understands my weakness and is even now interceding for me before the Father (Rom 8:34). And the one on the other side of the door is not an official who must be won over before he opens it. Paul calls him "God our Savior," who himself "desires all people to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:3–4); he is the one who sent this Mediator. Today I do not need to find the right person or prepare anything first; I can come to God through him. I can say to the Father directly: I have come through Jesus; he has already paid in full for me.

verse_parts.text: 倘若我耽延日久，你也可以知道在神的家中当怎样行。这家就是永生神的教会，真理的柱石和根基。大哉，敬虔的奥秘，无人不以为然！就是神在肉身显现，被圣灵称义，被天使看见，被传于外邦，被世人信服，被接在荣耀里。

entries.content:
本章脉络

第三章分成三段。监督（1-7节）：「人若想要得监督的职分，就是羡慕善工」；作监督的必须无可指责，有节制，善于教导，好好管理自己的家，不可是初入教的，在教外也要有好名声。执事（8-13节）：执事要端庄、不一口两舌、存清洁的良心，要先受试验；女执事（或执事的妻子）也要端庄、不说谗言、凡事忠心；善作执事的，在真道上大有胆量。神的家与敬虔的奥秘（14-16节）：保罗写这些，是要提摩太知道在神的家中当怎样行；这家是永生神的教会，真理的柱石和根基；敬虔的奥秘就是基督：「神在肉身显现……被接在荣耀里」。

这一章前半部分像一张品格清单，最后是一首颂赞基督的诗。保罗把这两样放在一起，是要告诉我们：教会带领人的品格，不是从一套规条来的，而是从认识那位「在肉身显现」的主来的。

深读 3:1-7 作监督的，必须无可指责

1. 「人若想要得监督的职分，就是羡慕善工」。 「『人若想要得监督的职分，就是羡慕善工。』这话是可信的。」（提前3:1）

  • 「监督」： 原文是看守、照管的人。在新约中，「监督」和「长老」常指同一个职分（参徒20:17、28；多1:5、7）：「长老」着重这人的成熟，「监督」着重他的工作。彼得也称基督为我们「灵魂的牧人监督」（彼前2:25）。
  • 「善工」： 保罗说想作监督是好的，但他强调这是「工」，不是地位。在一个看重面子和头衔的文化中，这话提醒我们：教会的职分是服事，不是荣誉（参太20:26-28）。
  • 「想要」： 这不是说人只要想当就可以当；接下来的清单就是要看他是否合适。但保罗也不认为愿意承担这份工作是骄傲。在讲究谦让的文化里，人常以为说「我愿意」就是不谦虚；保罗却说，这是羡慕善工。教会需要有人愿意为群羊摆上自己。

2. 品格的清单。 「作监督的，必须无可指责，只作一个妇人的丈夫，有节制，自守，端正，乐意接待远人，善于教导；不因酒滋事，不打人，只要温和，不争竞，不贪财」（提前3:2-3）。

  • 「无可指责」： 这是总纲，下面的各项都是它的说明。不是说他没有罪，而是说他的生活中没有明显、公开、让人可以拿来指控的过错。
  • 几乎全是品格： 这份清单中只有「善于教导」是一种能力，其余都是品格。神看重的首先不是一个人的口才、学历、财富或在社会上的地位，而是他的为人。
  • 「不打人，只要温和」： 一个用暴力、用怒气、用权柄压制别人的人，不可以作监督（参彼前5:3「也不是辖制所托付你们的」）。教会如果发现带领人有欺压、暴力或性方面的不当行为，不可为了保全面子而掩盖，要按真理处理；涉及犯罪的，应当向警方报案。这样的人不再合乎作监督的资格；即使他悔改、蒙了饶恕，饶恕也不等于恢复他的职分，也不等于让他再接近受害者或孩子。
  • 「不贪财」： 以弗所的假教师「以敬虔为得利的门路」（提前6:5）。带领人不可以把服事当作赚钱的途径（参彼前5:2）。

3. 「只作一个妇人的丈夫」。 这句话有几种理解：

  • 对婚姻忠诚： 原文直译是：一个女人的男人。多数现代解经家（如奈特、孟恩斯、汤纳）认为，重点是在婚姻中对妻子忠诚，不可多妻，也不可有婚外的关系。
  • 一生只结一次婚： 一些初期教父认为，作监督的人即使丧偶，也不可再婚。这种看法最有力的根据是提前5:9，对寡妇也用了相同的说法：「从来只作一个丈夫的妻子」。可是保罗在提前5:14和罗7:2-3并没有反对丧偶的人再婚。
  • 没有离婚再婚： 有人认为，这句话是把离婚后再婚的人排除在外。各教会对此有不同的做法。
  • 一定要结婚： 很少人这样理解。保罗自己当时没有妻子（林前7:7-8），他在这里关心的是已婚者的忠诚，不是要求每一个监督都必须结婚。

4. 「好好管理自己的家」。 「好好管理自己的家，使儿女凡事端庄顺服。人若不知道管理自己的家，焉能照管神的教会呢？」（提前3:4-5）

  • 家是一个试验场： 一个人在家中怎样对待妻子和儿女，最能显出他的真实品格。教会也是一个「家」（提前3:15），在自己家里不能用爱心和忠心带领的人，在神的家中也难以照管人。
  • 不是要求完美的孩子： 「端庄顺服」是说儿女在他的管教下有秩序，不是说孩子永远不会犯错，或者孩子长大后的每一个选择都要由父母负责。
  • 「照管」： 这个词也用在好撒玛利亚人的故事中：「照应他」（路10:34-35）。照管教会，是带着怜悯去照顾，不是发号施令。

5. 「初入教的不可作监督」。 「初入教的不可作监督，恐怕他自高自大，就落在魔鬼所受的刑罚里。」（提前3:6）「初入教的」原文是新栽种的。一个人信主不久就被放在高位上，很容易骄傲。许多人认为「魔鬼所受的刑罚」指的是魔鬼因骄傲而受的审判。教会不可因为一个人有能力、有钱或有名望，就急着让他作带领人（参提前5:22）。

6. 「在教外有好名声」。 「监督也必须在教外有好名声，恐怕被人毁谤，落在魔鬼的网罗里。」（提前3:7）不信的人也在看教会的带领人。如果一个带领人在工作上不诚实，在邻舍中名声很坏，福音就会被人轻看。

要点：神为他的家选带领人，看的首先不是才干、财富或地位，而是品格。教会的职分是一份「善工」，是像基督那样为羊摆上自己的服事。
深读 3:8-13 作执事的，也是如此

1. 「作执事的」。 「作执事的，也是如此：必须端庄，不一口两舌，不好喝酒，不贪不义之财；要存清洁的良心，固守真道的奥秘。」（提前3:8-9）

  • 「执事」： 原文就是服事的人。许多人认为，执事的起源可以追溯到使徒行传第6章，那七个人被选出来管理供给寡妇的事，使使徒可以「专心以祈祷、传道为事」（徒6:3-4）。不过，使徒行传第6章没有称他们为执事。腓1:1也提到「诸位监督，诸位执事」。
  • 和监督的不同： 执事的清单没有「善于教导」，所以多数人认为，执事主要负责实际的服事和管理，不是教导和带领全教会。但品格的要求几乎是一样的。
  • 「不一口两舌」： 执事常常要在不同的人中间走动，处理实际的需要，很容易对这个人说一套，对那个人说另一套。
  • 「固守真道的奥秘」： 执事做的虽然是实际的事，但他也必须持守真道。实际的服事和纯正的信仰不可分开。

2. 「要先受试验」。 「这等人也要先受试验，若没有可责之处，然后叫他们作执事。」（提前3:10）保罗没有说怎样试验，可能是让教会观察一段时间。教会选立同工，要有耐心，不要因为急需人手就随便安排人。

3. 「女执事也是如此」。 「女执事也是如此：必须端庄，不说谗言，有节制，凡事忠心。」（提前3:11）原文只说：女人也是如此。这可以有两种理解：

  • 执事的妻子： 有学者（如加尔文）认为，这是指执事（或监督）的妻子。理由是：第11节夹在讲执事的经文中间，第12节又直接回到执事，若是介绍另一种职分，显得突然；而且这里的要求比执事的少。有些英文译本就译作他们的妻子。
  • 女执事： 另一些学者认为是指女执事。理由是：「也是如此」和第8节的结构一样，像是在介绍另一组服事的人；原文没有「他们的」；保罗在别处称非比为坚革哩教会的执事（罗16:1，原文与「执事」是同一个词）。初期教父金口约翰也这样理解。和合本译作「女执事」，就是采取这种理解。
  • 持这两种理解的人都同意： 女人在教会中有重要的服事，她们的品格和男人一样受到看重。

4. 「执事只要作一个妇人的丈夫」。 「执事只要作一个妇人的丈夫，好好管理儿女和自己的家。」（提前3:12）这和对监督的要求一样（参提前3:2、4）。

5. 「美好的地步……大有胆量」。 「因为善作执事的，自己就得到美好的地步，并且在基督耶稣里的真道上大有胆量。」（提前3:13）

  • 「美好的地步」： 可能指在教会中受人尊重，也可能指在神面前的好名声。无论哪一种，都不是世人所看重的地位。耶稣说：「我在你们中间如同服事人的。」（路22:27）
  • 「大有胆量」： 忠心服事的人，在信仰上会越来越坚定，也越来越能坦然地面对神、面对人。
要点：执事的服事看起来很实际，却和真道连在一起。在神的家中，摆桌子、探访、管账、照顾有需要的人，都是尊贵的服事；忠心的人在其中会越来越认识基督。
深读 3:14-15 在神的家中当怎样行

1. 「倘若我耽延日久」。 「我指望快到你那里去，所以先将这些事写给你。倘若我耽延日久，你也可以知道在神的家中当怎样行。」（提前3:14-15）保罗希望能快去以弗所，却不确定能否成行。他把教导写下来，提摩太和以弗所教会就可以照着行。今天我们读这封信，也是在读神藉着保罗留给教会的话。

2. 「神的家」。 「这家就是永生神的教会」（提前3:15）。

  • 「家」： 原文可以指房屋，也可以指家庭。保罗两层意思都用：教会是神的一家人（提前5:1-2），也是神居住的殿（参林前3:16；弗2:21-22）。
  • 「永生神」： 以弗所有亚底米的神像，那是不能说话、没有生命的偶像（参徒19:26）。教会的神是活的神。

3. 「真理的柱石和根基」。 「真理的柱石和根基」（提前3:15）。

  • 「柱石」： 柱子撑起屋顶，也让人从远处就看得见这座建筑。教会要高举真理，让世人看见。
  • 「根基」： 原文指地基或支撑物。教会要稳稳地守住真理，不让它被异教摇动。
  • 教会和真理的关系： 教会不是真理的来源，真理是从神来的，记在圣经里（提后3:16）。教会是支撑和保守真理的群体。这也提醒我们：真理不是只靠个人保守的，而是在教会的团契中一同持守的。
要点：教会是永生神的家，是真理的柱石和根基。我们在教会中怎样行，不只关乎人际关系，更关乎神的荣耀和真理的见证。
深读 3:16 大哉，敬虔的奥秘

1. 「大哉，敬虔的奥秘，无人不以为然」。 「无人不以为然」，原文的意思是：我们一同承认。这句话很可能是个引子，下面引的是初期教会一同诵念的认信或诗歌。

  • 「奥秘」： 在保罗的用法里，「奥秘」不是神秘难懂的事，而是从前隐藏、现在被神显明出来的事（参罗16:25-26；西1:26-27）。
  • 「敬虔的奥秘」： 敬虔不是从我们的努力开始的，而是从神所显明的基督开始的。前面第9节说「真道的奥秘」，这里说「敬虔的奥秘」，这两个说法都指向基督。

2. 「神在肉身显现」。 这里有一个抄本上的问题。和合本根据较晚的抄本，译作「神在肉身显现」；较早的抄本作那一位在肉身显现，指的是基督，多数学者认为这更接近原文。这两种读法在希腊文抄本中写出来非常相近。差别只在于是否直接称他为神，却不改变教义：这「在肉身显现」的一位，在取了人性以前就已经存在（参约1:14；腓2:6-7）。基督的神性也不倚靠这一处经文；圣经在别处清楚称他为神（约1:1；约20:28；多2:13）。

3. 六句诗。 许多人认为这首诗分成三组，每组两句，彼此对照（也有人认为是两段，每段三句）：

  • 「在肉身显现，被圣灵称义」： 他在肉身中显现，被人轻看，被钉十字架；许多人认为是圣灵使他从死里复活，证明他是义的，「以大能显明是神的儿子」（罗1:4）；也有人把原文理解为在灵里，指复活的生命，与「肉身」相对（参彼前3:18「按着灵性说」）。无论哪一种理解，复活都是神宣告他为义。「称义」在这里是被证明为义的意思。
  • 「被天使看见，被传于外邦」： 天上的天使看见他的得胜（参彼前3:22），地上的外邦人听见他的福音。天上和地上都知道他。
  • 「被世人信服，被接在荣耀里」： 世上的人信了他，他自己被接到天上的荣耀里（徒1:9）。
  • 次序： 「被接在荣耀里」在时间上早于福音传遍外邦，诗歌却把它放在最后。这首诗不是要排列时间表，而是用对照的方式，赞美基督从卑微到荣耀的全部工作。

4. 为什么放在这里？ 保罗刚讲完监督和执事的品格，就唱出这首诗。他是要告诉提摩太：敬虔的生活不是从一张清单开始的，而是从这位基督开始的。我们能够活出敬虔，是因为他在肉身显现，为我们死，又复活、升天；我们活出敬虔，是靠着他，也是为了他。下一章，保罗就要讲到那些把敬虔变成禁戒规条的人（提前4:1-5）。

要点：敬虔的奥秘就是基督自己：在肉身显现、被圣灵称义、被接在荣耀里的基督。教会的一切秩序和品格，都要从认识他、敬拜他开始。
默想

默想： 「大哉，敬虔的奥秘，无人不以为然！就是神在肉身显现，被圣灵称义，被天使看见，被传于外邦，被世人信服，被接在荣耀里。」（提前3:16）一听到「敬虔」这个词，我可能会想到一些习惯：每天读经祷告、主日不缺席、不抽烟、不喝酒、说话有礼貌。这些都可能是好的。可是保罗说，敬虔的奥秘不是一套习惯，而是一个人。当我读到前面那张监督和执事的清单，也许心里会想：我离这些还差得很远，心里也有骄傲、贪心和怒气。其实，真正完全合乎这张清单的，只有一位，就是基督自己。这不是降低对带领人的要求；乃是说，我和每一位带领人一样，都要先在他里面蒙接纳，才能被他改变。他无可指责，他温和，他不争竞，他好好照管神的家，他为羊舍命（约10:11）。今天，我可以慢慢地读这六句诗，每读一句就停一下。我最需要的是哪一句？是「在肉身显现」，知道他来到我所在的地方？是「被圣灵称义」？那被人定罪的，神已经证明他为义；他担当了我该受的定罪（参罗4:25），我在他里面也蒙了接纳。是「被传于外邦」，知道这福音也传给了像我这样的人？还是「被接在荣耀里」，知道他现在就在父的右边，我的将来也在他手里？我可以选一句，带着它过今天；然后和历代的教会一同说：大哉，敬虔的奥秘！
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 3 falls into three parts. Overseers (vv. 1–7): "If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task"; an overseer must be above reproach, self-controlled, able to teach, managing his own household well, not a recent convert, and well thought of by outsiders. Deacons (vv. 8–13): deacons must be dignified, not double-tongued, holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience, and tested first; women deacons (or deacons' wives) likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, faithful in all things; those who serve well gain great confidence in the faith. The household of God and the mystery of godliness (vv. 14–16): Paul writes so that Timothy may know how to behave in the household of God, the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of truth; the mystery of godliness is Christ: "He was manifested in the flesh... taken up in glory."

The first half of the chapter reads like a checklist of character; it ends with a hymn to Christ. Placed side by side, they tell us that the character of the church's leaders does not come from a set of rules but from knowing the one who was "manifested in the flesh."

Going Deeper: 3:1–7 An Overseer Must Be Above Reproach

1. "If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task." "The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task" (1 Timothy 3:1).

  • "Overseer": the word means one who watches over and cares for others. In the New Testament "overseer" and "elder" often refer to the same office (see Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5, 7): "elder" stresses the person's maturity, "overseer" his work. Peter calls Christ "the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls" (1 Pet 2:25).
  • "A noble task": Paul says aspiring to be an overseer is good, but he stresses that it is a "task," a work, not a status. In a culture that prizes face and titles, this reminds us that office in the church is service, not honor (see Matt 20:26–28).
  • "Aspires": this does not mean that anyone who wants the office may have it; the list that follows tests whether he is fit. But Paul does not regard willingness to take on this work as pride. The church needs people willing to give themselves for the flock.

2. The list of character. "Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money" (1 Timothy 3:2–3).

  • "Above reproach": this is the heading; the rest of the list fills it out. It does not mean he is sinless, but that his life has no obvious, public fault that could fairly be charged against him.
  • Almost all character: only "able to teach" on this list is a skill; everything else is character. What God values first is not eloquence, education, wealth or social standing, but what kind of person someone is.
  • "Not violent but gentle": someone who uses violence, anger or authority to crush others may not be an overseer (see 1 Pet 5:3, "not domineering over those in your charge"). If a church finds that a leader has been abusive, violent or sexually inappropriate, it must not cover it up to save face but deal with it truthfully; where a crime is involved, it should be reported to the police. Such a man is disqualified from office; even if he repents and is forgiven, forgiveness does not restore his office nor give him access to victims or children.
  • "Not a lover of money": the false teachers in Ephesus imagined "that godliness is a means of gain" (1 Timothy 6:5). Leaders must not treat ministry as a way to make money (see 1 Pet 5:2).

3. "The husband of one wife." This phrase has been understood in several ways:

  • Faithful in marriage: the Greek reads literally "a one-woman man." Most modern commentators (such as Knight, Mounce and Towner) think the point is faithfulness to one's wife in marriage: no polygamy and no relationships outside marriage.
  • Married only once in a lifetime: some early church fathers held that an overseer may not remarry even after his wife's death. This view's strongest support is 1 Timothy 5:9, where the same phrase is used of widows: "having been the wife of one husband." But in 1 Timothy 5:14 and Rom 7:2–3 Paul does not oppose the remarriage of the widowed.
  • Not divorced and remarried: some take it to exclude those who have divorced and remarried. Churches handle this in different ways.
  • Must be married: few read it this way. Paul himself had no wife at the time (1 Cor 7:7–8); his concern here is the faithfulness of married men, not a requirement that every overseer marry.

4. "He must manage his own household well." "He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?" (1 Timothy 3:4–5).

  • The home as a testing ground: how a man treats his wife and children at home shows his true character most clearly. The church is also a "household" (1 Timothy 3:15); someone who cannot lead his own home with love and faithfulness will find it hard to care for people in God's household.
  • Not a demand for perfect children: "submissive" means his children are orderly under his care, not that children never misbehave, or that parents are answerable for every choice their grown children make.
  • "Care for": the same word is used in the story of the Good Samaritan: "took care of him" (Luke 10:34–35). Caring for the church means looking after people with compassion, not issuing orders.

5. "He must not be a recent convert." "He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1 Timothy 3:6). "Recent convert" means literally "newly planted." Someone placed in high office soon after coming to faith can easily become proud. Many take "the condemnation of the devil" to mean the judgment the devil incurred through pride. A church must not rush someone into leadership because he is capable, wealthy or prominent (see 1 Timothy 5:22).

6. "Well thought of by outsiders." "Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil" (1 Timothy 3:7). Unbelievers are watching the church's leaders too. If a leader is dishonest at work or has a bad name among his neighbors, the gospel will be held in contempt.

The point: When God chooses leaders for his household, he looks first not at talent, wealth or status but at character. Office in the church is a "noble task," service that gives itself for the sheep as Christ did.
Going Deeper: 3:8–13 Deacons Likewise

1. "Deacons likewise." "Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience" (1 Timothy 3:8–9).

  • "Deacons": the word simply means "servants." Many trace the origin of deacons to Acts 6, where seven men were chosen to oversee the distribution to widows so that the apostles could "devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word" (Acts 6:3–4). Acts 6, however, does not call them deacons. Phil 1:1 also mentions "the overseers and deacons."
  • How they differ from overseers: the deacons' list lacks "able to teach," so most think deacons served mainly in practical service and administration rather than in teaching and leading the whole church. But the character required is nearly the same.
  • "Not double-tongued": deacons often move among many people handling practical needs, and it is easy to tell one person one thing and another person something else.
  • "Hold the mystery of the faith": though deacons do practical work, they must also hold to the truth. Practical service and sound faith cannot be separated.

2. "Let them also be tested first." "And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless" (1 Timothy 3:10). Paul does not say how they are tested; perhaps the church observes them over time. A church choosing workers needs patience and should not appoint people carelessly because it urgently needs hands.

3. "Their wives likewise" or "women likewise." "Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things" (1 Timothy 3:11). The Greek says only "women likewise," which can be read two ways:

  • Deacons' wives: some scholars (such as Calvin) take it to mean the wives of deacons (or of overseers). Their reasons: verse 11 sits in the middle of the instructions about deacons, and verse 12 goes straight back to them, which would be odd if a separate office were being introduced; and the list is shorter than the deacons'. The ESV translates "their wives" (its footnote gives "Wives likewise" or "Women likewise").
  • Women deacons: other scholars take it to mean women deacons. Their reasons: "likewise" follows the same pattern as verse 8, as if introducing another group of servants; the Greek has no "their"; and Paul elsewhere calls Phoebe a deacon of the church at Cenchreae (Rom 16:1, the same Greek word as "deacon"). The early church father John Chrysostom read it this way. The CUV translates "women deacons," taking this view.
  • Both views agree: women have important service in the church, and their character is valued just as men's is.

4. "Let deacons each be the husband of one wife." "Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well" (1 Timothy 3:12). This matches what is required of overseers (see 1 Timothy 3:2, 4).

5. "A good standing... great confidence." "For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 3:13).

  • "A good standing": this may mean respect in the church or a good name before God. Either way, it is not the kind of status the world prizes. Jesus said, "I am among you as the one who serves" (Luke 22:27).
  • "Great confidence": those who serve faithfully grow steadier in the faith and freer to face God and people openly.
The point: Deacons' work looks practical, yet it is bound up with the truth. In God's household, setting up tables, visiting, keeping the accounts and caring for people in need are all honorable service; the faithful come to know Christ more deeply in it.
Going Deeper: 3:14–15 How to Behave in the Household of God

1. "If I delay." "I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God" (1 Timothy 3:14–15). Paul hoped to come to Ephesus soon but was not sure. He wrote his teaching down so that Timothy and the Ephesian church could follow it. When we read this letter today, we too are reading what God, through Paul, left to the church.

2. "The household of God." "Which is the church of the living God" (1 Timothy 3:15).

  • "Household": the Greek can mean a house or a family. Paul uses both senses: the church is God's family (1 Timothy 5:1–2) and the temple where God dwells (see 1 Cor 3:16; Eph 2:21–22).
  • "The living God": Ephesus had images of Artemis, idols that could not speak and had no life (see Acts 19:26). The church's God is the living God.

3. "A pillar and buttress of truth." (1 Timothy 3:15).

  • "Pillar": a pillar holds up the roof and can be seen from far away. The church is to hold up the truth for the world to see.
  • "Buttress": the word means a foundation or support. The church is to hold the truth firmly so that false teaching cannot shake it.
  • The church and the truth: the church is not the source of truth; the truth comes from God and is written in Scripture (2 Tim 3:16). The church is the community that holds up and guards the truth. This also reminds us that the truth is not kept by individuals alone but held together in the church's fellowship.
The point: The church is the household of the living God, a pillar and buttress of truth. How we behave in the church concerns not only our relationships with one another but God's glory and the witness of the truth.
Going Deeper: 3:16 Great Indeed Is the Mystery of Godliness

1. "Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness." "We confess" means "by common confession," and very likely introduces a confession or hymn the early church recited together.

  • "Mystery": as Paul uses the word, a "mystery" is not something obscure but something once hidden and now revealed by God (see Rom 16:25–26; Col 1:26–27).
  • "The mystery of godliness": godliness does not begin with our effort but with Christ, whom God has revealed. Verse 9 spoke of "the mystery of the faith"; here Paul speaks of "the mystery of godliness"; both point to Christ.

2. "He was manifested in the flesh." There is a manuscript question here. The CUV follows later manuscripts and reads "God was manifested in the flesh"; the earlier manuscripts (which most scholars think are closer to the original) read "He who," referring to Christ, and the ESV translates it that way. The two readings differ (one calls him "God" outright), but neither changes the doctrine: the one "manifested in the flesh" already existed before he took human nature (see John 1:14; Phil 2:6–7). In Greek manuscripts the two words look almost alike (ΟΣ and the abbreviation ΘΣ). Christ's deity does not rest on this verse; Scripture plainly calls him God elsewhere (John 1:1; John 20:28; Titus 2:13).

3. Six lines. Many see three pairs, each pair a contrast (others, two stanzas of three lines):

  • "Manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit": he appeared in the flesh, was despised and crucified; many take "by the Spirit" to mean that the Holy Spirit raised him and so vindicated him, "declared to be the Son of God in power" (Rom 1:4); others read "in the spirit," the realm of resurrection life in contrast to "the flesh" (see 1 Pet 3:18). Either way, the resurrection is God's verdict that he is righteous. "Vindicated" here means shown to be in the right.
  • "Seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations": angels in heaven saw his victory (see 1 Pet 3:22); Gentiles on earth heard his gospel. Heaven and earth both know him.
  • "Believed on in the world, taken up in glory": people in the world believed in him, and he himself was taken up into heavenly glory (Acts 1:9).
  • The order: being "taken up in glory" came before the gospel spread among the nations, yet the hymn puts it last. The hymn is not laying out a timetable; it uses contrasts to praise the whole of Christ's work, from humiliation to glory.

4. Why here? Paul has just finished describing the character of overseers and deacons, and then he breaks into this hymn. He wants Timothy to know that a godly life does not begin with a checklist but with this Christ. We can live godly lives because he was manifested in the flesh, died for us, rose and ascended; we live by him and for him. In the next chapter Paul turns to people who have turned godliness into rules of abstinence (1 Timothy 4:1–5).

The point: The mystery of godliness is Christ himself: manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, taken up in glory. All the church's order and character must begin with knowing and worshiping him.
Meditation

Reflect: "Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory" (1 Timothy 3:16). When I hear the word "godliness," I may think of habits: reading the Bible and praying every day, never missing Sunday, not smoking or drinking, speaking politely. These may all be good. But Paul says the mystery of godliness is not a set of habits; it is a person. When I read the list for overseers and deacons, I may think: I am still far from all this, and my heart harbors pride, greed and anger. In truth, only one person fully fits that list: Christ himself. This does not lower the standard for leaders; it means that I, like every leader, must first be accepted in him before I can be changed by him. He is above reproach; he is gentle; he is not quarrelsome; he cares well for God's household; he lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Today I can read these six lines slowly, pausing after each one. Which line do I need most? "Manifested in the flesh," knowing he came into the place where I am? "Vindicated by the Spirit," knowing that the one people condemned, God has shown to be righteous, and that because he bore the condemnation I deserved (see Rom 4:25), in him I too am accepted? "Proclaimed among the nations," knowing this gospel has reached people like me? Or "taken up in glory," knowing he is now at the Father's right hand and my future is in his hands? I can choose one line and carry it through the day, and then say with the church of every age: Great indeed is the mystery of godliness!
