entries.content:
本章脉络

第四章分成三段。后来必有人离弃真道（1-5节）：圣灵明说，有人要听从邪灵和鬼魔的道理，禁止嫁娶，禁戒食物；但凡神所造的物都是好的，若感谢着领受，就没有一样可弃的，都因神的道和人的祈求成为圣洁了。作基督耶稣的好执事（6-10节）：提摩太要把这些事提醒弟兄们，弃绝荒谬的话，在敬虔上操练自己；操练身体益处还少，惟独敬虔凡事都有益处；我们的指望在乎永生的神，他是万人的救主，更是信徒的救主。不可叫人小看你年轻（11-16节）：提摩太要在言语、行为、爱心、信心、清洁上作信徒的榜样；要以宣读、劝勉、教导为念；不要轻忽所得的恩赐；要谨慎自己和自己的教训。

第三章以「敬虔的奥秘」作结，这奥秘就是基督；第四章就讲到假的敬虔和真的敬虔。假的敬虔是一套禁戒的规条，真的敬虔是在基督里，感谢着领受神所赐的一切，并且天天操练自己，越来越像他。

深读 4:1-5 凡神所造的物都是好的

1. 「在后来的时候，必有人离弃真道」。 「圣灵明说，在后来的时候，必有人离弃真道，听从那引诱人的邪灵和鬼魔的道理。」（提前4:1）

  • 「圣灵明说」： 可能指旧约或耶稣的预言（参可13:22；徒20:29-30），也可能指教会中的先知所说的话。无论哪一种，保罗都说：这是圣灵预先告诉我们的。
  • 「后来的时候」： 新约常说，从基督第一次来到他再来之间的整个时期，就是「末后的日子」（参来1:2；约一2:18）。所以保罗说的不只是遥远的将来，以弗所的教会已经在经历这样的事。
  • 「鬼魔的道理」： 这些教训看起来很属灵，甚至很严格，但背后有属灵的欺骗。错误的教训不只是想法错了，也是属灵的争战。

2. 「良心如同被热铁烙惯了一般」。 「这是因为说谎之人的假冒；这等人的良心如同被热铁烙惯了一般。」（提前4:2）

  • 「烙惯了」： 这个词可以指被烙铁烫过、失去感觉的皮肤；也可以指奴隶或罪犯身上被烙的印记。两种意思都很严肃：一个人一次又一次违背良心，最后良心就麻木了，或者他就被打上了另一个主人的印记。
  • 和第一章相连： 保罗在提前1:19已经说过，有人丢弃良心，在真道上如同船破坏了一般。

3. 「禁止嫁娶，又禁戒食物」。 「他们禁止嫁娶，又禁戒食物，就是神所造、叫那信而明白真道的人感谢着领受的。」（提前4:3）

  • 为什么禁止？ 这些人可能认为身体和物质是低等的，越远离它们就越属灵；也可能认为复活已经过去了（参提后2:18），信徒应该像天使一样不嫁不娶（参路20:35-36）。也可能和犹太人的洁净条例有关：保罗在提多书提到「犹太人荒谬的言语」之后，就说「在洁净的人，凡物都洁净」（多1:14-15；参西2:16）。这几种因素可能混在一起（参本书导读）。
  • 保罗的回答： 婚姻和食物都是「神所造」的（创1:31；创2:24）。拒绝神所造的好东西，看起来很敬虔，其实是在否认创造主的美善（参西2:20-23）。

4. 「若感谢着领受，就没有一样可弃的」。 「凡神所造的物都是好的，若感谢着领受，就没有一样可弃的，都因神的道和人的祈求成为圣洁了。」（提前4:4-5）

  • 「凡神所造的物都是好的」： 这句话呼应创世记第1章：「神看着一切所造的都甚好。」（创1:31）马可记述耶稣的教导时，也加上一句：「各样的食物都是洁净的」（可7:19）。
  • 「因神的道……成为圣洁」： 「神的道」可能指神在创造时宣告万物都好的话，也可能指饭前祷告中引用的圣经，或者指福音宣告食物洁净的话（参可7:19；徒10:15）。
  • 「和人的祈求」： 就是感谢的祷告。饭前谢恩不是一种迷信的仪式，而是承认：这一切都是从神来的。
  • 这不是说什么都可以： 保罗在别处也说，若吃某样东西会叫软弱的弟兄跌倒，就宁可不吃（林前8:13）。保罗在这里所反对的，是把禁戒当作得救或更属灵的条件。
  • 祭过的食物： 按林前8-10章的原则，参与祭拜（上供、烧香、跪拜、在供桌前同吃）是「与鬼相交」，不可有分（林前10:20-21）；平常买来或别人请吃、没有宗教意义的食物，可以感谢着吃（林前10:25-27）；若有人特别说明这是祭过的，为了那人的良心就不吃（林前10:28）。
  • 在华人处境中： 有些人信主以前许过吃素的愿，或者觉得某些食物不洁净；有些教会把不喝酒、不吃某种东西当作属灵的记号。信主以前向菩萨或神明许的素愿，应当在主面前认罪、弃绝，它不再约束在基督里的人；他可以感谢着吃。若良心一时还不安，也可以暂时不吃，但不是为了还愿（罗14:6）。教会为了见证或保护软弱的人（例如在劝酒成风的场合，或为了帮助受酒瘾困扰的人），提倡不喝酒，是出于爱心的智慧；但若把它当作衡量属灵与否、甚至得救的标准，就落入了保罗所警告的错误。
要点：神所造的都是好的。真正的敬虔不是远离神的恩赐，而是在感谢中领受它，在每一顿饭、在家庭、在工作中，承认那位赐恩的主。
深读 4:6-10 在敬虔上操练自己

1. 「基督耶稣的好执事」。 「你若将这些事提醒弟兄们，便是基督耶稣的好执事，在真道的话语和你向来所服从的善道上得了教育。」（提前4:6）

  • 「好执事」： 这里的「执事」是一般的意思，就是服事的人，不是第三章的职分。
  • 「得了教育」： 原文是现在式，许多人认为这是强调要不断从真道得着喂养。一个人要喂养别人，自己先要天天吃神的话（参太4:4）。

2. 「在敬虔上操练自己」。 「只是要弃绝那世俗的言语和老妇荒谬的话，在敬虔上操练自己。」（提前4:7）

  • 「老妇荒谬的话」： 这是当时的一句俗语，指没有根据的无稽之谈，不是要轻看年长的妇女（参提前5:2）。
  • 「操练」： 原文是体育场上锻炼身体的那个词。运动员要每天练习，有计划，有节制（林前9:25）。敬虔也是这样，不是一时的热心，而是长期的操练：读经、祷告、敬拜、团契、服事、认罪悔改。
  • 操练不是赚取恩典： 我们不是靠操练得救，而是因为已经蒙恩，就操练自己，在恩典中长进（参提后2:1；彼后3:18）。操练的人不是在争取神的接纳，而是在学习以那位已经接纳他的神为乐，并且顺服他。

3. 「操练身体，益处还少」。 「『操练身体，益处还少；惟独敬虔，凡事都有益处，因有今生和来生的应许。』这话是可信的，是十分可佩服的。」（提前4:8-9）

  • 「益处还少」： 保罗没有说操练身体没有益处，而是说它的益处有限，只在今生。今天许多人很看重养生、健身、饮食，这些都有它的价值；但如果我们花在身体上的心思远远多过花在灵魂上的，就本末倒置了。
  • 「今生和来生的应许」： 敬虔不只是为了将来，也带来今生的益处：平安、知足、与神同行的喜乐（参提前6:6）。
  • 哪一句是「可信的话」？ 解经家对「这话是可信的」指的是第8节还是第10节，看法不同。和合本把第8节放在引号里，采取前一种理解。主张指第8节的人指出，第10节开头有「因为」（和合本作「正是为此」），像是解释，而不像格言本身；第8节的对句形式也像一句格言。

4. 「他是万人的救主，更是信徒的救主」。 「我们劳苦努力，正是为此，因我们的指望在乎永生的神；他是万人的救主，更是信徒的救主。」（提前4:10）

  • 「劳苦努力」： 操练敬虔是辛苦的，但我们的盼望不在自己的努力上，而「在乎永生的神」。
  • 「万人的救主，更是信徒的救主」： 这句话有几种理解。
  • 「更是」的意思： 有些改革宗学者（如乔治·奈特）认为，「更是」在这里可以理解为进一步说明前一句：神是万人的救主，也就是说，他是信徒的救主。
  • 普遍恩典： 加尔文等改革宗解经家认为，神以普遍的恩典保守、供应所有的人（参太5:45；徒14:17），在这个意义上是万人的「救主」；但只有信的人才真正得着永远的救恩。
  • 为万人预备的救恩： 阿民念和卫斯理传统（如约翰·卫斯理；解经家如霍华德·马歇尔）认为，神为所有的人预备了救恩，愿意所有的人得救（参提前2:4），但只有信的人才真正领受。
  • 共同的地方： 这几种看法都不认为所有的人最后都必得救；保罗在同一章就说「有人离弃真道」（提前4:1），又说要「救自己，又能救听你的人」（提前4:16）。（参第二章对提前2:4、6的讨论。）
要点：敬虔需要操练，像运动员一样天天练习；但我们操练，不是为了赚取神的爱，而是因为我们的盼望在乎那位永生的神，他是信徒的救主。
深读 4:11-16 不可叫人小看你年轻

1. 「不可叫人小看你年轻」。 「这些事，你要吩咐人，也要教导人。不可叫人小看你年轻，总要在言语、行为、爱心、信心、清洁上，都作信徒的榜样。」（提前4:11-12）

  • 提摩太有多年轻？ 他跟随保罗已有十几年，所以这时可能是三十多岁。在当时的社会，四十岁以下仍常被看作「年轻」，而以弗所的长老中很可能有比他年长的人。
  • 怎样不叫人小看？ 保罗没有叫他用权柄压人，也没有叫他为自己辩护，而是叫他作榜样。这里有五个方面：言语、行为、爱心、信心、清洁。最好的回应不是争辩，而是生命。
  • 华人教会的处境： 我们的文化很看重辈分和年资。年轻的传道人和同工常常被说「你还年轻，不懂」。这段经文对年轻人说：不要因为年轻就退缩，也不要用骄傲来回应，要用生命作榜样（参耶1:6-7）。它也对年长的人说：不要因为一个人年轻就小看他，要看神在他身上所做的工。

2. 「以宣读、劝勉、教导为念」。 「你要以宣读、劝勉、教导为念，直等到我来。」（提前4:13）

  • 「宣读」： 指在聚会中公开诵读圣经。这是从犹太会堂继承下来的（参路4:16-21；尼8:8）。在许多人没有自己的圣经、也不识字的时代，公开读经非常重要。今天我们也不应该轻看在聚会中好好地读经。
  • 「劝勉、教导」： 读了经，还要讲解，使人明白，并劝人照着去行。

3. 「不要轻忽所得的恩赐」。 「你不要轻忽所得的恩赐，就是从前藉着预言、在众长老按手的时候赐给你的。」（提前4:14）

  • 恩赐是神给的： 提摩太的服事不是从他自己的能力开始的，而是神所赐的（参提后1:6）。
  • 「轻忽」： 恩赐不会自动长大，需要使用、挑旺。一个胆怯的人很容易因为别人的批评，就把神给的恩赐放在一边。
  • 「众长老按手」： 教会公开地承认、差派他（「藉着预言」，参提前1:18）。保罗在提后1:6说是藉着他自己按手；两处可能指同一件事，保罗和众长老一同按手。

4. 「使众人看出你的长进来」。 「这些事你要殷勤去做，并要在此专心，使众人看出你的长进来。」（提前4:15）神不要求提摩太一开始就完美，而是要他「长进」。人们看见的，不是一个没有缺点的人，而是一个在恩典中不断成长的人。

5. 「又能救自己，又能救听你的人」。 「你要谨慎自己和自己的教训，要在这些事上恒心；因为这样行，又能救自己，又能救听你的人。」（提前4:16）

  • 先谨慎自己： 保罗先说「自己」，再说「自己的教训」。一个传道人如果只顾教训，不顾自己的生命，最后两样都会失去（参林前9:27）。
  • 「救自己」是什么意思？ 这不是说我们靠自己的努力得救。救恩完全是神的恩典（提前1:15-16；提后1:9）。这里的「救」，是指在信心中坚持到底，最后完全得救；神使用我们的恒心和他所托付的道，来保守我们和听道的人（参腓2:12-13）。我们得救的根据，是基督舍自己作万人的赎价（提前2:6）；恒心是得救之人的路，不是得救的代价。
  • 听的人： 传道人的生命和教导，关系到别人的灵魂。这是一个严肃的责任，也是一个荣耀的托付。
要点：神不要提摩太先变得年长，才开始服事；他要提摩太在恩典中长进，用生命作榜样，谨慎自己和所教导的道。神的恩赐和神的话，就足以使用一个年轻又胆怯的人。
默想

默想： 「不可叫人小看你年轻，总要在言语、行为、爱心、信心、清洁上，都作信徒的榜样。」（提前4:12）也许我正是那个被人小看的人：在教会里，因为年轻，我的意见常常没有人听；我刚开始服事，别人一句「你还年轻，不懂」，就让我想放弃。也许正相反，我是那个小看别人的人：看见一个年轻的弟兄姊妹上台，心里就先打了折扣，也许是因为我把自己的价值放在了资历上，一个年轻人做得好，好像就显得我不那么重要了；或者在家里，从来不认真听儿女说他们从神那里学到了什么。无论我是哪一种，我都可以想到耶稣。他开始传道的时候「年纪约有三十岁」（路3:23），在他长大的地方，人们说：「这不是那木匠吗？」「他们就厌弃他」（可6:3）。他被人小看，「我们也不尊重他」（赛53:3）。可是他没有用争辩来证明自己，而是一直走下去，走到十字架，为那些小看他的人舍命，也为我舍命。我被人小看的时候，可以记得：他比我更明白这种滋味，而父对他的喜悦从来没有因为人的轻看而减少。我小看别人的时候，要先向主认罪：我自己也曾是「不尊重他」的人，他却没有小看我。今天，我可以求主帮助我在一件小事上作个小小的榜样，不是为了证明自己，而是因为他的恩典；也可以去听一个比我年轻的人说话，听他讲神在他身上做了什么。那位曾被人厌弃的主，父已经叫他从死里复活；我和那个年轻人身上的「长进」（提前4:15），都是他亲自在做的工。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 4 falls into three parts. Some will depart from the faith (vv. 1–5): the Spirit expressly says that some will devote themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods; but everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer. A good servant of Christ Jesus (vv. 6–10): Timothy is to put these things before the brothers, have nothing to do with silly myths, and train himself for godliness; bodily training is of some value, but godliness is of value in every way; our hope is set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe. Let no one despise you for your youth (vv. 11–16): Timothy is to set the believers an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity; to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching; not to neglect the gift he has; and to keep a close watch on himself and on the teaching.

Chapter 3 ended with "the mystery of godliness," which is Christ; chapter 4 turns to false godliness and true godliness. False godliness is a set of rules of abstinence; true godliness is, in Christ, receiving all that God gives with thanksgiving and training ourselves day by day to become more like him.

Going Deeper: 4:1–5 Everything Created by God Is Good

1. "In later times some will depart from the faith." "Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons" (1 Timothy 4:1).

  • "The Spirit expressly says": this may refer to prophecies in the Old Testament or from Jesus (see Mark 13:22; Acts 20:29–30), or to words spoken by prophets in the church. Either way Paul says: the Spirit told us this in advance.
  • "In later times": the New Testament often calls the whole period between Christ's first coming and his return "the last days" (see Heb 1:2; 1 John 2:18). So Paul is not speaking only of a distant future; the church in Ephesus was already living it.
  • "Teachings of demons": these teachings look very spiritual, even very strict, but behind them lies spiritual deception. False teaching is not only an intellectual error; it is also spiritual warfare.

2. "Whose consciences are seared." "Through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared" (1 Timothy 4:2).

  • "Seared": the word can mean skin burned by a hot iron until it loses feeling; it can also mean the brand burned onto a slave or criminal. Both senses are sobering: someone who violates conscience again and again ends with a conscience gone numb, or bears the mark of another master.
  • The link with chapter 1: Paul has already said in 1 Timothy 1:19 that some have rejected conscience and made shipwreck of their faith.

3. "Who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods." "Who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth" (1 Timothy 4:3).

  • Why forbid them? These people may have thought the body and material things inferior, so that the further one kept from them the more spiritual one became; or they may have believed the resurrection had already happened (see 2 Tim 2:18), so that believers should be like the angels, who neither marry nor are given in marriage (see Luke 20:35–36). They may also have drawn on Jewish purity rules: right after "Jewish myths" Paul says "To the pure, all things are pure" (Titus 1:14–15; see Col 2:16). These strands may have been mixed together (see the introduction).
  • Paul's answer: marriage and food are both things "God created" (Gen 1:31; Gen 2:24). Rejecting the good things God made looks godly, but it actually denies the goodness of the Creator (see Col 2:20–23).

4. "Nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving." "For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer" (1 Timothy 4:4–5).

  • "Everything created by God is good": this echoes Genesis 1: "God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (Gen 1:31). Mark notes that Jesus "declared all foods clean" (Mark 7:19).
  • "Made holy by the word of God": "the word of God" may mean God's word in creation declaring all things good, or the Scripture quoted in a prayer before meals, or the gospel word that declares foods clean (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15).
  • "And prayer": that is, the prayer of thanksgiving. Giving thanks before a meal is not a superstitious ritual; it acknowledges that everything comes from God.
  • This does not mean anything goes: Paul says elsewhere that if eating something will make a weak brother stumble, he would rather not eat it (1 Cor 8:13). What Paul opposes here is making abstinence a condition of salvation or of being more spiritual.
  • Food offered in worship: in a Chinese setting, 1 Corinthians 8–10 gives the lines: taking part in the offering (setting out offerings, burning incense, bowing, eating at the altar table) is fellowship with demons and must be refused (1 Cor 10:20–21); ordinary food bought or served without religious meaning may be eaten with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 10:25–27); if someone points out that it was offered, abstain for that person's conscience (1 Timothy 10:28).
  • In a Chinese setting: some people took a vegetarian vow before coming to faith, or feel certain foods are "unclean"; some churches treat not drinking or not eating certain things as a mark of spirituality. A vegetarian vow made to a bodhisattva or deity before conversion should be confessed and renounced before the Lord; it does not bind someone in Christ; he may eat with thanksgiving. If his conscience is not yet at rest he may abstain for a time, but not in order to keep the vow (Rom 14:6). A church that encourages abstaining from alcohol for the sake of witness or to protect the weak (for example amid pressure to drink at banquets, or where someone struggles with addiction) is exercising loving wisdom; but making it the measure of spirituality, or even of salvation, falls into the error Paul warns against.
The point: Everything God made is good. True godliness does not keep away from God's gifts but receives them with thanksgiving, acknowledging the gracious Lord in every meal, every home and every job.
Going Deeper: 4:6–10 Train Yourself for Godliness

1. "A good servant of Christ Jesus." "If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed" (1 Timothy 4:6).

  • "Servant": the word is the general one for someone who serves, not the office of deacon in chapter 3.
  • "Being trained": the Greek is a present participle, often taken to stress ongoing nourishment. Anyone who would feed others must first keep being fed by God's word (see Matt 4:4).

2. "Train yourself for godliness." "Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness" (1 Timothy 4:7).

  • "Silly myths": the Greek is literally "old wives' tales," a common expression of the time for baseless nonsense; it is not meant to belittle older women (see 1 Timothy 5:2).
  • "Train": the Greek is the word for exercising the body in the gymnasium. An athlete trains every day, with a plan and with self-control (1 Cor 9:25). So too with godliness: not a moment of zeal but long training: reading Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship, service, confession and repentance.
  • Training does not earn grace: we are not saved by training; because we have already received grace, we train ourselves to grow in it (see 2 Tim 2:1; 2 Pet 3:18). Someone in training is not striving for God's acceptance but learning to enjoy and obey the God who has already accepted him.

3. "Bodily training is of some value." "For while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come. The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance" (1 Timothy 4:8–9).

  • "Of some value": Paul does not say bodily training is worthless, only that its value is limited to this life. Many people today care a great deal about health, fitness and diet, and these have their value; but if we give far more thought to the body than to the soul, we have our priorities upside down.
  • "Promise for the present life and also for the life to come": godliness is not only for the future; it brings benefits in this life as well: peace, contentment, the joy of walking with God (see 1 Timothy 6:6).
  • Which is the "trustworthy saying"? Commentators differ on whether "the saying is trustworthy" refers to verse 8 or verse 10. The CUV puts verse 8 in quotation marks, taking the first view. Those who take it as verse 8 note that verse 10 begins with "for," which reads like an explanation rather than the saying itself, and that verse 8 has the balanced form of a proverb. The ESV leaves the question open.

4. "The Savior of all people, especially of those who believe." "For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe" (1 Timothy 4:10).

  • "Toil and strive": training in godliness is hard work, but our hope is not in our own effort; it is "set on the living God."
  • "The Savior of all people, especially of those who believe": this phrase is read in several ways.
  • "Especially" as "that is": some Reformed scholars (such as George Knight) think "especially" can here mean "that is": God is the Savior of all people, namely, of those who believe.
  • Common grace: Calvin and other Reformed interpreters hold that God preserves and provides for all people by common grace (see Matt 5:45; Acts 14:17), and in that sense is the "Savior" of all, but that only those who believe actually receive eternal salvation.
  • Salvation provided for all: the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions (for example John Wesley; among commentators, I. Howard Marshall) hold that God has provided salvation for all and desires all to be saved (see 1 Timothy 2:4), but that only those who believe actually receive it.
  • Common ground: none of these views holds that all people will finally be saved; in this same chapter Paul says "some will depart from the faith" (1 Timothy 4:1) and speaks of saving "both yourself and your hearers" (1 Timothy 4:16). (See the discussion of 1 Timothy 2:4, 6.)
The point: Godliness takes training, daily practice like an athlete's. But we train not to earn God's love; we train because our hope is set on the living God, who is the Savior of those who believe.
Going Deeper: 4:11–16 Let No One Despise You for Your Youth

1. "Let no one despise you for your youth." "Command and teach these things. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity" (1 Timothy 4:11–12).

  • How young was Timothy? He had been with Paul for over a decade, so he may now have been in his thirties. In that society men under forty were often still considered "young," and the Ephesian elders likely included men older than he was.
  • How does one avoid being despised? Paul does not tell him to use authority to pressure people or to defend himself, but to be an example in five areas: speech, conduct, love, faith, purity. The best answer is not argument but a life.
  • In Chinese churches: our culture values seniority and years of service. Young pastors and coworkers often hear, "You're still young; you don't understand." This passage tells the young: do not shrink back because you are young, and do not answer with pride; be an example with your life (see Jer 1:6–7). It also tells the older: do not despise someone for being young; look at what God is doing in him.

2. "Devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching." "Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching" (1 Timothy 4:13).

  • "Public reading": reading Scripture aloud in the gathering, a practice inherited from the synagogue (see Luke 4:16–21; Neh 8:8). In an age when many had no Bible of their own and could not read, public reading was vital. Today too we should not neglect reading Scripture well when we gather.
  • "Exhortation, teaching": after the reading comes explanation, so that people understand, and exhortation, so that they act on it.

3. "Do not neglect the gift you have." "Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you" (1 Timothy 4:14).

  • The gift is God's: Timothy's ministry did not begin with his own ability; God gave it (see 2 Tim 1:6).
  • "Neglect": a gift does not grow by itself; it must be used and fanned into flame. A timid person can easily set aside God's gift because of others' criticism.
  • "The council of elders laid their hands on you": the church publicly recognized and sent him ("by prophecy," see 1 Timothy 1:18). In 2 Tim 1:6 Paul speaks of his own laying on of hands; the two may describe the same event, with Paul and the elders laying hands on him together.

4. "So that all may see your progress." "Practice these things, devote yourself to them, so that all may see your progress" (1 Timothy 4:15). God did not require Timothy to be perfect from the start, but to "progress." What people see is not someone without flaws but someone growing steadily in grace.

5. "You will save both yourself and your hearers." "Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers" (1 Timothy 4:16).

  • Watch yourself first: Paul says "yourself" before "the teaching." A minister who attends only to his teaching and not to his own life will in the end lose both (see 1 Cor 9:27).
  • What does "save yourself" mean? It does not mean we are saved by our own effort. Salvation is wholly God's grace (1 Timothy 1:15–16; 2 Tim 1:9). "Save" here means persevering in faith to the end and being finally saved; God uses our perseverance and the word he has entrusted to us to keep us and our hearers (see Phil 2:12–13). The ground of our salvation is Christ, who gave himself as a ransom (1 Timothy 2:6); perseverance is the road the saved walk, not the price of being saved.
  • The hearers: a minister's life and teaching bear on other people's souls. This is a solemn responsibility and a glorious trust.
The point: God did not make Timothy wait until he was older to begin serving; he called him to grow in grace, to be an example with his life, and to keep watch over himself and the word he taught. God's gift and God's word are enough to use someone young and timid.
Meditation

Reflect: "Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity" (1 Timothy 4:12). Perhaps I am the one being despised: in church my opinions are seldom heard because I am young; I have just begun to serve, and one remark, "You're still young; you don't understand," makes me want to quit. Or perhaps it is the other way around, and I am the one who despises others: when a young brother or sister stands up front, I have already marked them down in my heart, perhaps because I have put my worth in my seniority, and a young person doing well seems to make me matter less; or at home I never really listen when my children tell me what they have learned from God. Whichever I am, I can think of Jesus. When he began his ministry he "was about thirty years of age" (Luke 3:23), and in the town where he grew up people said, "Is not this the carpenter?" "And they took offense at him" (Mark 6:3). He was despised, "and we esteemed him not" (Isa 53:3). Yet he did not argue to prove himself; he kept going, all the way to the cross, and laid down his life for those who despised him, and for me. When I am despised, I can remember that he knows the taste of it better than I do, and that the Father's delight in him never lessened because people looked down on him. When I look down on others, I confess it to him: I too was among those who "esteemed him not," yet he did not look down on me. Today I can ask the Lord to let me, in one small thing, be a small example, not to prove myself but because of his grace; and I can go and listen to someone younger than I am, and hear what God has been doing in their life. The Lord who was once despised, the Father has raised from the dead; the "progress" (1 Timothy 4:15) in me and in that younger person is his own work.

entries.content:
本章脉络

第五章分成四段。在神的家中彼此对待（1-2节）：要劝老年人如同父亲，劝少年人如同弟兄，劝老年妇女如同母亲，劝少年妇女如同姊妹，总要清清洁洁的。寡妇（3-16节）：要尊敬那真为寡妇的；寡妇若有儿女或孙子孙女，他们要先在自己家中行孝；那独居无靠的寡妇是仰赖神，昼夜祈求；记在册子上的寡妇要年满六十岁，有行善的名声；年轻的寡妇最好再嫁；信主的妇女家中若有寡妇，要自己救济她们。长老（17-25节）：善于管理的长老配受加倍的敬奉；控告长老要有两三个见证；犯罪的要在众人面前责备；不可有偏心；按手不可急促；有些人的罪和善行是明显的，有些是随后显出来的。中间还插进一句保罗对提摩太个人的关心：可以稍微用点酒，因为他屡次患病（23节）。

这一章看起来是一些实际的安排：怎样照顾寡妇，怎样对待长老。但每一条都建立在提前3:15的真理上：教会是神的家。一个家，要照顾软弱的，也要尊重带领的；要有爱心，也要有公义。

深读 5:1-2 如同父亲，如同弟兄

1. 「不可严责老年人，只要劝他如同父亲」。 「不可严责老年人，只要劝他如同父亲；劝少年人如同弟兄；劝老年妇女如同母亲；劝少年妇女如同姊妹；总要清清洁洁的。」（提前5:1-2）

  • 「严责」： 原文是用很重的话斥责。提摩太是教会的带领人，但对年长的人，即使需要劝诫，也要带着尊重，像儿子劝父亲一样。
  • 这是一个家： 保罗用了四个家人的称呼：父亲、弟兄、母亲、姊妹。在教会里，我们不是同事，也不是顾客，而是一家人（参可3:34-35）。
  • 「总要清清洁洁的」： 对少年妇女，要像对亲姊妹一样，在言语、行为和心思上都清洁。教会的带领人尤其要谨慎，不可利用牧养的关系，在情感或身体上越过界线。
要点：教会是神的家。我们成为一家人，是因为基督把我们带到同一位父面前；所以就连劝诫和纠正，也要带着家人的尊重和清洁的爱。
深读 5:3-8 尊敬那真为寡妇的

1. 「要尊敬那真为寡妇的」。 「要尊敬那真为寡妇的。」（提前5:3）

  • 「尊敬」： 这里不只是心里的尊重，也包括实际的供养（参提前5:17-18「敬奉」）。在当时，寡妇如果没有家人照顾，往往陷入贫穷。旧约一再吩咐以色列人照顾孤儿寡妇（申24:19-21），神自己也是「作寡妇的伸冤者」（诗68:5）。初期教会一开始就照顾寡妇（徒6:1；徒9:39）。
  • 「真为寡妇的」： 保罗接下来解释，就是没有家人可以依靠的寡妇。

2. 「先在自己家中学着行孝」。 「若寡妇有儿女，或有孙子孙女，便叫他们先在自己家中学着行孝，报答亲恩，因为这在神面前是可悦纳的。」（提前5:4）

  • 「行孝」： 原文是「敬虔」的动词形式。保罗把孝敬父母看作在家里活出敬虔。敬虔不只在聚会中，也在家里。
  • 「报答亲恩」： 父母曾经养育我们，现在我们照顾年老的父母，这是神的心意（出20:12）。耶稣曾经责备那些以「各耳板」为借口、不奉养父母的人（可7:10-13）。
  • 和华人文化的关系： 华人文化很重视孝道，这一点和圣经的吩咐相近，但根基不同。儒家的孝以人伦为本，也包括祭祖；圣经的孝道是「在神面前」的：我们孝敬父母，是因为敬畏神、遵行他的诫命（出20:12）。孝道不能高过神（太10:37），也不包括祭祖、烧香跪拜这些违背信仰的事；信徒可以用追思礼拜、扫墓献花来纪念先人、感谢神；而尽孝最要紧的，是好好照顾在世的长辈。另一方面，信主的人也不可以「属灵」为借口，忽略对父母的实际照顾。

3. 「那独居无靠、真为寡妇的，是仰赖神」。 「那独居无靠、真为寡妇的，是仰赖神，昼夜不住地祈求祷告。但那好宴乐的寡妇正活着的时候也是死的。」（提前5:5-6）

  • 「仰赖神」： 一个没有人可以依靠的人，把她的盼望放在神身上。路加福音中的亚拿就是这样一位寡妇：她「并不离开圣殿，禁食祈求，昼夜事奉神」（路2:37）。
  • 「好宴乐的」： 指放纵享乐、只为自己活的人。保罗说她「正活着的时候也是死的」，就是外表活着，灵里却已经死了（参启3:1）。

4. 「比不信的人还不好」。 「人若不看顾亲属，就是背了真道，比不信的人还不好，不看顾自己家里的人，更是如此。」（提前5:8）这是全章最重的一句话。连不信的人都知道要照顾自己的家人；一个自称信主的人若不照顾，就是在行为上否认了信仰。照顾家人不只是文化的要求，也是信仰的见证。若父母曾经虐待儿女，儿女仍可以用安全的方式、保持适当的距离来尽奉养的责任，不必回到危险之中。有些人身在海外，有些人自己身体不好，有些人经济实在困难，没有办法亲自照顾父母，心里常常内疚。保罗责备的是不肯看顾的人，不是有心无力的人；看顾可以有许多方式：常常打电话、尽量回去探望、在经济上支持、托可靠的人就近照顾。真有亏欠的地方，就向主认罪，他必赦免；力有不逮的地方，就交托给主，求他指引一条走得通的路。

要点：照顾年老和孤单的人，是神家的标记。孝敬父母是在神面前的敬虔；无依无靠的寡妇，有神自己作她们的依靠，教会也要成为她们的家。
深读 5:9-16 寡妇的名册

1. 「寡妇记在册子上」。 「寡妇记在册子上，必须年纪到六十岁，从来只作一个丈夫的妻子，又有行善的名声，就如养育儿女，接待远人，洗圣徒的脚，救济遭难的人，竭力行各样善事。」（提前5:9-10）

  • 这名册是什么？ 学者们有不同的看法。有人认为，这是教会长期供养的寡妇的名单；也有人认为，这是一群在教会中专门服事（如祷告、探访、接待）的寡妇，她们由教会供养，也承诺委身于这样的服事。后来的初期教会中，确实有一个专门服事的「寡妇」群体。
  • 「从来只作一个丈夫的妻子」： 和提前3:2对监督的要求相对应（参第三章的几种看法）。有人认为是指一生只结过一次婚；许多人认为是指在婚姻中忠诚：保罗在第14节劝年轻的寡妇再嫁，他不会因为她们听从了这个劝告，日后就把她们排除在名册之外。
  • 「洗圣徒的脚」： 指谦卑地服事别人，可能也包括实际地接待旅行中的信徒。耶稣自己为门徒洗脚（约13:14-15）。

2. 「至于年轻的寡妇」。 「至于年轻的寡妇，就可以辞她；因为她们的情欲发动，违背基督的时候就想要嫁人。她们被定罪，是因废弃了当初所许的愿」（提前5:11-12）。

  • 「当初所许的愿」： 原文这个词一般译作「信」。许多解经家认为这里指一种誓约：记在名册上的寡妇承诺专心服事基督、不再嫁人，后来若想再嫁，就违背了这个誓约；也有解经家认为是指离弃起初对基督的信，例如嫁给不信的人，或跟从假教师（参提前5:15「已经有转去随从撒但的」）。
  • 保罗不是反对再嫁： 他在第14节说：「我愿意年轻的寡妇嫁人，生养儿女，治理家务。」问题不在于再婚，而在于许了愿又背弃，以及在第13节所说的「挨家闲游……说长道短」。这可能也和假教师有关，他们在各家中传异教（参提后3:6）。
  • 今天的意义： 这不是说年轻的寡妇在属灵上比较软弱，而是保罗出于牧者的智慧，不让她们过早许下一个难以持守的誓愿。

3. 「信主的妇女，若家中有寡妇」。 「信主的妇女，若家中有寡妇，自己就当救济她们，不可累着教会，好使教会能救济那真无倚靠的寡妇。」（提前5:16）家人能照顾的，先由家人照顾；这样，教会有限的资源就能用在最需要的人身上。

要点：教会对寡妇的照顾既有爱心，也有智慧：家人先尽本分，教会照顾真正无依无靠的人，也尊重那些一生忠心服事的人。
深读 5:17-25 对待长老

1. 「配受加倍的敬奉」。 「那善于管理教会的长老，当以为配受加倍的敬奉；那劳苦传道教导人的，更当如此。因为经上说：『牛在场上踹谷的时候，不可笼住它的嘴』；又说：『工人得工价是应当的。』」（提前5:17-18）

  • 「加倍的敬奉」： 「敬奉」和第3节的「尊敬」在原文是同一个词根，包括尊重和经济上的供给。从第18节引用的经文看，这里显然包括工价。「加倍」可能是指尊重加上供给，也可能只是说丰厚的敬奉，不一定是精确的两倍工资。
  • 「劳苦传道教导人的」： 这可能表示，在长老中有一些人特别专注于讲道和教导。
  • 两处引用： 第一句出自申25:4（参林前9:9）。第二句和路10:7耶稣的话在原文中几乎一字不差。对「经上说」的范围有两种看法：许多学者认为，「经上说」同时引出这两句。若是这样，保罗已经把耶稣的话当作与旧约同等的圣经。这句话可能出自已经写成的路加福音（路加正是保罗的同工，参提后4:11），这也和路加福音较早成书的看法相合（参彼后3:16）。另一些学者认为「经上说」只引出第一句，「又说」引的是口传的主的话。无论哪一种，保罗都把主的话当作有权威的吩咐（林前9:14）。
  • 华人教会的处境： 有些教会觉得传道人清贫才属灵，给的生活费很少，甚至不够养家。保罗说，善于带领、劳苦教导的人，配受加倍的敬奉。尊重传道人，也包括让他们一家能够安心生活。

2. 「控告长老的呈子，非有两三个见证就不要收」。 「控告长老的呈子，非有两三个见证就不要收。犯罪的人，当在众人面前责备他，叫其余的人也可以惧怕。」（提前5:19-20）

  • 保护长老： 「两三个见证」出自申19:15（参太18:16）。带领人常常受人批评，教会不可以凭一个人的话，就随便定一位长老的罪。
  • 但不可成为掩护： 这条原则是要防止诬告，不是要保护犯罪的人。性侵和虐待常常发生在没有旁人的地方；但几位受害者各自的陈述、书面记录和其他证据，都可以成为「见证」。教会不可以用「没有两三个见证」为理由，拒绝认真调查对带领人的指控。「两三个见证」是教会处理控告的原则，不是报警的前提：涉及犯罪的事，应当向警方报案，不可只在教会内部处理；涉及儿童或性侵的事，不必等教会查清楚才报案（参罗13:4）。受害者也不必勉强与不安全的人修复关系，或继续留在危险中。即使犯罪的带领人真心悔改、受害者也饶恕了他，饶恕也不等于恢复他的职分，更不等于让他再接触受害者或儿童。
  • 「当在众人面前责备他」： 「犯罪的人」原文是现在分词，许多解经家认为是指那些继续犯罪、不肯悔改的长老。带领人的罪经过查证属实，教会就要在众人面前处理，不可因为事情原本隐秘，或为了顾全面子，就把它掩盖（「家丑不可外扬」不是圣经的原则）。这样，「其余的人也可以惧怕」，就是存敬畏的心，不敢轻看罪。

3. 「不可存成见，行事也不可有偏心」。 「我在神和基督耶稣并蒙拣选的天使面前嘱咐你：要遵守这些话，不可存成见，行事也不可有偏心。」（提前5:21）保罗用非常严肃的话嘱咐提摩太：处理这些事的时候，不可因为一个人有名、有钱、有恩赐，或者是自己的朋友，就偏袒他（参雅2:1、9）；也不可因为对一个人有成见，就先定了他的罪。

4. 「给人行按手的礼，不可急促」。 「给人行按手的礼，不可急促；不要在别人的罪上有分，要保守自己清洁。」（提前5:22）多数人认为，这是指按立长老。如果教会急着把一个还没有经过考验的人放在带领的位置上，他后来犯了罪，按立他的人也有责任（参提前3:6、10）。这也适用于犯过罪的带领人：不可急着恢复他的职分。（也有少数人认为，这里的按手是指接纳悔改的人重回教会。）

5. 「可以稍微用点酒」。 「因你胃口不清，屡次患病，再不要照常喝水，可以稍微用点酒。」（提前5:23）

  • 一句个人的关心： 在这些严肃的嘱咐中间，保罗突然关心起提摩太的胃。他不只是发出嘱咐的使徒，也是一位属灵的父亲（参提前1:2）。
  • 为什么要说这话？ 有人认为，提摩太完全不喝酒，可能有几个原因：受了当时禁戒风气的影响；不想让主张禁戒的假教师抓到把柄，说他放纵；也要在「不因酒滋事」（提前3:3）上作榜样。保罗说：为了身体的缘故，可以稍微用点酒。当时的水常常不干净，掺酒的水可能比较安全。
  • 这不是鼓励多喝酒： 「稍微」这个词很重要。保罗在别处也说「不要醉酒」（弗5:18）。他在这里所反对的，是把禁戒当作敬虔的标准，而忽略了身体的需要。

6. 「有些人的罪是明显的」。 「有些人的罪是明显的，如同先到审判案前；有些人的罪是随后跟了去的。这样，善行也有明显的，那不明显的也不能隐藏。」（提前5:24-25）选立带领人的时候，有些人的问题一眼就看得出来，有些人的问题要过一段时间才显出来。所以「不可急促」（提前5:22）。同样，有些人的善行很明显，有些人默默地服事，没有人注意；但神都看见，最后也都要显明出来（参太6:4）。

要点：神的家要尊重忠心的带领人，也要按公义处理带领人的罪；不可诬告，不可掩盖，不可偏心。在这一切背后，是那位在暗中察看、最后要显明一切的神。
默想

默想： 「那独居无靠、真为寡妇的，是仰赖神，昼夜不住地祈求祷告。」（提前5:5）有些人的生活走到一个地步，好像只剩下祷告了：丈夫或妻子走了，儿女在远方，身体也不如从前，能做的事越来越少。也许我就是这样的人：一天里大部分的时间，屋子里都很安静，我常常觉得孤单，有时连祷告都觉得空空的。路加福音记载了一位寡妇亚拿，她「现在已经八十四岁，并不离开圣殿，禁食祈求，昼夜事奉神」（路2:37）。几十年的祷告，看起来没有什么结果；可是有一天，马利亚和约瑟抱着婴孩耶稣进了圣殿，「正当那时，她进前来称谢神，将孩子的事对一切盼望耶路撒冷得救赎的人讲说」（路2:38）。这些年日的祷告，并不是她做不了别的事、才剩下来的一件事；那些年日，是她与神同在的日子。她最后得着的，不是别人重新觉得她有用，而是亲眼看见了她所盼望的那一位。那个婴孩后来长大，在十字架上替我们担当罪；临死的时候，他还看见站在十字架下的母亲，把她交托给所爱的门徒照顾（约19:26-27）。他自己最痛的时候，还记挂着母亲往后有人看顾。「神在他的圣所作孤儿的父，作寡妇的伸冤者。神叫孤独的有家」（诗68:5-6）。今天，我可以老实告诉主：我常常觉得孤单，有时连祷告都觉得空空的；然后像亚拿一样，在祷告中等候他，因为我所等候的，不是自己重新变得有用，而是主自己。如果我认识这样一位年长的弟兄姊妹，我也可以去问他：我能为你祷告什么？你也愿意为我祷告吗？说不定，主正要藉着我，叫一个孤独的人有家。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 5 falls into four parts. How to treat one another in God's household (vv. 1–2): encourage an older man as a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity. Widows (vv. 3–16): honor widows who are truly widows; if a widow has children or grandchildren, they are first to show godliness to their own household; the widow left all alone has set her hope on God and prays night and day; a widow to be enrolled must be at least sixty, with a reputation for good works; younger widows had better remarry; a believing woman with widows among her relatives is to care for them herself. Elders (vv. 17–25): elders who rule well are worthy of double honor; a charge against an elder needs two or three witnesses; those who persist in sin are to be rebuked in the presence of all; there must be no partiality; do not be hasty in laying on hands; the sins and good works of some are conspicuous, while others appear later. In the middle comes a personal word of care from Paul to Timothy: use a little wine, because of his frequent ailments (v. 23).

This chapter looks like a set of practical arrangements: how to care for widows, how to treat elders. But each instruction rests on the truth of 1 Timothy 3:15: the church is God's household. A household cares for the weak and honors those who lead; it has both love and justice.

Going Deeper: 5:1–2 As Fathers, as Brothers

1. "Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father." "Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father. Treat younger men like brothers, older women like mothers, younger women like sisters, in all purity" (1 Timothy 5:1–2).

  • "Rebuke": the Greek means to reprimand harshly. Timothy is the church's leader, but even when an older man needs correcting, Timothy is to speak with respect, as a son would appeal to his father.
  • This is a family: Paul uses four family words: father, brothers, mothers, sisters. In the church we are not colleagues or customers but family (see Mark 3:34–35).
  • "In all purity": toward younger women he is to act as toward his own sisters, pure in word, deed and thought. Church leaders especially must take care never to use a pastoral relationship to cross emotional or physical boundaries.
The point: The church is God's household. We are family because Christ has brought us to the same Father; so even correction and rebuke are to carry the respect of family and the purity of love.
Going Deeper: 5:3–8 Honor Widows Who Are Truly Widows

1. "Honor widows who are truly widows." "Honor widows who are truly widows" (1 Timothy 5:3).

  • "Honor": not only inward respect but practical support (see 1 Timothy 5:17–18, "double honor"). In that world a widow without family to care for her often fell into poverty. The Old Testament repeatedly commanded Israel to care for the fatherless and the widow (Deut 24:19–21), and God himself is the "protector of widows" (Ps 68:5). The early church cared for widows from the very beginning (Acts 6:1; Acts 9:39).
  • "Truly widows": Paul goes on to explain: widows with no family to depend on.

2. "Let them first learn to show godliness to their own household." "But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God" (1 Timothy 5:4).

  • "Show godliness": the Greek is the verb form of "godliness." Paul calls caring for one's parents the practice of godliness at home. Godliness is not only in the gathering but in the home.
  • "Make some return to their parents": our parents raised us; now caring for them in old age is God's will (Exod 20:12). Jesus rebuked those who used "Corban" as an excuse not to support their parents (Mark 7:10–13).
  • In relation to Chinese culture: Chinese filial piety resembles the biblical command but rests on a different foundation: Confucian human relations, which include ancestral rites. Biblical filial piety is "in the sight of God": we honor our parents because we fear God and keep his command (Exod 20:12); filial duty cannot rank above God (Matt 10:37), and it does not include ancestor rites, burning incense or bowing, or other things contrary to the faith; believers can remember the departed through memorial services and flowers at the grave, giving thanks to God; but filial duty is above all caring for living elders. On the other hand, believers must not use "spiritual" reasons as an excuse to neglect the practical care of their parents.

3. "She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God." "She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day, but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives" (1 Timothy 5:5–6).

  • "Set her hope on God": someone with no one else to lean on puts her hope in God. Anna in Luke's Gospel was such a widow: "She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day" (Luke 2:37).
  • "Self-indulgent": someone given to pleasure and living for herself. Paul says she "is dead even while she lives," alive outwardly but dead in spirit (see Rev 3:1).

4. "Worse than an unbeliever." "But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever" (1 Timothy 5:8). This is the weightiest sentence in the chapter. Even unbelievers know to care for their own families; someone who claims to believe and does not is denying the faith by his conduct. Caring for one's family is not only a cultural expectation but a witness of faith. Where a parent has been abusive, provision can be made safely and at a distance; it does not require returning to danger. Some, living abroad, ill themselves or in real financial hardship, cannot care for their parents in person and carry constant guilt. Paul rebukes those who will not provide, not those who cannot do all they wish. Provision can take many forms: regular calls, visits when possible, financial support, entrusting care to someone reliable. Where we have truly failed, we can confess it to the Lord, and he forgives; where we simply cannot do more, we can entrust it to him and ask him to show us a way forward.

The point: Caring for the old and the lonely is a mark of God's household. Honoring parents is godliness before God; and for those with no one to lean on, God himself is their support, and the church is to become their family.
Going Deeper: 5:9–16 The List of Widows

1. "Let a widow be enrolled." "Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work" (1 Timothy 5:9–10).

  • What was this list? Scholars differ. Some think it was a list of widows the church supported long term; others think it was a group of widows devoted to particular service in the church (such as prayer, visiting and hospitality), supported by the church and committed to that service. The early church did later have "widows" as a recognized group of servants.
  • "The wife of one husband": this parallels 1 Timothy 3:2 (see the views set out in chapter 3). Some take it to mean married only once; many take it to mean faithfulness in marriage, since in verse 14 Paul urges younger widows to remarry and would hardly bar them from the list later for doing so.
  • "Washed the feet of the saints": humble service of others, perhaps including practical hospitality to traveling believers. Jesus himself washed his disciples' feet (John 13:14–15).

2. "But refuse to enroll younger widows." "But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith" (1 Timothy 5:11–12).

  • "Their former faith": the CUV reads "the vow they first made." The Greek word is usually "faith." Many commentators take it here as a pledge: enrolled widows promised to devote themselves to Christ's service and not remarry, so a widow who later wished to remarry would break that pledge. Others take it as abandoning their first faith in Christ, for example by marrying an unbeliever or following the false teachers (see 1 Timothy 5:15, "some have already strayed after Satan").
  • Paul is not against remarriage: in verse 14 he says, "I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households." The problem is not remarriage but making a pledge and then abandoning it, along with what verse 13 describes: "going about from house to house... gossips and busybodies." This may also be connected with the false teachers, who spread their teaching from house to house (see 2 Tim 3:6).
  • What it means today: this does not mean younger widows are spiritually weaker; it is Paul's pastoral wisdom, not wanting them to take on too early a vow that would be hard to keep.

3. "If any believing woman has relatives who are widows." "If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are really widows" (1 Timothy 5:16). What the family can do, the family does first; then the church's limited resources can go to those in greatest need.

The point: The church's care for widows combines love with wisdom: the family does its part first, the church cares for those with no one to lean on, and it honors those who have served faithfully all their lives.
Going Deeper: 5:17–25 How to Treat Elders

1. "Worthy of double honor." "Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, 'You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain,' and, 'The laborer deserves his wages'" (1 Timothy 5:17–18).

  • "Double honor": "honor" is from the same root as "honor" in verse 3, including both respect and financial support. The verses quoted in verse 18 show that wages are clearly included. "Double" may mean respect plus material support, or simply generous honor; it need not mean exactly twice the pay.
  • "Those who labor in preaching and teaching": this may indicate that among the elders some gave themselves especially to preaching and teaching.
  • Two quotations: the first is from Deut 25:4 (see 1 Cor 9:9). The second agrees almost word for word in Greek with Jesus' saying in Luke 10:7. There are two views of how far "the Scripture says" reaches. Many scholars think it introduces both quotations: Paul already counts Jesus' words, perhaps the written Gospel of Luke (Luke was Paul's companion, 2 Tim 4:11), as Scripture alongside the Old Testament; this fits an early date for Luke (see also 2 Pet 3:16). Others think "the Scripture says" introduces only the first quotation, and "and" introduces a saying of the Lord known orally. Either way, Paul treats the Lord's word as authoritative command (1 Cor 9:14).
  • In Chinese churches: some churches feel that a pastor's poverty is a sign of spirituality and pay so little that it cannot support a family. Paul says that those who lead well and labor in teaching are worthy of double honor. Honoring ministers includes enabling them and their families to live without anxiety.

2. "Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses." "Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear" (1 Timothy 5:19–20).

  • Protecting elders: "two or three witnesses" comes from Deut 19:15 (see Matt 18:16). Leaders often face criticism, and the church must not condemn an elder on one person's word.
  • But never a shield: this principle exists to prevent false accusation, not to protect wrongdoers. In many cases of sexual abuse and other abuse, things happen where no one else is present; yet the separate testimonies of several victims, written records and other evidence can all serve as "witnesses." A church must not use "there are not two or three witnesses" as a reason to refuse a serious investigation of an accusation against a leader. Where a crime is involved, it should be reported to the police, not handled only inside the church; and victims do not need to reconcile with someone unsafe or stay in danger. "Two or three witnesses" is a rule for how the church receives a charge; it is not a precondition for going to the police. Where children or sexual abuse are involved, do not wait for the church to finish its own inquiry before reporting (see Rom 13:4). Even if an offending leader truly repents and the victim forgives him, forgiveness does not restore his office, nor does it give him access to victims or children again.
  • "Rebuke them in the presence of all": "those who persist in sin" translates a present participle, and many commentators take it to mean elders who go on sinning and will not repent. When a charge against a leader has been established, the church must deal with it before all, and must not cover it up because it happened in private or to save face ("don't air the family's shame outside," 家丑不可外扬, is not a biblical principle). Then "the rest may stand in fear," that is, hold God in awe and not take sin lightly.

3. "Without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality." "In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality" (1 Timothy 5:21). Paul charges Timothy in the most solemn terms: in handling such matters, he must not favor someone because he is famous, wealthy, gifted or a friend (see Jas 2:1, 9); nor may he condemn someone in advance because of a prejudice against him.

4. "Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands." "Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure" (1 Timothy 5:22). Most take this to refer to ordaining elders. If a church rushes someone untested into leadership and he later falls into sin, those who appointed him share responsibility (see 1 Timothy 3:6, 10). This applies also to a leader who has fallen: do not be hasty to restore him to office. (A minority take the laying on of hands here as restoring penitent sinners to fellowship.)

5. "Use a little wine." "(No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments)" (1 Timothy 5:23).

  • A personal word of care: in the middle of these solemn instructions, Paul suddenly shows concern for Timothy's stomach. He is not only an apostle giving orders but a spiritual father (see 1 Timothy 1:2).
  • Why say this? Some think Timothy may have been influenced by the ascetic climate, or wanted to give the ascetic false teachers no ground to accuse him of laxity, and to be an example of "not a drunkard" (1 Timothy 3:3), and so abstained from wine entirely. Paul says: for your health, use a little wine. Water at the time was often unsafe, and water mixed with wine was probably safer.
  • This is no license for heavy drinking: the word "little" matters. Elsewhere Paul says, "do not get drunk with wine" (Eph 5:18). What he opposes here is making abstinence the standard of godliness while neglecting the body's needs.

6. "The sins of some men are conspicuous." "The sins of some men are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later. So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden" (1 Timothy 5:24–25). In choosing leaders, some people's problems are obvious at a glance; others' appear only with time. That is why one must not be "hasty" (1 Timothy 5:22). Likewise, some people's good works are plain to see, while others serve quietly and no one notices; but God sees it all, and in the end it will all come to light (see Matt 6:4).

The point: God's household honors faithful leaders and deals justly with leaders' sins: no false accusation, no cover-up, no partiality. Behind all of it stands the God who sees in secret and will at last bring everything to light.
Meditation

Reflect: "She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day" (1 Timothy 5:5). Some people reach a point in life where prayer seems to be all that is left: a husband or wife has died, the children live far away, the body is not what it was, and there is less and less one can do. Perhaps I am such a person: for most of the day the house is quiet; I am often lonely, and sometimes even my prayers feel empty. Luke tells of Anna, who lived "as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day" (Luke 2:37). Decades of prayer seemed to produce nothing; then one day Mary and Joseph carried the infant Jesus into the temple, "and coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem" (Luke 2:38). Anna's decades of prayer were not a leftover task, the one thing she could still manage; they were her days with God. What she received in the end was not the sense of being useful again, but the sight of the One she had waited for. That child grew up and on the cross bore our sins in our place; even as he was dying he saw his mother standing below and entrusted her to the care of the disciple he loved (John 19:26–27). In his own worst hour he made sure she would be cared for. "Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. God settles the solitary in a home" (Ps 68:5–6). Today I can tell him honestly that I am often lonely and that sometimes even my prayers feel empty; and then, like Anna, wait for him in prayer, because what I am waiting for is not a more useful version of myself but him. If I know an older brother or sister like this, I can also go and ask: What can I pray for you? And would you pray for me? Perhaps the Lord means to use me to give one solitary person a home.

entries.title: 敬虔加上知足的心便是大利
entries.title_en: Great Gain in Godliness with Contentment
entries.verse: 提摩太前书 6:6-8，提摩太前书 6:12，提摩太前书 6:17

verse_parts.text: 然而，敬虔加上知足的心便是大利了；因为我们没有带什么到世上来，也不能带什么去。只要有衣有食，就当知足。
你要为真道打那美好的仗，持定永生。你为此被召，也在许多见证人面前，已经作了那美好的见证。
你要嘱咐那些今世富足的人，不要自高，也不要倚靠无定的钱财；只要倚靠那厚赐百物给我们享受的神。

entries.verse_text: 然而，敬虔加上知足的心便是大利了；因为我们没有带什么到世上来，也不能带什么去。只要有衣有食，就当知足。你要为真道打那美好的仗，持定永生。你为此被召，也在许多见证人面前，已经作了那美好的见证。你要嘱咐那些今世富足的人，不要自高，也不要倚靠无定的钱财；只要倚靠那厚赐百物给我们享受的神。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第六章分成五段。作仆人的（1-2节）：在轭下作仆人的，要尊敬自己的主人，免得神的名和道理被人亵渎；有信主的主人，更要加意服事。敬虔与钱财（3-10节）：传异教的人自高自大，专好争辩，以敬虔为得利的门路；然而，敬虔加上知足的心便是大利；想要发财的人陷在网罗里，贪财是万恶之根。打那美好的仗（11-16节）：属神的人要逃避这些事，追求公义、敬虔、信心、爱心、忍耐、温柔；要为真道打那美好的仗，持定永生；保罗在那向本丢‧彼拉多作过美好见证的基督耶稣面前嘱咐他，又颂赞那可称颂、独有权能的万王之王。嘱咐富足的人（17-19节）：不要自高，不要倚靠无定的钱财，只要倚靠那厚赐百物给我们享受的神；要行善，甘心施舍。保守所托付的（20-21节）：要躲避那似是而非的学问；愿恩惠常与你们同在。

这一章又回到书信开头的问题：假教师。他们的问题不只是道理错了，还有爱钱的心。保罗的回答是：真正的「大利」不是钱财，而是敬虔加上知足；真正的富足，是倚靠那厚赐百物的神，持定那真正的生命。

深读 6:1-2 凡在轭下作仆人的

1. 「当以自己主人配受十分的恭敬」。 「凡在轭下作仆人的，当以自己主人配受十分的恭敬，免得神的名和道理被人亵渎。」（提前6:1）

  • 当时的处境： 在罗马帝国，奴隶占人口的相当一部分（估计各地不同，大约一成到两成，城市里更多），早期教会中有许多信徒是奴隶。罗马的奴隶制度和近代跨大西洋的黑奴贸易有些不同：罗马的奴隶不以种族划分；许多奴隶，尤其是城里的家奴，后来可以得自由。但这仍然是把人当作财产、世代相传的制度，常常充满暴力和屈辱。
  • 保罗为什么这样说？ 他关心的是「神的名和道理」不被亵渎。如果信主的奴隶因为得了福音的自由，就轻看主人、不肯做工，外人就会说：这个新宗教叫人造反。保罗要信徒在一个不公义的处境中，仍然用好的品格为福音作见证（参多2:9-10）。

2. 「不可因为与他是弟兄就轻看他」。 「仆人有信道的主人，不可因为与他是弟兄就轻看他；更要加意服事他；因为得服事之益处的，是信道蒙爱的。」（提前6:2）

  • 在基督里是弟兄： 主人和奴隶在教会里同是弟兄，这在当时的社会是破天荒的事（参加3:28；门16「不再是奴仆，乃是高过奴仆，是亲爱的兄弟」）。
  • 但不可以此为借口： 有些信主的奴隶可能想：既然我们是弟兄，我就不必那么尊重他了。保罗说，正因为他是「信道蒙爱的」弟兄，更要好好服事他。

3. 保罗赞成奴隶制度吗？

  • 他没有号召革命： 保罗没有叫奴隶起来反抗，这在当时只会带来血腥的镇压，也会叫福音被看作政治运动。
  • 但福音埋下了种子： 保罗在提前1:10把「抢人口」（贩卖人口）的人列为违背律法的罪人；他劝作奴隶的「若能以自由，就求自由更好」（林前7:21）；他要腓利门把阿尼西母当作「亲爱的兄弟」（门16）；他也吩咐主人「不要威吓他们」，因为主人和奴隶「同有一位主在天上」（弗6:9）。历史上，许多信徒正是根据圣经反对奴隶制度：四世纪的教父尼撒的贵格利公开谴责蓄奴，英国的威伯福斯推动了废奴。
  • 不可误用： 历史上有人曾用这类经文为奴隶制度辩护，这是误用圣经，教会应当为此认罪。
  • 今天怎样应用？ 今天的雇员不是奴隶，但这段经文的原则仍然适用：信徒在工作中要尽心、诚实，不要因为老板或上司是信徒，就随便对待工作。但这不是要人忍受违法的对待。遭受剥削、欠薪、虐待或性骚扰的人，可以寻求法律保护；向警察或有关部门举报是正当的（罗13:4）；也可以离开不安全的工作环境（参林前7:21）。反过来，信主的老板也不可以拿「我们是弟兄」作借口，要信徒员工无偿加班或忍受不公平的待遇；保罗吩咐作主人的「要公公平平地待仆人」（西4:1）。如果欺压人的是教会里的弟兄，教会也不可为了面子、「家丑不可外扬」而包庇。
要点：福音没有用暴力推翻社会制度，却从根本上改变了人与人的关系：主人和奴隶在基督里成了弟兄。信徒在不公义的处境中仍忠心做事，是因为他们真正事奉的是主基督（西3:23-24），为要叫神的名得荣耀。
深读 6:3-10 敬虔加上知足的心便是大利

1. 「以敬虔为得利的门路」。 「若有人传异教，不服从我们主耶稣基督纯正的话与那合乎敬虔的道理，他是自高自大，一无所知，专好问难，争辩言词，从此就生出嫉妒、纷争、毁谤、妄疑，并那坏了心术、失丧真理之人的争竞。他们以敬虔为得利的门路。」（提前6:3-5）

  • 「专好问难」： 原文有病态的意思，指对争论上了瘾，像得了病一样。这正好和「纯正的话」相对（「纯正」原文是健康的意思）：纯正的道理叫人健康，好争论却叫人生病。
  • 「以敬虔为得利的门路」： 这些假教师把宗教当作赚钱的生意。今天也有人传成功神学（富足福音），说只要信得够、奉献得够，神就会让你发财。保罗说，这样的人是「失丧真理」的。
  • 在华人处境中： 有些人把信仰当作求平安、求发财的另一种方法，和从前拜财神、求签其实没有两样。保罗要我们分辨：我信主，是为了得着神自己，还是只为了得着神给的好处？

2. 「敬虔加上知足的心便是大利了」。 「然而，敬虔加上知足的心便是大利了；因为我们没有带什么到世上来，也不能带什么去。只要有衣有食，就当知足。」（提前6:6-8）

  • 保罗把话反过来说： 假教师以为敬虔可以带来钱财。保罗说，敬虔确实是大利，却不是他们想的那种利。
  • 「知足」： 这个词在当时的斯多亚哲学中很常见，指不依靠外在环境的自足。但保罗的知足不是靠自己的意志，而是靠基督：「我无论在什么景况都可以知足……我靠着那加给我力量的，凡事都能做。」（腓4:11-13）保罗在别处用同一个词说：「神能将各样的恩惠多多地加给你们，使你们凡事常常充足」（林后9:8）。信徒的知足，来自神的供应。
  • 「没有带什么到世上来」： 这句话叫人想起约伯说的：「我赤身出于母胎，也必赤身归回」（伯1:21；参传5:15）。人走的时候，银行存款、房子、头衔都带不走。
  • 「有衣有食，就当知足」： 这不是说信徒不可以工作赚钱、改善生活，也不是说越穷越属灵。箴言的祷告很有智慧：「使我也不贫穷也不富足；赐给我需用的饮食」（箴30:8）。

3. 「贪财是万恶之根」。 「但那些想要发财的人，就陷在迷惑、落在网罗和许多无知有害的私欲里，叫人沉在败坏和灭亡中。贪财是万恶之根。有人贪恋钱财，就被引诱离了真道，用许多愁苦把自己刺透了。」（提前6:9-10）

  • 问题不是钱，而是「贪」： 保罗说的不是「钱是万恶之根」，而是「贪财」，就是爱钱的心。一个穷人也可能贪财，一个富人也可能不贪财。
  • 「万恶之根」： 许多解经家认为，这句话像当时一句常见的格言，希腊的道德家也有类似的话，说贪财是众恶的根源。意思是各样的罪恶都可能从贪财长出来，并不是说一切罪都出于贪财；有些英文译本就译作各样罪恶的一个根。单看原文的文法（有没有冠词），不能决定这一点；但整段的语气支持这个理解：欺骗、偷窃、嫉妒、背叛，甚至离弃信仰，都可以从这个根长出来。
  • 「用许多愁苦把自己刺透了」： 想要发财的人以为钱会带来快乐，结果却是焦虑、失眠、家庭破裂、良心不安。耶稣说：「人的生命不在乎家道丰富。」（路12:15）
要点：真正的大利不是钱财，而是敬虔加上知足的心。我们赤身而来，也要赤身而去；到了永恒里，我们仍然拥有的，只有神自己，和我们在基督里的生命。
深读 6:11-16 打那美好的仗

1. 「但你这属神的人」。 「但你这属神的人要逃避这些事，追求公义、敬虔、信心、爱心、忍耐、温柔。」（提前6:11）

  • 「属神的人」： 这是旧约对摩西、以利亚等先知的称呼（申33:1；王上17:24）。保罗用这个尊贵的称呼来叫提摩太（提后3:17也用这个称呼，指一切因圣经「得以完全」的信徒）。
  • 「逃避」和「追求」： 敬虔的生活有两方面：逃避贪财和争论，也追求美好的品格。光是逃避不够，还要有所追求。

2. 「为真道打那美好的仗」。 「你要为真道打那美好的仗，持定永生。你为此被召，也在许多见证人面前，已经作了那美好的见证。」（提前6:12）

  • 「打那美好的仗」： 许多解经家认为这是竞技场上的用语，指运动员全力以赴的竞赛（参林前9:25）；这个词也可以指争战（参提前1:18）。信仰的路，需要拼上全部的力气。
  • 「持定永生」： 永生是神所赐的，但我们要紧紧抓住它。
  • 「那美好的见证」： 可能指提摩太受洗或被按立时，在众人面前公开承认信仰；也有人认为是指他曾在审问他的官长面前承认信仰，正和基督在彼拉多面前的见证相对应。

3. 「向本丢‧彼拉多作过那美好见证的基督耶稣」。 「我在叫万物生活的神面前，并在向本丢‧彼拉多作过那美好见证的基督耶稣面前嘱咐你：要守这命令，毫不玷污，无可指责，直到我们的主耶稣基督显现。」（提前6:13-14）

  • 基督的见证： 耶稣在彼拉多面前承认自己是王，又说：「我为此而生，也为此来到世间，特为给真理作见证。」（约18:37）他明知这见证会带他上十字架，仍然没有退缩。（原文也可以译作在本丢‧彼拉多的时候，指他一生直到受死的见证。）
  • 提摩太的见证和基督的见证： 保罗把提摩太的见证和基督的见证放在一起。提摩太的见证是跟随基督的见证，我们也是这样。我们能站稳，不是因为自己勇敢，而是因为基督已经先为我们作了见证，走完了那条路。他在彼拉多面前没有退缩，一直走上十字架，替我们这些常常退缩、甚至否认他的人，担当了罪的刑罚（提前2:6「舍自己作万人的赎价」）。他替我们站在了审判台前，所以我们站得住。
  • 「叫万物生活的神」： 提摩太面对的也许是危险甚至死亡，但他所事奉的神是叫万物生活的，也是叫死人复活的。

4. 「那可称颂、独有权能的万王之王、万主之主」。 「到了日期，那可称颂、独有权能的万王之王、万主之主，就是那独一不死、住在人不能靠近的光里，是人未曾看见、也是不能看见的，要将他显明出来。但愿尊贵和永远的权能都归给他。阿们！」（提前6:15-16）

  • 一首颂歌： 保罗在提前1:17讲到自己蒙怜悯，就忍不住赞美；这里他讲到基督的显现，又一次发出颂赞。两处都称神为不能看见、独一的君王。
  • 「万王之王、万主之主」： 这个称呼出自旧约：「耶和华－你们的神－他是万神之神，万主之主」（申10:17；参诗136:3；但2:47）。当时的亚细亚尊崇罗马皇帝，也有人称皇帝为「主」。在这样的环境里，这首颂歌自然形成一种对照：真正掌权的只有一位。启示录把同样的称号归给羔羊（启17:14；启19:16），可见子与父同享这尊荣。
  • 「住在人不能靠近的光里」： 神是圣洁的，人不能看见他而存活（出33:20）。可是这位不能看见的神，已经藉着他的儿子把自己表明出来（约1:18），也要到了日期，使他的儿子显现出来（14-15节）。
要点：信仰的生活是一场美好的仗。我们能打这仗，是因为基督已经在彼拉多面前作了美好的见证，走上了十字架；那位万王之王、万主之主，必在他的日期使基督显现。
深读 6:17-19 嘱咐那些今世富足的人

1. 「不要自高，也不要倚靠无定的钱财」。 「你要嘱咐那些今世富足的人，不要自高，也不要倚靠无定的钱财；只要倚靠那厚赐百物给我们享受的神。」（提前6:17）

  • 「今世富足的人」： 保罗没有说富人不能信主，也没有叫他们把财产全部变卖。但他提醒：他们的富足只是「今世」的。
  • 两个危险： 一是骄傲（「自高」），以为有钱就比别人高；二是安全感放错了地方（「倚靠无定的钱财」）。钱财是「无定的」：股市会跌，公司会倒闭，房子会贬值。
  • 「厚赐百物给我们享受的神」： 这句话很重要。保罗不是禁欲主义者（参提前4:3-4）。神「厚赐百物」，是要「给我们享受」的。问题不在于享受神所赐的，而在于倚靠恩赐而不倚靠赐恩的神。

2. 「在好事上富足」。 「又要嘱咐他们行善，在好事上富足，甘心施舍，乐意供给人，为自己积成美好的根基，预备将来，叫他们持定那真正的生命。」（提前6:18-19）

  • 另一种富足： 保罗巧妙地重复了「富足」这个词：今世富足的人，要「在好事上富足」。
  • 「积成美好的根基」： 这和耶稣的教导一样：「只要积攒财宝在天上」（太6:20）。这不是说用钱可以买到永生，而是说：一个真正认识神恩典的人，会用钱财去爱人；这就显明他的心在哪里（太6:21）。
  • 「那真正的生命」： 钱财所能买的生活，不是「真正的生命」。真正的生命是与神同在的生命，在今生就开始，到永远都不会失去。
要点：钱财是无定的，神是可靠的。富足的人要倚靠那厚赐百物给我们享受的神，并用今世的钱财在好事上富足，持定那真正的生命。
深读 6:20-21 保守所托付你的

1. 「保守所托付你的」。 「提摩太啊，你要保守所托付你的，躲避世俗的虚谈和那敌真道、似是而非的学问。」（提前6:20）

  • 「所托付你的」： 原文是一个法律用语，指托人保管的财物。福音不是提摩太发明的，是神托付给他的，他要原原本本地保守，再交给后来的人（参提后1:14；提后2:2）。
  • 「似是而非的学问」： 原文直译是冒称的知识，就是假冒的知识。假教师自以为有高深的知识，其实是虚谈。

2. 「愿恩惠常与你们同在」。 「已经有人自称有这学问，就偏离了真道。愿恩惠常与你们同在！」（提前6:21）

  • 「你们」： 在较早、较可靠的抄本里，这里是复数。这封信虽然是写给提摩太的，却是要在以弗所教会中宣读的。
  • 最后一句话： 这封信讲了许多规矩、品格和责任，但最后一句是恩惠。提摩太能保守所托付的，不是靠他自己的力量，而是靠神的恩惠。保罗在另一封信中说：我「知道我所信的是谁，也深信他能保全我所交付他的，直到那日」（提后1:12）。
要点：福音是神托付给教会的宝贵财物，我们要保守它，再传给下一代；但最终保守我们的，是那位赐恩惠的主。
默想

默想： 「然而，敬虔加上知足的心便是大利了；因为我们没有带什么到世上来，也不能带什么去。」（提前6:6-7）我心里是不是有一个数字：月薪到多少，存款到多少，房子换到多大，我就可以满足了？可是每一次快到那个数的时候，它又悄悄往上挪了一点。我开始想，是不是要换一份收入更高的工作，是不是要再拼几年、多加点班。保罗没有说想改善生活是罪，他说的是「想要发财」的心，是那种总觉得还不够、总想再多一点的心。这种心像一个网罗，越挣扎越紧，最后「用许多愁苦把自己刺透了」。我们赤身而来，也要赤身而去；那个一直往上挪的数字，最后一分也带不走。诗篇的作者也曾经羡慕恶人的兴旺，后来他进了神的圣所，才说：「除你以外，在天上我有谁呢？除你以外，在地上我也没有所爱慕的……神是我心里的力量，又是我的福分，直到永远。」（诗73:25-26）我的福分不在于我有多少，而是神自己。主耶稣离开这世界的时候，连身上的衣服都被兵丁拈阄分了（约19:23-24）；他在十字架上被剥去一切。他甘心舍弃一切，为我的贪心和不信舍了自己，好叫神自己成为我的福分。今天，我可以把那个数字在主面前老老实实说出来，承认这里面有贪心，也有不信他会供应：主啊，我一直以为到了那个数才算够。然后我可以记得：「你们存心不可贪爱钱财，要以自己所有的为足；因为主曾说：『我总不撇下你，也不丢弃你。』」（来13:5）下一次那个数字又往上挪的时候，我可以换一个问题问自己：不是我还差多少，而是这位为我舍己的主，今天是不是仍然是我的福分。

The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 6 falls into five parts. Slaves (vv. 1–2): those under a yoke as slaves are to regard their masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled; those with believing masters are to serve them all the better. Godliness and money (vv. 3–10): the false teacher is puffed up, craves controversy, and imagines that godliness is a means of gain; but there is great gain in godliness with contentment; those who desire to be rich fall into a snare, for the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. Fight the good fight (vv. 11–16): the man of God is to flee these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness and gentleness; to fight the good fight of the faith and take hold of eternal life; Paul charges him before Christ Jesus, who made the good confession before Pontius Pilate, and praises the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings. A charge to the rich (vv. 17–19): they are not to be haughty or set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy; they are to do good and be generous. Guard the deposit (vv. 20–21): avoid what is falsely called "knowledge"; grace be with you.

This chapter returns to the problem with which the letter began: the false teachers. Their problem was not only wrong doctrine but a love of money. Paul's answer is that the real "great gain" is not money but godliness with contentment, and that true wealth is to hope in God, who richly provides us with everything, and to take hold of that which is truly life.

Going Deeper: 6:1–2 Those Under a Yoke as Slaves

1. "Regard their own masters as worthy of all honor." "Let all who are under a yoke as slaves regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled" (1 Timothy 6:1).

  • The setting: in the Roman Empire slaves made up a substantial part of the population (estimates vary, roughly 10–20 percent, more in the cities), and many in the early church were slaves. Roman slavery differed in some ways from the later Atlantic slave trade (for example, it was not based on race, and many slaves, especially urban household slaves, were eventually freed), but it was still a hereditary system that treated people as property and was often full of violence and humiliation.
  • Why does Paul say this? His concern is that "the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled." If believing slaves, having found freedom in the gospel, began to despise their masters and refuse to work, outsiders would say that this new religion incites revolt. Paul wants believers, even in an unjust situation, to bear witness to the gospel with good character (see Titus 2:9–10).

2. "Must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers." "Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved" (1 Timothy 6:2).

  • Brothers in Christ: masters and slaves were brothers in the church, something revolutionary in that society (see Gal 3:28; Phlm 16, "no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother").
  • But not an excuse: some believing slaves may have thought: since we are brothers, I need not respect him so much. Paul says that precisely because he is a brother, "believing and beloved," they should serve him all the better.

3. Did Paul approve of slavery?

  • He did not call for revolution: Paul did not tell slaves to rise up; in that world it would only have brought bloody suppression and made the gospel look like a political movement.
  • But the gospel planted seeds: in this very letter Paul lists "enslavers" (traffickers in people) among the lawbreakers (1 Timothy 1:10); he tells slaves, "if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity" (1 Cor 7:21); he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus "as a beloved brother" (Phlm 16); and he tells masters to "stop your threatening," knowing that master and slave have the same Master in heaven (Eph 6:9). Many believers opposed slavery on the basis of Scripture: Gregory of Nyssa in the fourth century openly condemned slaveholding, and William Wilberforce in Britain worked for abolition.
  • Not to be misused: in history some used passages like this to defend slavery. That is a misuse of Scripture, and the church should confess it.
  • How does it apply today? Employees today are not slaves, but the principle still applies: believers are to work wholeheartedly and honestly, and not take their work lightly because the boss or manager is a believer. This does not mean enduring unlawful treatment: those who suffer exploitation, unpaid wages, abuse or sexual harassment may seek the protection of the law; reporting to the police or proper authorities is right (Rom 13:4), and one may leave an unsafe workplace (see 1 Cor 7:21). Conversely, a believing employer must not use "we are brothers" to demand unpaid overtime or unfair treatment; Paul tells masters to "treat your slaves justly and fairly" (Col 4:1). If the one doing wrong is a fellow church member, the church must not cover it up to save face.
The point: The gospel did not overthrow the social order by force, but it changed relationships at the root, from within: master and slave became brothers in Christ. Believers who serve faithfully even in unjust situations do so because the One they really serve is the Lord Christ (Col 3:23–24), for the glory of God's name.
Going Deeper: 6:3–10 Great Gain in Godliness with Contentment

1. "Imagining that godliness is a means of gain." "If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness, he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain" (1 Timothy 6:3–5).

  • "Unhealthy craving": the Greek suggests sickness, an unhealthy appetite for argument. It is the opposite of "sound words" (literally, "healthy words"): sound doctrine makes people healthy; controversy makes them sick.
  • "Godliness is a means of gain": these false teachers treated religion as a business. Today too some preach a "prosperity gospel," saying that if you believe enough and give enough, God will make you rich. Paul says this is to be deprived of the truth.
  • In a Chinese setting: some people treat faith as another way to seek safety and wealth, not essentially different from praying to the god of wealth or drawing fortune sticks in the past. Paul wants us to discern: do we believe in order to have God, or in order to have God's things?

2. "There is great gain in godliness with contentment." "Now there is great gain in godliness with contentment, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content" (1 Timothy 6:6–8).

  • Paul's reversal: the false teachers say godliness brings gain; Paul says: yes, godliness is great gain, but not the kind of gain they mean.
  • "Contentment": this word was common in Stoic philosophy at the time, meaning self-sufficiency independent of outward circumstances. But Paul's contentment does not rest on his own willpower; it rests on Christ: "I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content... I can do all things through him who strengthens me" (Phil 4:11–13). Elsewhere Paul uses the same word for a sufficiency God supplies: "God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things..." (2 Cor 9:8).
  • "We brought nothing into the world": this echoes Job: "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return" (Job 1:21; see Eccl 5:15). When we go, we take no bank balance, house or title with us.
  • "If we have food and clothing, with these we will be content": this does not mean believers may not work to earn money and improve their lives, nor that poverty in itself is spiritual. The prayer in Proverbs is wise: "give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me" (Prov 30:8).

3. "The love of money is a root of all kinds of evils." "But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs" (1 Timothy 6:9–10).

  • The problem is not money but love of it: Paul does not say "money is the root of all evil," but "the love of money." A poor person can love money, and a rich person can be free of that love.
  • "A root of all kinds of evils": many commentators take this as a proverb-like saying (similar maxims about love of money circulated among Greek moralists), meaning that every kind of evil can grow from it, not that every sin comes from it; the ESV renders it this way. The lack of an article does not settle the question by itself, but the flow of the passage supports this reading: deceit, theft, envy, betrayal, even abandoning the faith can all grow from this root.
  • "Pierced themselves with many pangs": those who desire to be rich think money will bring happiness; instead it brings anxiety, sleeplessness, broken families and a troubled conscience. Jesus said, "one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions" (Luke 12:15).
The point: The real great gain is not money but godliness with contentment. We came with nothing and will leave with nothing; what we will still have in eternity is God himself and our life in Christ.
Going Deeper: 6:11–16 Fight the Good Fight

1. "But as for you, O man of God." "But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness" (1 Timothy 6:11).

  • "Man of God": this is the Old Testament title for Moses, Elijah and other prophets (Deut 33:1; 1 Kgs 17:24). Paul gives Timothy this honored title (2 Tim 3:17 uses it of any believer equipped by Scripture).
  • "Flee" and "pursue": a godly life has two sides: fleeing the love of money and quarrels, and pursuing good character. Fleeing alone is not enough; there must also be something pursued.

2. "Fight the good fight of the faith." "Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses" (1 Timothy 6:12).

  • "Fight the good fight": many take this as the language of the athletic contest, an athlete's all-out effort (see 1 Cor 9:25); the word can also mean combat (see 1 Timothy 1:18). The life of faith calls for everything we have.
  • "Take hold of the eternal life": eternal life is God's gift, but we are to grasp it firmly.
  • "The good confession": this may refer to Timothy's public confession of faith before many at his baptism or ordination; some think of a confession made before hostile authorities, paralleling Christ's before Pilate.

3. "Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession." "I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Timothy 6:13–14).

  • Christ's confession: before Pilate Jesus acknowledged that he was a king and said, "For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world, to bear witness to the truth" (John 18:37). He knew that this testimony would take him to the cross, and he did not draw back. (The phrase can also mean "in the time of Pontius Pilate," pointing to his whole witness up to his death.)
  • Timothy's confession and Christ's: Paul sets the two side by side. Timothy's confession follows Christ's; so does ours. We can stand firm not because we are brave but because Christ has already borne witness for us and walked that road to the end. He did not draw back before Pilate because he was going to the cross to bear, in our place, the penalty for the sins of people like us who often draw back and deny him (1 Timothy 2:6, "who gave himself as a ransom for all"). We can stand because he stood in the dock in our place.
  • "God, who gives life to all things": Timothy may face danger, even death, but the God he serves gives life to all things and raises the dead.

4. "The blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords." "Which he will display at the proper time, he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen" (1 Timothy 6:15–16).

  • A doxology: in 1 Timothy 1:17 Paul broke into praise as he spoke of the mercy shown to him; here he does so again as he speaks of Christ's appearing. Both times God is the invisible, only King.
  • "King of kings and Lord of lords": the title comes from the Old Testament: "the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords" (Deut 10:17; see Ps 136:3; Dan 2:47). In a province where emperors were honored with cult and sometimes called "lord," such praise also implied a contrast: there is only one true Sovereign. Revelation gives the same title to the Lamb (Rev 17:14; Rev 19:16): the Son shares the Father's honor.
  • "Who dwells in unapproachable light": God is holy; no one can see him and live (Exod 33:20). Yet this invisible God has made himself known through his Son (John 1:18), and at the proper time he will display the appearing of his Son.
The point: The life of faith is a good fight. We can fight it because Christ has already made the good confession before Pilate and gone to the cross; the King of kings and Lord of lords will bring about Christ's appearing at the proper time.
Going Deeper: 6:17–19 A Charge to the Rich in This Present Age

1. "Not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches." "As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy" (1 Timothy 6:17).

  • "The rich in this present age": Paul does not say the rich cannot believe, nor does he tell them to sell everything. But he reminds them that their wealth belongs only to "this present age."
  • Two dangers: first, pride ("haughty"), thinking that money makes one better than others; second, security placed in the wrong thing ("the uncertainty of riches"). Riches are uncertain: markets fall, companies fail, houses lose value.
  • "God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy": this phrase matters. Paul is no ascetic (see 1 Timothy 4:3–4). God "richly provides" everything "to enjoy." The problem is not enjoying what God gives but trusting the gifts instead of the Giver.

2. "Rich in good works." "They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life" (1 Timothy 6:18–19).

  • Another kind of wealth: Paul plays on words: those who are rich in this age are to be "rich in good works."
  • "A good foundation for the future": this matches Jesus' teaching: "lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven" (Matt 6:20). It does not mean money can buy eternal life, but that someone who truly knows God's grace will use money to love others, and this shows where his heart is (Matt 6:21).
  • "That which is truly life": the life money can buy is not "truly life." True life is life with God, beginning now and never lost.
The point: Riches are uncertain; God is dependable. The rich are to hope in God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy, and to use this age's wealth to be rich in good works, taking hold of that which is truly life.
Going Deeper: 6:20–21 Guard the Deposit

1. "Guard the deposit entrusted to you." "O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called 'knowledge'" (1 Timothy 6:20).

  • "The deposit": the Greek is a legal term for property entrusted to someone for safekeeping. Timothy did not invent the gospel; God entrusted it to him, and he is to guard it intact and pass it on to those who come after (see 2 Tim 1:14; 2 Tim 2:2).
  • "What is falsely called 'knowledge'": the false teachers thought they had deep knowledge, but it was empty talk.

2. "Grace be with you." "For by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you" (1 Timothy 6:21).

  • "You": the better manuscripts have the plural. Though the letter was written to Timothy, it was meant to be read in the church at Ephesus.
  • The last word: this letter has spoken of many instructions, qualities and responsibilities, but its last word is grace. Timothy will guard the deposit not by his own strength but by God's grace. In another letter Paul says, "I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that Day what has been entrusted to me" (2 Tim 1:12).
The point: The gospel is a treasure God has entrusted to the church; we are to guard it and pass it on to the next generation. But in the end the one who guards us is the Lord who gives grace.
Meditation

Reflect: "Now there is great gain in godliness with contentment, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world" (1 Timothy 6:6–7). Is there a number in my head: a salary, a savings balance, a size of flat, and then I will be content? Yet each time I come close to it, the number quietly moves up a little. I start thinking about switching to a better-paid job, or pushing hard for a few more years and working more overtime. Paul does not say that wanting to improve one's life is sin; he speaks of the "desire to be rich," the heart that always feels it is not enough and always wants a little more. That desire is a snare that tightens the more I struggle, until in the end I have "pierced [myself] with many pangs." We came with nothing and will leave with nothing; that ever-rising number cannot be taken along. The psalmist once envied the prosperity of the wicked; then he went into God's sanctuary and said, "Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you... God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever" (Ps 73:25–26). My portion is not in how much I have; it is God himself. When the Lord Jesus left this world, the soldiers cast lots even for his clothing (John 19:23–24); at the cross he was stripped of everything. He willingly gave up everything and gave himself for my covetousness and unbelief, so that God himself might be my portion. Today I can name that number honestly before the Lord, confessing the covetousness in it and the unbelief in his provision: Lord, I have been telling myself that only at that number would it be enough. Then I can remember: "Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you'" (Heb 13:5). The next time the number moves up again, I can ask a different question: not how much I am still short, but whether this Lord who gave himself for me is still my portion today.
